_comment: Per-work orientation descriptions shown in Browse Corpus and the Reader. Keyed by language, then by base work id (the .tess filename without language directory, extension, or .part suffix). Two or three plain sentences describing the TEXT itself: its contents, structure, and interest, with author and date kept brief. Every text import should add its entry here.

la.justin.epitome: An epitome in Latin prose of the forty-four books of universal history composed by Pompeius Trogus, made by Justin in the later Roman imperial period. The opening preface explains that the compiler, while staying in Rome, excerpted from Trogus whatever most deserved to be known, omitting what was neither pleasant to learn nor useful as example, so that readers who knew Greek might be reminded and those who did not might be instructed. From there the work surveys world history from the Assyrian and Median monarchies of Ninus, Semiramis and Sardanapalus through the rise of Persia under Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius, the wars of the Athenians and Spartans from Marathon to the Sicilian expedition, the reigns of Philip and Alexander, and the struggles of Alexander's successors among the Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids, with digressions on Scythia, Carthage, Mithridates, Armenia and Parthia. It closes with the early history of Rome, including the Greek foundations of Massilia, and with Spain, from the story of Geryon through Hannibal's command to Augustus's reduction of the province.
la.hyginus.fabulae: The Fabulae of Hyginus, represented here by a selection of individual fabulae, is an early Imperial Latin collection of mythological summaries written in plain prose. It opens with Prometheus, who first fashioned humankind from clay and carried fire to them, and with Pandora, formed by Vulcan at Jupiter's command and endowed with gifts by the gods. From there the collection moves through compressed versions of the principal Greek myths arranged roughly by heroic generation: the loves and adventures of the gods, the Argonautic expedition and Medea, the labours and death of Hercules, Theseus and the Cretan cycle, the house of Oedipus at Thebes, the judgement of Paris and the Trojan War, and the calamitous returns of the Greek leaders, including the wanderings and death of Ulixes. Shorter closing items offer the allegory of Cura as an aetiology of humankind and tales of famous friendships such as those of Moerus and Selinuntius and of Harmodius and Aristogiton.
la.hyginus.astronomica: An early imperial Latin treatise in prose attributed to Hyginus, the Astronomica opens with a dedicatory preface to a learned correspondent that defends the author's project and surveys the topics to follow. The work proceeds from definitions of the world, the sphere, the celestial circles, and the position and habitability of the earth to the mythological histories of the constellations, recounting for each the stories of its placement among the stars. Subsequent sections set out the position of every constellation with respect to the great circles, the number and arrangement of its stars, and the relation of the circles to the signs, and conclude with discussions of the world's rotation, day and night, the courses of sun and moon, eclipses, the five planets, and the reckoning of months and intercalation.
la.isidore.etymologiae: Isidore's Etymologiae is a Latin prose encyclopedia of early medieval date, arranged in successive books by subject. It opens with the book on grammar, which defines discipline and art, lists the seven liberal arts, and then treats letters, syllables, accents, metrical feet, and the parts of speech. Rhetoric, dialectic, and philosophical definitions follow, after which the work passes through the human body and its ages, portents and monstrous peoples, the nations and kingdoms of the world, military and civic institutions, kinship and marriage, and alphabetical vocabularies of words for persons. Later books survey war and games, ships and buildings, clothing, food and drink, vessels, and many other instruments and practices, with each item explained through the derivation of its name.
la.petrarch.africa: Africa is a Latin epic in hexameters by the Renaissance poet Petrarch, recounting the Second Punic War. It opens with an invocation to the Muses and an appeal for the favour of King Robert before turning to Scipio's resolve to avenge Rome's losses. The poem follows the war from Scipio's campaigns in Spain to the invasion of Africa, incorporating Massinissa's love for the captive Sophonisba, a celestial vision in which Scipio's dead father foretells victory and surveys Rome's future history to its eventual decline, and the meeting and battle of the rival commanders before Zama. It closes with Hannibal's flight and exile, the terms of peace, Scipio's triumphal return to Rome, a dream in which Homer prophesies the poem itself and its author's fame, and the poet's lament that King Robert died before the work was finished.
la.pomponius_mela.de_chorographia: The De Chorographia of Pomponius Mela is a Latin prose geography of the early Imperial period which opens by declaring an account of the world's situation to be a laborious undertaking, ill suited to eloquence yet rewarding in itself. After setting out the form of the whole earth, its zones and its threefold division into Europe, Asia and Africa, the work surveys the coasts of the Mediterranean from Mauretania round through Africa, Egypt, Asia Minor, Greece and Italy to Spain, recording rivers, mountains, cities, harbours and islands together with the customs of the peoples dwelling along them. From the Pillars of Hercules it then follows the outer ocean circuit along Atlantic Europe, Scythia and the Caspian to India and the Red Sea, blending topographical description with ethnography and marvels, before returning at last to the African shore where it began.
la.varro.de_lingua_latina: De Lingua Latina is a Latin prose treatise on language and usage by Varro, written in the era of the Roman Republic. It opens with a preface addressed to Septumius in which Varro lays out a six-book plan for explaining how words were imposed on things in Latin, distinguishing objections to etymology from arguments in its favour and naming popular usage and the poets as the two sources of vocabulary. The exposition then ranges over the origins and corruption of words through age and change, sets out four graded levels of etymological explanation from popular understanding to the most recondite, and treats in turn the vocabulary of places and of times, with abundant examples drawn from early drama and from everyday speech. It closes with a systematic account of analogy, the like inflection of like words, giving formal definitions of the word, of likeness, and of inflection, and marking the classes of words in which analogy does or does not properly apply.
la.varro.res_rusticae: Varro's Res Rusticae is a three-book prose treatise on farming from the Roman Republic, opening with a preface in which the octogenarian author tells his wife Fundania that practical guidance is needed for the farm she has just bought. Book 1, cast as a conversation at the temple of Tellus during the festival of the Sementivae, covers the qualities of land, soil and farm buildings, labor and equipment, and the seasonal round of ploughing, sowing, harvesting and storing crops. Book 2 turns to animal husbandry, treating the purchase, breeding, feeding and care of sheep, goats, pigs, cattle, asses, horses and mules, along with shepherd dogs and the organization of herding labor. Book 3, addressed to Pinnius, expounds villatica pastio, the rearing near the villa of thrushes, peacocks, pigeons, poultry, waterfowl, hares, boars, dormice, snails, bees and fish for profit and enjoyment.
la.velleius_paterculus.historiae_romanae: A Latin prose universal history by Velleius Paterculus, an early Imperial writer, addressed to the consul Marcus Vinicius and compressed into two books, of which the second and greater part survives. The work opens with the aftermath of the Trojan War and the movements of Greek peoples, and then traces the succession of empires, the founding of colonies, and the growth of Roman power, giving particular weight to the Punic wars, the conquests of Greece, Africa, and Asia, and the careers of commanders such as the Scipios, Marius, Sulla, Pompey, and Caesar. From the Gracchi onward the narrative follows in detail the civil wars, the rise of Augustus, and the military achievements of Tiberius, including the German and Pannonian campaigns in which the author himself served, ending with a panegyric of the reigning emperor and a prayer for the stability of the Roman state.
la.frontinus.strategemata: Frontinus's Strategemata, a Latin prose work of military science from the early imperial period, opens with a preface that distinguishes strategika, the art of generalship at large, from strategemata, cleverly contrived deeds, and announces a collection of examples arranged in three books. Book 1 gathers stratagems used before battle: concealing and discovering plans, choosing the character of a war, moving armies through hostile country, evading difficult positions, ambuscades, stretching enemy resources, quelling sedition, and countering discouraging omens. Book 2 covers battle and its aftermath, from the choice of time, place, and formation of battle through ambushes, feigned retreats, and surprise attacks to measures for pursuing victory, repairing defeat, holding doubtful troops, and escaping; book 3 turns to siegecraft, treating sudden assaults, deception, inducing treachery, reducing defenders by hunger, diverting rivers and fouling water, terror tactics, messages and supplies smuggled into cities, countermeasures against traitors and deserters, sorties, and the steadfastness of the besieged. A closing supplement collects exempla of generalship proper, discipline and its effects, continence, justice, constancy, moderation, and miscellaneous devices, drawn chiefly from Greek and Roman military history.
la.frontinus.de_aquis: De Aquis is a Latin prose treatise on the aqueducts of Rome by Frontinus, written after his appointment as curator aquarum under the emperor Nerva, with a closing notice of improvements begun under Trajan. It opens with a preface in which the author explains the office entrusted to him and his resolve to learn its duties at first hand rather than rely on assistants. The work then surveys the nine aqueducts serving the city, Appia, Anio Vetus, Marcia, Tepula, Iulia, Virgo, Alsietina, Claudia, and Anio Novus, giving for each its builder, consular date, source, channel lengths, and delivery capacity, before turning to the standard pipe measures and the quinaria system, the distribution of water by region among public works, basins, imperial grants, and private users, and the frauds practiced by water-workers and landowners. Later sections quote senatus consulta and a protective statute, set out the staff, revenues, and responsibilities of the curator, discuss the maintenance and repair of the channels, and end with a list of Frontinus's predecessors in the office.
la.sidonius.carmina: Sidonius' Carmina form a Late Antique collection of Latin verse in mixed meters whose center of gravity is panegyric. The book opens with a mythological prologue in which gods, heroes, and demi-gods vie in celebrating Jupiter, before the poet offers his own modest song in praise of the emperor Anthemius. Later pieces extend the panegyrical mode to Majorian and Avitus, while the collection ranges across mythological narrative, epithalamia for Polemius and Ruricius, invocations and consolatory poems, and short occasional and invitation verse. It closes with lighter fare, including a valediction that sends the little book on a circuit of friends' country houses in Gaul.
la.sidonius.epistulae: Sidonius' Epistulae are a prose letter collection in nine books by the Late Antique author Sidonius, opening with a preface to Constantius in which letters of rather polished style, written on various occasions, are said to have been gathered and edited into a single volume, professing to follow the roundness of Symmachus and the discipline of Pliny. The addressees form a wide circle of aristocrats, holders of imperial office and bishops in Gaul, and the correspondence runs from short notes of recommendation, introduction, thanks and consolation to extended set pieces. Among these are a portrait of Theodoric, king of the Goths, from his physical appearance to his daily routine; a narrative of a journey from Gaul to Rome, taking in the wedding of the patrician Ricimer; an account of the trial and condemnation of the ex-prefect Arvandus; a detailed tour of a villa, its baths, porticoes and lake; and playful exchanges about the author's own verses, with panegyric, epigrams and metrical experiments embedded in the prose. A concluding book is addressed largely to bishops, praising their conduct, pleading for captives and refugees, and treating ecclesiastical affairs amid the disruptions of Gothic and Burgundian power.
la.fronto.epistulae: This correspondence of the orator Marcus Cornelius Fronto with his imperial pupils, chiefly Marcus Aurelius as Caesar and later as Augustus, opens with affectionate exchanges in which Fronto and the young prince debate whether love needs a reason and trade playful literary exercises over sleep. The collection as a whole ranges across the Later Imperial epistolary world: greetings and health reports, household news and condolences, commendations of friends, and, above all, sustained discussion of eloquence, with criticism of word choice, comparisons of Cato, Sallust, and Cicero, and advice on the composition and delivery of speeches. Many letters pass between Latin and Greek, and the correspondence extends beyond the imperial house to Antoninus Pius, Lucius Verus, Herodes Atticus, and other friends, closing with Greek letters and a miscellany of detached pieces, including a debate with a pupil over the value of rhetoric versus philosophy.
la.nemesianus.eclogae: The Eclogae of Nemesianus, a poet of the later Roman Imperial period, form a collection of four pastoral poems in hexameters. The first eclogue opens as an invitation to the old shepherd Tityrus to begin a song, but turns almost at once into a memorial lament for the recently deceased Meliboeus, a venerable arbiter of rural quarrels and patron of song. The second poem is a serenade in which the youths Idas and Alcon vie in alternate verse for the love of the girl Donace, and the third tells how two boys steal the pipe of the sleeping god Pan, who consoles them with a hymn to Bacchus on his birth, his nurture among Nymphs and Satyrs, and the first treading of the vintage. In the fourth, the shepherds Lycidas and Mopsus, one enamored of the boy Iollas and the other of the sorceress Meroe, exchange songs of thwarted love under the recurring refrain 'cantet amat quod quisque', 'let each sing what he loves, for songs relieve cares.'
la.nemesianus.cynegetica: The Cynegetica is a didactic poem in Latin hexameters on hunting, attributed to Nemesianus, a poet of the later imperial period. Its proem claims a thousand paths of the chase as its theme, calls on Calliope and Diana, sets aside the familiar mythological subjects of the great poets, and promises future verse on the victories of the sons of the deified emperor Carus. The instruction proper covers the choice of hounds from Laconian, Molossian, British, Pannonian and other stocks, their mating, whelping, rearing and training for the hunt, and the treatment of mange and rabies with a draught of castoreum. There follow precepts on hunting horses of Greek, Cappadocian and Maurusian breeds, their conformation, feeding and exercise, and on the weaving of nets and the dyeing of brightly coloured scare-cloths, before the poem closes with the hunters riding out at dawn across the dew-laden meadows.
la.nemesianus_pseudo.de_aucupio: The De aucupio is a brief Latin didactic poem in hexameters on bird-catching, of later imperial date and attributed to Nemesianus, though its authorship is uncertain, and it survives only as a short fragment. It opens in the midst of a survey of birds, declaring the tetrax, which at Rome they have begun to call 'taracem', the most foolish of them all because it runs heedlessly into the snares set before it. The poem then follows the fowler's craft across particular species, describing a bird that nests near Peltinum at the foot of the Apennines and the small-bodied guardian of the Tarpeian citadel, with a passing reference to Palamedes, before a second section, set when the grove is stripped of its green, instructs the hunter on taking the woodcock, a creature that feeds on worms along the water's edge and locates its prey by sharp scent rather than by sight.
la.symmachus.epistulae: The Epistulae preserve the Latin correspondence of Symmachus, a late antique Roman senator and urban prefect, and open with letters to his father that mix news of life in the Campanian resorts with an exchange of epigrams and remarks on literary style. The middle of the collection runs through letters to literary friends such as Ausonius and Agorius Praetextatus, together with a large body of letters of recommendation, congratulation, condolence, friendly reproach, and gift-giving addressed to relatives and unnamed correspondents. The closing portion consists of official reports (relationes) to emperors including Theodosius and Honorius, covering judicial appeals, fiscal disputes, and the provisioning of Rome, among them the plea for the restoration of the Altar of Victory and the traditional rites, and ends with prefectural correspondence on the contested episcopal election of Boniface and Eulalius.
la.abelard.historia_calamitatum: The Historia Calamitatum opens with the observation that examples console more effectively than words, and announces that the writer will set down the story of his own misfortunes so that an absent friend may judge his trials slight by comparison. Written by Peter Abelard, it is a medieval Latin prose epistle that traces his Breton origins, his renunciation of his inheritance for a life of study, and his rise as a controversial master of dialectic, including his quarrels with his teachers William of Champeaux and Anselm of Laon. The narrative continues with his love for Heloise, their secret marriage and its brutal punishment, his entry into monastic life at Saint-Denis, the condemnation and public burning of his treatise on the Trinity at Soissons, and his flight from the abbey after a dispute over the identity of its patron saint. It closes with his founding of the oratory of the Paraclete, its gift to Heloise and her nuns, his unhappy tenure as abbot of Saint-Gildas in Brittany amid violence from rebellious monks and a local tyrant, and a concluding exhortation to patience drawn from scriptural authorities.
la.abelard.epistolae: A medieval Latin epistolary collection attributed to Abelard, comprising the surviving correspondence between him and Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete. It opens with Heloise's letter saluting Abelard as her lord, father, husband, and brother, in which she replies to the letter he had addressed to a friend recounting his misfortunes and complains that he has sent her no consolation since their entry into religion. Abelard's responses follow, giving spiritual counsel, setting out forms of prayer for the sisters of the Paraclete, and answering Heloise's objections to his remarks on death and the manner of their conversion. The final and longest letter, written at Heloise's request, traces the authority and dignity of the monastic profession of women from its scriptural origins and presents a complete rule for the Paraclete community, ordering its officers, divine office, solitude, food, dress, and discipline.
la.gregorius_magnus.dialogi: A Latin prose dialogue in four books, ascribed to Gregory the Great (Gregorius Magnus), composed in the late sixth century, framed as conversations between Gregory and his deacon Peter. The work opens with Gregory lamenting the burdens of his pastoral office and recalling the contemplative peace of monastic life, at which point Peter urges him to recount the holy men of Italy. The first three books present a long series of lives and miracles of Italian saints and ascetics, including Honoratus and Libertinus of Fundi, Equitius, Benedict of Nursia in extensive detail, Germanus of Capua, Paulinus of Nola, Totila-era bishops, and martyrs under the Lombards, interwoven with doctrinal digressions on miracles, compunction, and prophecy. The fourth book turns to the fate of souls after death, offering visions and exempla concerning judgment, purgatorial fire, the efficacy of masses for the dead, and the eternal punishment of the damned.
la.gregorius_magnus.regula_pastoralis: Gregory the Great's Regula Pastoralis, an early medieval Latin prose treatise on the pastoral office, opens as a letter of dedication to a fellow bishop named John, in which the author answers criticism that he had fled the burdens of rule and announces the book's fourfold plan. The first part weighs who should and should not undertake spiritual rule, the second sets out how a ruler should live, pure in thought, eminent in action, discreet in silence and in speech, and combining contemplation with care for his subjects, humility with the exercise of authority. The third and longest part teaches how the pastor should admonish, in a long series of paired admonitions matched to opposite dispositions among his hearers, from the proud and the diffident to the gluttonous and the abstinent, while the fourth treats how a pastor who has taught well should remember his own infirmity lest success breed elation. The argument advances by continuous scriptural exposition, with Old Testament persons, priestly vestments, and ritual objects read allegorically as images of the pastoral life.
la.lactantius_placidus.in_statii_thebaida_c: Lactantius Placidus's commentary on Statius's Thebaid, a late-antique Latin prose gloss preserved without a secure date of composition, presents itself as a line-by-line explication of the epic's twelve books, beginning with an explanation of the poem's opening invocation ('fraternas acies alternaque regna profanis decertata odiis') as an account of the fraternal contest for the Theban throne. The commentary explains Statius's summary of the war between Eteocles and Polynices, the catalogue of Argive champions with their genealogies and homelands, Adrastus's double wedding, the fatal peregrinations of Oedipus's sons, the seer Amphiaraus's descent through the earth, and the battle scenes in which each of the seven champions meets his end. Subsequent passages gloss the deeds of Capaneus, Hippomedon, Parthenopaeus, Menoeceus's self-sacrifice, the mutual slaughter of Eteocles and Polynices at Thebes, Creon's prohibition of burial, and the arrival of Theseus's Athenian forces, concluding with the mourning of the widows and the resolution of the funeral rites. Throughout, the commentator pauses on mythological allusions, Homeric and Vergilian echoes, grammatical and metrical points, and the moral dimensions of Statius's narrative, while the marginal line markers allow the reader to follow the exposition verse by verse through the full span of the epic.
la.aquinas.summa_theologiae_1: The Prima Pars of the Summa Theologiae, a Latin summa of theology by the medieval scholastic Thomas Aquinas, opens with ten questions establishing the nature of sacred doctrine, its necessity, its standing as a science, and the senses of Scripture, before arguing for God's existence by five ways. It then treats the divine essence and attributes, including simplicity, perfection, goodness, infinity, and omnipresence, together with God's operations of knowledge, will, and power, followed by questions on the three persons of the Trinity. The latter portion follows the procession of creatures from God, covering creation in general, the nature, knowledge, will, and hierarchy of the angels, the work of the six days, and the composition and faculties of human nature. The part concludes with questions on divine government, treating providence, predestination, fate, miracles, the ministry of angels and demons, and the propagation of man, body and soul.
la.aquinas.hymni: A collection of medieval Latin hymns attributed to Thomas Aquinas, devoted throughout to the Eucharist and the presence of Christ under the forms of bread and wine. It opens with the Pange lingua gloriosi corporis mysterium, a hymn recounting the institution of the sacrament at the Last Supper and ending with the Tantum ergo. The remainder gathers the Lauda Sion, a long sequence in praise of the eucharistic bread; the Sacris solemniis, containing the Panis angelicus; the Verbum supernum prodiens, closing with the O salutaris hostia; and the Adoro te devote, a devotional address to the deity veiled in the consecrated host.
la.erasmus.moriae_encomium: Moriae Encomium (The Praise of Folly) is a Latin prose satire by the Renaissance humanist Desiderius Erasmus, cast as a mock encomium delivered by the personified Folly. It opens with a prefatory letter to Thomas More in which the author defends the levity of the undertaking and the punning dedication, after which Folly herself takes the floor before an assembly of gods and mortals. Over the course of the speech she catalogues the benefits she confers, youth, pleasure, self-love, friendship, marriage, and the happiness of simpletons, before turning to mock the learned professions: grammarians, poets, rhetoricians, lawyers, philosophers, and above all scholastic theologians with their syllogistic subtleties. The satire then widens to monks, priests, bishops, cardinals, popes, kings, and courtiers, and closes with an appeal to biblical authorities for the paradox that Christian piety is itself a kind of blessed folly and ecstatic madness.
la.erasmus.colloquia: Latin prose dialogues by Erasmus, written and revised during the early decades of the sixteenth century, presenting an imagined series of conversations among schoolboys, travellers, merchants, monks, soldiers, pilgrims, women and personified figures such as Charon and a letter-writing Virgin. The work opens with a narrative spoken by a shipwrecked traveller who recounts a violent storm at sea, the superstitious vows of his fellow passengers and the desperate swim that saved a handful of them. Across its many colloquies the collection moves through satirical accounts of religious pilgrimages and relic-vending shrines, the quarrels of mendicant orders at a deathbed, a pious household meal and its learned host, an exposure of fraudulent exorcism and alchemy, soldiering and mercenary life, courtship and unequal marriage, a dispute between wives on the dignity of women, a prostitute reclaimed by Evangelical reading, and catechetical examinations of the Creed, closing with a defence of the true Epicurean pleasure of a pious conscience.
la.alan_de_insulis.anticlaudianus: The Anticlaudianus is a Latin allegorical epic in hexameter verse by the medieval author Alan of Lille. It opens with a prose prologue in which the poet submits his work to the reader's correction and announces that its literal surface, moral instruction, and allegorical subtlety will suit different grades of understanding. The poem then recounts how Nature, grieving over the flaws of her creation, gathers the personified virtues to forge a perfect new man: Prudence is carried by a chariot whose parts are wrought by the arts of the trivium and quadrivium through the spheres of the planets and the fixed stars to the empyrean, where she obtains from God the soul that Nature's fashioned body requires. The completed hero receives gifts from Fortune and Nobility, routs the army of vices in battle, and the closing epilogue turns from contemplation of the created universe to its Creator.
la.alan_de_insulis.de_planctu_naturae: A medieval Latin prosimetrum attributed to Alan of Lille (Alan de Insulis), alternating elegiac verse with ornate prose. The work opens with the speaker's lament that laughter has turned to tears as mankind perverts the laws of Venus through unnatural unions, a disorder expounded through grammatical and rhetorical figures. There follows a vision in which Nature, personified as a resplendent woman borne in a glass chariot, appears to the narrator and discourses on her office as God's deputy in generation, on man as a microcosm of the universe, and on humanity's unique rebellion against her ordinances. Her plaint condemns in turn sexual deviance, gluttony and drunkenness, avarice, pride, envy, and flattery, and after the allegory of Venus's degenerate offspring Jocus and the arrival of Hymenaeus with the attendant virtues Castitas, Temperantia, Largitas, and Humilitas, the priest Genius bears stylus and tablets and solemnly pronounces excommunication upon the offenders, at which the dreamer wakes.
la.bernard_silvestris.cosmographia: A medieval Latin philosophical allegory in mixed prose and verse, the Cosmographia of Bernard Silvestris sets out the making of both the universe and man. It opens with a dedicatory letter in which the author, hesitant to expose so difficult a treatise on the world's origin to a judge's scrutiny, submits the work for correction, followed by prose summaries of its two books. The first book, the Megacosmus, recounts the ordering of the greater world: Natura's tearful complaint over the confusion of prime matter (hyle) moves Noys, divine providence, to separate the four elements, establish the nine angelic hierarchies, fix the stars, signs, and seven planetary orbits, and adorn the earth with its mountains, rivers, trees, herbs, animals, fish, and birds. The second, the Microcosmus, turns to the lesser world: Natura and Urania descend through the celestial spheres to gather the soul's celestial endowment, while Physis, found with her daughters Theorica and Practica, fashions the human body from the residue of the elements, and the work closes with an account of the head, the senses, the heart, the liver, and the organs of generation.
la.cassiodorus.institutiones: A didactic prose treatise in two books by Cassiodorus, written in Late Antiquity for the monks of the Vivarium monastery. The opening preface recounts the author's grief that public teachers of Scripture were lacking, recalls his failed plan, with Pope Agapitus, to endow a Christian school in Rome, and offers these introductory books in its place. Book 1 organises the study of Scripture around nine codices, surveying for each the Latin and Greek commentators and translators, giving rules for correcting, punctuating and copying manuscripts, and cataloguing the fathers, historians and other writers the monastic library should contain. Book 2 turns to secular learning, presenting compressed accounts of grammar, rhetoric and dialectic and of the four mathematical disciplines of arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy, so that worldly letters may serve divine reading.
la.cassiodorus.variae: The Variae is a Latin epistolary collection in twelve books by Cassiodorus, a Roman official of late antiquity who drafted state papers for the Ostrogothic rulers of Italy. The work opens with a preface in which friends persuade the reluctant author to gather into one corpus the dictations he had pronounced in his successive high offices. Its books assemble royal edicts and letters of appointment couched in praise and moral exhortation, instructions on justice, taxation, the grain supply, public building and games, and diplomatic correspondence with the Eastern emperors and neighbouring peoples, while the later books contain letters issued from the author's own praetorian prefecture. Books six and seven preserve formulae for the palatine offices, included, as the author explains, to assist successors pressed for time.
la.venantius_fortunatus.carmina: Venantius Fortunatus's Carmina is a late-antique Latin collection of occasional poetry in mixed meters, by a poet of Italian birth settled in Merovingian Gaul. It opens with a panegyric congratulating Bishop Vitalis on the consecration of his church at Bordeaux. From there the work ranges widely: verse letters and encomia for bishops such as Eufronius and Gregory of Tours; praise, petition, and condolence poems for Merovingian kings, queens, and courtiers (Sigibert, Chilperic, Childebert, Brunhild, Fredegund, Gogo, Dynamius, Lupus); the epithalamium for Sigibert and Brunhild and the long lament for the dead queen Gelesuintha; epitaphs and consolations; and poems for Radegund and Agnes of the convent at Poitiers, among them the hymns 'Vexilla regis' and 'Pange, lingua.' Prose supplements the verse in expositions of the Lord's Prayer and the Creed and in four books on the life and miracles of St Martin of Tours, with a light first-person travel poem on a journey up the Moselle among the closing pieces.
la.venantius_fortunatus.vita_martini: Venantius Fortunatus's Vita Martini is a late antique epic in Latin hexameters, in four books, recounting the life and miracles of Martin, bishop of Tours. The poem opens with Christ's triumphal return to heaven after despoiling hell, followed by a survey of earlier Christian poets and the author's self-deprecating prologue. The narrative then traces Martin from his birth in Pannonia and his renunciation of military service under Julian, through his gift of his cloak to a beggar at Amiens, his association with Hilary of Poitiers, and his episcopate at Tours, marked by the destruction of rural temples, resurrections, healings, exorcisms, visions of angels, and confrontations with emperors such as Maximus and Valentinian. It closes with Brictio's rebellion and reconciliation, further miracles of the saint's advocacy for prisoners, a closing itinerary to his shrine, and prayers asking Martin's intercession, including the restoration of the poet's own eyesight.
la.walter_de_chatillon.alexandreis: The Alexandreis is a medieval Latin epic in hexameters by Walter of Châtillon recounting the career of Alexander the Great. A prose preface in which the author explains why he had long withheld the poem from the public introduces the invocation that calls on the Muse to sing the deeds of the Macedonian king. The narrative follows Alexander from his boyhood and the moral instruction he receives from Aristotle through his accession, the subjugation of Greece, and his crossing into Asia, where victories over Darius at Granicus, Issus, and Arbela are followed by the fall of Tyre, Gaza, Persepolis, and Babylon. Set speeches and reflections on the mutability of Fortune punctuate the later books, which relate Darius's murder by the traitor Bessus, the Scythian war, the defeat of Porus in India, and Alexander's death by poison at Babylon, before an epilogue commends the finished work to its episcopal patron.
la.nigel_wireker.speculum_stultorum: A Latin verse satire of medieval date, attributed to Nigel Wireker and written in elegiac couplets, opening with a prologue addressed to one Willelme in which the author defends the use of humble and apparently inept matter to convey serious moral teaching. The work follows the talking ass Burnellus, who first seeks to lengthen his short tail against the advice of the physician Galienus, a counsel framed by the tale of the cows Brunetta and Bicornis and the losses that follow Bicornis's impatience. Setting out for Salerno for remedies, Burnellus is cheated of his goods, attacked by Cistercian dogs, and dispatches their prior Fromundus in the Rhone before turning to study at Paris, where he learns nothing in seven years, adopts the name Parisius, and after various mishaps resolves to found a new religious order combining whatever he likes from each of the existing orders. On his way to Rome for confirmation he encounters Galienus again, and their ensuing exchange unfolds into a long satirical survey of the vices of the age, attacking the greed of the Roman curia, the failings of kings, unworthy bishops and pastors, monastic orders, secular canons, and nuns, with embedded beast fables of the crow, cock, and other birds on ingratitude and the dangers of a loquacious tongue. A final exemplum of the rustico Bernardus, who rescues Dryanus and his animal companions from a pit and is rewarded while his ungrateful lord is punished, closes the poem, which the author ends by directing the reader to seek the moral sense beneath the surface of the tale.
la.johannes_hanville.architrenius: A medieval Latin satire in hexameter verse attributed to Johannes Hanville, the Architrenius takes its name from its hero, the 'arch-weeper', a young man who sets out to find Mother Nature and complain of the vices with which she has burdened humankind. After a prologue in which the poet addresses a patron and defends his work against envious critics, the hero journeys through a world of personified temptations: the golden house of Venus and its beautiful inhabitant, gluttonous banquets, the poverty of Parisian scholars, the mountain of ambition, the flatteries of courts, and the tyranny of avarice. Along the way he hears long moralising speeches from ancient philosophers and sages against anger, envy, luxury, lust and hypocrisy, before Nature herself appears to arrange his marriage to a modest and virtuous bride, celebrated with a wedding feast. The poem ends with a farewell address to the book and its author.
la.carmina_burana.carmina_burana: The Carmina Burana is a medieval Latin collection of goliardic verse of uncertain authorship, drawn principally from clerical and student circles of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and preserved in a manuscript associated with Benediktbeuern; the corpus assembled here transcribes the complete sequence of poems CB 1 to 228 together with the supplement, in mixed classical and medieval metres. The opening poem is a satire on the power of money, depicting how coin perverts courts, church offices, and judgement alike, and the collection continues through moral and satirical verse against avarice, simony, and corruption among prelates. The poems then turn to laments on Fortune and the wheel of fate, with its famous meditations on mutable prosperity, followed by love songs in springtime settings, drinking songs of the tavern, and pieces on gambling and decay of virtue. The later portion includes liturgical plays on the Nativity, the Passion, and the Resurrection of Christ, laments of the Virgin at the Cross, miracle and morality material such as the story of Mary Magdalene, and devotional poems to saints, closing with Easter and Passion-tide offices.
la.tiberianus.carmina: A small collection of Late Antique lyric poems in mixed meters, the Carmina are attributed to Tiberianus. The work opens with an ornate description of a springtime landscape, in which a clear stream winds between flowering banks amid birdsong and fragrant groves, and the rose reigns as queen of colors. The remaining pieces are shorter and varied in theme: an invective against gold, drawn out through mythological episodes that show its power to corrupt; a fable in which a bird weighted down by rain-soaked plumage falls from the sky, with a moral against those who soar on prosperous winds; and a hymn invoking a single omnipotent deity as the cause, soul, and sustaining order of the universe. The collection closes with a few epigrammatic lines, including one on Pegasus and another defining nature as a stream that mirrors what it receives.
la.pentadius.carmina: Pentadius was a Late Antique Latin poet, of uncertain date, whose few surviving elegiac epigrams are preserved in the Anthologia Latina. The collection opens with a series of couplets built on a repeated phrase whose sense is reversed or darkened between hexameter and pentameter, drawing moralising turns from mythological exempla such as Procne, Medea, Orpheus and Eurydice, Thisbe, Daedalus and Icarus, the Trojans undone by the Palladium, Busiris, Hippolytus, Ariadne, Phrixus and Helle, and Tantalus. A longer poem on the coming of spring, with its swallows, flowers, echoing streams and shade of the plane tree, passes into a set of couplets on the youth Narcissus, who wastes away gazing at his reflection in his father's river. The collection closes with epigrams on adultery and the supposed faithlessness of women, ending in the verdict that no woman is good, and that even a good one is made so by some strange fate.
la.prudentius.cathemerinon: Prudentius's Cathemerinon, a collection of twelve Latin hymns in varied metres, is a work of Late Antique Christian poetry. The book opens with a hymn on the singing of the cock at dawn, which becomes an allegory of Christ's call to awaken the soul from sin, and the remaining hymns take up the whole round of the day in a similar devotional key: morning praise at sunrise, prayer before meals, hymns for the lighting of lamps at nightfall and for the hours of sleep and fasting. The collection also includes longer narrative treatments of biblical subjects, such as the crossing of the Red Sea, Jonah at Nineveh, Daniel among the lions, the miracles and Passion of Christ, the resurrection of the body, and Christmas themes like the star of Bethlehem and the Massacre of the Innocents, concluding with hymns of universal praise to Christ as king.
la.matthew_of_vendome.ars_versificatoria: The Ars Versificatoria is a medieval Latin art of versification attributed to Matthew of Vendôme, composed largely in prose and illustrated throughout by Latin verse examples. It opens with a polemical prologue in which the author, defending his novelties against a detractor named Rufinus, presents the work as an introduction for the less advanced. The instruction then covers ways of beginning a composition (zeugma, hypozeusis, the general proverb), epithets, the eleven attributes of persons and the circumstances of a deed, and the threefold elegance of verse residing in meaning, verbal ornament, and manner of speaking. Later sections on figures of speech, tropes such as metaphor and antithesis, the execution and paraphrastic variation of material, and the correction of verses are punctuated by sustained original descriptions in praise and blame, of a pope, Caesar, Ulysses, the slavish Davus, Marcia, a beautiful girl, and a hideous old woman, before the treatise ends with a doxology and a mention of the author's Summula for teaching boys.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.poetria_nova: The Poetria Nova of Geoffrey of Vinsauf is a medieval Latin treatise on the art of composition, cast in hexameter verse. It opens with a dedicatory address to Pope Innocent, whose name the poet divides to satisfy the metre. The bulk of the poem is a systematic course in rhetorical craft: mental design of the work before writing, the choice between natural and artificial order, techniques of amplification and abbreviation, and a long succession of 'colours' of diction, transsumption, apostrophe, prosopopoeia, description, emphasis and their kin, illustrated by exempla ranging from a lament for King Richard and the complaint of the Holy Cross to descriptions of beauty, banquets and dancers. Advice on memory and on delivery in recitation, followed by a closing dedication to a William, brings the work to its end.
la.geoffrey_of_vinsauf.documentum: A Latin rhetorical treatise in prose, presented as the Documentum of Geoffrey of Vinsauf, a medieval grammarian and rhetorician. Opening with the claim that every work of artifice involves a beginning, a progression and a consummation, the text first catalogues the natural beginning and eight artificial ways of beginning, illustrating each with prose and verse examples drawn from the tale of Minos, Scylla and Androgeus. It then treats continuation of openings, the arts of expanding brief material through descriptions, circumlocutions, digressions, prosopopoeiae and apostrophes, and of contracting diffuse material by emphatic locutions, participial constructions and other devices of brevity, before turning to the two modes of speaking well, ornata facilitas and ornata difficilis, with extended discussion of tropes, determination, colorae rhetorici and general rules for elegant composition. The work closes with advice on handling common and humorous material, on avoiding stylistic faults such as turgidity and aridity with frequent appeal to Horace's Ars poetica, on delivery or pronuntiatio, and on methods of concluding a composition drawn from the matter itself, from proverbs or from examples.
la.eberhard_the_german.laborintus: The Laborintus, a medieval Latin didactic poem in mixed metres attributed to Eberhard the German, opens with the poet commissioned by his Muse to write on the burden of the schoolmaster's chair and the art of governing himself and his pupils. There follows an allegory of a boy born under baleful stars and doomed to poverty and teaching, whom Philosophy presents with her seven daughters, the liberal arts, while Grammar nurses him on Donatus, Cato and the elementary schoolbooks and instructs the master in the discipline of his students. The central and longest portion expounds metres, tropes, schemes and the composition of prose and verse, with a survey of authors suited to school reading from Cato, Avianus and Ovid to Virgil, Lucan and Prudentius, and displays unusual verse forms such as Leonine, rhymed, retrograde and rhythmic kinds. The work closes with the mother of elegies lamenting the teacher's miseries under avaricious patrons, unruly pupils and poverty, followed by devotional rhythmi addressed to Christ and the Virgin and an appeal for the reader's correction.
la.petrus_riga.de_ornatu_mundi: De Ornatu Mundi ('On the Adornment of the World') is a short medieval Latin religious poem in elegiac couplets by Peter Riga, distinct from the same author's much longer Aurora, though its printed source transmits it under the name of Hildebert of Lavardin. It opens with an invocation to Clio to sharpen the poet's style and fill his wax with honey. The body of the work is an elaborate encomium of paradise, describing in turn its trees, fruits and springs, its birds and beasts, the great cedar harbouring bees at its root, the encircling wall, river and bridge, and the towering gate wrought by Vulcan with the aid of the Cyclopes and gleaming with silver, gold, gems and ivory. The closing lines concede that this ornament, 'the rose of the world', must wither, and urge pursuit instead of the unfading rose, the 'flower of the field' that flowered in the heavens and withered in the world.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_africo: De Bello Africo is a Latin prose work of the Republican period, attributed to Caesar but of uncertain authorship, narrating Caesar's African campaign in the civil war against Scipio, Labienus, Cato, and the Numidian king Juba. It opens with Caesar assembling a small and largely untried army at Lilybaeum in Sicily and crossing to the African coast near Hadrumetum. The account follows his operations around Ruspina and Uzitta, his struggle with supply and reinforcement, the defection of Gaetulian troops, and the naval skirmishing, culminating in the battle of Thapsus, Cato's suicide at Utica, the deaths of Juba and Scipio, and the punitive settlements imposed on the African cities before Caesar's return to Rome. Alongside the military narrative it contains speeches, vivid episodes such as the veteran centurion's defiance of Scipio, and close attention to tactics, logistics, and the handling of elephants in battle.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_alexandrino: The Bellum Alexandrinum is a Latin prose narrative of uncertain authorship, transmitted with the commentaries attributed to Caesar and continuing their account of the civil wars after Pompey's defeat. It opens with Caesar summoning fleets and auxiliaries from Rhodes, Syria, and Cilicia as he presses the siege of Alexandria. The narrative follows the urban and naval fighting around the city, the intrigues of Arsinoe and her minister Ganymedes, the relief force led by Mithridates of Pergamum, the defeat and death of King Ptolemy, and Caesar's settlement of Egypt under Cleopatra; later chapters recount Domitius Calvinus's defeat by Pharnaces near Nicopolis, Vatinius's naval victory over Marcus Octavius in Illyricum, and the extortion, mutiny, and death of Quintus Cassius Longinus in Further Spain. The work closes with Caesar's rapid march through Syria, Cilicia, and Asia, his decisive victory over Pharnaces near Zela, his reorganization of the eastern provinces and client kings, and his hurried return to Italy.
la.caesar_pseudo.de_bello_hispaniensi: De Bello Hispaniensi, a Latin prose account attributed to Caesar but of uncertain authorship, narrates the Spanish campaign of the civil war against the younger Gnaeus Pompeius. It opens after Caesar's victories over Pharnaces and in Africa, with Pompeius ravaging Further Spain while Caesar is detained in Italy. The narrative follows Caesar's rapid arrival, the siege of Ategua and the fighting along the river Salsum, the encounters at Ulia and Corduba marked by frequent skirmishes, sieges and defections, and culminates in the decisive battle of Munda, in which Labienus and Attius Varus fall. It closes with the younger Pompeius's flight and death, the reduction of the remaining towns and of Pompeius's fleet, and Caesar's address to the provincials at Hispalis.
la.vegetius.epitoma_rei_militaris: Vegetius's Epitoma Rei Militaris, a late-antique Latin technical treatise on warfare addressed to an unnamed emperor, abridges the military doctrine of earlier authorities in four books. It opens with a preface that outlines the scope of each book and argues that victory derives from training and discipline rather than mere numbers. Book one treats the selection and training of recruits, book two the organisation, ranks, and administration of the legion, and book three the generalship and tactics of land battle, closing with a set of general maxims on war. Book four covers the fortification, siege, and defence of cities, the machinery of assault, and the conduct of naval warfare.
la.grattius.cynegetica: The Cynegetica, an Augustan didactic poem in hexameters by Grattius, opens with an invocation to Diana that frames the arts of hunting as a divine gift and a stage in human progress. The bulk of the work surveys the hunter's equipment, nets, lines, snares and spears, with remarks on the materials drawn from various regions, and invokes the legendary Arcadian huntsmen Dercylus and Hagnon as exemplars of the tracking dogs known as metagones. It then catalogues the breeds of dogs and their temperaments, offers instruction on breeding, rearing and training puppies, on the choice of a trainer and his arms, and on the diseases of dogs and their cures, ranging from practical treatments to a healing ritual at the volcanic spring of Vulcan. The poem ends with an account of the horses suited to the chase, where the surviving text breaks off.
la.germanicus.aratea: The Aratea is a Latin didactic poem in hexameters by Germanicus, of the Early Imperial period, adapting Aratus's Phaenomena into Latin verse. It opens with a dedication to the emperor, recalling Aratus's beginning from Jove and crediting the imperial peace with leaving mortals free to study the heavens. The body of the work surveys the constellations of both hemispheres, recounting the myths attached to them, Helice and Cynosura as nurses of Jupiter, the Heliades mourning Phaethon beside the Eridanus, and also treats of stars scattered through the sky that form no figure. The poem closes with the risings of the signs, which serve as markers of the hours of the night, of winds, and of weather.
la.solinus.collectanea_rerum_memorabilium: Solinus, a Latin author of uncertain date writing in later imperial times, composed the Collectanea Rerum Memorabilium, a prose compendium of geographical and natural wonders described as a condensed survey of the world. The work opens with a dedicatory preface explaining its method and sources, then begins its survey with Rome itself, treating the city's legendary origins, its kings, and the chronology of its founding before proceeding through Italy, its islands, Sicily, Greece, Macedonia, Thrace, and the northern regions of Europe. The greater part of the work is an ordered tour of the inhabited world by region, including Germania, Gaul, Hispania, Africa, Egypt, Arabia, Asia, and India, recording for each the notable rivers, mountains, cities, stones, plants, animals, and the customs of exotic peoples. It closes with a description of distant islands such as the Fortunatae and an account of the ocean surrounding the oikoumene.
la.censorinus.de_die_natali: De Die Natali is a Latin technical and antiquarian treatise by Censorinus, of the later imperial period, cast as a birthday offering to the dedicatee Quintus Caerellius. It opens with a dedicatory preface in which Censorinus praises the addressee and explains that, instead of moral precepts or rhetorical praise, he has gathered brief learned questions suited to the occasion. The body of the work ranges over the genius honoured on birthdays; ancient opinions on human origins, conception, and gestation; the Chaldaean doctrine that the months of birth are governed by planetary aspects; Pythagorean numerology with an account of musical harmonies and the harmony of the spheres; the ages of man and their climacteric years; natural and civil saecula, including the Etruscan saecula and the Roman secular games; the great years assigned by various peoples; the Roman year and Julius Caesar's calendar reform; the names of the months; and finally the civil and natural definitions of day and hour together with the traditional divisions of day and night. The transmitted text breaks off before the work's epilogue.
la.obsequens.liber_de_prodigiis: The Liber de Prodigiis ('Book of Prodigies') is a late-antique Latin work of historiographical character by Obsequens, assembling reports of portents drawn from Roman republican history. It opens with a terse notice that the temple of Juno Lucina was struck by lightning, the first entry in a record arranged year by year under consular dates and running from the early second century BC into the age of Augustus. Its entries catalogue rains of blood, milk, and stone; monstrous and hermaphrodite births; speaking oxen; statues that sweat, weep, or bleed; comets and celestial fires; and other marvels, most followed by the expiations prescribed by the haruspices or from the Sibylline books. Interwoven with these are concise notices of wars, pestilences, and political crises of the same years, from the struggles with the Celtiberi and the tribunates of the Gracchi through Caesar's assassination and the civil wars to Octavian's rise and the campaigns of Drusus in Germany.
la.adamnan.de_locis_santis: A Latin prose treatise of early medieval date, written by Adamnan on the basis of what the visiting pilgrim Arculf reported to him of his travels, and supplemented with excerpts from earlier written authorities such as Jerome. The work opens with the situation of Jerusalem, its walls, towers and gates, and then the round church of the Anastasis over the Holy Sepulchre, whose form is described from the plan Arculf drew on a wax tablet. From there it proceeds through Golgotha and Constantine's basilica, the relics preserved in the city, the Mount of Olives, Bethlehem, Hebron and the tombs of the patriarchs, Jericho, the Jordan, the Dead Sea and the lake of Tiberias, Sichem, Nazareth, Tabor, Damascus and Tyre, while later chapters turn to Alexandria and the Nile, to Constantinople with the veneration of the wood of the True Cross and several miracle stories, and finally to a volcanic island east of Sicily, closing with an appeal for the reader's prayers.
la.aethelwulf.carmen_de_abbatibus: Carmen de Abbatibus is a medieval Latin poem of the Carolingian era by Aethelwulf. It opens with a humble dedication to a bishop, offering rustic verses and asking indulgence for the poet's untutored song, before turning to Northumbrian history: the fall of King Ecgfrith to the Picts and the accession of his brother Aldfrith, under whom a monastery was founded. The poem goes on to recount the community's noble first abbot, Eanmund, who abandoned a military life for monastic service, and the succession of abbots whose deeds and piety form the work's principal subject.
la.agius_of_corvey.epicedium_hathumodae: A Latin epicedium, or funeral lament for an abbess named Hathumoda, composed in the Carolingian period by Agius of Corvey. It opens with the poet explaining that the words of consolation he had spoken amid weeping to Hathumoda's sisters at her death he now casts into verse at their request, adding further material. The greater part is a dialogue of mourning with her community: the speaker urges moderation of grief, catalogues the deaths of biblical figures from the patriarchs and prophets to the apostles and Christ himself to show mortality's universality, argues that the spirit rather than the flesh is to be loved, and assures the nuns that God and Hathumoda herself will continue to protect them. A closing exchange with Gerberga, Hathumoda's successor as abbess, includes the poet's recollection and interpretation of dream visions of a tottering wall and a tall tree, which concern her family and confirm her worthy succession.
la.agius_of_corvey.versus_computistici: The Versus Computistici is a Carolingian Latin didactic poem on the computus, the reckoning of calendar days and movable feasts, attributed to Agius of Corvey and addressed to a certain Rimbert. It opens with a prologue asserting that God is the source of all arts and that number, through which the beginnings of things and the divisions of time were made, excels the other disciplines, before explaining that the author has compiled the work at Rimbert's request and punning that his name means 'clear in number'. The main body expounds a set of tables constructed by means of letters and numerals: pages for finding the weekday of each kalends throughout the year, together with solar and lunar cycles, epacts and concurrents, and paired tables of thirty and twenty-nine days following the moon through its nineteen-year cycle. Later sections describe the paschal cycle, complete after 532 years though contained within a quarter of that span, and a 'great cycle' of the same length in which common years are entered in black ink and embolismic ones in red, with leap years marked by the letter B, closing with instructions for reckoning the date of Easter and of three feasts in any year, backward or forward.
la.agnellus_ravennatis.liber_pontificalis: The Liber pontificalis is a Latin ecclesiastical historiographical work by Agnellus of Ravenna, composed in the Carolingian period largely in prose, with a verse preface and verse inscriptions. It opens with a metrical preface in which Agnellus, a priest of Ravenna, recounts being urged by local priests to write down the lives of the city's pontiffs, long left unrecorded. The body of the work consists of numbered biographies of the bishops and archbishops of Ravenna, beginning with Apollinaris, the disciple of Peter sent to preach at Ravenna, and running through late antiquity down to the author's own contemporaries. Alongside the lives it preserves miracle narratives, accounts of church foundations and restorations together with their dedicatory verses, and the epitaphs of several Ravennate bishops.
la.aimoin_of_saint_germain.carmen_de_transl: A short medieval Latin poem, of Carolingian date and attributed to Aimoin of Saint Germain, on the transfer of the relics of Vincent, the Spanish deacon-martyr. It opens with a chronological formula and the introduction of Audaldus, a monk and priest of Castrum, who sets out with a single companion for Valencia in Spain. There the pair bribe Zacharias, the Muslim custodian of the relics, uncover the tomb after reading its inscription naming Vincent as deacon and martyr, and carry the sacred body home beneath the stars. The rest of the poem recounts the martyr's arrival at the cell of Saint Benedict, the collapse and healing of a woman who refused to believe the relics belonged to the saint rather than a Moor, the many miracles that followed, some of them recorded in prose, and the body's placement behind the altar of Saint Benedict, where it shines with continual signs of virtue.
la.alcuin.carmina: A Latin verse collection attributed to Alcuin, the Carolingian-era scholar, comprising long narrative, epistolary, and epigraphic poems. It opens with an invocation to Christ and the saints before a substantial poem on the church of York, tracing the city from its Roman foundation through the coming of the Saxons, the conversion of the Northumbrians under Edwin and Paulinus, the reigns and miracles associated with Oswald and Oswiu, the saints Cuthbert, Bede, Wilfrid, and John of Beverley, and ending with the poet's own masters, pupils, and library. The remainder gathers occasional and devotional verse: court poems and precepts addressed to Charlemagne (styled Karolus and David), riddling verse letters and farewells to pupils and friends, a contest between Spring and Winter, the fable of the cock and the wolf, laments in pastoral guise, verses on virtues and vices, tituli for altars, churches, and books, hymns, and epitaphs, including one in Alcuin's own voice.
la.amalarius.versus_marini: The Versus Marini is a short medieval Latin narrative poem of the Carolingian period, attributed to Amalarius, that follows a party of monks on a voyage by sea. It opens with a questioning address to an abba who presses back toward the narrow seas, evoking the seasickness of a monk named Gregory before turning to night watches, storm-tossed waters, and prayers requested for a buried priest. The narrative then carries the travelers to Constantinople, where they pass a long sojourn, are summoned to the royal palaces by the emperor Leo, and hear prayers for the life of Charles, his sons, the sacred order, and the Frankish people; the homeward leg brings fierce winds, a prophetic warning against Moors and Slavs, and finally a tearful welcome from the brethren at a church in green Italy. The poem closes with the speaker, wearied by the death of the late king Charles, praying that God may join him with Charles and the brothers without end.
la.ambrose.exameron: Ambrose's Exameron is a late antique work of Latin theology in prose, comprising nine sermons that expound the six days of creation in the opening chapter of Genesis. It opens with a survey of the opinions of Plato, Aristotle, and other Greek philosophers on the origin, matter, and eternity of the world, against which Moses' words 'In the beginning God created heaven and earth' are set. The sermons then follow the creation week day by day, treating the first light, the firmament and the waters above it, the gathering of the seas and the appearance of dry land with its vegetation, the sun, moon, and stars, the fish and birds of the waters and air, and finally the land animals and humankind, interweaving discussion of the elements and the heavens with refutations of philosophical, astrological, and heretical teaching and with moral exhortation drawn from the behaviour of animals. The work closes with an account of the human being made in God's image and likeness, a survey of the human body as a microcosm of the universe, and God's rest after the completion of the works.
la.ambrose.explanatio_psalmorum_xii: A Latin prose commentary by Ambrose, bishop of Milan, explaining twelve Psalms. Opening with a discussion of how delectation, or pleasure, figures both in the divine call to virtue and in the devil's promptings toward error, the work proceeds psalm by psalm, beginning with the first Psalm's 'Beatus vir' and passing through Psalms 30-50, including the penitential Psalms 38, 39 and 50, and Psalm 47. Each psalm is expounded verse by verse, with sustained attention to its title and inscription, and the exposition alternates between moral exhortation on virtue, silence, patience and poverty and christological and mystical readings that see the passion, priesthood and resurrection of Christ foreshadowed in the text. Ambrose draws extensively on the Old Testament narratives and on the Apostle Paul, quotes alternative Greek and Latin renderings of difficult verses, and closes discussions with doxological conclusions, while the opening book offers a broader encomium on the psalter as a school of doctrine, medicine for the soul and a discipline uniting the whole people in song.
la.ambrosiaster.pseudo_augustini_quaestione: A Late Antique Latin collection of 127 questions on scriptural and theological difficulties, attributed to Ambrosiaster but long transmitted under Augustine's name. It opens with a treatise on the divine nature, arguing that God surpasses all opinion and expression and that evil is not a substance but a transgression of the good arising from the will. The collection then moves through problems raised chiefly by Genesis and the Mosaic law, including creation, the apostasy of the devil, the fall, Cain and Lamech, the giving of the law, circumcision, the patriarchs, and Melchisedech, before turning to questions on the Psalms, the Gospels, and the Pauline epistles, together with discussions of the Trinity and the persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Woven into its exegesis are refutations of contemporary opponents, most prominently the Novatians' exclusion of lapsed Christians and readings of creation that deny the one God as maker.
la.ammianus.rerum_gestarum: A Late Antique Latin prose history by Ammianus Marcellinus, the Res Gestae is preserved in its later books, which open with the savage rule of the Caesar Gallus in the East under the Augustus Constantius. The narrative then proceeds through Constantius's reign and the purges of his court, the elevation of Julian to the Caesarship and then to sole rule, his Persian expedition and death, and the reigns of Valentinian and Valens, closing with the Gothic crossing of the Danube and the Roman defeat at Hadrianople in which Valens perished. Its course is punctuated by digressions on geography and peoples, Saracens, Gauls, Egyptians, Persians, Huns, and Alans among them, alongside accounts of court intrigue, justice, religion, and military affairs, together with summaries of each emperor's virtues and vices. The concluding lines frame the whole work as an account of Roman affairs from the emperor Nerva down to the death of Valens, with the author urging abler writers to carry the story further.
la.angilbert_carmina: A short collection of Latin occasional verse by Angilbert, a poet of Charlemagne's court who styles himself Homerus, made up of court poems, greetings, devotional pieces, inscriptions and epitaphs. The opening poem addresses Pippin returning from Italy, dwelling on the joy of his father Charles, his brother Chlodowih, and the royal sisters and courtiers who long for his arrival. A long central cycle, bound together by the refrain 'Surge, meis caris dulces fac, fistula, versus', praises the palace circle under the biblical king David, Charlemagne himself, his consecrated sister Gisla, the princesses Rothrude and Bertha, clerics and companions, before sending a personified letter to carry greetings through the palatine households. The remainder is religious and epigraphic: prayers entreating the intercession of Saints Richarius and Eligius, tituli celebrating the church and buildings that Angilbert erected at Centula, and epitaphs, among them his verse monument for the priest Chaidocus.
la.angilbert_versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem ascribed to Angilbert, an abbot, opening with praise of the sound doctrine that Aurelius Augustine set forth in his work De doctrina. The body of the poem runs through the contents of that work's four books: the first teaches Christ's precepts, distinguishing right use of temporal things from enjoyment of eternal ones; the second shows how signs are to be recognized; the third treats what signs and words signify and what is to be avoided; and the fourth gathers the sayings of the earlier books and sets forth the three manners of speech, humble, temperate and grand. The closing lines name the lowly abbot Angilbert as the one who had the little book made to give to the pious King Louis (Hlodoicus), offering blessings on the king and ending with praise of the Trinity.
la.angilbertus_miles.versus_de_fontaneto: The Versus de Fontaneto is a short Carolingian Latin poem on a battle fought at Fontaneto, a country village, between the armies of Lothar and of Charles and Louis; it is attributed to an Angilbertus who presents himself in the poem as a soldier and eyewitness of the fighting. It opens with dawn breaking on the day of battle and a picture of fratricidal strife, in which brother seeks brother's death and Christian law lies broken. The remainder is a lament for the carnage: God's right hand shields Lothar as victor, the fields on the side of Charles and Louis grow white with the garments of the dead, corpses are abandoned unburied to vulture, crow and wolf, and the speaker, sole survivor of his part of the front line, curses the day of battle and the grass where the brave fell. The poem ends with a prayer to the Lord for the souls of the slain.
la.anonymi.planctus_de_obitu_Karoli: An anonymous Latin lament on the death of Charlemagne, of uncertain date and belonging to the medieval planctus tradition. It opens with grief stretching from the rising to the setting sun, as all peoples beat their breasts at the news of the emperor's death. The poem goes on to enumerate the mourners, Franks and Romans, infants and elders, bishops and matrons, while portraying Charles as the common father of orphans, pilgrims, widows, and virgins; it utters woes against Rome, Italy, and Francia over his burial at Aachen, and closes with prayers to Christ and an address to the scribe Columbanus that the emperor may be received among the apostles in heavenly rest. Each stanza closes with the refrain 'Heu mihi misero!'
la.anonymous.breviarius_de_hierosolyma: The Breviarius de Hierosolyma is a brief anonymous Latin prose guide to the holy places of Jerusalem, of uncertain date. It opens with the city set upon its mountain and the basilica of Constantine, where the relic of the True Cross was kept, noting the silver and marble columns, the altars, and the marvels associated with each spot. The itinerary then leads through Golgotha and the round church of the Holy Sepulchre to the sanctuaries of the Passion, the reed, sponge and chalice, the basilica on Sion, the houses of Caiaphas and Pilate, the pinnacle of the Temple, and closes with the Mount of Olives, the valley of Josaphat and Galilee, marking at each station the biblical events there commemorated and the relics preserved.
la.anonymous_pilgrim_of_piacenza.itinerariu: A late antique Latin prose itinerary attributed to the anonymous pilgrim of Piacenza, who opens by recording, under the protection of the martyr Antoninus, his purpose of setting down the holy places through which he passed. From Constantinople the journey runs by way of Cyprus and the Phoenician coast into Galilee, Samaria, and Judaea, with careful accounts of the Jordan and its Epiphany rites, Jericho, and the churches, relics, and miracles of Jerusalem and Bethlehem. The pilgrim then crosses the desert to the monasteries of Sinai and descends into Egypt by Clysma, Memphis, and Alexandria, before returning to Jerusalem and making his homeward way through Syria and Mesopotamia as far as the shrine of St Sergius at Tetrapyrgium. Throughout, the narrative notes distances, local customs of Jews, Samaritans, and Saracens, liturgical observances, natural marvels such as the Dead Sea and the petrified host of Pharaoh, and the healing wonders worked at each shrine.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_ludovicum_pium: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, addressed to Louis the Pious, it opens with a dedication asking the king, likened to the wisdom of Solomon, to accept a book composed in dactylic verses so that his soul may be adorned by its precepts. The work then unfolds as a sustained mirror for a ruler, urging faith, love of God, hope, the reading of scripture, mercy, patience, humility, contrition and confession of sins, fear of God, fasting and almsgiving, and chastity, while warning against deceit, false witness, envy, pride, anger, vainglory, gluttony, lust, avarice, sloth, and sorrow. In its closing section the king is armed with the four virtues of justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance and with celestial armour, the breastplate of justice, helmet of hope, shield of faith, and sword of the word of God, so that he may prevail in the ceaseless battle against the enemy and receive the crown of justice at the dread day of judgement.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_compoti_ratione: The Carmen de compoti ratione is an anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date and authorship, that teaches the elements of computus in verse. It opens with the lengths of the months and the placement of their kalends, nones and ides, together with the regular numbers from which the day of the week may be found. The poem then explains how to reckon the moon's age from the epacts of the nineteen-year cycle, describes a method of reckoning on the joints of the hand, and shows how the movable feasts, Septuagesima, Quadragesima, Easter, Rogation and Pentecost, are located, with the adjustments required in bissextile years.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_conversione_saxonum: The Carmen de Conversione Saxonum is a short anonymous Latin poem of the medieval period, which places its own composition in the ninth year of Charlemagne's reign. It opens with an account of the six ages of the world, mankind's fall into death, and the Father's sending of Christ, who vanquished death and returned in triumph to heaven. The greater part describes the pagan Saxons, given to sacrificing cattle and venerating demons, and Charlemagne's conquest of them by arms, figured as the transformation of wolves into lambs, ravens into doves, and other fierce creatures into gentle ones. The poem closes with the Saxons' baptism in the name of the Trinity and a prayer that Charlemagne, while the wicked are consigned to punishment, may gain the rewards of the starry kingdom when God weighs all merits at the Last Judgment.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_nynia_episcopo: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Nynia Episcopo versifies the life of Saint Ninian (Nynia), the apostle and bishop of the Picts. It opens with an account of Christ's incarnation and the spreading of divine light through the world before introducing Ninian, who travels to Rome, receives episcopal rank, and returns to convert the Picts and to found the church of Candida Casa dedicated to Martin. The narrative then recounts his miracles, including the restoration of the blinded King Tudvael, the speaking infant that vindicates an accused priest, the instantaneous growth of garden herbs, and the punishment and revival of cattle thieves, before describing his death and ascent to heaven. Its closing section treats the wonders worked at his tomb, notably the healing of the boy Pethgils, of a leper, and of a blind woman, the vision granted to the priest Plecgils of Christ as an infant on the altar during mass, and a final encomium on the saint's virtues and heavenly reward.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_pippino: A short medieval Latin poem of anonymous authorship and uncertain date, the Carmen de Pippino celebrates the victory of the Frankish king Pippin over the Avars. It opens with an address to Christ, creator of all peoples, before turning to the Avars' destruction of shrines, monasteries and consecrated vessels in earlier times. God then sends Saint Peter to aid Pippin, son of a great king, who encamps with the Frankish army on the Danube; the terrified Avar khagan, urged on by his consort Catuna, comes with gifts to pay homage and surrenders his realm with its forests, mountains and children to the Christian ruler. The closing lines give thanks that God confirmed the king's rule over the Avar kingdom, acclaim Pippin with wishes for long life and heirs, and end with a doxology.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_temporum_ratione: The Carmen de Temporum Ratione is an anonymous medieval Latin didactic poem, of uncertain date, on the reckoning of time. It opens by distinguishing three bases for such reckoning, divine authority as embodied in the Sabbath, human authority as in the Olympiads, and custom, and then sets out the divisions of the day and its smaller parts. The poem proceeds through the Hebrew, Egyptian, Greek, and Roman calendars, with their month names and the kalends, nones, and ides, the signs of the zodiac month by month, and an extensive body of lunar doctrine covering the moon's phases, distance, and influence on the tides. Its later portions treat the solar year and equinoxes, climates and varying day-lengths, the zones of the earth, the seasons with their correspondence to the humours and ages of man, the planets and their cycles, leap years and the nineteen-year cycle, and finally the computus of Easter, with rules for the paschal moon, epacts, the dating of Easter Sunday, and the Lenten fast.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_timone_comite: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de Timone Comite opens with an address to a king, presenting Count Timo as his envoy who restores neglected law in the land of the Norici, punishing thieves and robbers and upholding justice. The poem supports its praise of the count with scriptural examples of just and merciful rule, recounting the deeds of David, Job, Moses, Joshua and Joseph. A later section describes a spring flowing on a mountain beside a hall, attributed to the gift of Christ through Bishop Corbinian, and the work closes with the tale of the count's dog, which died after tasting poisoned food at the mountain's summit.
la.anonymus.carmina_cenomanensia: Carmina Cenomanensia is an anonymous medieval Latin collection of poems, of uncertain date, centred on Aldric, bishop of Le Mans. The opening verses praise Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the relics of the martyrs Gervasius, Prothasius, and Stephen honoured in the cathedral, before turning to Aldric's upbringing at Metz, his progress through the ecclesiastical orders, and his elevation to the see of Le Mans under King Louis. Later poems record his benefactions to his church, including vestments, a golden chalice from Queen Judith, altar dedications, and the transfer of the monastery of Carilephus with its lands under a charter of the emperor Louis. The collection closes with epitaphs and petitions for eternal rest, including for Aldric himself and for a priest named Franco.
la.anonymus.corneli_translationes: Corneli Translationes is an anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date celebrating the translation of the relics of Pope Cornelius into a church founded by a king named Charles. It opens by hailing the blessed place where the martyr rests after his agonies, contrasting the Rome that once flourished through his deeds with the Francia that now glories in his triumph. The poem then narrates the solemn procession by which king, clergy, and people receive the relics into the royal palace church, records Charles's lavish endowment of gold, silver, vestments, and gems, and catalogues the miracles of healing and exorcism worked at the shrine, together with the repulse of barbarian raiders who sought to burn the temple.
