It closes with prayers asking Cornelius to intercede for the king, the Franks, and the monastery, from which his body had earlier been driven toward Senlis, and with a summons to the papal shepherd to return to his own flock.
la.anonymus.hymnus_nynie_episcopi: A medieval Latin hymn of uncertain date and anonymous authorship in honour of Bishop Nynia, built as an alphabetical poem in which successive couplets run from A to Z and each repeats its opening words at the close of the second line. It opens with an invocation of God enthroned on high, sole creator and source of light, before tracing the penalty of ancient sin and the healing advent of Christ, born of a virgin mother. The greater part celebrates Nynia himself: his radiance among the citizens of heaven, the many miracles of the gentle father on earth, his cleansing of leprosy from his tomb, his burial beneath the temple roof, and his spirit borne by angelic hands to the stars. It closes with the serpent groaning before the dominion of Christ, the gem prepared amid dark shadows for the wretched, and the good at rest through all ages, singing mystical words to the king day and night.
la.anonymus.karolus_magnus_et_leo_papa: Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa is an anonymous medieval Latin epic poem, of uncertain date, devoted to Charlemagne and Pope Leo III. It opens with a nautical figure in which the poet, spreading sail on shifting winds, launches into praise of the king, likened to the sun and to David, whose justice no storm can darken and whose wisdom, learning, and eloquence place him above all other rulers. The poem goes on to describe Charlemagne's building of a second Rome, complete with forum, senate house, temple, theatre, and baths, and a great hunting expedition in the nearby woods, joined by his queen Liutgard, his son Pippin, and his daughters, portrayed in elaborate detail. The narrative then turns on a dream in which the king sees the Roman pontiff weeping, blinded, and with his tongue cut out; it recounts the assault on Leo by a murderous Roman faction, his healing and flight to Charlemagne's court, the king's crossing of the Rhine with his army, and the reunion of king and pope amid mutual homage, a solemn mass, a banquet, and the exchange of gifts, ending with Leo honorably received as a refugee from Roman treachery.
la.anonymus.laudes_mediolanensis_civitatis: The Laudes Mediolanensis Civitatis is an anonymous medieval Latin encomium in praise of Milan, of uncertain date and authorship. Opening with a depiction of the lofty and spacious city long known as Mediolanum, the poem proceeds through an orderly survey of its strengths: the thickness and height of its walls, its nine iron-bound gates with their outworks, paved streets and water supply, and its glittering churches adorned with stone and gold. It then extols Milan as queen of cities and metropolis to which all Italy's bishops come, praises the piety and charity of its people, catalogues the saints whose relics rest within and around it, Ambrose, Protasius, Gervasius, Nazarius, Simplicianus, Benedict, and others, and dwells on the learning, chant, and daily observance of its churches. The closing lines touch on the city's abundance, its Lombard ruler Liutprand and the bishop Theodore who adorned it, its victories over impious peoples, and a final hymn and prayer to the Trinity for the city's protection.
la.anonymus.laudes_veronensis_civitatis: An anonymous medieval Latin encomium in verse praising the city of Verona, of uncertain exact date. It opens by extolling Verona's situation in Venetia, its square walls, forty-eight towers, labyrinth, paved forum, pagan temples, and bridges over the river Adige. The poem then passes through the Incarnation and Resurrection, the succession of Veronese bishops culminating in Zeno and his miracles, catalogues of the martyrs and confessors whose relics guard the city on every side, the gilded shrine prepared by Bishop Anno, and the commendation of neighbouring Italian cities, closing with King Pippin residing there and a doxology to God.
la.anonymus.tituli_metrici_saeculi_viii: A collection of Latin metrical tituli, chiefly sepulchral inscriptions, transmitted anonymously and assigned by its title to the eighth century. The opening poem is an epitaph spoken in the first person by Peter, bishop of Pavia, who recounts his exile and restoration under King Charles and addresses the reader from the tomb. The remaining poems assemble epitaphs for a broad range of the dead, including popes, bishops, abbots, monks, kings, nobles, and young men cut down in war, many of them commemorated at Italian sites, with some verses voiced by the deceased themselves and others by mourners, parents, donors, or the craftsmen of a monument. Throughout, the dead are praised for lineage, virtue, and benefactions, and passers-by are urged to pray for their souls.
la.anonymus.versus_ad_ebonem_remensem: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, addressed to Ebbo, archbishop of Reims. It opens with a long series of honorific epithets hailing Ebbo as the glory of Reims, shepherd, light of the clergy, and friend of Christ and St Peter. The body of the poem recounts how the humble abbot Peter, at Ebbo's command, wrought a Gospel book adorned with gold within and ivory without and dedicated it to the apostle Peter, celebrating the volume as the fourfold chariot of Christ, a vehicle of the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, and as a medicine that heals the sick, restores the feeble, and turns mourners to joy. It closes by inviting sinners to seek the book's remedies and with a prayer that Christ reward Ebbo and Peter with eternal peace in heaven.
la.anonymus.versus_de_eversione_monasterii_: An anonymous medieval Latin poem, the Versus de Eversione Monasterii Glonnensis recounts the burning of the monastery of Glonna and its restoration. It opens by summoning the Thracian lyre, Orpheus's responsive mountains, rivers and woods, and every kind of music to join a lament. The narrative then follows the basilica of Saint Florentius from its pious foundation by the great King Charles and its further enrichment by his son Louis, through the discord that follows Louis's death, when the kingdom divided among four claimants sinks into strife. Nemenoius, a poor farmer enriched by a buried treasure, rebels against Charles and, together with the men of Rennes and Nantes, crosses the Loire and burns the monastery; Saint Florentius appears from heaven and weakens the ravager, who begs pardon and returns to Brittany, after which Abbot Dido obtains from King Charles the grant of other abbeys and the splendid rebuilding of the ruined house, and the poem closes with a prayer to the saint.
la.apuleius.de_deo_socratis: A Latin philosophical oration of the later imperial period, the De deo Socratis attributed to Apuleius, expounding Plato's doctrine of the daimonion of Socrates. It opens with Plato's tripartite division of all nature into gods, daemons, and men, cataloguing the celestial gods, some visible as stars and planets, others grasped only by the intellect. The argument then establishes the daemons as intermediate beings dwelling in the air, whose subtle bodies and mediating offices account for divination, omens, and the varied rites of cult, before turning to the human soul as a kind of daimon, the Genius and the Lemures, Lares, Larvae, and Manes, and to the higher guardian spirit assigned to each person as an unseen witness of deeds and thoughts. The closing portion treats Socrates' familiar daimon as a perceived sign rather than an audible voice, one that forbade but never urged, and ends by exhorting hearers to cultivate the soul, illustrated by Socrates' indifference to wealth and by Odysseus' prudent passage through his wanderings.
la.apuleius.metamorphoses: The Metamorphoses of Apuleius, known also as The Golden Ass, is a Latin prose fiction of the later imperial period, written in eleven books. It opens with the narrator Lucius introducing himself as a Greek-educated traveller who promises a Milesian tale of human figures transformed into other shapes and restored again. The narrative follows Lucius to Thessaly, where his curiosity about witchcraft brings about his transformation into an ass; in that form he passes through robbers' caves, the households of successive owners, and the embedded story of Cupid and Psyche, amid many comic and perilous misadventures. The closing books recount his return to human form through the intervention of Isis and his initiations into her mysteries and those of Osiris, after which he resumes a career as a pleader at Rome.
la.audradus_modicus.carmina: Carmina is a Carolingian Latin collection of poems by Audradus Modicus. It opens with a visionary colloquy in which Hincmar urges the poet to seek out a wondrous fountain, whose guardian voice declares that its waters are denied to mortals who come without a vessel. The collection proceeds through the poet's disappointed vigil at the spring and turns to a versified martyrdom of Saint Julian, who before a tyrannical prefect steadies his weeping followers by likening his ordeal to gold refined in the furnace. Later poems recount the miracles that attend churches dedicated in Julian's name and the collection closes with a doxology praising the Trinity and invoking the intercession of the martyrs for the forgiveness of sins.
la.audradus_modicus.de_sancta_trinitate: A verse treatise on the Holy Trinity by the Carolingian author Audradus Modicus. It opens with a prayer for mercy and a survey of the author's own writings, including books dedicated to the apostle Peter, to Martin of Tours, and to ten-year truces, before turning to its doctrinal subject. The poem defends the full equality of the Son with the Father and the equal substance and procession of the Holy Spirit, then recounts the creation of the angels, the fall of the tenth of their number, the making and deception of man, and Christ's incarnation from the Virgin, his victory over hell, and his restoration of the place the fallen angel had lost. It ends with the risen Christ instructing the disciples in his eternal generation from the Father and his part in the making of the world.
la.augustine.confessiones: The Confessions, a Latin prose work of theology by the Late Antique author Augustine, is an extended first-person prayer addressed to God that interweaves autobiographical narrative with philosophical and scriptural meditation. It opens with praise of the Creator and the plea of a heart that is restless until it rests in him. The narrative portion then recounts the author's life from infancy and school days through youthful sin, an attachment to Manichaeism, and his gradual movement toward Christianity under Ambrose at Milan, culminating in conversion, baptism, and the death of his mother Monica at Ostia. The later books turn from memoir to sustained reflection on memory, time, evil, and a running commentary on the opening of Genesis and the account of creation.
la.augustine.contra_adimantum: An anti-Manichaean treatise in Latin prose by Augustine, directed against Adimantus, a disciple of Mani who had collected Old Testament passages to set against the New as contradictions. It opens with the first chapter of Genesis, which the Manichaeans had opposed to the Gospel saying that the world was made through Christ, and Augustine answers that charge in three ways before turning to a long sequence of similarly paired passages. Drawing on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah, he treats the sabbath, marriage and divorce, circumcision, the dietary laws, the love of enemies, temporal and eternal rewards, and the zeal and severity of God, arguing throughout that both Testaments come from one God and agree when their figures and signs are spiritually interpreted. The work closes with Isaiah's vision of the Lord and an account of three kinds of vision, corporeal, imaginative, and intellectual, showing that the prophet's seeing of God does not conflict with the apostolic declaration that God is invisible.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelegian: Augustine's Contra duas epistulas Pelagianorum is a four-book anti-Pelagian treatise in Latin prose, addressed to Pope Boniface, refuting a letter sent to Rome by Julian of Eclanum and a joint letter dispatched by eighteen Pelagian bishops to Thessalonica. The work opens as a personal letter in which Augustine explains how his friend Alypius had brought him into contact with the pope and how thePelagian writings, containing Augustine's name inserted calumniously, had come into Boniface's hands. Augustine then works through Julian's arguments point by point, defending against their denial the doctrines of original sin transmitted to all humanity through Adam, baptism as conferring full remission of sins even on infants, and the priority of God's unmerited grace over any preceding human merit, while closely expounding Romans 7 on the conflict of flesh and spirit. He also contrasts Pelagians with Manichaeans, showing that the two heresies err in opposite directions yet alike against the catholic faith, and the final book gathers patristic testimony from Cyprian and Ambrose to show that the doctrine Augustine defends is the old and universal one of the church rather than a recent novelty.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_fundamenti: Contra Epistulam Fundamenti is a Late Antique Latin anti-Manichaean treatise by Augustine, cast as a direct address to the Manichaeans and devoted to refuting the book they call the Letter of the Foundation. It opens with a prayer for a tranquil mind and a plea that the debate proceed without arrogance, before dissecting the letter's salutation, 'Manichaeus apostolus Iesu Christi,' to argue that Mani is neither Christ's apostle nor the promised Paraclete and that belief should rest on Catholic authority rather than on unverifiable promises of knowledge. The greater part of the work examines the cosmogony recounted in Mani's letter, criticizing the account of the realm of light bordered by the land of darkness and its five natures of darkness, waters, winds, fire, and smoke, and then argues that every nature is good insofar as it exists, that evil is corruption contrary to nature rather than a substance, and that corruptible things were made from nothing by God. The treatise ends by reserving the remaining doctrines for refutation in subsequent books.
la.augustine.contra_epistulam_parmeniani: Contra Epistulam Parmeniani is a Late Antique Latin polemical treatise by Augustine, framed as a reply to a letter in which the Donatist bishop Parmenian had rebuked Tychonius. Augustine opens by recalling his many earlier writings and sermons against the Donatists and explains that, at the request of the brothers, he now answers Parmenian's letter, which had attacked Tychonius's position that the church is diffused through the whole world. The main body rebuts Parmenian's charges that the churches of Gaul, Spain, Italy, and beyond were founded by traditores, recounts the hearings of Caecilian before African councils and before Miltiades of Rome and Constantine, and argues that wicked clergy within a church neither defile its sacraments nor justify rebaptizing those they baptize. Augustine presses the Donatists with their own divisions, notably the Maximianist schism and the readmission of bishops they had condemned, answers their proof texts from the prophets, the Psalms, and Paul, and closes by denying that punishment endured for schism can count as martyrdom.
la.augustine.contra_felicem: The Contra Felicem of Augustine, bishop of Hippo, is a stenographic record of a public disputation held in the church at Hippo in December 404, during the sixth consulship of Honorius, between Augustine and Felix, a Manichaean layman. The proceedings open with Augustine challenging Felix to defend the scriptures of Mani, and the first day is occupied with readings from the Gospels, Acts, and the Pauline epistles on the promise of the Paraclete before the opening of Mani's so-called Fundamental Epistle is read aloud, its cosmology of a luminous earth, a war with the race of darkness, and a divine substance polluted and released through obscene transformations being tested through sustained questioning. The second book records the adjourned session, in which Augustine attacks the Manichaean doctrine of two natures, defends free will and the incorruptibility of God against the claim that a part of the divine substance was captured, defiled, and purged, and concludes with both disputants subscribing a written anathema of Mani, his teaching, and the spirit said to have spoken through him.
la.augustine.contra_litteras_petiliani: Augustine's Contra Litteras Petiliani is a Latin polemical treatise against the Donatist bishop Petilian of Cirta, written while Augustine was bishop of Hippo. The work opens with Augustine's reply to an intercepted letter in which Petilian attacked Catholic baptism, arguing that the validity of baptism does not depend on the moral worth of the minister but on Christ himself. When the remainder of Petilian's letter came to light, Augustine produced a longer second book that answers it clause by clause, quoting Petilian's words and responding beneath them: he defends the unity of the Church spread through all nations, cites the case of the Maximianists, whom the Donatists had condemned yet whose baptism they accepted, and rebuts charges concerning traditores, persecution and rebaptism. The treatise closes with further argument on scripture, the exercise of imperial power against schism, and the insistence that no one is to be compelled into the faith unwillingly.
la.augustine.contra_partem_donati_post_gest: Contra Partem Donati post Gesta is a short Latin prose treatise by Augustine of the Donatist controversy, addressed to the rank and file of the Donatist party after their bishops' defeat in a public disputation at Carthage. It opens by taunting the Donatists with the gap between their own recorded statements at the conference, above all their admission that 'one cause does not prejudge another cause, nor one person another person', and their continuing refusal to return to Catholic unity. The argument then works through the gospel parables of the field, threshing floor, net, and flock to show that good and bad remain mixed in the church until the final judgment, defends Caecilian's acquittal before Constantine against the charge of a bribed judge, exposes the Donatists' inconsistencies over the Maximianist schism and their claim to be the church that suffers rather than inflicts persecution, and appeals to biblical cases such as Haggai's two peoples under one temple to refute their demand for bodily separation from the impure. It closes with an exhortation to the Donatists to abandon an error already confuted, to embrace peace and unity, and to acknowledge their Catholic opponents as brothers.
la.augustine.de_beata_vita: De Beata Vita is a short Latin prose dialogue by Augustine, a work of Late Antique philosophical theology dedicated to Manlius Theodorus. It opens with a dedicatory preface that figures the approach to philosophy as a voyage toward a harbour, distinguishing three kinds of seafarers and warning against the deceptive mountain of vain glory that rises before the port. The main body recounts conversations held over three days, beginning at a birthday banquet whose participants include Augustine's mother, his brother Navigius, his son Adeodatus, and the young Licentius and Trygetius, as the company seeks a definition of the happy life. Through successive arguments the speakers conclude that misery is need, that the soul's need is folly, and that the happy life consists in the possession of wisdom and truth, that is, of a propitious God, a conclusion Augustine's mother greets at the close with a prayer to the Trinity.
la.augustine.de_bono_coniugali: De Bono Coniugali is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date in which Augustine sets out why marriage is a good. It opens by grounding marriage in creation, where the union of the first man and woman forms the first bond of human society, sustained by the fellowship of friendship, the tie of kinship and the offspring that is the honourable fruit of wedlock. The discussion then moves through the three goods of marriage, offspring, fidelity between the spouses, and the indissoluble sacrament, to questions of the marital debt, adultery, divorce and remarriage, temporary concubinage, and the ranking of marriage below widowhood and virginity. A substantial closing section defends the plural marriages of the Old Testament patriarchs against heretical calumny, contrasts their procreative unions with the continence urged on Christians under the New Testament, and distinguishes the virtue of continence as it is exercised in act from its abiding presence in the soul.
la.augustine.de_civitate_dei: Augustine's City of God, a Latin work of Late Antique prose theology, opens with a dedication to Marcellinus undertaking the defense of the City of God against pagans who blame the Christian religion for the recent sack of Rome. The early books answer that charge by surveying the disasters that befell Rome and other peoples before the coming of Christ, by attacking the theatrical rites and obscene legends attributed to the pagan gods, and by arguing from Roman historians that the republic was already morally ruined. The later books turn to the two cities themselves, tracing the origins of the earthly and heavenly societies among the angels and the first human beings and following their history from Cain and Abel to their mingling in the present age. The final books defend the resurrection of the body against philosophical objection, record contemporary miracles at the shrines of the martyrs, and end with the last judgment and the eternal blessedness of the City of God, figured as an unending sabbath.
la.augustine.de_continentia: A Latin prose treatise on the virtue of continence by Augustine, written in Late Antiquity as a work of Christian theology. It opens by acknowledging the difficulty of treating so great a subject and asserting, from scriptural testimony, that continence is a gift of God, as is conjugal chastity. The argument then distinguishes outward deeds from the consent of the inner 'mouth of the heart', expounds Pauline teaching on the struggle between flesh and spirit under grace rather than law, and rejects excuses for sin drawn from fate, fortune, the devil, or God himself. A sustained anti-Manichaean section defends the goodness of the body and its resurrection, rules out the continence of heretics and pagans as severed from faith, and closes with the hope of a future peace in which concupiscence will be no more.
la.augustine.de_doctrina_christiana: The De Doctrina Christiana of Augustine is a late-antique Latin treatise in prose on the interpretation and exposition of the Christian Scriptures. It opens by distinguishing the two things on which every treatment of Scripture rests, the mode of finding what is to be understood and the mode of setting forth what has been understood. The first book treats 'things' (res), ordering love of God, neighbour, and self through the distinction between enjoying and using, while the second and third turn to 'signs', covering the canon of Scripture, the knowledge of languages, of nature, and of numbers needed to resolve obscurity, and the discrimination of literal from figurative expression, including the seven rules of Tychonius. A fourth book on eloquence discusses the Christian teacher's aims of teaching, delighting, and persuading, and the styles of diction suited to each.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_symbolo: De Fide et Symbolo is a Late Antique Latin prose theological treatise in which Augustine expounds the creed entrusted to newly baptised Christians, article by article. It opens by arguing that faith demands confession with the mouth as well as belief in the heart, the creed's few words having been fixed as a defence against the subtleties of heretics. The exposition then proceeds through the articles on God the omnipotent Father and creation from nothing, the eternal generation of the Word and his incarnation, passion, burial, resurrection, ascension and sitting at the Father's right hand, and the Holy Spirit as consubstantial with Father and Son, before closing with the church, the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the flesh, with sustained polemic against heretical misreadings throughout. A final notice drawn from Augustine's Retractationes qualifies his account of the transformation of the risen body.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram: Augustine's De Genesi ad Litteram is a Late Antique prose theological commentary in twelve books that interprets the opening chapters of Genesis according to the letter of the text. It opens by distinguishing scriptural narration of deeds from figurative discourse, and by asking whether the creation of heaven and earth 'in principio' took place in time or through God's coeternal Word. The work then moves through the six days, arguing that God created all things at once in their causal reasons while their temporal unfolding continues in his unceasing operation, and treats the formation of Adam's body from the earth and his soul by divine breathing, denying that the soul is part of the divine substance or subject to transmigration through animals. The later books consider Paradise and its rivers, the commandment and the first transgression, the serpent and the devil's fall, the punishment of the first parents, and the treatise ends with an extended analysis of corporal, spiritual, and intellectual vision occasioned by Paul's rapture to the third heaven.
la.augustine.de_gratia_christi: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a letter to Albina, Pinianus and Melania and devoted to the question of grace in the controversy with Pelagius. It opens with greetings to the three correspondents and an announcement that the matters on which they had consulted him will now be treated. The body of the work quotes and examines Pelagius's own words, attacking his division of possibility, will and action, under which divine aid reaches only the natural capacity of the will while grace is reduced to law and teaching, and arguing instead that God works in humans both the willing and the doing of good. Augustine contrasts law and grace through Pauline texts, reviews Pelagius's letter to Innocent and his profession of faith sent to Rome, considers his letter to the virgin Demetrias and his books on free choice, and adduces Ambrose's testimony that God calls and makes religious whom he wills; the treatise closes by affirming that human nature, vitiated by the first man's sin, is healed only by grace, and announces a further treatment of original sin.
la.augustine.de_nuptiis_et_concupiscentia: A two-book Latin prose treatise by Augustine on marriage and carnal concupiscence, composed for the distinguished count Valerius in the setting of the late-antique controversy over original sin and infant baptism. It opens with a dedicatory letter praising Valerius's faith, his resistance to the new heresy, and his conjugal chastity, and explaining why the book has been sent to him. The first book maintains that marriage remains good in its three goods of offspring, fidelity, and sacrament, while distinguishing from them the concupiscence of the flesh, a penal disorder of the body's obedience that followed the first sin and transmits original sin to every child born, who therefore needs the washing of regeneration. The second book answers, point by point, the objections excerpted from the writings of the Pelagian opponents, defending from Scripture and from earlier Catholic authors such as Ambrose and Cyprian that all born of Adam lie under the devil's power unless reborn in Christ.
la.augustine.de_peccato_originali: A short Late Antique Latin treatise by Augustine on original sin, the De peccato originali argues that Adam's transgression passes to all his descendants and that infants are therefore baptized for the remission of sin. It opens by warning its addressees to listen cautiously to Pelagius and Caelestius, who concede infant baptism while denying that any sin is transmitted from Adam. The work then reviews the ecclesiastical proceedings against the two men, quoting at length from the acts of the councils of Carthage and Diospolis, the letters of Popes Innocent I and Zosimus, and the writings and professions of Pelagius himself, whom Augustine accuses of evasive and self-contradictory answers. It closes by insisting that the question touches the core of the Christian faith rather than a matter of indifferent debate, and by adducing passages from Ambrose as orthodox testimony against the Pelagian position.
la.augustine.de_peccatorum_meritis_et_remis: De peccatorum meritis et remissione et de baptismo parvulorum is a Latin prose treatise on sin and grace by Augustine, a theologian of late antiquity, written in answer to questions put by his correspondent Marcellinus. It opens with a short exordium excusing the work's delay amid the author's cares before taking up the position of those who hold that Adam would have died even without sinning and that no fault of his passed to his descendants. The treatise argues that death and concupiscence entered the human race through Adam's disobedience, that infants are baptized for the remission of original sin rather than of any sins of their own, and that no one in this life is wholly without sin except Christ the one mediator, supporting each point with a dense chain of testimonia drawn from the Pauline epistles, the gospels, the Psalms, Job and other scriptures. A concluding section quotes and answers arguments which Pelagius had advanced in his expositions on Paul concerning the transmission of Adam's sin and the reach of Christ's justice.
la.augustine.de_perfectione_iustitiae_homin: A short late-antique treatise by Augustine, framed as a letter to his fellow bishops Eutropius and Paul, in which he answers a set of brief definitions circulating under the name of Caelestius concerning whether a human being can live without sin. The body of the work takes up each definition in turn, what sin is, whether it belongs to will or necessity, whether it is an act or a thing, whether it is commanded and willed by God, arguing throughout that nature, vitiated by the first man's fall, can be healed only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ. Augustine then reviews the scriptural testimonies advanced for human perfection, expounding the Lord's Prayer, the claim that the divine commandments are not grievous, the case of Job, and passages from the apostles, and maintaining that only the one mediator lived wholly without sin while the just, advancing daily, must still pray 'forgive us our debts.' The work closes by declaring that no one in this mortal life, apart from Christ, is free from the need for the remission of sins, and that whoever denies this contradicts both the gospel and the apostle John.
la.augustine.de_trinitate: The De Trinitate is a Latin theological treatise in prose by Augustine, a major doctrinal work of Late Antiquity on the nature of the triune God. It opens with a dedicatory letter to Aurelius in which Augustine recounts that he began the books in youth and published them in old age, having been compelled to finish and correct a work that had been taken from him before he could revise it to his satisfaction. The opening argument warns against three kinds of error in thinking about God, those who reason from bodily things, from the soul, and from false suppositions found in neither, and explains how scriptural language accommodates human weakness through bodily and spiritual figures. From this Augustine proceeds to the purification of the mind, nourished by faith, as the necessary path toward understanding the incomprehensible and unchangeable divine substance.
la.augustine.epistula_ad_catholicos_de_sect: A late-antique Latin epistolary treatise by Augustine, written as a bishop to the Catholics entrusted to his care, it opens with a greeting and with the announcement that the work now replies from the beginning to a letter of Petilian, Donatist bishop of Constantine. The central question is where the Church is to be found, whether with the Catholics or the Donatists, and the author argues that the one Church called catholic, diffused through the whole world as the body of Christ, cannot be confined to the African party of Donatus. Testimonies from Genesis, Isaiah, the Psalms, the Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the apostolic letters are marshalled to show that the Church was promised in Abraham's seed, began at Jerusalem, and spread through Judaea and Samaria to all nations, after which the letter answers Donatist claims of a worldwide apostasy and treats the mixture of wheat and chaff within the Church, the reception of heretics without rebaptism, the mutual charges of traditio and persecution, and the violence of the circumcellions. It closes by exhorting its readers to hold fast the shepherd's clear command, that his sheep hear his voice and follow him.
la.augustine.liber_qui_appellatur_speculum: The Liber qui appellatur Speculum ('Mirror') is a late antique Latin prose collection of moral precepts drawn from canonical scripture, attributed to Augustine. It opens by distinguishing scriptural passages meant to be known or believed from commandments and prohibitions still binding in the time of the New Testament, announcing the plan to gather the latter into a single book, as a mirror, so that the believer who already obeys God may inspect his progress in good conduct and see what he lacks. The compilation then proceeds book by book through the Old Testament, citing the precepts of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy at length and continuing with selections from Joshua, the Psalms, Proverbs and the other sapiential books, together with Tobit. The remaining material is taken from the New Testament, beginning with the Gospel of Matthew and continuing through the Pauline letters and the other apostolic epistles, and the work closes with precepts from the Apocalypse.
la.augustine.locutiones_in_heptateuchum: Locutiones in Heptateuchum, a prose work by the late antique writer Augustine, opens with a programmatic statement announcing its subject: the turns of phrase in scripture that appear, in its own words, to be governed by the properties of the Hebrew or Greek language, what Greek calls idioms. The entries that follow run in order through the seven books of the Heptateuch from Genesis to Judges, each quoting a verse in the Latin of the Septuagint and adding a short note on some unusual wording. The notes explain doubled words, singulars for plurals, shifts of gender, number and case, ellipses, hyperbaton, and part-for-whole expressions as Hebrew or Greek idiom rather than error, often setting the Greek reading against the Latin codices. Augustine also distinguishes genuine locutions from questions of sense and marks places where Latin interpreters altered or avoided an idiom.
la.augustine.psalmus_contra_partem_donati: Augustine's Psalmus contra Partem Donati is a Late Antique polemical work shaped as a psalm, addressed to the Donatists and urging their return to Catholic unity. It opens with the parable of the net cast into the sea, whose image of good and bad fish mixed together until the shore and whose refrain 'Omnes qui gaudetis de pace, modo uerum iudicate' recur throughout. The work then traces the origins of the schism in the charge against Caecilian of Carthage, the hearings before Roman and imperial judges, Donatus's appeal and his introduction of rebaptism, and the fustes and violence of the circumcellions; drawing on scriptural figures such as Judas at the supper, the threshing floor, and the see of Peter, it argues that the righteous must tolerate sinners within the one church until the final separation. A speech by Mother Church, reproaching her departing children and contrasting their refusal of imperial peace with her own endurance, closes with the announcement of the coming judge.
la.augustine.quaestiones_in_heptateuchum: Augustine's Quaestiones in Heptateuchum is a late-antique Latin work of biblical theology, written in prose, that collects and answers questions arising from the first seven books of the Old Testament. It opens with a prologue explaining that questions coming to mind during the author's reading of the canonical scriptures were to be set down briefly and 'as if in haste', some merely noted and some solved, so that they would not escape memory. The longest portion is devoted to Genesis, treating such problems as Cain's founding of a city, Methuselah's lifespan, the angels who consorted with the daughters of men, the capacity and construction of Noah's ark, and the chronologies of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Questions then follow on Exodus, the sacrificial and purity legislation of Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, the conquest under Joshua, and the judges down to Samson, with solutions ranging across literal, moral, and allegorical interpretation and often unfolding prophetic or figurative meanings in the narratives.
la.augustine.retractationum: Augustine's Retractationes is a late-antique Latin prose work of theology, written in the author's old age, in which he reviews and criticizes the whole body of his own writings. It opens with a preface announcing a long-considered resolve to go through his books, letters, and treatises with a certain judicial severity, marking with a censor's pen whatever now offends him, since self-reproach forestals the reproach of others. The two books proceed by numbered entries in the order of composition, covering ninety-three works in two hundred thirty-two books, from the early dialogues Contra Academicos, De beata vita, De ordine, and the Soliloquia, through anti-Manichaean, anti-Donatist, and anti-Pelagian polemics and commentaries on Genesis and the Pauline epistles, to major treatises such as De doctrina Christiana, the Confessiones, De trinitate, and De ciuitate dei. Each entry records the occasion and circumstances of a work, summarizes its contents and purpose, and notes passages the author would now correct, whether in wording, scriptural citation, or doctrine, the whole closing with a tally of what has been reviewed before the letters and sermons are taken up.
la.ausonius.cupido_cruciatus: A short late antique Latin poem by Ausonius, the Cupido Cruciatus opens in the plains of air, where the heroines who died for love gather in a shadowy myrtle grove and re-enact the circumstances of their deaths. Figures such as Semele, Procris, Sappho, Ariadne, Phaedra, and Dido pass in review, each bearing the tokens of her fate. Their rites are interrupted when Cupid blunders into their midst: the women seize him, bind him to a myrtle tree, and take turns scourging him with the instruments of their own deaths. Venus arrives to join the punishment, but when the heroines relent and intercede for the boy, he slips his captors and escapes through the ivory gate, the whole episode presenting itself as the phantasm of a troubled dream.
la.ausonius.de_bissula: A short lyric collection by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, framed by prose addresses to his friend Paulus. It opens with a prose letter in which Ausonius, yielding to Paulus's insistence, brings to light the playful verses he had composed privately about Bissula, a Suebian girl captured beyond the Rhine and raised in his household. The pieces that follow present the verses themselves: a preliminary poem urging the reader to set aside gravity and drink first, then a sequence of epigrams on Bissula's charm, her blend of German origins and Latin upbringing, the loveliness of her natural colouring set against painted cosmetics, and instructions to a painter who would depict her.
la.ausonius.de_herediolo: A short Latin lyric poem by the late antique poet Ausonius, De Herediolo opens with a prose note explaining that the author, now a consul, returned after many years to the small villa left him by his father and composed these verses in a Lucilian manner. The poem addresses the estate itself, greeting the property cultivated by his great-grandfather, grandfather, and father, and reflects on inheritance, the piety of succession, and the limits of desire through exempla including Croesus, Diogenes, Aristippus, and Midas. Its closing section inventories the land, two hundred iugera of field with a hundred-iugerum vineyard, meadows, and woodland, a spring, a well, and a navigable stream, and produce stored for two years, and concludes that the estate lies neither far from the city nor at it, so that its owner may alternate life in country and town.
la.ausonius.eclogarum_liber: The Eclogarum Liber is a book of short lyric pieces by the Late Antique poet Ausonius, opening with a dedicatory poem in which the poet hands his 'rude' little book to his dear friend Pacatus and bids his verses rest there without fear of any other judge. What follows is a miscellaneous assembly of gnomic and didactic poems: a survey of the miseries attending every age and condition of life, praise of the sage who weighs each day's deeds in the balance, a disputation over the monosyllables 'Est' and 'Non', reckonings of the lifespans of animals and of the great year of the cosmos, and verses on atoms and the libra that holds the world together. The collection then turns to time-reckoning, with the planets as givers of the weekdays, the Roman months and their names, the kalends, nones, and ides, the length of the year and its seasons, and the zodiac signs that govern the months and the hours of birth. Catalogue poems on the four great Greek games, Roman festivals, the twelve labours of Hercules, the sun's yearly course, and the bodily attributes of the gods, together with a set of monostichs, close the book.
la.ausonius.ephemeris_id_est_totius_diei_ne: A lyric poem in alternating Sapphic and iambic metres by the late-antique poet Ausonius, the Ephemeris lays out the business of a whole day in the life of a man of affairs. It opens at dawn with the speaker's exasperated efforts to rouse his sluggish servant Parmeno. The day then proceeds through washing, a long Christian prayer to the Father and the Son, dressing and the exchange of morning greetings, the ordering of luncheon with the steward Sosia, a comic address to a shorthand notary who records speech faster than the poet can dictate it, and further engagements that carry the hours toward dusk. It ends at night with the speaker's dreams of triumph and shame, a dismissal of nightmares to the moon's realm, and the dedication of a green elm grove to their harmless keeping.
la.ausonius.epicedion_in_patrem: The Epicedion in Patrem is a short late antique Latin funeral poem by Ausonius, prefaced by a prose note in which the poet commends the memorial for his father to the reader, asking for affection rather than praise. The verses are cast in the dead father's own voice as a self-composed obituary: he names himself Ausonius, recalls his medical practice at Vasates and Bordeaux, his membership of both the curia and the senate, his frugal and unblemished conduct, and his avoidance of factions, lawsuits and false friendship. He goes on to record a harmonious marriage of forty-five years that produced four children, the honours attained by a son who became prefect of Gaul, Libya and Latium and by a daughter of distinguished marriages, and finally his own prefecture of Illyricum. The poem closes with his account of ending a ninety-year life unimpaired by prayer to the divine, leaving hope, vows and fear behind among sorrowing friends, with a parting address to whoever reads his words.
la.ausonius.epigrammata_ausonii_de_diversis: The Epigrammata de Diversis Rebus is a collection of short epigrams by Ausonius, a poet of the late antique period. It opens with a joke addressed to the poet's own little book, which would rather be eaten by moths than cost him the sleep and lamp-oil its writing consumes. The poems that follow range widely: satirical pieces on rhetors and grammarians, riddling verses on names and letters, mythological vignettes on Narcissus, Hermaphroditus, Leda, and Myron's bronze heifer, and epigrams on doctors, haruspices, and other professions, alongside some openly obscene pieces. Other poems celebrate the contemporary emperors Valens and Gratian, and the collection closes with a running series of attacks on a Briton named Silvius Bonus.
la.ausonius.epistularum: A collection of letters by the late-antique poet Ausonius, addressed to friends, kinsmen, and fellow writers including Paulus, Symmachus, Theon, Proba, and Ursulus. It opens with prose letters in which Ausonius praises a correspondent's writings, weighs his eloquence against his character, and urges him to keep composing. The collection then proceeds through epistles in prose and in a wide range of metres, elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, iambics, Sapphics, and bilingual Greek-Latin verses, trading compliments, invitations to visit, jokes, and gifts of books, oysters, thrushes, and fish. A substantial sequence is devoted to Ausonius's attempts to draw the younger Paulus back from his withdrawal into Christian devotion and abandonment of poetry, together with Paulus's replies defending his new life.
la.ausonius.epitaphia_heroum_qui_bello_troi: A cycle of short metrical epitaphs composed by the late-antique poet Ausonius, giving imagined tomb-inscriptions for the figures of the Trojan War. A prose preface explains that the author, having come upon such epitaphs in old sources, rendered them into Latin and arranged them freely rather than by strict order. The poems then speak largely in the voices of the dead, Agamemnon and Menelaus, Ajax, Achilles, Ulysses, Diomedes, Nestor and Antilochus, Pyrrhus, Deiphobus, Hector, Astyanax, Sarpedon, Polydorus, Priam, Hecuba, Polyxena and Niobe each lament or narrate from beyond the grave. A closing series moves beyond the Trojan matter to epitaphs for Diogenes the Cynic, a damaged inscription whose name has broken away, a circus charioteer, and family tombs such as those of Carus and the young Anicia.
la.ausonius.griphus_ternarii_numeri: The Griphus ternarii numeri ('Riddle of the Number Three') is a short Latin lyric poem by the late-antique poet Ausonius, devoted wholly to the occurrences and powers of the number three. It opens with the drinking injunction 'Ter bibe', drink threefold, proclaimed a mystical law. The poem then proceeds as a dense catalogue of triads: mythological (Cerberus, Hecate, the Fates, the Graces, the Sibyls), historical such as the three Punic Wars, legal and philosophical (threefold law; god, world and matter), and arithmetical, geometrical and musical, alongside the threefold divisions of Rome itself, tribes, tribunes and the orders of the city. It closes by returning to its opening toast, asserting that three is the number above all others, 'tris numerus super omnia, tris deus unus', and playfully reckoning the poem's own length in nines and tens.
la.ausonius.ludus_septem_sapientum: The Ludus Septem Sapientum is a short dramatic poem in verse by the Late Antique poet Ausonius. It opens with a preface addressed to Pacatus (Drepanius), asking him to judge the carmina with severity or indulgence as he sees fit. The play proper shows the seven sages of Greece, Solon, Chilon, Cleobulus, Thales, Bias, Pittacus, and Periander, appearing palliati in the theatre, introduced by a Roman speaker who explains their Greek dress and the place of the theatre at Athens and Rome; each sage in turn delivers in Greek and expounds in Latin the maxim ascribed to him, from 'know thyself' and 'measure is best' to 'surety brings ruin' and 'practice is everything.' Solon's speech is the longest, narrating the story of Croesus, Tellus, and Aglaus before the captive king before yielding the stage to Chilon, and the sages depart one by one amid applause.
la.ausonius.mosella: The Mosella is a Latin poem in hexameters of Late Antique date, a celebration of the river Moselle by Ausonius, a native of Burdigala (Bordeaux) in the far southwest of Gaul who names himself at the close. It opens with the speaker crossing the mist-covered Nava and following lonely woodland tracks until, from the Belgic borderland at Noiomagus (Neumagen), the vine-clad slopes and riverside villas of the Moselle valley come into view, recalling his homeland. The poem then catalogues the river's translucent waters and their many kinds of fish, the terraced vineyards and the vintage with its playful mythological excursus, the boatmen and fishermen mirrored in the stream, and the villas and bathhouses lining the banks. It ends with a survey of the Moselle's tributaries, a claim that the river might rival the Tiber itself, a summons to the Rhine to share in celebrating recent triumphs, and the poet's self-identification together with his promises of further works.
la.ausonius.oratio_consulis_ausonii_versibu: A late antique Latin prayer by Ausonius, styled in the title as consul, composed in rhopalic verses whose lines lengthen by one syllable at each step. It opens with an appeal to God as the reconciler of eternal rest, begging Christ the Trinity for pardon and grace. The prayer then ranges over night, fasting, and the cleansing font of baptism, recalls the redemption wrought by Christ's suffering on the cross, and invokes the witnesses Stephen, Paul, and the penitent thief, before closing with the petition of the aged servant to be numbered among the glorified in heaven, repeating its own first line as the final verse.
la.ausonius.ordo_urbium_nobilium: The Ordo urbium nobilium is a short late-antique Latin poem by Ausonius, ranking the famous cities of the empire in lyric verse. It opens with Rome placed first and Constantinople and Carthage contending for precedence, before the survey moves on to Antioch and Alexandria. Subsequent passages celebrate Trier, Milan, Capua, Aquileia, Arles, Hispalis, Athens, Catania and Syracuse, Toulouse and Narbo, each praised for its origins, wealth, site or monuments. The poem ends at Burdigala, the poet's native city, extolled at length for its climate, walls and the spring Divona, with the closing antithesis that he is citizen of Burdigala and consul in both cities, his cradle in one and his curule chair in the other.
la.ausonius.parentalia: The Parentalia of the late-antique poet Ausonius is a cycle of short commemorative poems mourning members of the poet's own family. It opens with a prose preface explaining the title and the duty of annual remembrance owed to the dead, followed by a programmatic elegy in which the poet announces the names of his departed kinsmen. The collection then proceeds through a roll of epitaphs for father and mother, the uncle and teacher Arborius, grandparents, aunts, paternal uncles, siblings, brothers-in-law, nephews and nieces, and friends joined by marriage, each recording lineage, character, offices and manner of death. The sequence is punctuated by longer laments, above all for the poet's wife Sabina, mourned unwedded for nine Olympiads, and for an infant son and the grandson Pastor, before closing with commemorative pieces for further relatives and their kin.
la.ausonius.praefatiunculae: The Praefatiunculae ('Little Prefaces') is a short collection of introductory pieces that the late-antique poet Ausonius of Bordeaux attached to individual books of his works, written mostly in lyric verse with one prose item. It opens with an autobiographical preface in which the poet records his family origins in Aquitaine and his career from teaching grammar and rhetoric at Bordeaux to life at the imperial court and the consulship. There follow a preface addressed to his friend Syagrius and a prose letter in which the emperor Theodosius, addressing Ausonius affectionately, asks for the poet's writings. The collection closes with a verse preface declaring that the emperor commanded the poems to be composed and that refusal of such a command is unsafe.
la.ausonius.technopaegnion: The Technopaegnion is a late antique Latin poem of verbal play by Ausonius, addressed to the proconsul Pacatus, in which every verse begins and ends with a monosyllable, the closing monosyllable of each line serving as the opening word of the next. The work opens with two prefatory epistles to Pacatus explaining the game and its difficulty, followed by a chain of verses on Fors, Spes, and Mors and on the parts of the human body. Later sections catalogue gods, foods, flowers and plants, and peoples in the same monosyllabic frame, pose riddle-questions answered in single monosyllables, and treat the Latin and Greek letters as well as disputed words, etymologies, and points of grammar. The poem closes with a final address to Pacatus asking indulgence for the performance.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_consolatoria_laude_c: A Late Antique Latin Christian poem by Avitus of Vienne, a consolatory exhortation addressed to his sister Fuscina, a consecrated virgin. It opens with an apostrophe in which the poet, styling himself Alcimus, offers his brotherly gift and commends her vow of chastity. The greater part of the work argues for virginity over marriage, dwelling on the pains and perils of wedlock and childbirth and urging vigilance against backsliding, and supports its case with a long series of biblical and hagiographic exempla, including Deborah and Jael, Susanna and Daniel, Joseph, Esther and Judith, the Virgin Mary, the wise and foolish virgins, the parable of the talents, Martha and Mary, the barren fig tree, and the virgin Eugenia. It closes with praise of Fuscina's kindred, among them bishops distinguished for holy lives, and a call for her to lead her family by her example as their patron and intercessor.
la.avitus_of_vienne.de_spiritalis_historiae: De Spiritalis Historiae Gestis is a late antique biblical epic in five books of dactylic hexameter by Avitus of Vienne, retelling the events of sacred history from creation to the Exodus. It opens with an address to the first man Adam and an account of God's creation of the world, the fashioning of Adam's body from clay, and the formation of Eve. The poem then follows the serpent's temptation and the Fall, the penalties pronounced on serpent, woman and man, and the miseries of post-lapsarian life, before turning to Noah and the Flood, the Tower of Babel, and the plagues of Egypt. The final books narrate the departure of the Israelites under the pillar of fire and cloud, their passage through the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh's host, closing with the song of triumph and a meditation on baptism as the fulfillment of the sea crossing.
la.bede.historiam_ecclesiasticam_gentis_ang: Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum opens with a dedicatory letter to King Ceolwulf, in which the author names his informants and asks the king to read and approve the work before it is copied further. The five books that follow, in Latin prose, trace the church among the English from the Roman invasions of Britain and the earliest Christianity on the island, through the Anglo-Saxon settlement and Augustine of Canterbury's mission despatched by Pope Gregory, to the conversion of the several kingdoms and the settlement of the Easter and tonsure disputes at the Synod of Whitby. Woven through the political and ecclesiastical narrative are the deeds of kings, bishops, and abbots, the lives of saints such as Aidan, Oswald, and Cuthbert, and numerous miracle stories and visions of the afterlife. The history runs down to Bede's own day, closing with a survey of the state of Britain about 731, a chronological recapitulation of the whole work, and the author's autobiographical account of his writings.
la.bernowinus.carmina: A collection of Latin verses by the Carolingian poet Bernowinus, composed in the reign of Charlemagne, whose rule the poems invoke. The work opens with a poem passing through the annunciation, nativity, passion, resurrection and ascension of Christ, each scene closing in a prayer for mercy. The remaining pieces are devotional and epigraphic: verses on the house of prayer that Bernowinus founded and presented to the priest Illidius, long acrostic prayer sequences addressed to Christ, a lament in the voice of a once-wealthy dead man warning against riches, an acrostic intercession for Angilbert, praise of a priest who built and consecrated a church, and epitaphs for Hebrarius, for a youth, and for Dida, wife of Ardoinus. Throughout, visitors to the house are urged to pray for the souls of the founder and of the departed.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto, a Latin verse legend of St Benedict by the Carolingian author Bertharius of Monte Cassino, opens with an apostrophe to the saint as father, way and pastor, praising the divine protection that attended him from childhood. The poem then proceeds through a series of episodes from the saint's career: a broken vessel restored, a poisoned meal turned aside, the rescue of the drowning Placidus, a Goth's iron drawn back from the waters, and boys entrusted to the saint's threshold. Further miracles follow, including the cleansing of a possessed monk, empty granaries filled through a vision, the words of slanderous sisters returned to their tombs, a crushed boy whose body the sepulchre cannot hold, and a serpent that vomits itself out before a brother fleeing to Benedict's shelter. The legend closes with the healing of a crippled Welsh youth styled a second David and with a prayer to Benedict and Christ for the safekeeping of the faithful, in which the poet names himself as the humble composer Bertharius.
la.boethius.commentaria_in_porphyrium_a_se_: Latin prose commentary by the late-antique philosopher Boethius on Porphyry's Isagoge, the introductory treatise to Aristotle's Categories. Cast as a dialogue between Boethius and Fabius, begun during a winter retreat in the Aurelian mountains, it works through the six standard preliminary questions about a philosophical work, aim, utility, order, authenticity, title, and the part of philosophy to which it belongs, and identifies Porphyry's subject as genus, species, difference, property, and accident. The dialogue also refers to the Latin version said to have been made by the orator Victorinus, and divides philosophy into theoretical and practical parts, distinguishing within the theoretical the intellectible, the intelligible, and the natural.
la.boethius.liber_de_persona_et_duabus_natu: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Boethius, cast as a letter to the deacon John. It opens with the author's account of a council debate over the Eutychian formula that Christ consists of two natures but not in two, which moves him to set out his position in writing. The work first distinguishes several senses of natura and defines persona as the individual substance of a rational nature, sorting out the Greek terms ousia, hypostasis, and prosopon; it then argues against Nestorius that Christ cannot be two persons, and against Eutyches that his two natures were neither converted into one another nor confused. It closes by affirming the catholic teaching that Christ consists both in and from two natures within one person, and by weighing in what state of human nature his assumed flesh stood.
la.boethius.utrum_pater: Utrum Pater is a short late-antique Latin prose treatise by Boethius, addressed to John the Deacon, which asks whether the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are predicated of the divinity substantially or in some other way. Opening with a resolve to take the path of inquiry from the foundations of the catholic faith, it argues that whatever is said alike of each person singly and of all three together, deity, truth, goodness, justice, omnipotence, and the like, belongs to the one simple and indivisible substance and so is predicated substantially. Against these it sets the personal names, including even trinitas itself, which hold only relatively (ad aliquid), arising from the plurality of persons rather than from the unity of substance. The treatise ends by asking John either to accept the argument or, should he differ, to examine the points more closely and, where he can, join faith with reason.
la.caesar.de_bello_gallico: The De Bello Gallico is a Latin prose account of Julius Caesar's campaigns in Gaul, written in the Roman Republican era and composed as year-by-year commentaries on his commands. It opens with a tripartite ethnographic survey of Gaul and the Helvetian migration, then traces the campaigns against the Helvetii and Ariovistus, the subjugation of the Belgae, operations against coastal and Aquitanian peoples, two crossings of the Rhine, two expeditions to Britain, and the great revolt of Vercingetorix culminating in the siege of Alesia and the final pacification of Gaul. Ethnographic and geographic digressions on Gallic institutions, druids, and Germanic customs are interspersed with the military narrative. A concluding book, introduced by an address to Balbus explaining its composition, continues the record through the suppression of the last revolts and the growing political tensions in Italy and Rome on the eve of the civil war.
la.calpurnius_siculus.eclogae: A collection of seven pastoral poems in Latin hexameters of early Imperial date, attributed to Calpurnius Siculus. The first eclogue opens with two herdsmen who find verses carved on a beech tree, in which the god Faunus prophesies the return of a golden age of peace under a young Caesar. The remaining poems likewise unfold as dialogues and formal singing contests among shepherds, taking in a jealous lover's complaint against the fickle Phyllis, an old goatherd's detailed instruction of his pupil in the seasonal care of goats, and prayers for the welfare of the reigning emperor. The last eclogue describes a countryman's visit to Rome and the spectacle games, beasts and wonders he witnesses in the amphitheatre there.
la.candidus_of_fulda.epitaphia_aegili: Two short Latin epitaphs for Eigil, abbot of Fulda, transmitted under the name of Candidus of Fulda and belonging to the Carolingian period. The first opens with an address to a reader entering the small cave of the tomb and bidden to read the inscription, then recounts in the third person Eigil's happy rule of the monastery, his translation of a martyr's sacred bones together with the bishop, his dedication of two churches, and his death, naming Hrabanus, his successor as abbot, as the composer of the titulus. The second epitaph speaks in Eigil's own voice, recording that his limbs lie in the modest tomb he built himself while living and expressing his confidence that the Lord, whose coming will loose the bonds of death, will raise him up.
la.candidus_of_fulda.vita_aegili: The Vita Aegili, a Latin verse life of Carolingian date ascribed to the Fulda monk Candidus, opens with the poet entreating his brother Modestus to receive his account of the celebrated deeds of the old man Aegil. The poem follows Aegil from his boyhood journey from the Norican region to Fulda, where Sturmi receives him, through his schooling, ordination by Bishop Lullus, and service under the abbots Sturmi and Baugolf. It then recounts the discord among the Fulda brethren after Baugolf's departure, the intervention of Louis, Aegil's election as abbot, his consultation with Archbishop Haistolf of Mainz, the consecration of the church with its crypts, and the solemn translation of the relics of the martyr Boniface, including the liturgical hymns sung at the ceremony. After narrating Aegil's final illness and burial, with an epitaph by Hrabanus, the work closes with reflections on mortality and on the virtues of the dead abbot.
la.cato_the_elder.de_agricultura: De Agricultura is a Latin prose manual of estate management from the Roman Republican era, by Cato the Elder. It opens with a preface praising agriculture over trade and moneylending as the source of the strongest citizens. The work then proceeds as a miscellany of practical instruction: buying and siting a farm, equipment inventories for an olive grove and a vineyard, the duties of the bailiff and his wife, seasonal operations of ploughing, planting, grafting, manuring, and harvesting, the care and doctoring of livestock, recipes for breads, cakes, wines, and salted pork, and the prayers, sacrifices, and purifications proper to field and household. It closes with contracts for hiring harvesters and selling oil, wine, and pasture, followed by an extended account of the cabbage as food and medicine and a charm for setting dislocated limbs.
la.catullus.carmina: Catullus's Carmina, a collection of lyric and epigrammatic verse in mixed metres from the late Roman Republic, opens with the dedication of a 'new little book' of polished nugae to the historian Cornelius Nepos. The short poems that follow range over hendecasyllabic and choliambic pieces on the poet's passion for Lesbia, on companions such as Veranius, Fabullus, and Calvus, and on targets of invective like Mamurra, Egnatius, and various social rivals. A group of longer compositions then presents the epithalamia for the wedding of Manlius and Vibia, the Galliambic lament of Attis, the mythological epyllion on the marriage of Peleus and Thetis with its extended tableau of Ariadne on Naxos, a star-myth poem on the lock of Berenice, and an elegy to Allius entwined with mourning for the poet's brother. The collection closes with a run of epigrams that continue the satirical attacks and the alternating despair and devotion of the Lesbia cycle, ending in the epitaphic farewell to the dead brother.
la.celsus.de_medicina: Celsus' De Medicina, an early Imperial Latin technical treatise in prose spread over eight books, opens with a prologue that traces the history of medicine from Aesculapius and Hippocrates down to the author's own day and weighs the claims of the rationalist, empiricist and Methodist schools before sketching the work's plan. Books 1 and 2 treat regimen, first the maintenance of health in sound bodies and the care of particular constitutions, then general therapeutic measures such as bleeding, cupping, purging, friction, diet and sweating. Books 3 and 4 set out the signs, prognostic indications and treatment of individual diseases, from fevers and affections of the whole body to ailments of particular organs and regions, while book 5 turns to pharmacology, cataloguing the properties of simple drugs and giving numerous compound recipes before passing to wounds, ulcers and other external affections. The remaining books are devoted to surgery, covering wounds, ulcers, tumours and morbid growths, operative procedures on the head, mouth, abdomen and other parts, and finally the treatment of fractures and dislocations.
la.cicero.de_divinatione: Cicero's De Divinatione, a philosophical dialogue in two books written during the Roman Republic, examines whether the future can be known and foretold. It opens with the old opinion, confirmed by the consensus of the Roman people and of all nations, that divination exists among humankind, the power the Greeks call mantike. In the first book Quintus, the author's brother, defends divination in both its artificial forms, augury, extispicy, portents, lots, and astrology, and its natural forms of dreams and inspired prophecy, while in the second Marcus refutes him, taking each practice in turn and closing with a distinction between religion and superstition.
la.cicero.de_domo_sua: The De Domo Sua is an oration by Cicero of the late Roman Republic, addressed to the college of pontiffs in support of his claim to the Palatine house that Publius Clodius had demolished and consecrated as a shrine of Libertas while Cicero was in exile. It opens with an appeal to the pontiffs to place the welfare of the state alongside the claims of religion. The body of the speech combines sustained invective against Clodius with legal argument: Cicero defends his recall and his conduct as consul, denies the validity of Clodius's tribunate, adoption, legislation, and of the consecration itself, and discusses the broader questions of extraordinary commands and of the inviolability of a citizen's house. It closes with a prayer to Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Vesta, and the household gods for his restoration to his home.
la.cicero.de_haruspicum_responso: A prose oration in Latin by Cicero of the Roman Republic, opening with the speaker's account of his clash on the previous day with Publius Clodius in the senate and his resolve to answer Clodius' exploitation of a fresh response from the haruspices. The body of the speech takes the Etruscan diviners' pronouncements item by item: Cicero argues that his Palatine house was lawfully freed of religious scruple by the verdicts of the pontiffs, the senate and the Roman people after Clodius had consecrated it, and he denounces the riot that polluted the Megalesian games of the Great Mother as an omen of servile violence. He catalogues Clodius' sacrileges, from the profanation of the rites of the Bona Dea and the destruction of shrines to the sale of the sanctuary at Pessinus to Brogitarus, and reviews the scandalous career by which a patrician reached the tribunate. The closing section dwells on the haruspices' warnings of discord among the optimates, of murder threatening the leading citizens and of the state falling under one man's power, ending with an exhortation to concord and to expiation of the portents.
la.cicero.de_imperio_cn_pompei: An oration by Cicero, delivered before the Roman people during the Republic in support of the tribune Manilius' proposal to confer supreme command of the war against Mithridates and Tigranes on Gnaeus Pompeius (the speech is also known as the Pro Lege Manilia). It opens with the speaker's explanation of why, though the Rostra had always beckoned, he had hitherto abstained from popular addresses, having devoted his early career to the defense of private clients. The speech then assesses the necessity and magnitude of the war, the devastation of Asia and Bithynia, the peril to allies, revenues, and the fortunes of Roman citizens, and the collapse of credit at Rome, and goes on to argue Pompey's fitness under four heads, military knowledge, courage, authority, and good fortune, refuting the objections of Q. Catulus and Q. Hortensius, defending Gabinius' role in the command, and closing with an appeal to Manilius himself to stand firm against threats and intimidation.
la.cicero.de_natura_deorum: De Natura Deorum is a three-book philosophical dialogue by Cicero, composed during the Roman Republic. It opens with a preface addressed to Brutus on the obscurity of the question of the nature of the gods and on the Academic practice of suspending judgement. The conversation, set at the house of C. Cotta during the Latin holidays, presents the theology of three schools: the Epicurean Velleius first expounds gods that are blessed, idle, and human in form, whom Cotta rebuts; the Stoic Balbus then argues in the second book that the world and its celestial order are divine, governed by providence and arranged for the benefit of gods and humans. In the third book Cotta subjects Balbus's Stoic case to a sustained critique, and the dialogue ends with the disagreement unresolved.
la.cicero.de_oratore: De Oratore is a three-book rhetorical dialogue in Latin prose by Cicero, composed during the late Roman Republic. It opens with a dedication to Cicero's brother Quintus on the troubled state of public life before turning to a remembered conversation. The dialogue is set at the Tusculan villa of Lucius Crassus shortly before his death, where Crassus and Marcus Antonius, with Q. Mucius Scaevola, Catulus, and Caesar as participants, debate the education and character of the ideal orator. Across the three books the speakers discuss whether eloquence can be reduced to an art, the need for wide learning in law, philosophy, and history, and then treat invention, arrangement, memory, style, humour, and delivery, the frame closing with an account of Crassus's death soon after the conversation.
la.cicero.de_republica: Cicero's De Republica, a philosophical dialogue in six books on the best constitution and the statesman's role in public life, survives in a fragmentary state, with substantial portions preserved through quotation in later authors. The surviving opening argues for the active political life against the philosophers' case for retreat, citing Roman exemplars such as Cato, Marcellus, and Scipio Africanus. From there the dialogue ranges over the classification of simple and mixed constitutions, a long account of Rome's constitutional history from Romulus through the kings, consuls, decemvirs, and tribunes of the plebs, and the qualities required of the ruler who governs the state. It closes with the Dream of Scipio, in which Africanus appears to Scipio in a vision, expounding the harmony of the spheres, the smallness of the inhabited earth, the vanity of earthly glory, and the celestial reward reserved for those who have laboured for their country's welfare.
la.cicero.de_senectute: A Latin prose philosophical dialogue of the Roman Republic by Cicero, De Senectute opens with a metrical address to Atticus and a preface explaining that the argument on old age is placed in the mouth of the elder Cato, with Laelius and Scipio Aemilianus as his admiring young interlocutors. In the main dialogue Cato answers the four standard complaints against old age, that it withdraws men from active affairs, weakens the body, cuts off pleasures, and brings death near, countering each with exempla from Roman history and his own career, including Fabius Maximus, Appius Claudius, and the old farmers Cincinnatus and Curius. The speech goes on to praise the studies and rural delights befitting age, dwells on the authority that an honorably lived old age confers, and closes with Platonic and Pythagorean arguments for the immortality of the soul and a serene acceptance of death as nature's maturity.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_q_caecilium: Opening with an address to the judges explaining why a man who has spent his career defending clients now steps forward as an accuser, the Divinatio in Q. Caecilium is Cicero's speech, of the Roman Republic, in the preliminary contest over who should prosecute Gaius Verres for extortion committed in Sicily. Cicero maintains that the Sicilian communities, plundered during Verres' three-year praetorship, have themselves chosen him as their advocate, whereas his rival Quintus Caecilius, who served as quaestor under Verres and was implicated in his dealings, is disqualified by partiality, by the obligations owed to a former superior, and by lack of forensic ability. The argument ranges over Verres' depredations and particular cases of injustice in the province, derides the maneuvering of Verres' defenders, and closes by urging the judges to appoint the accuser best able to sustain so great a cause.
la.cicero.in_catilinam: Cicero's In Catilinam gathers the four consular speeches of the Roman Republic directed against the conspiracy of L. Sergius Catilina. The first, delivered in the senate, opens with the challenge 'quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?' and confronts Catiline with the evidence of his plots until the consul bids him leave the city; the second, spoken to the Roman people, announces his departure and reviews the classes of indebted and desperate men who remain in Rome. The third reports to the people the interception of the Allobrogian envoys and the letters that incriminated Lentulus, Cethegus and their fellow conspirators, while the fourth, before the senate, sets Caesar's proposal of perpetual imprisonment against the call for execution and closes with an exhortation to judge decisively for the safety of the state.
la.cicero.in_vatinium: An oration of the Roman Republic by Cicero, In Vatinium is the portion of his defence speech for Publius Sestius in which he cross-examines a witness for the prosecution, Publius Vatinius. It opens with Cicero declaring that contempt alone would have moved him to send so sordid a witness away unheard, and that he interrogates him instead to crush his ferocity and entangle his loquacity in a few questions. A relentless chain of interrogations then pursues Vatinius through his disreputable youth, his quaestorship at Puteoli, his irregular journeys as legate in Spain and Africa, and a tribunate in which he trampled the auspices, the Aelian and Fufian laws, and the consul Bibulus, with further questioning on the Vettius conspiracy, his professed Pythagoreanism, and his servility toward Caesar. The examination closes with his private disgraces, including a banquet attended in mourning dress, prosecution and obstruction of his trial, and a self-granted legation, before pressing the contradictions between his earlier statements and the testimony he has just given against Sestius and Titus Annius.
la.cicero.letters_to_atticus: The Letters to Atticus form the correspondence of the late-Republican orator and statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero with his close friend and confidant Titus Pomponius Atticus, arranged in sixteen books. The collection opens with letters from Cicero's canvass for the consulship, reporting on his candidacy and the prospects of his rivals. Across the correspondence Cicero mixes running commentary on public affairs, from elections, trials and the rivalry of Pompey and Caesar through the civil war and the crisis following Caesar's assassination, with intimate news of family, finances, property purchases, legal business, and his literary and philosophical projects. Written throughout in a conversational prose studded with Greek phrases, the letters trace Roman politics and private concerns together across the closing decades of the Republic.
la.cicero.pro_a_caecina: A forensic oration of the Roman Republic by Cicero, spoken in defense of Aulus Caecina before recuperatores in a suit arising from the interdict de vi armata. It opens by contrasting Aebutius' armed audacity in the fields with his impudence in court, claiming that his opponent's own confession will carry the case. The narrative section recounts the tangled history of the Fulcinian estate: the widow Caesennia's purchase of it through the scheming Aebutius, her marriage to Caecina, the armed ambush at the ravine of the olive trees by which Aebutius barred Caecina from entering the land, and the examination of the witnesses on both sides. The bulk of the speech is then devoted to a long legal argument against the opposing advocate Piso, weighing whether Caecina was 'expelled' within the meaning of the interdict, whether intimidation without bloodshed counts as violence, the relation of verbal formulae to equity and to the authority of the jurists, and Caecina's citizenship despite Sulla's settlement of Volaterrae, before closing with an appeal to the panel's sense of justice and to Caecina's standing in Etruria.
la.cicero.pro_a_cluentio: The Pro Cluentio is a forensic oration of the Roman Republic in which Cicero defends Aulus Cluentius Habitus of Larinum against a charge of poisoning. It opens with an exordium announcing that the defense will treat the case in two parts, the inveterate prejudice left by the so-called Junian trial and the formal charge before the standing poisoning court.
