The body of the speech refutes the allegation that Cluentius bought the conviction of Statius Albius, exposes the crimes of the dead Oppianicus and the agitation of the tribune Quinctius, answers the censors' notations of the jurors, and then dismantles the poisoning accusation itself, attributing it to the schemes of Cluentius' mother Sassia and the prosecutor Titus Attius. A peroration invokes the support of Larinum and the neighboring municipalities and entreats the judges to save the defendant from his mother.
la.cicero.pro_archia: A judicial oration by Cicero, dating from the era of the Roman Republic, spoken in defense of the Greek poet A. Licinius Archias, whose claim to Roman citizenship was being contested in court. The speech opens with Cicero acknowledging Archias as the first guide of his rhetorical studies and asking the judges' leave to speak in a manner removed from ordinary forensic usage. After arguing the case itself from Archias's career from Antioch through Greece and Italy, his enrollment at Heraclea, and the testimony of Lucullus and the allied city's envoys, the oration turns into a sustained encomium of literary studies as refreshment, discipline, and moral formation, illustrated by the poets' celebration of great Romans and by Archias's own verses on the Mithridatic War and Cicero's consulship. It closes with Cicero's confession of his love of glory and an appeal to preserve a poet who has promised lasting witness to the deeds of the Roman people.
la.cicero.pro_balbo: The speech opens with Cicero acknowledging that men of the highest authority, eloquence and friendship, above all Pompey on the previous day, have already defended the cause, and with him falls the task of finishing it. His client is Lucius Cornelius Balbus of Gades, prosecuted over the Roman citizenship Pompey had conferred on him by the verdict of his council under the lex Gellia Cornelia. Cicero argues that Pompey acted lawfully, denies that the treaty with Gades barred the grant, disputes the prosecution's doctrine of 'municipal' peoples and the supposed 'sacrosanctity' of the Gaditanian treaty, and marshals precedents from Marius, Pompey's father, Crassus, Sulla and Metellus alongside Rome's long-standing practice of admitting new citizens from Romulus and the Sabine treaty onward. The latter part rebuts oblique charges over Balbus's wealth, luxury, tribal enrolment, adoption by Theophanes and closeness to Caesar, closing on the claim that the judges are really passing on Pompey's benefaction rather than on any crime of Balbus.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_perduellionis_reo: A forensic speech by Cicero defending Gaius Rabirius, an elderly senator prosecuted for perduellio (treason) by the tribune Titus Labienus and tried by the archaic duumviral procedure with appeal to the Roman people. The opening sets out Cicero's reasons for undertaking the defence, presenting his client's acquittal as bound up with the survival of senatorial authority, consular imperium, and the concord of the optimates. The body of the oration answers the various charges Labienus has raised and then turns at length to the death of the tribune Saturninus, defending the senatus consultum by which the consuls Marius and Valerius called citizens to arms and arguing that Rabirius acted honourably among the defenders of the state. Throughout, Cicero denounces the threatened penalty of scourging and crucifixion as alien to the liberty of Roman citizens, and the speech closes with an appeal that the defendant be allowed to die a natural death at home rather than at the executioner's hands.
la.cicero.pro_fonteio: A defence oration by Cicero of the Roman Republic, spoken on behalf of Marcus Fonteius, a former governor of Transalpine Gaul prosecuted for extortion on the testimony of Gallic communities. The surviving portion opens mid-argument, with Cicero defending the propriety of Fonteius's handling of public money during his quaestorship. Across the speech Cicero dismantles the accusations, illegal exactions of money, grain and cavalry, a levy on wine, and profiteering from road-building, by setting the word of hostile Gallic envoys against that of Roman colonists, Massiliote allies, merchants and publicani, and by urging the judges to weigh rather than merely accept testimony. He dwells on the Gauls' earlier wars against Rome and their barbarous rites, invokes the support of Fonteius's family, including a Vestal virgin sister, and closes by calling for the acquittal of a citizen portrayed as loyal to the Roman people.
la.cicero.pro_ligario: Pro Ligario is a forensic oration by Cicero of the Republican era, spoken before Julius Caesar in defense of Quintus Ligarius, whom his kinsman Quintus Tubero accused of having been in Africa and taken up arms against Caesar. The speech opens with Cicero conceding the charge outright and declaring that his case will rest not on denial but on an appeal to Caesar's mercy. Cicero then argues that Ligarius went to Africa only as a legate in peacetime, kept clear of Varus's usurped command, and that Tubero himself had drawn his sword at Pharsalus, so that the accusation invites scrutiny of the accuser's own conduct in the civil war. The oration closes with an extended plea for clemency, invoking the grief of Ligarius's brothers and the Roman knights who plead for him, and asking Caesar to pardon the absent man as he has pardoned those present.
la.cicero.pro_milone: Cicero's Pro Milone is a prose forensic oration of the Roman Republic, a defence of Titus Annius Milo on a charge of murdering Publius Clodius on the Appian Way. It opens with the advocate confessing that the novel sight of a court ringed with soldiers unnerves him as he rises to speak for so valiant a defendant. The body of the speech argues that killing in self-defence is permitted by nature and sanctioned by Roman precedent, defends the senatorial decree and Pompey's special statute from the charge that they condemned the deed, and reconstructs the meeting on the Appian Way to show that Clodius, not Milo, had laid an ambush. An extended invective against Clodius's life and designs gives way to a peroration in which Milo's imagined stoic speeches and Cicero's own tears plead for acquittal.
la.cicero.pro_plancio: A forensic oration of the Roman Republic by Cicero, the Pro Plancio is a defense speech on behalf of Gnaeus Plancius, recently elected aedile and prosecuted for electoral corruption (ambitus) by Marcus Laterensis. It opens with Cicero telling the judges that Plancius' fidelity in guarding his life has earned the goodwill that now aids the defense. The speech then argues that the people's verdict in the aedileship election ought not to be overturned in court, attacks the prosecution's edicting of tribes under the lex Licinia de sodaliciis as unfairly chosen, rebuts the witnesses and charges of bribery, and dwells on Cicero's own quaestorship and political conduct. It culminates in a personal plea of gratitude to Plancius, who sheltered and protected Cicero during his flight and exile through Brundisium, Dyrrachium, Macedonia, and Thessalonica, closing with emotional appeals to the judges' mercy.
la.cicero.pro_publio_quinctio: A forensic speech by Cicero, a Roman orator of the Republican era, delivered in a civil action on behalf of Publius Quinctius against Sextus Naevius before the judge Gaius Aquilius. It opens with Cicero lamenting that the influence of Naevius and the eloquence of Hortensius, who speaks for the opposing side, are both arrayed against him and his client. The body of the speech reconstructs the partnership between Quinctius' brother and Naevius in Gaul, the brother's death and the inheritance by Quinctius, the disputed debt, the alleged abandonment of the vadimonium, Naevius' seizure of Quinctius' goods under the praetor's edict, and the forcible expulsion of Quinctius from the common estate, before arguing in sequence that nothing was owed, that Naevius had no grounds for his petition, that the goods were never lawfully possessed ex edicto, and that Quinctius had been duly defended through his procurator Alfenus. It closes with an appeal to the judge's equity and mercy, presenting the case as one in which Quinctius' reputation and entire fortune hang on a single verdict against a wealthy and unscrupulous adversary.
la.claudian.carmina_minora: The Carmina Minora gathers the shorter poems of Claudian, a late antique Latin poet writing in hexameters, most of them occasional pieces in a panegyric mode. The collection opens by telling Stilicho to crown his gleaming hair and bid war yield to festive torchlight, hailing him as once the emperor's son-in-law and now his father-in-law. The remaining poems move through praise of the imperial circle, epigrams on marvels such as the phoenix, a magnetic stone, and crystal, invectives against literary rivals, mythological narrative pieces, and marriage songs. The sequence closes with Christian poems on the birth of Christ, his miracles, and redemption.
la.claudian.de_bello_gothico: De Bello Gothico ('On the Gothic War') is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian in praise of the general Stilicho. The opening proem, in which the poet, roused after a long silence, invokes the Muse and compares Stilicho's deliverance of Italy to Tiphys steering the Argo past the Clashing Rocks, introduces the Gothic invasion of Italy under Alaric. The narrative then records the omens that terrify Rome, among them the prodigy of two slain wolves foretelling the death of a Gothic leader, an elder Goth's plea for retreat that Alaric proudly rejects, and Stilicho's winter crossing of the Alps to Rhaetia, where troops gather from Britain, Germany and the Rhine frontier. Rallying his forces, he brings the invaders to battle, and the poem ends with the Roman victory at Pollentia, the recovery of captives and spoils, and the comparison drawn between Stilicho and Marius, who defeated the Cimbri on the same plain.
la.claudian.de_consulatu_stilichonis: The De Consulatu Stilichonis is a Latin panegyric in hexameter verse, in three books, by the late antique poet Claudian, celebrating the consulship of Stilicho, the general of the Western Roman empire. It opens in heaven, where the gods prolong their rejoicing over the imperial wedding and the triumph over the defeated Gildo, while the poet weighs how any single song could encompass the mass of Stilicho's deeds. The poem then traces his career from boyhood, his justice, courage, and achievements in peace as in war, with personified provinces, Gaul, Britannia, and Africa among them, testifying to his defense against Franks, Picts, Scots, and Saxons and to the recovery of Africa. The closing section turns to triumphal spectacle, culminating in a fantastic maritime procession in which elephants, sea monsters, and a Bacchic fleet of Silenus and the Satyrs attend the victor.
la.claudian.de_raptu_proserpinae: De Raptu Proserpinae is a Latin epic in three hexameter books by the late antique poet Claudian, on the abduction of Proserpina. After a brief prelude on the first mariner to dare the deep, the poet invokes Phoebus and the gods below for a song of the ravisher's horses, and the first book shows Pluto, chafing at his unwedded state, restrained by the Fates from renewed war yet promised Jupiter's daughter as bride, while Ceres conceals the girl in Sicily and departs for Cybele's rites on Ida, amid extended description of the island and Etna. The second book brings Venus, Minerva and Diana to lure Proserpina from her half-woven tapestry of the universe into a flowering meadow, where Pluto bursts from a fissure in the earth and carries her off despite the virgin goddesses' protests, consoled by a vision of her future throne as queen of the dead, and the underworld keeps festive wedding rites. The third book follows Ceres, warned by omens and a dream, as she lights her torches on Etna and wanders land and sea for her lost daughter, Jupiter having forbidden any god to reveal the abductor; the poem breaks off during this search as she turns towards Scylla's cave.
la.claudian.epithalamium_de_nuptiis_honorii: A Latin hexameter epithalamium by the Late Antique poet Claudian, celebrating the marriage of the emperor Honorius to Maria, daughter of Stilicho. The poem opens with the mythological wedding of Peleus and Thetis, where Apollo's song foretells Achilles, before turning to Honorius pining in secret love for his bride. The greater part of the work follows Venus and Amor: Amor carries news of the union to Cyprus, Venus sails to Italy attended by sea deities bearing bridal gifts, prepares the wedding chamber, and adorns Maria, whose beauty she praises at length. It closes with the nuptial procession and a wedding song that extols Stilicho's virtues and blessings on his children and hoped-for descendants.
la.claudian.in_consulatum_olybrii_et_probin: A late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, celebrating the joint consulship of the young brothers Olybrius and Probinus, sons of the noble Probus. The poem opens with an invocation to the Sun and an encomium of the Anician house, whose members are said to be born to the consulship. It then recounts an allegorical episode in which Rome, personified as a warrior goddess, journeys to the war god fresh from victory over Alpine foes to plead for the brothers; his assent is followed by the Tiber's vision of the consuls entering the forum attended by the senate, a festive banquet among the river gods, and a closing prayer that the seasons and the fasti favour their year of office.
la.claudian.in_eutropium: Claudian's In Eutropium is a late-antique Latin invective in hexameter verse, in two books, directed against the eunuch Eutropius, who rose from slavery to the consulship at the eastern imperial court. The poem opens with a catalogue of cosmic portents that yield in horror to the greater prodigy of a eunuch consul, before recounting Eutropius' castration, his careers as slave, pimp, and courtier, and his traffic in offices and commands. The first book dwells on his dishonorable rise and military pretensions, and brings the personified Roma to plead with Stilicho to defend Italy's dignity; the second follows the Gothic revolt of Tribigild through the cities of Phrygia, the rout of the court's forces, and Eutropius' fall from favor into condemnation and exile.
la.claudian.in_rufinum: Claudian's In Rufinum is a late antique Latin panegyric in two books of hexameters that combines invective against the eastern minister Rufinus with praise of the general Stilicho. The poem opens with Apollo's slaughter of Python and a meditation on whether the world is governed by providence or chance, a doubt the poet says Rufinus's punishment finally dispels. The narrative then follows the Fury Megaera's rearing of Rufinus, his rise to power at the court of Arcadius, his avarice, cruelty, and collusion with barbarian peoples, and the resistance of Stilicho, whose eastern campaign against him is halted by an imperial command. The second book carries the story through Rufinus's killing by the soldiers at an imperial muster, his dismemberment by the populace of Constantinople, and his trial before Minos, who consigns his shade to the deepest pit of Tartarus.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_quarto_consulatu: A Latin hexameter panegyric by Claudian, opening with the celebrations of Honorius' fourth consulship: the returning fasces, the soldiery reassuming civilian dress, and Bellona herself bearing the consular trabea. The poem then traces the dynasty's rise, recounting the conquests of Theodosius the Great from Britain to Ethiopia and his suppression of two western tyrants, before a long paternal address in which the dying emperor instructs his son in self-mastery, piety, justice and the conduct of war, with exempla drawn from early Roman history. There follow Stilicho's pacification of the Rhine peoples, his repulse of the barbarians who had overrun Greece, and praise of his justice and moderation in peacetime. The closing sections return to Honorius, describing his training in arms and horsemanship, his journey to Rome and consular procession, the defeat of the Greuthungi under Odothaeus, and the prospect of marriage and of shared triumphs with his brother Arcadius.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_sexto_consulatu_: The Panegyricus de Sexto Consulatu Honorii Augusti is a Late Antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian, celebrating the emperor Honorius' entry upon his sixth consulship. It opens with a dream-vision in which the poet recites verses before Jupiter in the heavens, an omen confirmed by news of the emperor's approach to Rome. The body of the poem traces Honorius' upbringing and rooted devotion to the city, his cession of the eastern court to his brother, the suppression of the rebel Gildo in Africa and of Alaric through Stilicho, the Gothic defeat at Pollentia and the fighting at Verona, and Alaric's despairing retreat over the Alps, with speeches assigned to the river god Eridanus and to Alaric himself. Roma then pleads in person for the emperor's presence, recalling Stilicho's night rescue of the young Honorius across the Addua, and travels to Rome to adorn the adventus, after which the poem closes with the civic spectacles of the games and the inauguration of the consulship, prized as a victory over a foreign foe rather than, as in earlier imperial visits, over fellow citizens.
la.claudian.panegyricus_de_tertio_consulatu: Claudian's Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius is a late antique Latin poem in hexameters celebrating the young Western emperor's assumption of the consulship. It opens with the image of an eagle exposing its fledglings to the sun's fire, an allegory of imperial upbringing and testing. The poem then traces Honorius's birth amid the camps of his father Theodosius, his harsh martial training and the tales of his grandfather's campaigns, the overthrow of the usurper who had seized the Western throne and the victory at the Frigidus river, and Honorius's triumphal progress through Italy to his father's embrace. It closes with Theodosius, ascending to the heavens, entrusting his sons to Stilicho and prophesying that the brothers will together subdue the peoples of the East.
la.claudius_mamertinus.panegyricus: A Latin prose panegyric of the later imperial period, spoken in the person of Claudius Mamertinus to thank the emperor Julian for conferring upon him a consulship. The speech opens with an apology for tardy gratitude and a survey of the offices Julian had earlier bestowed on the speaker as a public administrator and praetorian prefect. It then follows the emperor's deeds and character at length: the recovery of Gaul, his frugality and justice, his rapid Danube voyage, his provisioning of Rome and restoration of Greek cities, the revival of learning, and his grant of honours without petition or bribery, contrasted with the corruption of earlier courts. It closes with the consular salutation and procession in the senate and the speaker's pledge to commemorate the emperor's benefactions with lifelong devotion.
la.columella.de_re_rustica: De Re Rustica is a Latin prose treatise on agriculture, the work of Columella in the Early Imperial period. It opens with an address to Publius Silvinus rejecting the claim that the earth has grown old and barren, lamenting the neglect of husbandry, and surveying earlier Greek and Roman writers on the subject. Successive books then take up the choice of land and the siting and arrangement of the villa, the management of coloni, slaves, and overseers, soils, ploughing, and sowing, and the cultivation of vines, the arbustum, olives, and fruit trees. Later books pass to farm animals, birds kept for the table, fishponds, and bees, closing with a promise of a verse treatment of gardens.
la.commodian.carmen_apologeticum: The Carmen Apologeticum is a Latin work of apologetic theology by Commodian, an author of the later imperial period. It opens with the speaker's recollection of his own wandering in error, the illumination he found in the book of the law, and his resolve to turn others from deception. The body of the poem argues from the law and the prophets that the one God foretold to Israel came in the flesh as Christ, rehearsing prophetic testimonies, Christ's miracles and the promise of resurrection, while rebuking Jewish unbelief, idolatry, and worldly pursuits such as the law courts and classical letters. Its final movement is apocalyptic, foretelling a last persecution, the return of Nero as Antichrist, Elijah's preaching, the burning of Rome, a judgment by fire, and the raising of the just to eternal life.
la.commodian.instructiones: The Instructiones is a two-book Christian didactic work by Commodian, a writer of the later Roman Empire. It opens with a preface in which the author recalls his own long wandering in pagan error and his conversion through reading the divine law, announcing his intention to instruct the ignorant. From there the work mounts a sustained polemic against paganism and Jewish unbelief alike: the gods and their myths, Saturn, Jupiter, Apollo, Mercury, Dionysus and the rest, are ridiculed, idols, diviners, haruspices and venal priests are denounced, and arguments are drawn from the law and the prophets, with figures such as Adam, Cain and Abel read as types of Christ. The second book turns to believers, reproving worldliness and laxity in the face of persecution and prescribing conduct for catechumens, women, the wealthy, deacons and pastors, with precepts on baptism, penance, charity to the sick and poor, martyrdom and funerary display, before closing with a full scheme of last things, a revived Nero and Antichrist, the return of Elijah, a thousand-year reign, the final judgment by fire, and the resurrection of the just.
la.corippus.johannis: A Late Antique Latin epic in hexameters attributed to Corippus, the Johannis spans roughly 4,700 lines in eight books and celebrates the campaigns of the Byzantine general John against the Moorish peoples of North Africa under Justinian. The poem opens with an invocation and panegyric to Justinian and an account of the devastation of Africa, then follows John's voyage from Constantinople to Carthage, his battles with Antalas and the Laguatan, his discipline of the troops, the death of Stutias in civil strife, the usurpation of Guntarith, and successive campaigns against Carcasan and the Nasamones. Throughout, the narrative alternates set-piece battle scenes with speeches, divine interventions, episodes of famine and mutiny, and reflections on divine providence governing Roman victory.
la.cyprian.ad_donatum: A short Latin prose treatise of late antique Christian theology, addressed by Cyprian to his friend Donatus, it opens with the recollection of a promised conversation to be held in the pleasant seclusion of a garden. The speaker then gives a first-person account of his conversion, recalling how implausible moral rebirth once seemed to him and how baptism and the Holy Spirit made possible what he had thought impossible, ascribing all to the free gift of divine grace. A long central survey, framed as a vision of the world seen from a mountain height, catalogues the corruptions of secular life, including warfare, gladiatorial games, theatrical spectacles, sexual vice, the law courts, political honours, wealth, and power, concluding that peace and security are found only in withdrawal to God. The work closes with exhortations to purity, constant prayer and reading, and a day ended in sober psalmody.
la.cyprian.de_lapsis: De Lapsis is a Latin prose treatise on church discipline by Cyprian, composed in the aftermath of a persecution during which many Christians had sacrificed to idols or compromised themselves with certificates of compliance. It opens in thanksgiving for the peace newly restored to the church and in praise of the confessors who endured prison and torture, before turning to lament those who had lapsed. Cyprian attributes the collapse to greed, luxury, and slackened observance within the community, condemns the hasty reconciliation of the fallen on the strength of martyrs' petitions or through certain clergy without prior penance, and argues from scriptural examples that the power to forgive sins committed against God belongs to God alone. Recounting the divine punishments that struck unworthy communicants, the treatise closes by urging the lapsed to full confession, satisfaction, fasting, almsgiving, and tears, holding out the hope that true penitents may be restored to grace and even to the crown of martyrdom.
la.cyprian.de_mortalitate: Cyprian's Latin treatise De Mortalitate, a work of Late Antique Christian prose theology, opens by acknowledging that while many believers stand firm amid a present pestilence, the weak in faith require strengthening against the fear of death. Drawing on the Lord's prophecies of wars, famines and plagues as signs that the kingdom of God is at hand, the argument cites Simeon, Job, Tobias, Abraham and the apostle Paul to show that adversity tests and proves the just, and contends that the mortality Christians share with pagans is no ground for complaint, since for the faithful death is a liberation from the devil's warfare and a passage to immortality. Later sections answer the objection of those prevented by death from achieving martyrdom, urge that the departed be received with joy rather than mourning as they depart for their true homeland, and close by likening the collapsing world to a tottering house and a storm-tossed ship from which the faithful should hasten toward paradise, where patriarchs, apostles, martyrs and other departed loved ones await them.
la.cyprian.epistulae: The Epistulae of Cyprian, composed in Late Antique Latin prose, consist of correspondence dealing with church order and clerical conduct. The letters collected here take up questions of ecclesiastical discipline, including a ruling that clergy may not be named as guardians or curators in wills, the exclusion from communion of a stage performer who persists in his trade, and the reproof of a deacon who insulted his bishop. Biblical precedent is cited throughout in support of the decisions, and each letter closes with a formulaic wish for the recipient's continued health.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_senatorem_ex_christian: A short Latin admonition of uncertain authorship, attributed to Cyprian and belonging to the later imperial period, addressed to a senator who has abandoned the Christian religion for the worship of the old gods, and of Isis in particular. The speaker opens by declaring that, shocked to find his correspondent once more enslaved to vain rites, he has hastened to answer in song because the senator has always loved poetry. The work then proceeds as a sustained rebuke: it ridicules the effeminate dress and conduct of Isiac priests, mocks the spectacle of a former consul now ministering with the sistrum, and argues from a series of examples that excess of every kind destroys what it feeds, adducing even Maro's line on the eternally seated Theseus. It closes by warning that known truth knowingly abandoned is no light offence and urging the senator to amend before old age recalls him, since remorse can excuse only a first lapse.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_pascha: A brief Latin poem on Easter, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and of uncertain date. It opens at Golgotha, named as the centre of the world, where a tree cut from barren stock has borne wholesome fruit. The allegory unfolds as the tree grows to heaven and spreads twelve branches over the whole earth, and fifty days later a heavenly breath pours divine nectar upon them, while beneath their shade a clear spring draws peoples of every age, sex and rank. Of those who taste the sweet fruits, some reject the unfamiliar flavour and others fall back into the mire, but the faithful come on the seventh day to bathe fasting in the waters and are purified for the journey to heaven, the poem closing by identifying the tree as the wood of life for all who believe.
la.cyprianus_cordubensis.cypriani_et_samson: A short Latin collection of epigrams and sepulchral verses from medieval Cordoba, transmitted under the names of Cyprian of Cordoba and Abbot Samson. It opens with poems praising Count Adulfus, who renewed at his own expense a book-case housing the books of the Old and New Testament as nourishment for the soul, and includes an admonition to his son Fredenand together with a piece on a gilded fan inscribed with the name Guifredus. The greater part consists of epitaphs and memorial inscriptions for figures such as Abbot Samson, Hermildis, John, a priestly virgin, the abbot Athanagild, and Valentinian, one of which bears the year 918.
la.cyprianus_gallus.heptateuchos: The Heptateuchos is a late-antique Latin epic in hexameters, attributed to Cyprianus Gallus, which versifies the historical narrative of the first seven books of the Bible, from Genesis to Judges. It opens with the six days of creation, the fashioning of Adam and Eve, their temptation by the serpent, and the expulsion from Eden. The poem then follows the patriarchal narratives of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph before turning to Moses and the Exodus, treating the plagues of Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea, the manna and water of the desert, the law-giving at Sinai, and the subsequent wanderings and rebellions of Israel, with extended passages of legal and ritual prescription drawn from Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. Its closing books carry the story through the conquest of Canaan under Joshua and the allotment of the land among the tribes, and end within the period of the judges, from Othniel through Gideon and Samson.
la.descartes.meditations: A philosophical treatise in Latin prose by René Descartes, cast as a sequence of meditations conducted over successive days, which opens with a resolve to demolish all former beliefs and to entertain systematic doubt concerning the senses, the difference between dreaming and waking, and the hypothesis of a deceiving God or malignant genius. From that doubt the work derives the certainty of the thinker's own existence as a thinking thing, examines the nature of mind through the example of a piece of wax, and argues from the idea of an infinitely perfect being to the existence of God and to the truth of whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived. The later meditations explain error as the will's assent extending beyond what the intellect apprehends, demonstrate the real distinction between mind and body, and re-establish the existence of material things, showing the senses to be reliable in their proper office of signalling what benefits or harms the composite of mind and body.
la.dhuoda.rhythmy_ex_manuali_dhuodanae: A Carolingian collection of Latin rhythmic verses drawn from the Manual of Dhuoda, written by a mother for her young son William. It opens with an invocation to God as maker of light and eternal king, praying that the boy may come to know, love and praise his creator. The verses then move through prayers for William's welfare of body and soul and exhortations to humility, chastity, reverence for the clergy, just judgement, and generosity to widows, orphans, pilgrims and the poor, interspersed with Dhuoda's own remarks on the haste and illness that constrained her writing. The collection closes with an epitaph and burial prayer for Dhuoda herself, followed by shorter pieces on the creation and fall, the foolish talker, peace and strife, and rich and poor.
la.dicuil.versus: A short Latin poem by the Carolingian author Dicuil. It opens by declaring an intention to please Charles in speech and song, presenting playful arguments and asking the hearer to mark which month it is, reckoning from April. The poem then salutes Louis as Charles's successor, states that it was completed in May, eight hundred and fourteen years from the conception of the Lord, and expresses hope of soon beholding the king. It ends by likening the poet's humble offering to the widow's two mites, which outweighed the many gifts of the powerful.
la.dracontius.de_laudibus_dei: De Laudibus Dei ('On the Praises of God') is a Late Antique Latin Christian epic in three books of hexameters by the poet Dracontius. The opening invites whoever wishes to know God in wrath and in mercy to read the poem attentively, since all goods and calamities alike descend from his throne. The first book celebrates creation across the six days, the ordering of sky, sea, plants and animals, the fashioning of Adam and Eve, their temptation by the serpent and their expulsion from paradise. The second and third books set God's justice and forbearance against human sin through biblical punishments and pardons, contrast pagan feats of rash valour with acts of faith, and end in a first-person penitential prayer in which a captive speaker confesses his offences and begs for release, health and restoration.
la.dracontius.romulea: The Romulea of Dracontius is a Late Antique Latin collection of shorter lyric poems, of uncertain date, comprising eleven pieces. It opens with a preface that evokes Orpheus and apostrophises a revered master of letters before turning to a narrative of Hylas, the beloved companion of Hercules, among the nymphs. The remaining poems range across mythological narrative and occasional verse, including festive scenes of personified virtues, Bacchic and bridal revelry, and the arrival of Venus before the walls of Carthage, and the collection ends with the image of a gleaming serpent trailing through the clouds.
la.engelmodus.carmina: A small collection of Latin verse by the Carolingian poet Engelmodus, consisting of a personal epistle and a long panegyric to the same addressee. The opening poem is a complaint addressed to a beloved friend named Agi, reproaching him for neglect and changed affections while pleading for the renewal of their bond despite the gulf of wealth and rank between them. The remainder of the work is an extended encomium and prayer to Agi, now addressed as pope, praising his noble upbringing, eloquence, learning, and manifold virtues, his care for the poor and defence of his flock, and concluding with visions of the last judgement in which the poet begs the pontiff's protection and intercession. Throughout, exaltation of the prelate's sanctity is interwoven with the poet's professions of humility and devoted dependence on his favour.
la.ennius.annales: The Annales of Ennius, an epic in hexameter verse composed during the Roman Republic, survives only in a scattered body of fragments. It opens with an invocation of the Muses and a dream in which Homer himself appears to the poet, alongside famous short passages on the pietas of the soul and its transmigration into other bodies. The poem as a whole traced Roman history from its legendary origins, the fall of Troy, the wanderings of Aeneas, and his arrival in Saturnian Hesperia, the land of Latinus, through the early kings and the wars of the Republic down to military campaigns and embassies of Ennius's own day, with much space given to battle on land and sea. Among the fragments are set pieces such as the widowed heroine's tearful dream of her dead father, the figure of Sisyphus straining at his rock, and the 'lateralis dolor' that announces approaching death.
la.ennodius.carmina: The Carmina of the late antique poet Ennodius is a varied collection of Latin poems in a range of metres. It opens with an itinerary poem describing a journey through wintry Alpine country to the shrines of martyrs such as Saturninus, Crispinus, and Daria. The rest of the collection ranges across praise poems addressed to friends and patrons, pieces on nature, love, and mythological subjects such as Phaethon and Venus, and a substantial devotional sequence on Christ, the Virgin Mary, and the saints and martyrs Stephen, Cyprian, Ambrose, Nazarius, Martin, and Dionysius, closing with hymns and prayers.
la.ermenricus_elwagensis.epistola_ad_grimal: The Epistola ad Grimaldum is a Carolingian Latin verse letter by Ermenricus Elwagensis, dedicated to one Grimald and devoted to Saint Gall. It opens with prayers to the Trinity and to Gall himself for the gift of worthy song, with Greek words woven into the Latin verses. A geographic prologue then surveys the Alps, the Danube, the Rhine and Lake Constance, pausing on the island monastery of Augia and its abbot Folcwinus, before a jesting apostrophe to Homer renounces epic matter in favour of the saint's story. The remainder of the poem undertakes an account of where Gall was born, whence he came to these lands, where he dwelt beside the Rhine, and the deeds he performed there, told in humble verse.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_honorem_Ludo: A Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters by Ermoldus Nigellus, addressed to the emperor Louis the Pious. It opens with a prayer to Christ in which the poet rejects the Muses and asks aid for his exile before turning to praise of Louis. The narrative recounts Louis's Aquitanian campaigns and the capture of Barcelona from the Moors, Charlemagne's partition of the realm and coronation of his son, the visit of Pope Stephen, war against the Breton ruler Murman, the conversion and baptism of the Danish king Herold, the painted halls of the palace at Ingelheim, and miracle tales connected with a Strasbourg church of the Virgin. It closes with the exiled poet's direct appeal to Louis and his wife Judith for pardon and restoration.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carmen_in_laudem_pippi: A Latin panegyric in hexameter verse by the Carolingian poet Ermoldus Nigellus, addressed to King Pippin and written throughout from the standpoint of an exile seeking the ruler's favour. The poem opens with an invocation to Thalia, who is sent to the royal palace to herald the exiled poet's arrival and convey his greetings to the court. Its course then takes in a dispute between the personified Rhine and the Vosges region over their respective gifts, a portrait of Strasbourg and its learned bishop Bernold, exempla of celebrated exiles and of biblical and Frankish rulers, and the humorous episode of the cat whose presence hinders a monk's vision of Christ; counsel on kingship and praise of Louis the Pious lead to a closing prayer for Pippin and his wife and a passage spelling out the author's own name.
la.ermoldus_nigellus.carminum_appendix: A short Carolingian Latin poem in hexameters, the Carminum Appendix is attributed to Ermoldus Nigellus. It opens as a song for King Pippin, in which counsels to a boy, to learn whatever wisdom teaches, to read the dicta of Cato and the verse of Virgil, to sing what the psalm sings, alternate with refrain-like lines, amid catalogues of ivory, incense, agates and gold from India, Saba, Attica and Arabia, and praise of golden Rome and triumphant Francia. The poem then recalls Louis made emperor by the coronation of Pope Stephen and the bishop Ebbo's renewal of the foundations of his see, before passing into the epitaph of Himiltrudis, Ebbo's humble mother, who recounts her upbringing on the German Rhine, later life by the Loire and the Seine, her only son's elevation as bishop and rebuilding of the church, and the ten years they laboured there together. It closes with her death recorded at the Kalends of September, a warning to the passing traveller against excess, and a prayer that God pardon sinners.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.formulae_spiritalis_in: The Formulae spiritalis intellegentiae is a late-antique Latin manual of allegorical biblical interpretation in prose by Eucherius of Lyon. It opens with a dedicatory preface addressed to the author's son Veranus, which argues that divine scripture must be read figuratively and sketches the scheme of scriptural senses as historical, tropological, allegorical and anagogical. The body is arranged under ten numbered headings, bodily members of the Lord, supernal creatures, earthly things, animals, appellations, the interior man, objects of daily use, various verbal significations, Jerusalem and its adversities, and numbers, each entry giving a biblical term's spiritual meaning, often in both a good and a bad sense, with a supporting citation. The work closes with a catalogue of symbolically charged numbers from one to one hundred, interpreted as bearers of doctrinal meaning.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.instructiones: Instructiones is a two-book Latin work of scriptural explanation by Eucherius of Lyon, composed in the late antique period and dedicated in a preface to his son Salonius. The first book proceeds in questions and answers that resolve difficulties in passages running from Genesis through the historical books, Job, Psalms, and the Prophets to the Gospels, the Pauline epistles, and Acts, favoring allegorical and moral senses alongside the literal. The second book is a compact glossary giving the meanings of Hebrew and Greek proper names, obscure biblical terms for objects, animals, vestments, weights, and measures, the names of peoples, places, months, and festivals, and the chief vocabulary of ecclesiastical usage. Eucherius presents his explanations as drawn from the judgments of earlier doctors rather than his own ingenuity, and closes by describing the collection as a seed-bed of understanding spread over nearly the whole body of Scripture.
la.eutropius.breviarium: A Latin prose epitome of Roman history by Eutropius, a magister memoriae who dedicated the work to the emperor Valens and composed it during his reign. The opening dedication explains that the author has gathered, in brief narrative ordered by time, the outstanding events of Roman history in war and civil affairs, together with notable deeds from the lives of the emperors. The account runs from Romulus and the seven kings through the struggles of the early Republic, the Samnite wars, and the Punic wars against Carthage, with extended treatment of Hannibal's invasion of Italy. It then follows the eastern conquests and civil conflicts of the late Republic, the emperors from Augustus through the Severans and the third-century crises, the tetrarchy and Constantine, and closes with Julian's Persian expedition, the author himself claiming a part in it, and the death of Jovian.
la.fardulfus.carmina: Carmina is a short Carolingian Latin poem by Fardulf, who identifies himself in its closing lines as an abbot. It opens with an address to the reader announcing that Fardulf made these verses for his Charles, before recounting how adverse fortune drove him from the sceptre of his own people into exile. The narrative follows his loyal service to Charlemagne, the king's abundant gifts in reward for his fidelity, his appointment as head of the church of Saint-Denis, and the construction there of a richly adorned basilica in fulfilment of vows first made amid the hardships of banishment. It closes with Charlemagne's approval of the work, prayers that the king's friendship and days may long increase, a description of the abbey as a house of grace and salvation where God dwells among the bodies of the saints, and a final notice that Abbot Fardulf made its ciborium.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_gratia_libri_duo: The De gratia is a two-book prose treatise on grace and free will by Faustus of Riez, a theological writer of the late antique period. It opens with a dedicatory address to Leontius, in which the author pledges his aid to a council summoned for condemning the error of predestination and sets out a double aim: refuting the Pelagian exaltation of unaided human labour and the opposite error that ascribes everything to grace. The first book combats Pelagian positions chapter by chapter, treating the baptism of infants, the interpretation of Pauline sayings on grace, faith and works, the survival and weakness of free choice, Christ's death for all humanity, the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, and divine prescience, which it presents as following human acts rather than compelling them. The second book, lacunose in places, argues more positively that the will retains its freedom even before Christ and the written law, adducing Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius and the Ninevites as gentiles able to know God by natural reason, and closes with an imagined deliberation among divine power, goodness, wisdom and justice over the creation of a man left free to sin so that he may merit.
la.faustus_of_riez.sermones: A collection of prose sermons by the Late Antique author Faustus of Riez, addressed to mixed lay and monastic hearers across the liturgical year. The opening piece urges purification of conscience and body so as to celebrate the Lord's nativity and receive the Eucharist worthily, and the cycle continues with homilies on the Epiphany, the martyrdoms of Stephen and Vincent and the Holy Innocents, and the commemorations of Honoratus and Augustine. Moral discourses on penitence, almsgiving, fasting, love of enemies and the last judgment alternate with typological readings of Abraham, Isaac and Joseph and doctrinal sermons on the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, culminating in Pentecost instruction.
la.florus.epitome_bellorum_omnium_annorum: The Epitome bellorum omnium annorum, a Latin prose historical epitome by the early imperial writer Florus, compresses the military history of Rome from the founding of the city to the reign of Augustus. It opens with a preface that divides Roman history into the ages of a human life, describing the people's infancy under the kings, adolescence in the conquest of Italy, and robust manhood in the overseas wars, with old age briefly renewed under Trajan. The narrative follows that scheme through the seven kings, the struggles of the early Republic, the Samnite and Punic wars, and the conquests of Macedonia, Syria, Spain, and Gaul, together with the northern invasions, the war against Mithridates, and the suppression of the pirates. It closes with the civil wars of Marius, Sulla, Caesar, and Pompey, the victory of Octavian at Actium, the pacification of the frontiers, and Augustus's establishment of peace and the closing of the gates of Janus.
la.gerwardus.versus: A six-line Latin epigram of Carolingian date, attributed in the source record to Gerwardus. It opens with the poet offering these verses to a prince so that his praise and eternal memory may be secured. The speaker styles himself a suppliant servant who raises his patron's distinguished name to the stars, and the closing couplet addresses the reader directly, bidding that the deed concerning Einhard, the glorifier of great Charles, be set down in writing.
la.giovanni_aurelio_augurelli.chrysopoeia: Chrysopoeia ('The Making of Gold') is a Renaissance Latin didactic poem in four books by Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli on the alchemical art of transmuting base metals into gold. It opens with a proem in which the poet asks a pope's protection for his enterprise and invokes Apollo, Vulcan, and the other powers presiding over metallurgy. The poem then treats the origin of metals in the veins of the earth, mining and its perils, the theory of metallic generation, and the preparation of the 'golden powder' or elixir by which imperfect metals are perfected, describing the apparatus, furnaces, materials, and gradual sequence of color changes of the great work. Digressions on pearls, gemstones, pigments, and glassmaking lead to warnings against fraudulent practitioners, an exhortation to secrecy, and a closing lament for the wars then devastating Italy.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carminum_appendix: A short Latin appendix of two poems attributed to Godescalcus Saxus and assigned to the Carolingian period. It opens with a penitential prayer in which the speaker, hailing Christ as the light of his darkness, begs deliverance from the pit of sin, pardon for his lapses, and a heart that loves God. The longer closing poem addresses Christ as maker and governor of all things, recounting the creation of the heavens, stars, seas and fields, his birth from the mouth of the omnipotent Father, his enclosure in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and his conquest of death, before turning into a blessing on a dear friend: the speaker celebrates the friend's keen understanding, ready eloquence, and mastery of both prose and verse, hails him as a shining star and a teacher worthy of honour, and prays that Christ, who holds the paternal sceptre through all time, grant him prosperity.
la.hegesippus_pseudo.de_excidio_hierosolymi: The De Excidio Hierosolymitano, a late-antique Latin prose history attributed to Hegesippus and hence ascribed to Pseudo-Hegesippus, opens with a preface announcing an account of Jewish history carried beyond the biblical narrative in historiographical style, while faulting Josephus for insufficient attention to religion and truth. From there the work traces the fortunes of the Jews from the Maccabean revolt under Mattathias, Judas Maccabaeus, and their successors down to the Roman campaigns of Vespasian and Titus: the sieges of Jotapata, Jopa, and Jerusalem, Josephus's capture and his debate over suicide, the burning of the temple, and the destruction of the city. Long set speeches, including Titus's address to the besieged and Eleazar's final exhortation, punctuate the narrative, which closes with the mass suicide of the defenders at Masada, a single woman alone surviving to reveal it.
la.hibernicus_exul.carmina: Latin poems of Carolingian date attributed to the court poet known as Hibernicus Exul ('the Irish exile'). The collection opens with a prayer that God grant victory, long life and firm peace to the emperor Charles, and then ranges across court panegyric, a debate between poet and Muse over what gift befits a king, and a long allegorical narrative in which the serpent's whispers break the peace between Charles and the duke Dasilo until a restored bond of fidelity reconciles them. Later pieces include a letter carried to the imperial palace with petitions for the ruler, his sons and his daughters, an exhortation urging boys to study while youth is pliant, epitaphs for priests, monks and Carolingian kings, an elegy recording the death of Charles at seventy, and a guided tour of a house whose seven rooms hold grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy and medicine. The book ends with a verse letter in which Dungal, separated from his old master Baldo, protests his constancy and affection.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_historica: A Late Antique Latin prose work transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, the Fragmenta historica preserves fragmentary documents from the ecclesiastical conflicts surrounding the councils of Nicaea and Ariminum. Its contents are chiefly episcopal correspondence, opening with a synodal letter of the Gallican bishops to their Eastern counterparts that upholds the confession of homoousios, denounces the silencing of the term ousia at Ariminum, and excommunicates Auxentius, Ursacius, Valens, Gaius, Megasius, Justinus and Saturninus. A further letter from Eusebius to Gregory reports Ossius' resistance to the Rimini settlement and laments the exile of orthodox bishops, attributing the Arian cause to dependence on secular power. The collection as a whole records the anti-Arian position of Western bishops through professions of faith, doctrinal argument and notices of condemnation.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_mysteriorum: The Tractatus mysteriorum is a work of Late Antique Latin prose theology by Hilary of Poitiers. It opens with a declaration that everything contained in the sacred books announces, expresses, and confirms through words, deeds, and examples the advent of Christ, together with a promise to treat in order, from Adam onward, all that prefigured his preaching, passion, resurrection, and the gathering of the Church. The treatise then proceeds sequentially through Genesis, Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Lamech, Seth, Noah with the ark and the dove, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac's blessing of Jacob over Esau, interpreting each person and event as a figure of Christ and of the Church, and continues through Moses' rescue from the Nile, the burning bush, the signs before Pharaoh, the sweetening of the bitter waters, the manna and quails, Hosea's marriage, and Rahab's preservation at the fall of Jericho. A closing reflection argues that these histories were committed to writing for posterity's instruction, and that in all of them God the Father, God the Son, and Christ as God and man are to be recognized.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_evangelico: De evangelico is a short later imperial Latin poem in hexameter verse, attributed to Hilary of Poitiers. It opens with a lyrical account of the Nativity: Christ as flower and light born of the virgin, a rejoicing earth, the terror of the serpent, and the Magi bearing gold, incense and myrrh. The central portion addresses Christ as the true Son of God, at once divine and human, lion and lamb, judge of the living and the dead, and then interprets the four winged creatures about the heavenly throne, man, lion, calf and eagle, together with the twenty-four elders and the Trisagion, as figures of Christ amid the universal worship of all creation and the groping blindness of the nations. The poem closes with Gospel episodes of healing, as the paralytic rises to carry his bed and the man born blind is granted new eyes toward heaven.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.hymni: A short Latin collection of two hymnic pieces transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and placed in the later imperial period, though the attribution is doubtful. It opens with a hymn greeting the returning day, addressing Christ as the giver of light and the true morning star who outshines the lesser star of night, and praying for inward illumination, freedom from the deceiver's frauds, and chastity of body and mind amid the daily business of life. The remainder, by far the longer portion, is an alphabetical penitential hymn whose quatrains run from A to Z: the speaker confesses himself crushed under the weight of sins beyond counting, catalogues the personified vices that wound him, pride, envy, discord, vainglory and gluttony among them, calls on stars, beasts, sea and mountains to weep with him, and appeals to Christ the sole redeemer for mercy, cleansing and restoration, professing an orthodox faith that rejects the dogmas of Arius and Sabellius. A doxology to the undivided Trinity closes the collection.
la.hilary_saint_archbishop_of_arles.epistul: A single short Latin letter of the late antique period, written in prose by Hilary, archbishop of Arles, and addressed to Eucherius. It opens with the writer explaining that he has sent back Eucherius's books as promised in an earlier letter, unable to resist the insistence of the messenger Eucherius had sent, and anxious lest the works, not yet copied out, be harmed by the heavy and ceaseless rains. He then records his admiration at reading the whole collection through at a sitting, expresses the hope of one day studying the works again with Eucherius's own pages as his guide, and asks to be reckoned among the young men whom Eucherius's teaching has formed, the more earnestly since the weakness of age presses upon him. The letter closes with a prayer that the Lord long preserve Eucherius, addressed as most blessed pope, mindful of the writer and for the advancement of his church.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.collecta: A Late Antique Latin theological dossier compiled by Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, gathering conciliar acts, episcopal letters, creeds and synodal documents from the mid-fourth-century Arian controversy. The collection opens with a confession of faith set out by Gallic bishops, condemning those who returned from the Council of Ariminum having accepted silence over the term ousia, and proceeds through the correspondence and decrees of the Eastern bishops at the Council of Sardica, their accusations against Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, and parallel Greek and Latin versions of the synodal letter to Emperor Constantius. Later items include the exchanges between Liberius of Rome, Ossius of Corduba and the Eastern hierarchy, professions of faith composed at Ariminum and Sirmium, and Hilary's own defense of the Nicene doctrine of the Son's consubstantiality with the Father.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmen_in_libros_r: A medieval Latin verse retelling of the four Books of Kings (1–2 Samuel, 1–2 Kings), attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin. The poem opens with Elkanah, husband of Peninnah and Hannah, offering sacrifice at Shiloh, and proceeds continuously through the biblical narrative. Its course embraces Samuel's birth and judgeship, Saul's reign and rejection, David's rise, persecution by Saul, and troubled kingship, Solomon's wisdom and the building of the Temple, the division of the kingdom, the ministries of Elijah and Elisha, and the alternating fortunes of the kings of Israel and Judah. The closing books carry the story through Hezekiah, Manasseh, and Josiah's reform to Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem and the carrying off of the Temple treasures, including the bronze columns, to Babylon.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carmina_minora: A medieval Latin collection of shorter poems ascribed to Hildebert of Lavardin. The book opens with verses addressed to a Bishop William on how Nature created him free of vice, and then ranges widely over epistolary poems to bishops, queens, countesses, abbots, and kinsmen; epitaphs and elegies for churchmen and nobles; moral meditations on fortune, wealth, exile, and mortality; satirical and witty pieces; and religious verse on the Trinity, the sacraments, the Incarnation, and the passion of Christ. Among the longer items are two laments on fallen Rome and a prophetic poem on England's coming peace under a future king, alongside shorter pieces on Lucretia, Ganymede, the Egyptian plagues, the twelve stones of the sons of Israel, and the canonical hours.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.carminum_supplemen: A medieval Latin collection of poems by Hildebert of Lavardin, opening with an allegory in which water, sun, crystal and fire figure the Trinity and the virginal birth of Christ, so compounded that they revive the dead, open the tombs and restore order to the fallen. The bulk of the work expounds the twenty-four hours of day and night, tying each hour to a biblical event, such as Adam's first fear of nightfall, the deluge, Moses' crossing of the Red Sea and the Passion of Christ, and urging praise and prayer at the corresponding time. A longer elegy follows, denouncing a wealthy rival whose gold rather than character won away the speaker's beloved, lamenting that riches now outweigh faith, beauty and nobility, and warning young men against mercenary women. The collection closes with short satirical epigrams on the effects of heavy drinking.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_machabaeis: A medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin, De Machabaeis narrates in verse the oppression of the Jews under the Seleucid kings and the outbreak of the Maccabean revolt. It opens with the Macedonian conquest of Persia, Alexander's death, and the partition of his empire, from whose successors arises the persecutor Antiochus. The poem goes on to recount the attempt of Heliodorus on the Temple treasury, the Hellenizing pontificates of Jason and Menelaus, and Antiochus's sack of Jerusalem, abolition of the Law, and desecration of the sanctuary. It closes with the uprising of Mattathias at Modin, his deathbed exhortation to his sons, and the first victories of Judas Maccabeus over the generals Apollonius and Seron.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_mysterio_missae: De Mysterio Missae is a medieval Latin poem in which Hildebert of Lavardin expounds the rite of the Mass as a system of figures fulfilled in Christ. The opening couplets present the author by name, announce the aim of showing what the mystic rites of the Mass represent and what the minister performs, and beg the reader's pardon for the work's faults. From there the poem follows the liturgy in sequence, introit, Kyrie, Gloria, lections, Gospel, offertory, secret prayers, preface, Sanctus, and canon, assigning to each element an Old Testament counterpart, above all the ministry of Aaron, the sacrificial law, and the temple ritual, read as anticipations of Christ's sacrifice on the cross. Later sections treat the Lord's Prayer, the fraction and mingling of bread and wine, communion, and the conversion of bread into Christ's flesh, closing with the claim that the types and signs of the old law have ceased at the cross.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_ordine_mundi: De Ordine Mundi is a medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin that retells the whole sweep of sacred history in verse. It opens with a prayer urging Christ to come at the end of an exhausted age, as the prophets foretold, and announces the poet's aim of retracing in verse the redemption begun with the birth from the Virgin. The poem then moves from Adam's fall through Cain's fratricide, the flood, Babel, the patriarchs, the plagues of Egypt and the giving of the law, celebrating figures such as David, Judas Maccabaeus and Judith, before turning to the incarnation, virgin birth, miracles, passion, resurrection and ascension of Christ. It closes with an exposition of the Trinity, a denunciation of the pagan gods as products of fear and royal tyranny, and an account of Peter's preaching that turns Rome from idolatry.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_querimonia_et_c: A medieval Latin poem attributed to Hildebert of Lavardin stages the complaint and conflict of the Flesh and the Spirit. It opens with a voice lamenting captivity in the narrow, crumbling house of the body, recalling a former betrothal to Christ and grieving that a scheming seducer has robbed it of chastity. A consoling reply promises a lasting dwelling beyond the grim prison and broadens into instruction: a denunciation of worldly care and of an age when vice outweighs honesty, an exemplum of Peter's patient acceptance of Paul's correction, and an account of the soul's seven acts, from vegetative growth and sense perception through reason, conscience, and the law up to contemplation and union with God. In the closing exchange the weary Flesh protests against dying daily and longs for a single death, while the poet explains that the will becomes sinful only when the Spirit, figured as a wife, consents to the Flesh as husband.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.in_primum_caput_ec: A medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin, In Primum Caput Ecclesiastes is a verse exposition of the first chapter of Ecclesiastes, opening with the words 'Vanitas vanitatum' and a portrayal of King Solomon, ever greedy for wisdom, surveying a created order in which everything is mutable and vain. The body of the poem follows the Vulgate chapter lemma by lemma, quoting each scriptural verse and glossing it in turn: the sun's rising and setting that temper cold and heat, the rivers that flow into the sea without filling it, the generations that succeed one another like waves, and the impossibility of grasping the hidden causes of things except through enigmas until the faithful behold God face to face. Later passages explain that nothing under the sun is new, since every thing returns through its seed, and that oblivion has swallowed the titles and pomp of the world's tetrarchs, praetors and monarchs. The poem closes in Solomon's voice, recalling the wisdom and wealth with which he surpassed all crowned kings, and ends with the admonition that God's judgments come by measure, number and weight, and that those who strive to fathom them will be held detestable.
la.hincmar.carmina: The Carmina gathered under the name of Hincmar, a Carolingian author who speaks in them as bishop of Reims, collect occasional and devotional Latin verse. The collection opens with a poem on an altar of the Virgin Mary adorned by the bishop, followed by epitaphs for his predecessors Tilpinus and Remigius. Later pieces include a long poem addressed to Mary on the incarnation and the Eucharist, memorial verses for Remigius with chronological notices, a gift-poem accompanied by verses to King Charles, and a pointed exchange between two clerics named Hincmar over the right of free appeal to the apostolic see. A closing epitaph, which bids the reader remember Hincmar and pray for his soul, ends the collection.
la.horace.ars_poetica: The Ars Poetica of Horace, a didactic poem in hexameters by the Augustan poet addressed to the Pisones, opens with the grotesque image of a painter joining a human head to a horse's neck to argue that a work of art must be single and unified. From there it ranges across the whole craft of poetry: choice of subject proportioned to the writer's powers, diction and the life of words under the rule of usage, the metres and conventions of the several genres, the portrayal of character suited to age and condition, dramatic structure and stage decorum, and the proper union of instruction with delight. Later sections review the history of drama from Thespis and Aeschylus to Roman tragedy and comedy, insist on patient revision and honest criticism, and weigh natural talent against trained art, ending with warnings against the poet's vanity and the flattery of admiring friends.
la.horace.carmen_saeculare: Horace's Carmen Saeculare is a short Augustan choral lyric, a public hymn addressed on behalf of the Roman state to Apollo and Diana. It opens with an invocation of Phoebus silvarumque potens Diana, asking the deities worshipped on the seven hills to grant the prayer that Sibylline verses prescribed for chosen maidens and chaste boys to sing at the sacred season. The poem then calls on Ilithyia, the Parcae, Ceres, and the bright sun for fruitful marriage, safe childbirth, abundance of corn and cattle, and wholesome air and water; it recalls Aeneas' escape from burning Troy and his settlement of the Romulean stock in Latium, petitions the gods for good morals in the young and gentle rest for the old, and declares that Rome's power is now feared by the Mede, the Scythian, and the Indian alike. It closes with the return of Fides, Pax, Honos, Pudor, and long-neglected Virtus amid a horn of plenty, with prayers that Apollo, augur and healer, favourable to the Palatine, and Diana on the Aventine and Algidus may prolong the life of Roman and Latin greatness, as the trained chorus reports good hope to Jupiter and all the gods.
la.horace.epistles: The Epistles of Horace, written in hexameter verse during the Augustan age, cast ethical and practical reflection in the form of verse letters. The opening epistle to Maecenas announces the poet's withdrawal from public striving and his resolve to weigh what is true and fitting, professing allegiance to no single philosophical master. Across the two books the speaker counsels a gallery of friends, Lollius, Albius, Torquatus, Numicius, and others, on avarice, envy, moderation, friendship, and contentment with one's lot, often through anecdote and fable; the second book then turns toward literary matters, addressing Julius Florus and Augustus on poetic talent, the judgment of audiences, patronage, and the condition of Roman poetry.
la.horace.epodes: The Epodes are a book of seventeen iambic poems by the Augustan poet Horace, each composed in couplets of a longer iambic line followed by a shorter line of varying metre. The opening poem addresses Maecenas, promising the poet's company through every danger of Caesar's campaigns. From there the collection ranges over praise of country life undercut by a moneylender's backsliding, comic invective on garlic and on unattractive lovers, attacks on an upstart ex-slave and on the poetaster Mevius, scenes of sorcery dominated by the witch Canidia, laments and warnings over Roman civil bloodshed, a celebration of Caesar's naval victory at Actium, and a prophetic call for the virtuous to abandon a doomed city for the blessed isles, closing with the speaker's unsuccessful appeal for release from Canidia's incurable curse. Themes of friendship, love, politics and personal abuse alternate in poems whose tone shifts between lyric charm and savage invective.
la.horace.odes: Horace's Carmina, four books of lyric poetry by the Augustan poet, open with the ode to Maecenas that surveys the ambitions driving men to racing, politics, wealth, farming, war, and hunting, and claims a place among the lyric singers for the poet himself. Across the books the odes alternate between private and public registers: love poems to Pyrrha, Chloe, Lydia, and others, drinking songs and invitations, hymns to Venus, Mercury, Bacchus, Faunus, and Fortune, and reflections on friendship, avarice, fortune's reversals, and the approach of death, alongside civic odes on Roman virtue and the achievements of Augustus, from Cleopatra's defeat to the campaigns of Drusus and Tiberius. Among the famous pieces stands the ode in which the poet raises himself a monument more lasting than bronze, and the collection closes with the renunciation of war themes to sing, under the peace of Augustus, of Troy, Anchises, and the offspring of Venus.
la.horace.satires: Horace's Satires (Sermones) are two books of hexameter verse satire composed in the Augustan age. The work opens with an address to Maecenas asking why no one is content with the lot that fate or reason has assigned him. The first book ranges over discontent, greed, ambition, and the failings to be pardoned in friends, includes an autobiographical account of the poet's upbringing by his freedman father, follows the poet on a satirical journey from Rome to Brundisium, and discusses the satiric art in dialogue with Lucilius's practice. The second book proceeds largely through dialogue, presenting Ofellus's praise of frugal living, Damasippe's lecture on universal madness, Catius's precepts on gastronomy, Ulysses's consultation of Tiresias on legacy-hunting, the fable of the town mouse and the country mouse, the slave Davus's reproach of his master, and the disastrous banquet of Nasidienus, before closing on Horace's contentment with his modest Sabine estate.
la.hrabanus.carmen_evangeliorum: A short medieval Latin poem on the four evangelists, attributed to Hrabanus and belonging to the Carolingian period. It introduces Matthew as the foremost maker of the evangelical art, then Mark as Peter's disciple who carried the teaching from Italy to Egypt, Luke as the evangelist linked with Achaia, and John as the Lord's beloved table-companion, whom Asia honours. A central passage makes all four bear common witness to Christ, begotten of the Father, who humbly became man and brought hope to the world. The latter half expounds the four symbolic creatures, man, calf, lion and eagle, first as emblems of the evangelists and then in a tropological reading as figures of reason, bodily discipline, victory in struggle and contemplation of heaven, closing with the Church's celebration of Christ's name in prayers and chants and the concord of the four Gospel writers.
la.hrabanus.carmina: Latin poems by Hrabanus, a Carolingian poet whose verses repeatedly name him as a humble servant, and later abbot, of the church of Fulda. The collection opens with a dedicatory poem presenting, on behalf of a Frankish pupil, a book on the passion of Christ composed with figured numbers and tropological figures. The rest is chiefly occasional verse: dedications accompanying his writings to popes, bishops and Queen Judith; letter-poems of friendship and spiritual counsel to fellow clerics; didactic pieces on the virtues and on the transience of worldly things; and a long poem narrating salvation history from the Creation through the life of Christ to the Last Judgement. A substantial group of poems describes the altars, relics and tombs of Fulda, and the collection closes with epitaphs and tituli for monks, bishops and lay notables, ending with one for Hrabanus himself.
la.hrabanus.carminum_appendix: A Carolingian appendix of Latin verse attributed to Hrabanus, made up of short hymnic and devotional poems, many in four-line stanzas with refrains. The collection opens with a poem in praise of charity, tracing its working from creation and the incarnation to Pentecost and the gathering of the church. The poems that follow treat the chief feasts of the liturgical year, including the nativity, the Holy Innocents, Epiphany and the baptism of Christ, the resurrection and the ascension, together with pieces on the apostles Peter and Paul and on Andrew, a confessor's feast, a penitent's prayer, an alphabetical poem contrasting charity with avarice, verses on the cross and the books of Moses, and a lament for Hatto, the abbot honoured at Fulda.
la.hrabanus.laudes_crucis: Laudes Crucis is a Carolingian Latin poem in praise of the Cross, attributed to Hrabanus; it opens with an invocation to the muse to sing the gifts of the supreme Father and the sacred trophy of the crucified King. The work then unfolds a sustained encomium of the cross as the instrument of redemption, celebrating its victory over the serpent, death, and hell, and gathering Old Testament prefigurations of the Passion alongside the symbols of the four evangelists and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Much of the poem is devoted to number symbolism, fives, tens, twelves, eights, and sixes, which the poet expounds as figures of the cross's mysteries, together with catalogues of virtues, angelic orders, prophetic testimonies, and the ranks of saints and virgins. It closes with a personal prayer in which the author names himself Hrabanus and offers his song to Christ as a sacrifice upon the altar.
la.iulius_firmicus_maternus.liber_de_errore: The Liber de errore profanarum religionum is a Latin Christian polemic against pagan worship by Iulius Firmicus Maternus, a later-imperial prose treatise addressed to the emperors Constantius and Constans. It opens with the argument that divination was invented by the devil and then surveys the cults of the four elements, the Egyptian veneration of water through the myth of Osiris, the Phrygian earth cult of Attis, rites of air, and the Persian fire cult of Mithras, together with Liber, Proserpina, Serapis, the Penates, Vesta and the Palladium, contending that each consecrates the death or the crimes of its god. The author contrasts these rites with the Christian sacraments, arguing that bread, light, the bridegroom, the stone and similar symbols announced by the prophets are fulfilled in Christ, and rehearses the adulteries and murders attributed to the pagan deities as evidence of their corruption. The treatise closes with an exhortation urging the emperors to abolish idolatry, destroy temples and idols, and thereby complete the triumph of the Christian faith in the empire.
la.jerome.epistulae: A large corpus of Latin prose letters by Jerome, the late-antique Christian writer, addressed over the course of his career to correspondents including bishops, priests, monks, and noble women such as Paula and Eustochium. The collection opens with a preface in which the author, protesting his inadequacy through an extended nautical metaphor, takes up the ordeal of a woman accused of adultery at Vercellae, who withstands repeated torture while refusing to condemn herself. Across the correspondence as a whole the letters alternate among personal news, moral and ascetic counsel, scriptural exposition, biographical narrative, and doctrinal polemic, with sustained attacks on Origenist teaching and, toward the end, on Pelagians and other heretics. The final pieces, composed in evident old age and frailty, urge their recipients to firmness against heretical teaching and record the deaths of friends within the author's circle.
la.jerome.in_hieremiam_prophetam: Jerome's Latin commentary on the Book of Jeremiah, addressed to his friend Eusebius and written in the late fourth century as part of his series of commentaries on the prophets. The work opens with a preface in which Jerome explains his plan: he will follow the Hebrew text rather than the Septuagint, will pass over Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah, and will keep his annotations brief so that meaning is not lost in verbosity. The six books proceed verse by verse through the prophet's oracles, offering philological discussion of the Hebrew, comparison of the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, and interpretation that moves between the literal history of Judah and its kings, moral exhortation to the church and its teachers, and Christological readings of the prophecies, extending from the call of Jeremiah through the oracles against the nations to the promises of restoration.
la.jerome.vulgate: The Vulgate is the Latin version of the Bible translated by Jerome in the late antique period, presenting the whole of Christian scripture in prose. It opens at the head of Genesis with the creation of heaven and earth and the six days of God's work. From there it runs through the patriarchal narratives of the Pentateuch, the histories of Israel, the Psalms, the wisdom of the Proverbs and the prophetic books, together with apocryphal writings such as the visions of Esdras, before reaching the books of the New Testament.
la.johannes_hymonides.versiculi_de_cena_cyp: A Carolingian Latin poem by Johannes Hymonides that recasts the Cena Cypriani in verse, its prologue invoking Cyprian as the rhetor and pope of Libyan Carthage and playfully imagining performance at the banquets of Emperor Charles. The poem assembles a vast company of biblical figures, patriarchs, kings, prophets, apostles and notorious sinners alike, as guests at a wedding feast, assigning each a fitting seat, dish and garment drawn from scriptural incident. The narrative proceeds from the arrivals and seating arrangements to the serving of the meal and the king's distribution of vestments to his guests.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carmina: The Carmina of John Scotus Eriugena gather the Latin poems of a Carolingian author, opening with a long poem on Christ's cross and harrowing of hell addressed to King Charles, into whose Latin Greek terms are woven. The collection goes on to offer verse on Easter and the passover, a panegyric on Queen Irmintrud, Greek acrostics and prayers on Charles's behalf, and a glowing description of the royal church the king has built, complete with the enthroned ruler. Other pieces touch on Dionysius the Areopagite and Maximus the Confessor, on the zodiac signs said to mark the dates of Christ's conception and birth, and on the nativity at Bethlehem. The collection ends with a short satirical epitaph on Hincmar.
la.juvenal.satires: Juvenal's Satires is a collection of sixteen satiric poems in dactylic hexameter by the Roman poet Juvenal of the early imperial period. The opening satire announces, amid complaints at the endless recitals of rival poets, that indignation itself compels verse, and that the hopes, fears, angers, pleasures and bustle of mankind furnish the medley of the book. The remaining satires range across Roman society: the hypocrisy of ostentatious moralists, the perils of the city streets, the humiliation of the client at his patron's table, a sweeping attack on women and marriage, the dependence of letters on patronage, the hollowness of aristocratic pedigree, the follies of ambitious prayer, legacy-hunting, avarice, superstition and cannibal frenzy in Egypt, and finally the legal privileges of soldiers, in a poem that breaks off unfinished. Throughout, contemporary types and institutions are portrayed with savage irony and sustained moral indignation.
la.juvencus.historia_evangelica: Juvencus's Historia Evangelica recasts the gospel narrative in four books of Latin hexameters, a Christian epic of the later imperial age.
