It opens under the bloody king Herod, with the angel's annunciation to the priest Zacharias of the birth of John and the annunciation to Mary. The poem then follows the whole gospel course: the nativity and the Magi, John's preaching and the baptism of Christ, the temptation in the wilderness, Christ's Galilean ministry of sermons, parables and healings, and the journey to Jerusalem for the Passion, crucifixion and resurrection. It closes with the risen Christ's commission to his disciples and a dedication praising the emperor Constantine.
la.lactantius.carmen_de_passione_domini: A short late-antique Latin poem attributed to Lactantius, the Carmen de Passione Domini is cast as a first-person speech by Christ, who greets a passer-by at the doors of a temple and bids him contemplate the Passion. After this opening appeal, the speaker recounts his incarnation and humble birth in Judaea, the flight from Herod into Egypt and return, and a ministry of teaching and miracles, before turning to the betrayal, the trial before Pilate, the scourging, and the crucifixion, described in close physical detail from the crown of thorns to the wound in his side. The closing lines urge veneration of the cross, endurance of adversity, and detachment from fleeting worldly goods, promising in return eternal joy with Christ in heaven.
la.lactantius.de_ave_phoenice: The De Ave Phoenice is a late antique Latin work by Lactantius that opens with a description of a blissful eastern land, untouched by disease, old age, death, and vice, where the solitary phoenix dwells in the sun's grove. The work goes on to trace the bird's thousand-year life, its flight to Syria, its building of a nest of aromatic spices that serves as both tomb and cradle, its death in flames, and its rebirth from the ashes in the form of a worm that gradually recovers its former shape. It then describes the young phoenix's journey to the temple of the Sun, where it deposits the remains of its predecessor amid the homage of Egypt and the assembled birds, and closes with reflections on the creature's self-generation, its abstinence from sexual union, and the eternal life it attains through death.
la.lactantius.epitome_divinarum_institution: The Epitome of the Divine Institutes is a Late Antique Latin Christian apology in prose, opening with a dedicatory preface in which Lactantius explains to his brother Pentadius that he has condensed his seven-book Divine Institutes into a shorter form. It argues for providence and the unity of God from pagan poets, philosophers, and the Sibyls, maintains that the deities of Greco-Roman religion were mortal men deified after death and that daemons are fallen angels who led humanity astray, and then rejects philosophy as false wisdom by surveying the sects' conflicting doctrines of the supreme good. The second half presents true religion and true wisdom as united in Christ, covering his divine generation and birth in the flesh, the prophetic testimonies of his Passion and resurrection, the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, and the meaning of the cross. Closing chapters prescribe Christian conduct, justice toward God and neighbour, mercy, continence, fidelity in marriage, and penitence, before concluding with proofs of the soul's immortality and an account of the last things, from the tribulations of the world's end and the reign of an impious king to Christ's return, the thousand-year kingdom, the final judgement, and the renewal of the world.
la.lios_monocus.libellus_sacerdotalis: A Carolingian Latin verse treatise attributed to Lios Monocus, the Libellus Sacerdotalis styles itself a little book on the priestly art and opens with a prayer to Christ for the gift of eloquent speech. Addressed to ministers and clergy, the poem proceeds largely through moral exhortation: it dramatizes the devil luring churchmen into complacency about sin, dwells at length on the torments of hell, and sets out the seven virtues that cleanse the seven deadly sins together with the seven causes of the remission of sins. Much of the work is cast as quoted teaching attributed to the psalmist, Paul, Solomon and above all Christ, including a versified rendering of the beatitudes, denunciations of worldly riches, and injunctions to almsgiving and forgiveness of one's neighbour. It closes with a vision of the heavenly city, its never-failing light and rivers, and the everlasting rewards prepared for the humble and the merciful.
la.livy.ab_urbe_condita: Livy's Ab Urbe Condita is an Augustan prose history narrating the fortunes of the Roman people from the city's origins onward. Its preface weighs the difficulties of the undertaking and presents Roman history as a record of conduct to be imitated or avoided, before the narrative opens with the Trojan settlement of Latium under Aeneas, the founding of the city, and the reigns of the early kings. Composed in annalistic Latin prose, the work proceeds year by year, recounting wars, domestic politics, and the leading figures and institutions of the Republic.
la.lucan.bellum_civile: The Bellum Civile (also called the Pharsalia) of Lucan is a Latin epic in ten books of hexameter, composed in the early Imperial period, on the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey. The poem opens with a proem deploring wars 'more than civil' and addressing the emperor Nero, before moving to Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon and the flight of the Senate from Rome. Its course runs through the earlier massacres of Marius and Sulla, Caesar's Italian campaign, the siege of Massilia, Pompey's crossing to Greece, the battle of Pharsalus, Pompey's murder in Egypt, and Cato's march through the African desert and Syrtes, including a long catalogue of serpents. The narrative breaks off, apparently incomplete, during Caesar's struggle in Alexandria, and throughout is marked by speeches, storm scenes, portents, and necromantic episodes in a heavily rhetorical style.
la.lucretius.de_rerum_natura: Lucretius's De Rerum Natura is a didactic epic of the Roman Republic, composed in six books of hexameters and addressed to Memmius. It opens with a hymn to Venus and a celebration of Epicurus before setting out Epicurean physics: nothing arises from nothing, and all things consist of atoms moving through void in an infinite universe. Later books extend this system to the mortality of the soul, the formation and eventual destruction of the world, the natural origins of life, language, religion, and civilization, and finally meteorological phenomena and the plague of Athens. Throughout, the argument is that knowledge of natural causes dispels the fear of gods and of death.
la.lupus_servatus.versus: A short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Lupus Servatus, cast as a dedicatory address to a patron named Evrardus. It opens by inviting whoever wishes to know the causes of all the laws to seek out the book that Evrardus has had compiled. The body of the poem enumerates the law codes gathered in that collection, the Salic law of the Franks, then the Ripuarian, Lombard, Alamannic and Bavarian laws, each paired with the depicted figures of the people whose law it is, and it exclaims over the shining countenances of Charles, Pippin, Louis and Lothar and the far-resounding force of their laws. It closes with the poet signing himself Lupus, the least of men, promising worthier song should God grant him further years, and calling on Father, Son and Holy Spirit to protect, exalt and honour Evrardus.
la.macrobius.fragment: A short Latin prose fragment attributed to the late-antique author Macrobius. It opens with a group of idle men dicing, drenched in perfume and surrounded by courtesans. The sketch follows them through their day: they send a boy to the comitium to learn what has been done in the forum, who argued for and against, and how the tribes voted; on the way they drain every wine jar in the alley, and in court the judge demands witnesses while stepping out to relieve himself, then examines documents with eyelids heavy from wine. The closing speech dismisses involvement with such triflers in favour of drinking honeyed Greek wine and eating fattened thrush and fine fish caught between two bridges.
la.macrobius.in_somnium_Scipionis_commentar: A late-antique Latin prose commentary in which Macrobius expounds the Dream of Scipio, the concluding portion of Cicero's De re publica, addressing the work to his son Eustathius. A long prefatory essay sets Cicero's dream alongside Plato's myth of Er, defends the philosopher's use of figurative narrative against its critics, classifies the five kinds of dreams, and fixes the dream's purpose as the teaching that souls of the just return to heaven after death. The commentary then follows Cicero's words through the numerological significance of seven and eight in gestation and the ages of life, the soul's immortality and its descent through the planetary spheres, the order, zones and measurements of the heavens and earth, the harmony of the spheres, and the self-moved nature of the soul maintained against Aristotle's objections. It closes with exhortations to public virtue and contempt for fame, together with the observation that moral, natural and rational philosophy are all comprised within the dream.
la.macrobius.saturnalia: The Saturnalia is a learned Latin dialogue in seven books composed in late antiquity by Macrobius, framed as the gatherings of Roman aristocrats and men of letters at the house of Vettius Praetextatus during the Saturnalia festival at Rome. An opening preface, addressed to the author's son Eustachius, presents the work as a digest of varied reading arranged into an ordered whole. The dialogue then ranges over the origins and rituals of Roman religious festivals and cults, linguistic and antiquarian questions, and an extended appreciation of Virgil as orator and poet, including analysis of his rhetorical art and a gathering of earlier writers' passages beside his own. The final book poses questions on physiology, medicine, astronomy, and other natural phenomena, answered in turn by the physician Disarius and the other speakers.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.benedictio_cerei_i: A late-antique Latin prose blessing of the Easter candle by Magnus Felix Ennodius, opening with the declaration 'Dignam et iustum est' that humanity owes God at least vocal thanks for what it has received. The prayer praises the Creator who fixed the earth and waters, joined the seasons, made all things from nothing, and divided light from darkness, before turning to the night that freed mankind from the yoke of servitude, at whose ministry the candle is offered to dispel the ancient gloom. Its symbolism treats the wax, wick and flame, engendered without union like the offspring of the Virgin, and the slain Lamb whose sacrifice replaces animal victims, while the burning column recalls the pillar that led Israel through the sea, the Hebrew crossing and the Egyptian drowning. It closes with petitions that the blessed light protect the faithful against winds and storms and that, as spring renews the earth at the season of the passion and resurrection, God grant fruitfulness of the times and preserve the priest and his clergy.

The Benedictio Cerei II is a Latin prose liturgical prayer by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a blessing of the paschal candle belonging to the Easter vigil of late antiquity. It opens with the preface formula 'Dignum et iustum est', proclaiming that the offices of the blessed night be unlocked as with a worthy key so that the noble messenger of life may herald the resurrection. The prayer then moves through praise of the creator who formed man from the dust, an account of the fall into voluntary error and exile, and a celebration of regeneration in baptism, where water and flame are reconciled beyond the order of nature; the candle itself, fed by rivers and by wax from bees whose virginity suffers no loss, recalls Christ burning in the bush without harm. It closes with an invocation that the consecrated light, borne at the season of resurrection, withstand every storm and that the celebrating priest and his clergy be granted abundance of the earth together with innocence of life.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_1_praefati: Two prose prefaces introduce the first book of the Carmina of Magnus Felix Ennodius, a Latin author of late antiquity. The first opens by observing that gladness ever attends a man's return to his native soil and that such joy owes a clear voice lest mute rejoicing take on the likeness of mourning; it then defends the practice of eloquence against envious detractors, invokes the prophets who set their prayers into verse as precedent, and closes by commending a gifted young addressee whose gifts restore the writer's own flagging powers. The second, much shorter preface thanks an unnamed correspondent for support already conferred, laments the postponement of further favour, admits that verses have been appended to the accompanying poem, and bids the reader take pleasure in the poetry that follows.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.petitorium_quo_abs: The Petitorium of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a short late Antique prose petition, composed in the author's own voice, seeking the formal manumission of his slave Gerontius before the ecclesiastical authorities of the Roman city. It opens with a meditation on God as arbiter of human affairs, who rewards the faithful, relieves the toil of the devout, and makes hardship pass into renewed devotion. Ennodius then attests Gerontius's good faith, integrity and free bearing, explains that he had acquired him by an exchange but now prefers the verdict of a solemn judgement to the profit of possession, and restores his liberty together with the service owed to him. The petition closes by asking that the ecclesiastical acts record Gerontius as released from every obligation, that he be admitted to perpetual fellowship in the Roman college, and that his whole peculium be conceded to him without diminution.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.vita_epiphanii: The Vita Epiphanii of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a late-antique Latin prose saint's life of Epiphanius, bishop of Pavia (Ticinum). A prologue weighing the perils of praising eminent persons, answered by an invocation of the Holy Spirit as witness and companion, opens into an account of Epiphanius's birth at Pavia, his childhood entry into clerical service under Bishop Crispinus, and his early advancement as lector, subdeacon, and deacon. The body of the work follows his consecration to the episcopate and ascetic discipline, his embassies to the emperor Anthemius to reconcile him with Ricimer and to the Visigothic king Eurich, his protection of captives during Odoacer's sack of Pavia, his rebuilding of ruined churches and exorcisms, and a mission to the Burgundian king Gundobad that won the release of more than six thousand Italian prisoners. Petitions for tax relief directed first to Odoacer and then to Theoderic lead to a final journey to Ravenna, after which Epiphanius dies at Pavia in his fifty-eighth year, the thirtieth of his episcopate, and the closing chapters narrate his funeral, the lustre of his relics, and the universal grief of a people among whom the narrator claims eyewitness standing.
la.manilius.astronomica: The Astronomica of Manilius is a didactic poem in five books of Latin hexameters, written during the Augustan era, that expounds the principles and practice of astrology. It opens with an invocation to Caesar and a claim that the poet is the first to sing in Latin of the stars' governance of human fate. The opening books describe the fabric of the heavens and the earth, survey the constellations and the celestial circles, and classify the signs of the zodiac by their natures, subdivisions, aspects, and tutelary deities. The later books set out the reckoning of the horoscope and the rising times of the signs, the character and callings that each sign, degree, and decan bestows on the newborn, the distribution of the world's peoples and regions among the signs, and the influence of the constellations that rise in company with the zodiac.
la.marbodus_redonensis.certamina_septem_fra: A medieval Latin poem by Marbod of Rennes on the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother. It opens with a royal edict that would force the Israelites to eat forbidden food, which seven brothers, steadfast with their mother, refuse on pain of death. Each brother in turn confronts the tyrant Antiochus with a speech of defiance before dying under torment, including flaying, mutilation, fire, and the frying pan, while the king's attempt to win over the youngest with promises collapses when the mother exhorts her son to stand firm. The work closes with the youngest brother's tortured death and that of the mother, who shines last among her sons, crowned with seven crowns as victor of the contest.
la.martial.epigrams: The Epigrams of Marcus Valerius Martialis, a poet from the Spanish town of Bilbilis writing in the early Imperial period, assemble a large collection of short satirical poems arranged in successive books. The collection opens by presenting the poet as known throughout the world and asking the reader's indulgence for wanton pages written in an honest life. Its range runs from scathing portraits of Roman social types such as legacy-hunters, sponging dinner guests, plagiarists, doctors and needy patrons, through erotic and obscene verses, epitaphs for children and freedmen, and flattering addresses to the emperor, to closing books of two-line verses attached to Saturnalia gifts.
la.martialis.de_spectaculis: The De Spectaculis of Martial is a sequence of short poems in hexameter verse from the early Imperial period, celebrating the spectacles staged in the newly built Flavian Amphitheatre. It opens by proclaiming the new arena superior to the fabled wonders of the ancient world and to the despised works of Nero that had occupied the site. The collection then surveys the games in their variety: spectators gathered from every province of the empire, criminals executed in scenes drawn from myth, hunts and combats with exotic beasts, and naval battles fought in a flooded arena. It closes with epigrams on the gladiators Priscus and Verus, on animals that showed unexpected clemency, and on the fortunes of the Flavian house.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.opus_prosodiacum: A very short Latin poem attributed to Micon of Saint-Riquier, a Carolingian author, transmitted under the title Opus Prosodiacum. The opening lines invoke one who washes the pious with fire and the offerings of living water, and the poem then turns to the occasion at hand, a gift of soap, praying that its cleansing power dissolve the heaps of sin, that lactean whiteness guard the virginal adornment of the breast, and that the casket breathe the fragrance of virtues instead of standing empty. The speaker goes on to say that what is now given drives out the fluid humour of phlegm and wipes away the sharp bites of the innards, and the final line breaks off incomplete.
la.micon_of_saint_riquier.prologus_in_tract: A verse prologue to the grammatical treatise De primis syllabis, composed in Carolingian Latin by Micon of Saint Riquier. It opens by declaring that, since no art existed for recognising which first syllable is long or short, the author will set the matter out briefly so that young learners can find it without labour. The bulk of the poem outlines the treatise's plan: metric titles introduced after an account of the courses of the sun and moon, a six-part treatment of initial syllables of fixed quantity across the parts of speech, with the interjection deliberately set aside as a category the Greeks do not number, and further discussion of the particle pro, of verbs in the present and perfect, of defective impersonal verbs and the gerund, and of the vowel, mute and liquid letters, including the common syllable and the behaviour of s before the metre. The prologue closes by announcing that the metrical portion ends there and that the remaining teaching, framed for boys at their studies, will proceed in prose.
la.minucius_felix.octavius: The Octavius is a late-antique Latin apologetic dialogue of uncertain date, attributed to Minucius Felix, framed as the narrator's affectionate recollection of the debate in which his friend Octavius converted the pagan Caecilius to Christianity. It opens with the narrator recalling his bond with the deceased Octavius and the walk along the shore from Rome to Ostia, where Caecilius, after kissing an image of Serapis, consents to argue against the Christian cause. Caecilius speaks first, defending traditional religion and philosophical doubt and rehearsing the stock accusations against Christians, before Octavius replies with a long oration that argues from the order of the universe to a single provident creator, exposes pagan myth, idolatry and imperial conquest, ascribes oracles and portents to demons, refutes the slanders of infanticide and incest, and defends resurrection and Christian conduct. The dialogue closes with Caecilius' submission to the argument and the narrator's joy that his friend has both believed and triumphed.
la.moduin.carminum_appendix: A brief Carolingian Latin poem by Moduin, preserved as a short self-contained piece. It opens with the speaker, who describes himself as old and broken in body, urging a young brother to turn his muse away from Virgil, whose eloquence he dreads, toward Arator. The body consists of paired contrasts between the two poets: Virgil sings of pastoral causes and Aeneas' wars, keeps company with Jove, is seized by Cerberus and praised an incestuous Venus, while Arator recounts apostolic virtues and the Lord's sweet words, sings how Paul overcame the world, and shares Peter's heavenly kingdom with the mother of God invoked at his side. The closing lines exhort the young man to follow the better writings, which drive sordidness from the heart and fix the mind on God.
la.moduin.eclogae: Carolingian Latin eclogue attributed to Moduin, opening with the singer's dedication of his verses to Charles and a defence of his rustic poetry against envious detractors. The work is cast as a dialogue between shepherds: the elder poet, called David, is consoled in his leafy retreat, while the younger Meliboeus hails the renewed golden Rome of the Carolingian court, catalogues the rewards poetry won for figures from Ovid, Virgil, Lucan and Ennius to contemporaries at Charles's court, and summons his companion to sing together amid bees, heat and grazing flocks. A long closing vision proclaims a universal peace under Charles's rule, with war chained and buried, wild beasts at rest with the herds, rivers rejoicing, and the untilled earth yielding its harvest. The final lines send these rustic songs to David and to the pious king, asking that he read them to the end and correct any fault with his clemency.
la.nithardus.historiae: Nithard's Historiae, a prose history in four books of Carolingian Latin, opens with a preface to a royal patron in which the author, caught up in the very troubles he records, explains his commission to commit the deeds of his times to writing, before turning to the career of Charlemagne and the succession of the emperor Louis. The narrative follows the arrangements and divisions of the empire among Louis's sons and then the wars in which Charles and Louis contend against their brother Lothar, with campaigns, river blockades, forced marches, and embassies punctuated by storms, eclipses, and comets. The account takes in the mutual oaths sworn at Strasbourg, set down in Romance and Teutonic as well as Latin, together with the Saxon Stellinga rising and Norse raids on the coasts, and moves through Lothar's defeats and the brothers' brief concord. A fourth book carries the story into renewed negotiations for a tripartite division of the kingdom and Charles's marriage, interrupted by a digression on the author's own kindred and his resolve to continue the record.
la.optatian.epistula: A Latin prose epistle by Optatian, addressed to the emperor Constantine and counted among the panegyric writings of the later imperial period, the letter presents the poet's verse for the emperor's acceptance. It opens by acknowledging that a song bound in the tighter fetters of the Muses has come into the emperor's victorious hands to be read with his serene eyes. In place of the customary invocations of Helicon, the Castalian spring, Apollo and the Muses, the writer sets the eternal felicity of Constantine's name, contrasting Virgil, the Mantuan priest of the Roman Muses who exulted under Maecenas' testimony, with himself, a poet of slender talent whose work gains its immense weight from the judgement of an emperor who applauds the Muses amid his triumphs, laws and victories. The letter closes with thanks and a plea that Constantine, whose clemency has kindled such boldness, will graciously admit the verses the poet has dared to bind.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.s_optati_: A seven-book Latin prose treatise by Optatus, bishop of Mileve in Numidia, belonging to the late antique controversy between the catholic church of Africa and the Donatist schism. The work opens by appealing to the one faith of all Christians and to the peace that Christ left them, a peace the author says has been broken by the authors of schism. Addressed over its course to the Donatist bishop Parmenianus and written against his treatises, it argues for the unity of the one catholic church throughout the world, defending the catholic clergy against charges concerning the armed soldiers sent under Macarius, rejecting Donatist rebaptism and their treatment of penance and consecrated virgins, condemning their violation of altars and chalices, discussing the traditores and whether children inherit their fathers' guilt, and urging the schismatics' return to the see of Peter and communion with the universal church.
la.ovid.ars_amatoria: The Ars Amatoria is a didactic poem in elegiac couplets by Ovid of the Augustan period, cast as instruction in the art of love delivered by a self-styled praeceptor amoris. It opens with the poet's claim that love, like ships and chariots, must be governed by ars, and with a summons to readers not yet versed in the art of loving. Books 1 and 2, addressed to men, move from where a lover may find women in Rome, theatre, circus, forum, porticoes, banquets, through courtship, letters, and persuasion to the sustaining of desire by complaisance, endurance, and tactful service, with digressions on Daedalus and Icarus and on Mars and Venus. Book 3 turns to women, treating dress, cosmetics, hair, song, and games, then the deceiving of guardians and husbands and the conduct of the bedchamber, and ends by asking its pupils to inscribe upon their spoils the words 'Naso magister erat.'
la.ovid.ex_ponto: Ex Ponto is a collection of elegiac epistles in Latin, attributed to Ovid and written during his exile at Tomis on the Black Sea. The four books comprise roughly fifty verse letters addressed to named friends, relations and members of the imperial house, in which the poet pleads for a mitigation or recall of his banishment, describes the harsh climate and warfare of the Pontic frontier, reflects on friendship, fame and the poet's craft, and commemorates events such as the triumphs of Tiberius and Germanicus. The opening poem presents the new book itself to Brutus, explaining that its letters differ from those of the Tristia only in being openly addressed to their recipients; the collection then runs through petitions, consolations, descriptions of Tomis and the Getae, poems of thanksgiving and friendship, and closes with an invective against an envious detractor of the poet's verse.
la.ovid.fasti: The Fasti of Ovid is an Augustan poem in elegiac couplets that follows the Roman calendar month by month, its six books running from the first rites of January to the close of June. The opening address to Germanicus sets out the poet's programme: to sing of times and their causes and of the risings and settings of the stars, beginning with Janus, god of the year's origin. Each month then unfolds as a sequence of festival days and commemorations, Carmentalia, Lupercalia, Parilia, Vestalia, Quinquatrus and Matralia among them, explained through etymologies, aetiological myths, antiquarian lore and dialogues between the poet and deities such as Mars, Flora and Vesta. Astronomical entries punctuate the flow, and legends and events are fixed to their dates, from the exposure of Romulus and Remus and the rape of Lucretia to temple dedications and anniversaries of the Augustan age.
la.ovid.heroides: Ovid's Heroides is an Augustan collection of fictional letters in elegiac couplets, written in the voices of mythological women to absent lovers or husbands: Penelope addresses Ulysses, Phyllis Demophoon, Briseis Achilles, Phaedra Hippolytus, Oenone Paris, Hypsipyle Jason, Dido Aeneas, and so on down to Sappho's epistle to Phaon. The work opens with Penelope's letter from Ithaca, in which she reproaches Ulysses for his long delay and reports the suitors consuming his household. The remaining letters vary this situation of separation and betrayal, each heroine blending complaint, reminiscence, entreaty and occasional threats of self-destruction. The collection closes with three paired exchanges, between Paris and Helen, Hero and Leander, and Acontius and Cydippe, in which both parties of each love affair write in turn.
la.ovid.ibis: Ovid's Ibis is an Augustan curse poem in elegiac couplets aimed at an enemy whom the speaker pointedly declines to name. It opens with the poet's complaint that, after a long career of harmless verse, a hostile figure is harassing him even in his northern exile, compelling him to take up weapons and devote his foe, after the manner of Callimachus, under the veil of the name Ibis. The bulk of the work is a vast catalogue of imprecations: drawing on a host of figures from myth and legend, the speaker wishes upon the addressee every conceivable calamity in birth, life, death, and the underworld, from bodily torments and disgrace to unending punishment among the damned. The poem closes with the warning that these curses, sent for the moment in a small book under a false name, will be followed by a fiercer attack in iambics that names its target outright if the enmity persists.
la.ovid.medicamina_faciei_femineae: The Medicamina Faciei Femineae is a short didactic elegy by the Augustan poet Ovid, composed in elegiac couplets and addressed to women on the care and adornment of the face. It opens by bidding girls learn what care commends beauty, arguing from fields, fruit, wool and ivory that cultivation improves whatever nature supplies, and adding that in an age when even men are groomed a woman's toil to please carries no reproach. The poem then urges that character is the surest and most enduring basis of charm, before setting out recipes for facial preparations: barley moistened with eggs and ground, blended with narcissus bulbs, gum and honey; roasted lupins and beans; cerussa and Illyrian iris; frankincense with Ammonian salt; fennel with myrrh; and, last, poppies steeped in cold water to be pounded and smoothed over the cheeks.
la.ovid.metamorphoses: Ovid's Metamorphoses is a Latin epic in dactylic hexameter, written in the Augustan age and divided into fifteen books, which traces the history of the world from creation to the poet's own day through an unbroken sequence of tales of transformation. It opens with an invocation to the gods and an account of the world's formation from chaos, followed by the decline of mankind through the golden, silver, bronze, and iron ages. The poem then ranges in roughly chronological order through Greek and Roman legend, including the flood of Deucalion, the stories of Phaethon, Narcissus, Daedalus, Pygmalion, and Orpheus, the Calydonian boar hunt, and the Trojan War, before turning to the early legends of Rome. It closes with the apotheoses of Romulus and Julius Caesar, praise of Augustus, and the poet's claim to enduring fame.
la.ovid.remedia_amoris: The Remedia Amoris is an Augustan didactic elegy by Ovid, composed in elegiac couplets to instruct lovers in how to free themselves from love. It opens with the poet's apology to Cupid and an appeal to lovers whom his earlier precepts have deceived, promising that the hand which taught love will also teach its cure. The teaching first urges resistance at love's onset and an active life in the courts, war, agriculture, hunting, and travel; where the passion is already established, the poet prescribes dwelling on the beloved's faults, avoiding the places, letters, and erotic poetry that feed desire, moderating wine, and diverting the affections toward a new love. Mythological exempla of ruined lovers such as Phyllis, Dido, Medea, and Circe punctuate the instruction, a passage defends the licence of erotic elegy against its critics, and the poem closes with the healed summoned to pay votive garlands to the poet.
la.ovid.tristia: The Tristia is a collection of five books of elegiac couplets composed by Ovid during his banishment from Rome under Augustus, from Tomis on the Black Sea coast. It opens with the exiled poet addressing his book as it journeys to Rome in his place. The remaining poems, cast as letters to the emperor, to his wife, and to various friends, lament the poet's fall, recount the perilous sea voyage and the fierce winters of the Pontic shore among the Getic and Sarmatian peoples, defend the erotic poetry that led to his punishment, and petition repeatedly for mitigation of his sentence; an autobiographical elegy in the fourth book surveys his upbringing, family, friendships, and poetic career.
la.paschasius_radbertus.carmina: A short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Paschasius Radbertus, of uncertain exact date, cast as a funerary lament with allegorical dialogue. It opens with a summons to men of every age to weep for a departed spiritual father and to lay him to rest at Corbie amid flowers, tears, and song. The lament then unfolds through alternating speeches, by a grieving daughter-figure, a mother, and a maiden named Galathea, who bewail death's indiscriminate power, console themselves with the soul's ascent to the heavenly bridechamber, and invoke the sister virtues Faith, Hope, and Charity as the means by which the soul reaches the royal banquet of Christ. The closing section addresses the virgin Sophia, bidding her go before King Charles to present, on behalf of one who styles himself abbot Radbertus, an offering that reveals the mysteries of the body and blood of Christ.
la.paul_the_apostle_saint.epigramma: A brief Latin item attributed in the source record to Paul the Apostle under the title Epigramma, its six lines being the edition's prefatory prose rather than verse: a note on transmission followed by an argumentum. The note reports that the piece survives in Parisinus 7558 appended to Claudius Marius Victor's Alethia under the inscription 'S. Paulini epigramma', that Gagneius first printed it as Victor's work, and that Wernsdorf judged it a sermon rather than an epistle, so that its authorship remains disputed; the accompanying summary relates how Salmon, a priest revisiting the city of his upbringing after long absence, discusses with the aged monk Thesbo the vices of its men and, more severely still, of its women despite the blow of barbarian ravages. Dated in the record to the Early Imperial era and classed as theology, the item serves readers of intertexts chiefly as evidence for the attribution history of a Christian moral dialogue and for themes of civic corruption in Christian Latin poetry.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.carmina: Paulinus of Aquileia's Carmina is a Carolingian collection of religious verse that opens with a first-person confession of Trinitarian faith, complete with anathemas against ancient heretics from Cerinthus to Sabellius. Occasional pieces follow, among them a poem asking the Irish priest Zacharias for his prayers and a lament for a warrior named Heric, in which the rivers and cities of the Aquileian countryside mourn his death in battle. Longer biblical narratives come next: a retelling of the raising of Lazarus, worked out at length in typological, allegorical and moral senses, and a versified life of Joseph running from his dreams and betrayal by his brothers to the reunion with Jacob in Egypt. A penitential abecedary in which personified vices assail the sinner, together with liturgical poems on the nativity, charity, the resurrection, the presentation in the temple, the Lenten fast, the feasts of Mark and of Peter and Paul, a church dedication, a prayer for God's command over the winds, and a Kyrie eleison, rounds out the collection.
la.paulinus_of_aquileia.versus_de_destructi: A Carolingian Latin lament by Paulinus of Aquileia on the destruction of Aquileia, addressed to the ruined city itself. The poem opens with the speaker finding no tears or words equal to mourning Aquileia's ashes, then unfolds across twenty-three four-line stanzas, each beginning with a successive letter of the alphabet. It contrasts the city's former glory as metropolitan seat of Venetia, crowded with clergy, churches and nobility, with the pride that drew divine wrath, Attila's devastating siege, the massacre and enslavement of its people, the burning of its sacred books and vessels, and its reduction from a royal city to a lair of beasts and thieves. It closes with Attila himself tormented in hell and prayers to Christ to avert such wrath and protect the faithful.
la.paulinus_of_nola.carmina: The Carmina gathers the Latin Christian poetry of Paulinus of Nola, opening with a prose preface and accompanying verses on a gift of ficedulae (figpeckers) sent to the poet's elder correspondent Ausonius. From there the collection ranges across verse epistles defending the poet's turn from secular letters to Christ, a narrative poem on the birth of John the Baptist, metrical renderings of psalms, and a series of annual natalicia in honour of St. Felix of Nola that recount the saint's life, miracles, and the growing basilica complex at Nola. Further pieces commemorate the return of the priest Niceta, console the poet's friends over the death of the child Celsus, polemicize against pagan cult, and record inscriptions and prayers for the churches Paulinus built.
la.paulinus_of_nola.epistulae: A Latin collection of letters by Paulinus of Nola, the late antique aristocrat turned priest, bishop of Nola and prolific correspondent. The opening letter addresses a recipient in the language of honeyed sweetness, praising the words of scripture and the correspondent's renunciation of wealth for Christ, before turning to questions of how the faithful should answer those who demand a reckoning for their conduct. Over the course of the correspondence Paulinus consoles a bereaved husband, urges a widow to perseverance, exhorts a young soldier to leave Caesar's service for Christ's, and recounts marvels attending a shipwrecked sailor preserved alone at sea. The collection closes with letters of pastoral instruction and scriptural interpretation addressed to figures such as Severus, Augustine, and Alypius, covering topics from almsgiving to the significance of the discovery of the cross in Jerusalem.
la.paulinus_of_pella.eucharisticus: Paulinus of Pella's Eucharisticus is a Late Antique Latin autobiography composed as an act of thanksgiving to God for the course of the author's life. It opens with a prose preface in which the aged writer explains that, worn down by long exile and troubled idleness, he was moved by divine mercy to record his life in gratitude. The narrative then follows him from his birth at Pella in Macedonia and upbringing at Bordeaux, through his Greek and Latin schooling, youthful ease, marriage and management of the family estates, into the disasters of the Gothic invasions: his father's death, the burning of Bordeaux and loss of his property, the siege of Bazas, and his dealings with the usurper Attalus, the Goths of Ataulf and the Alans. It closes with his impoverished resettlement at Marseilles, his embrace of a religious way of life, the trials of old age, and prayers of continuing thanksgiving.
la.paulus_albarus.carmina: The Carmina attributed to Paulus Albarus, here placed in the Carolingian era, is a collection of medieval Latin devotional verse of uncertain date. It opens with an invocation urging the nightingale to let her song surpass all instruments, birds, and the Muses in praise of Christ. The remainder assembles several longer pieces: a poem in which the cock and other creatures join in lauding the Creator, followed by a versified survey of the books of Scripture from Genesis through the prophets to the Apocalypse, expounding their historical and mystical senses; a poem on the cross shining in the full moon, admonishing unbelievers and extolling Jerome as the authoritative interpreter; and a hymn narrating the martyrdom of Eulogius, closed by an epitaph in which Albarus names himself, confesses his sins, and asks the reader for tears and prayer.
la.paulus_diaconus.carmina: The Carmina transmitted under the name of Paul the Deacon collect the Latin poetry of a scholar of the Carolingian age whose pieces are rooted in Lombard Italy and the circle of Charlemagne. The collection opens with a chronological poem reckoning the years of the world from creation, through the patriarchs, the giving of the law, and the Babylonian captivity, down to the poet's own day in Lombard Italy under Desiderius and Adelchis. The remainder ranges from verses on the miracles of St Benedict and a praise poem on Lake Como to a riddle exchange with Charlemagne, a verse catalogue of the bishops of Metz from Clement to Angilramn, epitaphs and laments for Carolingian queens and princesses and for the Beneventan prince Arichis, and a fable of the sick lion and the flattering fox. Hymns and devotional pieces close the collection, among them the Baptist hymn beginning 'Ut queant laxis resonare fibris' and a metrical life of St Paulinus of Aquileia.
la.persius.saturae: The Saturae of the Early Imperial poet Persius are a book of satiric poems in hexameters, opening with a prologue that stages the poet's exchange with an imagined reader who doubts that anyone will read such verse. The poems that follow mount a severe moral critique of contemporary Roman life, attacking literary affectation and fawning audiences, empty prayers for riches, neglected study and self-discipline, and the hidden vices men conceal behind a respectable exterior. A later poem considers how a young heir should use his patrimony, urging plain and moderate living against luxury and gluttony, and the book closes with a dialogue in which a legacy-hunter, Chrysippus, reckons up the profits he has wrung from the dead.
la.petronius.satyricon: A collection of the verse fragments surviving from the Satyricon, a sprawling satirical prose work of the early Imperial period attributed to Petronius. It opens with a trochaic prologue in which an aspiring poet is urged to temper his art with frugal morals before drinking deep of the Homeric spring. The remaining lines gather the poems embedded in the narrative as it has come down: moralising epigrams on money, fortune, friendship and theatrical pretence; a long account of the Trojan horse and the death of Laocoon; a declamatory passage on civil war; verses on baldness, gluttony and the defence of plain speech; the prayer of a penitent to Priapus and the god's own boastful reply; and a witch's swaggering catalogue of her power over nature, beasts and the heavenly bodies.
la.petrus_riga.aurora: The Aurora is a medieval Latin verse work by Petrus Riga that paraphrases the books of the Bible in hexameter-style verse while folding in spiritual exposition. It opens with prefatory matter, including verses by a certain canon praising the book through a catalogue of scriptural figures, comparing it to the manna sent from heaven, to Ezekiel's scroll written within and without, and to Moses' veiled face unveiled by the light of Christ. The body of the work follows the order of Scripture, versifying the narrative of each book and interlacing allegorical and moral interpretation, as when the stone rejected from the building of the temple is read as Christ the Mediator joining synagogue and Church. Its closing books expound the Song of Songs as the discourse of Christ the Bridegroom with his bride, the faithful soul, whose answer to the perverse ends the poem.
la.phaedrus.fabulae_aesopiae: The Fabulae Aesopiae of Phaedrus is a Latin verse-fable collection of the Early Imperial period, recasting material inherited from the Greek fabulist Aesop in senarii. The opening prologue claims a twofold dowry for the book, that it moves laughter and counsels a prudent life, before leading into the wolf and the lamb quarrelling at the stream. Across its several books the work offers brief animal fables each rounded off with a moral, anecdotes in which Aesop himself appears among Athenians, masters and patrons, episodes from Greek and Roman history, and prologues and epilogues defending fable as veiled speech under servitude, with satirical jabs at busybodies, flatterers and the rich. It closes with mythological exempla of fruitless punishment, Tantalus, Sisyphus and the Danaids, followed by the precepts voiced by the Delphic oracle.
la.philastrius.diversarum_hereseon_liber: The Diversarum Hereseon Liber, a Latin prose heresiology of the late antique period by Philastrius, opens with a declared programme of enumerating the pestilent errors that arose from the beginning of the world, first among the Jews and then after the Lord's coming in the flesh, the devil being likened to the partridge of Jeremiah's prophecy. The work proceeds as a sequential catalogue of sects: Old Testament-era Jewish groups and idolatries (Ophites, Cainites, Sethians, Sadducees, Pharisees, Samaritans, Essenes, sun- and Baal-worshippers) are followed by the Christian heresiarchs from Simon Magus through Menander, Basilides, Valentinus, Marcion, Tatian, the Montanists, Manichaeans, Sabellians, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Arians, Novatians and Donatians, each entry naming a founder and summarising his doctrine with refutations drawn from scripture. A closing and far longer stretch treats dozens of further 'heresies' defined chiefly by misreadings of the Bible, on creation, the soul, angels, the giants, the origin of languages and the Greek versions of the Old Testament, the Psalter, the Canticle and the Christian fasts, interlaced with standing polemic against Judaism and paganism.
la.plautus.amphitruo: In Plautus' Amphitruo, a comedy of the Roman Republic, the god Mercury opens the play by asking the audience for silence and declaring that, since kings and gods appear in it alongside a slave, it will be a 'tragicomoedia' rather than pure tragedy or pure comedy. The action turns on Jupiter's impersonation of Amphitruo, general of the Theban forces against the Teloboans, in a night made marvellously long for his liaison with Amphitruo's wife Alcmena, while Mercury takes the shape of the slave Sosia to keep the household at bay. When the real Amphitruo arrives home with Sosia fresh from victory, each finds himself doubled, and mutual charges of madness and adultery drive Alcmena to swear her chastity while Amphitruo seeks a witness from the fleet. The entanglement dissolves when the slave girl Bromia reports Alcmena's painless delivery of twin boys and the infant Hercules' strangling of two serpents, after which Jupiter reveals himself, restores Amphitruo to his wife's favour, promises the hero immortality, and closes by calling for applause.
la.plautus.bacchides: The Bacchides is a Latin comedy in dramatic meter by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic. The preserved play begins abruptly in mid-scene, without a prologue, as the young Pistoclerus, distracted by the courtesan Bacchis, is berated by his tutor Lydus. The plot centers on two sisters who bear the same name, Bacchis, one of them the Samian beloved of Mnesilochus, and above all on the resourceful slave Chrysalus, who repeatedly cheats the two elderly fathers, Nicobulus and Philoxenus, out of gold for the young lovers, triumphantly likening each deception to episodes from the Trojan War. After the claims of a soldier, Cleomachus, on the Samian Bacchis are bought off with promised money, the fathers arrive to reclaim their sons, only to be charmed by the sisters into joining the banquet themselves, and the play closes with an appeal to the audience for applause.
la.plautus.cistellaria: The Cistellaria is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republican period by Titus Maccius Plautus, composed in dramatic metres within the palliata tradition of Roman plays adapted from Greek models. The work survives only in part, and the 680 lines preserved in Leo's 1895 edition centre on the world of the courtesans: the opening scene follows Selenium and her companions as they weigh friendship, freedwoman status, and the raising of daughters against the hazards of their trade, while the plot as a whole turns on recognition and a young woman's recovered parentage, as the title 'The Casket' suggests. For readers hunting intertexts, the play offers parallels with Greek New Comedy and with other Plautine and Roman comic treatments of recognition tokens, stock lovers, and courtesan diction.
la.plautus.curculio: The Curculio is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, named for the parasite Curculio whose errand sets the plot in motion. The action centers on the young Phaedromus, in love with Planesium, a slave girl held by the pimp Cappadox, and on the trickery by which money is procured to ransom her, ending in a recognition scene that restores the heroine to free birth. Composed in dramatic meters for the Roman stage, the play includes the celebrated fourth-act monologue in which a speaker surveys the trades and characters gathered in the Roman Forum.
la.plautus.epidicus: Epidicus is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a fabula palliata of the Roman Republic set in Athens, named for its quick-witted slave protagonist. The play opens without a prologue, mid-conversation, as the slave Epidicus is stopped in the street by the soldier Thesprio and learns that his young master Stratippocles, son of Periphanes, has bought a captive girl from war booty with money borrowed at Thebes. The plot follows Epidicus's efforts to raise the debt behind the father's back: he dupes Periphanes into paying for a hired piper-girl in the belief that she is the daughter he fathered long ago, deflects a wealthy soldier who arrives to purchase the captive, and is exposed when the imposture collapses, until a recognition reveals that the captive girl Telestis is in fact Periphanes' long-lost daughter and so Stratippocles' half-sister. The closing scene leaves the two old men comically outwitted, and Epidicus wins his freedom as reward for his roguish services.
la.plautus.menaechmi: The Menaechmi is a Roman comedy of the Republic by Plautus, written in dramatic meter. A prologue addressed to the spectators announces the poet and recounts the backstory: twin sons of a Syracusan merchant, alike beyond telling apart, were separated as boys when one was carried off at Tarentum and brought up in Epidamnus, and both were afterwards given the name Menaechmus. The action follows the Syracusan brother's arrival in Epidamnus with his slave Messenio in search of the lost twin, and the tangle of mistaken identity that ensues as the resident Menaechmus's wife, his mistress Erotium, and the parasite Peniculus mistake first one brother and then the other. Scenes of feigned madness before the wife's father and a physician, Messenio's rescue of the brother he takes for his own master and his subsequent manumission, and the recognition of the twins through their shared name, parentage, and childhood memories lead to the closing announcement of an auction of the Epidamnian's household, slaves, land, and wife, and a farewell to the audience.
la.plautus.miles_gloriosus: Plautus's Miles Gloriosus, a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic composed in dramatic meter, opens with the braggart soldier Pyrgopolynices and his parasite Artotrogus inflating one another with extravagant tales of martial prowess. Set in Ephesus, the play follows the cunning slave Palaestrio as he schemes to reunite the Athenian Pleusicles with Philocomasium, whom the soldier has abducted from Athens and keeps as his concubine. Aided by the neighbour Periplectomenus, Palaestrio has Philocomasium pass as her own twin sister, slipping through a hole in the party wall to fool the watchman Sceledrus, and then stages a courtesan in the role of Periplectomenus's wife to entice the soldier into giving up the girl. Philocomasium departs by sea with her lover, and the comedy closes with the duped soldier, caught as an adulterer in the neighbour's house, beaten and bound to silence.
la.plautus.stichus: Stichus, a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Republican period, opens with two sisters lamenting the three years' absence of their husbands and fearing that their father intends to marry them to other men. Their father, Antiphon, questions the daughters on wifely conduct and tries to persuade them to leave their husbands' houses, while the hungry parasite Gelasimus stages a mock auction of his slender 'goods' in pursuit of a dinner invitation. News brought by the slave Pinacium reveals that the husbands, Epignomus and Pamphilippus, have returned from Asia enriched; the brothers greet their wives, reconcile with their father-in-law in a scene of pointed banter, and grant their slaves a day of freedom. The comedy closes with the drinking party of Stichus and Sangarinus, rival lovers of the courtesan Stephanium, whose songs, dancing, and farewell to the spectators end the play.
la.plautus.truculentus: Truculentus is a Latin comedy by Plautus, a dramatist of the Roman Republic. Its prologue, spoken in the poet's own person, asks the audience for a small piece of their city so that the scene may be set at Athens, where the courtesan Phronesium and her maid Astaphium exploit the men who love them. The action turns on Phronesium's feigned childbirth: to extract gifts from the bankrupt Diniarchus and the soldier Stratophanes she passes off a supposititious infant, in fact the child Diniarchus fathered on the daughter of Callicles, to whom he had once been betrothed, while the rough country servant Truculentus, who gives the play its name, is tamed by Astaphium and the young Strabax squanders his father's money at the same door. When Callicles uncovers the deception, Diniarchus admits his fault and marries Callicles' daughter, the child is restored to its family, and the rival suitors are left still outbidding one another for the courtesan's favor.
la.pliny_the_younger.letters: A collection of Latin prose letters by Pliny the Younger, composed in the early Imperial period. The opening letter to Septicius Clarus explains that Pliny gathered letters he had written with unusual care, arranging them not chronologically but as each had come to hand. The nine private books address friends and acquaintances on matters ranging from villa life, hunting, and literary recitations to court advocacy, senatorial trials, recollections of Domitianic tyranny, and the eruption of Vesuvius that killed the author's uncle. A tenth book preserves official correspondence with the emperor Trajan from Pliny's governorship of Bithynia and Pontus, treating public works, provincial administration, and the handling of Christians.
la.poeta_saxo.annales_de_gestis_karoli_magn: The Annales de Gestis Karoli Magni is a Carolingian Latin epic in hexameters by the poet known as Poeta Saxo, narrating the reign of Charlemagne in five books. It opens with Christ's birth from the Virgin and Charles's accession to sole rule of the Franks on the death of his brother Carloman. The first four books proceed year by year through his wars against the Saxons, Lombards, Basques, Bavarians, Avars, Slavs, Saracens and other enemies, alongside embassies from distant rulers, church synods, his imperial coronation in Rome by Pope Leo, and the settlement that finally ends the long Saxon wars. The work closes with a lament for the emperor's death and a fuller account of his ancestry, bodily appearance, dress, diet, learning, piety and building works.
la.polignac.antilucretius: The Antilucretius is a Latin philosophical poem in hexameters, presented as a rebuttal addressed to a friend named Quinti against the atomistic and hedonistic doctrine of Epicurus and Lucretius. It opens with the speaker invoking divine Wisdom and announcing his undertaking to demolish the Sect of Epicurus, warning Quinti against the seductions of pleasure. The work then proceeds through a long systematic refutation: it attacks the theory of atoms, the void, the motion of matter, the origin of mind from matter, the Epicurean gods, the denial of providence, the claims of contemporary physics from Gassendi through Descartes, Huygens, Newton, and Spinoza, and the Hobbesian account of justice, arguing throughout for a supreme, provident Creator, the immateriality and immortality of the soul, free will, and natural law, before closing with an appeal to the divine origin of religion and the promise of rewards and punishments after death.
la.pontius_diaconus.acta_proconsularia: A brief Latin prose record, ascribed to Pontius the Deacon, of the judicial examinations and martyrdom of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus. It opens with Cyprian's interrogation by the proconsul Aspasius Paternus at Carthage, in which the bishop confesses himself a Christian and is banished to Curubis. The remainder follows his recall and second hearing before Galerius Maximus, his condemnation to death by the sword, his execution before a crowd of the brethren, the burial of his body by night near the fishponds on the Mappalian road, and the proconsul's own death a few days later.
la.priscian.perihegesis: The Perihegesis is a Latin geographical work of Late Antique date attributed to Priscian. It opens with a prayer to the creator, asking leave to sing of the lands, seas, rivers, cities and peoples of the world, and presents the earth as an island girdled by Ocean and divided among Libya, Europe and Asia. The body of the work tours each continent in turn, covering Africa with Egypt and the Nile, Europe from Spain and Italy through Greece to its islands, and Asia from the Black Sea and Caucasus across Syria, Arabia, Persia and India, with sustained attention to mountains, rivers, seas, cities and peoples. Woven through the geographic description are accounts of natural marvels, above all stones and gems credited with remarkable properties.
la.propertius.elegies: The Elegies of Propertius are a four-book collection of Latin love elegy in elegiac couplets by Sextus Propertius, a poet of the Augustan age. The collection opens with the poet's declaration that Cynthia was the first to ensnare him with her eyes, an account of his amorous servitude accompanied by warnings to his friend Tullus against the miseries of love. Books 2 and 3 continue the turbulent relationship with Cynthia through jealousy, quarrels, and reconciliations, alongside reflections on wealth, faithlessness, and the poet's own art and calling, including addresses to Maecenas and claims for his place among earlier elegists. The fourth book widens to Roman themes, presenting poems on the god Vertumnus, the wife Arethusa writing to her absent soldier husband, the treachery of Tarpeia, Hercules and Cacus, the temple of Apollo and the battle of Actium, a nocturnal visit from Cynthia's ghost, and the farewell speech of Cornelia delivered from beyond the grave.
la.prudentius.apotheosis: The Apotheosis is a didactic poem in Latin by the Late Antique Christian poet Prudentius, a polemical treatise on the divinity of Christ and the unity of the Trinity written to confute a series of heresies. It opens with a confession of the threefold God, one in substance, and a prayer for sure guidance through the false paths of erring teachers. The poem then takes up successive errors in turn: Sabellian confusion of Father and Son, doctrines that deny the Word's full deity, Jewish rejection of Christ, lingering paganism, illustrated by an episode in which a Christian page at the imperial court disrupts a sacrificial rite, the Manichaean denial of Christ's real body, and the claim that the human soul is divine or a part of God. It closes with an affirmation of the resurrection of the flesh, as the poet addresses his own members and bids them rise with Christ, wholly restored to their former state.
la.prudentius.contra_symmachum: Contra Symmachum is a two-book Latin polemical poem by the late antique Christian poet Prudentius, written against the plea of the pagan senator Symmachus for the restoration of the Altar of Victory. The first book opens with an allegory of the apostle Paul, shipwrecked on Malta, shaking off a venomous serpent that stands for resurgent paganism striking at the church, then turns to a satirical survey of the births, loves and disgraces of the traditional gods, the deification of emperors, and Constantine's victory under the sign of the cross and Rome's conversion. The second book stages a debate in which a learned orator defends the ancestral cult of Victory and personified Faith replies, arguing for the one Creator against fate and the city's genius, presenting Roman conquest as providential preparation for Christian unity, and closing with a defense of Christian virginity against the Vestals and an appeal to end gladiatorial slaughter.
la.prudentius.dittochaeon: The Dittochaeon is a short Late Antique Latin Christian poem by Prudentius, made up of four-line verses each devoted to a single biblical scene. The opening quatrains deal with Eve and the Fall, Cain and Abel, Noah's dove, and the patriarchs Abraham and Joseph. The sequence then follows Moses and the Exodus before turning to the Gospel narrative, treating the Annunciation, Nativity, adoration of the Magi and shepherds, the massacre of the Innocents, and figures such as John the Baptist. It closes with episodes from Acts and the Apocalypse, among them the martyrdom of Stephen, Peter's vision, the conversion of Saul, and the elders who praise the Lamb.
la.prudentius.epilogus: The Epilogus is a short Latin poem in which the late antique Christian poet Prudentius closes his collected verse with a statement of humble offering. It opens by contrasting the pious donor who gives money to feed the poor with the poet who can consecrate only his swift iambics and rolling trochaic measures, poor in holiness and powerless to relieve the needy, yet assured that God benignly approves the lowly song. The poem then pictures a rich man's house stocked with vessels of every sort, golden cups, polished bronze basins, earthenware pots, silver dishes, ivory pieces and bowls hollowed from oak or elm, where any vessel is serviceable if it fits its master's use. In that house the poet likens himself to a worn little earthenware vessel that Christ fits to humble purposes in the father's hall, ending with the thought that even the least service to God has its profit and that whatever may befall, it will have been a joy to sound Christ's name aloud.
la.prudentius.hamartigenia: The Hamartigenia ('Origin of Sin') is a late-antique Latin didactic poem by Prudentius that attacks the Marcionite doctrine of two gods, one good and one evil, and argues that the one God is not the author of evil. It opens with the offerings of Cain and Abel, reading the fratricide as a figure of the heretic who divides the Godhead while claiming to worship rightly. The poem then refutes the dualist position at length, attributing evil instead to the pride and envy of a fallen angel and to the free choice of human beings, whose sins corrupt both themselves and the created world; a catalog of vices, a defense of free will supported by the exempla of Lot and his wife and of Ruth and Orpah, and a survey of the soul's fate after death in hell and paradise carry the argument forward. It closes with a prayer to Christ for pardon and for mitigation of punishment.
la.prudentius.peristephanon: Prudentius's Peristephanon, a Late Antique collection of Christian poems, comprises fourteen hymns in varied metres celebrating individual martyrs and groups of martyrs, including Lawrence, Eulalia, the eighteen martyrs of Saragossa, Vincent, Fructuosus, Quirinus, Romanus, Hippolytus, Peter and Paul, Cyprian, and Agnes. The poems narrate the saints' trials, tortures and deaths, describe their shrines and relics, and include accounts of the author's own pilgrimages and prayers at martyrs' tombs in Spain and Rome.
la.prudentius.psychomachia: A late-antique Latin allegorical poem by Prudentius, the Psychomachia opens with a preface that reads Abraham's rescue of Lot and his encounter with Melchisedech as a figure of the soul's inner warfare, followed by a prayer to Christ to arm the mind against sin. The main narrative stages a battle in which personified Virtues, Faith, Chastity, Patience, Humility with Hope, Sobriety, and Good Works, defeat their opposing Vices, from the Worship of the Old Gods and Lust through Wrath, Pride, and Luxury to Avarice, with biblical exempla such as Judith, David, and Jonathan woven into the victors' speeches. After the victory, the disguised Discordia, also called Heresy, infiltrates the camp and wounds Concordia before being destroyed, and the work closes with the Virtues building a jeweled temple for the enthroned Wisdom, followed by a final prayer of thanks to Christ.
la.pseudo_cyprian.adversus_judaeos: A Latin theological treatise of the later Roman Empire handed down under Cyprian's name, Adversus Judaeos is a polemical work in prose defending the Christian claim to the scriptural inheritance. It opens with an exhortation to perceive the divine sacrament of Christ with the eyes of faith rather than by hearing alone. The argument then surveys salvation history from Adam through Noah, Abraham, and Moses, casting Israel's persecution of the prophets and the killing of Christ as a breach of the paternal testament that justifies God's transfer of the covenant to the Gentiles, who are summoned to baptism and the new testament without distinction of rank, age, or condition. It closes with Israel depicted as an exile stripped of temple, kingdom, and homeland yet offered pardon on repentance, and with a vision of the humble and unlearned, children, women, and rustics, now teaching the scriptures to those who once instructed them.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_duplici_martyrio: A Latin prose treatise on theology attributed, pseudepigraphically, to Cyprian and of uncertain date in the later Roman imperial period. It opens as a letter of thanks to a correspondent named Fortunatus, presenting the work as a promised second book on the twofold kind of martyrdom. The treatise surveys the open martyrdom of blood, the meaning of witness, the efficacy of Christ's blood, and the way God's name is glorified or dishonoured by the conduct of the baptized, before turning at length to the hidden, unbloody martyrdom of daily life, condemning avarice, lust, drunkenness and idolatry as covert apostasy and censuring monks and virgins whose outward discipline conceals inward vice. It closes by urging believers in every state of life to bear loss, illness and temptation with patience, so that the whole life may render testimony to God.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_singularitate_clericor: A Latin prose treatise of the later imperial period on clerical discipline, transmitted under Cyprian's name and of uncertain date and authorship, which argues that clergy must live apart from women. It opens as an address to 'dearest sons', where the author recalls promising a general letter on the conduct of clerics but reports being compelled, by a divine warning and by scandals in his community, to write instead against clergy who cohabit with women. The argument proceeds chiefly through authorities such as Solomon and Paul to portray female proximity as a snare, rebuts objectors who cite the examples of Elijah, the apostles, Christ, angels and martyrs in defence of such households, and concedes only liturgical gatherings and works of charity as legitimate occasions for contact with women. It closes with a sustained encomium of 'singularitas', the single chaste life, together with practical directions on clerics' households and hospitality, gathered under a final exhortation drawn from Paul.
la.quintilian_pseudo.major_declamations: The Major Declamations (Declamationes maiores) are a collection of extended fictional courtroom speeches in Latin prose of the early imperial period, transmitted under the name of Quintilian though attributed to him rather than securely his. The corpus opens with the case of a blind son and his stepmother who accuse one another of the murder of the boy's father, the pleadings turning on evidence such as a sword left in the wound and bloodied palm-prints on a wall. Each subsequent speech is likewise prefaced by a brief statement of a hypothetical case and then argued at length before the judges, whether in prosecution or in defence. The collection ranges over disputed inheritances, alleged poisoning, an astrologer's prediction that a brave soldier will kill his father, a doctor who dissects one twin to cure the other, a poor man's son who dies in the arena to ransom his rich friend, ghosts bound by magic, suspected incest, and conflicts of parental severity, fate, suicide and vengeance, sustained throughout by dense moral and psychological argument in the manner of the declamation schools.
la.rufinus_of_aquileia.interpretatio_oratio: A late-antique Latin rendering by Rufinus of Aquileia of nine orations of the Cappadocian bishop Gregory of Nazianzus, made at the request of his friend Apronianus. The collection opens with a dedicatory preface recounting Gregory's life, chastity and eloquence, before turning to the Apologeticus, Gregory's defence of his withdrawal from priestly office after ordination, an extended meditation on the care of souls, the discipline required of teachers and the danger of disputing about God unseasonably. The remaining books translate further discourses, among them sermons on the Nativity or Epiphany of the Lord and orations against the Arians and against those who contend indecently over the law, moving through biblical exempla of prophets and apostles to reflections on speech, silence and the duties of shepherds.
la.rusticus_presbyter.epistula_ad_eucherium: A brief Late Antique prose letter of theological content, written by a presbyter named Rusticus to Eucherius of Lyon. It opens with word that the writings Eucherius sent to be copied at Rusticus's request have been transcribed and both volumes returned to him, and with the confession that the recipient's doctrine, which most fully opens the great questions and enigmas of both Testaments and pours the light of spiritual understanding into the eyes of the heart, cannot worthily be praised. Rusticus then recalls an epigram read in boyhood beneath the portrait of Virgil in a library, declaring the poet best praised by his own songs, and applies it to Eucherius's work, which needs no external panegyric; he foretells that Eucherius will be celebrated by the mouths of all Christians as a teacher of posterity, and closes by asking him, as a holy friend of God and father in Christ, to pray for his correspondent.
la.rutilius.de_reditu: De Reditu is a Late Antique Latin elegy by Rutilius, composed in elegiac couplets. The opening lines pair an address to the reader with a hymn to Rome as mother of men and gods, 'urbem fecisti, quod prius orbis erat,' before turning to the speaker's reluctant departure from the city. The poem then recounts a sea voyage from Rome toward the speaker's native Gallic estates, a route taken because 'Getic' devastation has wrecked the Tuscan countryside and the Via Aurelia. Its contents combine first-person travel narrative, topographical description, patriotic panegyric, and lament for a war-torn Italy.
la.sallust.catilina: Sallust's Catilina, a prose historiographical monograph of the Roman Republic, recounts the conspiracy of L. Sergius Catiline against the Roman state and its suppression during the consulship of Cicero. It opens with a preface on the worth of exertion of mind and body and the pursuit of lasting glory, followed by a portrait of Catiline's character and a digression on Rome's decline from the austerity of its early institutions to the corruption fostered by Sulla's victory. The narrative follows the growth of the plot among indebted nobles, Sullan veterans and ruined plebs, the betrayal of the city conspirators through Q. Curius, Fulvia and the envoys of the Allobroges, and their arrest, with opposing senate speeches in which Caesar argues for imprisonment and Cato for execution, before the condemned are put to death in the Tullianum prison. The work ends with Catiline's march into Etruria, his exhortation to his troops, his defeat and death in battle against the army of Antonius under the legate Petreius, and a closing picture of mingled grief and joy in the victorious camp.
la.sallust.jugurtha: Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum, a Latin prose monograph of Roman Republican historiography, opens with a preface on the superiority of mental virtue to bodily goods and the author's withdrawal from politics into writing history. The narrative then follows Rome's war against Jugurtha, king of Numidia, from his murder of his adoptive brother Hiempsal and expulsion of Adherbal through the siege and massacre at Cirta, the failure of Roman embassies, and the corruption of senators and commanders by the king's bribes. Subsequent sections recount the Mamilian inquiry, the campaigns of Metellus, the rise of the new man Marius to the consulship, the capture of Capsa and of the mountain fortress by the Muluccha, and Sulla's negotiations with King Bocchus of Mauretania, which culminate in Jugurtha's betrayal into Roman hands. The work ends with Jugurtha led in chains to Rome and Marius celebrating a triumph as consul.
la.salvianus.ad_ecclesiam: A Latin prose homily or epistolary treatise on almsgiving, addressed in the voice of a humble servant to the catholic church, whose authorship is assigned to the presbyter Salvian of Massilia in the edition's heading. The work opens with an apostrophe to the church lamenting that many of her children hoard their wealth rather than use for mercy the goods God has entrusted to them. From this starting point it develops a sustained argument that wealth is held from God only in usufruct, that avarice is a form of idolatry, and that failure to dispense riches, whether in life or at death, brands even the professedly religious as unbelievers. The greater part of the treatise rebuts a series of anticipated objections: that parental affection justifies leaving inheritances to children, that widows, virgins, continent couples, monks, and clerics are exempt, and that Christ has no need of human gifts, each answered by appeal to scriptural precept and example, including the parable of Lazarus and the rich man. It closes by refuting the claim that kinship should outweigh Christ at the hour of death, and with exhortations to redeem sin through repentance and alms before the final judgement.
la.scriptores_historiae_augustae.historia_a: A late-antique Latin prose collection of imperial biographies of uncertain authorship and date, transmitted under the names of various scriptores such as Spartianus, Capitolinus, Lampridius, Gallicanus and Vulcacius, and traditionally entitled the Historia Augusta. Its file opens with the life of Hadrian narrated from his Spanish origins and upbringing through his reign, travels, building projects and troubled succession, and the work proceeds through the lives of emperors and claimants from Hadrian's adopted heirs and the Antonines down through the Severan dynasty, the rival usurpations of Pescennius Niger and Clodius Albinus, the reigns of Caracalla, Geta, Macrinus and Elagabalus, the virtuous Alexander Severus and the brutal Maximinus Thrax, ending with the Gordians and the brief joint rule of Maximus and Balbinus. The biographies mix genealogy, omens and portents, military campaigns, administrative and legal measures, personal habits and physical descriptions, and frequently quote letters, speeches and verses attributed to their subjects, while naming earlier writers such as Marius Maximus, Herodian and Dexippus as sources.
la.secundinus.epistula_secundini_ad_augusti: A late-antique Latin letter in prose from Secundinus to Augustine, composed from a Manichaean standpoint in answer to Augustine's writings against Manichaeus. It opens with a salutation and thanksgiving that extol Augustine's holiness and pray for protection against the evil spirit assailing him. The argument denies that Augustine was ever a genuine Manichaean, rebukes his attacks on the Old Testament and his scriptural proofs, and portrays the devil's long campaign of deception from the fall of the apostles to the rise of heresies. Doctrinal passages defend the two natures and the primal battle between light and darkness, offer to settle remaining points in a peaceful colloquy, and close with repeated pleas that Augustine renounce his errors and return to the truth.
la.sedulius.a_solis_ortus_cardine: A Solis Ortus Cardine is a late antique Latin hymn by Sedulius, cast in twenty-three quatrains whose opening letters run alphabetically from A to Z. It opens with a call to sing of Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, from the rising of the sun to the bounds of the earth. The poem then proceeds through the nativity narrative, the annunciation, the birth in the manger, the angels and shepherds, Herod, the Magi and the mourning mothers of the innocents, before surveying Christ's miracles, among them the water changed to wine, the healing of the centurion's servant, Peter walking on the waves, the raising of Lazarus and the staunching of the woman's flow of blood. It closes with the betrayal, scourging and crucifixion, the resurrection and the women at the sepulchre, Christ's triumph over hell and his return to the heavens, ending with an invitation to sing his victory.
la.sedulius.carmen_paschale: The Carmen Paschale is a Christian epic in six books of Latin hexameters by the Late Antique poet Sedulius. Its prologue sets the fictions of pagan poetry against the saving miracles of Christ, whom the poet invokes as his theme and guide. The poem first surveys Old Testament wonders, from Enoch, Sarah, and the crossing of the Red Sea to Jonah, the fiery furnace, and Daniel, presented as anticipations of Christ, and then proceeds through his life: the virgin birth and the adoration of the magi, the miracles and teaching of his ministry, and at length the Passion, with the two thieves, the earthquake and opened tombs, and the resurrection, appearances to the disciples, and ascension. A short elegiac epilogue offers the finished work as a modest dish of greens from a poor garden, set against the rich banquets of learned writers.
la.sedulius.carmina_ad_sedulium_spectantia: Carmina ad Sedulium spectantia is a small late-antique Latin collection of poems associated with, but not certainly composed by, the Christian poet Sedulius.
