It opens with an elegiac epigram by Turcius Rufus Asterius praising Sedulius' truthful verse and urging him to remember Asterius, whose care brought the poems before the public. Two acrostic pieces by the scholastic Bellesabius follow, their initial letters spelling the poet's name: the first commends Sedulius' verses on Christ's miracles while contrasting a modest banquet with noble luxury and recalling the feeding of the five thousand, the second pictures Sedulius in a flowering field hearing David's song and taking up the plectrum of Christian poetry. The collection closes with an anonymous Carmen de incarnatione of uncertain authorship, which narrates the Father's resolve to send the Son, the annunciation to the Virgin, the birth marked by a guiding star, and a final promise of peace, prosperity, and eternal reward to those who keep the feast.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium: The Epistola ad Macedonium is a prose dedicatory letter by the late-antique Christian poet Sedulius, addressed to a priest named Macedonius as the preface to his Paschale carmen. It opens with the author's apology for having ventured, untrained in ancient learning, upon the vast sea of the paschal mystery in a small skiff. Sedulius then recounts his conversion from fruitless secular studies, defends his choice of verse on the grounds that readers more readily retain sweetened lines than rhetorical prose, and answers an imagined objection that worthier figures, among them Ursinus, Laurentius, Gallianus, Felix, Jerome, the virgin Syncletica, and her sister Perpetua, might better have received the work. The letter ends with the commendation of his four books of Christ's miracles, gathered from the four gospels up to the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, and with the explanation that he has named the poem Paschale carmen because Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.
la.sedulius.hymnus_i: A Latin hymn in short paired verses by the late-antique Christian poet Sedulius, in which a longer line is followed by a shorter one that recasts it, typically turning a statement about an Old Testament event or figure towards its fulfilment in Christ. The opening line invites companions to sing praise to the Lord and to sound forth the sweet love of Christ with devout mouth. From there the hymn runs through the whole of salvation history: Adam's fall, Eve and the serpent, Cain's murder of Abel, the flood and the ark, the patriarchs, Pharaoh and the plagues, the Passover lamb, the crossing of the sea, the manna, the law and the promised land. A closing stretch treats the virgin birth, Christ's miracles, passion, resurrection and enthronement above the stars, the ending of the old shadow in his coming, the promise of judgement for the faithless, and a final doxology to Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
la.sedulius_scotus.carmen_pastorale: The Carmen pastorale is a short Carolingian Latin didactic poem attributed to Sedulius Scotus, addressed throughout to a priest and arranged in brief rubricated sections. It opens by urging the shepherd to guard his flock against the wolf, since any loss through negligence must be answered for before its creator. The poem then proceeds through the honour and burdens of the priestly office, zeal for reading, the sevenfold daily hours of praise, and proper conduct at synods, before taking up fraternal charity, baptism, and the reverent celebration of the mass. Its closing sections cover diligence in the service of the church, the right use of gifts received, the prohibition on clergy bearing arms, the priest's relation to wife and bride, the administration of penance, and the prayers and burial owed to a priest at his death.
la.seneca.agamemnon: A Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Seneca, the Agamemnon dramatizes the victor's homecoming from Troy and his murder at Mycenae. The play opens with the ghost of Thyestes, who surveys the crimes of the house of Pelops and foresees fresh bloodshed in the palace above. Clytemnestra and Aegisthus debate and harden their resolve against the returning king, whose fleet a long messenger speech reports scattered by a storm on the voyage home; Cassandra, possessed by Apollo, prophesies the deed before it is done, and the murder is consummated at a banquet through the trap of the fatal robe. The closing scenes bring Electra's concealment and flight of the boy Orestes, the leading away of Cassandra to die, and threats of further vengeance to come.
la.seneca.apocolocyntosis: Apocolocyntosis is a short Latin verse satire of the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca, which mocks the death of the emperor Claudius and his abortive reception among the gods; its title twists 'apotheosis' into a 'gourdification' of the deified emperor. It opens with the Fates spinning a golden thread for the young Nero while Apollo sings of the golden age to come. The narrative then carries Claudius up to heaven, where the gods, persuaded by Augustus, refuse him divine honours and send him down to the underworld. The scene shifts finally to earth, with a mock dirge over the dead emperor and laments from his dependants, chief among them lawyers and dice-players whose patron's dice now refuse to fall in his favour.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_helviam: A Latin prose consolation of the early imperial period, Seneca's De Consolatione ad Helviam is addressed by the philosopher to his mother Helvia from the exile into which he has been sent. It opens with Seneca's explanation of why he hesitated to console her and his resolve to prove by his own equanimity, rather than by borrowed precepts, that his circumstances are not truly wretched. The body of the work argues in turn that banishment is merely a change of place of the kind humanity has always undergone, that poverty and loss of standing cannot injure a mind schooled in virtue, and that Helvia's grief must be tempered by the example of steadfast Roman women such as Cornelia and Rutilia. It closes by directing her to her surviving sons, grandchildren, and kinswomen as living consolations, and with Seneca's portrait of his own contented devotion to study and the contemplation of nature amid adversity.
la.seneca.medea: Seneca's Latin tragedy Medea, a drama of the early imperial period in dramatic meter, opens with Medea's incantation summoning infernal deities and her wedding oaths as she calls down ruin on Jason, who is about to marry Creon's daughter. The action follows Creon's order of banishment, Medea's debates with the Nurse over revenge and flight, and her preparation of a poisoned robe and crown delivered to the bride through her own children, amid choral odes on the first voyage of the Argo and the fury of love. A messenger recounts the bride's death by unquenchable fire and the burning of the palace, after which Medea, torn between maternal feeling and vengeance, slaughters her two sons. The play closes with Jason confronting the corpses and Medea escaping overhead in a chariot drawn by winged serpents, taunting him that no gods exist where she has come.
la.seneca.octavia: The Octavia is a Latin drama of the early imperial period transmitted among the tragedies of Seneca but generally regarded as the work of a later imitator of uncertain date. It is the sole surviving fabula praetexta, a tragedy drawn from recent Roman history rather than myth, dramatizing Nero's repudiation of his wife Octavia in favor of Poppaea and Octavia's banishment to her death. The play opens with Octavia lamenting the ruined house of Claudius and the deaths of Agrippina and Britannicus in conversation with her nurse, and proceeds through dialogue and lyric chorus to depict Nero's fury, the counsel of the philosopher Seneca, and the princess's final condemnation.
la.seneca.oedipus: A Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Seneca, Oedipus dramatizes the Theban king's discovery of his own crimes. The play opens with Oedipus lamenting the plague that is destroying Thebes and recalling the Delphic oracle that drove him from Corinth for fear of killing his father. Creon brings back the god's demand that the murderer of Laius be banished, and when sacrifice proves equivocal, Tiresias raises the ghost of Laius by necromancy; the shepherd Phorbas's account of the exposed infant then confirms that Oedipus is Laius's son and his mother's husband, whereupon he puts out his own eyes and Jocasta kills herself over his body. Choral songs on the symptoms of the plague, on the cult of Bacchus, and on the inescapability of fate punctuate the action.
la.seneca.phoenissae: The Phoenissae is a Latin tragedy of Early Imperial date by Lucius Annaeus Seneca, preserved in roughly 672 lines of dramatic verse. Bearing the traditional title of dramas on the Theban legend, the play opens with the blind Oedipus, guided by his daughter Antigone toward Cithaeron, and belongs to the cycle of stories surrounding Oedipus' cursed house and the strife of his sons. Even its opening speech displays the compressed mythological texture typical of Senecan tragedy, piling up exempla of Actaeon, Pentheus, and Ino in rapid rhetorical succession. For readers of intertexts, the play stands as a major Latin reworking of Greek tragic material on Thebes and a rich source of verbal and thematic echoes for later European drama.
la.seneca.quaestiones_naturales: Quaestiones Naturales, a Latin prose treatise on natural philosophy by Seneca of the Early Imperial period, opens with a preface to Lucilius contrasting the part of philosophy that concerns human conduct with the higher part that contemplates the gods and the heavens. The work proceeds through seven books surveying the physical world, treating celestial fires, thunder and lightning, the annual flooding of the Nile, clouds, rain, hail, snow, winds, and earthquakes, and closing with an extended discussion of comets. Throughout, Seneca sets out and tests explanations proposed by earlier Greek thinkers such as Aristotle, Theophrastus, Posidonius, and Diogenes of Apollonia, frequently rejecting them in favor of his own physical arguments. Moralizing prefaces and digressions, on the smallness of human affairs beside the cosmos, on luxury, and on contemporary neglect of philosophy, frame the scientific inquiry.
la.seneca.thyestes: Seneca's Latin tragedy Thyestes, an Early Imperial drama, opens with the ghost of Tantalus summoned from the underworld to plant renewed fury in the doomed house of Pelops. The action follows Atreus, who feigns reconciliation and draws his exiled brother Thyestes back to Argos with the promise of a shared throne, despite the misgivings of Thyestes and his sons. Choral odes on kingship, fortune and the fears that attend the powerful alternate with scenes in which Atreus resolves upon a revenge beyond all precedent and has Thyestes' three sons slaughtered and cooked for a banquet. A messenger then reports the butchery and the meal, the sun reverses its course in horror, and in the closing scene Atreus reveals the crime to his brother, who in turn curses him and prophesies vengeance still to come upon his line.
la.seneca.troades: The Troades is a Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period transmitted under the name of Lucius Annaeus Seneca. It opens with the captive Trojan women and Hecuba lamenting amid the smoking ruins of Troy as the Greek leaders quarrel over Polyxena. Calchas demands the girl's sacrifice at Achilles' tomb together with the death of Astyanax, and Andromache's attempt to hide her son within Hector's sepulchre is defeated by Ulysses' stratagem. The play carries the double killing to its end, allots Hecuba among the spoils to Ulysses, and closes with a chorus of the captive women departing from the coast of Troy.
la.seneca_the_elder.controversiae: Seneca the Elder's Controversiae, a Latin prose work of oratory from the early Imperial period, preserves in excerpt the declamations of Roman orators and rhetors. It opens with a preface addressed to the author's three sons, in which the aged writer undertakes to draw on his memory for the sayings of declaimers of an earlier generation and laments the decline of eloquence since Cicero. The remainder is arranged in five books around successive controversiae, imaginary legal cases involving such matters as parricide, disputed wills, captives, and the crimes of tyrants: under each case Seneca records the striking sententiae of individual named speakers, adds divisiones and colores setting out how they ordered their arguments and shaded their treatment of the parties, and interweaves anecdotes and critical remarks about the declaimers, with sayings delivered in Greek standing alongside the Latin.
la.seneca_the_elder.fragmenta: A small collection of fragments attributed to Seneca the Elder, the early Imperial rhetor, preserved only as quotations in later writers. The collection opens with a report from Quintilian that in Seneca's youth Pomponius and Seneca debated whether a certain phrase could properly be spoken in tragedy. The remaining items likewise come down through Quintilian and Donatus: a striking exchange from a controversia in which a father kills his son and stepmother discovered in adultery, a dry remark that oath-taking is the business of witnesses rather than advocates, and an anecdote in which the poet Julius Montanus says he would steal certain verses from Virgil if he could also take his voice and presence, since the same lines sound well in his delivery but fall mute without it.
la.sigloardus_remensis.rhytmi: Rhytmi is a short collection of medieval Latin poems from Carolingian Reims, the work of the monk Sigoard, whose own name appears in a closing prayer. The opening piece is a lament for Fulco, bishop of Reims, extolling his nobility, eloquence, and governance of church and realm before cursing Guinemarus, who attacked and killed him with armed followers. Subsequent poems commemorate the translation of the relics of St Remigius, an event dated in the verse to 901, narrating the sudden healing of a lame man during the procession and the enshrinement of the body in the church of the martyr Timothy. The collection closes with epitaphic verses on Fulco's tomb recording the length of his episcopate and his violent death, and with prayers commending the souls of Sigoard himself and a certain Adeloldus to St Remigius.
la.smaragdus.carmen_in_psalterio: A brief Latin prefatory poem on the Psalter by the Carolingian author Smaragdus. It opens with the image of a beautiful golden casket enclosing a little book that holds the holy teachings of the fathers. The poem goes on to contrast the book's plain outward appearance with the mystical meaning it bears within, saying that David's mystically sung songs lie veiled under a literal covering until the new fathers of the church expounded more lucidly the sacred proclamation of the old prophets. It ends with Smaragdus speaking in his own voice, declaring that he wished to pluck gems from the book so that its pages might be made illustrious.
la.smaragdus.carmina: The Carmina of Smaragdus, a Latin verse collection of the Carolingian period, opens with an elegiac prologue that invites the reader through a 'little book' joining scriptural material to grammatical instruction. The greater part of the work is an allegorical grammatical poem treating the parts of speech in turn, noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, conjunction, and interjection, under images of money, seafaring, roads, and royal rule. A substantial passage praises the Rule of St Benedict as the narrow path leading monks to the heavenly kingdom, and the collection closes with a trochaic poem addressing Christ as fount of light and life and describing the eternal joys of the heavenly Jerusalem.
la.smaragdus.epitaphium: A short Carolingian Latin epitaph attributed to Smaragdus. It opens by placing Smaragdus's tenure as abbot within the reign of the pious emperor Louis, recording that because the original site was ill suited to human uses he transferred his seat to a location nearby. The poem then relates that, on being called to the heavenly kingdom, he gave his body back to the old place for burial. It closes by fixing the moment of his death at the hour when the sun stood in Scorpio and the heavens lay open to him as a theologian.
la.smaragdus.versus_ad_filium_ludovici_pii: The Carolingian author Smaragdus addresses a son of Louis the Pious in didactic Latin verse that opens with the prayer that the Lord's love fill the young king's heart and with a summons to keep God's commandments. The poem then ranges through the duties of a Christian ruler: wisdom and prudence, simplicity of heart, patience, the dove's innocence joined to the serpent's cunning, justice in judgement, care for the poor, widows and orphans, payment of tithes, generosity against the plague of avarice, peace and fraternal zeal, clemency, sound counsel and trust in the Lord's protection. It closes in prayer that God arm the king against rulers who refuse to acknowledge Christ, expanding into praise of Christ the creator of sea, land, sky, stars, birds, fish, fire and storm, all things hastening to obey him.
la.statius.achilleid: The Achilleid is an epic in Latin hexameters by the early imperial poet Statius, left incomplete after two books, the second of which breaks off in mid-sentence. Its proem invokes the Muse to sing Achilles' life from his concealment on Scyros onward rather than confining itself to the Homeric story of Troy. The first book follows Thetis as she removes her son from the centaur Chiron's care on Pelion and hides him disguised among the daughters of Lycomedes on Scyros, where he seduces Deidamia and fathers Pyrrhus, before Ulysses and Diomedes unmask him by presenting arms among the princesses and speed his departure for the war. The fragmentary second book contains Deidamia's parting lament, the voyage, Ulysses' account of Paris and Helen, and Achilles' autobiographical recital of his upbringing and training under Chiron, at which point the poem stops.
la.statius.silvae: The Silvae of Statius, a work of the Early Imperial period, are a collection of occasional poems in hexameters, arranged in five books. The first poem welcomes a colossal equestrian statue of Domitian newly set up in the Roman Forum. The books that follow gather pieces on a wide range of occasions: panegyrics of emperors and noble friends, descriptions of villas, trees, and works of art, birthday and wedding poems, and consolations for the bereaved. The final book closes with a grieving father's remembrance of a young child, recalled from his first words and earliest sleep.
la.statius.thebaid: Statius's Thebaid is a Latin epic in twelve books of hexameter verse, composed in the early imperial period, recounting the war of the Seven against Thebes and the destruction of the house of Oedipus. It opens with a proem invoking the Muses, announcing the theme of fraternal strife at Thebes, and deferring celebration of the reigning emperor's deeds to a future poem. The narrative runs from Oedipus's malediction and the collapse of the brothers' alternate rule, through the exile of Polynices to Argos, the muster of the champions, the failed embassy of Tydeus, the fighting before the walls with the gods divided among the combatants, the self-sacrifice of Menoeceus, the deaths of the seer Amphiaraus and of Capaneus beneath Jupiter's bolt, the funeral games for Archemorus, and the single combat in which Eteocles and Polynices kill one another. It then follows the refusal of burial under Creon, the widows' appeal to Theseus at Athens and at the altar of Clementia, the deaths of Antigone and Argia on the contending pyres, and closes with an envoi bidding the poem itself farewell.
la.sulpicius_severus.chronica: The Chronica, a prose work of sacred history by the Late Antique author Sulpicius Severus, compresses biblical and ecclesiastical narrative from the creation of the world into two books, interweaving scriptural events with secular chronology so that the succession of times may be fixed. After a preface in which the author announces his design of brevity and his decision to continue beyond the passion of Christ and the acts of the apostles to the destruction of Jerusalem and the fortunes of the churches, the work runs through the patriarchs, Moses and the giving of the law, the judges, kings, exile and return, and the Maccabean age, down to the birth of Christ under Herod. The second part carries the narrative into Roman history, treating Nero's persecution, the fall of Jerusalem under Vespasian and Titus, the later persecutions, Constantine's conversion, Helena's finding of the cross, and at length the Arian controversy and the Priscillianist affair in Gaul, closing amid the discords that trouble the episcopate of the author's own day.
la.sulpicius_severus.vita_martini: The Vita Martini, a Latin prose saint's life of late antique date by Sulpicius Severus, recounts the career of Martin, monk and bishop of Tours. It opens with a prologue contrasting the futile pursuit of lasting fame in writings about pagan heroes with the author's declared purpose of recording the life of a holy man as an exemplar. The narrative follows Martin from his Pannonian birth and military service under Constantius and Julian through his baptism, his gift of half his cloak to a beggar, his renunciation of arms, and his association with Hilary of Poitiers and life as a monk, to his election as bishop of Tours. The later chapters record his destruction of rural pagan shrines, his healings, exorcisms, and raisings of the dead, his visions of angels and confrontations with the devil, his encounters with the emperor Maximus, and a closing portrait of his humility and unceasing prayer.
la.tacitus.agricola: The Agricola is a Latin prose biography of Gnaeus Iulius Agricola, conqueror of much of Britain and father-in-law of the author, composed in the Early Imperial period after the accession of Trajan. It opens with a preface contrasting the Republic's readiness to commemorate great men with the enforced silence of writers under Domitian, and announces the book as an act of homage to the author's father-in-law. The narrative follows Agricola from his ancestry, education, and early posts through his magistracies and command in Aquitania to his governorship of Britain, giving in the course of it a survey of the island's geography, inhabitants, and Roman conquest, an account of his campaigns culminating in Calgacus' speech of defiance before the battle at Mons Graupius, and then his recall, retirement, and death amid Domitian's suspicion. A closing lament and consolatory address to the dead man marks the work's turn from public history to personal mourning.
la.tacitus.annales: Latin prose historiography by Tacitus narrating the Roman principate from the death of Augustus in AD 14 through the reign of Tiberius and, in the later books preserved here, the reigns of Gaius, Claudius and Nero; the opening books, from Augustus's obsequies and Tiberius's accession onward, cover the mutinies on the Rhine and in Pannonia, the German wars of Germanicus and his death, and the rise and fall of Sejanus, with Tiberius's withdrawal to Capri and the delations and executions that follow. Later annalistic sections treat the murder of Agrippina and Octavia, the Pisonian conspiracy and its suppression, the great fire of Rome, Nero's artistic pretensions and Oriental campaigns, notably Corbulo's Armenian war and the settlement with Tiridates, together with the trials and deaths of figures such as Seneca, Thrasea Paetus and Petronius. The narrative closes with Nero's reign still unended, since the work is incomplete and its later books survive only in part. The famous preface declares the author's programme of writing subsequent history 'sine ira et studio', with few words on Augustus and then the reign of Tiberius, free of the flattery and fear that had distorted earlier accounts.
la.tacitus.de_origine_et_situ_germanorum_li: An early Imperial Latin ethnographical treatise by Tacitus, De Origine et Situ Germanorum opens by setting the boundaries of Germany between the Rhine, the Danube and the Ocean, and by weighing what may be said of the origins and distinctive purity of its inhabitants. The longer first half describes the land and its peoples in general terms: their cults and divination, assemblies and forms of government, military organisation, marriage and domestic life, hospitality, entertainments, slavery, land tenure and funerary customs. The second half proceeds people by people through the nations east of the Rhine and north of the Danube, from the Batavi and Chatti to the Suebian tribes and the remote nations of the northern Ocean. It closes with the obscure races of the far northeast, of which the author reports rumours while leaving the truth undecided.
la.tacitus.dialogus_de_oratoribus: The Dialogus de Oratoribus, a prose dialogue on the condition of oratory attributed to Tacitus and of early Imperial date, opens with a narrator recalling for Fabius Iustus a debate he had witnessed as a young man on why his own age produces no great orators. The conversation is set in the sixth year of Vespasian at the house of the tragic poet Curiatius Maternus, in the company of Marcus Aper, Julius Secundus, and Vipstanus Messalla. Aper first argues for the practical rewards and pleasures of oratory against the fleeting fame of poetry, then defends the eloquence of the moderns against Messalla's admiration for Cicero and the Republican masters; Messalla in turn ascribes the decline of eloquence to faults of upbringing and education, the artificial exercises of the rhetorical schools, and above all the changed political conditions of the empire, in which settled peace and concentrated power leave no room for the great oratory bred of civic discord. The participants part amicably, each jesting that the others will accuse him of favouring poets, antiquarians, or rhetoricians.
la.tacitus.historiae: The Historiae is a Latin prose history by Tacitus, an early imperial account of the civil wars that convulsed Rome after the death of Nero. It opens with a programmatic preface fixing the starting point at the consulship of Galba and Titus Vinius, lamenting the distortion of truth under one-man rule, and reserving the reigns of Nerva and Trajan for a later work. The narrative then traces Galba's adoption of Piso and his murder, the coup of Otho, the rise and march of Vitellius, and the proclamation of Vespasian in the East, following the Flavian commanders through the battle and sack of Cremona to the overthrow of Vitellius. Its later books move to the aftermath: senatorial recriminations and trials, the rebuilding of the Capitol, the Jewish war and Titus' assault on Jerusalem, and the great revolt of Civilis and the Gallic conspirators on the Rhine.
la.terence.adelphi: A Latin comedy by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic, written in dramatic verse. It opens with a prologue in which the poet appeals to the audience to judge the controversy surrounding the play and announces that the two old men of the first scene will disclose the plot as the action begins. The work turns on the opposed methods of two brothers in bringing up their sons: Micio, the indulgent city-dweller and adoptive father of Aeschinus, and Demea, the harsh countryman father of Ctesipho. Aeschinus, ostensibly to further his brother's love affair, carries off a music-girl from the procurer Sannio, while his seduction of the citizen maiden Pamphila comes to light in the tenth month of her pregnancy; the resulting entanglements end in marriage for Aeschinus, a wife and further concessions forced upon Micio, the manumission of the slave Syrus, and a demonstration of Demea's sudden conversion to liberality.
la.terence.andria: A comedy of the Roman Republic, Terence's Andria opens with a prologue in which the poet defends his practice of adapting and combining the plots of Menander against the attacks of a rival playwright. The action follows the Athenian Simo, who arranges mock wedding preparations for his son Pamphilus with Chremes' daughter in order to probe the young man's attachment to Glycerium, a woman from Andros left pregnant by him. The schemes of the slave Davus, a simulated childbirth, and the exposure of the newborn at Simo's door drive the tangled plot toward crisis, until the arrival of Crito reveals that Glycerium is in fact an Athenian, the daughter of Chremes' brother Phania. Recognition follows, the marriage is settled, and Davus, threatened with the mill for his meddling, is released as the comedy closes with the usual appeal for applause.
la.terence.heautontimorumenos: The Heautontimorumenos ('The Self-Tormentor') is a Latin stage comedy by Terence, composed during the Roman Republic and adapted, as its prologue announces, from an integral Greek original to which a second plot has been joined. It opens with an actor speaking on the poet's behalf, defending his practice of combining Greek plots in Latin comedies against a malicious rival and asking the audience for a fair hearing. The action turns on two neighbouring fathers: Menedemus, whose harshness drove his son Clinia away to military service in Asia and who now torments himself with remorse and ceaseless farm labour, and Chremes, whose son Clitipho is secretly infatuated with the courtesan Bacchis. Through the schemes of the slave Syrus, Bacchis is passed off as Clinia's mistress, Chremes feigns the grant of his whole estate as her dowry to recall Clitipho to his senses, and the recognition of Antiphila as Chremes' long-lost daughter clears the way for her marriage to Clinia and for Clitipho's reconciliation and betrothal elsewhere.
la.tertullian.adversus_hermogenem: Adversus Hermogenem is a Late Antique Latin theological polemic in which Tertullian attacks the doctrine of Hermogenes that God fashioned the world out of pre-existing, eternal matter. The treatise opens with the conventional argument that heresy is a latecomer to the truth and with an invective against Hermogenes as a painter who turned from the church to Stoic philosophy. The refutation that follows seeks to establish that God made all things out of nothing: Tertullian rebuts Hermogenes' proofs that matter is unbegotten and coeternal with God, distinguishes the divine names of God and Lord, identifies the Wisdom and the Word of God rather than any material substrate as the medium of creation, and takes apart claims about matter's corporeality, moral quality, location, and motion, while also addressing whether God can be the author of evil. A closing section argues that what was made from nothing will pass back into nothing, appealing to scriptural promises of the world's end.
la.tertullian.adversus_marcionem: Tertullian's Adversus Marcionem, a Latin prose theological polemic of the late second or early third century, argues against Marcion's doctrine of two gods, a just creator and an alien benevolent deity. The opening preface recounts the loss and reworking of earlier versions of the treatise before launching a vitriolic portrait of Marcion as a Pontic barbarian and heretic, and the work then proceeds systematically: it refutes the possibility of a second or unequal god by philosophical argument on the divine essence, defends the creator's goodness, justice, foreknowledge and patience, and vindicates Christ and the apostle Paul as belonging to the creator by adducing the law, the prophets, the Gospels and Paul's letters, with sustained discussion of the resurrection of the flesh, judgment, marriage, and the falsified text of Marcion's own gospel. In its surviving course the treatise moves book by book through the whole Marcionite system, from the doctrine of God through Christology and the epistles to questions of bodily resurrection, testing each claim against the Old and New Testament writings that Tertullian takes as the one God's own revelation.
la.tertullian.de_anima: De Anima is a Latin prose treatise on the soul by Tertullian, a work of late-antique Christian theology. It opens by turning from a controversy with Hermogenes over the soul's material origin to a confrontation with philosophy in general, taking Socrates' composed death in prison as a test case for whether pagan wisdom can attain truth. The argument proceeds from the soul's creation by God's breath rather than from matter to its corporeality, simplicity, and propagation together with the flesh through procreation, rejecting Platonic pre-existence, recollection, and the transmigration of souls into beasts. Subsequent chapters treat the senses and the intellect, sleep and dreams, the timing and order of death, and the underworld, closing with the soul's condition there in expectation of judgment and resurrection.
la.tertullian.de_idololatria: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Tertullian, De Idololatria opens by declaring idolatry the principal crime of humankind and argues that it encompasses every other sin, from murder and adultery to fraud and cupidity. The work then maps the breadth of idolatry beyond overt sacrifice, condemning the artisans who fashion images, the allied crafts and trades that supply temples, and professions such as astrology and the teaching of pagan letters, while rejecting the plea that the necessity of earning a living excuses such activity. Further chapters examine participation in pagan festivals and household customs such as lamps and laurels at the door, the limits of honour owed to emperors, whether Christians may hold office or serve as soldiers, and the idolatry incurred in speech, oaths, blessings and written contracts. It closes with the figure of faith as a ship sailing by the Spirit of God through the shoals and whirlpools of idolatry, safe if cautious.
la.tertullian.de_pudicitia: De Pudicitia is a late-antique Latin prose treatise on church discipline by Tertullian, arguing against opponents he calls psychici who admitted the lapsed to reconciliation for sexual sins. It opens with an exalted encomium of chastity and a denunciation of an episcopal edict remitting the sins of adultery and fornication to those who have done penance. The argument then ranks these offenses with idolatry and murder among the capital and irremissible sins, rereads the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son as concerning gentiles rather than fallen believers, and works through the Pauline letters (including the case of the incestuous Corinthian), 1 John, Revelation, the Epistle of Barnabas, and the leprosy laws of Leviticus in support of a stricter rule. It ends by denying that bishops or martyrs possess any authority to grant ecclesiastical peace to fornicators and adulterers, reserving judgment on such sins to God alone.
la.tertullian.scorpiace: The Scorpiace, a prose treatise of Christian theology by the Late Antique author Tertullian, argues that martyrdom is willed by God and must be accepted rather than evaded, against Christians, especially Gnostics and Valentinians, who discouraged confession of the faith under persecution. The work opens with the figure of the scorpion, whose sting at the tail figures the venomous pressure of persecution and heretical teaching, and offers the treatise itself as an antidote to that poison. From the Old Testament the argument establishes that God ordained martyrdom, adducing the prohibition of idolatry, the repeated punishments of apostates, and the vindication of the faithful such as the three youths and Daniel, while the charge that such a God is cruel is answered through medical and athletic analogies and the allegory of Wisdom slaying her sons. Christ's sayings on confession and persecution, the sufferings of the apostles as witnessed by Peter, John, Paul and Acts, and a closing refutation of the claim that confession is due in the heavens rather than on earth before human powers complete the case.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.carmina: Latin verse attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a Carolingian bishop, poet, and courtier, this collection spans some seventy-two book files and about five thousand lines of didactic, devotional, occasional, and satirical poetry. It opens with a long poem on the vices and virtues, treating sorrow, anger, pride, and patience in the manner of a moral physician, before turning to exhortations on pastoral duty addressed to bishops. The collection also includes works on monastic rules, verses on the ecclesiastical arts, an allegory of the liberal arts as branches of a tree, verses of greeting and exhortation to Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and other Carolingian figures, hymns and prayers, epigrams on altars and churches, letters in verse, and lines of exile, including appeals to charitable readers from prison. One extended poem narrates marvels of rivers and birds, and others record visions, dreams, and courtly anecdotes.
la.theodulf_of_orleans.epitaphia: A Latin verse epitaph composed by Theodulf of Orleans, a Carolingian bishop. It opens by recording that the ashes of one who was once both bishop and abbot to his people lie preserved in stone. The poem then proceeds in the poet's own voice through his life and fall: born in Hesperia and nurtured in Gaul, he held the populous see of Orleans above the Loire, served under Charlemagne, whose virtues he celebrates at length, and lost his position when Louis succeeded by paternal right and gave credit to slanderous accusations, so that after confinement by the emperor's order he died in exile and was buried in a foreign land far from the shores where he wished his bones to rest. The closing lines profess trust in the judge who knows the weight of his cause, hope of rising from the dust at the divine command, and a plea that readers pray for 'Theodulf the servant' and ask Christ the king for mercy upon him.
la.unknown.corpus_scriptorum_ecclesiasticor: A brief Latin prose excerpt of uncertain date, attributed to Augustine, which argues that the law serves as a pedagogue driving transgressors toward the grace of God. It takes up the question whether any human being can be without sin, finding that Scripture names no one so except Christ, and answers objections drawn from the Letter of James, above all the saying that no one among men can tame the tongue. Such sayings are read as showing that command of the tongue and fulfilment of the precepts rest not on natural strength but on divine aid, for which the soul must pray, and the discussion closes with an examination of the 'wisdom of the flesh' that is enmity against God. The author also refers to books he had written on the same question to Marcellinus.
la.valerius_flaccus.argonautica: The Argonautica of Valerius Flaccus is an early Imperial Latin epic in eight books of hexameters recounting Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece. It opens with a proem on the first ship to traverse the seas and a prayer for poetic inspiration before turning to the action. Pelias, alarmed by prophecy, sends Jason from Iolcus at the head of the Argonauts; the narrative follows the Argo's voyage with its storms, rites and episodic labours, the arrival in Colchis, Medea's overpowering passion for Jason, and her aid in his subjection of the fire-breathing bulls, the earthborn warriors and the sleepless dragon that guards the fleece. The narrative ends abruptly in the midst of Jason and Medea's flight from Colchis with the prize.
la.vergil.aeneid: A Latin epic in hexameters in twelve books, written by Vergil in the Augustan period, the Aeneid tells of the Trojan Aeneas' flight from Troy, his arrival in Italy, and the war fought there to secure a home for his followers, the forebears of the Roman people. It opens with an invocation to the Muse of arms and the man, ascribing the hero's many trials to the wrath of Juno, who drives his fleet across the seas. The first six books recount the fall of Troy as narrated by Aeneas at Carthage, his love for Dido, the funeral games for Anchises, and his descent to the underworld, while the remaining six shift to Latium, where Allecto's intervention embroils Trojans and Italians in war against the Rutulian Turnus. The poem closes in single combat, as Aeneas, catching sight of the spoils of young Pallas on Turnus' shoulders, plunges his sword into his enemy, whose life flees indignant beneath the shades.
la.vergil.eclogues: The Eclogues are a collection of ten pastoral poems in hexameter by Vergil, composed in the Augustan age. The first poem opens with the dialogue between Tityrus, who has been freed and restored to his land by a divine benefactor, and Meliboeus, who must abandon his confiscated farm. The remaining eclogues offer a varied cycle of shepherd scenes: the hopeless love of Corydon for the boy Alexis, a bitter contest of abuse and song, the prophecy of a new golden age at the birth of a wondrous child, a lament for the dead Daphnis, Silenus's cosmological song before his youthful captors, paired singing matches between rival herdsmen, refrained song exchanges woven around love-magic, the dispossession of farmers by land confiscation, and the lovesick lament of Gallus. Throughout, the herdsmen's songs and conversation blend rustic idyll with the intrusion of love, violence, and political upheaval.
la.vergil.georgics: The Georgics is a didactic poem in four books of hexameter verse, composed by the Roman poet Vergil in the Augustan age and addressed to Maecenas. It opens with an invocation to Maecenas and the tutelary gods of agriculture, joined to a prayer for Caesar. The four books successively treat the cultivation of arable fields, with weather signs and the constellations that govern the farmer's year; the planting of trees, vines, and olives, interspersed with an encomium of Italy and a celebration of the countryman's life; the breeding and management of horses, cattle, and goats, closing with a devastating plague of livestock; and the keeping of bees. The last book also contains the tale of Aristaeus, whose quest for the cause of his bees' death brings forth the story of Orpheus and Eurydice, and the poem ends with the poet's recollection of his earlier pastoral verse.
la.vergil_pseudo.aetna: The Aetna is a Latin poem in hexameters transmitted under Virgil's name but of uncertain authorship and date. Opening with an invocation to Apollo, the poet announces his subject, the fires of Mount Etna and the causes of its eruptions, and rejects the mythological explanations of earlier singers, from Vulcan's forges and the Giants' revolt to the tales of an underworld beneath the mountain. The bulk of the poem offers a physical account of volcanic activity: the hollow interior of the earth, winds compressed in its caverns, the combustible stones and materials that feed the flames, and the behaviour of molten rock as it hardens into streams, with a digression defending the study of nature against the pursuit of mineral wealth. It closes with the story of two brothers who bore their aged parents unharmed through an eruption, the fire yielding before their piety and earning them the name of the Pious.
la.vergil_pseudo.ciris: A Latin mythological epic in hexameters, of Augustan date, attributed to Vergil but of uncertain authorship. The opening prologue, addressed to Messalla, renounces a loftier philosophical theme and dedicates the poem as the first-fruits of the poet's early years, with a digression that distinguishes its Scylla from the Homeric monster and surveys rival versions of the legend. The narrative then recounts how Minos besieged Megara, where King Nisus's life and the city's safety depended on a purple lock of hair, and how Scylla, inflamed with love for the enemy king and encouraged by her nurse Carme, cut the lock and betrayed both father and city, only for Minos to reject her and tow her behind his ship. As she dies over the waves, the sea god transforms her into the ciris bird and Nisus into a sea eagle, the two fated to pursue one another endlessly through the air.
la.vergil_pseudo.dirae: The Dirae is a short Latin poem in dactylic hexameters of Augustan date, ascribed to Pseudo-Vergil, in which a farmer exiled from land confiscated after civil war calls down curses upon it. It opens with the speaker urging his companion Battarus to join him in renewed song of the divided estates and the imprecations laid upon them. The poem then works through a sequence of curses, sterile fields and vines, drought-stricken meadows, a beloved grove consumed by heavenly fire, the sea let loose upon the land and rivers turned back upon their banks, punctuated by refrains recalling Battarus' sadder and sweeter counter-songs and by laments for the soldier rewarded with the confiscated farm. It closes with the exile's farewell from a distant hilltop to his fields, fountains and Lydia, dearer than them all, and with a vow that his love will outlast every reversal of nature.
la.vergil_pseudo.moretum: The Moretum, a short Latin poem of the Augustan era attributed to Pseudo-Vergil, opens on a winter night as the smallholder Simylus rises before dawn and coaxes a fire from dying embers. The narrative follows his morning's labour in sequence: he grinds grain at a hand-mill with the help of his African slave Scybale and sets a loaf to bake, then gathers herbs, garlic, and cheese from his kitchen garden and pounds them in a mortar to make the savoury paste that gives the poem its name. With bread and moretum prepared, he ends the early morning by yoking his oxen and driving his plough into the fields.
la.vergil_pseudo.priapea: The Priapea is a short Latin poem of the Augustan era, attributed to Pseudo-Vergil, spoken largely in the voice of Priapus, the god who guards gardens. It opens with the god lamenting that winter alone among the seasons is his pest and fearing that his wooden body will serve only as firewood for idle farmers. The bulk of the poem has him describe his rustic image set up to watch over a poor man's plot, catalogue the seasonal offerings he receives, garlands, ears of corn, grapes, olives, milk, a kid and a lamb, and threaten would-be thieves with obscene punishment, including the club fashioned from the wrenched-off arm of the farm bailiff. It closes with his advice to two boys to spare his own garden and plunder instead the nearby estate of a rich and negligent neighbour.
la.victor_vitensis.historia_persecutionis_a: The Historia persecutionis Africanae provinciae is a Latin prose ecclesiastical history in five books recording the persecution of African Catholics under the Arian Vandals, composed in Late Antiquity by Victor Vitensis, bishop of Vita. The opening prologue, addressed to the bishop Diadocus, announces the author's purpose of setting down what befell the African provinces while the Arians raged there, a task undertaken in obedience to another's command. The first book traces the Vandal crossing from Spain under Geiseric and the ensuing devastation of cities, churches, and clergy, together with episodes of exile, confession, and martyrdom under Vandal rule. The remaining books follow Huniric's persecution: the elevation of Eugenius to the see of Carthage, the banishment of nearly five thousand clergy toward the desert among the Moors, the public disputation with Arian bishops and the king's anti-Catholic edict quoted at length, the tortures and mutilations of noble confessors, the famine and pestilence presented as divine judgment, and the closing account of Huniric's death.
la.victorinus_saint_bishop_of_poetovio.comm: A Latin commentary on the Apocalypse attributed to Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, a later imperial theological work transmitted here together with a preface and supplementary material apparently added by a later hand. The commentary proceeds through the Book of Revelation section by section, interpreting the letters to the seven churches as addresses to classes of believers, the visions of the throne, seals, trumpets and bowls as figures of the church's preaching, tribulation and final judgement, and the beasts, Babylon and the millennial reign within a survey of the last times. It closes with an account of the two resurrections, the defeat of Antichrist and the heavenly Jerusalem, expounded in allegorical and literal senses together.
la.vitruvius.de_architectura: De Architectura is a Latin prose treatise on architecture in ten books, written during the Augustan period and dedicated in its opening preface to the emperor Caesar. The work begins with the education and proper qualifications of the architect and the siting and planning of cities, then covers building materials, timber, and methods of walling; Books 3–4 set out the proportions of temples and the Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Tuscan orders. Later books treat public buildings such as fora, basilicas, theatres, baths, palaestras, and harbours, private houses in both Roman and Greek styles, and wall plaster, pavements, and pigments. The final books deal with the finding, testing, and conducting of water, with sundials and water clocks, and with machines ranging from cranes, hoists, and water-lifting devices to catapults, ballistae, and engines of siege and defence.
la.vulfinus_diensis.vita_marcelli_metrica: The Vita Marcelli metrica is a Carolingian Latin poem, attributed to Vulfinus of Die, who names himself as the see's bishop near its close. It opens by praising Marcellus radiant on the episcopal throne of Die, then traces his austere youth, his renunciation of family wealth, and his service as deacon and helper to his elder brother Petronius, bishop of the city formerly called Essa. The narrative follows Marcellus's deathbed exhortation to his flock, his flight from election to a cave on a neighbouring mountain, his discovery there by a searching crowd, and miracles performed in life, including the cure of a possessed queen and the rescue of a tottering column in a church he founded, described in a lengthy account of its painted and gilded decoration. The poem ends with wonders at Marcellus's tomb, healings of a paralyzed mother, a blind girl and a girl with a crippled hand, culminating in the cure worked at the intercession of the poet-bishop Vulfinus himself.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_cultu_hortorum_carmen: A Carolingian didactic poem in Latin by Walafrid Strabo, De cultu hortorum describes the cultivation of a small kitchen and herb garden. It opens with a defence of gardening as a worthy pursuit within the quiet country life and an account of clearing the neglected plot beside the speaker's door as spring arrives. The body of the work surveys plant after plant, sage, rue, gourds, melons, wormwood, horehound, lovage, lilies, poppies, mint, pennyroyal, celery, betony and radish among them, combining instructions for sowing, watering and transplanting with remarks on each species' appearance and medicinal virtues. The poem closes allegorically on the rose and the lily as emblems of martyrdom and faith addressed to the Virgin, followed by a dedicatory epilogue in which Strabo offers the finished work to his revered master Grimald.
la.walafrid_strabo.de_vita_et_fine_mammae: A Latin hagiographic poem attributed to the Carolingian author Walafrid Strabo, telling the life and martyrdom of Saint Mammes of Caesarea in Cappadocia. It begins with a prologue in which the poet confesses his sins and asks his friends Anshelm, Wulfing, and Lantwine for their prayers before invoking his subject. The narrative follows Mammes from a pious childhood in Caesarea to his retreat as a young shepherd onto a mountain, where he tames wild beasts, receives a heavenly staff and gospel book, and supplies the poor with milk and cheese; summoned under Aurelian's persecution, he is interrogated and tortured by the governor Alexander with the rack, hooks, and a furnace, feeds his fellow prisoners through the gifts of a dove, and is spared by a bear and then a lion, which speaks with a human voice and slaughters the spectators. After emerging unharmed from a stoning, Mammes dies and is received into paradise, and the poem closes with an epilogue in which the poet, naming himself Strabo, lists the biblical shepherds, patriarchs, prophets, and martyrs whose virtues Mammes combines in himself.
la.walafrid_strabo.in_natalem_s_mammetis_hy: A short Latin hymn of Carolingian date, attributed to Walafrid Strabo, composed for the feast day (natale) of the martyr Saint Mammes. It opens by calling on humble suppliants to sing the blessed martyr's praise to the glory of the Trinity, who gives the crown to his witnesses. The central stanzas recount Mammes' contempt for worldly wealth and prosperity, his virtue, eloquence and abounding charity, his life among the beasts, and his victory through spiritual arms over the fury of princes and the savage dragon, with faith, hope and charity dwelling within him. The poem then bids the whole assembly of suppliants rejoice and seek his intercession, addresses Mammes directly with pleas for favour, protection, deliverance from evil and solace in good, and closes with a doxology to the Trinity.
la.walafrid_strabo.visio_wettini: The Visio Wettini is a Carolingian Latin afterlife vision composed in hexameter verse by Walafrid Strabo. It opens with a prayer for grace in the poetic undertaking and a survey of the island monastery of Augia (Reichenau), its abbots, and Wettin, a learned monk of the community. The bulk of the poem recounts the vision Wettin received during an illness: led by an angel, he tours the places of punishment, where clerics, monks, and laypeople suffer for avarice, lust, and other vices, hears detailed moral admonitions to proclaim what he has seen, passes through the dwellings of saints, martyrs, and virgins, and returns to dictate his experiences before dying the next day as foretold. The work closes with the narrator's lament for his dead master.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carmina: Carmina is a collection of Latin verse by the Carolingian poet Walahfrid Strabo. The opening poem is an admonition addressed to a bishop, urging him to strengthen the members of the church in sound teaching and to purge vice before calling newcomers to the fold, after the example of Paul. The collection then ranges over devotional and epistolary pieces, including a poem in which the poet vows perpetual service in deed, prayer, heart, and faith to a revered spiritual father. It closes with short mnemonic verses that attach numbers to the Kalends, Nones, and Ides of the months, drawing on biblical and liturgical matters.
la.walahfrid_strabo.carminum_appendix: A short appendix of Carolingian Latin verse attributed to Walahfrid Strabo, though its opening poem is an epitaph spoken over Walahfrid himself, lamenting his death while crossing the Loire and his burial at Auua through the care of the scribe Reginbert. The collection then turns to dedicatory and inscriptional pieces for a church rebuilt by Abbot Haito while a Louis ruled the Franks, praising the altar wrought in silver by Geroltus and recording the gifts of donors such as Odilo and Bishop Waldo. Later verses address travellers at the church door and communicants at the altar, urging repentance, concord and worthy reception, and exhort the brethren to unity and to the reading of the fathers under Benedict's rule. The sequence closes with eucharistic imagery drawn from the marriage feast at Cana and the miraculous feeding, as Christ satisfies all who gather at his table.
la.walahfrid_strabo.versus_de_Blaithmaic: The Versus de Blaithmaic is a Latin hagiographic poem by Walahfrid Strabo, a writer of the Carolingian period, recounting the life and martyrdom of the Irish saint Blaithmaic. The opening presents the poet, born of Alamannian soil, undertaking at the urging of a venerable father named Felix to write of the blessed Blaithmaic's life and end. The narrative follows the saint from his birth into royal stock: he renounces his inheritance for the cloister, withstands his father's efforts to reclaim him, grows in learning and humility to govern communities of monks, and at last slips away with a small band of disciples to the island of the Picts where Columba's body rests. Forewarned of pagan Danish raiders, he gives leave to any who wish to flee, refuses to reveal the hiding place of Columba's relics, is slain, and is honoured as a martyr buried on the spot where miracles are reported, the poem closing with a prayer that his merits may win pardon for the author's sins.
la.wandalbert.de_creatione_mundi: De Creatione Mundi is a Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, giving a versified account of the six days of creation. It opens by invoking the eternal, triune God who fashions the world through the Word, and then follows the Genesis narrative through the appearance of light, the firmament, seas and dry land, plants, the sun, moon and stars, fish and birds, land animals, the forming of woman from man's rib, and the Creator's rest on the seventh day. The latter part of the poem turns to man himself, presenting him as a second world endowed with the light of mind, called to govern the lower senses, cultivate virtue like seed brought to fruit, distinguish deeds of light from darkness, and look toward the eternal paradise promised to a worthy heir.
la.wandalbert.horarium: The Horarium is a short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Wandalbert, a didactic piece on the changing length of a sundial's shadow through the hours of the day across the year. It opens with December and January, giving in feet the shadow measured at each of six successive hours. The remaining months follow in pairs of equal daylight, February with November, March with October, April with September, May with August, and June with July, each pair set out with the same hour-by-hour figures, and a precept directs that this method of reckoning be observed everywhere.
la.wandalbert.horologium: The Horologium is a short didactic poem in Latin attributed to the Carolingian author Wandalbert. Opening with an address to the reader and a promise to teach in a few verses how the sun's course joins the months, it pairs January with December, February with November, and the remaining months likewise by equal daylight. The poem then sets out which hours correspond in every month, notes that shadow lengths vary with latitude, from lands scorched under the south wind to those lying frigid beneath the northern pole, and anchors its instructions in a region stretching from the Danube westward, marked by Lyon and the Rhône and facing the Britons surrounded by the Ocean. It ends by warning that shadow measurements should not be fixed at the kalends and carried to the month's end, since shadows grow and diminish gradually from mid-month to mid-month as the rising of the signs turns.
la.wandalbertus.martyrologium: A Latin verse martyrology of the Carolingian period by Wandalbert. It opens with an invocation to God, an exhortation to imitate the saints, a commendation of earlier Christian writers, and a dedication to a Carolingian ruler, followed by an account of how the year is divided into months, weeks, seasons, and feast-keeping. The main body proceeds month by month through the calendar, recording the feast days of martyrs, confessors, popes, and virgins, often noting where each suffered or how each was venerated. A concluding prayer in the author's own voice and a hymn to Christ close the work.
la.william_of_tyre.historia_rerum_in_partib: A Latin prose chronicle in twenty-three books by William of Tyre, minister of the church of Tyre and chancellor of the kingdom of Jerusalem, composed in the late twelfth century at the command of King Amalric. A prologue on the hazards and duties of writing history precedes an account that runs from the departure of the Western princes who won the promised land and nearly all Syria, through the successive rulers of the Latin kingdom from Godfrey to Baldwin IV, a span of some eighty-four years. The narrative covers campaigns against the rulers of Damascus and Egypt, the captivity and deliverance of King Baldwin II, the Venetian fleet and the siege of Tyre, the Council of Nablus, and the charters and privileges of the realm. It closes with the quarrel between Baldwin IV and the count of Joppa and the entrusting of the kingdom's administration to the count of Tripoli.
la.ambrose.apologia_altera_prophetae_david: The Apologia altera prophetae David is a late-antique Latin prose homiletic treatise by Ambrose that defends the prophet David against the scandal of his adultery with Bathsheba and his contrivance of Uriah's death. It opens by acknowledging the offense many take at the title of the fiftieth psalm, which recalls Nathan's coming to David when he entered to Bathsheba, and at the gospel reading in which Christ dismisses an adulteress without condemnation. The defense then unfolds in the three divisions announced: against pagans, who reproach Christianity with the crimes of its forefathers; against Jews, who object that so guilty a man cannot be the ancestor of God's son, a point broadened into a refutation of Photinian, Sabellian, Arian, and Manichean errors about Christ's person and incarnation; and among Christians, where the biblical history is read allegorically, Bathsheba figuring the human condition or the church sought out by Christ, Uriah the law, and David's name, interpreted as 'the humble one,' the humbled Lord. Nathan's parable of the rich man and the poor man's ewe is expounded as synagogue against church, and the treatise concludes with a running exposition of the Miserere psalm on confession of sin, the magnitude of divine mercy, and the unity of God against heretical division.
la.ambrose.apologia_prophetae_david_ad_theo: An apology for the prophet King David, written in Latin by Ambrose and addressed, as its title states, to the emperor Theodosius. It opens with the author's declaration that he takes up the defence not because David, who flourished with such merits and virtues, needs it, but because many readers, following the bare sequence of his deeds, wonder how so great a prophet failed to avoid the contagions first of adultery and then of homicide. The work proceeds to recount the sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah, argues that David was justified by God and redeemed his fault through immediate confession and immense sorrow, and holds that the lapses of the saints were permitted so that later generations might take from their lives a lesson in penitence as well as innocence. It reads figures of the Old Testament, from the brazen serpent, Joseph, and Judah to Solomon and Bathsheba, as types pointing to Christ and the church, surveys David's virtues and acts of forbearance, and closes with a long exposition of the fiftieth psalm, the Miserere, as David's own testimony to confession, baptism, and the forgiveness of sins.
la.ambrose.de_benedictionibus_patriarcharum: The De Benedictionibus Patriarcharum is a single-book exegetical treatise by Ambrose, the late fourth-century bishop of Milan, expounding the deathbed blessings that Jacob pronounces over his twelve sons in Genesis. It opens by dwelling on the dignity of a father's final blessing and on Joseph's presentation of his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, whom Jacob adopts in place of his own children. The body of the work proceeds tribe by tribe through the blessings of Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, and Benjamin, reading each as a prophecy fulfilled in Christ and the Church and incorporating Moses' later blessings from Deuteronomy. Along the way Ambrose repeatedly sets his allegorical and christological interpretations against the explanations of the Jews, identifying Judah's lion with Christ, the serpent of Dan with the future Antichrist, and the rapacious wolf of Benjamin with the apostle Paul.
la.ambrose.de_cain_et_abel: De Cain et Abel is a late antique Latin theological treatise in prose by Ambrose. It opens by looking back to an earlier treatment of Paradise and the fall of Adam and Eve, and then follows the subsequent scriptural narrative of Cain and Abel. The two brothers serve throughout as figures of opposing tendencies within the soul, one referring all good to God and the other arrogating it to itself, and as types of synagogue and church, with Cain figuring the unbelieving people and Abel the Christian who adheres to God. The exposition ranges widely over the meaning of the brothers' offerings, the rival figures of Pleasure and Virtue drawn from Proverbs, Christ's three temptations, the secrecy and discipline of prayer, the spiritual 'births' of virtue in the soul, the Levites as a figure of redemption, and the closing episodes of Abel's blood crying from the ground, Cain's mark and punishment, and Lamech.
la.ambrose.de_fuga_saeculi: A short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose on the spiritual duty of fleeing the world. It opens by observing how frequently such escape is urged yet how rarely accomplished, since the enticements of earthly desires and the senses continually recapture the mind. The main body allegorizes the six Levitical cities of refuge as refuges in God and in Christ the eternal high priest, whose death releases the fugitive, and gathers scriptural exemplars of holy flight, Jacob, Moses, David, Jonah, Lot, Susanna, and Paul let down in a basket, to urge flight from sin, vice, and worldly corruption. The work closes with the counsel that one may flee the world in spirit even while detained in the body, dying to the age with Christ and taking refuge in penitence and the grace of God.
la.ambrose.de_helia_et_ieiunio: De Helia et Ieiunio is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on fasting by Ambrose. It opens with the biblical trumpet-call to war recast as a summons to the approaching solemn fast, in which Christ's forty-day fast in the wilderness and his victory on the cross set the pattern for the Christian contest. The work then ranges through the praise of abstinence: Elijah's heaven-closing fast leads into exempla from Elisha, John the Baptist, Moses, Daniel and the three youths in the furnace, while the discipline of fasting is traced back to the six days of creation and the command laid upon Adam in paradise, whose transgression by eating brought sin and death into the world. A long closing movement denounces drunkenness and luxurious banqueting through the stories of Noah, Lot, the rich man and Lazarus, Judith and Esther, through satirical pictures of gluttons, drinking contests and merchant ventures, and through the prophecies against Tyre, ending with exhortations to conversion, baptism and readiness for the day of judgement.
la.ambrose.de_iacob: De Iacob, a Latin prose treatise on theology by Ambrose, belongs to late antiquity. It opens with a discussion of good discourse and the rule of reason over the passions, arguing that concupiscence can be tempered but not eradicated, and illustrating the point from David, Jacob, and Joseph. The argument then proceeds through free will and servitude to sin, the relation of law and grace after Paul's letter to the Romans, and the nature of the blessed life, before taking the patriarch Jacob's career as its principal exemplar: his exile and reconciliation with Esau, his marriages to Lia and Rachel as figures of law and grace, his wrestling with God, and his deathbed prophecies and blessings are read both morally and christologically. A concluding section presents the Maccabean martyrs, Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother, as exemplars of beatitude maintained under persecution and torment.
la.ambrose.de_joseph: A Late Antique Latin prose sermon by Ambrose, it opens with the premise that the lives of the saints offer a pattern for living and announces the history of Joseph the patriarch as its subject, above all as a mirror of chastity. The work follows the Genesis narrative of Joseph throughout: Jacob's partiality for his son, Joseph's dreams, his betrayal and sale by his brothers into Egypt, his service in an Egyptian household and rejection of his master's wife, his imprisonment and interpretation of dreams, his rise to power, and his eventual reconciliation with his brothers and father. The story is read throughout allegorically as a figure of Christ, with the sale into Egypt prefiguring the passion, Benjamin foreshadowing Paul, and the famine prefiguring the hunger for divine teaching, alongside moral exhortation on chastity, patience toward enemies, freedom within servitude, and the emptiness of worldly power. A closing section treats Jacob's descent into Egypt and his prophetic blessing of his sons.
la.ambrose.de_mysteriis: De Mysteriis is a Late Antique prose treatise of sacramental theology by Ambrose, a catechetical exposition addressed to the newly baptized. It opens by recalling the moral sermons on the patriarchs and on Proverbs that preceded it and by explaining why the mysteries were not disclosed to those not yet initiated. The exposition then follows the neophytes' experience in order: renunciation of the devil and turning toward the east; the baptismal water prefigured from the Spirit moving over the primeval waters through the flood, the crossing of the Red Sea, the sweetening of Marah, Naaman's washing in the Jordan, and the pool of Bethesda; the threefold witness of water, blood, and Spirit together with confession of the Trinity; and the rites that follow the font, namely anointing, footwashing, and the white garments, interwoven with nuptial allegories of the Church as Christ's bride drawn from the Song of Songs. The final part treats the Eucharist, arguing that the Church's sacrament is older than the synagogue's rites through Melchizedek's offering and superior to the manna in the desert, that the words of consecration change bread and wine into the true body and blood of Christ, a change supported by biblical transformations of nature and by the Virgin Birth, before closing with exhortations to guard the mysteries inviolate.
la.ambrose.de_nabuthae: A Latin prose work of late-antique moral theology attributed to Ambrose, De Nabuthae expounds the biblical story of Naboth's vineyard as a sustained sermon against avarice. It opens by declaring the story of Naboth ancient in time yet daily in experience, since Ahab's covetousness is reborn in every age and the poor are despoiled without cease. The argument then follows the narrative in which Ahab and Jezebel procure false witness and Naboth's death to seize his vineyard, expanding it into an indictment of the rich that covers luxury and jewels, hoarded granaries, a father driven to sell his children in famine, almsgiving as a loan made to God, and allegorical treatments of the rich fool's barns, Lazarus, and the horses and riders of the psalmist. The closing sections weigh Ahab's remorse and its limits, his wars with the king of Syria, and the deferred divine sentence fulfilled in his bloody death.
la.ambrose.de_noe: De Noe is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique theology in which Ambrose expounds the biblical flood narrative, opening with the announcement that he will set forth the life, character, and deeds of holy Noah and the depths of the just man's mind. The work moves through the Genesis account from God's threat to destroy humankind and the building of the ark, through the deluge, the sending of the raven and the dove, and the disembarkation, to Noah's viniculture and drunkenness, the sin of Cham, and the blessings of Sem and Iapheth. Literal and allegorical exegesis alternate throughout: the ark is read as a figure of the human body, the flood as the inundation of the passions, and details such as the birds, the rainbow, and the recurring numbers of the story as signs of vice, virtue, and divine providence.
la.ambrose.de_paradiso: De Paradiso ('On Paradise') is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise on theology and Scripture by Ambrose. It opens by citing Genesis on God's planting of a garden in Eden and acknowledges, invoking Paul's rapture to the third heaven, the difficulty of determining what and where Paradise is. The work then follows Genesis 2–3 in continuous commentary, discussing the site and nature of Paradise, allegorizing it as the fruitful soul, and interpreting its four rivers as the cardinal virtues of prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice, which are further mapped onto successive ages of sacred history. The latter part takes up the two trees, the command laid on Adam and the making of Eve from his rib, answers a series of objections, some drawn from heretics such as Apelles, about divine foreknowledge of the fall and the threat of death, and expounds the serpent's deception, Eve's transgression, and the sentences pronounced on serpent, woman and man.
la.ambrose.epistula_ad_sororem: A Latin prose letter attributed to Ambrose and addressed to his sister, of late antique date. Opening in answer to her repeated inquiries about the state of the church, the author promises a full account of recent events. It then narrates a standoff with the emperor Valentinian over the surrender of the city's basilicas: the author refuses on the grounds that divine things are not subject to imperial power, recounts the occupation of a basilica by soldiers, fines imposed on merchants, threats against his own life, and the sermons he preached on Job and Jonah amid the crisis. The account closes with the withdrawal of the troops and restitution of what had been exacted, tempered by the author's foreboding of graver disturbances to come.
la.ambrose.epistulae_variae: Epistulae Variae is a Latin prose collection of letters by Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the Late Antique period, most of them addressed to the emperors Gratian, Valentinian II, Theodosius, and Eugenius. It opens with a letter to Gratian praising his piety and defending the full divinity of Christ and the Holy Spirit. The remaining letters follow the course of Ambrose's episcopate: reports of the Council of Aquileia and its judgments against Arian, Photinian, and other dissident bishops; disputes with Valentinian over the restoration of the altar of Victory in the Roman senate house and over the attempted surrender of Milanese basilicas to Arians; and correspondence with Theodosius on the burning of a synagogue at Callinicum, the massacre at Thessalonica, the burial of Valentinian II, and money left to pagan temples under Eugenius. Throughout the collection Ambrose asserts that matters of faith belong to episcopal judgment, urges clemency and penance on Christian rulers, and treats the emperor as subject to God.
la.ambrose.expositio_evangelii_secundum_luc: The Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam is a Late Antique Latin work of theology by Ambrose, a continuous prose commentary on the third Gospel. It opens with a prologue on Luke 1:1, in which Ambrose argues that the evangelist, unlike the many who undertook to narrate without completing the task, wrote all things diligently under divine inspiration. The exposition then follows Luke's narrative from the annunciations to Zacharias and Mary, through the birth and preaching of John the Baptist, the parables and miracles of Jesus's ministry, and his discourses, to the Passion, crucifixion, and the resurrection appearances. In the course of the commentary Ambrose draws moral and mystical meanings from each episode, discusses disputed points such as the agreement of the evangelists' genealogies and resurrection accounts, and repeatedly defends the full divinity of Christ, the perpetual virginity of Mary, and the unity of the Trinity against heretical readings.
la.ambrose.expositio_psalmi_cxviii: A prose theological exposition of Psalm 118, the alphabetical psalm on the law of the Lord, by the late-antique Latin author Ambrose, who comments on the psalm verse by verse as it runs through the twenty-two Hebrew letters, eight verses to each. The opening ranks the psalm as the summit of David's moral teaching, like the sun at midday among his moral psalms. The bulk of the work expounds the verses as instruction in the moral life, amendment of conduct, custody of God's commandments, resistance to temptation and persecution, readiness for martyrdom, while moving continually from the moral to the mystical sense, above all through the Song of Songs' figures of the bride as soul or church and Christ as bridegroom. Recurring topics include baptismal purification, the relation of law and gospel, the discipline of speech and silence, and the passage of divine truth from synagogue to church, until the last letter, Tau, closes with the confession of straying like a lost sheep and the plea that the Lord seek out his servant.
la.anonymous.laudes_domini: Laudes Domini ('The Praises of the Lord') is an anonymous Latin poem of uncertain date, transmitted among medieval works; its closing prayer for the victory of a Constantine is the only fixed point in its chronology. It opens with rhetorical questions about the apparent slowness of divine rewards, answered by the story of a devoted couple among the Aedui on the Arar, whose vow of a shared tomb is confirmed when the dead wife's outstretched hand invites her husband to join her. The greater part of the poem addresses Christ directly, praising his ordering of sea, land, vines, trees, animals, seasons and nightly rest, and then recounting the virgin conception, his teaching, miracles and raising of the dead, and his ascent to heaven. The final lines describe his opening of hell's gates to release all but the wicked, his apportioning of places of punishment, and the prayer that Christ grant Constantine victory and joy.
la.anonymus.carmen_ad_agobardum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem in four-line stanzas, addressed to an Agobard whose name the poem itself spells out through the initial letters of its stanzas. It opens with an invocation to the immense creator who holds the whole earth within his fist and is begged, as omnipresent witness and judge, to be appeased. The bulk of the poem is a penitential lament in which the speaker, thrust into the prison of a dreadful death, contemplates the punishment awaiting the proud, sees his life draining away as guilt pours in, awaits the terrible shore where the spirit must leave its fleshly seat, and asks that friends, kinsmen, and the dear survivor who will bear out his cold body come to his aid, before calling on Christ to strengthen him for both life and death. It ends by offering the verses to the addressee as 'father', bidding him read his own name in the poem's initial letters, and closing with petitions for the addressee's welfare, a request to be commended to fellow Christians, and a trinitarian doxology.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_exordio_francorum: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, the Carmen de exordiis Francorum addresses a Frankish ruler named Charles and undertakes a versified account of the origins of the Frankish people. It opens with a declaration that a prose narrative of the nation will now be supplemented in verse. The poem then traces a line of descent from the decline of Rome through Ansbertus, who marries Blithild, daughter of the Frankish king Hlotharius, and their children, among them the martyred bishop Feriolus, the confessor Modericus, and the miracle-working virgin Tharsicia, before continuing through the line of Arnulf, Ansgise, and Pippin to the deeds of Charles himself, praised for subduing the Saxons and checking the Northmen. A closing section celebrates the pious reign of Louis, exhorts the young Charles to temper the valour of David with the wisdom of Solomon as his successor, and promises a further verse account of Christ's miracles and deeds under the figures of man, lion, calf, and eagle.
