la.anonymus.carmina_augiensia: The Carmina Augiensia is a medieval Latin collection of anonymous verse whose title points to the monastery of Reichenau (Augia), transmitted in a fragmentary state with many lacunae. It opens with a greeting to St Valentine, whom Christ admits to the apostolic choirs above the stars. The collection consists mainly of inscriptional verses for altars, images and the cross, in the manner of tituli: poems in honour of an altar of St Mary offered by a priest-monk and invoking Peter, Paul, John the Baptist, Sebastian and Valentine; a poem on a cross dedicated to the Virgin in which Egino is named; verses on the signs of the cross; and a series naming the four evangelists, with short pieces on Gospel miracles, including the raising of Lazarus and of the widow's son, an exorcism, the stilling of wind and wave, and cures wrought by touch and spittle.
la.anonymus.carmina_bibliothecarum_et_psalt: An anonymous medieval Latin collection of dedicatory and descriptive verses composed for a royal Bible and for psalters. The opening lines name the four companions of David, Asaph, Eman, Ethan, and Idithun, and then praise a King Charles, likened to Josiah and Theodosius, crediting Jerome with transcribing David's psalms and the scribe Liuthard with the completion of the book. Further poems enumerate the uses of the two Testaments gathered in the bibliotheca, count the years since Christ's birth and of Charles's reign, and expound the evangelist symbols depicted in the manuscript, including the calf and the eagle. The closing verses retell episodes from Paul's conversion, his baptism by Ananias and flight in a basket, and Christ the Lamb's unsealing of the seven seals of the Apocalypse.
la.anonymus.carmina_de_ludovico_ii: An anonymous medieval Latin poem on the emperor Louis II, consisting of a narrative lament followed by an epitaph. It opens with a summons to all the ends of the earth to hear of the crime committed at Benevento, where Adelpherius and the citizens, fearing for their kingdom, seize the pious emperor, lead him from his palace as though to martyrdom, and resolve on his death, while Louis protests in words recalling Christ's passion. The narrative goes on to tell how the imperial crown is set on the head of the scheming tempter, who is then vexed by a demon and falls to the ground amid wondering crowds, after which the Lord's judgment brings a Saracen invasion into Calabria and up to Salerno, and an oath is sworn on the holy relics to defend the kingdom and seek another ruler. The poem closes with an elegiac epitaph on Louis Caesar, recalling the sceptres of Italy handed on by his grandfather, the imperial name conferred by Rome, his strong and peaceful rule and his endurance of frequent Saracen attacks, and the mourning of Rome, Latium and Gaul at his death, while his spirit rejoices in heaven.
la.anonymus.carmina_libris_saec_viii_adiect: A collection of anonymous Latin verses transmitted as additions to books of the eighth century, opening with an invocation that Christ preserve one Ragnard and a note naming the young scribe Hieronimus of noble stock. The remainder assembles dedicatory prefaces and praise poems largely bound up with the circle of Charlemagne: a verse epistle to Pope Hadrian celebrating the overthrow of the Lombard king Desiderius; prefaces to a golden psalter naming the scribe Dagulf and his pupil Deodatus; a dedication by Adam son of Haynhard written at Worms; verses recording how the deacon Godesscalc completed a gospel book after a journey to Rome and the baptism of Carloman under the name Pippin; Wigbod's preface to a compilation of Mosaic verses made at the king's command; and closing lines accompanying a herbal. Throughout, the poems dwell on golden letters on purple parchment, royal piety toward the apostolic see, and the humility of servile scribes offering small works to great patrons.
la.anonymus.translatio_sancti_mercurii: An anonymous medieval Latin poem, of uncertain date, narrating the translation of the relics of Saint Mercurius; it opens by announcing that the saint's passio has been told in the verses preceding it. The poem recounts how the emperor Constans, campaigning to subdue Apulia, took charge of the martyr's body with three monks and sacked the wealthy city of Quintodecimum near Benevento before meeting a violent death in Sicily on his homeward way, while the monks buried the body beneath a basilica threshold marked by a stone, where it lay forgotten for some ninety-five years. Prince Arechis, having built a basilica of Holy Wisdom at Benevento and entombed the twelve martyr brothers there, resolved to join Mercurius' bones to theirs; with the bishop he excavated the half-ruined shrine, and after the martyr appeared urging the work's completion, the body was carried toward Benevento, the bier halting miraculously outside the walls. The people's lamentations and Arechis' prostrate vows, including the donation of Quintodecimum itself, together with the heaven-sent lightness of the bier, lead to the saint's honourable entombment in the basilica, an event the closing lines date to the seventh of August in the 738th year from the Incarnation.
la.anonymus.translatio_xii_martyrum: Translatio XII Martyrum is a medieval Latin poem, anonymous and of uncertain date, that gives a versified account of the removal of the relics of twelve martyrs to Benevento under the prince Arechis. It opens by observing that the bodies of many saints long lay hidden in obscure graves until divine grace brought them to light. The narrative then follows Arechis's petition for relics from Apulia, the joyous procession of the whole populace into the city, the gifts of land and treasure offered by citizens and prince alike, the construction of a marble church beside the princely palace where the martyrs are buried together in a single altar, the enclosure of dedicated virgins in a cloister there, and the prince's night vision in which the martyrs promise that his devotion will be rewarded. The closing lines state that Abbot Matthew ordered the book to be made and commend the work to Christ.
la.apuleius.apologia: Apuleius' Apologia (Pro se de magia) is a prose defense speech delivered before the proconsul Claudius Maximus against a capital charge of magic, pressed by Sicinius Aemilianus and other kinsmen of Apuleius' wife, the wealthy widow Pudentilla. It opens by portraying the accuser as a reckless calumniator and claiming the trial as an occasion to vindicate philosophy itself. The argument then works through the alleged evidence in turn, amatory verses, a mirror, the purchase of fish, an incantation that supposedly felled a boy, an inscribed wooden image, and excerpts torn from Pudentilla's letters, interleaving digressions on Plato, Aristotle, natural history, and medicine, and defending the motives, the modest dowry terms, and the domestic concord of the marriage. It closes with the speaker summarily rebutting each accusation in turn and declaring that he fears the proconsul's judgment less than his disapproval.
la.apuleius.florida: The Florida is a Latin prose miscellany of excerpts from the public display speeches delivered at Carthage by Apuleius, a philosopher and orator of the later imperial period. It opens with a comparison between the reverent pauses travellers make at sacred spots along the road and the ceremonial pause a speaker owes on entering so venerable a city. The excerpts then range over anecdote, encomium and moral reflection: Socrates's manner of judging men, the piping contest of Marsyas with Apollo, the gymnosophists of India, Alexander's edict confining his portraiture to three artists, Hippias of Elis with his self-made implements, the talking parrot, the Cynic Crates, Pythagoras's schooling and rule of silence, the comic poet Philemon dying over an unfinished play, Asclepiades reviving a man already prepared for burial, and Protagoras's paradoxical bargain with his pupil Euathlus. Many of the pieces praise the learning of Carthage, thank its magistrates and proconsuls, and speak of a statue decreed to the author by the city.
la.arnobius.adversus_nationes: Arnobius's Adversus Nationes is a seven-book Latin prose defense of Christianity written in the late antique period. It opens with Arnobius answering the charge that the world has suffered calamity after calamity since the Christian religion first appeared on earth. Across the seven books the author contends that pestilence, drought, and war long antedate the Christians; derides the births, loves, and crimes that poets and theologians ascribe to the gods; condemns temples, cult statues, sacrifice, and divination as unworthy treatments of deity; and rejects the Platonic doctrines of the soul's divine origin and natural immortality. A sustained defense of Christ's miracles and messianic mission, together with the claim that the one supreme God is the only object of worship, binds the treatise together.
la.augustine.adnotationes_in_iob: A late-antique Latin exegetical work by Augustine, the Adnotationes in Iob consists of short interpretive notes on the Book of Job, expounding the biblical verses chiefly in a spiritual or allegorical rather than literal sense. It opens with the sacrifices Job offers for his children in the book's first chapter, read as figures of confession and charity. The commentary then follows the whole course of the poem, from Job's laments and the speeches of his three friends Eliphaz, Bildad and Sophar, through the intervention of Elihu and the Lord's answer out of the whirlwind with its questions about creation, to Job's final reply and submission. Throughout, Job and his trials are read as bearing on Christ, the Church, the relation of Jews and Gentiles, and the penitent sinner's confession and correction of life.
la.augustine.breviculus_collationis_cum_don: The Breviculus Collationis cum Donatistis is a Latin prose summary by Augustine, of Late Antique date, of the official acts of the conference between Catholic and Donatist bishops held at Carthage by imperial command before the tribune and notary Marcellinus as cognitor. It opens by explaining that the full transcript of the proceedings was so prolix as to be hard to read, and that a breviary was therefore compiled with numbered headings so that any passage could readily be found. The work then follows the three days of disputation in order: the reading of the imperial rescript and edicts, the written petitions and mandates of both parties, the procedural conflicts and the dispute over the numbers of bishops present, the scriptural arguments over whether evil men are mixed within the church in this age, the recitation of the earlier councils and imperial judgements concerning Caecilianus of Carthage and his ordainer Felix of Aptunga, and the Donatists' repeated efforts to obstruct the reading of documents unfavourable to their case. It ends with the cognitor's final sentence pronouncing the Donatist position confuted by the evidence.
la.augustine.contra_academicos: Contra Academicos, a Late Antique Latin prose dialogue by Augustine, opens with an exhortation to his friend Romanianus, urging him toward the philosophical life and offering the disputation that follows as a first taste of it. The work records discussions at a country villa in which Augustine, Alypius, Licentius, and Trygetius first debate whether a happy life is possible for one who seeks truth without finding it, and then turn to Augustine's promised attack on the Academics, whose doctrines that nothing can be perceived and that the wise must suspend assent he expounds before arguing that many truths, mathematical, moral, and sensible, are known with certainty and that wisdom itself can be attained. The dialogue distinguishes the old from the new Academy and traces the school from Arcesilas and Carneades through Antiochus to Plotinus, closing with Augustine's declaration that he will hold fast to the authority of Christ while pursuing truth by reason chiefly among the Platonists.
la.augustine.contra_cresconium_grammaticum_: A polemical work in Latin prose by Augustine, written against Cresconius, a Donatist grammarian who had composed a reply to Augustine's earlier letter to Petilian. The opening addresses Cresconius directly, explaining the circumstances of the correspondence and defending both eloquence and dialectic against Cresconius's accusations that these arts served falsehood. The work then proceeds through the whole range of the Donatist controversy: it argues at length that the validity of baptism does not depend on the moral condition of the minister, defends the Catholic practice of not rebaptizing converts from schism, contests the appeal to Cyprian's authority, and examines at great length the case of the Maximianists, whom the Donatists had condemned and later received back without rebaptism, arguing that this concession refutes their own principles. It also treats the accusations of traditor and the violence of the circumcellions, and closes with a summary recapitulation of the argument, urging Cresconius and his party to return to Catholic unity.
la.augustine.contra_faustum: Augustine's Contra Faustum is a Late Antique Latin prose polemic against the Manichaean Faustus, an eloquent African adherent of that sect whose volume attacking the Christian faith had been read in Augustine's community. The work opens with an account of Faustus and of the brothers' request for a reply, and then proceeds by quoting Faustus's words section by section and answering them in turn. Over its course Augustine defends the Old Testament against Manichaean rejection, arguing that the Gospel fulfils rather than abolishes the law of Moses, and refutes Manichaean teaching on the two principles, the sun and moon, marriage and divorce, food prohibitions, and the Paraclete. The later books take up the Christian feasts, the authority of the apostolic scriptures, the fate of the patriarchs, and the comparison of Manichaeans with pagans, closing with an exhortation to abandon the sect's error.
la.augustine.contra_gaudentium_donatistarum: A late antique prose polemic in which Augustine refutes two letters addressed by Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, to the imperial tribune and notary Dulcitius, who had been charged by the emperor with enforcing the laws for Christian unity; the letters were written after Gaudentius threatened to burn himself and his followers in a church. The work opens with Augustine explaining his plan to answer the letters by quoting each passage and replying to it, a form he adopts in place of the disputed 'Petilianus dixit' arrangement of his earlier rejoinder. The main body takes up Gaudentius's arguments point by point, defending imperial coercion, rejecting the Donatist claim to persecution and to martyrdom through self-immolation, denouncing the violence of the circumcelliones, and discussing the hearing of Emeritus of Caesarea, the exemplum of Razias in Maccabees, rebaptism, and the traditor charges against Secundus of Tigisis. It closes with an extended appeal to Cyprian's witness that the catholic church spreads through the whole world and bears the wicked within it, set against the Donatist claim to be the one true church.
la.augustine.contra_mendacium: A late-antique Latin prose treatise cast as a letter to Consentius, Augustine's Contra Mendacium argues that lying is never lawful, not even for a pious purpose. It opens with Augustine apologising for a year's delay in answering the writings his correspondent sent him, praising his zeal against the Priscillianists while rejecting their claim that falsehood may rightly be used to hunt hidden heretics. The bulk of the work refutes that claim on the ground that sin cannot be fought with sin, and then examines the scriptural passages alleged to sanction lying, the Hebrew midwives, Rahab, Jacob's deception of Isaac, Lot at Sodom, David's rash oath, and Christ's apparently false words and actions, showing them to be either truthful signification or sins not to be imitated. Augustine closes by urging Consentius to overturn the Libra of Dictinius on these lines and insisting that no cause, not even the saving of a life or of a soul, justifies lying, perjury, or blasphemy in matters of religion.
la.augustine.contra_secundinum: Contra Secundinum is a short anti-Manichaean treatise in Latin prose by Augustine of the Late Antique period, composed as a reply to a letter from Secundinus, a Manichaean who had questioned the motives for Augustine's departure from the sect. It opens with an acknowledgment of the correspondent's goodwill and a refusal to trade suspicions over why the author left Manichaeism, insisting that only his conscience before God matters. The argument then turns to doctrine, attacking the Manichaean cosmogony of two opposed natures of light and darkness and defending instead creation from nothing, the immutability of God, evil as a voluntary defect rather than a substance, and the distinction between Christ as unigenitus and as primogenitus of all creation. It closes by answering Secundinus's objections to episodes of the Old Testament, upholding the reality of Christ's flesh, death, and resurrection against Manichaean teaching, and urging the correspondent's return to the catholic faith.
la.augustine.de_agone_christiano: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine on the Christian combat, it sets out how the believer triumphs over the devil, whom Christ has already conquered by taking on human nature. It opens with the claim that the crown of victory is promised only to those who fight, identifying the adversary as the devil, who reigns through cupidity and is cast out when the heart renounces the world. Augustine then explains that the invisible enemy is defeated within, through submission of the self and body to God under his providence, and presents the Incarnation as the medicine that heals every human vice of pride, avarice, anger, impiety and fear. The latter part rehearses a rule of faith in the one unchangeable Trinity and answers in turn a series of heretical denials, concerning Manichaean teaching, the Son's divinity, the reality of Christ's body and mind, his resurrection, ascension and session at the Father's right hand, the last judgment, the coming of the Spirit, the worldwide catholic church against Donatists and Luciferians, and the resurrection of the flesh, closing with an exhortation to grow in charity and so merit the promised crown.
la.augustine.de_baptismo: A late-antique Latin prose treatise of Augustine, composed amid the Donatist controversy, arguing that baptism administered by heretics and schismatics is Christ's own sacrament, valid though unprofitable outside the unity of the Catholic Church, and therefore not to be repeated for converts. It opens by recalling Augustine's promise, made in earlier books written against Parmenian's letter to Tychonius, to treat the question of baptism more fully, and announces a twofold aim: to refute the Donatists' objections and to answer their appeal to the authority of Cyprian the martyr. The body of the work sustains the case that the sacrament keeps its integrity wherever the gospel words are used, distinguishing holding baptism from holding it usefully, and treating remission of sins, John's baptism, the baptism of infants, and the effect of unworthy ministers and recipients. In its later portion Augustine turns to Cyprian, citing his letters to Jubaianus, Quintus and Pompey and the opinions of the African bishops gathered with him at Carthage, and contends that Cyprian, though in error on rebaptism, remained in communion with colleagues of a different view and so offers no warrant for schism.
la.augustine.de_bono_viduitatis: A brief Late Antique prose treatise in the form of a letter, written by Augustine the bishop to Juliana, a devout Christian widow who had pressed him to make good a promise to write on the profession of holy widowhood. It opens with an apology for the delay and a remark that, although addressed to one woman, the letter is meant to profit others through her. The doctrinal first half expounds Paul in 1 Corinthians 7 to set the goods of marriage, widowhood and virginity in order, maintaining that widowhood excels wedlock without condemning it and rebutting those who denounce second marriages, before weighing the merits of widows against the scriptural exempla of Anna and Ruth and asking whether third or later marriages can be condemned. A longer exhortatory second half urges perseverance in the widowed vow, defends the necessity of prayer and divine grace against those who rest perseverance on free will alone, and closes with practical counsels on prayer, fasting, almsgiving and the safeguarding of a good reputation.
la.augustine.de_conjugiis_adulterinis: De coniugiis adulterinis is a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a reply to his correspondent Pollentius on whether adultery dissolves a marriage. It opens with Pollentius's question whether Paul's injunction that a departed wife remain unmarried applies only to a woman who has left an adulterous husband. Augustine contends that the marital bond endures as long as both spouses live, so that neither divorce for fornication nor separation from an unbelieving partner frees anyone to remarry, and he defends the reconciliation of penitent adulterers against objections drawn from human law, the weakness of the flesh, and the double standard that judges male and female incontinence differently. The work closes with discussion of the baptism of catechumens and of persons living in adulterous unions who, near death, can no longer answer for themselves.
la.augustine.de_consensu_evangelistarum: A Late Antique theological treatise in Latin prose by Augustine, written to defend the mutual agreement of the four canonical Gospels against pagans and others who allege contradictions among the evangelists. It opens by ranking the gospel above all other scriptures and by assigning each evangelist a distinct role, Matthew's royal and Luke's priestly emphasis on the human Christ, Mark's position as abridging follower, and John's soaring account of Christ's divinity, before rebutting objections that Christ wrote nothing himself and that his disciples taught magic. The greater part of the work then proceeds through the gospel narratives, from the genealogies and infancy of Jesus through his ministry, parables, Passion, resurrection, and post-Easter appearances, comparing the four accounts episode by episode to show that omissions, variations of wording, and differences of narrative order do not entail real disagreement.
la.augustine.de_cura_pro_mortuis_gerenda: Augustine's De Cura pro Mortuis Gerenda is a brief Latin prose treatise cast as a letter to the bishop Paulinus, opening with an answer to a widow's question whether burial beside a saint's memorial benefits the deceased. Augustine argues that funerary care, burial, and the choice of a grave at martyrs' shrines are solace for the living rather than aid to the dead, while prayer, almsgiving, and altar offerings profit only those whose lives merited such help. The treatise then examines scriptural passages on burial, reports of the dead appearing in dreams and visions, most fully the case of Curma and his vision of paradise, and the question whether martyrs assist petitioners in person or through angels, a point Augustine declines to settle. He closes by restating that burial is an office of humanity and a testimony to the resurrection, and that commendation of the dead at the martyrs' memorials serves chiefly to quicken the supplications of the living.
la.augustine.de_fide_et_operibus: Augustine's De fide et operibus is a late-antique prose treatise on theology that opens by setting out the position of certain opponents, namely that all who present themselves should be admitted to the baptismal washing without exception, even those who openly profess their resolve to persist in sins such as adultery. In reply, Augustine argues that those seeking baptism must first be instructed both in the rule of faith and in the conduct proper to Christian life, since faith without works is dead, drawing on the rich young man of the Gospel, John the Baptist's preaching to publicans and soldiers, and Peter's call for repentance before the three thousand were baptized at Pentecost. The argument then answers a series of scriptural objections, including the baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch, Paul's claim to have known nothing among his hearers but Christ crucified, the two precepts of charity, and Israel's passage through the Red Sea before the giving of the Law, and takes up the parables of the wheat and the tares, the net, and the wedding feast to show that the presence of the wicked in the church requires patient tolerance without any relaxation of ecclesiastical discipline, a discussion that touches the Donatist schism. A long concluding section treats the saying in 1 Corinthians 3 about building on the foundation with wood, hay, and stubble and being saved as through fire, which Augustine, together with the Epistle of James, reads as excluding any promise of salvation to those who remain in manifest sins on the strength of faith alone.
la.augustine.de_genesi_ad_litteram_imperfec: An unfinished Latin prose treatise of late antiquity by Augustine on the literal interpretation of the Genesis account of creation. It opens with a preface insisting that obscure questions about natural things be treated by inquiry rather than rash assertion, briefly names four recognised modes of scriptural exposition (historical, allegorical, analogical and aetiological), and then states the Catholic faith in summary: the consubstantial Trinity created all things from nothing, evil is either sin or the punishment of sin, and humanity is renewed through Christ. The main body works through the opening verses of Genesis, asking what 'in the beginning' signifies, whether time itself is a creature, how the angels and the first light are to be understood, what it means that the spirit of God moved over the waters, and how the firmament, the waters above and beneath it, the dry land, plants, the heavenly bodies, fish and birds, land animals, and finally man made in the image and likeness of God are to be expounded, with sustained discussion of the plural 'let us make' as spoken of the Trinity. Questions are posed and rival readings weighed rather than affirmed, and the exposition breaks off within the first chapter of Genesis, in keeping with its designation as an unfinished book.
la.augustine.de_mendacio: De Mendacio is a Late Antique prose treatise on lying by Augustine, opening with the observation that the question of falsehood disturbs ordinary daily conduct and announcing an inquiry pursued with little care for verbal elegance. The work first defines lying, distinguishing the speaker who declares what he takes to be true from the liar who has one thing in his heart and another in his words, and then asks whether any lie can be useful, weighing the scriptural cases that defenders of lying adduce, such as Sarah's denial, Jacob's deception of Isaac, and the Egyptian midwives. Augustine goes on to test the divine prohibitions of falsehood and disputed passages about oaths and false witness, considers whether bodily chastity may ever be shielded by a lie, and arranges eight kinds of lies in descending order of gravity, from falsehood in religious teaching down to lies that harm no one. He concludes that lying is never permitted under any of these heads, rejects the claim that the apostle Paul lied in the episode involving Peter and Barnabas, and closes with a prayer for strength against temptation.
la.augustine.de_natura_boni: De Natura Boni ('On the Nature of Good') is a compact Latin theological treatise of late antiquity by Augustine, directed against the Manichaeans. It opens by identifying God as the supreme, immutable, and eternal good from whom every other good, great or small, derives, all created things having been made from nothing and therefore mutable. From that premise the work argues that evil is not a nature or substance but the corruption of the measure, form, and order proper to each creature, treating sin, pain, punishment, prime matter, and the eternal fire as privations within goods rather than things in themselves, and reinforcing its case with a series of biblical testimonies. The closing section assails the Manichaean mythology in detail, the war between the kingdom of light and the race of darkness, the mixture and supposed purification of the divine substance, and the practices of Mani's elect, and ends with a prayer for the conversion of those ensnared in the error.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_gratia: On Nature and Grace (De natura et gratia) is a Latin prose treatise by Augustine, composed in Late Antiquity and addressed to Timasius and Jacobus. It opens with the author's report that he has read with close attention the book they sent him, written against people who excuse their sins by blaming human nature rather than their own wills. The body of the work is a sustained rejoinder to that book's claim that human beings, by natural capacity and free choice, can be without sin: Augustine argues that human nature, injured by Adam's transgression, requires the grace of Christ both for the forgiveness of past sins and for aid in avoiding future ones, adducing Pauline passages on original sin and infant baptism and weighing texts from Ambrose, Hilary, Jerome, and his own De libero arbitrio. He excepts the Virgin Mary alone from the universality of sin and ends by expounding the charity that, poured into human hearts by the Holy Spirit, makes the divine commandments light.
la.augustine.de_natura_et_origine_animae: De Natura et Origine Animae is a Late Antique theological treatise in prose by Augustine, directed against the doctrines of Vincentius Victor on the nature and origin of the soul. It opens as a letter to Renatus, thanking him for forwarding two books by Victor, a young writer lately converted from Rogatist Donatist circles. The remainder comprises further letters, addressed to the presbyter Peter and to Victor himself, in which Augustine refutes Victor's claims that the soul emanates from God's own breath rather than being created from nothing, that it is a body rather than a spirit, that it merited guilt before its bodily existence, and that infants dying unbaptised may reach paradise and even the kingdom of heaven, for whom sacrifice ought to be offered. Throughout, Augustine maintains a suspended judgment as to whether individual souls are propagated from their parents or newly infused by God, while insisting that the soul is a mutable creature made from nothing and not of the substance of God.
la.augustine.de_opere_monachorum: De Opere Monachorum, a late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, takes the form of a letter written at the request of his fellow bishop Aurelius. It opens by acknowledging that commission and posing its question: whether monks who refuse manual labour may rightly appeal to Paul's precept that whoever will not work shall not eat and to the Gospel's counsel against anxiety for food. The main body argues from Paul's letters that the apostle's admonition concerns bodily labour, reviews Paul's own practice of supporting himself by handwork while preaching and his refusal of the support owed to evangelists, discusses the alms supplied to needy servants of God, and rebukes idle wandering monks who trade on relics and feigned sanctity under the name of the monastic profession. A concluding admonition censures long-haired brethren who justify uncut hair by claiming that self-castration has made them neither male nor female, and the letter closes with instructions for its circulation among Augustine's monks.
la.augustine.de_ordine: De Ordine is a Late Antique Latin prose dialogue in the genre of theology, by Augustine. It opens with a preface addressed to Zenobius on how difficult and rare it is to see or set forth the order by which the world coheres and is governed. The greater part of the work stages conversations at a country villa among Augustine, the youths Licentius and Trygetius, Alypius, and Augustine's mother: a night dispute over whether anything happens outside divine order, prompted by the varying sound of water in a channel, leads through a definition of order, the place of evil and justice within providence, an observed cockfight read as evidence of natural law, and a discussion of authority and reason in education. The dialogue closes with an ordered survey of the liberal disciplines from grammar and dialectic through rhetoric, music, geometry, and astronomy, showing how number purifies the soul for contemplation of God and of truth, and ends with praise of Pythagoras.
la.augustine.de_patientia: A late antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine on patience, De Patientia (On Patience) opens by asking how patience can be predicated of a God who cannot suffer, concluding that divine patience is real though ineffable. The work then defines human patience as the equanimous endurance of evils for the sake of higher goods, distinguishing it from the endurance of the greedy, the ambitious, and the criminal, which springs from cupidity rather than virtue and merits no praise. Job figures as the exemplar of endurance; the argument rejects self-inflicted death and contends that true patience is not the fruit of unaided free will but a gift of God, poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit by charity. The closing pages answer objections concerning grace and election, weigh whether endurance shown in schism counts as this gift, and end with the assurance that the patience of the poor of Christ will not perish but yield eternal fruit.
la.augustine.de_sancta_virginitate: Augustine's Latin treatise De Sancta Virginitate, a work of Late Antique prose theology, opens by recalling his recently published De Bono Coniugali and urging Christ's consecrated virgins not to despise the married faithful on account of the greater gift they have received. The argument sets holy virginity above wedlock and widowhood without condemning marriage, treating Mary's bodily and spiritual motherhood, Paul's counsel on virgins, the eunuchs who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, the parable of the denarius, and the new song of the hundred and forty-four thousand in the Apocalypse. It closes with a long exhortation on humility, warning the virgins against pride and vainglory and holding up the meek and lowly Christ as both teacher and exemplar whose grace alone guards so great a good.
la.augustine.de_spiritu_et_littera: A Late Antique Latin prose theological treatise by Augustine, opening as a letter to the correspondent Marcellinus in which Augustine answers his objection that nothing can be held possible if no example of it exists, in this case, a human being living without sin through divine aid. The work's central argument opposes those who hold that the human will can attain righteousness without God's help, expounding Paul's saying that 'the letter kills, but the spirit gives life' and maintaining that even human justice is God's work accomplished through grace. Augustine proceeds through sustained exegesis of Romans, contrasting the law of works with the law of faith, the Decalogue written on stone with the law written in the heart, and the old and new testaments, and closes by defending free will as established rather than annulled by grace and asking whether the will to believe is itself God's gift.
la.augustine.de_utilitate_credendi: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, addressed to his friend Honoratus, in which the author defends the Catholic practice of believing before understanding against the Manichaean promise of pure reason. It opens with a distinction between the heretic, who begets or follows false opinions for the sake of gain and glory, and the honest man deceived into crediting heretics, together with a pledge to explain how truth is to be found and kept. The body of the work recalls Augustine's own some nine years among the Manichaeans, sets out a fourfold reading of the Old Testament as history, aetiology, analogy and allegory, answers Manichaean attacks on the Old Law and the Catholic faith, and separates blameless belief from culpable credulity through examples of error in reading. It argues that in religion authority, confirmed by miracles and the assent of the multitude, must precede reason for minds not yet capable of grasping truth directly, and closes by urging Honoratus to commit himself to the teachers of the Catholic church and to prayer, while noting that Augustine has not yet begun a direct refutation of the Manichaeans themselves.
la.augustine.epistulae: The Epistulae of Augustine form a Latin prose collection of Late Antique correspondence with friends, fellow clergy, and lay men and women. The collection opens with a letter in which the author defends his treatment of the Academics, arguing that he imitated rather than attacked their veiling of Platonic truth. It then moves through exchanges with Nebridius and Alypius on beatitude, the soul, and the intelligible world, a lengthy inquiry into how God may be seen, discussion of the spiritual body of the resurrection, and instruction on baptism and penance set against Novatianist teaching. Shorter letters handle practical and pastoral business, including a debt of seventeen solidi, appeals for alms, the dedication of a basilica, and encouragement of correspondents in faith and charity.
la.augustine.gesta_cum_emerito_donatistarum: The Gesta cum Emerito is a Latin prose record of a disputation held at Caesarea in the greater church, under the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the eighth of Theodosius, between Augustine of Hippo, attended by fellow Catholic bishops including Alypius and Possidius, and Emeritus, a Donatist bishop. Opening with Augustine's account of how Emeritus entered the city and consented to come into the church, the proceedings turn on his demand that Emeritus state why he has come, and on the Donatist's persistent refusal to speak. Augustine then has Alypius read aloud the letter addressed to the tribune and notary Marcellinus, in which the Catholics undertook to surrender their sees if defeated at the Conference of Carthage, and expounds at length the Donatists' own condemnation of the Maximianist schism, arguing that their reception of bishops once excommunicated exposes their inconsistency over rebaptism and schism. The record closes with an appeal to the congregation to pray for Emeritus rather than despair of him.
la.augustine.liber_de_divinis_scripturis_si: The Liber de divinis scripturis sive Speculum is a late antique Latin florilegium transmitted under Augustine's name, which gathers proof texts from Scripture under a long sequence of doctrinal and moral headings. It opens with a table of more than a hundred chapter titles, running from the one God and the distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit through precepts on almsgiving, oaths, idolatry, virginity, and widowhood to chapters that explain figurative names in Scripture such as the vine, the mountains, the stars, and the dogs. The body then supplies the corresponding passages, introduced by formulae such as 'In genesi' and 'Item apostolus ad romanos' and drawn from the Pentateuch, the Psalms, the wisdom books, the prophets, the Gospels, the apostolic epistles, and the Apocalypse. The chapters move from Trinitarian doctrine through conversion, fear of the Lord, peace and charity, just judgment, and the care of the poor, widows, and orphans, to penitence, prayer, resurrection, the tribulations of the just, and warnings against idolatry, fornication, drunkenness, usury, and false prophets, concluding with the sanctity of Samuel and Paul, the washing of feet, and the Lord as the fountain of life.
la.augustine.liber_de_unico_baptismo: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, the Liber de unico baptismo is a polemical reply to a Donatist composition claiming that baptism administered outside their communion is no true baptism and must be repeated. It opens with an address to Constantine, explaining that Augustine has often been compelled to answer those who err from the rule of truth and now responds to a Donatist sermon on the one baptism that reached him through a Donatist presbyter. The main argument holds that God's truth may be held even in iniquity, as among Jews, idolaters, and demons who confessed Christ, so that baptism given by heretics and schismatics is to be acknowledged rather than destroyed, while rebaptism is condemned as diabolical presumption. Augustine further reviews the old dispute over rebaptism between Cyprian of Carthage and Stephen of Rome, defends bishops such as Caecilian, Miltiades, and Marcellinus against Donatist accusations, and closes by reaffirming that the church spread through the whole world corrects men's iniquity without violating the divine sacrament.
la.augustine.sermo_ad_caesariensis_ecclesia: A Latin prose sermon of Augustine, addressed to the people of the church at Caesarea and preserved among his writings against the Donatists. It opens with the preacher's joy that Emeritus, a Donatist bishop, has shown willingness toward unity, and with the congregation's acclamation 'aut hic aut nusquam'. The sermon then argues that schismatics may be received because the baptism they bear belongs to Christ rather than to Donatus, distinguishing the sacramental sign from salvation and urging the wanderer to return so that the sign may profit rather than condemn him, with an extended exposition of charity from 1 Corinthians and of the inheritance of peace under the figure of Sara and her rivals. It closes by rehearsing the origins of the Donatist party in the persecution of Caecilian and the colloquy at Carthage, defending the Catholic pursuit of the stray brother, and praying that Emeritus may communicate in peace, unity and love.
la.aurelius_victor.de_caesaribus: The De Caesaribus of Aurelius Victor is a short Latin prose history of the Roman emperors, a work of Late Antique historiography arranged as a succession of reign-by-reign biographical notices. It opens with the collapse of republican institutions and the concentration of power in the hands of Octavian, who took the name Augustus after his victory over Antony. From there the narrative runs through the Julio-Claudian house and the civil wars of 69, the Flavians, the adoptive and Severan emperors, and the military turbulence of the third century, closing with Diocletian's tetrarchy, the rise of Constantine, and the reign of Constantius II. Throughout, portraits of individual rulers alternate with sketches of their deeds and with frequent moralizing judgments on character, luxury, cruelty, and the fortunes of the Roman state.
la.aurelius_victor.epitome_de_caesaribus: A Latin prose work of imperial historiography of the Late Antique era, attributed to Aurelius Victor, the Epitome de Caesaribus consists of short biographies of the Roman emperors. It opens by recording how, in the 722nd year from the founding of the city, the Roman practice of obedience to a single ruler was revived and Octavian, renamed Augustus for his victory, assumed supreme power. The narrative then proceeds reign by reign, giving each emperor's family, deeds, character, vices and manner of death: the Julio-Claudians and the brief reigns of Galba, Otho and Vitellius, the Flavians and the adoptive emperors, the soldier-emperors and usurpers of the third century, the tetrarchy of Diocletian, Constantine and his sons and rivals, and finally the dynasty of Valentinian and Theodosius. The work ends with the death of Theodosius at Milan and the translation of his body to Constantinople.
la.ausonius.de_xii_caesaribus: De XII Caesaribus is a Late Antique Latin work by Ausonius, a series of short epigrammatic notices on the Roman emperors. It opens with a proem promising a single monostich apiece for the twelve Caesars whose names, deeds, lives and deaths Suetonius had set out at length, and the opening is followed by verse tallies of the length and the manner of death of each of the twelve reigns. The work then announces an extension to rulers beyond the original dozen, proceeding emperor by emperor from Julius Caesar and Augustus through Tiberius, Gaius, Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho and Vitellius to the Flavians, Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Pertinax, Didius Julianus, Septimius Severus, Caracalla and Macrinus, and closing with a denunciation of the emperor who falsely bore the Antonine name as the foulest monster ever seated in Roman power.
la.ausonius.gratiarum_actio: A Late Antique Latin prose oration by Ausonius, a formal speech of thanks addressed to the emperor Gratian on behalf of the speaker, once the emperor's tutor and now raised to the consulship. It opens with the declaration that the emperor's benefactions, matching his majesty in scale, require no repayment and can be answered only by gratitude felt more richly than it can be spoken. The body of the speech dwells chiefly on the consulship, the divine sanction of the appointment, the precedence in its official announcement, and the consular robes sent from Illyricum, while extolling Gratian's piety toward his deified father Constantius, his victories on the Danube and the Rhine, his remission of tribute, and his personal care for sick soldiers. Anticipating objections to a schoolmaster's elevation, the speaker compares his case with those of earlier imperial tutors such as Seneca, Quintilian, and Fronto, and closes with a prayer to God.
la.ausonius.libri_de_fastis_conclusio: A short closing poem in lyric verse by the late-antique poet Ausonius, the Conclusio collects the concluding verses of his books of Fasti, a verse reckoning of Roman time reaching from the city's foundation to the poet's own consulship. It opens by offering the completed fasti as the fruit of the poet's sleepless nights, an ordered account of Rome's eternal years and of names from the early age scattered through Latin history. The remaining sections give arithmetical rules for summing the whole span of years from Rome's origin, tell whoever reads to add further entries himself should fate grant the poet no more, and direct anyone curious about the author to a title where he may read the name of consul Ausonius. The poem closes with an address to Proculus, who will receive the yearly series deduced from king Quirinus down to Ausonius's consulship, with the expectation that he will mark the finished count of Olympiads.
la.ausonius.precationes: A short sequence of lyric prayers by the late antique poet Ausonius, opening with the repeated invocation 'Iane, veni' as the January fasces are taken up for a new consular year. The prayers ask Janus and the sun for seasonable weather month by month, the favourable course of the planets, and peace throughout the world. Further stanzas call for victories over the Franks, Suebi, Sarmatians, Huns, Getae and Alans, and anticipate a Caesar succeeding the speaker to the consulship in the year ahead. The sequence closes with a renewed petition to the two-faced Janus to renew the year and to guide the sun and moon through their monthly and annual courses.
la.ausonius.versus_paschales_pro_augusto_di: A short late antique Latin poem in lyric metre by Ausonius, composed for Easter and spoken in honour of the emperor. It opens with the return of Christ's saving feast and the devoted observance of his worshippers, then addresses God as father of all things, whom earth, sea, air, the underworld and the heavens obey. The hymn credits God with granting eternal life, delivering law and prophets to humankind, pitying Adam deceived by Eve, and sending his son, true from true and living from the living source. It closes by finding an earthly counterpart in the elder Augustus, sire of two co-emperors, who embraces brother and son and shares with them an undivided rule, and ends in prayer that Christ present these rulers, mild governors of earth and ministers of heaven, before the eternal father.
la.bede_the_venerable.de_locis_santis: A short Latin prose treatise by Bede the Venerable, of early medieval date, describing the holy places of Palestine and the wider eastern Mediterranean. It opens with the site, walls and gates of Jerusalem, then moves through the church of the Holy Sepulchre with its Martyrium and Anastasis, Mount Sion, the Mount of Olives, Bethlehem, Hebron, Jericho, the Jordan, the Dead Sea and Galilee, before turning to Damascus, Alexandria and Constantinople. Throughout it records churches, tombs, relics and measurements alongside local marvels, contemporary conditions under Saracen rule, and scattered wonders and legends. The concluding chapter states that the account follows the report of Arculf, a bishop of the Gauls, as set down by Adamnan, together with older written sources.
la.bertharius_of_monte_cassino.carmen_de_sa: The Carmen de Sancto Benedicto Interpolatum is a Carolingian Latin verse life of St Benedict of Nursia, ascribed to Bertharius of Monte Cassino, whose name the poet introduces in the closing prayer; its title marks the version as interpolated. The poem opens by apostrophising Benedict as the confessor chosen by God from boyhood to be father and guide of those who seek the heavenly kingdom. The body then runs through a long sequence of episodes from the saint's career: the broken sieve restored, exorcisms, the spring and the recovered billhook on Monte Cassino, Maurus's rescue of Placidus, the poisoned loaf carried away, the conversion of pagan temples, prophecies to Totila and concerning Rome, the Lombard sack of the monastery, the shared tomb of Benedict and his sister, the visions witnessed by Servandus, and the praise of his Rule. It ends with healing miracles at Benedict's shrine, including the cure of the lame Andreas, and a prayer in which the poet begs Christ to guard his flock and to protect Bertharius himself.
la.boethius.consolatio_philosophiae: Boethius' Consolatio Philosophiae, a late-antique Latin work of philosophy, opens with the poem in which the fallen statesman laments that his former career of song has turned to mournful measures and that premature age and disgrace have overtaken him. Personified Philosophy then appears at the prisoner's bedside, banishes the seductive Muses, and leads him through a dialogue that moves from complaint against Fortune's reversals to an account of true happiness as the possession of the supreme good, which is God. Subsequent books argue the powerlessness and misery of the wicked, the rule of divine providence over the series of fate and apparent chance, and, in the final book, the reconciliation of God's timeless foreknowledge with human free will. Across five books the prose argument is punctuated by short lyric metres that gloss and reinforce each stage of the discussion.
la.boethius.de_fide_catholica: A brief late-antique prose treatise attributed to Boethius that sets out the essentials of the Christian faith. It opens by proclaiming that the authority of the Old and New Testaments reveals the Christian religion, which rests on the eternity of the one divine substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, noting along the way the errors of Arius, the Sabellians, and the Manichaeans. The tract then recounts salvation history: the creation of the world and the fall of the angels and of Adam, the patriarchs from Abraham through Jacob, the deliverance from Egypt and the law given through Moses, the kings from David onward, and the birth of Christ from the Virgin of Davidic stock, with the teachings of Pelagius, Nestorius, and Eutyches rejected in passing. Its closing pages follow Christ's baptism, passion, resurrection, and ascension, describe the sacraments and the spread of the church, distinguish the sources of doctrinal authority, and end with the expectation of the world's end, the resurrection and last judgment, and the eternal contemplation of the creator.
la.boethius.quomodo_substantiae_in_eo_quod_: A short late-antique Latin prose treatise by Boethius, composed as a letter to the same recipient as a companion work and opening with a promise to expound more clearly a question drawn from the author's Hebdomads: how substances are good in virtue of their existence without being substantial goods. The body first sets out nine axioms or 'common conceptions of the mind', including the distinction between being (esse) and that which is, and then states the puzzle that if all things are good only by participation they cannot of themselves tend to the good, while if they are good by substance everything that exists would turn out to be God. The solution proceeds by a mental separation: setting the first good aside in thought, the argument shows that things are good in their being because their existence flows from the will of the first good, not because they resemble or participate in it. A closing passage contrasts goodness, which belongs to essence, with justice, an act that does not extend to all things.
la.boethius.quomodo_trinitas: A short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Boethius, the 'Quomodo Trinitas' sets out to show how Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and not three gods, and is dedicated to the author's father-in-law, Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus. It opens with the dedicatee being told why the question is difficult and why the argument is veiled in deliberately chosen philosophical vocabulary. The work then rejects Arian attempts to rank the divine persons by degrees, distinguishing the various senses of 'same' and 'different' by genus, species, and number, and separating speculative disciplines into the natural, mathematical, and theological. Applying Aristotle's categories to divine predication, it argues that 'deus' and terms like 'iustus' and 'magnus' signify what is beyond substance and accident, that repeated predication of 'deus' creates enumeration rather than plurality, and that relational predicates such as 'pater' and 'filius' alter nothing in the divine essence, so that unity resides in substance while relation alone multiplies the trinity into persons, with the argument closing by submitting the question to Symmachus's judgment.
la.caesar.de_bello_civili: A prose historiographical account in Latin of Caesar's civil war, in three books of uneven length, conventionally attributed to Caesar himself, though the date of composition and the question of authorship are debated. The narrative opens with the tribunes Antony and Cassius fleeing from Rome to Caesar at Ravenna and carries the story through the surrender of Corfinium, the campaign in Spain against Afranius and Petreius, the siege of Massilia, Curio's African expedition and death, the blockade at Dyrrachium, the battle of Pharsalus, and finally Caesar's arrival in Egypt, where it breaks off amid the Alexandrian war. The work follows Pompey's flight and death and the outbreak of the Alexandrian conflict, presenting Caesar's own justification of his conduct from his crossing of the Rubicon down to the last events recorded.
la.caesar_augustus.res_gestae_divi_augusti: The Res Gestae Divi Augusti is a first-person Latin prose account in which the emperor Augustus summarises his achievements and expenditures, presented as the copy of an inscription cut on two bronze pillars at Rome. It opens with a preamble naming its subject and the claim that at nineteen Augustus raised a private army at his own expense to free the republic from a dominating faction. The work proceeds thematically through his career: civil and foreign wars, the offices and priesthoods he held or declined, his censorial lustra and counts of citizens, gifts of land, money and grain to soldiers and the plebs, the temples, aqueducts and public buildings he built or restored, the games and spectacles he gave, and the pacification of the seas together with the extension of the empire's frontiers in Gaul, Spain, Germany, Egypt, Armenia, Pannonia and Arabia. It closes with the submissions and embassies of foreign kings, the restoration of the state to the senate and people, the honours of the name Augustus and the title pater patriae, and a summary of his total outlay.
la.cicero.brutus: A Latin prose dialogue of the Roman Republic by Cicero, the Brutus casts its history of Roman eloquence as a conversation among Cicero, Atticus, and Brutus. It opens with Cicero grieving the death of the orator Quintus Hortensius, news of which reaches him on his return from Cilicia, before the three men fall to talk. The dialogue then surveys oratory at Rome from its earliest practitioners down to Cicero's contemporaries, sketching the careers and styles of successive generations and weighing such questions as popular versus expert judgment, the Attic and Asiatic manners of speaking, and the parts and training of the orator. Woven through the survey is an autobiographical account of Cicero's own rhetorical education, forensic career, and rivalry with Hortensius, and the work closes with an address to Brutus, whom Cicero encourages to pursue eloquence amid the disorders of the state.
la.cicero.cum_populo_gratias_egit: A prose oration of the Republican era, delivered by Cicero to the Roman people in formal thanks for his recall from exile. It opens with the vow he had once made to Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the other immortal gods, devoting himself and his fortunes to the safety of the citizens, and with his joy that the judgment of the gods, the testimony of the senate, the consent of Italy, and the confession of his enemies have vindicated that devotion. The speech goes on to recount how absence taught him the worth of his brother, his children, his property, his friendships, and his fatherland, contrasts his restoration, effected through the senate, the consul P. Lentulus, and above all Cn. Pompeius, with those of Popilius, Metellus, and Marius, and closes with promises of perpetual gratitude and unwavering service to the res publica.
la.cicero.de_fato: A philosophical dialogue of the late Republic by Cicero, set at his Puteolan villa after Caesar's death, De Fato opens with a preface on the Academic practice of arguing on both sides and a conversation in which the consul-designate Hirtius asks for a disputation on fate. The discussion then examines whether all events occur from antecedent causes, whether divination implies necessity, and how the logical puzzles of Chrysippus and Diodorus over the truth and possibility of future-tense statements bear on the question. Along the way it treats Posidonius's appeals to the influence of place and the stars, the Epicurean doctrine of the swerving atom, Carneades' defense of voluntary motion without external causes, Chrysippus's distinction between principal and auxiliary causes together with the analogy of the pushed cylinder, and the refutation of the 'lazy argument' and of objections drawn from 'co-fated' events such as the birth of Oedipus. The work breaks off unfinished in the midst of the argument against Epicurus.
la.cicero.de_finibus_bonorum_et_malorum: Cicero's De Finibus Bonorum et Malorum is a philosophical dialogue in five books, composed in prose during the Roman Republic, on the question of the highest good and the highest evil. It opens with a preface addressed to Brutus in which Cicero defends the writing of philosophy in Latin against anticipated objections. The first two books stage an Epicurean defence of pleasure as the supreme good, followed by Cicero's refutation; books three and four give Cato's Stoic exposition of virtue as the only good and Cicero's counter-argument; and the fifth book presents Piso's Old Academy account of goods according to nature, answered by Cicero in conversation with Quintus and Pomponius. The work closes as the disputants, their debate concluded, set off together into town.
la.cicero.de_inventione: A Latin treatise on rhetoric in two books by Cicero, composed in the Republican era, De Inventione opens with a prolonged meditation on whether the power of speech has brought men and states more good or more harm. The first book defines the art, its office, end and subject-matter, enumerates the parts of rhetoric, and concentrates on invention: the four constitutions or issue-types of a cause, the six parts of the oration from exordium to conclusion, and argumentation by induction and ratiocination, together with the commonplaces. The second book supplies hypothetical cases and precepts for accuser and defender under each constitution, treats controversies arising from written instruments, including ambiguity, letter versus intent, conflicting laws, inference and definition, and closes with instruction on deliberative and demonstrative oratory, covering the honourable, the useful, necessity and the topics of praise and blame. The work ends by announcing that the remaining subjects, notably style, are reserved for later books.
la.cicero.de_officiis: A philosophical treatise in three books written by Cicero in the last years of the Roman Republic and addressed as a letter of instruction to his son Marcus, then studying philosophy in Athens. Opening with paternal counsel on uniting Greek and Latin learning, the work sets out a theory of moral duty in the Stoic tradition, following Panaetius's scheme while supplying parts that Panaetius left unfinished. The first book treats the morally honourable, tracing it to wisdom, justice, greatness of spirit, and propriety; the second examines the expedient, covering goodwill, glory, beneficence, and the management of wealth; the third addresses apparent conflicts between honour and advantage, arguing that nothing can be truly useful which is not honourable, with historical examples from Regulus to Caesar.
la.cicero.de_optimo_genere_oratorum: A short Latin rhetorical treatise by Cicero of the Republican era, De Optimo Genere Oratorum opens by rejecting any division of oratory into genera on the analogy of poetic genres, arguing instead that there is one perfect kind of orator, who teaches, delights and moves his hearers. The work goes on to enumerate the qualities of words, thoughts and arrangement required for that ideal, distinguishes the Attic manner from the abundance characteristic of Asia, and holds up the orators of Athens, and Demosthenes above all, as the standard of excellence. It closes by presenting itself as the preface to Cicero's Latin versions of the opposing speeches of Aeschines and Demosthenes in the case arising from Ctesiphon's decree honouring Demosthenes with a golden crown, summarising the laws, accusations and history of that trial and defending a method of translation that preserves the force and figures of the original rather than rendering word for word.
la.cicero.de_provinciis_consularibus: A prose oration of the Roman Republic in which Cicero, addressing the senate as a senator, offers his formal opinion on the assignment of the consular provinces. The speech opens with the speaker remarking that the senators can work out for themselves whose removal from their provinces he will propose, since his known grievances make his view plain. The greater part denounces Piso and Gabinius for the extortion, violence, and military ruin that have overtaken Macedonia and Syria under their command, arguing that both must be recalled, while contending that Caesar should remain in Gaul until the conquest there is complete. The close is given to a long justification of Cicero's political reconciliation with Caesar, weighing their earlier dealings, his own exile and restoration, and the public advantage of finishing the Gallic war.
la.cicero.epistulae_ad_familiares: The Epistulae ad Familiares is a Latin prose collection of Cicero's letters to family members, friends and political associates, arranged in sixteen books that group the correspondence largely by addressee. The opening letter, sent during Cicero's consulship to Lentulus Spinther, then in Cilicia, reports on the senate's troubled handling of the restoration of the Alexandrian king. From there the collection ranges across the final decades of the Republic: the political struggles over Caesar's command, the outbreak and course of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, and the uneasy aftermath under the victors, taking in letters of bereavement for Tullia and humorous exchanges with Papirius Paetus along the way. Throughout, news of the senate, the forum and the camp mingles with letters of recommendation, requests for favours, domestic and financial arrangements, family affection and philosophical reflection.
la.cicero.letters_to_brutus: Letters to Brutus is a Latin prose collection of Cicero's correspondence from the closing phase of the Roman Republic, written during the civil war against Mark Antony in the aftermath of Caesar's assassination. The opening letter, addressed to Brutus, offers reassurance about the loyalty of the tribune-designate Clodius and reports on Antony's standing. The collection then ranges across Cicero's accounts to Brutus of senatorial debates, honours decreed to the Caesarian leaders, the deaths of the consuls Hirtius and Pansa, and operations against Dolabella in Asia, together with Brutus's long and severe reply rebuking Cicero for appealing to the young Caesar, and shorter letters to Servilius, Plancus and Cassius on troops, money and strategy. The correspondence breaks off abruptly without a formal close.
la.cicero.letters_to_quintus: Letters to Quintus is a collection of epistolary prose by Marcus Tullius Cicero, addressed to his brother Quintus in the final decades of the Roman Republic. The opening piece is a long fraternal admonition urging Quintus, then governing the province of Asia, to integrity, mildness and self-command in his administration. The remaining letters range across Cicero's own fortunes, including his exile at Thessalonica, reports on senatorial debates, trials and the manoeuvres of Pompey, Caesar and Clodius, alongside family news, building work on the brothers' estates and remarks on Cicero's literary projects. The correspondence as a whole blends political commentary, private business and fraternal affection in a conversational Latin.
la.cicero.lucullus: The Lucullus is Cicero's Latin prose dialogue on Academic skepticism, composed during the Republic and transmitted as part of the Academica. It opens with a eulogy of Lucius Licinius Lucullus, celebrating his campaigns against Mithridates, his devotion to Greek letters and philosophy, and his attachment to the philosopher Antiochus of Ascalon. The dramatic setting is Hortensius's villa at Bauli on the day after a debate at Catulus's house, where Lucullus delivers a long speech in defense of Antiochus's position that truth can be grasped and known, marshaling the evidence of the senses, memory, the arts, and virtue against Arcesilas and Carneades. Cicero replies at length on behalf of the New Academy, expounding the Carneadean doctrine of the probable, turning the Stoics' dialectic and the sorites against them, and surveying the schools' irreconcilable disagreements over nature, the gods, and the supreme good, before Catulus and Hortensius close the conversation with brief pronouncements.
la.cicero.orator: A Latin treatise on rhetoric by Cicero of the late Roman Republic, cast as a direct address to Marcus Brutus, whose repeated urging overcomes the author's professed hesitation to take up so great a question. The work presents the perfect orator as an ideal form grasped by the mind rather than fully realized in any single speaker, grounding eloquence in philosophy and answering the narrow standard of the Atticists with a broader account of what it means to speak Attically. It distinguishes three styles of oratory, the plain, the temperate, and the grand, and considers what befits each in subject, person, and occasion, along with the orator's need of dialectic, civil law, history, and philosophical knowledge, and the power of delivery and emotional appeal. A long closing portion examines the arrangement of words, prose rhythm, cadence, and the periodic sentence, illustrated throughout from Greek and Roman orators and poets and from Cicero's own speeches, before submitting the whole account to Brutus's judgment.
la.cicero.paradoxa_stoicorum_ad_m_brutum: A short prose treatise by Cicero of the late Republic, addressed to Marcus Brutus, setting out and defending six famously counter-intuitive Stoic doctrines. It opens with a preface explaining that admiration for Cato of Utica moved Cicero to test whether doctrines admired for their severity could be made acceptable to a Roman audience through oratorical polish. The body takes up the paradoxes in turn, that moral rectitude alone is a good, that virtue of itself suffices for the happy life, that all offences are equal, that every fool is mad (a section preserved only in part), that only the wise man is free while all fools are slaves, and that only the wise man is rich, each argued declamatorily with exempla from early Roman history and pointed attacks on contemporary figures such as Clodius, Hortensius and Crassus.
la.cicero.post_reditum_in_senatu: A Latin prose oration by Cicero, addressed to the Roman senate upon his return from exile during the late Republic, offering thanks for the body's role in his recall. The speech opens with the claim that no abundance of eloquence could repay the senate's benefits, which had restored to him his brother, his children, his fortunes, and his fatherland. It proceeds to recount the senate's steadfast support during his absence, hurls sustained invective against the consuls of his exile year, Piso and Gabinius, and praises a long series of benefactors, above all the consul Lentulus, Pompey, the tribunes Annius and Sestius, and his brother Quintus. It closes with Cicero's account of his own decision to withdraw rather than fight, his sense that he returned together with the republic itself, and his resolve to defend it with undiminished freedom.
la.cicero.pro_c_rabirio_postumo: A forensic oration by Cicero, dating to the Republic, in defense of Gaius Rabirius Postumus, a Roman eques charged under the Julian extortion law on the ground that money taken by the condemned governor Gabinius had reached him. The speech opens with Cicero conceding that Rabirius acted rashly in entrusting his fortune to King Ptolemy of Alexandria while begging the judges not to add ruin to a man already crushed by fortune. Cicero then argues that the charge rests on a novel and inapplicable clause of the statute, since Rabirius was neither named nor called as a witness in Gabinius's trial, and that a conviction would set a dangerous precedent against the whole equestrian order. He refutes the accusations that Rabirius served as the king's financial minister, wore Greek dress, and skimmed a tithe from the monies collected, praises Caesar's generosity in sustaining the bankrupt defendant, and closes with an appeal to pity recalling Rabirius's support of Cicero and his family during the exile.
la.cicero.pro_m_caelio: A forensic defence speech of the Roman Republic, composed by Cicero on behalf of Marcus Caelius Rufus, a young man prosecuted under the law on public violence. The opening reflects on the odd circumstances of the trial, held during public festival days, and on the disproportion between the grave statute invoked and the youthful, promising defendant actually accused. The argument goes on to neutralise the moral slanders against Caelius, his indulgent youth, his former association with Catiline, his debts and his removal to a house on the Palatine, before confronting the two formal charges, that he took gold from Clodia and plotted poison against her; Cicero dismantles these by ridiculing Clodia through imagined speeches of a stern censorial ancestor and her urbane younger brother, dissecting the implausible account of the poison's handover at the baths of Senias, and appealing to the sworn testimony of L. Lucceius. The peroration pleads for acquittal on the strength of Caelius's ability and ambition, his father's dependence on him, and a pledge of his future loyalty to the res publica.
la.cicero.pro_marcello: A short oration of the Roman Republic in which Cicero addresses the senate and Julius Caesar after Caesar's victory in the civil war, giving thanks for the pardon and recall of Marcus Marcellus, an adversary whom the senators had begged Caesar to spare. It opens with Cicero explaining that the day's proceedings break a long silence he had kept out of grief and a sense of shame, and it turns at once to gratitude for Marcellus's restoration. The speech goes on to rank Caesar's clemency above his military exploits, to defend Cicero's own record as a consistent advocate of peace during the war, and to confront Caesar's suspicion of plots against his life, arguing that the safety of the commonwealth and of all the pardoned citizens now depends on his. It closes by urging Caesar to complete the settlement of the state through restored courts, credit, and laws, and with renewed thanks on behalf of the senate, of Marcellus's brother Gaius, and of Cicero himself.
la.cicero.pro_murena: Pro Murena is a forensic oration in which Cicero, speaking as consul, defends Lucius Murena, consul-elect, against a charge of electoral bribery brought by M. Cato, Servius Sulpicius, and C. Postumus. It opens with the prayer Cicero had offered when he announced Murena's election at the comitia centuriata, now repeated for the defendant's safety, and with his answer to critics who held that a consul who had himself carried a law against bribery ought not to undertake such a defence. The body of the speech answers the slurs on Murena's conduct in Asia and his service as legate under Lucullus, rebuts Cato's taunt that the soldierly defendant was a 'dancer', and argues that military distinction counts for more towards the consulship than Servius's legal expertise, with an extended mockery of the jurists' art. Its later portions treat the evidence about canvassers, shows, and dinners, weigh Cato's Stoic severity, dwell on the Catilinarian conspiracy and the danger of leaving the state with a single consul, and close with an appeal to the judges' pity for the afflicted defendant and his family.
la.cicero.pro_rege_deiotaro: Cicero's Pro Rege Deiotaro is a forensic oration of the late Roman Republic, spoken before Julius Caesar in defence of Deiotarus, king and tetrarch of Galatia, accused by his grandson Castor of plotting Caesar's assassination and of harbouring treasonous intentions. The speech opens with Cicero professing that the strangeness of pleading a capital case inside a private house before a single judge has unsettled him more than usual. The argument then turns to discrediting the accusers, above all a grandson against his grandfather and a corrupted slave against his master, before rehearsing Deiotarus's long record of service to Rome, his alliance with Pompey down to the battle of Pharsalus, and his subsequent cooperation with Caesar. Cicero dismantles each alleged proof in turn, including the supposed ambush at Blucium and the reported remarks of Blesamius, praises the king's gravity, temperance and loyalty, and closes with an appeal to Caesar's clemency to preserve the accused in both life and reputation.
la.cicero.pro_s_roscio: A forensic oration of the Roman Republic in which Cicero, presenting himself as a young advocate who has never before spoken a public case, defends Sextus Roscius of Ameria against a charge of parricide brought by the prosecutor Erucius. The opening explains why he alone has risen while orators of the highest rank sit silent for fear of the times, and states the defence's premise: the murdered man's estates, bought for a trifling sum by the powerful freedman Chrysogonus, will be secure only if the son is destroyed. The narrative reconstructs the killing near the baths of Pallacine, the flight of the news to Ameria and to Sulla's camp, the seizure of the property by Titus Roscius Magnus and Capito in partnership with Chrysogonus, and the accused's refuge with Caecilia at Rome; the refutation then dismantles the alleged motives of paternal hatred and intended disinheritance, with digressions praising the rural life and describing the Roman penalty of the sack for parricides. The later part turns to counter-accusation, arguing that the two Roscii, who profited from the death and refused the interrogation of the slaves, are the likelier murderers, arraigning Capito's betrayal of the legation sent to Sulla, exposing Chrysogonus' luxury and the irregularity of his purchase under the proscription laws, and closing with an appeal that the judges prevent a fresh proscription of the victims' children.
la.cicero.pro_sestio: Pro Sestio is a forensic oration in which Cicero opens by asking why so few citizens of courage now come forward in the state's defence, before taking over from Hortensius the case of Publius Sestius, charged with public violence (vis). The speech traces the political crisis of the preceding years: the gang warfare of P. Clodius, the complicity of the consuls Piso and Gabinius, Cicero's own exile and recall, and the tireless work of Sestius as tribune of the plebs on Cicero's behalf, which exposed him to prosecution. Embedded in the argument is a lengthy digression defining the optimates as the men who pursue otium cum dignitate in contrast with popular agitators, together with praise of Milo's resistance to Clodius and an exhortation to the young nobility to imitate the great defenders of the commonwealth. Cicero closes by appealing to the jurors to acquit Sestius and his fellow defendants Milo and Lentulus, whose ruin would dishonour his own restoration.
la.cicero.pro_sulla: A defense oration by Cicero, composed in the late Roman Republic, in which he pleads the case of Publius Sulla against the charge of complicity in the Catilinarian conspiracy. It opens with Cicero lamenting Sulla's fallen fortunes and explaining that he must at once defend his client and answer the prosecutor Lucius Torquatus, who has attacked Cicero for testifying against some alleged conspirators while defending Sulla. The speech then works through the prosecution's evidence, the testimony of the Allobroges, the purchase of gladiators through Faustus Sulla, an alleged alteration of the public record of the indictment, while repeatedly vindicating Cicero's own consulship and suppression of the conspiracy, and it closes with an appeal to the judges' mercy based on the defendant's life and character.
la.cicero.pro_tullio: The Pro Tullio is a fragmentary forensic speech of Cicero's from the Republican period, delivered in defence of Marcus Tullius, a landowner of Thurii, in an action for damages against Publius Fabius. It opens with Cicero explaining that his task has changed from proving the deed to arguing its legal character, now that the opponent's household has confessed the killing. The surviving portions recount the night raid in which Fabius' armed servants killed Tullius' slaves and wrecked a farm building, and then argue at length over the force of 'dolo malo' and 'iniuria' in the formula of the special action de vi hominibus armatis, covering the origin of that action under Lucullus, the jurisdiction of the recuperatores in assessing quadruple damages, the interdicts on forcible dispossession, and the Twelve Tables' rules on killing a thief in self-defence.
