la.cicero.timaeus: A Latin philosophical prose work of the Republic by Cicero, being a version of Plato's Timaeus that breaks off before the dialogue's end. It opens with a preface in which Cicero recalls his disputations on natural philosophy with P. Nigidius, a reviver of Pythagorean teaching, and a meeting with the Peripatetic Cratippus, before turning to Timaeus' distinction between what always is and what is generated. The rendering then follows the cosmology of that speech: a benevolent craftsman god brings order out of disorderly matter, fashions the world as a single, spherical, rational living being, builds the world-soul from blended indivisible and divisible substance in harmonic numerical proportions, sets the orbits of the fixed stars, sun, moon and planets to measure time, and creates the celestial gods and the daemones or Lares. The creator then charges the younger gods to fashion mortal beings; souls are allotted to the stars and sown into bodies, the fortunes and transmigrations of human souls into women and beasts are set out, and an account of the formation of bodies and of the eyes and their divine gift of philosophy carries the work to its abrupt close.
la.cicero.tusculanae_disputationes: Cicero's Tusculan Disputations is a philosophical treatise in five books, written during the Roman Republic and addressed to Brutus, which recounts the disputations Cicero held over five days at his villa at Tusculum. The opening preface explains that, freed from forensic and senatorial labours, Cicero has undertaken to set forth Greek philosophy in Latin, and it describes the Socratic method whereby a thesis is proposed and Cicero argues against it. The five books argue in turn that death is no evil, that pain can be borne through fortitude, that grief does not befall the wise, that the remaining disturbances of the soul arise from judgement and opinion rather than nature, and finally that virtue alone suffices for a happy life. Throughout, the discussions are presented as they were conducted, with Cicero weighing the doctrines of the several philosophical schools in an Academic, probabilistic manner.
la.cicero_pseudo.in_sallustium: A Latin prose invective, preserved among the works ascribed to Cicero but of uncertain authorship and date, cast as a speech delivered in the senate in answer to a denunciation by C. Sallustius. It opens by asserting that a man's words should accord with his life, and that the speaker's task is to answer a slanderer whose own record will not bear examination. The speech alternates between self-defence and attack: the Ciceronian speaker recalls his consulship, his verses on civic harmony, his exile and recall, and his public friendships, while cataloguing Sallust's alleged youthful vices, a publicly confessed adultery, a corrupt quaestorship, extortion as governor of Africa, and sudden wealth acquired through Caesar. It ends with the observation that open denunciation of others' disgraces usually offends an audience more than the offences themselves.
la.cicero_pseudo.pridie_quam_in_exilium_ire: A Latin oration transmitted under Cicero's name and framed as the address he delivered to the Roman people on the day before his departure into exile, though it is preserved as a pseudo-Ciceronian piece and its actual date of composition is uncertain. The speaker opens by urging the citizens to defend, with one accord, the man who risked his own head so that they might not all be consumed. The speech proceeds as a sustained apologia: the speaker recounts his suppression of the Catilinarian conspiracy, protests that he is banished without witness, accuser, or trial through tribunician fury and the envy of the wicked, appeals to the Roman knights and to Jupiter and the other gods of the Capitol for aid against his enemies, invokes the precedents of Marius, Scipio, and Pompey, and finally resolves to withdraw into exile rather than let civil bloodshed follow, asking the people to protect his children, his household, and the reputation won by his virtue.
la.claudian.de_bello_gildonico: A short late antique Latin panegyric in hexameters by Claudian on the war against Gildo, the Moorish count whose seizure of Africa's grain supply brought famine to Rome under the western emperor Honorius. The poem opens with the startling swiftness of Gildo's overthrow and with the personified Roma pleading before Jupiter against the starvation his rebellion has caused. The bulk of the work consists of formal speeches: Roma's lament for her lost greatness, Africa's counter-complaint against the tyrant's outrages, the ghost of Theodosius reproaching his son Honorius and vindicating Stilicho, the proposal that Mascezel, Gildo's wronged brother, lead the expedition, and a satirical portrait of Gildo's cruelty and luxury as the forces muster. The narrative ends with the fleet, assembled at Pisa, lying in the harbour of Caralis in Sardinia and waiting for a favourable wind, with no battle yet narrated.
la.claudian.panegyricus_dictus_manlio_theod: Claudian's hexameter panegyric for the consulship of Manlius Theodorus, a court poem of the Late Antique period, opens with the poet's Muse hesitating before so august an audience and with an emblem of winged envoys from East and West meeting to survey the whole world. The body of the poem follows Theodorus from precocious eloquence and advocacy through judicial posts in Libya and Macedonia to his recall as palatine judge answering for Spain, Germany, Britain and the Gallic rivers, then his withdrawal into philosophy, surveyed in a catalogue of the Greek schools and their cosmologies. Personified Justice descends to summon him back to public life, and after a dialogue with her he assumes the governance of Italy, Africa, Illyricum and the islands, his mildness in punishment and tranquillity in power receiving extended praise. The closing movement, entrusted to Uranie and the Muses, describes the consular games of beast hunts, mimes, acrobats and musicians in lavish detail, ending with a prayer that consulships never fail in the Manlian line.
la.claudianus_mamertus.de_statu_animae: De Statu Animae is a Late Antique philosophical treatise in prose and three books by Claudianus Mamertus. It opens as a reply to a reverend priestly correspondent on how to answer Arians who claim that the begotten Son is younger than the unbegotten Father, with discussion of how divine names signify persons rather than natures. The bulk of the work addresses an anonymous opponent who held the soul to be a body, defending the soul's incorporeality, immortality, and local independence through reasoned argument and through testimonies from Plato, the Pythagoreans, Roman writers such as Varro and Cicero, and Christian authorities including Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Augustine, Hilary, and Eucherius. Along the way it treats measure, number, and weight as marks of bodies and of souls, and it closes with a recapitulation of syllogistic proofs that the soul is not a body, an admonition to the adversary, a disquisition on the genera of bodies and spirits, and an appended diagram summarizing the whole argument.
la.claudianus_mamertus.epistolae: The Epistolae of Claudianus Mamertus, a Late Antique author writing in Latin prose, form a small collection of letters addressed to a learned and eloquent correspondent. The opening letter protests that opportunities to visit are rare and rebukes the addressee for his long silence, threatening to avenge it with an equally persistent stream of writing. The remaining letters dwell in lavish praise: they extol the addressee's treatise on the state of the soul, celebrate one of his hymns and its subtle metres, and set his eloquence beside a roll-call of Greek and Latin orators, philosophers and Church Fathers. One letter laments the neglect of liberal studies in the author's own day and urges the addressee, as citizen and teacher of Vienne, to shun modern novelties and model his style instead on Naevius, Plautus, Cato, Varro and Cicero.
la.commodianus.instructiones: The Instructiones is a two-book collection of Christian instructional pieces in Latin by Commodianus, a writer of the Later Imperial period whose dates are uncertain. The work opens with a preface, after which the first book moves through short chapters attacking pagan religion, with sections on individual gods such as Saturn, Jupiter, Apollo, Mercury, Bacchus and Hercules, on idols and their cults, and on gentiles and Jews, before closing with chapters on the time of Antichrist. The second book is directed chiefly at Christians, addressing catechumens, the faithful, penitents, apostates, soldiers of Christ, matrons and clerics, and treating the first resurrection, the day of judgement, penance, martyrdom, funeral customs and the duties of readers, ministers and pastors.
la.couplet_et_alii.confucius_sinarum_philos: A Latin prose treatise by Couplet and collaborators presenting the Chinese sage Confucius to a European royal audience. It opens with a dedication to Louis XIV in which Confucius is imagined transported to France to admire the king's triumph over heresy. The body of the work examines the doctrines of the Chinese literati and rival sects, disputes whether the ancient classics attest knowledge of a supreme deity, and recounts Matteo Ricci's deliberations and labours in establishing the Jesuit mission at Peking. A concluding life of Confucius narrates his birth, career, disciples, teachings, death, and posthumous honours, arguing that the rites observed at his academies are civil rather than religious in character.
la.cyprian.ad_quirinum_aut_testimoniorum_li: Addressed to a correspondent named Quirinus, the treatise opens with a preface in which Cyprian explains that, at the recipient's request, he has compiled a compact anthology of scriptural passages arranged under numbered chapter headings. Book I assembles Old and New Testament citations to argue that the Jews forfeited God's favor by rejecting the prophets and Christ, that the old law, circumcision, sacrifice, and priesthood gave way to new ones, and that Christians drawn from all the nations took the Jews' place. Book II gathers testimonies on the person and work of Christ, covering his pre-existence as the wisdom, word, and arm of God, his virgin birth at Bethlehem, his humble advent, passion, crucifixion, descent to the underworld, and resurrection on the third day, and his future coming as judge and everlasting king. Book III, likewise introduced by a preface and a list of 120 chapters, collects scriptural precepts for Christian conduct and church discipline, ranging from almsgiving, humility, and patience under persecution to baptism, virginity, the duties of masters and slaves, and separation from idolaters, heretics, and schismatics.
la.cyprian.de_bono_patientiae: The late-antique Latin treatise De bono patientiae, by Cyprian, opens with the author addressing his audience as 'beloved brothers' and observing that patience is required even to hear a discourse on the subject. The work presents patience as the foremost of the heavenly disciplines, a virtue originating in God the Father and distinguished from the false patience professed by the philosophers, and it traces the divine patience that grants sun and rain alike to just and unjust. Christ's incarnation, temptation, teaching, and above all his passion supply the central exemplar, reinforced by the endurance of Abel, Abraham, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, David, Job, Tobias, and Stephen, while impatience, beginning with Adam's transgression, is shown to be the devil's work and the source of idolatry and heresy. The treatise closes with an account of the many operations of patience, governing anger, tongue, and mind, and sustaining bodily affliction and persecution, and with an exhortation to await steadfastly the day of divine vengeance rather than seek vindication.
la.cyprian.de_dominica_oratione: A Latin treatise of Late Antique date, the De dominica oratione sets out Cyprian's teaching on the prayer Christ gave his followers. It opens by presenting the evangelical precepts as divine instruction and by arguing that Christ, who both prayed and taught, himself supplied the form of prayer the faithful should use. The body of the work first considers how to pray, urging quietness, modesty, and humility before God with examples drawn from scripture, and then expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, from the invocation 'our Father' through the hallowing of God's name, the coming of the kingdom, the doing of God's will in heaven and on earth, daily bread, the forgiveness of debts, and deliverance from temptation and from the evil one. A closing section points to Christ's own practice of prayer as an example and urges vigilance of heart, fasting, almsgiving, and prayer at the traditional hours, in the morning, the evening, and through the night.
la.cyprian.de_habitu_virginum: A Latin Christian treatise attributed to Cyprian, De Habitu Virginum opens by praising disciplina as the guardian of hope and the foundation of religious life, through which believers attain the divine promises. From this general theme the work narrows to consecrated virgins, the flower of the church, whose calling it defines as the devotion of both body and spirit to Christ alone. The bulk of the treatise exhorts virgins against outward adornment, jewellery, dyed hair, cosmetics, and costly dress, supported by a dense weave of biblical citation, together with warnings against the misuse of wealth, attendance at mixed baths and wedding feasts, and any conduct that excites the desire of others. It closes by ranking the reward of virginity second only to that of the martyrs, likening virgins to angels and to the heavenly Adam, and urging them to persevere in purity and to remember the author in their prayers.
la.cyprian.de_opere_et_eleemosynis: The De Opere et Eleemosynis is a brief Latin prose treatise on almsgiving by the Christian writer Cyprian, belonging to the late-antique period. It opens by enumerating the divine benefits bestowed on humanity through Christ and presents alms as the appointed remedy for sins committed after baptism. The body of the work assembles scriptural precepts and exempla, Isaiah's summons to feed the hungry, Raphael's counsel in Tobit, Peter's raising of Tabitha, the widow's mites, the widow sustained by Elijah, and Job's sacrifices for his children, to urge the faithful to exchange earthly wealth for treasure in heaven. Cyprian answers the objection that generosity toward the poor will impoverish donors and their families, contrasts the spectacle of almsgiving before God and Christ with pagan public games, and closes with the Last Judgment scene of Matthew 25 and an exhortation to continued works of mercy on the model of the earliest Christian community.
la.cyprian.de_unitate_ecclesiae_catholicae: A Latin Christian treatise by Cyprian on the unity of the Catholic Church, directed against heretics and schismatics. It opens with an exhortation to vigilance against the devil, who threatens believers not only through open persecution but by creeping in secretly under the guise of peace. The work then builds its central argument on scriptural grounds, presenting Peter as the starting point of the church's oneness, insisting that the episcopate is one and that each bishop holds its power entire, and illustrating indivisible unity through figures such as the sun's rays from a single light, the many streams of one fountain, Noah's ark, and Christ's seamless tunic. It closes by warning that neither martyrdom nor confession avails outside the church, deploring the growth of heresy and schism in the last days and the decline of unanimity among believers, and urging its audience to hold fast to peace, charity, and watchfulness for the Lord's coming.
la.cyprian.de_zelo_et_livore: A late antique Latin prose treatise on zeal and envy, composed by Cyprian. It opens by presenting envy as a deceptively light sin that, unnoticed, lets the watchful devil work his way into the soul, and urges constant vigilance against his hidden attacks. The argument then ranges over the whole history of the vice, from the devil's own fall through Cain's murder of Abel, Esau's hatred of Jacob, the selling of Joseph, Saul's persecution of David, and the Jews' blindness to Christ, before cataloguing the envy that breeds hatred, avarice, ambition, discord, schism, and heresy within the church. Citing the Psalms and the apostolic letters, the treatise exhorts believers to humility, charity, and peace, ranks the victories over such passions among the crowns won in daily spiritual struggle, and closes with a final address to the once envious, urging them to love those they had hated and to set their minds on paradise and the heavenly kingdom.
la.cyprian.quod_idola_dii_non_sint: A short late-antique Latin apologetic treatise attributed to Cyprian, Quod idola dii non sint argues that the gods worshiped by the nations are not gods at all. Opening with the observation that the deities of the common people were originally kings honored after death with temples, images, sacrifices, and festivals, the work surveys mythological and Roman examples, from Aesculapius, Hercules, and the Cretan tomb of Jupiter to Romulus and the native gods of Rome, to expose the mortals behind the divinities, and goes on to ascribe oracles, augury, and religious deception to deceiving demons. It then proclaims the one invisible God, whose temple is the whole world rather than any shrine, and closes with an account of Christ sent as the Son of God after the Jews forfeited the grace once given them, his miracles, passion, resurrection on the third day, and ascension, together with the confession of Christians who acknowledge him under torment.
la.cyprian_pseudo.de_iona: De Iona is a later imperial Latin work on the prophet Jonah, transmitted under the name of Cyprian. It opens by recalling God's punishments of Sodom and Gomorrah and his practice of warning sinners through prophets before sending Jonah to preach Nineveh's destruction. The narrative then follows Jonah's flight by ship from Joppa, the storm raised against the fugitive, his confession to the sailors and his being cast into the sea, where a great fish swallows him alive. Preserved within the creature's belly, Jonah is presented not as one destroyed but as a witness to death overcome and a future sign of the Lord.
la.cyprian_pseudo.orationes: A short Latin collection of prose prayers spuriously attributed to Cyprian and of later Roman imperial date, comprising three orations followed by a brief preface. The first prayer opens with the trisagion 'Hagios, hagios, hagios' and invokes God as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, asking for integrity of heart and deliverance from the devil's snares with appeal to Sara, the three youths in the furnace, Daniel and the apostles. The second and third orations commend the soul to God and petition the Father and the Son for mercy, marshalling a catalogue of scriptural precedents, Jonah, the Ninevites, David, Tobias and Sara, Susanna, Hezekiah, Thecla, Peter and Paul, and rehearsing Christ's miracles at Cana, his healings, death and resurrection as grounds for aid. A concluding preface on the twelve abuses of the world enumerates moral failures, from the wise without works and the old without religion to the negligent bishop and the people without law, through which, it says, justice is suffocated and the wheel of the world turns toward the darkness of hell.
la.cyprian_saint.de_exhortatione_martyrii: A Latin prose treatise of the later Roman imperial period transmitted under the name of Cyprian, addressed to a correspondent named Fortunatus who had asked for scriptural exhortations with which to steel fellow Christians for the persecutions weighing upon them and the approaching time of antichrist. The work proceeds as a compendium of biblical testimonia arranged under numbered headings rather than as a continuous argument, opening with proofs that idols are not gods and that God alone is to be worshipped, together with the divine threats against idolaters. Its central and longest portions assemble passages on steadfastness under trial: the foretold hatred of the world, God's protection and aid in persecution, perseverance rewarded with the martyr's palm, and the contrast between the water baptism that remits sins and the baptism of blood that wins the crown. The closing sections retell the Maccabean martyrs, the seven brothers, their mother, and Eleazar, as models of confession and gather the biblical promises of the rewards awaiting the just, whether they actually suffer or hold fast in faith.
la.dracontius.orestes: Orestes is a Latin tragedy in dramatic metre by the late-antique poet Dracontius, retelling the fortunes of the house of Atreus from Agamemnon's homecoming to his son's formal acquittal. The poem opens with a prologue invoking Melpomene and announcing the lamentable triumphs of a hero who was pious in his very impiety. The narrative follows Agamemnon's return from Troy and his discovery that Iphigenia still lives as a priestess of Diana, his murder by Aegisthus and Clytaemestra, Electra's rescue of the child Orestes, and the youth's upbringing in Athens beside Pylades until their father's ghost rouses both men to revenge. After the slaying of Aegisthus and Clytaemestra, the poem traces Orestes' torment by his mother's ghost, his madness, his recognition by Iphigenia among the Taurians, and his trial at Athens, where a court evenly divided between life and death yields to the verdict of the gods and the acquitted hero returns in triumph to Mycenae.
la.ennodius.epigrammata: The Epigrammata is a late-antique Latin collection of short poems by Ennodius. It opens with an epitaph on a young man of noble house, mourning his sudden death and affirming that merit outlives the tomb. The collection then ranges widely: funerary and consolatory pieces; poems praising bishops and clergy, including Ambrose and Simplician; inscriptions and descriptions of churches dedicated to Lawrence, Sixtus, and other saints; riddling verses on animal mimes, pictures, gems, and works of art; and satirical invective against gluttons, drunkards, a eunuch, a magpie, and a man falsely styling himself Virgil. Epigrams on gifts, books, horses, and dining, together with the first-person epitaph of a woman named Melissa, close the book.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.de_laude_heremi: A short Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Eucherius of Lyon, framed as a letter to a beloved friend Hilarius, which celebrates the desert as God's chosen dwelling and the nursery of the spiritual life. It opens by commending the addressee's withdrawal from family and wealth into solitude, surpassing even the bond with a brother. The body assembles scriptural exempla, Moses before the burning bush and on Sinai, the Israelites guided and fed in the wilderness, Elijah and Elisha, John the Baptist, and Christ's fast, temptation and miracles, before turning to the desert monks John and Macarius and closing with praise of the island community of Lérins, its founder Honoratus and its monks. Throughout, the barren wilderness is figured as paradise, temple and battlefield over the devil, fruitful in grace precisely where the Garden of Eden proved fatal.
la.eucherius_of_lyon.unknown: The Passio Agaunensium martyrum, a late-antique Latin prose account by Eucherius of Lyon, opens by announcing its purpose of setting down in writing the passion of the martyrs who illumined Agaunum with their glorious blood. The narrative tells how the Theban legion, six thousand six hundred strong and summoned from the East to serve under Maximian, refused the order to persecute Christians, endured successive decimation, and, urged on by Maurice, Exuperius and Candidus, submitted to the sword in the narrow Alpine valley of Agaunum rather than deny their faith. It continues with the soldier Victor, killed on the spot after refusing a banquet held over the martyrs' spoils, the martyrdoms of Ursus and Victor at Solothurn, Maximian's own death by strangling after his plot against Constantine, the revelation of the bodies to bishop Theodore, and two miracles worked at the basilica raised in the martyrs' honour. The account closes in epistolary form, presenting the written passion to its addressee and tracing the tradition through Isaac of Geneva back to Theodore himself.
la.eugippius.epistula_ad_probam_virginem: A short Latin prose epistle of Late Antique date by Eugippius, addressed to the virgin Proba. The letter opens with the compiler's defense of his undertaking: at the prompting of his abbot Marinus and other holy brethren he had assembled excerpts from the works of Augustine, and fearing a charge of presumption he sets out the causes of what he has done. The remainder of the epistle praises Augustine's erudition and authority, admits the poverty of the compiler's skill and means in gathering so few passages from a vast meadow strewn with heavenly flowers, and notes that each chapter of the collection indicates the work or book from which it is drawn. It closes by justifying the ordering of the excerpts, which begin with Augustine's letter to Jerome on the question of the soul and are framed at start and finish by titles on charity, the perfection of all the virtues and the fullness of the divine law.
la.eugippius.exerpta_ex_operibus_augustini: A late-antique Latin anthology of excerpts from the works of Augustine, compiled by Eugippius to present his thought through selected passages on theological and moral questions. The collection opens with Augustine's letter to Jerome asking how individual souls arise and how infants come under the bond of sin that baptism dissolves. Its excerpts then range across treatises, letters, and sermons, taking in the figurative interpretation of Gospel sayings and parables, a classification of kinds of lying, the discipline and patience owed to sinners within the church, the origin and propagation of souls, and the nature of the resurrection body. The compilation closes with an extended praise of caritas, set forth as the fulfillment of the law and the heart of the divine Scriptures.
la.eugippius.vita_sancti_severini: The Vita Sancti Severini, a late-antique Latin prose saint's life by Eugippius, opens with the death of Attila, when Pannonia and the Danube frontier were thrown into confusion, and introduces Severinus as a holy man from the eastern provinces who settles at Asturis in Noricum Ripense and warns its people of an impending barbarian raid. The body of the work follows Severinus through the fortified towns of Noricum and Raetia, including Comagenis, Favianis, Batavis, Lauriacum and Quintanis, recounting his relief of famine, redemption of captives, prophecies, healings and exorcisms, his ascetic discipline and founding of monasteries, and his dealings with the Rugian kings Flaccitheus and Feletheus, the queen Giso, and the young Odoacer. It closes with his prophecy that the Roman population must migrate to Italy, his final exhortation to his monks, his death, Odoacer's war against the Rugi, and the translation of his uncorrupted body into Italy, where it is laid in a mausoleum at the castellum Lucullanum and further miracles are recorded. The author presents himself as a companion of the saint who draws on his own memory and the testimony of others, and ends by offering the book to his addressee as a commemoratorium to be turned to fruit under his direction.
la.evagrius_monachus.altercatio_legis_inter: The Altercatio legis inter Simonem Iudaeum et Theophilum Christianum is a late-antique Latin theological dialogue in prose, ascribed to Evagrius Monachus. It opens with a dedicatory note in which Evagrius reports to his correspondent Valerius a recent disputation over the law between Simon, a Jew, and Theophilus, a Christian. The bulk of the work consists of Theophilus's replies to Simon's successive challenges, marshalling testimonies from the Pentateuch, Psalms, and prophets to establish Christ's divinity and sonship, his two advents, his virginal birth at Bethlehem, the circumcision of the heart that supersedes the carnal rite, the passion foretold despite the curse of Deuteronomy, the resurrection and ascension, and the Christian observance of sabbath and food. Vanquished by these arguments, Simon asks for instruction and is anointed, and the dialogue closes with his prayer of thanksgiving to Christ.
la.evodius.de_fide_contra_manicheos: A late-antique Latin theological treatise in prose, attributed to Evodius, written as a polemic against the Manichaean religion. It opens with a compact confession of one God, invisible, incomprehensible, and alone holding immortality, and at once takes up the Manichaean claim that an unbegotten prince of darkness stands against him. The argument maintains throughout that evil is not a nature but a sin of the will, citing Mani's own Thesaurus and Epistula Fundamenti, together with the apocryphal Acts of Leucius, to show that the sect's founder concedes that souls sin by their own volition; it defends the reality of Christ's passion against the teaching that the prince of darkness was crucified in his place, affirms the virgin birth and the resurrection of the flesh, upholds the harmony of the two testaments, and ridicules the myth of the divine substance held captive in plants and bodies and freed by means of the 'lucid ships.' It closes by setting before Manichaean readers the choice between the immutable, partless God of the Catholic confession and the suffering, composite deity of Mani, and urging them to return to the church.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_ratione_fidei: The De Ratione Fidei ('On the Rule of Faith') is a short late-antique Latin treatise on the Trinity, written in prose in a question-and-answer form by Faustus of Riez. It opens by asking what answer should be made to readers of the gospel who take 'the Father is greater than I' to mean that the Son is inferior in divinity, and replies with an account of Christ's two births and two natures, whereby he speaks now as man and now as God. A second question defends the full divinity of the Holy Spirit against those who call him lesser, a creature, or a mere minister, arguing from his role in creation, prophecy, the forgiveness of sins and the charismatic gifts that he is the one God dwelling in the faithful. The work concludes that the three persons possess one power, one glory and one nature, warning against denying the distinct persons, after the manner of the Jews and Patripassians, or believing in three gods, after the manner of the pagans.
la.faustus_of_riez.de_spiritu_sancto_libri_: A two-book Latin theological treatise of the Late Antique period by Faustus of Riez, De Spiritu Sancto defends the full divinity and distinct personhood of the Holy Spirit against the Macedonian claim that the Spirit is a creature. It opens with a sequence of chapter headings and an exposition of the creedal confession 'credo in spiritum sanctum', distinguishing believing that God exists from believing in him and insisting that faith is owed to the Spirit rather than to the church, which is believed with, not in. The treatise then assembles testimonia from prophets, evangelists, and apostles to show that the Spirit is creator and not creature, proceeds eternally from the Father, and shares one substance and operation with Father and Son, treating such topics as his titles (finger of God, Paraclete), his work in baptism, sanctification, prophecy, and the forgiveness of sins, and answering objections drawn from passages where only Father and Son are named. The closing chapters press the argument that only God can know and indwell the human heart, ending with an exhortation to make oneself a worthy temple of the Holy Spirit.
la.faustus_of_riez.epistulae: The Epistulae of Faustus of Riez is a late-antique collection of Latin prose letters treating doctrine and pastoral discipline. It opens with a letter urging a wavering brother to hold together the grace of God and the obedience of the baptized servant, ending in a series of anathemas against Pelagian positions and subscriptions from a college of bishops. Later letters refute Arian arguments for the Son's subordination, argue that only God is truly incorporeal while souls and angels are corporeal substances, and take up whether faith suffices without works, the fate of sinners after death, and the discipline of fasting and abstinence. The collection closes with letters of spiritual direction and recommendation, mingling counsel on humility, almsgiving, and the ransoming of captives, and an appended note on clerics who return to their wives.
la.favonius.disputatio_de_somnio_scipionis: A Latin prose treatise by Favonius Eulogius, a writer of the later Roman empire, expounding the arithmetic, numerology, and music theory embedded in Cicero's Dream of Scipio. It opens with a preface arguing that Cicero, unlike Plato in the myth of Er, composed the dream as rational philosophy rather than fable, and promising to show that Scipio's death at fifty-six was fixed by number. The body proceeds number by number from the monad through the octonarius, treating the monad and dyad as principles, the triad and tetrad in the world's structure, the pentad and the five planets, the perfect senarius, the septenarius in the heavens, the soul, and the ages of human life, the octonarius and its cubes, and the perfect number twenty-eight, two such perfect numbers summing to the fifty-six years of Africanus's life. A closing section expounds the harmony of the spheres, defining sound, interval, and symphony, the four numerical ratios, and the Pythagorean tuning by which the eight celestial circles sound a disdiapason consonance.
la.flavius_josephus.de_iudaeorum_vetustate_: A Latin translation of Josephus's two-book apologetic treatise against those who denied the antiquity of the Jewish people, addressed to Epaphroditus and presented as a sequel to the Jewish Antiquities. The work opens with an argument that the Jews are an ancient nation ignored by Greek historians, whose own records are late and mutually contradictory, and then marshals testimony from Egyptian, Phoenician, and Chaldean writers such as Manetho, Menander, and Berosus, along with Greek authors from Pythagoras's circle to Hecataeus, to establish Jewish antiquity. Book 1 proceeds to refute the Egyptian accounts of Manetho, Chaeremon, and Lysimachus that portray the Jewish ancestors as expelled lepers; Book 2 answers the grammaticus Apion on Moses, the sabbath, the status of Alexandrian Jews, and slanders about the Temple, and closes with a substantial defence of the Mosaic legislation, its divine monotheism, and the endurance with which the Jews have kept their laws.
la.fulcher_of_chartres.historia_hierosolymi: A Latin prose chronicle of the First Crusade and the early Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, covering the years 1095 to 1127, written by Fulcher of Chartres, a participant in the expedition who later served as chaplain to Baldwin of Boulogne. The work opens with a prologue on the profit of recording the deeds of God's warriors, followed by an account of the Council of Clermont and Pope Urban II's preaching of the journey to the Holy Sepulchre. Subsequent sections trace the crusaders' march through Asia Minor, the sieges of Nicaea and Antioch, the discovery of the Holy Lance, and the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, then turn to Fulcher's own service with Baldwin, the consolidation and defense of the Latin settlements in Edessa and Palestine, the campaigns and captivity of King Baldwin I and Baldwin II, and the taking of Tyre in 1124. Alongside its military and political narrative the chronicle incorporates digressions on the geography, marvels, animals, and customs of the eastern Mediterranean, closing with events of the year 1127.
la.gellius.attic_nights: A Latin prose miscellany in twenty books by Gellius, composed in the later imperial period and titled from the author's claim to have gathered his notes during winter nights in the Attic countryside. The opening preface explains this origin and contrasts the work's plain name with the more ornate titles other compilers of miscellanies have chosen. Thereafter the books proceed in no fixed order, presenting short chapters on grammar and etymology, literary criticism of Greek and Roman authors, points of law, augury, and pontifical practice, philosophical disputes such as Chrysippus and Diodorus on ambiguity, and anecdotes about figures from Romulus to Gaius Gracchus. The final chapters return to the preface's themes, catalogue the varied titles such works have borne, and promise further volumes as leisure allows.
la.giraldus_floriacensis.carmina: A medieval Latin collection of poems attributed to Giraldus Floriacensis. The opening poem recounts the Lombard devastation of Italy and Monte Cassino and then follows Aigulf on the journey by which the relics of Benedict and his sister Scholastica were brought to Fleury on the Loire, together with the miracles attending their remains and the founding of a convent there. The rest of the collection turns to shorter celebratory pieces: verses on Benedict's feast, virtues and miracles, some composed in mirrored parallel lines, poems on the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, and a Nativity poem in heroic verse addressed to a noble matron.
la.godescalcus_saxus.carmina: A collection of Carolingian Latin religious verse by Godescalcus Saxus, preserved in two books. It opens with a long rhythmic and heavily rhyming prayer to Christ begging pardon for a fallen sinner. The poems that follow are chiefly penitential: laments built on refrains, a complaint of exile likening the poet to Israel singing in Babylon, a paraphrase of the prodigal son, a plea for resurrection modelled on the raising of Lazarus, and a verse epistle to the teacher Rathramnus accompanying questions on a saying of Augustine. A cycle of hymns for the hours of the day, running from evening through cockcrow, matins, prime, terce, sext and none, closes the work with renewed praise of the Trinity and prayers for forgiveness.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.fragmenta_minora: A short Latin collection of excerpts attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the Gallic bishop, of uncertain date and compiler, assembling sayings of his on theological themes. It opens by citing Hilary's writing to the emperor Constantius on the incarnation of the Lord, affirming that the Son of God, made man, is God. The remaining excerpts gather passages on the exaltation of the servile form Christ assumed, on the devil's ceaseless war against humankind as taught from the book of Job, with divine mercy turning the devil's malice to our purgation, and on the petition for daily bread understood of Christ the bread of life dwelling daily in the faithful. Further items come from the prologue of Hilary's exposition of the Gospel of Matthew and from his exposition of the epistle to Timothy on the two natures in Christ, while a closing notice hails him as the Catholic Church's most vehement defender against heretics and quotes his treatment of Christ sent in the likeness of sinful flesh.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.hymni: A short collection of Latin hymns transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, a bishop of the late antique period. It is introduced by a note presenting the prophet David as the first to announce Christ to the world in song, and the opening hymn meditates on the Son's eternal generation from the unbegotten Father, the fullness of the godhead communicated in that begetting, and the unity of the two divine persons. A second hymn, whose successive lines run through the alphabet, is spoken in the voice of Christ and recounts the incarnation, the scourging and crucifixion, the descent into the underworld where even the rivers of hell grow cold, the defeat of death, and the resurrection. A third hymn on the glorious battles of Adam moves through Satan's despair before the nativity, the angelic message to the shepherds, John the Baptist's preaching and Christ's baptism in the Jordan, and the voice from heaven at the approach of the temptation.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.oratio_synodi_sardice: A Latin prose oration of late antiquity addressed to the emperor Constantius and attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, the work presents itself as the petition of the council of Sardica. It opens with praise of the emperor's benign nature and a plea, offered in words and tears, that the Catholic church be spared further injuries, persecutions and contempt at the hands of its own brothers. The bishops ask that judges keep out of ecclesiastical causes and that exiled bishops be restored to their sees; they name the two Eusebii, Narcissus, Theodore, Stephen, Acacius, Ursacius and Valens as inventors and spreaders of the Arian corruption, and defend the acquittal of Athanasius as duly settled by synodal judgment. The closing section recounts recent events at Milan, where Eusebius of Vercelli, Dionysius of Milan and Lucifer of Sardinia, appealing to the faith expounded at Nicaea, resisted demands to subscribe a condemnation of Athanasius.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.tractatus_super_psalm: A Latin prose commentary on selected Psalms attributed to Hilary of Poitiers, a fourth-century bishop of Gaul. It opens with a lengthy prologue discussing the unity and authorship of the Psalter, the Septuagint translation, the significance of superscriptions and musical terminology, and the numerical arrangement of the psalms into three fifties, before turning to verse-by-verse exegesis. The work proceeds through psalms including the first two, several penitential psalms, and portions of Psalm 118, reading each throughout as prophecy of Christ's incarnation, passion, resurrection, and eternal kingdom, with appeal to both Old and New Testament texts.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.libri_tr: A Latin theological compilation by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, directed against Valens and Ursacius and assembled in three stages dated 356, the winter of 359/360, and 367. It opens with a preface followed by a section on the council of Arles and the exile of Paulinus, bishop of Trier, now lost, and then presents the letter of the Eastern bishops at Sardica with their creed and the names of the subscribing bishops. The remainder gathers, with brief connecting narrative, the acts and correspondence of the Western Sardican council and its address to Constantius, the letters of Valens and Ursacius, the documents of Bishop Liberius of Rome and of Emperor Constantius, the records of the councils of Milan, Ariminum, and Seleucia, and, from 367, the letter of the synod of Paris, two letters on reconciling lapsed bishops, and the creed and letters of Germinius of Sirmium. Conciliar letters, creeds, and imperial letters are thus arranged in chronological sequence to set out the course of the mid-fourth-century doctrinal controversy from Sardica to the 360s.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.spuria: Short pieces in Latin transmitted among the spuria of Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, of uncertain date and authorship. The opening item is a prose letter, Accepi litteras tuas, in which a father on a long journey tells his daughter how he sought from a beautiful youth a garment and pearl of inestimable worth, and how the youth promised to grant them on condition that she renounce silk, dyed and gilded clothing and other jewels; the letter closes with a plea that she await these gifts and with an enclosure of morning and evening hymns. There follow a morning hymn, Lucis largitor splendide, which hails Christ as the true light of the world, and the alphabetical Versus de paenitentia, in which a penitent recounts his subjection to personified lust, pride, envy, discord, vainglory and gluttony, calls on the whole creation to weep with him, professes right faith while rejecting the teachings of Arius, Sabellius and Simon, and implores the redeeming Trinity for mercy.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.vita_mariae_aegypt: The Vita Mariae Aegyptiacae is a medieval Latin verse life of the penitent Mary of Egypt by Hildebert of Lavardin, cast around the figure of the monk Zosimas. It opens with Zosimas as a boy spurning wealth and worldly glory for monastic life, outstripping his teachers in virtue until a warning against pride sends him across the Jordan to the desert monks. There he encounters a naked fugitive who proves to be Mary, and the poem's centre is her long confession: a corrupt youth in Alexandria, passage to Jerusalem bought with her body, exclusion from the church by an unseen power, repentance before an icon of the Virgin, and decades of penance in the desert sustained first by three loaves and then by herbs and heavenly consolation. Zosimas returns at her bidding with the Eucharist a year later and finds her dead and incorrupt after she has crossed the Jordan unaided, whereupon a lion helps him dig her grave and he carries her story and her pastoral charges back to his monastery.
la.italicus.ilias_latina: An early Imperial Latin epic in hexameters, attributed to Italicus, that condenses the whole Iliad into a compact verse narrative. It opens with an invocation to a goddess to unfold the wrath of Peleus' proud son that brought misery upon the Greeks, echoing Homer's proem. The poem then runs through the entire course of the war story: the plague sent by Apollo and the quarrel of Agamemnon and Achilles, the duel of Menelaus and Paris, the catalogue of the Greek fleet, the exploits of Diomede and Hector, the night exploit against Rhesus, and Patroclus' death in Achilles' borrowed arms, down to Achilles' vengeance, the slaying and dragging of Hector, Priam's ransom of the body, and Hector's funeral. It closes with a valediction in which the poet, addressing Calliope and Phoebus, declares that his ship has reached the port and goal of mighty Homer.
la.john_cassian.conlationes: John Cassian's Conlationes is a Late Antique Latin work of monastic theology, cast in prose as a series of recorded conferences with the Egyptian desert fathers. It opens with a preface dedicating the teaching of the anachorets of Scetis to Pope Leontius and the monk Helladius. The body comprises twenty-four conversations in which Cassian and his companion Germanus put questions to successive elders, Abba Moses, Chaeremon, Theonas and Abraham among them, on the goal of the monastic profession, purity of heart as the scopos, discretion, the interplay of divine grace and free will, mortification, chastity and charity. The final conference gathers up and concludes the traditions and statutes of all the elders.
la.john_cassian.de_incarnatione_domini_cont: De Incarnatione Domini contra Nestorium is a Latin prose treatise of Late Antique date by John Cassian, composed at the entreaty of Leo, a deacon of the Roman church whose praise and importunity fill the preface. The work is a polemic against the recently arisen Nestorian heresy, which the author introduces under an extended image of heresy as a hydra whose severed heads regrow. It first catalogues earlier Christological errors, those of the Ebionites, Sabellians, Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Photinians and Apollinarians, before turning to the contemporary error, of uncertain name but sprung from the old Ebionite stock, that the title identifies with Nestorius.
la.john_cassian.institutiones: A Late Antique Latin treatise on the monastic life by John Cassian, addressed to Bishop Castor, who asked him to record the customs of the Egyptian and Palestinian monasteries for a new foundation in Gaul. The opening preface figures the undertaking as the building of the true temple of God, not of lifeless stones but of the congregation of holy men, whose vessels are sanctified souls rather than gold and silver. From there the work proceeds through the outward institutions of coenobitic observance: the monk's dress and its symbolism, the canonical hours and psalmody as practised in Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia, the testing, stripping, and obedience of those received into a monastery, and the discipline of silence, work, and the refectory. Successive books then treat the eight principal vices, gluttony, lust, avarice, anger, dejection, acedia, vainglory, and pride, setting out for each its origins, causes, and remedies, illustrated with sayings and deeds of the desert elders and sustained scriptural exposition.
la.lactantius.de_ira_dei: A Latin prose theological treatise by the late antique author Lactantius, addressed to one Donatus and directed against the widespread view, shared by many philosophers, that a beneficent deity cannot be angry. The work surveys the positions of the Epicureans, who strip God of both anger and favor, the Stoics, who retain favor while denying anger, and the atomists who reject providence altogether, before arguing for a single divine creator, the unity of God, and the making of the world for the sake of human beings. Further sections explain that good and evil were both set before humanity so that wisdom and virtue could exist, distinguish a just anger that corrects and coerces sinners from the furious passion unworthy of God, and defend divine patience in deferring punishment so that correction remains possible. An epilogue in Ciceronian style closes the work by assembling Sibylline verses and other pagan testimonies to God's indignation at the impious, ending with an exhortation to consecrate God in the heart rather than in temples.
la.lactantius.de_mortibus_persecutorum: Lactantius's De Mortibus Persecutorum, a Late Antique Latin prose treatise in the tradition of Christian apologetic, is framed as an address to Donatus, opening with thanksgiving that a recent persecution has ended and the church has been restored. The work then surveys in chronological order the emperors who assailed the Christians, from Nero through Decius, Valerian, Aurelian, Diocletian, Maximian Herculius, Galerius, Maxentius, and Maximinus Daia, recounting each ruler's crimes and the agonizing deaths by which divine vengeance was executed upon them. Woven into this scheme is a detailed political narrative of the tetrarchy, Diocletian's abdication, the rise of Constantine, the victory at the Mulvian Bridge, Licinius's defeat of Maximinus, and the edict granting freedom of worship. The treatise closes by cataloguing the extinction of the persecutors' houses and ends in praise of God's triumph and a prayer for the church's lasting peace.
la.lactantius.de_opificio_dei: De Opificio Dei ('On the Workmanship of God') is a Latin prose treatise by the late-antique author Lactantius, framed as a letter of moral admonition and instruction to a young correspondent named Demetrianus. The work sets out to demonstrate divine providence through a detailed account of the construction of the human body, presented by its author as a fuller treatment of a theme he finds only summarily handled in Cicero. It argues that man's nakedness and weakness are marks of rational dignity rather than defects, then surveys the body part by part, from the frame, senses, and organs of speech to the internal viscera and the process of generation, punctuated throughout by polemic against Epicurean atomism and the doctrines of Lucretius. The closing portion turns to the mind and soul, treating their seat and nature, the mechanism of sleep and dreams, the soul's divine origin and immortality, and the gift of wisdom, before ending with a promise of further writings in defense of truth.
la.lactantius.divinarum_institutionum: The Divinae institutiones, a Latin apologetic treatise in seven books by the Late Antique author Lactantius, opens by contrasting the ancient philosophers who sought truth without finding it with divine revelation, and announces a plan of seven volumes that joins true wisdom to true religion. The first three books refute pagan religion, arguing that the gods were mortals deified after death and that their cults stem from demons, poets' fictions, and human credulity, before turning against philosophy itself as a human wisdom able to expose error but never to attain truth. The fourth book expounds the Christian faith, treating the unity of God, the two births of Christ, his miracles, passion, resurrection, and ascension, while the remaining books set out justice and its precepts, the worship owed to God in place of sacrifice, and an account of the last things, the second coming, the final judgement, the thousand-year reign, the resurrection of the dead, and the renewal of the world, closing with an exhortation to embrace wisdom and religion together.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_conven: De non conveniendo cum haereticis ('On not meeting with heretics') is a late antique Latin prose treatise of anti-Arian polemic attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, framed as a direct address to the emperor Constantius. It opens with the author's reply to the charge that he and his fellow bishops are enemies of peace, defending their withdrawal from the Arians by the example of Moses pitching the tabernacle of the testimony outside the camp. The body of the work assembles a long chain of biblical exempla, Moses and the Midianites, Jericho and Rahab, the man of God of Bethel, Jehoshaphat's alliances, the Psalms and Proverbs, the Maccabees, and the apostolic epistles, each marshalled to prove that Christians must refuse communion with heretics, whom Lucifer brands as spiritual adulterers, serpents, and servants of the devil. Along the way Constantius is denounced as a persecutor and his court bishops (Valens, Ursacius, Epictetus, Saturninus) named, the author's exile and imprisonment recalled, and Arianism ranked among the sects excised from the church alongside Sabellianism, Marcionism, and the doctrine of Paul of Samosata.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_non_parcen: A late antique Latin prose treatise by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, defending his rebuke of the emperor Constantius for introducing Arian idolatry into the church. It opens with Lucifer answering the emperor's complaint that the servants of God have treated him with contumely, insisting that he has spoken only the truth. The rest of the work assembles a long chain of scriptural exempla, Moses and Phinehas, Samuel and Saul, Achan, Uzziah, Josiah, the Maccabean martyrs, the apostles before the council, and Daniel's fourth beast, to show that rebuking persecutors of God's house has always been the duty of prophets, priests, and apostles. Throughout, Constantius is likened to Judas, to the tyrant Antiochus, and to the forerunners of Antichrist, with repeated exhortations to abandon the Arian heresy and return to the faith described at Nicaea.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.epistulae: A late-antique Latin collection of epistles in prose attributed to Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, bound up with the Arian controversy. The corpus opens with a letter from Lucifer to Bishop Eusebius urging him to hasten the overthrow of the Arian doctrine, comparing its fall to that of Simon Magus. The remaining letters comprise greetings from Liberius of Rome and Athanasius commending Lucifer's confession amid exile and persecution, exchanges with the official Florentius concerning a codex offered to the emperor, an embassy in which Lucifer and his companions plead with Constantius Augustus for a council on the faith, and a closing exhortation warning the faithful and monks against prayer or communion with those of Arian sympathies.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.moriendum_ess: A Late Antique Latin prose treatise of theology by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, cast as an invective addressed to the emperor Constantius. It opens with a rebuke of Constantius as an interpolator of the divine scriptures who has fallen into the Arian heresy and persecuted Christians. The bulk of the work argues that it is necessary to die for the Son of God, exhorting believers to endure torments, exile and execution rather than deny his divinity; it catalogues the emperor's cruelties against martyrs such as those in Alexandria, defends the Son's equality and coeternity with the Father against Arian teaching, and supports its case with extensive quotations from the Psalms, the Gospels and the apostle Paul. It closes by contrasting the eternal glory promised to those who confess Christ with the unending punishment awaiting the unrepentant emperor and his adherents.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.ennodius_ambrosio_: A late-antique Latin prose work by Magnus Felix Ennodius, a didactic exhortation (paraenesis) written at the repeated request of its addressee, a youth named Ambrosius. It opens with the author explaining that he has yielded to petition and deliberated whether to issue his instruction in verse or in the manner of a letter. The body of the work brings forward a sequence of personified virtues and liberal arts, including Verecundia, Pudicitia, Fides, Grammatica and Rhetorica, each of which addresses the pupil in turn, with verse passages interspersed among the prose. The exhortation closes by naming contemporary aristocrats and Christian matrons, among them Symmachus, Boethius, Barbara and Stephania, as living models of eloquence and conduct, and ends with a short verse appeal.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.libellus_adversus_: A polemical treatise in Latin prose by the Late Antique writer Magnus Felix Ennodius, composed in defense of Pope Symmachus and of the synod convened to hear charges against him. The opening prologue justifies the author's recourse to speech after silence, dedicating his oratory to the priesthood against whom detractors of the council had unleashed their attacks. The body of the work takes up, point by point, the arguments of an adversarial libellus, that not all bishops were summoned, that the pope ought to have called the synod himself, that Christ and Peter submitted to judgment, and that the assembly acted before any crime was established, answering each with scriptural citation and sustained invective while defending the pope's retreat from his accusers and the conduct of the gathering. It closes with imagined addresses in which the Apostle Peter rebukes the schismatics and the personified city of Rome laments their discord and summons them back to concord.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.panegyricus_theodo: A Latin prose panegyric of late antique date by Magnus Felix Ennodius, addressed to Theodoric, ruler of Italy. It opens with a reflection on the duties and limits of the speaker's office of praise before turning to the king's deeds. The speech then recounts Theodoric's victories over the Bulgar leader and the Gepids, his defeat of Odoacer at Verona and on the Athesis, and the campaigns of his generals Pitzia and Herduic at Sirmium, presenting these conquests as the restoration of Roman order. It closes with praise of Theodoric's rebuilding of Rome, his patronage of learning and eloquence, his clemency and personal magnificence, and a prayer that an heir be born to him.
la.maximianus.elegiae: A cycle of late antique Latin elegies in elegiac couplets by Maximianus. The opening poem gives voice to an old man's plea for death as release from bodily decay, recalling the fame he once won as orator and poet and the athletic, military and amatory prowess of his youth. The remaining elegies follow the same first-person speaker through the amours of old age, an aged former mistress, a courtship of a young woman conducted on sufferance, and a final liaison in which his young beloved consoles him and then departs as if from his funeral. The close finds the poet reckoning himself in part already dead and hurrying along the road that boys, old men, rich and poor alike must take towards a common death.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carminum_appendix: A Carolingian Latin collection of occasional verse preserved as the Carminum Appendix of Milo of Saint-Amand. It opens with couplets honouring the scribe Lotharius, who copied the book, and verses on the shrine enclosing the relics of Saint Amandus. The collection then gathers epitaphs for abbots, sacristans, teachers, and other figures buried at the monastery, a hymn and further versified lauds celebrating Amandus as shepherd, healer, and intercessor, and a courteous verse address to a patron named Haimin. It closes with a long sequence of short, often numerical and figured verses, repeatedly addressed to a Charles and playing on motifs of gold, theft, concord, and discord among brothers.
la.optatus_saint_bishop_of_mileve.appendix_: A late-antique Latin collection of ten documents bearing on the Donatist schism in Roman Africa, transmitted as an appendix to the seven books of Optatus, bishop of Mileve. It opens with a numbered index of its ten items and then the proceedings held before the consular governor Zenophilus, in which witnesses from Cirta testify about the bishop Silvanus and the charge of surrendering the scriptures during the persecution under Diocletian and Maximian. There follow the acts by which Felix, bishop of the Autumnitani, was purged of the same accusation, and then a series of letters in which Constantine labours to settle the dispute between Caecilian of Carthage and his opponents, arranging a hearing at the council of Arles, receiving that council's synodal letter to Pope Silvester, rejecting the appeal of the Donatist bishops, and instructing officials such as the vicar Celsus and the prefect Petronius. The collection closes with an appeal for patience addressed to the African episcopate and people and a letter restoring to the Catholics the basilica at Constantina that their rivals had seized.
la.ovid.amores: The Amores of Ovid are a three-book collection of love elegies in elegiac couplets from the Augustan period. The opening poem announces that five booklets have been reduced to three and recounts how Cupid stole a foot from the poet's attempted epic, conscripting him into the service of love verse. The books then follow the first-person lover's affair with Corinna through dinner parties under her husband's eye, midnight pleas at locked doors, the machinations of the bawd Dipsas and of servants, disputes over gifts and payment, a circus meeting, a prophetic dream, a flooded river, an episode of impotence, the death of Corinna's parrot, her perilous abortion, and the funeral of Tibullus. Throughout, love is cast as military service and poetry as the poet's immortality, and the collection ends with a farewell to elegy in favor of loftier work.
la.paulus_orosius.historiae_adversum_pagano: The Historiae Adversum Paganos ('Histories Against the Pagans') is a seven-book prose history in Latin by Paulus Orosius, written in the late antique period; it opens with a dedicatory preface in which Orosius answers Augustine's charge to compile the misfortunes of past ages. To rebut the pagan claim that the Christian era suffers more than earlier times, the work gathers accounts of wars, famines, plagues, earthquakes, floods, fires, and other calamities from the creation of the world onward. The narrative begins with the geography of the three continents and proceeds through the Assyrian, Persian, Greek, and Carthaginian powers before following Roman history in detail from the founding of the city through its kings, its republican wars at home and abroad, the civil wars, and the succession of emperors. It concludes with the Christian emperors, the Gothic sack of Rome within the author's own lifetime, and an extended argument that earlier ages endured miseries no lighter than those of the present.
la.petronius.fragmenta: A collection of scattered Latin verse fragments by Petronius, an early Imperial satirist, transmitted without book division and in a mixture of meters. The opening poem stakes a programmatic claim that genuine poetry springs from inner torment rather than from the levity of the pleasant poets. The remaining pieces, chiefly elegiac couplets alongside hendecasyllabic, choliambic, and lyric meters, take up the origin of religion in fear, the flight of rumor, Midas and his hidden ears, the deceptions of the senses and of dreams, the turns of fortune and nature, and a series of amorous poems, including an epigram on golden apples sent by Marcia, verses on Julia's snow-cooled touch, a poem on the anchoring of Delos, and a closing love letter in which the speaker begs his addressee for an embrace that would restore him to life.
la.plautus.aulularia: The Aulularia of Plautus is a Latin comedy of the Republican period in dramatic metres, built around a pot of gold buried beneath the hearth of a house and unearthed by the miser Euclio. The play opens with a prologue spoken by the Lar familiaris, the household's guardian spirit, who explains that an ancestor entrusted the treasure to his keeping and that he has now let Euclio find it so that the man may more readily dower his daughter, who has been secretly seduced by a young man of the highest rank. The action follows Euclio's obsessive guarding of the hoard, the marriage proposal of a wealthy neighbour who is uncle to the girl's seducer, the cooks and wedding preparations that fill the miser with alarm, the theft of the pot from his house, and the sharp exchanges between Euclio and the slave who took it as the theft comes fully to light.
la.plautus.captivi: Captivi (The Captives) is a comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, the Latin playwright of the Roman Republican period. Its prologue lays out the plot: Hegio of Aetolia, whose younger son was kidnapped and sold into slavery in Elis and whose elder son has been taken prisoner in the war between the Aetolians and the Eleians, buys captives in the hope of arranging an exchange, whereupon the Eleian prisoner Philocrates and his slave Tyndarus swap names and clothing so that master and servant may each serve the other's hidden designs. The prologue also notes that the play departs from comic convention by omitting such stock figures as the brothel-keeper, the wicked courtesan, and the boastful soldier, and by keeping its battles offstage.
la.plautus.casina: Casina is a Latin comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic. Its prologue addresses the spectators directly, extols old plays over new, and identifies the Greek original as Diphilus's Kleroumenoi (Latin Sortientes) before outlining the situation: an old husband and his son are both enamoured of Casina, a foundling raised as a slave in their house. The action follows the rivals' manoeuvres, as the father arranges the girl's marriage to his bailiff Olympio to secure access to her himself, while his wife Cleostrata backs the absent son's claim through the armour-bearer Chalinus; after lots are drawn in Olympio's favour, the women substitute Chalinus dressed as the bride, so that the bailiff and then the old man are each humiliated at the rustic wedding. The play closes with a spoken summary of the resolution rather than the scene itself: Casina is revealed to be the freeborn daughter of a neighbouring household and is promised in marriage to Euthynicus, the son.
la.plautus.mercator: Mercator is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic era, a stage work in dramatic verse built around a trading voyage. It opens with the young Charinus, sent by his father Demipho to trade at Rhodes, telling how he there fell in love with and bought a beautiful slave woman and brought her home, hoping to keep her hidden from his father. The plot follows Demipho, who on seeing the girl conceals his own desire and maneuvers her sale to his friend Lysimachus, whose wife returns unexpectedly from the country, finds the young woman installed in her house, and protests both her husband and the laws that let offending husbands go unpunished, while Charinus, believing his beloved lost to an unknown buyer, despairs and contemplates exile. Resolution comes when the girl is restored to Charinus and the wives appeased, and the comedy closes with a jesting proposal that old men who keep mistresses be judged by the same standard as their wives.
la.plautus.persa: The Persa ('The Persian') is a comedy in dramatic verse by Plautus, a playwright of the Roman Republic. It opens with the lover Toxilus declaring the labours of love worse than those of Hercules, before he undertakes to raise six hundred nummi to free his beloved Lemniselenis from the pimp Dordalus. With the slave Sagaristio and the parasite Saturio he passes off Saturio's daughter as a captive Persian girl, using a forged letter and a Persian disguise to extract the price from the credulous pimp, after which a second imposture as the girl's 'twin brother' robs Dordalus again. The play ends with the ruined pimp beaten and mocked, and Toxilus holding a banquet in celebration of Lemniselenis' liberty.
la.plautus.poenulus: The Poenulus, a comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, opens with a mock edict in which a stage herald, the 'commander of actors,' bids the audience keep silence and comically regulates who may watch, from hungry and well-fed spectators to slaves, nurses, and matrons. The action centers on the young Agorastocles' love for a girl kept by the pimp Lycus at Calydon and on the schemes of his slave Milphio, which are overtaken by the arrival of Hanno, a Carthaginian merchant who speaks partly in Punic as he searches for two daughters kidnapped from Carthage years before. Hanno proves to be the girl's father and a kinsman of the young man, and the pimp, trapped into accepting stolen gold, is forced to surrender her and submits to threats of prosecution and imprisonment. The play closes with the rival soldier mollified, the pimp pardoned after punishment, and preparations for Hanno's journey home to Carthage.
la.plautus.pseudolus: Pseudolus is a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by the playwright Plautus, named for the cunning slave who drives its plot. It opens with the lovesick young Athenian Calidorus showing Pseudolus a letter from the courtesan Phoenicium, whom the pimp Ballio has sold to a Macedonian soldier and will surrender the next day unless twenty minae are paid. Pseudolus promises to outwit Ballio and to wring the needed money from Calidorus' father Simo, staking it on a wager; with a forged letter, a stolen seal, the help of a garrulous cook and the crafty slave Simia, he deceives soldier, pimp, and old men alike and delivers the girl to her lover. A drunken scene follows in which the defeated Simo sues for mercy, and the play closes with Pseudolus declining to summon applause until the morrow.
la.plautus.rudens: The Rudens, a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, is set on the coast of Cyrene. Its prologue is spoken by the star Arcturus, who explains that Jupiter has stirred a storm to wreck the ship of the leno Labrax as he carries off the Athenian girl Palaestra and her companion Ampelisca, whom the young Plesidippus had contracted to buy. Cast ashore near the villa of Daemones, an Athenian exile living by the sea, the girls are sheltered by the priestess of Venus and defended by the slave Trachalio at the goddess's altar against the leno's violence. Daemones' slave Gripus, fishing after the storm, dredges up a chest whose gold and childhood tokens lead to the recognition of Palaestra as Daemones' long-lost daughter, and the play closes with the shipwrecked Labrax compelled to pay the talent he has sworn and free Gripus, the girls restored to freedom, and betrothals arranged between Palaestra and Plesidippus and between Ampelisca and Trachalio.
la.plautus.trinummus: The Trinummus is a comedy of the Roman Republic, Plautus's Latin version of the Greek Thensaurus by Philemon, as the prologue itself declares. It opens with the allegorical figures Luxuria and Inopia and an expository prologue that sketches the situation: the elderly Charmides has sailed abroad, entrusting to his friend Callicles a daughter of marriageable age, a dissolute son, Lesbonicus, and a treasure hidden in the house, which the spendthrift Lesbonicus has meanwhile sold. The action turns on the debates of Callicles and Megaronides over friendship and fidelity, the negotiations of Philto and his reformed son Lysiteles, who asks for Lesbonicus's sister without a dowry while Lesbonicus refuses to give her undowered, and the hiring of an impostor to pose as a messenger bringing gold from Charmides as a dowry so that the treasure may remain secret. The ruse collapses when the real Charmides returns and confronts the deceiver, and the play ends with a double betrothal, Lysiteles to the sister and Lesbonicus to Callicles's daughter, together with the father's reconciliation with his repentant son.
la.pliny_the_elder.naturalis_historia: The Naturalis Historia of Pliny the Elder, a Latin prose encyclopaedia of the Early Imperial period, opens with a dedicatory epistle to the emperor in which the author sets out his method, his catalogue of sources and a book-by-book summary of the work. The thirty-seven books then proceed systematically through the natural world: cosmology and astronomy, the geography and ethnography of Europe, Asia and Africa, the animal kingdom from elephants to insects, and the trees, crops and gardens of the earth. Later books are given over to medicine drawn from plant, animal and mineral substances, then to metals, stones, pigments and the arts of painting, sculpture and gem-engraving. Each book carries an index of its topics and lists of the Greek and Roman authorities excerpted, presenting nature as a single ordered whole from the heavens down to the smallest gemstones.
la.pontius_diaconus.vita_caecilii_cypriani: A later-imperial Latin prose life of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, composed by a deacon Pontius who presents himself in the narrative as an exile accompanying his subject. The opening prologue defends the recording of the deeds of a man already celebrated for his writings; the work then follows Cyprian's conversion under the presbyter Caecilian, his rapid elevation to the episcopate despite his reluctance, his almsgiving and leadership of the church during a devastating plague, his banishment to Curubis with its attendant visions foretelling his death, and his trial and execution before the proconsul at Carthage. A concluding passage notes that he was the first African bishop to win the martyr's crown and ends with the author's mingled exultation in his master's victory and grief at having survived him.
la.priscian.carmen_in_laudem_Anastasii_impe: A Late Antique Latin panegyric poem by Priscian in praise of the emperor Anastasius, it opens with a request that the ruler accept a song of thanksgiving for the peace and justice restored to the Roman world. The main body catalogues the emperor's virtues, justice, wisdom, clemency, piety, by comparison with Nerva, Titus, Trajan, Antoninus and Marcus, and gives a long account of his suppression of the Isaurian rebels, whom heaven itself is said to have defeated with storms, floods and lightning near the Lycian coast. Later sections praise his mercy toward the vanquished, his rebuilding of cities, harbours and farmland, his reform of taxation and the grain supply, his protection of plaintiffs and soldiers, and the rout of raiders who had advanced as far as the Euphrates. The poem closes with commendation of the Augusta and of Hypatius, and with a promise to speak only truth, rejecting the mythological flattery customary in verses about emperors.
la.priscillian.tractatus_undecim: The Tractatus Undecim is a collection of eleven Latin prose tractates of Late Antique date attributed to Priscillian. The first tractate takes the form of a confession of faith addressed to 'the most blessed priests', in which the author professes the creed, answers the accusations raised against him and his followers, and pronounces anathemas against a long catalogue of named heresies. The remaining tractates continue this defensive and instructional course through discussions of the unity of God and Christ, the authority and right reading of scripture within and beyond the canon, the discipline of Lent and the paschal fast, and allegorical expositions of the opening Psalms read as accounts of the soul's warfare against vice. The series closes with a doxology addressed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
la.priscillian_bishop_of_avila.canones_in_p: A Latin theological work in prose by Priscillian, bishop of Avila, composed in the late antique period. It opens with a dedicatory letter in which the author answers a correspondent's request for a compact scriptural defence against heretics who twist or deny the apostolic testimony, explaining that he has divided the fourteen Pauline epistles into numbered testimonia and distilled from them ninety short doctrinal canons, each annotated with the references of the passages it gathers. The body of the work consists of these canons, each beginning 'Quia' and followed by strings of numbers keyed to Romans, the letters to the Corinthians and Thessalonians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the letters to Timothy and Titus, Philemon, and Hebrews. Their subjects run from the veracity of God and the contrast between the two spirits and the two wisdoms, through the incarnation of Christ as God and man, the sacrament once hidden and now revealed, the opposition of the carnal old law and the spiritual law of faith, and the duties of clergy, laity, and ascetics, to baptism, the resurrection of the body, the final judgement by Christ, the coming of Antichrist, and the everlasting reign of the just with God.
la.proba_active_4th_century.cento: The Cento is a Late Antique Latin biblical epic by the fourth-century poet Proba, composed by recasting verses of Vergil to retell the narrative of scripture. It opens with a dedication urging the emperor to acknowledge Maro 'transformed into the better' and commending the poem to Arcadius, after which the poet renounces the pagan Muses and announces her design to sing Christ's gifts in Vergil's words. The poem proceeds from the creation of the world and of humankind through the temptation and fall, the first fratricide, the flood, and the fortunes of the patriarchs and their deliverance from Egypt, before turning to the coming of Christ foretold by the prophets. Its later movement recounts the annunciation and infancy, the baptism, the temptation in the wilderness, the teaching and miracles, the passion and crucifixion, and the resurrection, closing with the risen Christ's appearance to his followers and their charge to continue his work.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_novatianum: A Latin prose treatise of uncertain date and authorship, preserved among the works of Cyprian and written against the rigorist Novatian over the question of receiving back Christians who lapsed in persecution, a matter the work connects with the Decian persecution. It opens with the speaker's anguished deliberation over wounded brethren and with Novatian's appearance as a new adversary who denies the fallen the Father's mercy and the grace of penance. The argument then ranges widely through scripture, reading Noah's ark, the raven, and the twice-released dove as figures of the church and of two persecutions, in the first of which the lapsed fell and in the second of which they stood victorious, while Novatian is assailed as a new Cain who usurps a judgment Christ reserves to himself. Prophetic, gospel, and apocalyptic passages on divine clemency, repentance, and the day of judgment are amassed in support, and the treatise closes by urging confession and full satisfaction while the way of forgiveness stands open.
la.pseudo_cyprian.ad_vigilium_de_iudaica_in: A Latin epistolary treatise of uncertain date, transmitted among the works attributed to Cyprian, addressed to one Vigilius and concerned with the unbelief of the Jewish people.
