It opens with a lament over the inherited obstinacy of Israel, who, though Christ has proclaimed himself the light of the world, persist in refusing to turn to God. The body of the work assembles scriptural proofs of Christ's manifestation, the psalmists and prophets, the evangelists' narratives of the magi and Simeon, and Malachi's promised sun of righteousness, upholds the faith of Abraham as the model by which believers become his sons while unbelieving Israel has forfeited that name, and includes the author's account of his Latin rendering of the disputation between Jason the Christian and Papiscus the Jew. The letter closes with personal words to Vigilius, presented as a bishop unexpectedly chosen by God and destined for martyrdom, with a request for his prayers on the author's behalf.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_disciplina_et_bono_pud: De disciplina et bono pudicitiae is a Latin prose treatise of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage and taking the form of a bishop's written address to his congregation. It opens with an apology for time spent on daily gospel exposition and a resolve to exhort the faithful by letter. The work then praises chastity in encomiastic terms as the honor of bodies and ornament of morals, ranks it first among virgins, then the continent, then the married, and grounds its precepts in apostolic teaching on marriage and divorce. From there it denounces adultery and unnatural lust, celebrates Joseph and Susanna as examples of victorious chastity, criticizes elaborate female adornment, and closes with counsel on governing the body through the soul and seeking divine aid, ending with a farewell to the brothers.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_laude_martyrii: De Laude Martyrii is a Latin prose sermon on the glory of martyrdom, attributed to Cyprian and so transmitted among the Pseudo-Cyprianic works, of uncertain date in the later imperial period. It opens with an exordium in which the speaker pleads the inadequacy of his powers before a subject whose grandeur both incites and restrains him. The argument proceeds through three heads, what martyrdom is, how great it is, and to whom it brings profit, expounding martyrdom as the end of sin and the foundation of salvation, illustrating it with scriptural exempla such as Daniel, the three youths in the furnace, and Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac, and ranking the martyrs' crown above virginity and every other merit. Denunciation of love for the world, a vision of hell for deniers and of a seasonless paradise for the faithful, and calls to imitate Christ's passion carry the sermon to a closing glimpse of the shining host of martyrs.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_rebaptismate: The De Rebaptismate is a short Latin theological treatise of uncertain authorship, transmitted in the corpus of Cyprian of Carthage and generally counted among the pseudo-Cyprianic works, of later imperial date. It opens with a question circulating among the brethren about what should be done with those baptized in heresy, yet in the name of Christ, who return in penitence to the church: whether the bishop's imposition of hands alone suffices, or whether they must be baptized again. The author argues throughout that rebaptism is unnecessary, assembling scriptural testimony from John the Baptist's preaching, Acts, and the Gospels to show that a baptism invoking the name of Jesus is perfected rather than annulled when the Spirit is supplied through episcopal laying on of hands, and treating baptism by water, by blood in martyrdom, and by the Spirit as one baptism in diverse forms. The work closes by defending the church's venerable custom against innovators and by denouncing the fraudulent fire-tricks of heretical baptizers and the apocryphal book known as the Praedicatio Pauli.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_spectaculis_liber: De Spectaculis Liber is a Latin prose treatise of uncertain date in the later imperial period, transmitted under the name of Cyprian of Carthage as the work of a pseudo-Cyprianic author, which argues on theological grounds that Christians may not attend the public spectacles of the pagan world. It opens as an address to fellow believers, welcoming the occasion to write and lamenting that flattering patrons of vice twist the divine scriptures into an apology for the pleasures of the shows. The body of the work maintains that idolatry, the mother of all games, lies behind every kind of spectacle, races in the circus, theatrical plays, musical and athletic contests, and the gladiatorial arena, and condemns each in turn for its cruelty, obscenity, and vanity, showing that scripture's silence on such entertainments forbids rather than permits them. It closes by setting against the pagan shows the better spectacles of the believer, the beauty of the created world and the wonders wrought by God in scripture, above all the devil defeated beneath the feet of Christ, and ends with a doxology and a farewell to the brethren.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_xii_abusionibus_saecul: A late-antique Latin theological treatise ascribed to Cyprian but of uncertain date and authorship, De duodecim abusivis saeculi deals with twelve 'abuses' that corrupt the world. It opens by cataloguing these in summary fashion: the wise man without good works, the old man without religion, the youth without obedience, the rich man without almsgiving, the woman without chastity, the lord without virtue, the contentious Christian, the proud pauper, the unjust king, the negligent bishop, the undisciplined people, and the people without law. Each abuse is then taken up in turn and expounded with moral argument and copious scriptural quotation, the chapters on kingship and episcopal office setting out at length the duties of rulers and bishops, those on the laity treating humility, discipline and observance of God's law. The work closes by warning that a people without law is a people without Christ, since Christ is the end of the law.
la.pseudo_cyprian.epistulae: Latin letters attributed to Cyprian of Carthage but of uncertain authorship, composed in the theological idiom of the later imperial church. The collection opens with an exhortation to hold fast to a single, unified reading of divine scripture. The remaining pieces address the controversies of a divided Christian community: one letter rebukes a bishop for writings against the catholic faith concerning baptism and demands their retraction, another transmits conciliar rulings barring traditores, those who surrendered the scriptures under persecution, from clerical and liturgical standing, and a long consolatory epistle urges a father grieving his daughter's death to accept it as a passage to God rather than a loss. Throughout, the letters combine pastoral exhortation with scriptural argument on faith, martyrdom, resurrection, and ecclesiastical discipline.
la.pseudo_cyprian.liber_de_aleatoribus: The Liber de Aleatoribus is a Latin theological treatise against dice-playing, transmitted under Cyprian's name and attributed to a pseudo-Cyprianic author of the later imperial period. It opens with a bishop's account of his pastoral office and his alarm at the audacity of gamblers among the faithful. The work then expounds the bishop's duty as shepherd and steward of the gospel to correct sinners rather than pardon them laxly, before passing into a long denunciation of the gaming table as the devil's snare, ruinous of wealth and reputation and fertile in perjury, quarrels, blasphemy, and secret vice, together with a legend of the game's inventor, who demanded sacrifice to himself from all who played. It closes by declaring gamblers estranged from Christ and unworthy of his sacraments, and urges them to abandon the dice, distribute their goods to the poor and the church, and lay up treasure in heaven.
la.pseudo_eucherius.de_situ_hierusolimitana: De situ Hierusolimitanae urbis atque ipsius Iudaeae is a short late antique Latin prose treatise, handed down under the name of Eucherius and addressed in its opening to Faustus, a presbyter of the island, whose brief preface promises a treatment as compact as the work itself. The body surveys the hilltop site, walls and gates of Jerusalem, Mount Sion with its clerics and monks, and the Constantinian sanctuaries of the Martyrium, Golgotha and the Anastasis, before moving outward to the ruined Temple, the pool of Bethsaida, Siloa, the valley of Jehoshaphat, the Mount of Olives and neighbouring places from Bethlehem, Jericho and the Jordan to the Dead Sea, Hebron and Joppa, with distances reckoned in miles. A closing section sets out the length and breadth of Judaea from Dan to Beersheba, incorporating long excerpts from Jerome's letter to Dardanus and from Josephus on the bounds, cities and fertility of Galilee, Samaria and Judaea, the Jewish historian being cited as a witness to the truth of the account.
la.pseudo_severus_sulpicius.epistolae_septe: Seven prose letters of Christian exhortation handed down under the name of the late antique writer Sulpicius Severus, though their attribution to him is doubtful. The first letter, written to a devout woman, gives thanks for her progress in faith and urges perseverance against the assaults of the devil and the ridicule of the world. The rest of the collection turns to moral and ascetic instruction: a long admonition to a consecrated virgin argues that virginity, however great its merit, profits nothing without observance of all the commandments, and enjoins purity of soul as well as body, modesty in speech, dress and conduct, and contempt for worldly nobility and glory; further letters praise the conversion of a stage performer, playfully send a monastery a rustic cook ignorant of pepper but skilled in beans and porridge, commend a youth guilty of boyish error, argue over the tenant farmers of an estate, and close with a reflection on how letters sustain affection between absent friends.
la.pseudo_tertullian.adversus_omnes_haerese: A short Latin heresiological treatise transmitted under Tertullian's name, of the later Roman imperial period and of uncertain date, which surveys in summary fashion the sects its author counts as departures from Christian truth. It opens with a declaration that only a selection of heresies will be sketched, passing swiftly over Jewish groups such as the followers of Dositheus, the Sadducees, the Pharisees, and the Herodians before turning to those who erred from the gospel. The body of the work proceeds heresiarch by heresiarch through Simon Magus, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, Nicolaus, the Ophites, Cainites, and Sethians, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Ebion, Valentinus and his school, Marcus and Colarbasus, Cerdon, Marcion with his successors Lucanus and Appelles, Tatian, the Cataphrygians, Blastos, two Theodoti, and finally Praxeas and Victorinus, giving for each an outline of doctrines, especially concerning the origin of the world, the nature of Christ, and the resurrection. Denial of Christ's real flesh, rejection of the resurrection of the body, and disparagement of the law and the prophets recur throughout as the marks of the errors being catalogued.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.passio_septem_mon: A short Latin martyr narrative doubtfully attributed to Victor of Vita, recounting the sufferings of seven monks during the persecution of African Catholics under the Vandal king Huneric. The work opens with a prologue begging divine aid for the task of narrating the martyrs' triumphs. It then describes Huneric's edicts of exile, the closing of churches and confiscation of monasteries, and the arrest of the seven brothers, Bonifatius, Servus, Rusticus, Liberatus, Rogatus, Septimus and Maximus, who are brought to Carthage, refuse the promises of wealth and the rebaptism urged by an Arian bishop, and are condemned to be burned on a ship at sea; when the fire repeatedly fails, they are slain with oar-stocks, their bodies are miraculously returned to the shore, and they are buried with hymns beside the basilica of Celerina. The account ends with a doxology to the Trinity, under whose confession the martyrs completed their course.
la.q_cicero.on_running_for_consul: A Latin epistolary treatise of the Roman Republic, attributed to Quintus Cicero, in the form of a letter of advice to a candidate for the consulship. It opens with the writer explaining that he sets down in one ordered view the thoughts that came to him day and night about the reader's campaign, so that considerations scattered across the whole enterprise may be arranged and distributed. The body sets out the means of building support among the publicani, the equestrian order, the municipal towns of Italy, noble youths and consulars, and prescribes daily attention to callers, escorts and companions, together with flattery, liberality, constant presence and careful management of promises and refusals, illustrated by the practice of C. Cotta; it classes potential enemies under three heads, urges the cultivation of popular favour and rumour, including reliance on Pompey's goodwill, and supplies pointed invective against competitors such as Antonius and Catiline. The closing pages turn to preserving the esteem of senate, equites and plebs alike and to countering electoral bribery through vigilance, the intimidation of wrongdoers and the restraint of the divisores, ending with the writer's wish that the little handbook on electioneering be regarded as complete and his invitation to corrections.
la.quintilian.institutio_oratoria: The Institutio Oratoria is a twelve-book Latin prose treatise on the training of an orator by Quintilian, written after some twenty years of teaching in early imperial Rome and addressed to his friend Marcellus Victorius. It opens with a preface explaining the work's genesis and defining the orator as 'a good man skilled in speaking', before proceeding systematically: the first book covers the education of a child from infancy, nurses, schools, the branches of the encyclopedic arts and the study of letters; the second passes to the teacher's duties and the first exercises of the school of rhetoric. Five books are then given to invention and disposition, four to elocution, memory and above all delivery, treated in the eleventh book, which ends with prescriptions on voice and gesture. The twelfth and longest book forms the orator himself, insisting on character and wisdom, examining which causes he may undertake, offering practical advice on pleading, discussing the schools of style and the proper kind of eloquence, and closing with an exhortation to pursue virtue and eloquence together.
la.remigius_of_auxerre.expositione_in_pasch: A Latin prose commentary on Sedulius's Paschale Carmen, composed in the early medieval period and transmitted under the name of Remigius of Auxerre. It opens with an accessus that draws on Jerome's catalogue of illustrious men to recount Sedulius's life, his earlier prose treatment of the same story, and his dedication of the poem to the priest Macedonius. The body of the work proceeds lemma by lemma through the dedicatory epistle and the poem itself, glossing difficult vocabulary with etymologies and notes on grammar and rhetoric. Alongside these verbal explanations the commentary offers allegorical and moral readings of the narrative, which runs from the fall of Adam through the Old Testament figures the poet recapitulates to Christ's birth, miracles, passion, resurrection, appearances after Easter, and closing prayer.
la.rufius_festus.breviarium: The Breviarium of Rufius Festus is a late-antique Latin prose epitome of Roman history, presented to the reigning emperor with the promise that its compressed record may be counted rather than read. It opens by reckoning 1,117 years from the founding of the city, dividing the whole span into the ages of the kings, the consuls, and the emperors, and sketching how far Roman power advanced under each. The body of the work then recounts, province by province, how Sicily, Africa, Spain, Gaul, Illyricum, Thrace, Asia, and the Eastern lands were acquired and how each is governed in the author's own day, listing the provincial organization of the empire as it stood under the emperors. A long final section narrates the wars between Rome and Parthia and Persia, from the defeat and death of Crassus through the campaigns of Lucullus, Pompey, Trajan, and Diocletian to the peace concluded under Jovian, closing with the hope that victory over the Goths will add a Babylonian palm of peace to the emperor's achievements.
la.ruricius_i_bishop_of_limoges.epistulae: The Epistulae is a Late Antique Latin letter collection by Ruricius, Bishop of Limoges. It opens with a highly wrought letter to a revered priest, in which the bishop praises his correspondent's sanctity and pleads for his prayers and correction. The remaining letters, addressed chiefly to fellow bishops, clergy, monastic friends, and members of Ruricius's own family, are composed in ornate, rhythmical prose studded with biblical quotation and cover a wide range of business: requests and loans of books, letters of commendation for travelers and fugitives claiming sanctuary, exchanges of gifts such as horses, pears, and game, consolations on the deaths of children and kinsmen, appeals for leniency toward offenders, exhortations to penance and renunciation of the world, and notes on synods and other ecclesiastical affairs.
la.sallust.histories: A Latin prose historical work of the late Republic by Sallust, the Histories are preserved in fragments, consisting principally of speeches and letters. It opens with a public speech exhorting the Quirites to throw off the tyranny of Sulla and his partisans. The surviving material follows the discord of the decades after Sulla's dictatorship: senatorial speeches urging and resisting war against Lepidus, a consul's ritual self-dedication for the state, a commander's letter from the Spanish war protesting the neglect of his army, an oration on the restoration of tribunician power, and a letter in which Mithridates calls on Arsaces of Parthia to join him against Rome, reviewing Roman aggression from Philip of Macedon onward.
la.salutati.de_laboribus_herculis: De Laboribus Herculis, a Renaissance Latin prose treatise by Salutati, opens with a compendious defense of poetry against its detractors, who are chided for despising the art despite Aristotle's own reliance on the poets. From there the work unfolds a systematic account of poetry itself, defining it as praise and blame cast in figured, metrical speech, tracing its origin alongside religion and idolatry, and arguing that it is composed of all the liberal arts, a claim illustrated at length through musical proportion and the harmonies of the heroic hexameter. The greater part of the treatise expounds the myth of Hercules, running through the labors and further deeds, the Hesperides, Cacus, Cerberus, and the descent to the underworld, with digressions on Orpheus, Theseus, and Pirithous, and reads each fable as both history and moral, physical, or theological allegory in which Hercules figures the virtuous man. The closing portions follow Eneas's descent among the shades, expounding the golden bough, Charon, and the death of Misenus in the same allegorical vein.
la.salutati.de_tyranno: A Renaissance Latin treatise in epistolary form by Coluccio Salutati, chancellor of Florence, written in answer to Antonio di Aquila, a student of arts at Padua. It opens with a salutation and a protest against the correspondent's extravagant praise, before the writer announces five questions for treatment: the definition and kinds of the tyrant, the lawfulness of killing a tyrant, the character of Caesar's principate, the justice of his assassination, and Dante's condemnation of Brutus and Cassius. Drawing on etymology, authorities such as Gregory, and Roman legal and historical exempla, the argument permits force against an invader of a people's liberty but insists that a ruler with a lawful title may be opposed only by the authority of a superior or of the citizen body, and on this basis it acquits Julius Caesar of tyranny and condemns his assassins as murderers rather than liberators. A closing section vindicates Dante's placing of Brutus and Cassius in the lowest hell beside Judas, and the work ends with a briefer, deliberately undecided survey of ancient testimony on whether Antenor and Aeneas betrayed Troy.
la.salvianus.de_gubernatione_dei: De Gubernatione Dei is a Late Antique prose treatise by Salvian, a presbyter of Massilia, defending divine providence against the charge that God is careless of human affairs. It opens by contrasting the author's declared aim of writing remedies rather than verbal displays, and then frames the objection that the good suffer while the wicked prosper, as though God neither guarded the one nor restrained the other. The bulk of the work argues, by reason, by biblical examples running from Adam, Cain, and the Flood through Abraham, Moses, and David, and by scriptural testimonies, that God continually sees, governs, and judges the world, and that the calamities befalling the Roman Empire are deserved punishment. In its later portions it lists the vices of Roman Christians, greed, oppressive taxation, sexual impurity, fondness for the circus and theater, and casual swearing by Christ, contrasts them with the chastity and piety of barbarian peoples such as the Goths and Vandals, and ends by denouncing as blasphemy the claim that God neglects mankind.
la.saxo_grammaticus.gesta_danorum: A Latin history of the Danes, the Gesta Danorum was composed by Saxo Grammaticus at the urging of Archbishop Absalon and is of uncertain date. Its prologue, addressed to Absalon, to the canon Andrew, and to King Valdemar, announces an account of Danish deeds beginning with a description of the homeland and extending from legendary antiquity to the author's own day. The work draws on old Danish songs, whose matter is rendered in Latin metres, on the reports of Icelandic informants versed in antiquity, and on Absalon's own testimony of deeds he performed or learned of. Written in elaborate prose interspersed with verse, it traces the deeds of Danish kings across their whole recorded past.
la.sedulius.epistola_ad_macedonium_altera: A late-antique Latin dedicatory letter by the Christian poet Sedulius, addressed to the priest Macedonius and prefixed to his prose Paschale Opus. It opens with a greeting and an acknowledgment of Macedonius's command to render the earlier Paschale Carmen from verse into prose. The body defends the new edition against anticipated critics, appealing to Hermogenianus and Origen as precedents for reissuing and expanding one's own work, and distinguishes between altering what is complete and supplying what was left unfinished. It closes by naming the verse work Paschale Carmen and the prose rendition Paschale Opus, both offered in prayer to Christ.
la.sedulius.hymnus_ii_a_solis_ortus_cardine: A Late Antique Latin Christian hymn by Sedulius, opening with the call 'A solis ortus cardine' to sing of Christ the prince, born of the Virgin Mary, from the rising of the sun to the limits of the earth. The work is an alphabetic hymn whose quatrains begin with the successive letters A through Z, and its stanzas follow the course of Christ's life from the annunciation and nativity, through the angels and shepherds, the magi and Herod's fear, and the slaughter of the innocents, to his baptism and a sequence of miracles including the water made wine, the healing of the centurion's servant, Peter walking on the sea, and the raising of Lazarus. The later stanzas move to Judas's betrayal, the passion and crucifixion between thieves, the women bearing myrrh after the sabbath, and end with Christ trampling the envious dragon and the mouth of the lion before returning to the heavens.
la.sedulius.opus_paschale: The Opus Paschale is a Late Antique Latin prose treatment of the life of Christ in a biblical and exegetical mode, opening with a preface contrasting pagan poetry unfavourably with Christian truth and invoking God's aid. The work surveys Old Testament miracles, Enoch, Abraham, Lot's wife, Moses, Jonah and others, as figures fulfilled in the Gospel narrative, then follows the course of Christ's life from the Virgin birth through the miracles and teachings of the ministry, the Lord's Prayer, the Passion with its extensive allegorical interpretation, the Harrowing of Hell, and the Resurrection and Ascension, closing with allusions to the evangelists. It expounds each episode with sustained rhetorical and allegorical commentary directed against pagan idolatry and heresy, notably Arianism, throughout.
la.seneca.ad_lucilium_epistulae_morales: Seneca's Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales is a Latin prose collection of moral-philosophical letters, composed in the early Imperial period and addressed throughout to the author's friend Lucilius. The opening letter urges Lucilius to reclaim the time that habit and society waste, since time is the only possession that is truly his own. The sequence that follows forms a continuous course of moral instruction, each letter opening with the same salutation and generally closing with a pithy saying, often quoted from Epicurus, as its 'payment' for the day. Its subjects range across friendship, reading and style, solitude and the crowd, gladiatorial spectacles, the fear of death, poverty, wealth and frugality, the passions, drunkenness, gratitude, and Stoic definitions of the good and the honorable, interwoven with anecdotes from Roman life, notices of Seneca's own health and travels, and occasional digressions into physics and dialectic.
la.seneca.carminum_fragmenta: A brief collection of lyric fragments in mixed metres attributed to Seneca and belonging to the Early Imperial period. It opens with an address to a parent and lord of the lofty heaven, in which the speaker allows no delay in obedience and concedes that the fates lead the willing while dragging the unwilling. The remaining excerpts, many of them single-line sententiae, dwell on wealth and virtue: whether men seek riches rather than goodness, the wish to be called the worst so long as one is called rich, the resolve to live rich or die poor, and a passage styling money a great good of humankind, beyond a mother's delight in her children. Gnomic sayings such as 'the speech of truth is simple' and a fragment on a thick woollen gausapa garment close the assemblage.
la.seneca.de_beneficiis: A Stoic philosophical treatise in Latin prose, in seven books, composed by Seneca in the early imperial period and addressed to Aebutius Liberalis. It opens with the complaint, voiced to Liberalis, that nothing in the erring life of mankind is more unworthy than that people know neither how to give nor how to receive a benefit. The work defines the benefit as residing in the giver's willing mind rather than in the gift itself, and then considers how recipients should be chosen and how benefits should be given, received and repaid, the many varieties and causes of ingratitude, whether benefits can be taken away or outweighed by later injury, and what is owed to parents, children, slaves and the gods, illustrating its arguments with examples from Roman history and legend. A closing book urges forbearance toward the ungrateful and ends with the Cynic Demetrius and the question whether anything can be given to the sage, who in a sense possesses all things.
la.seneca.de_clementia: A Latin prose philosophical treatise of the Early Imperial period, Seneca's De Clementia is addressed to the young emperor Nero, whom the opening preface promises to confront with his own clemency as in a mirror. From there the work argues that clemency is the virtue most proper to rulers, holding that a prince's safety rests on the love of his subjects rather than on fear, and illustrates the case with an extended narrative of Augustus sparing the conspirator Cinna and with cautionary examples of cruelty such as Sulla and Vedius Pollio. A later section defines clementia, distinguishes it from misericordia (pity) and from formal pardon (venia) in Stoic terms, and considers when punishment is owed and how far it should be tempered. The main argument breaks off in the discussion of reforming offenders, after which the surviving copy appends a set of aphoristic chapters on clemency for princes introduced as from an epistle attributed to Hildebert of Le Mans.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_marciam: A prose consolatio by the early Imperial philosopher Seneca, addressed to Marcia, daughter of the historian Cremutius Cordus, who has spent three years in unrelenting mourning for a son; it opens with praise of her fortitude and of her restoration of her father's suppressed writings. Seneca contrasts the endless grief of Octavia over Marcellus with Livia's self-command after losing Drusus, then argues that sorrow is a matter of opinion rather than nature, that all life's goods are held on loan from fortune, and that death can be a release and even a gain, illustrated by examples of men and women from Sulla, Paulus, Caesar, and Cornelia to Lucretia and Cloelia. The work closes with an imagined speech in which Cordus, speaking from the heavens to his daughter, sets human loss within the vast scale of cosmic time and the world's eventual conflagration, and urges her to accept her son's early death as a return to blessed company and lasting peace.
la.seneca.de_consolatione_ad_polybium: A Latin prose consolation by Seneca of the early imperial period, addressed to Polybius, a powerful figure close to the emperor, on the death of his brother. It opens by setting the fragility of human life against cities and monuments of stone, which seem firm by comparison with human affairs yet perish like everything nature has made. The argument proceeds that grief benefits neither the mourner nor the dead, that loss is the common lot illustrated by examples of Roman nobles and Caesars who endured the deaths of brothers and kin, and that the bereaved should honour the deceased through studies and writings that outlast marble; an extended encomium of the emperor's clemency incorporates the author's own account of exile and plea for recall. The work ends with counsel to temper tears while not wholly suppressing them, and with an apology that the author's own misfortunes among barbarians have left him ill-furnished with Latin words for another's consolation.
la.seneca.de_constantia: De Constantia is a Latin prose dialogue in which Seneca, writing in the early Imperial period, addresses Serenus and opens by ranking the Stoics above all other professors of wisdom and asserting that the sage, exemplified by Cato, stands beyond the reach of injury. The body of the work argues that iniuria cannot befall a man whose only true good is virtue, illustrating the thesis with Stilbo's reply to Demetrius Poliorcetes after the fall of Megara, Socrates' equanimity under abuse, and the insults of Gaius Caesar. A second part distinguishes contumelia from injury, treats the slights of slaves, women, and kings alike as the behaviour of children, and closes with counsel on despising contumelies and on the liberty of a mind set above fortune.
la.seneca.de_ira: Seneca's De Ira is a three-book prose treatise, addressed to his brother Novatus, that examines anger as the most destructive of the passions. The first book defines anger, denies that it is natural or useful, and refutes the Aristotelian view that it can serve courage; the second analyses how anger arises in the mind and sets out preventive remedies, including the education of children and the restraint of first impressions; the third addresses the management of one's own anger and the pacification of others, illustrated with anecdotes of rulers such as Cambyses, Alexander, and Augustus. Throughout, Seneca argues that anger must be eradicated rather than moderated, and closes with reflections on mortality and the brevity of life as arguments for calm.
la.seneca.de_providentia: A short Latin prose treatise by Seneca, written in the Early Imperial period and addressed to Lucilius, opens with the question why, if the world is governed by providence, so many misfortunes befall good men. The argument answers in Stoic terms that adversity is assigned by the gods to test and discipline the virtuous, illustrated with exempla such as Cato, Socrates, Regulus, Mucius Scaevola, Fabricius and Rutilius, and contrasted with the softness of figures like Maecenas and Sulla. Later chapters treat fate and the ordered course of the universe, the wise man's willing assent to divine will, and the readily available escape of death, closing with an exhortation to despise poverty, pain, fortune and mortality.
la.seneca.de_tranquillitate_animi: De Tranquillitate Animi, a philosophical prose dialogue of the Early Imperial period, opens with Annaeus Serenus confessing to Seneca a restless malaise of spirit, caught between frugality and luxury, public ambition and withdrawal into leisure. Seneca answers by naming the goal the euthymia of Democritus, which he calls tranquillitas, and surveys the causes of self-discontent: inconstant desire, wandering restlessness, envy of others' progress, and hidden shame over one's own failings. He then offers remedies in turn, public service or useful private study, honest self-assessment, choice of friends, moderation in wealth and expenditure, acceptance of fortune and readiness for death, avoidance of aimless busyness, and the alternation of solitude with society and of labour with relaxation. The work ends with counsel to regard human folly with laughter rather than tears, in the manner of Democritus rather than Heraclitus, and with the warning that only constant vigilance can preserve the wavering mind.
la.seneca.de_vita_beata: A Latin prose treatise on the happy life by Seneca, a philosopher of the early imperial period, addressed to his brother Gallio. It opens with the observation that all men wish to live happily but go astray because they do not first determine what the happy life is, so that the swifter their course the further they stray. The argument then sets out a Stoic account of beatitude as a life in accord with nature, grounded in virtue as the sole good, and attacks the doctrine that pleasure can be joined with virtue, defending Epicurus against those who use his name as a cover for luxury. Later sections take up the wise man's relation to wealth, which may be possessed and given away with profit though it is not a good, and answer critics who charge philosophers with failing to live by their own precepts, closing with the sage's rebuke of those who malign virtue and with the example of Socrates.
la.seneca.hercules_furens: A Latin tragedy of the Early Imperial period by Seneca, on the madness of Hercules. It opens with Juno's prologue, in which the goddess, displaced in Jupiter's favour by Alcmene and her son, summons the Furies to madden Hercules at the height of his success. The plot follows the Theban usurper Lycus, who has slain Creon and seized the throne and now threatens Megara, her children, and Amphitryon while Hercules descends to the underworld for Cerberus; Hercules returns in time to kill Lycus, but Juno's frenzy overtakes him and he slaughters his wife and children in the belief that they are enemies. Waking, he learns of the massacre from Amphitryon and Theseus, whose account of the lower world and of the capture of Cerberus fills much of the later action, contemplates suicide, and is persuaded by his father and his friend to live on, withdrawing from Thebes to expiate his crime.
la.seneca.hercules_oetaeus: Hercules Oetaeus is a Latin tragedy of Early Imperial date, attributed to Seneca and transmitted with his dramatic works. It opens with Hercules, his labours complete yet still refused a place in heaven, petitioning Jupiter and sending Lichas ahead with the spoils of Oechalia to the altar of Cenaeian Jove. The action then turns on Deianira's jealousy of the captive Iole: trusting to the supposed love charm of the dying Nessus, she sends her husband a robe whose clinging poison consumes his flesh, drives him to slay Lichas and to build a pyre on Mount Oeta, and prompts her own suicide in remorse. Alcmene's laments, the burning reported by Philoctetes, the deified Hercules' appearance to console his mother and promise vengeance on Eurystheus, and closing choruses on virtue's ascent to the stars bring the drama to its end.
la.seneca.phaedra: Seneca's Latin tragedy Phaedra, a drama of the Early Imperial period, opens with Hippolytus mustering his companions and hounds for the hunt through the hills of Attica and invoking the goddess Diana. The action then follows Phaedra's consuming passion for her stepson: she confesses her love, is rebuffed, and, fearing exposure, falsely accuses Hippolytus of assault before his father Theseus, who has just returned from the underworld and answers by calling down a curse through his father Neptune. A messenger then narrates how a sea monster destroys Hippolytus as he drives his chariot along the shore, after which Phaedra takes her own life with a confession of the truth, leaving Theseus to lament over the youth's dismembered remains. Choral odes interspersed among the acts meditate on the dominion of love, the inconstancy of Fortune, the merits of the simple country life, the transience of beauty, and the fickleness of fate.
la.seneca_the_elder.excerpta_controversiae: A Latin prose work of the Early Imperial period, attributed to Seneca the Elder, collecting rhetorical material from the declamation schools: the excerpted Controversiae preserve imaginary legal cases together with sample sententiae, divisions and colores drawn from the declaimers who argued them. The surviving portion opens with themes such as the disinherited son who supported his uncle and the captive priestess who killed her abductor, each followed by opposing arguments in the voices of various rhetoricians. The work then runs through a long sequence of controuersiae on themes of family conflict, piracy, tyranny, adultery and inheritance, interspersed with anecdotal asides about individual declaimers, and concludes with the prefaces addressed to Seneca's sons in which he discusses famous orators such as Cassius Severus, Asinius Pollio and Haterius.
la.seneca_the_elder.suasoriae: The Suasoriae is a Latin prose compilation assembled by Seneca the Elder in the early Imperial period, preserving a series of deliberative declamation exercises together with the memorable sayings, argument divisions, and stylistic treatments contributed by celebrated orators and rhetoricians. The collection opens in the midst of the suasoria in which Alexander is counselled whether to sail beyond the Ocean, its speakers weighing the bounds that nature sets upon empire. Subsequent themes include the three hundred Spartans deliberating withdrawal from Thermopylae, the Athenians debating whether to take down the trophies of Xerxes, Agamemnon deliberating the sacrifice of Iphigenia, and Cicero weighing whether to burn his speeches against Antonius or plead with the triumvir for his life. Throughout, the compiler interlaces judgments on individual declaimers and their mannerisms, anecdotes of their lives and rivalries, extended descriptive passages from their performances, verse excerpts from poets such as Cornelius Severus, and historical narratives, including several historians' accounts of Cicero's death.
la.servius_honoratus.in_virgilii_georgicon_: A late antique prose commentary by Servius Honoratus on Virgil's Georgics, transmitted in four books corresponding to the four books of the poem and composed as a running sequence of Virgilian lemmata, each followed by explanation. The opening preface situates the Georgics among Virgil's works, holding that he followed Homer in the Aeneid, Theocritus in the Bucolics, and Hesiod in this poem, and that a single Hesiodic book on farming was deliberately expanded into four and addressed to Maecenas as Hesiod addressed Perses. Through the body of the work the notes gloss Virgil's wording with grammatical and stylistic analysis of forms, cases, and figures, etymologies of names and terms, alternative explanations introduced by 'et aliter', and mythological narratives such as those of Achelous, Orpheus, and Eurydice. The commentary also treats seasonal and astronomical lore, Stoic allegorization of the gods invoked in the poem, the agrarian, veterinary, and apicultural precepts themselves, and passages quoted from earlier Latin authors, closing at the end of book four with the sign of the bees from the oxen and the verses in which Virgil reviews his Bucolics and his theme of Caesar's wars in the East.
la.silius_italicus.punica: Silius Italicus's Punica, an epic in hexameters of the early Imperial period, recounts the Second Punic War between Rome and Carthage across seventeen books. It opens with Hannibal's oath against Rome and the siege of Saguntum, then traces the war's course through the Roman disasters at the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae, the long resistance under Fabius Cunctator, the campaigns of Scipio in Spain and Africa, the deaths of Hasdrubal and other commanders, and the war's end with Hannibal's defeat, exile and the triumph that closes the poem. The work also treats dynastic and divine machinery surrounding the conflict, the Numidian politics of Syphax and Masinissa, and Hannibal's final withdrawal from Italy.
la.suetonius.de_vita_caesarum: The work opens with the life of Julius Caesar, beginning in his youth with the loss of his father, his appointment as flamen Dialis, his marriage to Cornelia, and his defiance of Sulla. It continues through a sequence of biographies of the rulers from Caesar to Domitian, including the brief reigns of Galba, Otho, and Vitellius, whose lives round out the period of civil war between the Julio-Claudian and Flavian dynasties. Rather than proceeding as continuous annals, each life is arranged topically under headings such as ancestry and family, omens and portents, military campaigns and public offices, buildings and games, private habits, physical appearance, and manner of death. In compiling these accounts Suetonius cites letters, memoirs, senatorial records, and earlier writers, preserving a mass of anecdote, quotation, and documentary detail on the public conduct and personal character of each emperor.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_Bassulae_p: A short late-antique prose epistle of Sulpicius Severus, addressed to his mother Bassula, which opens with mock-legal banter accusing her of purloining and circulating his private letters as fast as he writes them. The bulk of the work is the promised account, given only on condition that she show it to no one, of the death of Martin of Tours: the saint's journey to Candes to reconcile discordant clerics, his expulsion of a flock of birds with a word of command, his sudden failing strength, his refusal to choose between life and death in his prayers, and his passing with a vision of the devil rebuked and Abraham's bosom before him. It closes with the luminous appearance of the saint's body, the vast funeral gathering of monks, virgins and crowds from city and countryside, and a rhetorical comparison of his exequies with a worldly triumph.
la.sulpicius_severus.epistula_ad_aurelium: In this Late Antique prose letter, Sulpicius Severus writes to a correspondent named Aurelius. It opens with the writer, alone after their parting and weighed down by thoughts of his sins, falling into a sleep in which he sees Martin, bishop of Tours, radiant in white, bless him and ascend to heaven, followed by the presbyter Clarus, only to wake to the news of Martin's death. The remainder is an outpouring of grief, urging Aurelius to come and mourn with the writer, who insists that Martin, though denied martyrdom in blood, achieved a bloodless martyrdom through fasting, vigils, and every hardship borne for the faith, and would gladly have faced beasts, fire, or the sword had a persecuting age demanded it. The letter closes with the hope that Martin's intercession may make up for the writer's own sins, together with an apology for having dwelt so long upon his sorrow.
la.terence.eunuchus: A Latin comedy in verse by Terence of the Republican period, adapted from a Greek original by Menander. Its opening prologue has the poet answer a charge that he took the parasite and the boasting soldier from an earlier Latin play, and invites the audience to judge the case for themselves. The action turns on the young Phaedria's rivalry with the braggart soldier Thraso for the courtesan Thais, and on Phaedria's brother Chaerea, who slips into Thais's house disguised as a eunuch sent among the gifts, where he rapes a young woman who proves to be Thais's long-lost Athenian sister. Recognition, a threatened lawsuit before the archon, the soldier's abortive assault on the door, and the servant Parmeno's punishment carry the plot to a resolution in which Chaerea marries the girl, Thais is taken under the family's patronage, and Thraso is brought into the household as an obliging rival.
la.terence.phormio: Phormio is a Latin comedy in dramatic verse by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic. The opening prologue has a poet answer the attacks of an older rival before announcing the play, a Greek comedy rendered in Latin as Phormio after its title character. The plot follows two young Athenians whose guardians are away: Antipho, advised by the bold parasite Phormio, marries Phanium under a law allowing next of kin to wed an heiress, while Phaedria seeks money to ransom his beloved from a procurer. Deception, fabricated kinship, and a promised dowry pile confusion upon the returning fathers Demipho and Chremes until the discovery that Chremes fathered Phanium long ago in Lemnos untangles the marriages, and the resourceful Phormio is welcomed into the family.
la.tertullian.ad_martyres: A short Latin prose exhortation of the late antique period by the Christian author Tertullian, addressed to designated martyrs held in prison while awaiting their contest. It opens by urging them to nourish the spirit along with the flesh while the mother church and fellow believers supply their bodily needs in confinement. The work goes on to warn against discord as the devil's weapon within the prison, reverses the comparison by calling the world rather than the cell the true dungeon, likens the imprisonment to the desert retreat of the prophets and to the training of soldiers and athletes under God, and sets the flesh subject to the spirit in anticipation of sword, cross, beasts, and fire. It closes by marshalling pagan exempla of endured and self-inflicted suffering, from Lucretia and Mucius Scaevola to Regulus, Cleopatra, and the Spartan flagellation rite, to argue that endurance for a heavenly reward should come more readily than endurance for earthly glory, since human life confronts everyone with unavoidable suffering and death.
la.tertullian.adversus_valentinianos: A late-antique Latin prose polemic by the Christian author Tertullian against the Valentinian heresy. It opens by likening the sect's obsessive secrecy to the Eleusinian mysteries and by pleading for Christian simplicity against their professed wisdom. The main body recounts the school's origins in Valentinus, disappointed of a bishopric, and its development under Ptolemy, Heracleon, Secundus, and Marcus, before expounding with sustained irony the whole Valentinian mythology: the thirty Aeons of the Pleroma, the fall of Sophia and the generation of Achamoth, the Demiurge's creation of the world, the threefold division of humankind into material, animal, and spiritual natures, and the sect's eschatology of spiritual marriages in the Pleroma. The work closes with a survey of variant versions of the system taught by Ptolemy, Secundus, and other Gnostic masters, through which the doctrine of the Valentinians branches into the wilder growth of the Gnostics.
la.tertullian.de_carnis_resurrectione: Tertullian's De Carnis Resurrectione is a Latin prose treatise in defence of the bodily resurrection, addressed against pagan ridicule and, above all, against heretics such as the Marcionites, Valentinians, and followers of Basilides and Apelles who admitted only a spiritual resurrection. It opens with the claim that the resurrection of the dead is the Christians' chief confidence and the very thing the crowd mocks while yet practising funeral rites for those it believes insensible. The work then proceeds by a systematic argument: it defends the dignity and divine origin of the flesh from Genesis, marshals the authority of scripture, the power of God shown in nature and in the phoenix, and the necessity of divine judgement, and refutes at length the allegorising and 'spiritual' readings by which opponents explain away the promises made to the flesh. It closes by addressing objections about the condition and functions of the risen body, concluding that all flesh, the same flesh, and the whole of it, shall rise, preserved with Christ as pledge in heaven.
la.tertullian.de_ieiunio_adversus_psychicos: The De Ieiunio aduersus psychicos is a Latin prose polemic on fasting by the Late Antique theologian Tertullian, written in defense of the stricter dietary discipline taught by the New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. It opens with scorn for the psychics, whom Tertullian accuses of pairing frequent marriage with a hatred of fasts, framing the dispute as whether fasting or marrying more often befits the Christian. The body of the work assembles biblical exempla from Adam's fall through eating, Israel's craving in the wilderness, Moses and Elijah, Daniel, Nineveh, and Ahab to Anna the prophetess, Christ's fast, Cornelius, and Paul, arguing that fasting expiates sin, averts divine anger, and wins revelation; it then treats in turn the xerophagies (abstinence from meat, wine, and moist foods) and the station-days, defending both as ancient observance rather than novelty and answering scriptural objections against imposed abstinence. Along the way it denounces the gluttony and banquet customs of its opponents, ties the discipline of hunger to endurance of prison and martyrdom, and closes with the taunt that a lean flesh is better fitted for the narrow gate of salvation and for a lighter resurrection.
la.tertullian.de_patientia: De Patientia ('On Patience') is a Latin prose treatise on Christian patience by Tertullian, a Christian writer of Late Antiquity. It opens with the author's confession that he is scarcely fit to compose such a work, being himself afflicted with the impatience he would prescribe against. The treatise then surveys divine patience as shown in God's forbearance toward humankind and supremely in Christ's incarnation and passion, traces impatience to the devil and to the first sins of Adam, Eve, Cain and Israel, and sets out the practice of patience under precepts governing loss of property, insult, grief for the dead, the desire for revenge, forgiveness, penance and charity, extending it to bodily discipline in fasting, continence and persecution, with Job as the great exemplar. It closes with a personification of Patience enthroned beside the Spirit of God, set against the false patience of the pagans.
la.tertullian.de_spectaculis: Tertullian's De Spectaculis is a Latin treatise of Christian moral theology arguing that believers must renounce all public games and spectacles. It opens by addressing new converts on how the rule of faith and the baptismal renunciation of the devil and his pomp bar the pleasures of the circus, theatre, stadium and amphitheatre. The argument then surveys in turn the origins, titles, equipment, venues and performers of each kind of entertainment, tracing chariot racing, the stage, athletic contests and gladiatorial combat alike to idolatry and the agency of daemons, while answering pagan objections and the claim that scripture nowhere names such prohibitions. It closes by opposing the fleeting shows of the world to the Christian's true spectacle, the coming Last Judgment, when persecutors, philosophers, poets and performers alike will stand revealed before Christ's tribunal.
la.tertullian.de_testimonio_animae: A brief Late Antique treatise of Latin theology attributed to Tertullian, the De Testimonio Animae sets out to prove Christian truth from a witness available to all, the human soul itself. The work opens by dismissing appeals to pagan philosophers and poets as sources of testimony, and instead summons the soul as she exists in ordinary people, unformed by schools and libraries. The bulk of the argument shows that common speech and instinctive belief, confession of a single God, terror of divine judgement, abhorrence of demons and Satan, and the conviction that the dead still feel reward and punishment, reveal knowledge implanted by God, and that this natural, universal testimony outweighs the divergent doctrines of Plato, Pythagoras and Epicurus. The treatise concludes that the soul is at once guilty of error and a witness to truth, destined to stand before the courts of God on the day of judgement.
la.thedulf_of_orleans.carmina_appendix: A short appendix of Latin poems attributed to Theodulf of Orleans, a writer of the Carolingian period. It opens with a sequence of riddling pieces in which objects, creatures and natural things speak in the first person, defining themselves through paradox, enumeration and wordplay while leaving their solutions unspoken. The enigmatic manner continues through verses on speech, harmony and healing, before the closing lines turn to Christian admonition and a prayer in horticultural imagery, asking that the root of the heart be transplanted to the fields of heaven and bear fruit.
la.theodosius.de_situ_terrae_sanctae: The De Situ Terrae Sanctae attributed to Theodosius is a late antique prose guide to the holy places of Palestine, of uncertain date. Opening with the gates of Jerusalem and the distances from the city to Jericho and the Jordan, it proceeds through measured itineraries across Judaea, Samaria, Galilee, and the coastal plain, recording mileages and identifying churches, martyria, and the biblical events attached to each site. Later sections extend farther afield, describing saints' cults and holy places in Arabia, Mesopotamia, Cappadocia, Cilicia, Egypt, and the Black Sea region, together with notes on provinces, rivers, monasteries, and local marvels such as the field at Galgala and the salt statue of Lot's wife.
la.valerius_maximus.facta_et_dicta_memorabi: Valerius Maximus's Facta et Dicta Memorabilia, a Latin prose compilation of memorable deeds and sayings composed in the early imperial period and addressed to the ruling Caesar, opens with a preface in which the author explains that worthy acts and words of Rome and of foreign peoples have been gathered from distinguished writers so that those seeking examples may be spared long research. The nine books are arranged by theme rather than chronology: the first treats religion, auspices, omens, prodigies, dreams, and miracles, and the remainder pass in turn through Roman and foreign institutions and customs, military discipline and the law of triumphs, and long sequences of virtues and vices, from fortitude, continence, clemency, gratitude, piety, chastity, liberty, justice, friendship, and liberality to luxury, cruelty, anger, avarice, pride, perfidy, sedition, and rashness. Each chapter assembles brief anecdotes drawn largely from Roman history, with foreign examples appended for variety, and the final book closes with notable kinds of death and accounts of bodily resemblance.
la.vergil_pseudo.catalepton: The Catalepton is a small collection of short lyric poems attributed to Vergil and of Augustan date. It opens with epigrams on a mistress who hides herself from the speaker's friend Tucca and on a rhetorician so devoted to Thucydides that he mangles his Greek. From there the collection ranges over a meditation on Fortune's sudden overthrow of a mighty man, a poem of friendship, and the speaker's renunciation of rhetoric and the Muse as he sets sail for the 'blessed harbors' of Siro's teaching. Lighter and later pieces include jests on a quarrelsome father- and son-in-law, a farewell to the little farm once Siro's, praise of a triumphing general, a comic dedication to a renowned mule-driver named Sabinus, a lament for the young Octavius, coarse wedding jests at the expense of Noctuinus, an invective against Licinius, and a closing vow to honor Venus with sacrifice if the poet's Latin song of Trojan Aeneas proves worthy.
la.ambrose.de_interpellatione_iob_et_david: A Latin prose theological treatise of late antiquity by Ambrose, De interpellatione Iob et David examines how the righteous may question God in the midst of adversity. It opens from the scriptural commonplace that life is full of disturbances yet supplied with consolations that outweigh them, citing Paul on the present sufferings and coming glory. The greater part of the work follows Job's pleas to God, his losses, his ulcers, his replies to the friends who charge him with sin, and draws from his speeches discussions of human frailty, the vanity of riches, the inaccessibility of divine wisdom, and the promise of resurrection, before turning to David's laments in the Psalms, above all the soul's longing for God like a deer for the waters in the forty-first psalm and Asaph's puzzlement at the prosperity of the wicked in the seventy-second. Throughout, a moral and allegorical exposition insists that God's justice, though hidden, and his consolations surpass every present affliction.
la.ambrose.de_tobia: De Tobia is a Late Antique Latin prose treatise by Ambrose, homiletic in form and beginning from a reading of the biblical Book of Tobit with praise of its hero's virtues of justice, mercy, hospitality, burial of the dead, and patience under blindness. The bulk of the work is a sustained invective against usury, depicting the seductions and exactions of moneylenders and the progressive ruin of debtors who pledge and lose property, freedom, and even their children, with digressions on debtors' despair, the gaming obsession of the Hunnish peoples, and the devil as the archetypal creditor. Scriptural prohibitions of interest are marshalled from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Leviticus, the Psalms, Ecclesiastes, and the Gospels, before the latter part of the treatise recasts lending in a positive key, urging alms to the poor as a loan to God that repays a heavenly return, illustrated from Peter's healing of the lame man and the parable of the two debtors. The work closes with Tobit's counsels to his son on almsgiving, prompt payment of the hired labourer, and sobriety.
la.anonymous.s_silviae_peregrinatio: An anonymous Latin prose pilgrimage account, transmitted under the name of Silvia and of uncertain date, reporting an extended journey to the holy places of the Near East. The surviving portion opens mid-journey in the mountains of Sinai, where the narrator, guided by local monks and clergy, tours sites associated with Moses and the Israelites, climbing the holy mountain and visiting the burning bush. The itinerary then carries the pilgrim through the land of Goshen, to Mount Nebo and the Jordan valley, to the shrine of Job, and onward to Edessa, where the story of King Abgar and the letter of Christ is retold, and to Harran, Seleucia, and the shrine of St Thecla, before reaching Constantinople. A long final section sets out in detail the life of the Jerusalem churches, describing the daily services at the Anastasis and the order of offices, processions, and catechetical instruction through Lent, Holy Week, Easter, Pentecost, and the feast of the dedication, the whole framed as a report addressed to a community of women far away.
la.anonymus.carmen_de_aquilegia: An anonymous medieval Latin poem of uncertain date, its lines are arranged alphabetically, each beginning with a successive letter of the alphabet. It opens with praise of Aquileia as a glorious and warlike city, chief city of the Venetians, until laid waste long ago by the savage Attila. The poem then recounts the city's evangelization through the apostle Mark and the martyr-bishop Hermagoras, before turning to the sins that provoked its destruction at the hands of the pagan Avars, the passing of the faith to the Venetians, and the heresy of the Lombard-era patriarch John, who divided the church as Jeroboam had divided Israel. It closes with God's delivery of Italy to the Franks, the deposition of the deceitful patriarch Maxentius under Louis and his son Lothar, and a prayer to the undivided Trinity for victory over the false Aquileians.
la.aristotle.economics_book_3: The third book of the Economics attributed to Aristotle sets out the reciprocal duties of wife and husband in the governance of a household. It opens by requiring a good wife to rule the interior of the house under written law, admitting no one without her husband's knowledge, keeping modest dress and expenditure, and leaving public and marital business to him. The argument then turns to the husband, who must instruct his wife gently rather than with servile fear, honour her above all others, keep faithful to her, and beget children from a worthy union as a farmer commits seed only to well-tilled ground, with Homer's Penelope, Odysseus, Agamemnon and Nausicaa episodes cited as instances of conjugal fidelity and its failures. The book closes by urging concord of will between husband and wife in prosperity and adversity alike, so that together they govern children, parents, friends and goods in common and reap an honourable old age.
la.augustine.commonitorium: A short Latin prose document attributed to Augustine and of late antique date, the Commonitorium sets out how converts from Manichaeism are to be received back into the catholic church. It opens by prescribing the steps whereby Manichaeans who confess their error must anathematise the heresy in a set form, submit a written confession, and obtain from a bishop a dated letter protecting them from further public or ecclesiastical penalty, while remaining catechumens or penitents until proved over time. The greater part of the work consists of a series of anathemas against specific Manichaean doctrines, including the two opposed principles, the captivity of the divine substance in plants and in humanity, the fabulous generation of Adam, the transfiguration of divine virtues into beautiful figures to liberate the vital substance through the sun and moon, the eternal globe of damnation, and the denial of the Mosaic law, of Christ's true flesh, and of the true Holy Spirit, with a final curse upon Manes himself. It closes with the prescribed form of the bishop's letter to converts and with rules confining former Manichaean elect to monasteries or hostels and restricting their movements until the sincerity of their conversion is evident.
la.augustine.contra_duas_epistulas_pelagian: A late-antique Latin prose treatise by Augustine, cast as a letter to Boniface, bishop of Rome, and written against two Pelagian epistles, one sent by Julian to Rome and another by eighteen bishops of like mind to Thessalonica. The work opens with an amicable dedication in which Augustine explains why he must answer writings that entice the unwary away from catholic teaching. The three books then take up the Pelagian positions point by point, defending the priority of grace to all human merit, affirming original sin washed away in baptism though human infirmity remains, and treating of the law, marriage, free will, and the impossibility of living without sin in this life. The final book supports the argument with extensive quotations from Cyprian and Ambrose, presented as witnesses that the doctrine defended is the faith handed down from antiquity rather than a novel opinion.
la.augustine.contra_fortunatum: The work is a stenographic record of a public disputation conducted by Augustine against Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter, in the baths of Sossius at Hippo before the people, its opening heading dating the occasion by the consulship of Arcadius and Rufinus. The debate centres on the nature of God and the origin of evil: Augustine argues that the Manichaean claim, that a divine substance or power sent against the race of darkness became mingled with the world and with souls, cannot be reconciled with a God who is incorruptible and inviolable, while Fortunatus maintains that the soul is of divine origin and sins under constraint of a contrary nature. In reply Augustine appeals to creation from nothing, the free choice of the first man, and the binding force of habit, supporting each step with citations from the apostle Paul. After a second day's session before the notary the disputation breaks off without agreement, Fortunatus deferring his answer until he has consulted his seniors, and the record closes with Augustine's thanksgiving.
la.augustine.de_divinatione_daemonum: De Divinatione Daemonum ('On the Divination of Demons') is a Latin prose theological treatise by Augustine of the late antique period, opening with a recollected conversation with Christian laymen during the octave of holy days concerning pagan pretensions to knowledge and a demon's foretelling of the overthrow of the temple of Serapis in Alexandria. The dialogue then works through successive objections, whether what almighty and just God permits can be evil, and why sacrifices once permitted are now suppressed, before taking up the central question of whence the divinations of demons arise. Augustine ascribes their forecasts to the keen sense, speed, and long experience of their aerial bodies: demons often predict what they themselves will bring about, read natural and bodily signs inaccessible to humans, and at times report what they have heard from angelic and prophetic oracles, yet such knowledge is not divine in itself, and the demons are often deceived and deceive. The treatise concludes by setting the prophesied destruction of temples and false gods, attested in Zephaniah and the Psalms and fulfilled through Christ, against the dwindling remnant of pagans who still mock the simplicity of the Christians.
la.augustine.de_duabus_animabus: A late-antique Latin theological treatise by Augustine, it opens with the author, delivered from Manichaean error and restored to the Catholic church, resolving to consider and deplore the doctrine he had once accepted that there are two kinds of souls, one of the very substance of God and the other of no relation to him. The argument then proceeds rationally to show that every soul, grasped by intellect rather than by bodily sense, surpasses visible light, so that even souls the Manichaeans call evil must, insofar as they live, come from the same creator as sun and moon. It goes on to define the will and sin, sin as the will to retain or pursue what justice forbids, to locate wrongdoing in the will alone, to explain the fluctuation of deliberation without positing two souls, and to argue that repentance for sin presupposes a single created nature capable of both good and evil. Gospel and apostolic sayings seemingly denying that sinners are 'of God' are reconciled with the affirmation that all things are from him, and the work ends with a prayer for friends still attached to the sect and with the defense of the Catholic scriptures against Manichaean accusation deferred to other volumes.
la.augustine.de_gestis_pelagii: Augustine's De gestis Pelagii is a Late Antique Latin theological treatise addressed to Bishop Aurelius, written after Pelagius had been pronounced catholic by the fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine. It opens with Augustine explaining that the arrival of the official acts of that examination has ended his hesitation and led him to comment more fully on the defense Pelagius had earlier sent him in a short note. The bulk of the work goes through the synodal record point by point, weighing each objection and Pelagius's reply, on the help given by knowledge of the law, on all men being ruled by their own will, on eternal punishment of sinners, on the kingdom of heaven promised in the Old Testament, and on the possibility of living without sin, and argues that the bishops acquitted the man while their verdict condemned the doctrines connected with him and Caelestius, above all the reduction of grace to human nature endowed with free will. The closing chapters recapitulate the anathematized propositions, cite letters of Timasius and Jacobus together with Augustine's own earlier letter to Pelagius, and examine a disputed letter attributed to Pelagius that treats the acquittal as a triumph, concluding that the heresy stands condemned even though Pelagius was absolved.
la.augustine.sermo_de_rusticiano_subdiacono: A short Latin sermon of Augustine, preserved among the writings against the Donatists, opens with the bishop standing before his congregation in tears, having three times tried and failed to preach through grief. The occasion is twofold: the community has lost a venerable pastor, and Rusticianus, a deacon of Mutigena, has neglected his charge, fallen into debt, incurred excommunication, and fled to the Donatists, by whose bishop Macrobius he was received, rebaptized, and ordained a deacon. Augustine recounts his interventions and reads aloud the letter he sent to Macrobius, so that the people may see how peaceably the matter was handled. The sermon then widens into an argument against rebaptism, defending the sanctity of the Catholic font against Donatist charges of defilement and closing with a plea for one baptism, one faith, and one profession of charity.
la.ausonius.cento_nuptialis: The Cento Nuptialis of Ausonius is a late-antique Latin wedding poem in hexameters, pieced together almost wholly from lines and half-lines of Virgil. It opens with a prose preface to Paulus defining the cento, apologising for the triviality of the undertaking, and attributing the commission to the emperor Valentinian. The poem then follows a wedding from the banquet and the bride's and groom's arrival through the gifts and songs of the guests to the wedding night, which is first wrapped in periphrasis and then set out in a closing sequence of patched verses of remarkable frankness. An epilogue, mingling verse and prose and appealing to Juvenal, Martial, Pliny, and other classical writers, pleads that the wanton page accompanies a chaste life, sets a limit to reading, and leaves the remainder to the curious.
la.cicero.de_lege_agraria_contra_rullum: De Lege Agraria contra Rullum is a series of prose speeches delivered to the Roman people by Cicero, as consul in the Roman Republic, against the agrarian bill of the tribune P. Servilius Rullus. The opening imagines the bill's young colonists occupying Capua and holding other towns with garrisons and fortifications. The argument then follows the proposed law clause by clause, attacking the sweeping powers it gives the land commissioners (xviri) to sell public lands, revenues, and the spoils of commanders across Italy and the provinces, and dwelling on its intrusion into the eastern conquests of Cn. Pompeius in the war against Mithridates. The closing sections take up the law's dealings with Sulla's land assignments, rebutting the charge that Cicero protects Sulla's beneficiaries, and end with a defiant appeal to the people to stand by a consul who claims to have secured their peace and possessions.
la.cicero.de_partitione_oratoria: A Latin prose treatise on rhetoric composed during the Roman Republic, De Partitione Oratoria is cast as a dialogue that opens with the younger Cicero asking his father to set out in Latin the doctrine of speaking he had previously received from him in Greek. The exchange then proceeds in strict question-and-answer form through the whole of rhetorical theory, dividing the art into the power of the orator, the speech, and the question, and covering the discovery and arrangement of arguments from their loci, style and word choice, delivery, and memory. The work goes on to expound the four parts of the oration, introduction, narration, confirmation, and peroration, together with amplification, before turning to the kinds of questions and causes, distinguishing praise and blame, deliberation, and judicial pleading. Its closing portions treat the statuses of conjecture, definition, and quality, disputes over written documents and ambiguous wording, and the grounding of oratory in Academic dialectic, ending with the father's exhortation to his son to pursue these studies further.
la.cicero.divinatio_in_c_verrem: The Divinatio in C. Verrem is a forensic speech in Latin prose by Cicero, delivered as an accusation in the Roman courts of the late Republic. It opens with Cicero claiming that the trial of the corrupt ex-governor Gaius Verres offers the senatorial judges a heaven-sent chance to restore the reputation of their order, and with warnings against the bribery and delay tactics he alleges Verres is attempting. The bulk of the speech surveys Verres' career in order: his quaestorship under Carbo, his legateship in Asia under Dolabella, and above all his three-year praetorship in Sicily, against which Cicero marshals charges of extortionate grain levies, theft of temple treasures and artworks, the bribery surrounding a fleet commanded by Cleomenes, and the flogging, imprisonment and crucifixion of Roman citizens. The oration closes with a defence of the Roman franchise that Gavius died invoking, and a prayer that the gods violated by Verres' sacrilege will favour the verdict.
la.cicero.in_l_pisonem: In L. Pisonem is a prose invective of the Roman Republic, delivered in the senate by Cicero against Lucius Calpurnius Piso, his political enemy and a former consul. The speech opens with an apostrophe to the immortal gods for granting the speaker the spectacle of the 'monster of the city' before the house. From there it ranges over Piso's lowly Gallic origins and debased character, contrasts his discreditable consulship with Cicero's own preservation of the state from the Catilinarian conspiracy, holds him responsible together with his colleague Gabinius for Cicero's exile and the humiliation of the senate, and ridicules his Epicurean doctrines, drunken revels, and obscure return from the province of Macedonia. It closes with a full indictment of his provincial misgovernment and Cicero's declaration that he seeks Piso's disgrace and self-condemnation rather than his blood.
la.cicero.philippicae: The Philippicae is a collection of fourteen prose speeches that Cicero delivered in the Senate and before the Roman people during the late-Republican crisis that followed Caesar's assassination, directed against Marcus Antonius. The first oration opens with Cicero explaining to the senators his recent departure from and return to Italy, praising Antony's early conduct after Caesar's death before warning against his laws and acts. The speeches grow steadily harsher: a long published invective surveys Antony's whole career and consulship, later orations press the Senate to declare him a public enemy, to reject embassy and any negotiated peace, and to honor Decimus Brutus, the young Caesar, Lepidus, and the legions defending Mutina. The final orations welcome news of victory over Antony, decree thanksgivings for the commanders, monuments and rewards for the fallen soldiers, and denounce Dolabella as a public enemy.
la.cicero.pro_q_roscio_comoedo: A prose forensic speech of the Roman Republic by Cicero, defending the comic actor Quintus Roscius against a claim by Gaius Fannius Chaerea arising from their partnership in the slave performer Panurgus. The speech opens amid an attack on the plaintiff's accounts, contrasting the official codex accepti et expensi, in which Roscius's name is absent, with his informal adversaria, and pressing Fannius to explain why so large a sum lay unrecorded for years. The argument then establishes that the money claimed was neither given, entered as paid, nor secured by stipulation, contrasts the all-or-nothing rigour of a judicium with the moderation of arbitrium, and turns Fannius's own earlier resort to arbitration into proof that the debt was fictitious. The later sections weigh the parties' characters against each other, argue that Panurgus's value lay chiefly in Roscius's training, defend Roscius's settlement with Quintus Flavius as made for his own share alone, and rest the case on Cluvius's testimony, reported on oath by the senators Manilius and Luscus.
la.curtius_rufus.historiae_alexandri_magni: Curtius Rufus's Historiae Alexandri Magni is an early Imperial Latin prose history narrating the campaigns of Alexander the Great. The work opens with Alexander's operations in Asia Minor, taking in the capture of Celaenae and the episode at Gordium, where he cuts the knot of the royal chariot. From there the history follows Alexander to his victories over Darius at Issus and Arbela, the sieges of Tyre and Gaza, the conquest of Egypt with its consultation of Ammon's oracle, the foundation of Alexandria, and the pursuit that ends with Darius's murder. The later portions carry the war through Bactria and Sogdiana amid purges of the king's own officers, then on to India and the hard-won victory over Porus at the Hydaspes, the army's mutinies, the expedition to the Ocean, Alexander's death at Babylon, and the succession struggles that close with the division of his empire among his generals.
la.cyprian.ad_demetrianum: Ad Demetrianum is a Late Antique prose treatise in Latin by Cyprian, written as an apology addressed to a pagan named Demetrianus. It opens with Cyprian explaining that he had long scorned to answer Demetrianus's railings against the one true God, but can no longer keep silent now that Christians are blamed for wars, famine, plague, and failing rains. The argument then proceeds that the world is undergoing the natural decline of old age, that such calamities were foretold in Scripture as signs of the approaching day of judgement, and that they fall upon humankind for its sins and neglect of God rather than for abandoning the old deities. Cyprian goes on to catalogue the moral corruptions of pagan society, protests the persecution of Christians, contrasts their patient endurance and hope with pagan despair, and closes with a warning of eternal punishment together with an appeal to Demetrianus to seek God's forgiveness, which remains open even at the end of life.
la.cyprian.sententiae_episcoporum: The Sententiae Episcoporum records the opinions given by the bishops who gathered at Carthage on 1 September, drawn from the province of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, together with presbyters, deacons, and a great part of the laity, to decide whether converts from heresy must be baptized on entering the church; it belongs to the controversy over heretical baptism in which Cyprian of Carthage figures as presider and correspondent. It opens with the reading of Cyprian's correspondence with his colleague Jubaianus on the unlawful baptism of heretics, followed by Cyprian's own address to the assembled bishops. The greater part of the work is a sequence of short verdicts delivered one by one by the participants, who with near unanimity hold that there is only one true baptism, that of the church, that heretics and schismatics therefore cannot baptize, and that those coming over from them must be baptized, and where needful exorcized, before communion.
