The individual speeches range from terse rulings to extended scriptural argument for the nullity of rites performed outside the church and for the subordination of custom to truth, and a few opinions reach the council by proxy from absent bishops.
la.cyprian_pseudo.ad_flavium_felicem_de_res: Ad Flavium Felicem de Resurrectione Mortuorum is a Latin poem of the later Roman Empire, transmitted under the name of Cyprian and addressed to a Flavius Felix, setting out the case for the resurrection of the dead. It opens with the speaker laying aside his earlier rustic songs to take up loftier themes, beginning with creation, the true God, and the fall of Adam and Eve, through which death entered the world. The body of the work argues that God, who made all things from nothing, can likewise reassemble dissolved bodies, adducing seeds that spring up again, the daily return of light, and the phoenix, before depicting the last judgment: angels gather all humanity from their graves, the just are welcomed into an eternally flowering paradise rich in streams, gems, and fruit, while the wicked, their manifold crimes rehearsed, are driven into everlasting fire. A closing exhortation urges amendment of life and repentance while the day of grace yet endures.
la.dante.divina_comedia: A medieval Latin hexameter version of Dante's Divine Comedy, the epic recounting the poet's imagined journey through the realms of the Christian afterlife. It opens with the pilgrim astray in a dark wood at the midpoint of life, where Virgil appears to lead him down through the circles of Hell among its classes of damned souls. The second book follows their toilsome ascent of Mount Purgatory, whose terraces purge souls of the seven deadly sins, and closes as Virgil withdraws and Beatrice assumes the role of guide. The third book carries Dante upward through the celestial spheres of Paradise under Beatrice's direction, culminating in a final vision of divine light and love.
la.dracontius.satisfactio: The Satisfactio is a Late Antique Latin poem by Dracontius, cast as a penitential apology in which a captive poet begs pardon from an offended ruler. It opens with a hymnic invocation of God as maker and governor of all things, whose anger and favour direct human affairs, before the poet confesses that his fault was to write in praise of another lord while keeping silent about his own. The greater part of the work sustains the plea with examples drawn from Scripture, Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, David, Solomon and the martyr Stephen, and from Roman rulers such as Caesar, Augustus, Titus and Commodus, arguing that clemency is godlike, that guilt is universal, and that punishment should correct rather than destroy. Meditations on the mixture of good and evil in creation and on the ordered passage of time lead to the closing petition for the captives' lives and the poet's restoration, sealed with the image of a horse checked by the spur rather than maimed.
la.ennodius.epistulae: Epistulae is a collection of prose letters by Ennodius, a Latin author of the late antique period. The collection opens with an ornate literary epistle in which the writer praises the eloquence of a young friend, comparing his speech to the restless sea. The remaining letters, addressed to aristocrats, clerics, women, and friends in Italy and beyond, form a body of highly rhetorical epistolary prose: many pieces chide a correspondent's silence and exhort him to renewed exchange, while others carry recommendations and petitions for patronage, console the bereaved, report the writer's illnesses and recoveries, and conduct ecclesiastical and secular business, with occasional verse insertions such as an epitaph and a poem on the hot springs of Aponus.
la.eobanus.iliad: Eobanus, Iliad (20265 lines, 24 book files). A Latin verse rendering of the Iliad in twenty-four books, by the Renaissance German humanist Eobanus Hessus (input gives only "Eobanus"), who brought the Homeric epic into neo-Latin hexameters for sixteenth-century readers. The poem opens with the invocation to the Muse and the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over Briseis, much expanded and glossed relative to Homer. Its course follows the whole Trojan war: the catalogue of ships, the duel of Paris and Menelaus, the embassy to Achilles, the death of Patroclus, Achilles' return to battle and slaughter around the Scamander, the funeral games for Patroclus, Priam's ransom of Hector's body, and the burial and mourning that close the epic. Throughout, the adaptation regularly amplifies Homer's narrative with explicit speech, moralising, and versified commentary rather than offering a bare translation.
la.florus_of_lyon.carminum_appendix: A brief appendix of Latin poems associated with Florus of Lyon, a poet and scholar of the Carolingian period. It opens with a summons to rejoice on a day brightened by light, and then dwells on the sweet songs a dear friend has sent, praising a faithful love that outdoes hills, valleys, rivers, and winds. The speaker prays that this implanted love endure untouched by wealth or glory, calls it a treasure stored in heaven beyond the reach of thief, rust, and moth, and closes by begging the friend to accept the verses and keep sending his own in return. The appendix ends with short fragmentary pieces, among them lines on a festival day for Florus and a broken invocation of Christ as witness.
la.glass.washingtonii_vita: Washingtonii Vita is a prose Latin life of George Washington by Francis Glass, an Ohio schoolmaster who composed it for school use in 1824 and died before its publication in 1842. It opens with a lengthy English preface by the editor recounting how he found Glass teaching the classics in a log schoolhouse near Lebanon, Ohio, and arranged for the manuscript to be completed and printed. The Latin narrative then traces Washington from his Virginia birth in 1732 and years as a surveyor through his embassy to the French, Braddock's defeat, and the Revolution, from Lexington and Bunker Hill to Trenton, Princeton, and the surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown in 1781. It closes with Washington's resignation of his commission, his presidency and its diplomatic difficulties, his death in 1799, sketches of other commanders of the Revolutionary era, and an appendix on the proper method of teaching the ancient languages.
la.hilary_of_poitiers.liber_ad_constantium_: The Liber ad Constantium Imperatorem is a late-antique Latin prose treatise of theology and self-defence by Hilary of Poitiers, addressed to the emperor Constantius. It opens with the author's protest that he, a bishop of the churches of Gaul, lies in exile through faction and the false reports of a synod rather than through any crime, with the emperor's own Caesar, Julian, as witness to his cause. The plea then widens into an attack on the creeds composed since the synod of Nicaea, whose successive novelties have made as many faiths as there are wills and undermined the baptismal confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and into a charge that Marcellus, Photinus, Sabellius, Montanus, Manichaeus, and Marcion all speak the scriptures without their sense. It ends by asking to be heard before the synod now disputing over the faith and by setting out a creed confessing one God the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, the image and word of God, born before eternal times and incarnate of the Virgin.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.ad_leonem_papa: A Latin work of uncertain date, transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers and addressed to Pope Leo, retelling the biblical history of creation and early humankind. It opens with a dedication to the pontiff, announcing a song of thanks to God the omnipotent father, the origin and source of all things. The narrative moves from primordial chaos through the days of creation, the separation of sky, land and waters, the sun, moon and constellations with their guidance for farmers and sailors, the springing up of plants and the birth of animals, to the making of man in the divine image, endowed with reason, speech, memory of the past and foreknowledge, and given dominion over the world. After the transgression of the forbidden tree brings mortality and a race increasingly given to war, perjury and fraud, the work recounts the flood that washes away the world's crime and the preservation of Noah, prefiguring the church and the coming baptism, and closes with the renewed people, boys unharmed among flames and lions, and kings and prophets praising God, while the remnants of the ancient poison await cleansing by better waters from a better teacher.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.de_martyrio_ma: A late Latin poem of uncertain date transmitted under the name of Hilary of Poitiers, recounting the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under Antiochus, king of Syria. It opens with Antiochus failing to win the mother over through promises of gold and treasure, and then turning to torments that leave her defiant. The greater part of the work is a sequence of martyrdoms in which each son, encouraged by a speech of his mother that invokes the patriarchs Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob and Esau, and God's wonders from the crossing of the Red Sea to the water struck from the rock, refuses the king's commands and dies unafraid in the flames. The poem closes with the ordeal of the youngest and only remaining boy, the mother's own collapse and death, and the reception of her and her sons among the saints.
la.hilary_of_poitiers_pseudo.epistula_ad_ab: A late antique Latin prose letter attributed to Hilary of Poitiers and addressed to his beloved daughter Abra, it opens with the writer excusing a long absence: he has journeyed far to seek a marvellous garment and pearl for her. The body recounts his quest in narrative form: after travelling many long and difficult roads he prostrates himself before a beautiful young man, weeping and praying until shown a garment finer than silk, snow or gold and a pearl whose beauty surpasses heaven, sea and earth. A bystander explains that the garment never wears out and that the pearl preserves its wearer from sickness, age and death, but the young man consents to grant both only to a daughter who renounces dyed, silken and gilded clothing and all other jewels. The father accordingly urges Abra to refuse such adornments, sends her morning and evening hymns to keep him in her memory, and promises to reveal the youth's identity and promises once she has written back.
la.hildebert_of_lavardin.de_operibus_sex_di: A medieval Latin poem by Hildebert of Lavardin, De Operibus Sex Dierum gives a running allegorical exposition of the six days of creation. It opens with the Almighty making heaven and earth in the beginning, then proceeds day by day, reading each work of the Genesis account as a figure of spiritual realities: the first light as the faith that follows baptism, the firmament as Scripture set between the waters of angels and men, dry land and sea as the just and the wicked, plants and trees as teachers, the sun and moon as Christ and the Church, the creatures of the fifth and sixth days as the motions of man's outer and inner life, and the making of humanity in the divine image as the gift of reason. The poem closes with the seventh day, explaining God's rest not as relief from weariness but as the cessation of new creation, and ends by contrasting divine bounty, which creates without need of the world's goods, with human labor undertaken for the sake of rest.
la.hrabanus.de_imagine_caesaris: A short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Hrabanus, De imagine Caesaris opens with a prayer to Christ, king of kings, who absolved the sins of humankind through the cross. The poem then turns to a ruler addressed as Caesar and Augustus, whose image, standing armed in faith, goes before the work: it depicts his God-granted dominion over the whole world, the homage and gifts of nations such as Greeks and Persians, and his role as protector of the flock under divine guardianship. It closes with the author offering his 'libellum', composed in both verse and prose, to the emperor, whose triumphant image precedes the book.
la.john_scotus_eriugena.carminum_appendix: The Carminum Appendix is a brief collection of Latin poems attributed to the Carolingian scholar John Scotus Eriugena. It opens with verses on the weaving of a sindon, a cloth wrought with gems and golden thread, whose image of Christ's body, face and hands and head and all its members, is promised to guard its beholder from blows, bonds, hunger, torments, wild beasts and the serpent's venom. The collection then turns to a lament on Rome, once built by noble patrons but now subjected to slaves and deserted by its kings, its name and honour passed to the Greeks, while Constantinople flourishes as the 'new Rome' and the ancient city declines in morals and walls alike. The final lines charge Rome with pride and avarice, with mutilating living saints and selling their dead limbs, and with trafficking in false relics while the voracious earth consumes the bones of the dead.
la.lactantius.fragmenta: Latin fragments and testimonia for Lactantius (L. Caelius Firmianus Lactantius), the late-antique Christian Latin writer whom Jerome's notice preserved here describes as teaching rhetoric at Nicomedia under Diocletian and later instructing Crispus in Latin letters. The collection opens with Jerome's quotation of the third book of Lactantius's letters to Probus, tracing the Galatians to the milk-white Gauls named by the Sibyl and Vergil. The remaining excerpts, drawn principally from Jerome and Rufinus, preserve remnants of the letters to Probus, Demetrianus and Severus, treating comic metre and the Holy Spirit, together with a fragment on the affections of the soul from an Ambrosian codex of ecclesiastical excerpts, a metrical remark reported by Victorinus, a Vergilian scholion citing Firmianus as a commentator, and a Greek preface to the Sibylline oracles that names Firmianus and quotes a Sibylline acrostic. Biographical and evaluative notices from Jerome, the chroniclers, Damasus, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Eucherius, Sidonius, Gennadius and papal decretals, covering his life, works, eloquence and doctrine, bring the collection to a close.
la.lucifer_bishop_of_cagliari.de_regibus_ap: A polemical theological treatise in Latin prose by Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, addressed to the emperor Constantius, whom the author reckons an apostate and an Arian. It opens with Lucifer announcing that he will recount the deeds of a few ancient kings comparable to Constantius in apostasy and cruelty, so as to refute the emperor's boast that his long possession of power proves his faith pleasing to God. The body of the work argues from a long series of biblical examples, including Gideon, Saul, Solomon, Jeroboam, Ahab and Manasseh, that rulers who fell into idolatry or heresy often reigned and prospered for many years before retribution came, so that survival on the throne is no evidence of divine approval. It closes with scriptural testimony on the prosperity of the wicked and pressing exhortations to Constantius to repent and return to the faith confessed at Nicaea.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.carmina_2: Carmina 2 is the second book of the collected poems of the late-antique poet Magnus Felix Ennodius, consisting largely of short epigrams on funerary, religious, encomiastic, and satirical themes. It opens with an epitaph lamenting a young man of good family cut off in his twentieth year, before the appointed order of death. Much of the book consists of verses on churches, their founders, and their ornament, above all the basilica of Saint Lawrence, alongside inscriptions for painters, goldsmiths, gardeners, and other donors, and praise of bishops and aristocrats such as Ambrose, Simplicianus, Senator, and Boethius. Satirical attacks on named enemies, including one against a man falsely calling himself Virgil, epigrams on animals, gifts, and vices, and occasional prose prefaces complete the collection.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.eucharisticum_de_v: The Eucharisticum de vita sua of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a Late Antique Latin prose work that sets an autobiographical account of the author's life in the form of a confession and thanksgiving to God. It opens with a meditation on weakness, illness, and contrition as the means by which divine power restores the sinner. The narrative then recounts the writer's youthful absorption in secular rhetoric and poetry, a grave fever that directed him toward the martyr Victor as intercessor and moved him to vow the renunciation of worldly writing, and later episodes of his life, including his orphaning at about sixteen during Theodoric's entry into Italy, an arranged marriage into a noble family, his pride and estrangement from God, and the ecclesiastical office through which he says he was corrected. The work closes with an appeal to Victor, praise of the author's wife's steadfast piety, and the doxology 'Gloria Patri et Filio et Spiritui Sancto'.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.praeceptum_quando_: A brief Latin prose decree, the Praeceptum of the late-antique writer Magnus Felix Ennodius, is cast as an instruction to all bishops issued with the authority of the apostolic see. It opens with a disquisition on the man who, schooled in divine discipline, has subdued carnal desire, arguing that detraction can no more extinguish the brightness of an innocent life than night can dim the stars. The argument then turns to the duty of pastors to cut away every occasion for scandal, prompted by a recent violent uprising against the bishop of the apostolic see and by the danger that the careless and solitary may fall under false accusation. The operative ruling forbids any bishop, priest, or lower cleric to dwell alone without a well-approved companion, commands that all their dealings be open rather than clandestine, prohibits them from keeping women in their households beyond those the canons allow, and threatens offenders with the loss of their honours while censuring those who give rise to suspicion as themselves at fault.
la.nepos.vitae: The Vitae is a Latin collection of prose biographies by Cornelius Nepos, a Roman writer of the Republican period, devoted to the lives of outstanding commanders and set out in brief, anecdotal form. An opening preface addressed to Atticus defends the author's attention to Greek customs that Romans might judge improper or humble, before announcing the design of writing on excellent generals. The ensuing lives cover the Greek commanders Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristides, Cimon, Lysander, Alcibiades, Thrasybulus, Conon, Dion, Iphicrates, Chabrias, Timotheus, Epaminondas, Pelopidas, Agesilaus, Eumenes, Phocion, and Timoleon, together with the Persian Datames. After a compact survey of Persian and Macedonian kings and the successors of Alexander, fuller lives of Hamilcar and Hannibal follow, and the work closes with the Romans M. Cato and T. Pomponius Atticus and the reflection that character shapes fortune.
la.orientius_saint.carmina: The Carmina of Saint Orientius is a small late-antique collection of Latin Christian poems. It opens with a brief piece on the Nativity of the Lord, presenting the day of Christ's birth as outshining every other day of the year. There follows a catalogue of the Saviour's names and titles, door, lion, word, shepherd, cornerstone and many others, which the greater part of the work elaborates in a long poem on the Trinity that moves through Christ's divinity, his passion and the triumph of the cross, including a symbolic reading of the Greek letters of the crucifix, and then in a verse-by-verse explanation of each epithet in turn. The collection closes with a laudatio that passes into direct prayer, as the poet calls himself unworthy and begs Christ for mercy on himself and his own.
la.orientius_saint.commonitorium: The Commonitorium is a Late Antique Christian didactic poem attributed to Orientius, written as moral instruction for whoever would win eternal life. It opens by inviting the reader who desires the rewards of heaven to learn the way, with a prayer to Christ for the eloquence to teach it. The first book expounds the two lives granted to humankind, the love of God and neighbour, and warns at length against lust, envy, and avarice, drawing examples from biblical history; the second turns to vainglory, restraint in speech, gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly ambition, meditates on the brevity of life and the approach of death, and closes with a vivid account of the Last Judgement, the punishments of the wicked and the blessedness of the righteous, followed by a plea that the reader remember the author in prayer.
la.paschasius_radbertus.epitaphium_arsenii: A Carolingian prose dialogue by Paschasius Radbertus, the work opens with the speakers Adeodatus, Paschasius, and Theophrastus resolving, after long distraction and toil, to complete the epitaph of their deceased 'Father' Arsenius, which they had begun to set down in writing years before. The conversation then unfolds as a sustained lament and defence, rehearsing Arsenius's fearless remonstrances before the emperor, bishops, and senators against the corruption of ecclesiastical order and the seizure of church property, his denunciation of the adulterous tyranny that endangered Augustus and his sons, and his share in the council by which that danger was averted. It follows him through a series of exiles, a lofty cavern by the Pennine Alps, the remote island of Herium in the Ocean, a monastery in Germany, and back to his own community, and then on a hazardous journey, undertaken at papal command amid warring factions, to assist the pontiff in reconciling father and sons. After the failure of that mediation and further alternations of power, he withdraws to the monastery of St. Columbanus in Italy, which he governs until his death, and the dialogue closes with his burial beside that saint, meditations on the good of death, and the report carried to Queen Ermengard that nuns at Brescia had heard angelic choirs bearing his soul to heaven.
la.paulinus_petricordiae.de_vita_sancti_mar: The De Vita Sancti Martini of Paulinus of Périgueux (Petricordiae) is a late-antique Latin epic in six books recounting the life, miracles, and afterlife of Martin of Tours. It opens with a prose epistle in which the poet, replying to the bishop who commissioned the work, excuses the presumption of versifying an account of the saint's merits and pledges obedience to the task. The verse narrative then traces Martin from his Pannonian birth and unwilling military service, through his conversion, the famous division of the cloak, his association with Hilary of Poitiers and his life as hermit and monk, to his episcopate at Tours, his confrontations with pagan cult, demons, and emperors, and his many miracles of healing, exorcism, and rescue, closing with the wonders worked at his tomb, from which the city of Tours rejoices in its bishop for ever.
la.paulus_orosius.commonitorium_de_errore_p: A brief Latin prose memorandum of theology, the Commonitorium de errore Priscillianistarum et Origenistarum is addressed by Paulus Orosius to a revered bishop, opening with an apology for the writer's boldness in offering a catalogue of heresies and a plea that their malign 'plantings' be uprooted and sound seed sown instead. The body of the work sets out the doctrines Orosius attributes to Priscillian, the descent of souls through circles and their imprisonment in bodies under a 'chirograph' annulled by Christ, the correspondence of patriarchs and zodiac signs with parts of the body, and a singular teaching on the Trinity, citing Priscillian's own letter and a book called 'Memoria apostolorum' in support. It then reports, on the authority of two fellow citizens named Avitus and of the Greek Basil, doctrines he links to Origen, including the eternal existence of creation in God's wisdom, a single substance shared by angels, souls and demons, a purgatorial and non-literal eternal fire, and a successive, ever-thinning assumption of Christ's body. The memorandum closes with Orosius's assurance that he has recorded only what he could retain and with a petition that the addressee hasten to apply the remedy to the plague of error.
la.petrus_of_pisa.carmina: A short collection of medieval Latin verses attributed to Petrus of Pisa, a poet of the Carolingian court. The opening lines form a hymn to Christ as creator and redeemer, born before the ages, who conquered hell and led the lost to paradise. The remainder addresses a Paul described as the most learned of poets and teachers, praising his command of Greek, Latin and Hebrew letters and thanking him for instruction in grammar; later pieces exchange verses with him, set him three riddling questions to be answered by letter, and recount a dawn vision in which a beautiful youth propounds a riddle about what a father gives the son, alongside gnomic maxims on restraint of tongue and peace between brothers. The sequence closes with a prayer that God preserve Charlemagne, whose prosperous sceptre the poems celebrate and whose daughter's journey overseas to a kingdom they record.
la.plautus.asinaria: The Asinaria is a Latin comedy by Plautus of the Roman Republic, written in dramatic verse. Its prologue announces the Greek model, the Onagos of Demophilus, rendered into Latin by 'Maccus', and gives the work its title, 'the comedy of asses', before the dialogue opens between the old man Demaenetus and his slave Libanus. The plot follows Demaenetus' effort to help his lovesick son Argyrippus secure the courtesan Philaenium from her pimp, as he and the slaves Libanus and Leonida raise the necessary money while concealing the scheme from Demaenetus' harsh wife.
la.plautus.mostellaria: The Mostellaria, a Latin comedy of the Roman Republic by Plautus, opens with the slave Tranio driving the rustic Grumio from the kitchen while his young master's household carouses. Philolaches, during the three-year absence of his father Theopropides abroad, has squandered the estate on a freed mistress, feasting, and a neighbouring house bought with borrowed money. On the father's unexpected return, Tranio fends him off with a fiction that the house is haunted by the ghost of a murdered guest, and sustains the deception through further trickery involving a moneylender and the neighbour Simo until the truth comes out. Cornered, Tranio takes sanctuary at an altar, and the intercession of Philolaches' friend Callidamates wins Philolaches reconciliation with his father, who at last pardons the slave.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_montibus_sina_et_sion_: A pseudonymous Latin treatise on the two mountains Sinai and Sion, written against the Jews and transmitted under Cyprian's name, of later imperial date. It opens with a probatio capitulorum declaring that what was written figuratively in the Old Testament must be understood spiritually in the New, through its fulfilment in Christ. The main argument, carried forward in prose through paraphrase and quotation of scripture, opposes the earthly Sinai, whence the law was given to the carnal people of the Jews, to the heavenly Sion, which the author identifies with the wood of the cross, whence the law went forth to the Christians; along the way it offers etymologies of Hebrew names from Adam to Moses, reads Rebecca's twins as synagogue and church, interprets the two thieves as the two peoples, and expounds the Passion, Pilate's trilingual titulus, and the heavenly Jerusalem. A closing figurative comparison likens Christ, crucified on high, to a boy set on a scaffold in a vineyard with a mirror of reeds, guarding God's vine, the Christian people, against the marauding devil.
la.pseudo_cyprian.de_pascha_computus: A short Latin prose treatise on the reckoning of Easter, transmitted among the works attributed to Cyprian and belonging to the later imperial period. It opens with the author describing his anxious search of the divine scriptures to discover the first day of the new month in which the Israelites in Egypt were commanded to immolate the Passover on the fourteenth moon. The argument proceeds from the separation of light and darkness in Genesis and the institutions of Exodus to establish the true first day of the month, sets out a pinax or table in which a sixteen-year cycle, extended through seven sedecennitates to 112 years, fixes the dates of the fourteenth moon and of the Jewish and Christian Easters, and reckons the years from the Exodus to Christ through the judges and kings, the seventy years of captivity, the rebuilding of the temple in the mystic number of Adam, and the seventy weeks of Daniel, expounded of the restoration, the reign of Antichrist and the ministry of Enoch and Elijah. Numerological arguments on Abraham's servants, the sign of the cross and the courses of sun and moon culminate in fixed dates for Christ's birth, baptism, passion and resurrection, and the whole reckoning, carried down to the fifth year of the emperor Gordian, closes with thanksgiving to God for the mysteries revealed.
la.pseudo_victor_vitensis.notitia_provincia: The Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae, a Late Antique Latin work preserved under the name of Victor of Vitensis, opens by announcing the names of the catholic bishops of the African provinces who came to Carthage by royal command in the sixth year of the Vandal king Huneric to render an account of their faith. The body of the work lists these bishops see by see, province by province, Proconsular Africa, Mauretania Caesariensis, Mauretania Sitifensis and Tripolitana, followed by the bishops living in exile on Sardinia, with head-counts appended to each roll, together with a note of sees left without bishops. A concluding tally sums the whole episcopate and distinguishes those who perished, those relegated to Corsica, those who remained in their sees, and those who fled.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae: The Epistulae of Salvian of Marseilles are a small collection of late-antique Latin prose letters that opens with a meditation on love, at once good and evil, sweet and harsh, which leads into an appeal on behalf of a young kinsman taken captive at Agrippina and commended to the charity and material aid of the addressees. The remaining letters are largely short notes of recommendation, apology and courtesy addressed to clerical and lay correspondents, among them the bishops Eucherius and Agroecius, the correspondent Ursicinus, his kinsfolk Hypatius and Quieta together with Palladia and Auspiciola, his sister Cattura, Limenius, Apro and Verus, and Salonius; their subjects include breaches of epistolary etiquette, the spiritual profit of bodily sickness, the proper humility in exchanging letters with superiors, and thanks for books received. The collection closes with a long letter to Salonius defending the libelli addressed 'to the church' that bear Timothy's name, explaining why their author wrote for the whole church, concealed his own name out of humility, chose Timothy's as expressing the honour of God, and thereby escaped the suspicion of apocrypha.
la.sedulius_scotus.carminum_appendix: A short Carolingian Latin poem attributed to Sedulius Scotus, opening with lines on the two laws that war within a person, the bad law ruling the body and the good law resisting in the citadel of the mind. The poem then unfolds as a dream vision: on a dark night a radiant maiden of towering stature appears to the weary poet and names herself Wisdom, Sophia among the Greeks and sapientia among the Latins. She bids the dreamer go to the house of Guntarius, whose praises she recites at length: a venerable bishop, gentle, humble and generous, chosen shepherd of his flock, who mortifies the flesh, delights in the study of wisdom, in the pages of scripture and in songs to God, and provides for the poor, the blind and the lame, a man of noble Frankish descent. Near the close the vision recalls the twin laws of human nature with which the poem began, and the verse breaks off in the midst of the bishop's encomium.
la.seneca.de_brevitate_vitae: A philosophical prose treatise of the early imperial period by Seneca, addressed to Paulinus, arguing that life is long enough for anyone who spends it well and short only for the 'occupied.' It opens with the common complaint that nature grants too brief a span and immediately rebuts it with the claim that people are prodigal, not poor, in time. The argument proceeds through portraits of wasted lives, Augustus craving leisure amid power, Cicero calling himself 'semifree,' busy officials, devotees of luxury and grooming, antiquarian pedants, and turns to praise of the sage, who by communing with past thinkers possesses all the ages. It closes with a direct exhortation to Paulinus to withdraw from administering the public grain supply to higher study, illustrated by the elderly S. Turannius, who feigned death rather than give up his duties.
la.seneca.de_otio: De Otio is a Latin prose treatise on leisure by the philosopher Seneca, of the early imperial period, transmitted in incomplete form and opening mid-sentence with a defense of withdrawal from public affairs as a path to moral consistency and release from the sway of popular judgment. The argument then asks whether the sage may rightly retire, contrasting the Stoic position that the wise man engages in public life unless prevented with Epicurean withdrawal chosen on principle, and concludes that both sects lead to leisure by different roads. The treatise distinguishes the greater commonwealth that embraces gods and humans from the particular city of one's birth, whose corruption may justify retreat, and holds that one serves humanity in leisure by investigating virtue, God, and the cosmos, since nature made humans for both action and contemplation. Closing passages argue that contemplation benefits posterity, adducing Zeno, Chrysippus, and Cleanthes as men whose teaching and writings served all humankind more than armies, offices, or laws.
la.severus_sulpicius.epistulae_tres: The three epistles of Sulpicius Severus, a Christian writer of Late Antiquity, are addressed to the venerable Bassula and centre throughout on Martin, bishop of Tours. The collection opens with a reply to a detractor who mocked Martin for nearly perishing in a house fire, in which Sulpicius retells the episode in full and compares the bishop's trial with the Apostle Paul's shipwreck and serpent. The second letter recounts Martin's foreknowledge of his end, his last days during a visitation, his death, and his solemn funeral procession, attended by monks and crowds. The third records the author's grief after Martin's passing and the dream vision in which the saint appears to console him with promises of his continuing presence.
la.sulpicius_severus.dialogi: The Dialogi of Sulpicius Severus is a Late Antique Latin prose work in dialogue form, cast as conversations among the author, his friend Postumianus, and Gallus, a disciple of Martin of Tours. It opens with Postumianus's return from three years in the East and the joyful reunion of the three friends at a secluded retreat. The dialogue then unfolds as a pair of reports: Postumianus narrates his journey through Carthage, Alexandria, Bethlehem, and the Egyptian desert, including the Origenist controversy, a stay with Jerome, and many miracles performed by monks, hermits, and even animals, while Gallus answers with an extended account of the virtues and miracles of Martin of Tours, his clashes with imperial officials and doubting clergy, and his prophecies of the end times, presenting Martin as a match for the ascetics of the East. The work closes with Postumianus charged to carry Martin's fame to Paulinus and the churches of the East and to visit the grave of the dead Pomponius, after which the friends part in tears.
la.terence.hecyra: The Hecyra (The Mother-in-Law) is a Latin comedy in dramatic metre by Terence, a playwright of the Roman Republic. It opens with a prologue in the poet's own person, which recalls how the play twice lost its audience to rope-dancers and gladiators and pleads for a quiet hearing now that the stage is free. The plot follows Pamphilus, married to Philumena while still devoted to the courtesan Bacchis, who leaves for Imbros soon after the wedding; his wife withdraws to her mother's house claiming illness, while in fact concealing a pregnancy begun before her marriage. Quarrels between the two mothers-in-law, Sostrata and Myrrhina, embroil both households until a ring torn from Philumena by her assailant in the dark is identified as one once given by Pamphilus, proving him father of her child; in an unusual turn it is Bacchis who brings reconciliation, swearing an oath that she has kept apart from Pamphilus since his marriage, and the families are reunited around the newborn son.
la.tertullian.ad_nationes_libri_duo: Ad Nationes is a two-book Latin apologetic treatise in prose by the late-antique theologian Tertullian, addressed to the pagan nations and written in defence of Christianity. It opens by arguing that the hatred aimed at Christians springs from their accusers' own ignorance, since those who come to know the name cease to hate it and often embrace it. The first book replies to the stock charges of infanticide, incest, and ritual crime by turning each accusation back on Greek and Roman practice, and defends the steadfastness of Christians under torture as grounded in their hope of resurrection and judgment. The second book attacks pagan religion directly, arguing that the gods were only men deified after death, exposing the contradictions of philosophical, poetic, and civic theology, ridiculing the Roman apparatus of cult from Saturn and Jupiter down to the tutelary spirits of childbirth and everyday life, and denying that the empire's dominion was a reward for piety.
la.tertullian.adversus_praxean: A Latin theological polemic of late antiquity by Tertullian, the Adversus Praxean refutes the view that the Father himself was born of the virgin and suffered on the cross, defending instead one divine monarchy ordered through a threefold economy of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It opens with an account of the devil's counterfeit of truth and a denunciation of Praxeas as the man who expelled the new prophecy at Rome and so 'crucified the Father'. The argument then sets out the rule of faith and establishes the Word (sermo) as a second person of one substance with the Father by analogies of root and shoot, source and stream, and sun and ray, before reviewing Genesis, the Psalms, the prophets, the Gospel of John above all, and the apostolic letters for evidence that Father and Son are distinct yet inseparable. Closing chapters treat the appearances of God under the patriarchs and in the Gospel, the divine and human substances conjoined in Christ, the sense of the name Christ, the suffering of the flesh rather than of the divinity, and the Spirit as the third name and grade of divinity, which together mark the difference between Christian confession and Jewish monotheism.
la.tertullian.apologeticum: The Apologeticum is a Latin prose apology for Christianity by Tertullian, addressed to the magistrates of the Roman empire. It opens with a plea that Christians be granted a fair hearing instead of being condemned on the bare confession of their name. The work then argues the whole case at length: it exposes the injustice of punishing without inquiry, refutes the charges of infanticide, incest, impiety, and disloyalty to the emperor, contends that the pagan gods were mortal men or deceiving demons, defends the antiquity and truth of the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, describes Christian worship, charity, and communal life, and ends with an account of resurrection and judgement and of the steadfastness of martyrs, whose blood Tertullian famously calls the seed of Christians.
la.tertullian.de_baptismo: De Baptismo is a Latin prose treatise on the sacrament of baptism by Tertullian, composed in Late Antiquity. It opens by celebrating the 'happy sacrament' of water and denouncing a recent heretical teacher who had been drawing followers away by undermining the rite. The argument then establishes the dignity of water from creation, the flood, and the crossing of the Red Sea, defends baptism's necessity against those who would rest salvation on faith alone, and takes up John's baptism, the questions whether Christ and the apostles were baptized, the single administration of the sacrament, and the 'second' baptism of blood through martyrdom. The latter part turns to discipline and practice: who may administer baptism, the advisability of delaying it for the young and the unmarried, the proper days for the rite, and preparation through prayer and fasting, ending with an appeal for prayer on the author's own behalf.
la.tertullian.de_oratione: De Oratione is a late-antique Latin theological treatise in prose by Tertullian, devoted to the form and discipline of Christian prayer. It opens by presenting the prayer taught by Christ as a new form suited to the new covenant, grounded in the Word, Spirit, and Reason of God and comprising in brief the whole gospel. The work then expounds the petitions of the Lord's Prayer one by one, the hallowing of the divine name, the coming of the kingdom, daily bread, the remission of debts, and deliverance from temptation, before taking up accessory questions of observance: reconciliation and purity before prayer, posture and dress at worship, the kiss of peace on fast days, the stations, the veiling of virgins, kneeling on the day of resurrection, fixed hours of prayer, and the singing of psalms. A closing encomium celebrates the power of Christian prayer as a spiritual sacrifice that prevails with God.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_iona_propheta: A later-imperial Latin theological work of uncertain authorship, transmitted under Tertullian's name. It opens with the living deaths of Sodom and Gomorrah and the question of how sinful Nineveh might escape a like punishment, before God commands Jonah to preach the city's destruction. The narrative follows Jonah's flight by ship from Joppa toward Tarsos, the storm God raises in pursuit, the sailors' jettisoned cargo and prayers to their gods, Jonah's confession of his guilt, and his casting into the sea at his own urging, where a great sea creature swallows him alive. The account ends with the storm subsiding, the sailors sacrificing in gratitude, and Jonah kept untouched by the waters within the creature's belly as a sign of the Lord and the glory of heaven.
la.tibullus.elegies: The Latin elegiac corpus transmitted under the name of Tibullus belongs to the Augustan age and comprises three books of erotic and occasional elegies. Book 1 opens with a prayer to the Lares contrasting rural poverty with wealth, then follows the poet's devotion to Delia, his servitude to the boy Marathus, and celebrations of his patron Messalla, including a song for the Egyptian festival of Osiris. Book 2 introduces Nemesis as a new and grasping mistress and adds festival hymns, a birthday poem for Cornutus, and verses on Messalla's son Messalinus and the omens of his day. The third book, the work of several hands besides Tibullus, contains six elegies under the name Lygdamus on his beloved Neaera, an anonymous hexameter panegyric of Messalla, a cycle concerning Sulpicia and her lover Cerinthus, six short elegies in Sulpicia's own voice, and a closing epitaph for Tibullus that pairs his death with Virgil's in the fields of Elysium.
la.vergil_pseudo.copa: The Copa is a brief Latin lyric poem of the Augustan period, handed down among the poems attributed to Vergil, though its authorship is disputed and it is conventionally classed as the work of a pseudo-Vergilian imitator. It opens with the figure of the Syrian barmaid, her head bound in a Greek headband, swaying her trained flanks to the castanets as she dances drunkenly in a smoky tavern. The rest of the poem is cast largely as her invitation to the weary traveller, cataloguing the inn's pleasures: rough wine and running water, roses, violets and lilies, cheese, plums, chestnuts and apples, the shade of the arbour, the sound of the shepherd's pipe and the cicadas. The closing lines press the invitation with an admonition to drink and crown the head now rather than hoard garlands for ungrateful ashes, since death itself whispers 'live, for I am coming'.
la.vergil_pseudo.culex: The Culex is a short Latin epic in hexameters attributed to Virgil and of Augustan date. It opens with a playful dedication to the young Octavius, acknowledging that the poem has been composed in a lighter strain than warfare and giants demand and promising a graver Muse hereafter. The narrative relates how a shepherd sleeping at noon among his grazing goats is roused by the sting of a gnat just as a huge serpent is about to seize him, and how he kills the serpent while unwittingly crushing his tiny rescuer. In a dream the gnat's ghost appears, bewails its death, and rehearses the lower world at length, with punished giants and mythological transgressors, the tale of Orpheus and Eurydice, the heroes of Troy, and the noble dead of Roman history, before departing; the shepherd then raises a burial mound, plants it with flowers, and sets an epitaph in the gnat's honor.
la.vergil_pseudo.lydia: Lydia is a short Latin lyric poem of the Augustan age, preserved under Vergil's name but of uncertain authorship. It opens with the speaker's envy of the meadows in which his beloved Lydia now plays, speaks, and sings the songs she once sang to him. The remainder is a lover's complaint: he wastes away in separation from her, congratulates the bull and the he-goat whose mates stay with them, and upbraids Nature, the moon, and Phoebus for denying him such companionship, citing the liaisons of Jupiter in the form of a bull, of Mars and Venus, and of Aurora as proof that gods and heroes loved freely in a kinder age. The poem closes with the lament that, born too late into a harsher world, he has been so ravaged by fate that his condition can scarcely be recognized.
la.victor_claudius_marius.alethia: The Alethia is a late antique Latin epic by Claudius Marius Victor, a versified retelling of Genesis in three books. It opens with an invocation to the triune God as the source of all being and goodness and a prayer for aid in setting before young souls the true origin of the world from the scrolls of Moses. The first book narrates the six days of creation, the formation of Adam and Eve, life in Paradise, and the temptation, Fall, and judgment of the first parents; the second follows their expulsion into a barren earth, their prayers for relief, the discovery of metals and the arts, Cain's murder of Abel, the spread of violence among the giants, and Noah's ark and the flood. The third book takes up Noah's sacrifice and covenant, the curse of Ham, the origins of idolatry, magic, and divination, the tower of Babel and the confusion of tongues, the call and wanderings of Abraham, his meeting with Melchisedech after the war of the kings, and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, down to Lot's wife and the salt lake left where the cities stood.
la.victor_claudius_marius.commentariorum_in: The Commentariorum in Genesim Libri Tres is a late antique Latin epic in three books retelling the early narrative of Genesis, attributed in its headings to Claudius Marius Victor, an orator of Massilia (Marseille). It opens with a prefatory prayer to God that praises the Trinity and invokes divine aid to set forth, from the writings of Moses, the origin of the world and the mysteries of eternal life. Book 1 narrates the six days of creation, the fashioning of Adam and Eve, the delights of paradise and its four rivers, and the fall and expulsion of the first parents; Book 2 follows their life after Eden through Cain's murder of Abel, the spread of wickedness, and Noah's ark amid the flood; Book 3 treats Noah's covenant and curse of Ham, the tower of Babel and confusion of tongues, and closes with Abraham's call, journeys, covenant, circumcision, and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.
la.victorinus.de_machabeis: The De Machabeis is a Latin poem of the Later Imperial period, attributed to Victorinus, which retells the martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother under the Syrian king Antiochus. It opens with Antiochus seeking by promises and then by torments to make a mother of holy lineage and her seven sons abandon the law of their people. The sons are put to death one by one in fire, each strengthened by the mother's exhortations, which recall creation, the patriarchs from Abraham through Jacob, and God's delivery of Israel from Egypt under Moses, while the king's fury and the hesitation of his ministers punctuate the sequence. After the youngest boy casts himself into the flames, the exhausted mother collapses and dies, her soul received with her sons among the saints.
la.walafrid_strabo.vita_sancti_galli_confes: A Latin verse life of the Irish missionary saint Gall, composed by the Carolingian author Walafrid Strabo. Its prologue, addressed to Gozbert, announces fulfilment of an old promise to recast the deeds of Gall, earlier written in prose, in metrical form. The poem recounts Gall's journey from Ireland as a companion of Columbanus, the mission to the Alamanni and their expulsion through the hostility of Brunihild and the king, and the stay at Arbona on Lake Constance, where illness keeps Gall behind when Columbanus departs for Italy, followed by his solitary life of asceticism, exorcisms, and miracles in the wilderness. Its later portions tell of the healing and consecration to virginity of Gunzo's daughter, Gall's refusal of the see of Constance and of the abbacy of Luxeuil, the building of his church, his death in old age, and the posthumous miracles at his burial, including the bier that only untamed horses could move and the discovery of his hair shirt and bloodstained chain.
la.wandalbert.de_mensium_nominibus: De Mensium Nominibus is a Latin didactic poem of the Carolingian period by Wandalbert on the origins of the names of the twelve months. Its opening lines announce an account of how the month names arose, which zodiac signs attend the twelve divisions of the year, and what the succession of the months brings to land and livelihood. The poem then passes month by month from January to December, deriving each name from Roman gods, kings, and emperors, assigning its zodiac sign, and describing the occupations of the season, from ploughing, sowing, and the pruning of vines to harvest, the vintage, hunting, fishing, and the fattening and slaughter of swine, together with the changing weather and the turnings of the solar year. The closing lines observe that Gallic lands preserve these customs and record the poet's statement that he wrote at a friend's urging while living on the banks of the Rhine, beneath the walls of old Cologne.
la.alcuin.carmina_rhytmica: A Carolingian Latin collection of rhythmical verse attributed to Alcuin, the work opens with a hymn to God the creator and proceeds through an alphabetical series of couplets, each beginning with a successive letter from A to Z. The doctrinal couplets treat creation, the Trinity and the procession of the Spirit, the incarnation and the twofold nativity of Christ, the motherhood of the Virgin, and the Passion, resurrection and redemption of humankind. A middle group of penitential prayers and doxologies confesses sin in detail, begs cleansing, virtue and protection from the devil, and appeals to Christ as both saviour and judge. The collection closes with polemical verses that set orthodox teaching against the heresiarchs Arius, Sabellius, Manichaeus, Photinus, Nestorius and Eutyches, marshalling scriptural formulae on the unity of the Father and the Son and the single person of Christ.
la.anonymous.itinerarium_hierosolymitanum: An anonymous Latin prose itinerary, commonly known as the Itinerarium Burdigalense, that records a journey from Bordeaux to Jerusalem and back by listing road stations, distances in miles, and the changing-points and overnight halts between them. The outward route runs through Gaul and northern Italy, crosses the Alps and the Balkan provinces to Constantinople, and then leads through Asia Minor and Syria into Palestine. At Jerusalem and its environs the itinerary slows to fuller prose, describing the city's pools and the site of the former temple, the places of the crucifixion and resurrection, the Mount of Olives, Bethlehem, Jericho, the Jordan and Hebron, together with the biblical events attached to each. A consular notice dates the return journey to the consulship of Dalmatius and Zenophilus (333), after which the route passes through Macedonia, crosses by sea from Aulona to Brindisi, and makes its way through Italy to Rome and finally Milan, with summary totals of stations and mileage closing each stretch.
la.augustine.de_dialectica: De dialectica is a short Late Antique Latin prose treatise on dialectic, the science of disputing well, attributed to Augustine. It opens by defining dialectic as the art of disputation and dividing words into simple and conjoined, framing these as the matter and the working of the discipline and announcing its several parts. The treatise then defines word, thing, and sign, distinguishing verbum, dicibile, dictio, and res, before surveying the origin of words, including Stoic claims about etymology, and the force of words by which they move a hearer in respect of both truth and decorum. Its main burden is the classification of obscurity and ambiguity as impediments to judging truth, covering univocal and equivocal terms, ambiguity arising from art and from usage, and finally ambiguity found only in writing, where the surviving text breaks off.
la.augustine.libellus_adversus_fulgentium_d: A late-antique Latin polemical treatise attributed to Augustine, answering the libellus that a Donatist named Fulgentius had addressed to him. It opens with the author's acknowledgement of Fulgentius's little book and his resolve to reply from divine scripture, taking up its claims of one baptism, one enclosed garden and one oil that 'dying flies' corrupt. The greater part of the work is a point-by-point refutation staged as alternating speeches, Fulgentius's objections answered under the headings 'Catholicus respondit' and later 'Augustinus respondit', drawing on the Samaritan woman, the waters of Jericho healed by Elisha, the widow's vessel of oil and Haggai on clean and unclean touch to argue that baptism is one and retains its force outside the Donatist communion. It also rehearses charges of traditio against named Donatist clerics, discusses the compulsion of schismatics, the rebaptizer as a 'pirate' and the case of the Maximianists, and closes by appealing to the decrees of the Donatist elders and the gospel saying that a kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.
la.cicero.academica: Academica is a Latin philosophical dialogue by Cicero of the Roman Republic, opening at Cumae, where Cicero, Atticus, and Varro meet and agree to discuss the history of the Academy in Latin. Varro speaks first, expounding the doctrine of the Old Academy as Antiochus taught it, presenting Plato, Aristotle, and the early Stoa as heirs of a single philosophy and setting out its teachings on the highest good, on nature, and on logical method. Cicero then answers on behalf of the sceptical New Academy, recounting Arcesilas's denial that anything can be known and Carneades's doctrine of the 'probable' as a sufficient guide for action. The dialogue breaks off unfinished, and the work survives only in fragmentary form.
la.cicero.pro_l_flacco: Cicero's defense speech for Lucius Flaccus, a Republican forensic oration in Latin prose, opens with an exordium pleading on behalf of a man who stood by the consul in the Catilinarian crisis and now stands accused of extortion arising from his praetorship in Asia. The body of the speech dismantles the prosecution's case in sequence: it attacks the reliability of Greek and Asiatic witnesses and their popular decrees, defends Flaccus's requisition of money for a fleet and his sequestration of Jewish gold, and rebuts the charges brought by Roman individuals such as Decianus, Lurco, and Falcidius. The peroration widens the stakes to the condition of the republic, presenting the verdict as a judgment on all who suppressed the conspiracy, and closes with an emotional appeal centered on Flaccus's young son.
la.cicero.pro_scauro: A prose oration of the Republic, the Pro Scauro is Cicero's defence of Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, who faced accusations pressed by Sardinian witnesses concerning his administration of the province, above all a grave charge relating to the grain levy. The speech opens with Scaurus' wish to preserve the dignity of his family and name without incurring hatred, and then reviews his client's earlier prosecutions before taking up the deaths of Bostar of Nora and his wife, which the prosecution ascribed to poison and to fear of violation. The heart of the argument meets that charge by conjecture and circumstance, weighing the two explanations current in Sardinia for the woman's death, and digresses on voluntary death with Greek and Roman examples and Plato's teaching on the soul. Its later portions discredit the Sardinian prosecutors as degenerate Phoenician stock whose unanimous testimony was bought, arraign the haste and motives of the prosecutor Triarius and of the presiding consul, and close with an appeal to the temples, ancestral honours and enduring name of the Scauri.
la.cyprian_pseudo.sodoma: A Latin poem of the later Roman Empire transmitted under the name of Cyprian, its authorship uncertain, retelling the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah from Genesis. It opens with God's covenant after the Flood, the rainbow pledging that water would no longer destroy the world, before the renewed wickedness of humankind calls instead for punishment by fire. The narrative then follows Lot's hospitality to the two angelic visitors, the onslaught of the Sodomite mob, the flight urged on Lot's household and his journey to Segor, the rain of sulphur and flame, and the transformation of Lot's wife into a pillar of salt. A final survey describes the ruined region's ash-covered fields, its bitumen-bearing waters in which nothing floats and bodies cannot sink, closing with the punishment as an enduring sign teaching unjust nations to fear God.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.de_vita_beati_anto: The De Vita Beati Antoni Monachi is a late-antique Latin prose life of the hermit Antony, written by Magnus Felix Ennodius for the abbot Leontius, who had commissioned the work. It opens with a preface in which the author asks Leontius to sustain him with prayer and argues that written remembrance preserves the deeds of the saints beyond their lifetimes. The narrative then traces Antony's course from his birth at Valeria on the Danube in Pannonia and his upbringing under Severinus and the bishop Constantius, through his flight from the barbarian devastations to Italy and his eremitical settlement on a mountain above Lake Como beside the shrine of the martyr Fidelis, his exposure of a murderer hidden in monastic garb and his taming of a marauding bear, to his final withdrawal to the island of Lérins, where he spent the last two years of his life.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.carmina_figurata: Carmina Figurata is a short sequence of Latin figure verses attributed to the Carolingian poet Milo of Saint Amand, addressed throughout to a King Charles. It opens with repeated petitions that Charles accept the poem with kindly favour, hailing him as one who holds his sceptre by God's eternal rule. The poems sustain this acclamation, celebrating the king's justice, piety, and a dominion reaching to Thule, while describing their own verses as painted figures, including shapes of the cross, wrought in the poet's modest craft. The sequence also professes to record the blessed deeds of a beloved bishop's life, is composed in Amand's name, and closes with a farewell to the poet Milo and a prayer for mercy that names Haimo.
la.paulus_orosius.liber_apologeticus: The Liber Apologeticus, a late antique Latin prose treatise in theology by Paulus Orosius, opens with an address to the bishops excusing the author for speaking not from presumption but from the necessity of injury, as defender of his own faith and unmasker of another's error. The work is a polemic against Pelagius and Caelestius: it recounts the condemnation of Caelestius in Africa, Augustine's written reply to Pelagius, and Orosius's disputation in Jerusalem before Bishop John over the reported assertion that a man cannot be without sin even with God's help, a quarrel referred to the Roman see. Its bulk refutes the Pelagian claim that a person may live sinlessly in this life, marshalling scriptural figures such as Job, David, Solomon, Zechariah, Peter and Paul to argue that perfection is reserved for the resurrection, that God's aid operates continually in all times and among all peoples, and that human nature is weak rather than evil, with free will upheld. It closes with Orosius's confession that he hates heresy but not the heretic, and with an appeal for fraternal correction within the bond of the church.
la.petrus_diaconus.de_locis_santis: De locis sanctis is a medieval Latin prose treatise attributed to Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino. Its dedicatory prologue, addressed to Guibaldus, abbot of Monte Cassino and Stavelot, explains that the work was compiled from various books and from the oral accounts of pilgrims who had visited the Holy Sepulchre, and commends the little book to the abbot's approval. The body of the treatise is a survey of the sacred sites of Palestine and Egypt: it begins with the Holy Sepulchre, Golgotha, and the Temple precincts of Jerusalem, proceeds to Mount Sion, Bethlehem, Jericho, the Jordan, and the towns of Galilee and Samaria, and concludes with Egypt, the route of the Exodus by the Red Sea, and the mountains of Sinai and Horeb, recording throughout the relics, churches, tombs, and monuments shown at each place, together with distances measured in miles.
la.salvian_of_marseilles.epistulae_selectio: A short Latin prose epistle by Salvian of Marseilles, a Christian writer of the late antique period, addressed to an unnamed correspondent who has sent him books. The letter opens by praising the volumes as brief in style but abundant in teaching, composed above all for the instruction of the writer's sons, whom he has formed as a temple to God crowned with doctrine. Salvian then prays that God make the young men equal to the books, that their teaching may become the fruit of the churches, and that they may bring credit both to the father who begot them and to those whom they have in turn instructed. He ends by asking that his former pupils stand as his daily intercessors and closes with an affectionate farewell.
la.tertullian_pseudo.de_sodoma: De Sodoma is a short Latin poem in hexameters on the sin and punishment of Sodom, transmitted under Tertullian's name but of uncertain authorship, belonging to the later imperial period. Opening with the flood by which God destroyed the first age of mankind and set the rainbow in the clouds as a pledge, it turns to the renewed impiety of a second race of men and to Sodom, whose lusts against nature mark the city out for destruction by fire rather than water. The poem then follows the arrival of two angelic youths at the gate, the hospitality of the righteous Lot, the assault threatened by the Sodomite mob, Lot's offer of his daughters in his guests' stead, and the divine decree of the city's coming annihilation, to which his sons-in-law respond only with incredulous laughter.
la.vergil_pseudo.elegiae_in_maecenatem: The Elegiae in Maecenatem are a pair of Latin laments in elegiac couplets for the death of Maecenas, handed down under Vergil's name as pseudepigrapha and of Augustan date. The first poem opens with the speaker declaring that he has lately bewailed a young man's fate in sad verse and must now give songs to a deserving old man, Maecenas, of Etruscan royal stock and the devoted companion of Augustus. Its course embraces praise of Maecenas' loyalty to Caesar, his harmless candour and his patronage of poets, recollections of Philippi, the eastern war and Actium, extended comparisons of Augustus with Bacchus and Hercules, and a wish that Medea's rejuvenating herb or the length of days granted to Tithonus and Nestor might restore him, ending with his dying words of devotion to Augustus. The second elegy, voiced in the person of Maecenas, consoles Augustus with the promise of unending remembrance and closes with blessings on him, on Livia, and on the continuation of the Caesarian line.
la.ausonius.commemoratio_professorum_burdig: The Commemoratio Professorum Burdigalensium is a late antique Latin work by Ausonius, a sequence of memorial notices for deceased teachers of grammar and rhetoric in his native Bordeaux. It opens with an invocation to men joined to the author not by kinship but by fame, devotion to his homeland, and a shared life of study, whom he undertakes to commemorate after their deaths. The body of the work proceeds through individual encomia and laments, among them celebrated rhetoricians, teachers of druidic lineage, kinsmen such as his uncle Arborius, and humbler grammarians whose names might otherwise perish, praising each one's eloquence, character, family fortunes, and manner of death. It closes with a statement of the commemorative rule observed throughout and a farewell to the spirits of the honoured dead, whose names, it says, should live on while their ashes rest.
la.cicero.de_amicitia: De Amicitia is a philosophical dialogue on friendship composed by Cicero during the Roman Republic, cast as the record of a discourse delivered by Gaius Laelius, who was renowned for wisdom, a few days after the death of his close friend Scipio Aemilianus. It opens with a prologue in which Cicero explains to Atticus his choice of Laelius as speaker, before Fannius and Scaevola, Laelius' sons-in-law, visit the old man at home and draw him into conversation. Laelius first answers his visitors' concern over his grief for Scipio, praising the dead man's life and death, and then at their request discourses on friendship: its origin in nature and affection rather than in need or profit, its existence only among good men, the rule that nothing dishonourable may be asked or done for a friend, the subordination of private ties to the welfare of the state, the choice and testing of friends, the superiority of long-standing attachments, the menace of flattery, and the proper way to loosen rather than rupture a failing friendship. The dialogue closes with Laelius' recollection that his friendship with Scipio, rooted in shared public and private life, endures in memory and will live on for posterity.
la.cicero.topica: Cicero's Topica, a prose treatise on rhetoric of the Republican era, opens with a dedicatory preface to the jurist Gaius Trebatius, recounting how Trebatius chanced upon Aristotle's Topica in the library at Cicero's Tusculan villa and, finding them obscure, was promised an account of their teaching, which Cicero set down from memory during a sea voyage while without his books. The work then expounds the art of discovering arguments, defining a locus as the 'seat' from which an argument is drawn, and surveys first the topics inherent in the subject under discussion, definition, partition, notation, conjugates, genus and form, similitude, difference, contraries, adjuncts, antecedents, consequents, repugnants, causes, effects, and comparison, and then the extrinsic topics grounded in testimony and authority. Examples are drawn largely from Roman civil law to suit the dedicatee, and the closing sections classify questions of cognition and action, the three kinds of cause (judicial, deliberative, and laudatory), the statuses of defence and legal disputation over ambiguous or conflicting writings, and the bearing of the topics on each part of an oration.
la.einhardus.rythmus_de_passione_marcellini: Einhard's Rythmus de Passione Marcellini et Petri is a Carolingian Latin poem recounting the passion of the Roman martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. It opens with the exorcist Peter imprisoned in Rome, whose preaching and healings win over his jailer Artemius and free Artemius' daughter from a demon. The poem goes on to narrate the saints' trial and torments before the judge Serenus, an angel's consolations in prison, the martyrdom of Artemius together with his wife Candida and daughter, and the beheading of Marcellinus and Peter in a dark wood, where they clear the ground and die singing praise. It closes with the burial of their remains near the tomb of Tiburtius by the women Lucilla and Firmina, the conversion of the executioner Dorotheus, and the report that Pope Damasus had committed the whole story to writing.
la.hilary_saint_bishop_of_poitiers.hymni: The Hymni attributed to Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, gather Late Antique Latin hymns on Christian doctrine and the life of Christ. The collection opens with a hymn addressing Christ as existing before the ages, expounding the eternal generation of the Son from the Father, the unity of the two, and the creation of all things through him. A second hymn, headed De resurrectione Christi, celebrates Christ's triumph over death and the underworld together with the believer's promised rising, while a third, De tentationibus Christi, follows Satan's alarm at Christ's birth and the beginning of the temptation before breaking off incomplete. The collection closes with a hymn of doubtful attribution, Hymnum dicat turba fratrum, which runs through the whole gospel narrative from the virginal conception and nativity, through the miracles, passion, and resurrection, to the founding of the church, ending with a summons to sing praise before dawn.
la.maffeo_veggio.aeneid: A Renaissance Latin epic in hexameters by Maffeo Veggio, which takes up the story of Aeneas in Italy at the moment Turnus dies in single combat and the Rutuli submit to the Trojan victor. The narrative then follows the aftermath of the war: the funerals and laments for Turnus voiced by Latinus and by his father Daunus, the burning of Ardea, and an embassy led by Drances that sues for peace. Latinus and Aeneas are reconciled, the marriage with Lavinia is celebrated with feasts and songs of Trojan and Latin history, and a flame shining over Lavinia's head is explained by Venus as an omen of the future glory of their line. The poem closes with Latinus yielding the kingship, Venus washing away Aeneas's mortality in the Numicius, and his ascent to the heavens as an Indiges.
la.magnus_felix_ennodius.dictiones: The Dictiones of Magnus Felix Ennodius is a late-antique Latin prose collection of set speeches and rhetorical declamations. It opens with an elaborate congratulatory address to Bishop Laurentius of Milan on his consecration, praising his endurance through persecution, war, and the desolation of his city. The remaining pieces range over panegyrics and addresses for bishops, aristocrats, teachers, and pupils, including speeches of thanks and recommendation delivered at dedications, commencements, and other civic occasions. Alongside these stand purely fictitious school exercises on both sides of imaginary cases, such as the redemption of sons from pirates, the enslavement of captured priests and Vestal virgins, accusations of parricide, and deliberative speeches cast in the voices of mythological figures like Medea, Dido, and Hercules.
la.florus.vergilius_orator_an_poeta: Vergilius orator an poeta is a short Latin prose dialogue attributed to Florus, an author of the early imperial period. It opens with the narrator, resting near a temple, being greeted by a stranger driven onto the shore while returning from Rome to Baetica, who recognises him as the Florus crowned in the poetic contest held under Domitian. The rest of the work consists of the narrator's answer: an account of his wanderings through Sicily, Crete, the Cyclades, Rhodes, Egypt, Gaul and Spain, an affectionate praise of the provincial city where he has settled, and a defence of teaching letters to boys as an office as honourable as military command.
la.milo_of_saint_amand.de_sobrietate: De Sobrietate is a two-book Latin didactic poem by the Carolingian writer Milo of Saint Amand. Its opening announces sobriety as the head and end of the work, casting the poet as a captive weeping by the rivers of Babylon who resolves to lament the gluttony for which Adam lost paradise. The body of the poem stages the conflict between sobriety and the vice it calls gastrimargia through a long allegorical survey of biblical history, from Noah's drunkenness, Esau's pottage, and the murmuring Israelites to Judith and Holofernes, Jael, Esther, the Maccabean martyrs, John the Baptist before Herod's banquet, and Christ fasting against the devil's three temptations. Later sections turn to humility, charity, almsgiving, and the duties of teachers and preachers, and the work closes with Milo's confession of his own sins, praise of the Virgin Mary, and a prayer for pardon.
la.catholic_church_pope.epistulae_imperator: A Late Antique Latin collection of uncertain compiler, transmitting letters and documents of emperors, popes, and bishops under the title Epistulae imperatorum pontificum aliorum. It opens with a narrative of persecution under the emperor Constantius, the exile of Pope Liberius, and the violent struggle for the Roman see between Damasus and Ursinus. The documents that follow range from theological discussion of the resurrection of the body to records of councils, episcopal rivalries in Alexandria and Constantinople, and the controversy surrounding Acacius. The collection closes with a formal profession of faith presented to Pope Hormisdas, affirming the orthodoxy preserved in the apostolic see.
la.florus_of_lyon.carmina: The Carmina are a Carolingian collection of Latin poems by Florus of Lyon on biblical and liturgical themes. The opening poem versifies the Gospel life of Christ as told by Matthew, from the evangelist's call at the tollbooth through the nativity, the magi led by the star, the flight into and return from Egypt, the calling of the fishermen, and the moral teaching on anger, alms, prayer, fasting, and trust in God's providence. Later pieces turn to devotional subjects, notably a first-person poem in which the almighty father governs and feeds the speaker as a shepherd, granting him pasture, streams, rod and staff, a prepared table, and a brimming cup as he pursues the straight paths of righteousness. The collection ends with a liturgical poem for the Easter vigil, in which wax formed by bees burns on the holy altar through the night, a night brighter than day, while every people on earth joins in singing Christ's everlasting praise.

grc.septuaginta.genesis: Genesis in the Septuagint is the Greek prose rendering of the first book of the Hebrew scriptures, translated in the Hellenistic period by unnamed translators. It opens with God's creation of heaven and earth and the ordering of the world in six days, then recounts Adam and Eve in Eden, Cain and Abel, the flood of Noah, and the tower of Babel before turning to the patriarchal narratives of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob with their covenants, migrations, and family strife. The final chapters follow Joseph, sold into Egypt, as he rises from slavery to power under Pharaoh and settles his kin in the land of Goshen. The book closes with Jacob's burial at Machpelah in Canaan and the death of Joseph in Egypt, his body laid in a coffin as the Israelites await their return.
grc.septuaginta.exodus: The Greek Exodus of the Septuagint, a Hellenistic rendering of the Hebrew book by translators whose names are not recorded, begins with the enumeration of Jacob's sons who went down to Egypt and the oppression of their multiplying descendants by a new king who did not know Joseph. It follows Moses from his rescue as an infant and upbringing at Pharaoh's court, through his flight to Midian and commissioning at the burning bush, to his contest with Pharaoh over the ten plagues and the institution of the Passover. There follow the departure from Egypt, the crossing of the Red Sea with the canticle sung by Moses and Miriam, and the wilderness marches marked by manna, water from the rock, and battle with Amalek. The later chapters tell of the theophany at Sinai with the Decalogue and covenant laws, the prescriptions for the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the priestly vestments, the apostasy of the golden calf and its aftermath, and finally the erection of the tent over which the cloud and glory of the Lord settle.
grc.septuaginta.levitikon: The Levitikon is the Greek version of the biblical Book of Leviticus, the third book of the Mosaic Torah, translated from a Hebrew original by an anonymous translator of Hellenistic date as part of the Septuagint. It opens with the Lord calling Moses from the tent of meeting to prescribe the manner of burnt, grain, and peace offerings. The laws then run on through sin and guilt offerings, the consecration of Aaron and his sons, the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, dietary rules, and purity regulations concerning childbirth, skin disease, bodily discharges, and the Day of Atonement. A closing section of 'holiness' legislation sets out sexual and moral prohibitions, the festival calendar, sabbath and jubilee years, and rules for vows and dedications, all cast as continuous divine speech to Moses at Sinai.
grc.septuaginta.arithmoi: Arithmoi is the Hellenistic Greek Septuagint version of the fourth book of the Pentateuch, the work of an anonymous translator and of uncertain precise date. It opens with the Lord's command to Moses, in the wilderness of Sinai in the second year after the exodus from Egypt, to muster the Israelite men of twenty years and upwards for war. The book combines narrative and legislation: the ordering of camp and march with the duties of Levites and priests, laws of purity, the ordeal for a suspected wife, the Nazirite vow and the priestly blessing; the mission of the spies, the sentence of forty years' wandering, and the rebellions of Korah, Dathan and Abiron; the oracles of Balaam summoned by Balak of Moab; and the defeats of Sihon and Og. It closes with a second census on the plains of Moab, laws of inheritance and festivals, the settlement of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh beyond the Jordan, and the designation of Joshua as Moses' successor on the eve of the crossing into Canaan.
grc.septuaginta.deuteronomion: The Deuteronomion is the Greek rendering of Deuteronomy contained in the Septuagint, the Jewish translation of the Hebrew scriptures made in the Hellenistic period by translators whose names are unknown. It opens with the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness in the fortieth year, as the people stand ready to cross into Canaan. The book consists chiefly of Moses' farewell discourses in Moab: a retrospective of the journey from Horeb and of the defeats and victories east of the Jordan, a repetition of the Decalogue and the command to love God alone, and a long legal corpus regulating worship and sacrifice, tithes and festivals, judges and kings, priests and prophets, cities of refuge, family and sexual relations, and conduct in war.
