Blessings and curses recited at Gerizim and Ebal, a renewal of the covenant, the Song of Moses foretelling apostasy and punishment, final blessings upon the twelve tribes, and an account of Moses' death on Mount Nebo and the succession of Joshua bring the work to a close.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_a: The Greek version of the biblical book commonly known as 1 Samuel, titled Basileion A ('Kingdoms I') in the Septuagint, is Hellenistic prose rendering a Hebrew narrative of Israel's passage from the rule of judges to the institution of the monarchy. It opens at Shiloh with the prayer of the childless Hannah, her vow, and the birth and dedication of Samuel. The account proceeds through Samuel's career as judge and prophet, the corruption of Eli's sons, the Philistine capture and return of the ark, and the people's demand for a king, which leads to the anointing of Saul and his eventual rejection after repeated disobedience. Its latter course follows David's rise, his victory over Goliath, his bond with Jonathan, and his flights from Saul's jealous pursuit, through Saul's resort to the medium at Endor to his death with his sons on Mount Gilboa.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_b: A Greek version of the second book of Samuel, transmitted in the Septuagint as the second of the four books of Kingdoms (Basileion Beta), a Hellenistic-era prose translation of biblical narrative by anonymous translators. The work opens after Saul's death with an Amalekite messenger's report to David and David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. It then follows David's rise to kingship, first over Judah at Hebron and then over all Israel, through the capture of Jerusalem, the transfer of the ark, Nathan's dynastic oracle, and campaigns against neighbouring peoples. The later chapters recount the Bathsheba episode and Nathan's rebuke, Amnon's violation of Tamar, Absalom's revolt and death, Sheba's rebellion, the execution of Saul's descendants on behalf of the Gibeonites, further wars with Philistine giants, David's victory song and last words, the roll of his warriors, and the census that brings plague, ending with David's purchase of Araunah's threshing floor for an altar.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_g: The Greek text of the Third Book of Basileion (1 Kings) from the Septuagint, the Old Testament as translated into Greek by Hellenistic-era Jewish translators; the precise dates and authors of that translation are not recorded, and the work survives here in an old Greek biblical form. It opens with the aged David, the succession intrigue of Adonijah, and Solomon's anointing as king, then follows Solomon's reign: his wisdom and judgment, the building of the temple with the help of King Hiram of Tyre, the visit of the queen of Sheba, and his eventual fall into idolatry. The narrative continues with the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam, the alternating accounts of the kings of Judah and Israel, and the prophetic activity of Ahijah, Elijah on Carmel, and the contest with the prophets of Baal, down through Ahab's wars with Ben-hadad of Syria, the episode of Naboth's vineyard, and Micaiah's prophecy at Ramoth-gilead. The book ends with the reign of Ahaziah, son of Ahab, who did evil in the sight of the Lord and worshipped Baal.
grc.septuaginta.basileion_d: The fourth book of the Reigns (Basileion D) in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament of Hellenistic date, gives in Greek prose the biblical account of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. It opens with Moab's rebellion after the death of Ahab and the prophet Elijah's denunciation of King Ahaziah of Samaria. The narrative then follows Elijah's fiery ascent and the ministry of Elisha, with the widow's oil, the Shunammite woman's son, Naaman's healing, and the wars with Syria, before turning to Jehu's bloody overthrow of the house of Ahab, the alternating reigns of Israelite and Judean kings, the fall of Samaria to Assyria and the deportation of its people, Hezekiah's defence of Jerusalem against Sennacherib, Manasseh's idolatry, Josiah's reform upon the rediscovery of the book of the law, and finally the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of Judah.
grc.anthologia_graeca: The Greek Anthology is a vast collection of Greek epigrams spanning the Hellenistic period through late antiquity, preserved in sixteen books whose poems cover an enormous range of subjects, meters and registers. The work opens with Christian dedicatory epigrams on church buildings and sacred images, and the corpus as a whole moves through books of amatory verse, funerary and dedicatory epigrams, epideictic pieces, satirical invective, epigrams on statues and works of art, epigrams on athletes and charioteers, and Christian subjects, alongside an extensive cycle of epigrams on famous poets and on the title figures of the works of art they accompanied. Traditional collections by poets such as Meleager, Philip and Agathias are woven into the larger arrangement, which mixes pagan mythological themes with late antique Christian material.
grc.achilles_tatius.leucippe_et_clitophon: Leucippe et Clitophon is an ancient Greek novel by Achilles Tatius, of uncertain date, told in the first person by Clitophon of Tyre. It opens at Sidon with a description of the city and an ecphrasis of a painting of Europa, which leads into Clitophon's account of his love for the Byzantine maiden Leucippe. After a courtship conducted within her father's house, the lovers elope by sea, suffer shipwreck off Egypt, and pass through bandit captivity, a staged human sacrifice in which Leucippe appears to be slain, slavery, and a series of trials at Ephesus, meeting several apparent deaths and improbable revivals along the way. The story closes with their reunion, the vindication of Leucippe's chastity before the Ephesian assembly, and the marriage long deferred by their fortunes.
grc.acta_joannis.acta_joannis: The Acta Joannis is an anonymous Greek apocryphal act of the apostle John, of uncertain date, opening with a prologue on Vespasian's destruction of Jerusalem and Domitian's subsequent persecution, which brings John from Ephesus to trial in Rome. John there drinks poison unharmed before the emperor, raises a condemned criminal to life, and is banished to Patmos, returning to Ephesus under Nerva and Trajan to resume his ministry. The Ephesian episodes that follow include the raising of Lycomedes and Cleopatra, the commissioning of John's painted portrait, a sermon in the theatre, the collapse of the temple of Artemis, a lesson commanded to bedbugs, and the death and restoration of Drusiana together with her would-be lover Callimachus. In a final revelatory section John teaches the believers about the polymorphic Christ, the cross of light, and the circle dance hymn sung before the passion, before lying down in a grave he has caused to be dug and giving up his spirit.
grc.aelian.de_natura_animalium: Aelian's De Natura Animalium is a Greek prose miscellany in seventeen books on the natures and habits of animals. A preface defends the claim that irrational creatures share in virtue by nature, after which the work proceeds through short, self-contained notices on beasts, birds, fishes, and insects. Its entries range from the fishing of the scarus and the mutual rescue behaviour of shoals to marvellous tales such as the herons of Diomedes' island, said to be the hero's transformed companions.
grc.aelian.varia_historia: The Varia Historia of Aelian (Claudius Aelianus) is a miscellany in Greek of anecdotes, apophthegms, and short notices ranging over natural history, human history, and moral exempla. It opens with chapters on animal behaviour: the predatory and colour-changing polyp, the weaving of spiders, the cunning of foxes, and the sagacity of Egyptian frogs, dogs, turtles, and mice. The collection then turns to human affairs, gathering stories of lawgivers and tyrants such as Solon and Archelaus, of orators and philosophers such as Demosthenes, Aeschines, Theophrastus, and Anaxagoras, and of other figures from Greek and Roman history. Later portions continue in the same manner with Spartan discipline, the virtues of Greek and Roman women, painters such as Zeuxis, and the conduct of kings such as Philip of Macedon and Ptolemy, the whole held together by loose thematic grouping rather than continuous narrative.
grc.aelius_aristides.orationes: The Orationes is a collection of Greek prose speeches by Aelius Aristides. The work opens with a hymn to Zeus, framed as thank-offerings made in fulfilment of a vow after escape from a storm at sea, in which the speaker laments the belatedness of his sacrifice and calls upon the Muses for aid. The hymn proceeds to celebrate Zeus as self-generated and eternal, first cause and craftsman of the cosmos, recounting his creation and ordering of earth, sea, air and aether, his adornment of the heavens with stars, and his allotment of proper dwellings to gods, humankind and the other races of living creatures. Further orations follow in the collection.
grc.aeschines.against_ctesiphon: A forensic oration by the Athenian statesman and orator Aeschines, delivered before Athenian jurors in the period following Philip's death and Alexander's accession, prosecuting Ctesiphon for proposing the decree honouring Demosthenes with a golden crown. The speech opens by urging the jurors that the laws are the safeguard of democracy and that in judging a case of an unlawful decree they cast their vote for their own freedom of speech. It then argues that Ctesiphon's decree is illegal both in honouring Demosthenes while he still owes an account of his offices and in ordering his proclamation in the theatre before the assembled Greeks, and proceeds to a long indictment of Demosthenes' career across four phases, alleging bribery in the Peace of Philocrates, the betrayal of Athenian interests in the Theban alliance and in Euboea, impiety over the sacred plain of Cirrha during Aeschines' service as pylagoros, and cowardice and desertion at Chaeronea. The closing sections contrast Demosthenes with Solon, Aristides, Themistocles and Miltiades, and urge the jurors to deny the crown as punishment for his political conduct.
grc.aeschines.on_the_embassy: On the Embassy is a defence speech by the Athenian orator Aeschines, answering a prosecution brought by Demosthenes on charges of bribery connected with the peace made with Philip of Macedon and the embassies that negotiated it. It opens with a plea to the Athenian jurors to hear the defendant with goodwill, mindful of the magnitude of his danger and of the prosecutor's devices. The greater part of the speech refutes the charges in order: Aeschines recounts the making of the peace and the first and second embassies, defends his conduct toward Cersobleptes, the Phocian cities, and the Amphictyonic settlement, and supports his case with decrees, letters, depositions, and witnesses, while portraying Demosthenes' own conduct as envoy and his character in hostile terms. It ends with an appeal for acquittal that invokes his family, his military service, and his record of goodwill toward the city.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, the Agamemnon opens with a watchman on the roof of the royal palace at Argos awaiting the chain of beacon fires that will announce the fall of Troy. The chorus of Argive elders recalls the expedition against Troy and the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, and a herald's report of the king's victory is followed by Agamemnon's homecoming with the captive prophetess Cassandra. Clytemnestra, avenging her daughter, lures her husband onto a costly robe and kills him, slaying Cassandra with him and acting together with her lover Aegisthus, whose father Thyestes was ruined by Atreus. The play closes with the triumphant pair exchanging threats with the defiant chorus, which looks ahead to the return of Agamemnon's son Orestes.
grc.aeschylus.agamemnon_hypothesis: A prose hypothesis, or plot-summary, to Aeschylus's tragedy Agamemnon, of uncertain date and transmitted with the play. It opens by recounting how Agamemnon, on departing for Troy, promised Clytemnestra a beacon signal on the day of victory, how she thereupon posted a paid watchman, and how the report of the fire brings together the elders who form the chorus. The summary then follows the whole course of the drama: Agamemnon's return in his chariot with Cassandra, her prophecy of her own death, the king's, and Orestes' future matricide, the murder of Agamemnon on stage, and the quarrel in which Clytemnestra and Aegisthus each defend the killing, she by the sacrifice of Iphigenia and he by the wrongs suffered by Thyestes. It closes with didascalic information, recording that the play was produced under the archon Philocles in the 78th Olympiad and that Aeschylus took first prize with the Agamemnon, Choephoroi, Eumenides, and the satyr-play Proteus, the choregos being Xenocles of Aphidnae, followed by a list of the dramatis personae.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides: The Eumenides is a Greek tragedy in verse by Aeschylus. It opens with the Pythia's prayer to the presiding deities of Delphi and her alarmed discovery of Orestes seated at the omphalos as a suppliant, with the sleeping Erinyes about him. The drama follows the pursuit of Orestes for the murder of his mother Clytemnestra, his flight under Apollo's protection to Athens, and the trial for bloodshed that Athena institutes on the Areopagus, where Apollo testifies and an equal count of votes, settled by Athena's ballot, acquits him. In the closing movement Athena persuades the resentful Furies to accept a home in Attica, establishing them as the Eumenides with cult honors, and the play ends with a torchlit procession and their blessings of fertility and civic concord upon the city.
grc.aeschylus.eumenides_hypothesis: A short prose hypothesis, or plot argument, prefixed to the Eumenides of Aeschylus, the concluding play of the Oresteia; the summary itself is anonymous and of uncertain date. It opens by recounting how Orestes, surrounded by the Erinyes at Delphi, went at Apollo's bidding to Athens and took refuge at the shrine of Athena. It goes on to relate that, acquitted through the goddess's counsel, he returned to Argos, appeased the angry goddesses, and renamed them the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones. A closing remark notes that the story is found in neither of the two poets.
grc.aeschylus.persians: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, set at the Persian court after the failure of Xerxes' invasion of Greece. It opens with a chorus of Persian elders at Susa recalling the muster of the king's vast host and voicing anxiety for news of his return. The queen mother Atossa recounts an ominous dream before a messenger arrives to tell of the annihilation of the Persian fleet at Salamis, and the ghost of Darius, summoned by offerings, interprets the disaster as divine punishment for hubris and prophesies a further defeat at Plataea. The drama closes as Xerxes himself returns in rags to join his elders in a sustained lament over the ruin of Asia.
grc.aeschylus.persians_hypothesis: A short prose hypothesis, or plot summary, transmitted as the prefatory argument to Aeschylus's Persians and of ancient date. It opens by citing Glaucus's account of Aeschylus's plots, which reports that the Persians reworked Phrynichus's Phoenissae and quotes the play's first line. The summary then sets the drama at the tomb of Darius and outlines its subject: Xerxes' invasion of Greece with vast land and naval forces, his defeat by sea at Salamis and on land at Plataea, and his flight back across to Asia. Concluding notes record Aeschylus's victory in the archonship of Menon with the Phineus, Persians, Glaucus Potnieus, and Prometheus, and distinguish the first Persian expedition under Darius, repulsed at Marathon, from the second under Xerxes at Salamis and Plataea.
grc.aeschylus.seven_against_thebes: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus dramatizing the assault of the Seven from Argos on Thebes. It opens with Eteocles rallying the citizens of Cadmus' city to man the walls, as a seer reports that the enemy is preparing an imminent attack. A long central scene follows in which a scout describes, gate by gate, the devices blazoned on the shields of the seven Argive champions while Eteocles assigns Theban defenders to meet them, and the chorus of Theban women prays to the city's gods amid an argument with the king over their panic and supplications. A messenger then announces that Eteocles and his brother Polynices have slain each other at the seventh gate; Antigone and Ismene lament the dead, and the closing exchange has Antigone defy a decree of the council forbidding Polynices burial, vowing to bury him herself.
grc.aeschylus.suppliant_women: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, of uncertain date, built around a chorus of suppliant maidens rather than a dominant individual protagonist. The play opens with the Danaids, daughters of Danaus, landing at Argos after fleeing Egypt to escape marriage to their cousins the sons of Aegyptus, and taking refuge at the altars of the local gods. King Pelasgus, recognizing their Argive descent through the lineage of Io, refers their plea to the citizen assembly, which votes to shelter them, and an Egyptian herald's attempt to seize the maidens by force is repelled. The drama closes with the refugees settled in the city, offering thanksgiving to the gods of Argos and a prayer that Zeus avert the hated marriage.
grc.andocides.on_the_mysteries: On the Mysteries is a forensic speech in which the Athenian orator Andocides defends himself against a charge of impiety arising from the profanation of the Eleusinian Mysteries and the mutilation of the Herms, opening with an appeal for the jurors' goodwill and a promise to recount every relevant event from the beginning. The narrative covers the successive informations laid over the secret rites, the panic that followed the mutilation of the Herms, Diocleides' false denunciation that saw his kinsmen imprisoned, and Andocides' own naming of the actual offenders, which he presents as an act that saved both his family and the city. He then contends that the decree of Isotimides under which he stands charged has been invalidated by the amnesty decrees and oaths sworn after the overthrow of the Thirty, adding invective against his chief enemies, Callias son of Hipponicus and Alcibiades. The speech closes with a public exhortation that Athens accept peace with Lacedaemon, reviewing earlier treaties to argue that peace has been salvation for the democracy where war has been its overthrow.
grc.anonymous.stadiasmus_magni_maris: The Stadiasmus Magni Maris is an anonymous Greek navigational treatise, a coastal guide or stadiasmos, of uncertain date. Its opening preface is addressed to a 'most honoured brother' and promises an exact account of the Great Sea, from Alexandria and the coasts of Europe and Asia as far as the Pillars of Heracles and Gades. The body of the work consists of numbered entries giving distances in stades between ports, anchorages, headlands, rivers and islands, with notes on harbours, watering places, shelter from particular winds and other navigational features. Its routes follow the North African coast from Alexandria through Cyrenaica to Carthage, pass on through Syria, Cilicia and the southern shores of Asia Minor, and take in Rhodes, the Aegean islands, Cyprus and Crete.
grc.apollodorus.library: A Greek prose compendium of mythology, the work known as the Library, attributed to Apollodorus and of uncertain date. It opens with the rule of Uranus over the universe, his offspring by Ge, and Cronus's usurpation of his father's power. From there the narrative runs through the Titanomachy, the Gigantomachy, and the assault of Typhon, before turning to genealogical saga: Deucalion and the flood, the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts to Colchis and its aftermath, the twelve labours and later campaigns of Heracles and the return of the Heraclids, the Theban cycle from Cadmus and Dionysus through Oedipus to the Seven Against Thebes and the Epigoni, the Arcadian and Spartan lines with Atalanta and the Dioscuri, the Trojan house from Dardanus to Priam and Paris, and the early kings of Athens. The surviving account breaks off amid Theseus's youthful exploits on the road from Troezen.
grc.apollonius_of_perga.conica: The Conica is a Greek mathematical treatise on conic sections by Apollonius of Perga, a geometer of the Hellenistic period. The preserved lines set out propositions in the Euclidean manner, each consisting of a general enunciation followed by a demonstration, and deal with tangents and secants drawn from external points to sections of a cone and to circumferences of circles. The hyperbola receives particular attention, with propositions involving its asymptotes and its opposite sections, and ratios of divided straight lines are used to determine where lines drawn from points of contact meet or touch the curve.
grc.apollonius_rhodius.argonautica: The Argonautica is a Hellenistic Greek epic in four books attributed to Apollonius of Rhodes, recounting Jason's voyage with the Argonauts to Colchis to win the Golden Fleece. It opens with a prayer to Apollo to sing of the men of old who drove the Argo through the Cyanean Rocks on Pelias's orders. The poem follows the muster of the heroes at Pagasae and their outward voyage through Lemnos, the land of the Doliones, the abandonment of Heracles and Hylas in Mysia, Polydeuces' boxing match with Amycus, Phineus's prophecies, and the passage of the Symplegades, before turning to the court of Aeetes, the tasks of the fire-breathing bulls and the dragon's teeth, Medea's love for Jason and her flight with him, the killing of Apsyrtus, and the long wanderings homeward by way of Circe, the Planctae, the Phaeacians, Libya, and Crete. It closes with the Argo's arrival back at Pagasae, the Greek shore from which the expedition set out.
grc.archimedes.arenarius: The Arenarius (Sand-Reckoner) is a treatise in Greek by Archimedes, dedicated to King Gelon, and it opens by recalling the opinion held by some that grains of sand are infinite in number and by others that no number can be named to exceed them, a view the author undertakes to refute through geometric demonstration. The work then sets out its assumptions, adopting figures deliberately larger than earlier estimates for the earth's circumference and the diameters of the sun and moon, describing an experiment with a long rule and a small cylinder to gauge the sun's apparent diameter, and proving that the sun's diameter exceeds the side of a chiliagon inscribed in the great circle of the cosmos. A system of orders and periods of numbers, built on myriads of myriads, is defined so that quantities far beyond ordinary nomenclature can be named, and bounds are established for the diameter of the cosmos as usually conceived by astronomers and, larger still, on the hypotheses of Aristarchus of Samos, who makes the earth circle the sun and places the sphere of the fixed stars at an immense distance. In the fourth and final section the number of grains of sand that would fill a sphere as large as Aristarchus's sphere of the fixed stars is shown to be less than a myriad of myriads of the eighth order of numbers.
grc.archimedes.de_corporibus_fluitantibus: De Corporibus Fluitantibus is Archimedes' hydrostatic treatise in Greek, cast as postulates, propositions and proofs, with some portions supplied in a Latin translation. It opens with a postulate on the behaviour of fluids, in which parts under greater pressure push out parts under less, and from this deduces that the surface of a fluid at rest is spherical and shares its centre with the earth. The following propositions set out how solids behave in fluid: bodies of equal weight with the fluid rest wholly submerged without sinking further, lighter bodies float partly above the surface and are driven upward with a force equal to the excess weight of the displaced fluid, and heavier bodies sink while losing weight in the fluid equal to that of the fluid they displace. The closing and longest portion determines the positions of equilibrium of segments of a right-angled conoid, lighter than the fluid, showing under what conditions of axis and weight such a segment rights itself, tilts, or rests with its base just touching the surface, with appeals to the Equilibria and the mechanical elements for centres of gravity.
grc.archimedes.de_lineis_spiralibus: Archimedes' On Spirals (De Lineis Spiralibus), a Greek geometrical treatise, opens as a letter to Dositheus recalling the death of Conon, surveying earlier problems of which some are now proved and others shown false, and announcing the theorems on the spiral. The body of the work first presents lemmas on uniform motion along a line, on sequences of lines exceeding one another by a constant difference, and on tangents and neuses to circles, followed by formal definitions of the spiral and its parts. The main theorems then establish the ratios of radii drawn from the origin to the spiral at equal angles, the property of the tangent at any point, the rectification of the circumference by the tangent at the end of each turn, and the areas enclosed between the spiral and the initial line, showing that the first turn bounds one third of the area of the first circle and that the areas of successive turns stand in simple multiple ratios. The treatise concludes with theorems comparing the areas cut off between two radii and the spiral with corresponding sectors and circles.
grc.archimedes.de_planorum_aequilibriis: A treatise on statics by Archimedes, the De Planorum Aequilibriis (On the Equilibrium of Planes) derives, from seven postulates on weights suspended from a balance, the law of the lever and the properties of the centre of gravity of plane figures, with propositions on commensurable and incommensurable magnitudes, composite bodies, and the parallelogram. It is written in the Doric dialect characteristic of ancient Greek mathematical prose, with forms such as τᾶς for τῆς, μακέων for the beam of the balance, and σαμεῖον for σημεῖον, which distinguish it sharply from Attic literary Greek. For readers tracing intertexts it offers the canonical formulation of mechanical vocabulary, κέντρον τοῦ βάρεος (centre of gravity), ἰσορροπέω (to balance), ῥέπω (to incline), on which later discussions of the lever and the balance in Greek technical and literary authors draw.
grc.archimedes.problema_bovinum: The Problema Bovinum is a short Greek arithmetical problem in verse that its introductory note presents as a challenge devised by Archimedes and sent to those pursuing such questions in Alexandria, in a letter to Eratosthenes of Cyrene. It opens with an address to a stranger, asking him to reckon how many bulls and cows of four colours, white, dark, yellow and piebald, grazed the fields of Sicily, their several numbers bound by stated fractional ratios. A further demand raises the difficulty: the white and dark bulls together must form a square number and the yellow and piebald a triangular number, with the promise that whoever satisfies every condition will be judged outstanding in wisdom. A closing prose scholion restates the rules for each colour and appends numerical totals for the bulls and cows of the four herds, expressed in Greek alphabetic numerals.
grc.archimedes.quadratura_parabolae: The Quadratura Parabolae is a short geometrical treatise by Archimedes, transmitted in Greek as a letter to Dositheus, on the area of a segment bounded by a straight line and a section of a right-angled cone (a parabola). It opens with a preface to Dositheus lamenting the death of Conon and announcing the central theorem, that every such segment is four-thirds of the triangle with the same base and equal height, together with the conic lemmas required for the proof. The body of the work first establishes the result mechanically, balancing portions of a segment against triangles and trapezia suspended from a lever, and then proceeds through inscribed triangles in a continued ratio of four to one, supported by a lemma showing that magnitudes in quadruple progression, with a third of the least added, sum to four-thirds of the greatest. The treatise closes with definitions of the base, height and vertex of a segment and a final proof by exhaustion that every such segment is four-thirds of the inscribed triangle.
grc.aretaeus.curatione_acutorum_morbum: A Greek medical treatise ascribed to Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a physician of uncertain date, transmitted under the Latin title De curatione acutorum morborum (On the Cure of Acute Diseases). The material gathered here gives a detailed clinical account of acute convulsive disorders, describing the warning signs, the seizure itself, and the aftermath of epilepsy, and the spasms of tetanus in its rigid, backward-arching (opisthotonic) and forward-curving forms. Further sections discuss the causes of these spasms, their incidence by season, age, and sex, and the physician's limited prospects of aiding those they strike.
grc.aristophanes.clouds: Aristophanes' comedy Clouds opens at night with the elderly farmer Strepsiades lamenting the debts incurred through his son Pheidippides' passion for horses and resolving to seek instruction at the neighbouring Thinkery of Socrates. There comic displays of Socrates' natural philosophy, astronomy, geometry and the meteorology that replaces Zeus with the chorus of Clouds, alternates with Strepsiades' own hapless schooling, until the chorus advises him to send his son in his place. Pheidippides masters the Unjust Argument, which defeats the Just Argument in an agon contrasting old and new education, and then turns his rhetoric against his father, defending the beating of parents and threatening his mother. Repenting of the sophistic training he sought, Strepsiades burns down the Thinkery and drives Socrates and Chaerephon from the roof.
grc.aristophanes.ecclesiazusae: Aristophanes' Ecclesiazusae is a Greek comedy that opens before daybreak with Praxagora addressing a burning lamp as she and her fellow plotters, disguised in men's cloaks, beards and heavy shoes, rehearse their plan to pack the Assembly. The disguised women carry the vote that hands the city over to female government, and Praxagora's programme abolishes private property, institutes common messes in the public buildings, and replaces marriage with an ordered community of partners in which the old have first claim on the young. Later episodes show the new laws at work: a husband left behind at home while his wife governs, reluctant citizens compelled to surrender their possessions to the common store, and a young man dragged off by two rival elderly women each claiming priority under the statute. The play ends with the chorus preparing a communal feast, cataloguing its outlandish ingredients, and leading an invitation to the citizens and the spectators to join the banquet.
grc.aristophanes.frogs: A comedy by Aristophanes, the Frogs opens with Dionysus and his slave Xanthias bantering over the loads they carry as the god, disguised in Heracles' lion-skin and club, asks his way down to the underworld. Having come to fetch Euripides back among the living, Dionysus crosses the lake with Charon amid the croaking of the frog chorus, joins the procession of initiates who hymn Iacchus, and endures humiliations including a whipping contest with Xanthias in Heracles' stead. In Hades he finds Aeschylus and Euripides disputing the tragic throne before Pluto, and the bulk of the play is their agon over prologues, lyrics, and the moral and political worth of poetry, which Dionysus, against his original purpose, settles in Aeschylus' favour, sending him back to counsel the city. Choral passages, including a parabasis on the treatment of deserving citizens, frame the contest and close with the poet's departure amid blessings for Athens.
grc.aristophanes.knights: Aristophanes' Knights is a political comedy whose chorus is drawn from the Athenian knights, the cavalry class whose members are praised in the play's choral odes and who name the demagogue Cleon as the target of their hostility. It opens in the house of Demos, the crotchety old man who personifies the Athenian people, where two slaves, ousted from their master's favour by the tanner Paphlagon, a bullying flatterer and informer, resolve to find him a rival in shamelessness. They recruit a vulgar sausage-seller from the agora, and the bulk of the play stages their escalating contests before Demos: rival professions of devotion, gifts of seats and delicacies, mutual accusations, duels of oracles, and appeals to council, assembly and courts, until the sausage-seller exposes Paphlagon's extortions and usurps his position. A lengthy parabasis defends the poet's art and laments the decline of earlier comic dramatists, and the play closes with Demos restored to the hearty simplicity of the age of Miltiades and Aristides, an idealised ancient Athens summoned to his side, and Paphlagon condemned to peddle sausages at the city gates.
grc.aristophanes.lysistrata: Lysistrata is a comedy by Aristophanes, first performed at Athens during the Peloponnesian War. The play opens with Lysistrata and Calonice assembling a congress of women from Athens and its allies, who swear an oath to withhold sex from their husbands until peace is made and seize the Acropolis and its treasury to enforce their resolve. The action follows the standoff between the women and their men, including failed attempts to storm the citadel, a debate before the council of old citizens, the tribulations of individual couples such as Cinesias and Myrrhine, and finally the arrival of Spartan envoys equally afflicted by the women's campaign. After the disputing parties present their claims, the goddess Reconciliation brings the sides together, and the play closes with united songs of thanksgiving and a Lakonian dance in celebration of the restored peace.
grc.aristophanes.peace: Peace, a comedy by Aristophanes, opens with the farmer Trygaeus fattening a dung beetle on barley cakes so that the insect will carry him up to heaven. There he finds the goddess Peace, long held captive while war ravages the land, brings her back to earth, and the remaining action celebrates her release: the chorus of farmers rejoices in the return of rural life, satirical scenes mock war-mongers, oracle-mongers and other public figures, and there are comic notices of poets such as Sophocles and Cratinus. The play concludes with a wedding hymn as Trygaeus marries Opora and the company is invited to share a festive meal.
grc.aristophanes.wasps: A comedy of Aristophanes belonging to Athenian Old Comedy, the Wasps takes its name from a chorus of elderly Athenians who serve as jurors and, with the sting at their backs, are likened to wasps. It opens with two slaves keeping watch over the old man Philocleon, whose mania for jury service leads his son Bdelycleon to confine him at home and attempt a cure. The action stages a mock household trial of a dog accused of eating a Sicilian cheese, a debate over the jurors' meagre pay and the demagogues who profit from the empire, and a parabasis in which the chorus defends the martial exploits of the older generation. Philocleon, having been weaned from the courts, relapses into wilder habits at a symposium, and the play closes with drunken brawling in the streets and a dancing contest of the sons of Carcinus.
grc.aristotle.analytica_priora: A Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on the syllogism, the instrument of demonstrative argument. It opens by defining its subject as demonstration and demonstrative knowledge, and by laying out the basic notions of proposition, term, and syllogism, with the distinction between perfect and imperfect forms. The treatise then works through syllogistic theory in detail: the three figures and their valid moods, the conversion of propositions, syllogisms built on necessary and possible premises, and the conditions under which no conclusion follows. Its later portions treat syllogisms from opposed premises, argument from false premises, circular demonstration, begging the question, and refutation, then the search for middle terms as causes and the construction of definitions with the aid of division, and finally the question of how the first principles of demonstration come to be known, arising from perception through memory and experience and grasped at last by a state of mind more certain than science.
grc.aristotle.de_caelo: A Greek treatise by Aristotle on the heavens, opening with the claim that natural science concerns bodies and magnitudes, their affections and movements, and the principles of such substance. Early chapters define the continuous, the divisible, and dimension, citing Pythagorean doctrine that the all and completeness are delimited by the number three, so that body, bounded in three dimensions, alone counts as perfect magnitude. Further argument distinguishes simple local motions as circular, upward, and downward, and holds that circular motion cannot belong by nature to fire or any of the elemental bodies, from which it follows that there exists another simple body, more divine and prior to the perceptible elements, whose proper motion is circular. The opening defers the question whether the universe as a whole is infinite in magnitude in order to treat first of its parts in kind.
grc.aristotle.de_generatione_animalium: Aristotle's treatise on the generation of animals, composed in Greek prose, takes as its subject how living things come to be, opening from the four causes already used in the study of animal parts and asking what causes serve the coming-to-be of the parts connected with generation. The work argues that male and female are the principles of generation, the male supplying form and the principle of motion, the female the matter, and it examines semen and menstrual fluid, the reproductive organs of blooded and bloodless animals, spontaneous generation, the role of heat in formation, the development of the embryo, birds' eggs, the gestation periods of different animals, and the causes of resemblances, monstrosities, barrenness and related phenomena, closing with a discussion of teeth and other features explained by necessity rather than purpose. Its five books move from general theory through the anatomy and reproduction of each class of animals toward detailed causal explanations of particular phenomena.
grc.aristotle.de_interpretatione: Aristotle's De Interpretatione is a short philosophical treatise in prose on simple assertions and the conditions under which they are true or false. It opens by defining the name and the verb as conventional signs that, taken by themselves, involve neither truth nor falsity. The treatise then examines affirmation and negation, contradiction and contrariety between propositions, and modal statements of necessity, possibility, and impossibility, including the famous discussion of whether claims about future events, such as a sea battle on the morrow, are already true or false. It closes with an analysis of the opposition between beliefs and of the corresponding opposition between affirmative and negative assertions.
grc.aristotle.de_sophisticis_elenchis: Aristotle's De Sophisticis Elenchis is a Greek treatise on sophistical refutations, arguments that appear to be refutations but are in fact fallacies. It opens by defining such apparent refutations and the sophist who profits from apparent rather than genuine wisdom, and by distinguishing four kinds of reasoning: didactic, dialectical, peirastic, and eristic. The main body sets out the five aims of contentious disputants, divides fallacies into six kinds dependent on language (homonymy, amphiboly, composition, division, accent, and form of expression) and others arising outside it, and then gives practical guidance on how to question, answer, and solve such arguments, with a discussion of what makes a piece of reasoning difficult or incisive. The treatise closes by returning to its original plan, remarking that nothing of the kind had existed before it, and asking its hearers for indulgence toward the first beginnings of the inquiry and thanks for what has been achieved.
grc.aristotle.divisiones_aristoteleae: A short Greek collection of dialectical divisions transmitted under Aristotle's name and of uncertain date. It opens with a passage quoted from Diogenes Laertius reporting that Aristotle divided goods into those of the soul, those of the body, and external goods. There follow a series of brief divisions and definitions covering, among many other subjects, the kinds of friendship, constitutions, justice, the sciences, medicine, written and unwritten law, the five kinds of discourse, rhetoric, music, nobility of birth, beauty, the parts of the soul, virtue and vice, forms of rule, benefaction, happiness, truth and falsehood, punishment, and pleasure and pain. Several topics are treated twice in closely parallel versions, and the compilation closes with discussions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity, contraries, and affirmation and negation.
grc.aristotle.epistulae: The Epistulae is a brief collection of six Greek letters attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date. The opening letter counsels a ruler to trust in virtue rather than in the shifting turns of fortune, warning against tyrannical rule and grandiloquent speech and recommending care for the soul through philosophy and for the body through health. The remaining letters keep to the same hortatory vein: they urge benefaction and mercy toward the unfortunate, invoking Theophrastus on gratitude, and recommend swift reconciliation after an injury. A short closing note on the acroamatic discourses remarks that, though published, they are intelligible only to those who heard them; throughout, the pieces are gnomic moral essays in epistolary form rather than letters of practical business.
grc.aristotle.magna_moralia: The Magna Moralia, a Greek ethical treatise transmitted under Aristotle's name but of disputed authorship, treats character as part of politics and argues that happiness is an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life. After an opening survey of earlier accounts by Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato, it defines moral virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency concerning pleasure and pain, and proceeds through the individual virtues, cowardice and courage, temperance, justice, friendship, and the relationship between practical wisdom, wisdom, and the passions. It closes with discussions of continence and incontinence, pleasure, good fortune, and the bearing of fortune on the virtuous life.
grc.aristotle.meteorologica: Aristotle's Meteorologica opens by defining its subject as the remaining part of natural philosophy after the study of first causes, the celestial bodies and the elements, namely the phenomena that all earlier thinkers had called meteorology. The work then surveys the region between the earth and the heavens, treating shooting stars, comets and the Milky Way, then clouds, rain, snow, hail, dew and frost, winds, earthquakes, rivers and springs, and the sea together with the cause of its salinity. Later sections deal with thunder, lightning, hurricanes, thunderbolts, halos, rainbows, mock suns and rods, explained through the reflection of sight and the mixture of moist vapour and dry exhalation. A final book examines the affections of bodies, combination, solidification, melting and kindred processes, and the composition of homogeneous materials such as metals, flesh and bone.
grc.aristotle.nicomachean_ethics: A Greek ethical treatise in ten books by Aristotle, asking what the human good is and how it may be attained. It opens with the claim that every art, inquiry, action and choice aims at some good, and identifies the highest good, studied by the science of politics, as happiness (eudaimonia). The body of the work defines happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, examines the moral virtues as means between excess and deficiency and treats individual virtues such as courage, temperance, magnanimity and justice, alongside the intellectual virtues, pleasure, weakness of will and friendship. It concludes by ranking the contemplative life as the most complete form of happiness and turns to the question of legislation and civic education.
grc.aristotle.physica: The Physica is Aristotle's treatise on natural philosophy, an inquiry into the principles and causes of things that exist by nature and are subject to change. It opens by arguing that knowledge depends on grasping first causes, principles, and elements, so that the science of nature must begin by determining its first principles, proceeding from what is clearer to us to what is clearer by nature. The argument then surveys the four causes, necessity, chance and spontaneity, the infinite, place, the void, and time as the number of motion in respect of before and after, before examining continuity and infinite divisibility, the species of change and motion, and their contrarieties. The closing books establish that motion is eternal, identify circular local motion as the first and only continuous kind, and conclude that there must be a first unmoved mover, without magnitude, as the source of all movement.
grc.aristotle.politics: Aristotle's Politics is a Greek philosophical treatise on the polis and the forms of association that constitute it. It opens by arguing that every polis is a natural community directed toward the good life and that man is by nature a political animal. From there the treatise treats the household and slavery, critiques earlier schemes for ideal states, classifies constitutions into kingship, aristocracy, polity, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny, and analyzes the deliberative, magisterial, and judicial parts of each. It then examines the causes of constitutional change and revolution and the means of political stability, and ends with the education of the citizen body, closing on the proper use of leisure and the ethical effects of music.
grc.aristotle.αριστοτέλους_φυσικά_προβλήματα: A large Greek collection of scientific and medical problems transmitted under Aristotle's name and of uncertain date, arranged by subject into series of short entries, each posed as a 'why?' question (dia ti) and followed by one or more attempted explanations. It opens with medical problems: why great excesses are diseased, why changes of season and of winds aggravate, judge, or cure illnesses, and why particular successions of weather bring fevers, eye inflammations, and epidemics. Later series range over mechanics and motion, including weighted knucklebones, the rolling of cylinders and cones, and the clepsydra, then over the rounded shapes of plant and animal parts, the priority of earlier and later and whether human affairs return in a cycle, sleep induced by reading, contentious argument, rhetoric, and the difference between philosopher and orator, and finally bodily matters such as the effects of rubbing and gymnastic practice, the sun's darkening or lightening of the skin, and the colouring of hair in old age or among seafarers.
grc.aristotle.φυσιογνωμονικά: A short Greek treatise on physiognomy preserved in the Aristotelian corpus and attributed to Aristotle, of uncertain date. It opens by arguing that mental dispositions accompany the states of the body, as drunkenness and illness show, so that bodily signs may reveal character. After defining the art and criticising earlier methods based on animal genera, individual body types, ethnic groups and transient passions, the main body of the work catalogues signs drawn from movement, shape, colour, hair, skin, voice and each part of the body, from feet to head, every sign being referred to an animal type or to male and female dispositions, as with the lion, the panther and the horse. It closes with remarks on bodily size and proportion and on which regions of the body, above all the face and eyes, yield the clearest signs.
grc.arrian.cynegeticus: Arrian's Cynegeticus is a short Greek prose treatise on hunting with hounds, framed as a supplement to Xenophon's work of the same name, whose omissions the author undertakes to supply. It opens with a list of chapters and an address to Xenophon son of Gryllus, noting that Xenophon did not know the Celtic breed of dogs or the Scythian and Libyan horses. The body of the work offers practical guidance on judging, feeding, exercising, tethering, and breeding hounds, above all the swift Celtic coursing dogs, and describes the pursuit of the hare without nets, the conduct of hunters on horseback and on foot, and Celtic and Libyan methods of taking larger game. It closes with injunctions to sacrifice to Artemis Agrotera and the other gods of hunting, illustrated with examples from Homer and a description of Celtic votive customs.
grc.bacchylides.dithyrambs: The Dithyrambs of the ancient Greek poet Bacchylides survive as a set of fragmentary choral songs, preserved largely in papyrus remains marked by extensive lacunae. The opening fragments, much broken, deal with the Greek expedition against Troy, naming Theano, Odysseus and Menelaus among the dramatis personae. Across the collection the poems move from Trojan narrative and gnomic reflection on Zeus, Justice and Hybris to episodes drawn from other myth cycles: Theseus carried by dolphins to the hall of Nereus, the birth of Dionysus to Semele at Cadmus' Thebes, and Idas' seizure of Marpessa at Sparta. Though the genre was rooted in choral song for Dionysus, the subjects treated here range well beyond the god's own legends.
grc.bacchylides.epinicians: The Epinicians gather the victory odes of the Greek lyric poet Bacchylides, songs in lyric metre composed for choruses in honour of victors at athletic contests. Each poem typically pairs praise of the victor, his family and his city with an extended mythological narrative drawn from heroic legend, as in an ode that opens with an address to the Pierian maidens and goes on to recount Minos' arrival with fifty ships and the Cretan host. Many of the odes are preserved only in fragmentary form, with long lacunae interrupting both metre and sense, while others survive as short excerpts.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.epistulae: A Greek collection of letters by Basil of Caesarea, the fourth-century bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. The correspondence opens with letters to Gregory of Nazianzus that recall their studies at Athens, question whether fortune and necessity rather than human choice govern events, and recount the writer's travels after leaving the city. A following letter defends withdrawal from the world, setting out the discipline of the solitary life in terms of silence, scriptural reading, prayer, fasting, simple diet, and night vigils as the means of purifying the soul. Elsewhere the collection ranges more widely, addressing friends, clergy, and civic officials on personal consolation, ascetic counsel, and the affairs of the church.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epitaphius: The Epitaphius Adonidis is a Greek bucolic lament for the dead Adonis, attributed to the poet Bion of Phlossa and of uncertain date. It opens with the repeated cry 'Woe for Adonis, fair Adonis is lost' as the Erotes take up the refrain and Cypris is roused from her couch to mourn her lover, gored in the thigh by a boar on the mountains. The poem then follows Aphrodite's frantic search through wood and crag, the weeping of nymphs, rivers, springs, flowers, and mountains, her address to the dying youth and to Persephone who detains him below, and the transformation of his blood into the rose and her tears into the anemone. It ends with Hymenaeus, the Charites, and the Moirai joining the mourning, and with the command that Cythera stay her cries for today, to weep again when a year has passed.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.epithalamium: A short fragmentary Greek epithalamium, or wedding song, in dactylic hexameters, attributed to the bucolic poet Bion of Phlossa and of uncertain date. It opens with a speaker asking why a sweet Sicilian pastoral melody of the kind Polyphemus once sang for Galatea is being performed, before turning to the story of Achilles on Skyros. The poem recounts Paris' abduction of Helen, the general muster of the Achaeans, and how Achilles alone lay hidden among the daughters of Lycomedes, disguised as a girl, performing women's work and sharing the chamber and bed of Deidameia, whom he addresses at night as his sole companion. The fragment breaks off mid-sentence as he begins a complaint that the crafty Nysaian, Dionysus, has wickedly parted him from her.
grc.callimachus.epigrams: Callimachus's Epigrams are a collection of short Greek poems, mostly in elegiac couplets, by Callimachus of Cyrene, a poet of the early third century BC active in Alexandria. The collection opens with an epigram in which a stranger consults the sage Pittacus on which of two prospective brides to choose, followed by laments for the poets Heraclitus of Halicarnassus and the cynic Timon. The rest of the corpus ranges over funerary verses for the drowned, the young, and the aged; votive epigrams recording offerings to Artemis, Demeter, Aphrodite, the Samothracian gods, and the Graces of Queen Berenice; and erotic and convivial pieces on boys, women, and the pains of love. Verse on poets and poetry recurs throughout, from praise of Aratus's subtle phrasing to the dismissal of the 'cyclic' poem and of everything hackneyed and public.
grc.callimachus.hecala: Callimachus' Hecale, an epic poem in Greek hexameters, survives only in fragments gathered with the ancient quotations and testimonia that transmit them. The collection opens with an epigram of Crinagoras praising the poem's celebration of Theseus' labours at Marathon. The surviving verses follow the hero's defeat of the Marathonian bull and the hospitality he receives from the poor old woman Hecale, with brief quotations, drawn largely from scholia and lexicographers, describing her household, her preparations for her guest, and her country speech. Later fragments trace a crow's narrative of its estrangement from Athena, Hecale's death and mourning, and the aetiology of the Athenian deme named in her honour.
grc.callimachus.hymns: The Hymns of Callimachus, a Hellenistic Greek poet, comprise six hexameter hymns in the Homeric manner, addressed to Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, Delos, Athena, and Demeter. The collection opens by asking what is fitting to sing of Zeus at libations, recounts his disputed birth and upbringing in Arcadia and Crete, and praises his gift of justice to kings. The remaining hymns mingle invocation with extended narrative: Apollo's titles and the slaying of Python alongside the founding of Cyrene; the child Artemis obtaining her privileges from Zeus and hunting in Arcadia; Leto's wandering before Hera until the drifting island Delos receives her and bears Apollo and Artemis; the Argive procession conducting Athena's image to her bath, which the young Tiresias unwittingly beholds; and Demeter's vengeance on Erysichthon, cursed with insatiable hunger for felling trees in her sacred grove. The last two hymns, in a literary Doric dialect, are composed as songs for ritual processions in honour of Athena and Demeter.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.μαθηματικὴ_σύνταξις: The Mathēmatikē Syntaxis ('Mathematical Treatise'), commonly known as the Almagest, is a comprehensive astronomical treatise in thirteen books by Claudius Ptolemy. The opening book contains a preface to Syrus on the place of mathematics among the theoretical sciences, followed by demonstrations that the heavens and the earth are spherical and that the earth lies motionless at the center of the cosmos. The remaining books supply the trigonometric and spherical astronomy on which the system rests, then treat solar and lunar theory with eclipse calculation, the fixed stars together with a catalog of their longitudes, latitudes, and magnitudes, and the motions of the five planets. Observational data, derivations, and numerical tables run throughout, and the treatise closes with an epilogue in which the author declares his account of the heavens complete.
grc.clement.exhortation: A short Greek Christian exhortation on the ordering of daily conduct, attributed to Clement and of uncertain date. It opens by urging quietness in word and deed, since a mind agitated by haste and passion falls prey to gluttony, anger, and the other passions. From there the instruction moves through bearing and speech, gentle address to those met, a voice measured to the hearers' need, listening and teaching in turn without envy or shyness, deference to elders, and firm refusal of falsehood, deceit, and insolence, to the reference of all works and words to God and Christ in constant prayer and hymnody by day and night. It closes with counsel on temperance in food and drink, freedom from anxiety for the body's needs, endurance under sickness, old age, and grief, and mercy towards the afflicted, in expectation of the coming of the Son of God, who restores good things to his own.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.protrepticus: The Protrepticus is an appeal to Greeks and other pagans to abandon their traditional religion and turn to Christianity, written in Greek by Clement of Alexandria, the Christian teacher of Alexandria. The work opens with the legend of Orpheus charming animals with his song, which Clement turns against the myths, arguing that the 'new song' of the divine Logos tames not beasts but humanity itself. It proceeds through a systematic exposure of Greek cult and myth, treating the mysteries of Demeter, Dionysus, and Cybele as scandalous fictions, the oracles as dead, the Olympic gods as deified men or shameful demons, and the philosophers' cosmologies as worship of the elements, while adducing Greek poets and philosophers themselves as witnesses for one true God. The argument culminates in an appeal to the Hebrew prophets and to the saving 'new song' of Christ, closing with a vision of the Christian mysteries that supersede the pagan ones and an urgent summons to conversion.
grc.demetrius.elocutione: A Greek treatise on prose composition and style, transmitted as Peri hermēneias (De Elocutione), attributed to Demetrius and of uncertain date. It opens by comparing the division of prose into clauses (kōla) with the division of poetry into metres, and explains how clauses and commata combine into periods. The work proceeds through the plain, grand, elegant, and forceful kinds of style, discussing rhythm and euphony, figures and similes, charm, jest, hyperbole, and allegory, word choice, and the guarded figure (eschematismenon), with illustrations drawn from Homer, Sappho, Plato, Xenophon, and other poets, philosophers, historians, and orators. It closes with remarks on smooth, hiatus-avoiding composition and on the ungraceful (acharis) in diction and arrangement.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_3: Attic forensic oration by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, fourth century BC, the third of his three speeches in the dispute with Aphobus, one of the guardians appointed under his father's will. It opens with the speaker recalling how easily he refuted Aphobus's falsehoods at the earlier trial and predicting that the present jury will likewise recognise the man's shamelessness. The speech as a whole is a defence in a suit for false witness that Aphobus brought against witnesses who had testified for Demosthenes in the inheritance case: the speaker maintains that their testimony, that Aphobus had acknowledged before the arbitrator that the slave Milyas had been freed by the speaker's father, was truthful, presses Aphobus's repeated refusal to submit the relevant household slaves to torture under challenge, reviews the provisions of the will, the eighty-mina dowry, the furniture and the house left unrented, and closes on the arbitrators' assessment of the loss at ten talents.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_2: An Athenian forensic speech in Greek, transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus as the second oration Against Boeotus. The speaker, contesting a claim on his deceased father's estate, argues that Boeotus and his brother Pamphilus were fraudulently passed off as the old man's sons through the machinations and perjury of their mother Plangon. He recounts his mother's first marriage and its dowry arrangements, the deceptive oath sworn at the Delphinium, his father's refusal to acknowledge the pair, and their forced introduction to the phrateres, presenting the whole inheritance dispute as the consequence of that deception.
grc.demosthenes.against_midias: Against Midias is a courtroom speech of the Athenian law courts, delivered by Demosthenes in prosecution of Midias on a charge of hubris arising from an assault committed against him while he was serving as chorēgos, or chorus-sponsor, at the Dionysia. It opens with the speaker telling the judges that Midias' insolence towards all the citizens is notorious and explaining how, after the assembly had condemned him in a probolē, he brought the matter to trial. The speech then sets the assault in the context of the festival, reads out the laws governing probolai and conduct during the Dionysia, and broadens into a sustained attack on Midias' whole career, taking in his dealings with Aristarchus and an inserted catalogue of his offences against individuals, the laws, and the gods, together with a warning against the wealthy friends who will come forward to intercede for him. It closes by urging the jury, now that the people have already voted against the defendant, to give a verdict that will vindicate the laws and preserve the security they afford to every citizen alike.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_30: A courtroom oration that opens with the speaker's account of his fruitless efforts to settle his differences first with Aphobus and then with Onetor, Aphobus' brother-in-law, before resorting to litigation. The case concerns Onetor's claim that a plot of land was pledged to him in lieu of the dowry of his sister, whom Aphobus married, and the speech argues that the dowry was never paid, that the supposed abandonment of the wife is a fiction since she openly lives with Aphobus, and that the pledge is a pretext to deprive the speaker of property recovered in his judgment against Aphobus. In support of these contentions the speaker arrays depositions and witnesses, presses offers to interrogate slave witnesses under torture, and builds a chronological argument from the dates of the marriage, the alleged abandonment, and the original lawsuit.
grc.demosthenes.against_phormio: A courtroom speech of the Demosthenic corpus, of uncertain date, spoken in an Athenian commercial court by the prosecuting merchant Chrysippus against Phormio over a maritime loan. It opens with an appeal for an impartial hearing, the speaker presenting himself as a complete layman who has long traded at the Athenian emporium without ever bringing suit there. The narrative recounts a loan of twenty minas for a voyage to the Pontus, the shipwreck of the vessel under the shipmaster Lampis, Phormio's claim that he repaid the gold in the Bosporus, and the speaker's arguments that the cargo was never laden as the contract required and that Lampis, having shared the money, later gave false testimony; contracts, witness statements, and laws are read out in support, the admissibility of the suit under the rules governing emporic agreements is defended, and an attempted arbitration before Theodotus is described. The speech closes with an accusation that Lampis illicitly exported grain to Acanthus during an Athenian shortage, a review of the speaker's services to the city in the grain trade, and an appeal to the jurors to protect lenders and the credit on which the emporium depends.
grc.demosthenes.against_polycles: A courtroom speech from classical Athens, attributed to Demosthenes, in which a trierarch prosecutes Polycles for refusing to take over his trireme when the speaker's term of service had expired. The speaker opens by arguing that the case concerns not the litigants alone but the whole city, since it touches the succession of ships and whether the laws are binding. The body of the speech recounts his outfitting and manning of the vessel at his own expense, his prolonged service under the general Timomachus in the Hellespont and northern Aegean, the escort of grain convoys, the episode involving Callippus and the exiled Callistratus, and his repeated, witnessed attempts to hand the ship over to Polycles at Thasos and Tenedos. It closes with the reading of laws, decrees, and testimony, a detailed reckoning of expenditures, and a plea for reimbursement and for punishment of a citizen who defied the rules of succession.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_2: A short forensic speech, attributed to Demosthenes, spoken in an Athenian prosecution for false witness against Stephanus, arising out of the dispute between Apollodorus and Phormion over the estate of the banker Pasion. The speech opens with the speaker anticipating Stephanus' defence that his testimony bore only on part of what was written in the document at issue. It goes on to argue that Stephanus swore falsely in attesting that the document held by Phormion contained copies of Pasion's wills, and it reads out a series of statutes, on wills made by men with legitimate sons, on heiresses and their adjudication, on betrothal and marriage, and on witness procedure, to show that Pasion could not lawfully have disposed of his property as alleged and that the testimony contravened the laws. The closing appeal urges the judges to punish a witness who testified falsely and against the law.
grc.demosthenes.against_timocrates: An Athenian forensic speech transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus, the 'Against Timocrates' is a public prosecution for proposing an illegal law (graphē paranomōn). It opens in mid-argument before a jury, the prosecutor declaring that Timocrates himself, having brought in a law 'contrary to the laws' in order to defraud the city of money it was about to recover, is the sole cause of the trial. The measure under attack would allow citizens condemned to state imprisonment for unpaid fines, whether sacred, public, or owed to the goddesses, to obtain release by furnishing sureties, thereby annulling verdicts already rendered and undermining the courts, the council, and the city's finances. The orator, an associate of Euctemon in earlier actions against Androtion and his circle, first rehearses those prosecutions and the embezzlement of sacred funds, then expounds the statutory procedure for legislation that Timocrates flouted, shows point by point that the new measure contradicts standing statutes on theft, mistreatment of parents, and military desertion, and closes with digressions on Androtion's public record, the melting down of dedicatory crowns for phialai, Athenian statesmen who submitted to imprisonment, the Locrian practice of legislating with a halter around the neck, and Solon's comparison of the laws to the city's coinage.
grc.demosthenes.exordia: A collection of exordia for speeches to the Athenian assembly transmitted under the name of the orator Demosthenes. The opening piece presents a speaker who rises only after others have had their say, ready to add counsel where their advice has fallen short. The remaining preambles, nearly all addressed to 'men of Athens', work through a recurrent repertoire of themes: that the assembly should hear all who wish to advise, that speakers should keep to the matter at hand instead of trading abuse, that policy demands preparation and means rather than confident words, and that politicians who flatter the demos for private gain are its worst enemies. The pieces stand as free-standing openings that could precede almost any deliberative speech, and several touch on the diplomatic affairs of the day, including relations with Sparta, Arcadia, Mytilene, Rhodes and Philip of Macedon.
grc.demosthenes.for_phormio: A forensic speech in the Demosthenic corpus, delivered in an Athenian court for the defence of Phormion, the former slave and business manager to whom the banker Pasion had leased his bank and shield factory and afterwards left his widow and the guardianship of his younger son. The opening concedes that Phormion is inarticulate, so that his friends undertake to instruct the judges in the case. The argument then traces the whole history of the affair: the terms of Pasion's lease and will, the division of the estate between Apollodorus and his brother Pasicles, the earlier suit and arbitration, Apollodorus' formal release of all claims upon payment, and the plea that a suit brought after such a release is inadmissible, supported by the reading of contracts, laws and testimony. Along the way it recounts Apollodorus' income and expenditure, defends with precedents the marriage of a banker's widow to a freedman, and closes with an appeal that the judges save a man who has proved useful to the city and to many of its citizens.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_2: The Second Olynthiac is a short deliberative oration by Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian assembly amid the war between Olynthus and Philip of Macedon. It opens by treating the emergence of peoples willing to fight Philip, above all the Olynthians, as a manifest sign of the gods' goodwill toward Athens. The bulk of the speech argues that a power built on perjury, deception and injustice must soon collapse, cataloguing Philip's betrayals of Amphipolis, Potidaea, the Thessalians and the Phocians, and probing the weakness of his kingdom, the hardship and resentment of his subjects and soldiers, and the disreputable circle of flatterers around him. Turning to Athens, it rebukes the citizens' idleness, their hesitancy over contributions and personal service, and the partisan conduct of the symmories, before closing with practical proposals: an embassy to the Thessalians, contributions from all according to their means, and common, resolute prosecution of the war.
grc.demosthenes.on_organization: A short deliberative speech of the fourth-century Athenian orator Demosthenes, addressed to the assembly and known as On Organization. It opens with the question of the public money and the two-obol payments that have occasioned the meeting, arguing that neither censuring the proposers nor counselling acceptance matters unless the citizens couple receipt of the dole with the organized mustering of the city's forces. The speaker then urges that hoplites, cavalry and all the rest be enrolled in a single trained body under a general of their own choosing, surveys the misdirection of public funds and the growth of private luxury, and contrasts the modest houses and unclaimed exploits of the men of Salamis and Marathon with the honours heaped on contemporary commanders and the grants of citizenship to corrupt foreigners. The speech closes with the claims that the city's safety lies in arms rather than in the lawcourts and that the citizens themselves, not the politicians who court them, determine the character of the state.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_chersonese: A deliberative oration of Demosthenes, addressed to the Athenian Assembly amid Philip of Macedon's campaigns in Thrace and the Athenian command of Diopeithes in the Chersonese. It opens with the speaker asking that those who address the people speak from judgement of the city's interest rather than from enmity or favour. The greater part of the speech argues that Philip is already at war with Athens whatever his denials, surveys his encroachments in Thrace, Euboea and the Hellespont, and defends Diopeithes against the accusations that threaten to dissolve his force. Demosthenes attacks the Athenians' ease-loving inaction and the orators who paralyse policy by prosecuting patriotic advisers, urges payment of the war tax, maintenance of the standing army and embassies to warn the Greeks, and closes with a defence of his own courage as a citizen and a summary of his proposals.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_crown: A forensic oration in Greek by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, spoken in the trial over Ctesiphon's decree awarding Demosthenes a golden crown, a decree Aeschines had prosecuted as illegal. It opens with a prayer that the judges grant the speaker the same goodwill he has shown the city, before he undertakes to answer Aeschines' slanders and give an account of his whole public life. The greater part of the speech reviews that career in opposition to Philip of Macedon: the Peace of Philocrates and the embassies, the delay over the oaths, the Amphictyonic quarrel at Amphissa that gave Philip his opening in Greece, the alliance with Thebes, and the war that ended in defeat, argued through the reading of decrees, Philip's letters, and witnesses. Demosthenes then defends the legality of the crown decree, maintains that the Theban alliance was the city's finest policy, and closes with sustained invective against Aeschines' parentage, theatrical career, and public conduct, ending in a prayer to the gods.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_false_embassy: Demosthenes' 'On the False Embassy' is a forensic speech delivered in an Athenian court at the scrutiny of Aeschines, prosecuting his former fellow ambassador for bribery and misconduct on the embassies sent to Philip of Macedon. It opens by urging the jurors to be swayed by their oath and by justice rather than by the supplications of the defendant's friends. The body of the speech recalls Aeschines' early denunciations of Philip, narrates the negotiations for the peace of Philocrates and the second embassy, and charges that Aeschines gave false reports, wasted crucial time, took bribes, and betrayed Phocis, Thrace, the Hellespont and the Pylae, calling the other ambassadors as witnesses and reading out letters of Philip. Its closing sections anticipate and answer counter-arguments, including a threatened prosecution by Charidemus, treat Aeschines' acting career and famed voice as irrelevant to his public conduct, and press for a conviction that will serve as a warning to corrupt envoys.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_1: The First Philippic is a deliberative speech of Demosthenes addressed to the Athenian assembly concerning Philip of Macedon. It opens with the speaker defending his decision to rise and speak first, since the habitual advisers have offered nothing to the point. The speech argues that Athens' setbacks stem from negligence rather than from Philip's strength, recalling the city's past success against Sparta when it attended to its affairs, and it attacks the habit of reacting to the enemy only after news of each fresh outrage. The greater part sets out a detailed program of permanent preparedness, fifty triremes, ten fast vessels, cavalry, and a standing force of two thousand men including five hundred Athenian citizens serving in rotation, to campaign continuously under an accountable general with specified pay and revenues, closing with an appeal to the Athenians to vote the measures and wage war in deeds and not merely in decrees.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_3: The third of Demosthenes' Philippics, a deliberative speech delivered in the Athenian assembly warning that Philip of Macedon, whatever his professions of peace, is already at war with the Greeks. It opens with the complaint that endless talk since the peace has let affairs drift toward ruin, and the speaker then undertakes to show that Philip's seizure of cities and territories, from Olynthus and Phocis to Thessaly, Euboea and the Chersonese, amounts to open war. Contrasting the old Athenian severity toward bribed traitors, as recorded on the bronze stele against Arthmius of Zeleia, with the present corruption of Greek politics by Macedonian gold, he recounts how Olynthus, Eretria and Oreus fell through heeding Philip's partisans rather than their own defenders. The speech closes by urging the Athenians to arm and equip themselves, send embassies to the Peloponnese, Rhodes, Chios and the Persian King, and take up the defence of Greek freedom.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_4: A deliberative speech in Attic Greek attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes and transmitted among his Philippics, the orations directed against Philip II of Macedon. The speaker opens by announcing that he will say what he judges advantageous for the city, lamenting that the Athenians' opinions have drifted away from the realities of the situation. The body of the speech rehearses Philip's successive encroachments, in Thrace, at Euboea, Megara, Olynthus and Cardia, to argue that Philip has already broken the peace and is at war with Athens and above all with its democracy, and it denounces both the citizens' indolence and the politicians who take Philip's pay. It closes by urging steady military and financial preparation, including the reallocation of the theoric funds and an embassy to the Persian King, and by warning that unless the Athenians mend their ways the whole of Greece will fall into servitude.
grc.diogenianus_of_heraclea.παροιμίαι_δημώδε: A Greek paroemiographical compilation of popular proverbs presented as drawn from the collection (synagōgē) of Diogenianus of Heraclea, a writer of uncertain date. The work opens with a short treatise on proverbs, discussing the term's etymology and definition, its kinship with the ainos or fable, and the varieties of Aesopian, Carian, Sybaritic, Cyprian and Libyan sayings, with illustrative verses from poets such as Archilochus and Aristophanes. The bulk of the work is an alphabetical catalogue running from alpha to the end of the Greek alphabet, in which each proverb is glossed with its sense ('said of...') and commonly supplied with an explanatory story drawn from myth, history, comedy or everyday life, from the gardens of Adonis and Midas' ass's ears to the oracle given Philip about silver spears. Cross-references to kindred sayings recur throughout, and quotations from authors such as Plato, Menander, Solon and Lucian are woven into the explanations.
grc.dionysius_calliphontis.dionysii_callipho: The Descriptio Graeciae, a short description of Greece attributed to Dionysius son of Calliphon and of uncertain date, opens with a preface addressed to Theophrastus, in which the author announces a rapid account of the whole of Hellas, its cities, groves, rivers, islands and harbours. The surviving work then proceeds as a periegesis beginning at Ambracia on the Ambracian gulf, moving through Acarnania, Aetolia, Locris and Phocis, where Delphi, Parnassus and the Corycian cave are described, and on through Boeotia, with Thebes, Plataea, Lebadeia and the oracle of Trophonius, to Megara and the approaches of the Peloponnese. Places are listed along the coast and inland with their sanctuaries, mountains, rivers, ports and distances in stades, in a compressed itinerary style. The preserved text is damaged, marked by lacunae and an interrupted sequence that resumes with the description of Crete.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isocrate: Dionysius of Halicarnassus's essay On Isocrates opens with a summary biography of the orator, covering his Athenian birth, his schooling under Gorgias, Prodicus and Tisias, his turn from public speaking to the writing of political speeches for want of boldness and voice, his long career as a teacher, and his death shortly after the battle of Chaeronea at nearly a hundred years of age.
