The discussion then weighs Isocrates against Lysias, crediting him with purity, grandeur and a periodic, quasi-poetic rhythm of diction while judging him inferior to Lysias in charm, concision and fitness for the lawcourts, yet superior in the arrangement and philosophical bearing of his subject matter. Individual speeches, the Panegyricus, the address to Philip, On the Peace, the Areopagiticus and the Archidamus, are surveyed, criticisms of his ornate and mannered style by earlier writers are reported, and the essay ends with extended specimens, the exordium of On the Peace and the forensic Trapeziticus, each analysed for what it shows of the orator's manner.
grc.epictetus.discourses: The Discourses (Diatribai) of Epictetus, a Stoic philosopher of the first and second centuries AD, were recorded in Greek by his pupil Arrian, whose prefatory letter opens the work by explaining that he transcribed his master's lectures from memory as notes for his own use. The surviving discourses, presented as dialogues between Epictetus and unnamed visitors or questioners, develop Stoic ethics chiefly through the distinction between what lies within our power, above all the faculty of choice, and what does not, covering topics such as providence, freedom, friendship, purity, and the proper conduct of argument, and repeatedly illustrating their points with examples drawn from Socrates, Diogenes, and figures of Roman public life.
grc.epictetus.enchiridion: The Enchiridion is a compact Greek manual of Stoic ethical teaching by the philosopher Epictetus, arranged as a sequence of very short chapters. It opens with the division between things that are and are not 'in our power,' grounding freedom and happiness in judgment, impulse, and desire alone. The remaining chapters gather precepts on the handling of impressions, on desire and aversion, on meeting death, loss, and insult with equanimity, on the duties arising from familial and social roles, on piety toward the gods and the proper use of divination, and on conduct in speech, company, and daily life. Later material treats the character and progress of the aspiring philosopher, placing practice above theoretical demonstration, and the work closes with verses on following Zeus and providence willingly.
grc.epicurus.epistula_ad_herodotum: The Epistula ad Herodotum is a letter of the philosopher Epicurus, one of three letters and a set of principal doctrines transmitted by Diogenes Laertius, addressed to a correspondent named Herodotus. It opens by explaining its purpose: to provide an epitome of Epicurus's writings on nature so that those unable to work through the longer books may retain the most important doctrines in memory. The body of the letter expounds Epicurean physics in sequence, covering the criteria of knowledge, the eternity of the whole, bodies and void, indestructible atoms moving in an infinite universe, the birth and dissolution of innumerable worlds, the role of images in vision, hearing and smell, the soul as a fine-parted mortal body, qualities, accidents and time, the natural origin of language, and celestial phenomena explained by multiple possible causes rather than divine agency. It concludes by directing attention back to sense-perceptions and feelings, through which fears concerning the gods and death are dispelled and tranquility of life secured.
grc.epicurus.gnomologium_vaticanum_epicureum: The Gnomologium Vaticanum Epicureum is a Greek collection of some eighty short Epicurean sayings, attributed to Epicurus and transmitted in a Vatican manuscript, its compilation being of uncertain date. It opens with the aphorism that the blessed and immortal being neither has troubles of its own nor gives them to others. The remaining maxims cover death, pain, and pleasure; the classification of desires; friendship, justice, and mutual trust; fate, necessity, and dreams; and the wealth, freedom, self-sufficiency, and plain living that philosophy makes possible. Several sayings are addressed directly to individual friends, and the collection closes with reflections on the wise man's freedom from disturbance.
grc.euclid.elements: Euclid's Elements is a Greek mathematical treatise that sets out geometry as a deductive system. It begins with definitions of the point, line, straight line, surface, plane, angle, circle, and rectilineal figures, together with five postulates and five common notions. The body of the work consists of propositions, each stated as a construction or theorem and accompanied by a formal proof; the opening propositions give elementary constructions, such as the equilateral triangle erected on a given straight line and the transfer of a length to a given point.
grc.euripides.alcestis: Alcestis is a Greek tragedy by Euripides that opens with Apollo recounting how he served Admetus, king of Pherae, and tricked the Fates into allowing him to escape death on condition that a substitute die in his place, a role the king's wife Alcestis has accepted. The action follows Admetus as Alcestis bids farewell to her household and dies, as he quarrels with his aged father Pheres, who refused to die for him, and as he receives the visiting Heracles into his house amid preparations for the funeral. Learning whose death he has intruded upon, Heracles wrestles Death at Alcestis' tomb and leads back a veiled woman, who is revealed to Admetus as his wife restored to life.
grc.euripides.andromache: Euripides' Andromache is a tragedy that opens with Andromache, Hector's widow, enslaved after the fall of Troy to Achilles' son Neoptolemus, taking refuge at the altar of Thetis as the Spartan Hermione, Neoptolemus' barren wife, threatens to kill her and her child Molossus. Menelaus, arriving in support of his daughter, seizes the boy as a hostage and forces Andromache from her sanctuary, but Peleus intervenes and drives him off. A messenger then reports that Neoptolemus has been killed at Delphi through the scheming of Orestes, who arrives and carries Hermione away to Sparta. After Peleus mourns over his grandson's corpse, Thetis appears from above to command the burial at Delphi, the marriage of Andromache to Helenus, the continuation of the Molossian royal line, and her own reunion with the now immortalized Peleus.
grc.euripides.bacchae: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, dramatising the arrival of the god Dionysus in Thebes and the resistance to him of the young king Pentheus. The play opens with Dionysus, in mortal disguise, declaring his intention to prove his divinity and punish the house of Cadmus for denying that Zeus fathered him on Semele. Pentheus imprisons the disguised god, who escapes as the palace is destroyed by miracles, and a messenger then reports both the wondrous rites of the Theban women on Mount Cithaeron and their savage attacks on the local settlements. Lured by Dionysus, Pentheus dresses as a woman to spy on the rites, is led to Cithaeron, and is torn apart by the maddened maenads, his mother Agaue returning in triumph with his head; the recognition of her deed, the exile of Cadmus and Harmonia, and Dionysus' final pronouncement of their transformation into serpents close the play.
grc.euripides.cyclops: The Cyclops is the only satyr drama to survive complete from Greek tragedy, Euripides' comic treatment of the episode in the Odyssey in which Odysseus blinds the man-eating Polyphemus. It opens with Silenus, who with his sons the Satyrs has passed from the service of Dionysus into slavery as the Cyclops' herdsman beneath Mount Aetna, lamenting his situation. When Odysseus and his crew, storm-driven from Troy, arrive seeking provisions, Silenus trades cheese and lambs for wine; Polyphemus returns, rejects the Greeks' appeal to the obligations of hospitality, and cooks and devours two of the sailors. Odysseus refuses to flee without his companions, gets the giant drunk with a potent wine of Dionysus under the assumed name Nobody, burns out his single eye with a heated stake, and escapes by ship, while the Cyclops recalls an oracle of his blinding and the Satyrs go over to the service of Bacchus.
grc.euripides.fragmenta: A collection of sententiae and detached iambic and lyric passages attributed to Euripides, preserving single lines and short segments from lost tragedies together with a few longer fragments, among them substantial portions of the Melanippe plays, a chorus in honour of Peace, the opening of a play about Danaë and Acrisius, and sections of the Alexandros, the Aeolus, the Andromeda, and the Autolycus. It opens with an interchange of brief gnomic utterances on such themes as poverty, nobility, slavery, wealth, and the power of Aphrodite and Love, and proceeds as a series of quotations, often headed by play titles, drawn from every part of the dramatic corpus: laments, reflections on fortune and necessity, political and moral maxims, lyrics on the seasons and the sea, and dramatic scenes of recognition and crisis, including the athletic fragment on athletes, the sceptical monologue of Sisyphus, and a long exhortation of a dying father to his son.
grc.euripides.hecuba: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, probably first performed in the years following the Athenian expedition against Macedonia, though its exact date is uncertain. The play opens with the ghost of Polydorus, the youngest son of Priam and Hecuba, who recounts how his Thracian guest-friend Polymestor murdered him for the gold sent with him from Troy. Hecuba, enslaved among the victorious Greeks, then learns that her daughter Polyxena is to be sacrificed on the tomb of Achilles, and after the discovery of Polydorus' washed-up corpse she exacts a brutal revenge on Polymestor, blinding him and killing his two sons. The drama concludes with a trial scene before Agamemnon, in which Polymestor defends his crime and in turn prophesies Hecuba's transformation and the murder of Agamemnon by Clytemnestra.
grc.euripides.helen: A Greek tragedy by Euripides, in which Helen, speaking at the tomb of Proteus beside the Nile, explains in the prologue how Hermes carried her to Egypt while a phantom likeness of her went to Troy with Paris, and how she now dreads being forced into marriage by Proteus's son Theoclymenus. Teucer passes through, and a shipwrecked Menelaus arrives; husband and wife recognize one another, and the seer Theonoe, Theoclymenus's sister, confirms that the report of Menelaus's death is false. Feigning that the castaway comes to announce his own end, they obtain a ship from the king for funeral rites at sea and escape, though the deception is soon discovered; the Dioscuri then appear, restrain Theoclymenus from killing Theonoe, and foretell for Helen divine honors and for Menelaus a dwelling on the Isles of the Blessed.
grc.euripides.heracleidae: A tragedy by Euripides in iambic trimeter with lyric passages, staged in Athens at the altar of Zeus Agoraios where the children of Heracles, fugitives pursued by Eurystheus, take sanctuary. The play follows the refugees' appeal to Demophon and Acamas, the oracle demanding the sacrifice of a maiden, the self-offering of Macaria, the aged Iolaus arming himself for battle, the defeat of Eurystheus through Iolaus' miraculous rejuvenation, and the closing dispute over the captive king's life in which Alcmene condemns him while Hyllus insists on sparing him, Eurystheus then prophesying that his tomb will protect Athens against the descendants of these children.
grc.euripides.hippolytus: Euripides' Greek tragedy Hippolytus opens with Aphrodite announcing from above her resolve to destroy the chaste Hippolytus, son of Theseus, because he honors Artemis and scorns her. The action then follows Phaedra's anguished and carefully concealed passion for her stepson, the nurse's fatal betrayal of the secret, and Phaedra's suicide, which leaves a written charge accusing Hippolytus of assaulting her. Believing the dying woman, Theseus curses his son with one of the three wishes Poseidon had granted him, and a monstrous bull from the sea terrifies Hippolytus' horses, dragging him to a mortal injury, after which Artemis reveals Phaedra's innocence and the young man's purity, consoles him as he dies, promises him enduring cult honors at Troezen, and reconciles him with his repentant father.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_tauris: A Greek tragedy by Euripides in which Iphigenia, spirited away by Artemis at the moment of her sacrifice at Aulis, serves unwillingly as priestess among the Taurians, a land whose king, Thoas, obliges her to put Greek castaways to death on the goddess's altar. It opens with her expository prologue recounting her lineage, the events at Aulis, her rescue by Artemis, and an ominous dream concerning her brother Orestes. Orestes and Pylades then arrive, sent by Apollo to steal the statue of Artemis from the temple, are captured and brought forward for sacrifice, and are recognized through the letter Iphigenia means to send to Argos; brother and sister contrive an escape disguised as a purification rite by the sea, carrying the statue with them. At the close Athena's epiphany halts Thoas's pursuit, secures safe passage for Orestes and the image, and ordains the cult of Artemis Tauropolos in Attica together with Iphigenia's service in the Brauronian rites.
grc.euripides.orestes: A tragedy in Greek by Euripides, first performed in 408 BC, dramatizing the fate of Orestes after his murder of Clytemnestra. It opens with Electra's prologue recounting the house of Atreus and Orestes' affliction by the Furies as he lies ill and awaits the Argive assembly's vote on his death. The drama follows the failed appeals to Menelaus, Orestes' condemnation, his attempted suicide pact with Electra, the seizure of Hermione as a hostage, the murder of Helen (averted by her deification), the burning of the palace, and Apollo's final appearance fixing Orestes' marriage to Hermione and his eventual trial at Athens.
grc.euripides.phoenissae: A Greek tragedy of uncertain date by Euripides, dramatizing the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices for the throne of Thebes. It opens with Jocasta's prologue tracing the misfortunes of the house of Cadmus down to Oedipus, as the Argive host musters before the city. The play then follows Antigone's survey of the seven champions from the walls, the oracle demanding the death of Creon's son Menoeceus, the repulse of the assault, and the mutual fratricide of the brothers in single combat, over which Jocasta kills herself. Creon's edict denying Polynices burial, Antigone's open resolve to defy it, and the departure of the blind Oedipus into exile toward Colonus bring the drama to its end.
grc.euripides.rhesus: Rhesus is a Greek tragedy transmitted among the plays of Euripides, though both its authorship and its date are disputed. It draws its story from the tenth year of the Trojan War and opens at night in the Trojan camp, where Hector, alarmed by Greek beacon fires, sends the scout Dolon to spy on the enemy ships in return for a promised reward. The action then follows Dolon's death at the hands of Odysseus and Diomedes, the late arrival of the Thracian king Rhesus as a Trojan ally, the pair's nocturnal raid in which Rhesus is slaughtered in his sleep and his famous white horses carried off, and the bitter recriminations between Hector and the Thracian charioteer over the disaster. The play closes with the entrance of the Muse, Rhesus' mother, who mourns her son, foretells his transformation into an underground power dwelling in a Thracian cave and Achilles' coming death, before Hector leads the Trojans off to arm for battle at dawn.
grc.euripides.trojan_women: A Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatising the immediate aftermath of the fall of Troy. It opens with Poseidon surveying the ruined city, describing Priam's death at the altar of Zeus and the Trojan women gathered as captives before the gates, among them Hecuba. The action follows the allotment of the captive women to their Greek masters, including Andromache, assigned to Achilles' son, alongside Cassandra's prophetic outbursts, the debate between Menelaus and Helen, and the killing of the child Astyanax. It ends with Hecuba and the chorus lamenting the burning of the city as they are led away to servitude in Greece.
grc.flavius_josephus.antiquitates_judaicae: Antiquitates Judaicae ('Jewish Antiquities') is a twenty-book historical work in Greek prose by Flavius Josephus, written after the author had separately composed his account of the Jewish war against Rome. In its preface Josephus explains that the work sets out the whole ancient history and constitution of the Jewish people, rendered from the Hebrew writings into Greek, and that its completion was urged by his patron Epaphroditus. The narrative runs from the creation of the world and the laws attributed to Moses through the biblical and later periods, carrying the account down to the final years before the war with Rome.
grc.flavius_josephus.josephi_vita: The Vita is a short Greek autobiography by Flavius Josephus, composed as an appendix defending his conduct during the Jewish War. It opens with a genealogy tracing his priestly and Hasmonaean descent, followed by an account of his education, his examination of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, and an embassy to Rome on behalf of imprisoned priests. The greater part of the work narrates his command in Galilee at the outbreak of the revolt, his feuds with John of Gischala and Justus of Tiberias, and his maneuvering among the cities and factions of the region. It closes with a polemic against Justus's history, an account of Josephus's fortunes under Vespasian, Titus, and Domitian, and a valediction to his patron Epaphroditus.
grc.gaius_romanus.fragmenta: Greek fragments attributed to Gaius, a Roman church writer of uncertain date, transmitted in the quotations of Eusebius's Ecclesiastical History and preserving part of the dialogue he held with Proclus, a champion of the Phrygian or Montanist heresy. The collection opens with Eusebius's report that Proclus concurred in an earlier discussion of the death of Philip and his daughters, whose tombs lay at Hierapolis in Asia. In the surviving exchange Gaius points to the 'trophies' of the apostles who founded the Roman church at the Vatican and on the Ostian road, enumerates only thirteen epistles of Paul apart from that to the Hebrews, and reproves Cerinthus for teaching an earthly kingdom of Christ and fleshly pleasures in Jerusalem after the resurrection. Further passages recount how Natalius, a confessor who accepted a salaried bishopric from the disciples of Theodotus the cobbler, was flogged through the night by angels and crawled back to communion with bishop Zephyrinus, and how the same heretics emended the divine scriptures while placing their confidence in the syllogisms of Aristotle, the geometry of Euclid and the authority of Galen rather than in the ancient rule of faith.
grc.galen.de_atra_bile: Galen's Greek treatise On Black Bile (De Atra Bile) sets out the nature, generation, and pathological effects of the melancholic humour within the four-humour framework of ancient medicine. It opens by surveying earlier treatments of the subject, praising Hippocrates' useful brevity and censuring Erasistratus for passing over the humours altogether. The work then distinguishes black bile from blood, phlegm, and yellow bile by its sensible qualities and its failure to coagulate, explains its production in hot and dry bodies, seasons, climates, and diets, and traces the disorders it causes, including melancholy, cancers, carbuncles, haemorrhoids, and varicose veins, with attention to the spleen's role in drawing off the sediment of the blood. A sustained polemic against Erasistratus and the newer sectarian physicians defends the presence of all four humours in the body, the selective action of purgative drugs such as hellebore, and the necessity of humoral theory to the practice of the medical art.
grc.galen.de_dignoscendis_pulsibus: De Dignoscendis Pulsibus ('On the Diagnosis of Pulses') is a Greek medical treatise by the physician Galen dealing with how the pulse is to be recognised and distinguished by touch. The work presents itself as the second of four parts of a complete account of pulse theory, the first part covering the genera and species of pulses, the third their causes, and the fourth their significance for practice, a division it argues has left diagnosis comparatively neglected by both philosophers and physicians. It maintains that accurate diagnosis of diastole, systole, and the differing qualities, rhythms, and uniformity of the arterial beat demands many years of disciplined practice, and it illustrates this claim from Galen's own experience as a young student of medicine and his slow attainment of certainty in distinguishing the movements of the artery.
grc.galen.de_dignotione_ex_insomniis: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on diagnosis from dreams, transmitted under the title De Dignotione ex Insomniis. It opens by setting out dream images with their humoral correspondences: fire betokens yellow bile, smoke or darkness black bile, rain cold moisture, and snow, crystal or hail cold phlegm, with due regard to the timing of the dream within an illness and to food recently eaten. The discussion then turns to the difficulty of separating dreams that arise from the body from those that recall daily occupations and cares or carry mantic foreknowledge, illustrated by anecdotes such as the dreamer whose leg seemed stone and was later paralysed and the wrestler who appeared to stand in a pool of blood, signifying plethora. Dreams of drinking, eating and intercourse are read as signs of thirst, hunger and seminal abundance, and the closing explanation holds that in sleep the soul enters the depths of the body and perceives its condition, so that visions of burdens, of running or flying, of foul or sweet smells and of wallowing in filth correspond to the quantity, lightness and corruption of the prevailing humours.
grc.galen.de_methodo_medendi: De Methodo Medendi ('On the Method of Healing') is a Greek treatise on therapeutics by Galen. Its opening section takes the form of a preface addressed to Hiero, in which the author explains his long hesitation to write on the therapeutic method, complains of an age in which patients favour obsequious and flattering physicians over the truly skilful, and delivers an extended invective against Thessalus, who professed to teach medicine in six months and vilified Hippocrates and the ancient Asclepiads. The preface also recalls the old rivalry among the medical schools of Cos, Cnidus and Italy, illustrating its argument with quotations from Hesiod on the two kinds of strife.
grc.galen.de_optima_doctrina: A Greek polemical treatise by Galen against the doctrine, associated with Favorinus, that the best teaching consists in arguing with equal force on both sides of every question. The opening reports Favorinus' account of the Academic suspension of judgment, older and newer, and his claim that pupils may judge opposing arguments without first learning any criterion of knowledge. The argument then contends that nature has furnished all people with trustworthy criteria in the senses and the intellect, that without these neither teacher nor pupil can judge anything, and that Favorinus contradicts himself in his own writings on the cataleptic impression. Its closing pages liken the teacher to a trainer or craftsman who corrects a learner's errors while leaving his natural faculties intact, and restate Galen's promise to equip pupils with the instruments and criteria by which true accounts are found and false ones detected.
grc.galen.de_ossibus_ad_tirones: De Ossibus ad Tirones ('On Bones, for Beginners') is a short Greek treatise on osteology by Galen. It opens by arguing that a physician must know each bone in itself and in its arrangement with the others if he is to treat fractures and dislocations correctly, then defines the skeleton and the technical vocabulary of its connections: arthrosis and symphysis, the kinds and subdivisions of each, the forms of synarthrosis (suture, gomphosis, harmonia), and the unions made through cartilage, sinew or flesh, with a corresponding distinction among nerves, tendons and ligaments. The preliminary definitions concluded, the treatise proceeds to the bones individually, beginning with the skull.
grc.galen.de_rebus_boni_malique_suci: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, known under the Latin title De rebus boni malique suci ('On the Good and Bad Juices'). It opens with an account of successive famines in provinces subject to Rome, describing the diseases, skin sores of many kinds, fevers, dysentery and mental disturbance, that arose when people were driven to eat unwholesome foods, and argues from such observations for the Hippocratic doctrine that diseased bodily humours are the cause of illness. It closes with an autobiographical passage in which Galen recounts his father's supervision of his diet in childhood, the recurring autumnal illnesses of his youth, and the regimen of moderation and exercise that he holds responsible for his continued good health.
grc.galen.de_semine: This treatise in Greek, attributed to Galen and preserved in the Kühn edition of his works, examines the nature, origin, and function of semen in both sexes. It opens with the question whether semen contributes only an efficient principle of generation, as Aristotle held, or also a material one, as Hippocrates supposed, and undertakes to decide the dispute by observation and dissection rather than plausible argument. The work marshals evidence from experiments on animals, from the testimony of women, and from anatomical dissections of pregnant beasts to show that the male seed remains within the womb, that females likewise emit semen, and that both parents contribute to the bodily substance of the embryo; it then traces embryonic development through its successive stages, the formation of the membranes and principal organs, and the causes of resemblance to either parent, while repeatedly refuting Aristotle, Athenaeus, Herophilus, and other earlier authorities on the generative parts, including the disputed role of the testes and spermatic vessels.
grc.galen.de_typis: Galen's short Greek treatise On Types (De typis) opens with the author remarking that many have treated the theory of periodicity in disease more diffusely, and announcing his intention to give a briefer, more sharply defined account, suited to newcomers to medicine. The work defines a typos as the ordered alternation of exacerbation and remission in an illness, observes that most diseases but above all fevers exhibit such periodicity, and distinguishes first from second, standing from moving, and simple from compound types. Its main body characterises the quotidian, tertian, quartan and semitertian fevers in turn, setting out their symptoms, pulses, attendant signs, seasonal prevalence, dangers and duration, with quotations from Hippocrates and a report of Agathinus's differing explanation of the semitertian's name. A concluding section treats doubled types and the ways in which quotidian, tertian, quartan and quintan fevers may be interwoven, illustrated by a worked example of a recurring daily pattern of exacerbations and remissions.
grc.galen.de_venereis_ap_oribasium: A short Greek treatise on sexual intercourse, attributed to Galen and transmitted among the excerpts of Oribasius. It opens by rejecting the Epicurean position that sexual activity is never beneficial to health, arguing instead that intercourse at sufficiently long intervals leaves a person feeling lighter and freer in breathing. The discussion then sets out the proper timing and bodily conditions for intercourse, neither overfull nor deficient, neither overheated nor chilled, and describes its contrary effects on strong and weak constitutions, including the exhaustion, feverishness and melancholy that can attend either excess or retention of semen. It closes with corrective measures for those harmed by abstinence or overindulgence: preparatory exercise, cold baths when the season permits, and a lighter, moister, moderately warming diet.
grc.galen.quos_quibus_catharticis_medicament: A Greek therapeutic treatise by Galen, the second-century CE physician, on which patients ought to be purged with which cathartic drugs and at what time. It opens by observing that purging healthy bodies is laborious and quickly weakening, since the drug, seeking its proper humour, finds the blood wanting and melts the flesh instead. The treatise then matches the humours requiring evacuation, namely phlegm, bitter and black bile, and serous residue, to the chronic diseases they cause, illustrating the practice with cases of gout, epilepsy, melancholy, elephantiasis, quartan fevers, and a cancerous condition of the breast checked by annual purging. Later sections set out the timing of purgation by season, region, age, habit, and critical days; the preparation of patients through trial emetics, moistening foods, and rest; the use of white and black hellebore and of colocynth; the draught of ptisan following the drug; and the blending of purgatives with fragrant, thinning ingredients so that they carry off the offending humour without harming the stomach.
grc.galen.thrasybulus_sive_utrum_medicinae_s: A short treatise of Galen addressed to a friend named Thrasybulus, it opens with the author recalling the question Thrasybulus had posed in conversation, whether what is called the 'healthful' belongs to medicine or to gymnastics, and his promise to set the oral answer down in writing. The argument then examines how such problems should be framed and defined, maintains that there is one art concerned with the body, divided into a therapeutic part (medicine proper) and a preservative or hygienic part, and assigns gymnastics to the latter as the knowledge of exercise, enumerating the materials of the art in food, drink, evacuations, surroundings and training. Galen supports the case with appeals to Hippocrates, Plato and Erasistratus, distinguishes the natural condition of the healthy body from the athletic condition 'not by nature', condemns athletic training and its trainers as a counterfeit art, and closes by explaining why the whole art of the body has come to bear the name 'medicine'.
grc.galen.περὶ_τῶν_ἐν_ταῖς_τροφαῖς_δυνάμεων: Galen's treatise on the powers of foods opens by criticising earlier physicians, from Diocles to Mnesitheus and Philotimus, for giving unqualified judgments about what is easy to digest, nourishing or laxative, and argues that the effects of any food depend on the constitution, age, habits and condition of the eater. The bulk of the work then goes food by food through cereals and their breads and porridges, pulses, seeds, fruits and berries, vegetables, roots and fungi, then animal foods including the flesh of land animals, poultry, fish, shellfish, eggs and milk, before closing with wine, salted fish and preserved foods, discussing throughout the preparation of each food, its humoral qualities of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, and its suitability for particular bodily conditions. It forms part of Galen's wider physiological project and frequently refers back to his own works on mixtures and on the powers of simple drugs.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ὑπέρ_παλαμήδους_ἀπολ: A Greek prose defence speech attributed to Gorgias of Leontini, put in the mouth of the legendary Palamedes, who stands accused by Odysseus of betraying Greece to the barbarians. The speech opens by distinguishing the real stake of the trial: not death, which nature has already passed on all mortals, but the choice between honour and disgrace. Palamedes then argues that the treachery was impossible, since no contact, pledge, payment, or entry of enemies could have escaped notice, and that he had no motive in tyranny, wealth, honour, safety, or friendship, cataloguing his services to mankind in letters, laws, numbers, and the arts of peace before turning to expose the accuser's self-contradiction in imputing at once wisdom and madness. It closes with an appeal to the Greek judges to decide by truth and deeds rather than slander, warning that to condemn him unjustly would be the gravest of crimes against a benefactor of Hellas.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.christus_patiens: The Christus Patiens is a Greek tragedy on the Passion, burial, and Resurrection of Christ, attributed to Gregory of Nazianzus and of uncertain date. It opens with a prologue spoken by the Virgin, who sets the deception of the first mother in Eden as the cause of her Son's redemptive death and begins her lament in the role of tragic mother. The action moves through Judas' betrayal, Peter's denial, the trial before Pilate, and the crucifixion, which the Mother and the Galilean women mourn amid cosmic portents, to the piercing of the side and the burial by Joseph and Nicodemus. After the tomb is sealed and guarded, the women find it empty, the risen Christ appears to Mary Magdalene and then to the disciples gathered behind closed doors, and the play closes with a prayer of the evangelist John to the Mother of God.
grc.heraclitus_of_ephesus.fragmenta: The work collects the surviving fragments of Heraclitus of Ephesus, a Presocratic philosopher of uncertain date, each preserved as a quotation from later Greek and Latin writers such as Sextus Empiricus, Clement of Alexandria, Plutarch, Hippolytus, Aristotle, and Stobaeus, with the citing source noted. It opens with the saying on the logos, according to which men remain without understanding of the account that governs all things, both before and after hearing it. The remaining numbered fragments range over the unity of opposites and the harmony born of strife, the ever-living fire and its measure-regulated transformations, the river sayings on ceaseless flux, the one divine law, the role of war, the critique of earlier sages such as Hesiod, Pythagoras, Homer, and Archilochus, and the disparagement of popular cult and mystery rites. Aphorisms on the soul, sleep and waking, sense perception, self-knowledge, and human folly and happiness fill out the collection.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.catoptrica: A Greek treatise on mirrors and reflected vision by Hero of Alexandria. The preserved opening takes as granted that nature does nothing in vain nor labours to no purpose, and argues from this that reflection occurs at equal angles, supporting the claim with a geometrical proof that the path of a visual ray broken at unequal angles against a straight mirror is longer than the equal-angled path. The work as a whole develops the geometry of reflection across plane, spherical and other curved mirrors, proving propositions about the courses of visual rays and the position and properties of the images formed in mirrors.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.dioptra: The Dioptra is a Greek treatise on surveying attributed to Hero of Alexandria, setting out the construction of a geared sighting instrument together with the measurements it makes possible. An opening preface defends the utility of dioptrics, criticises earlier writers on the subject, and argues that a single instrument suffices for all the tasks in hand. The body of the work proceeds as a sequence of numbered problems: establishing differences of level along water conduits, joining inaccessible points by straight lines, taking distances, heights, depths and the width of rivers, driving tunnels through mountains so that workings begun from both ends will meet, sinking vertical shafts onto underground channels, tracing harbour curves, levelling ground to spherical or inclined profiles, and measuring, dividing and restoring the boundaries of landholdings, with arithmetical rules for the areas of triangles and trapezia. Closing chapters add a spring-flow gauge, measurement of angular separations between stars, a reckoning of the distance from Alexandria to Rome from lunar-eclipse timings observed in both cities, a cart-borne hodometer for road distances, a paddle-wheel device for distances sailed, and gear trains by which a small force moves a great weight.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.geodaesia_sp: A short Greek treatise on geodesy, or land measurement, attributed to Hero of Alexandria. It opens with elementary definitions of the point, line, surface, plane, angle, circle, and the principal rectilinear figures. The work then traces the invention of measurement to the Egyptian surveyors who re-marked fields after the Nile flood, defines the terms and genera of plane geometry used by surveyors, tabulates linear measures from the finger to the schoinos and parasanges, and sets out conversions between areas measured in orguiai and the seed measures of land in modii and litrai. It closes with worked numerical problems on finding the areas and sides of squares, oblongs, and triangles of every kind, including right-triangle constructions ascribed to the methods of Pythagoras and of Plato and the computation of a triangle's area from its three sides.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.pneumatica: This Greek treatise on pneumatics, preserved among the works of Hero of Alexandria, expounds the theory and construction of devices that operate through air, fire, and water. It opens with a long physical argument defending the existence of dispersed vacua and the compressibility of air, drawing on phenomena such as drinking vessels, medical cupping glasses, and the diving of swimmers, before turning to practical machines. The bulk of the work describes, with numbered diagrams, a long series of contrivances: bent siphons, vessels that pour wine or water at will, altar figures that libate and dragons that hiss when fire burns, singing birds and trumpets, temple doors that open by fire on the altar, the water organ, an aeolipile, fountains and measuring vessels, lamps that feed themselves, and surgical suction instruments, each explained by appeal to the pressure and movement of trapped air. It closes with an animal automaton that appears to drink after being cut, operated by hidden tubes and valves.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.stereometrica: A Greek collection of worked problems in solid mensuration attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date. It opens with problems for finding the volume and surface of a sphere by numerical rules drawn from Archimedes' demonstration that the circumscribing cylinder is half again the sphere. The work then proceeds through long series of solved exercises for cones, truncated cones, cylinders, columns, cubes, wedges, obelisks, and pyramids with square, triangular, and polygonal bases, before turning to the measurement of theatres, amphitheatres, vaults, apses, apsed niches, pools, wells, jars, ships, granaries, and grain stores, with capacities reckoned in modii and Italian sextarii and short procedures for deriving heights from shadows, gauging pipes, sails, and roof tiles, and settling questions of weights and measures; the demonstrations cite Archimedes and Euclid's Elements. A closing section of elementary arithmetic teaches the multiplication of feet and fractional measures.
grc.herodianus.συμπόσιον: A very short Greek grammatical work by Herodian, the Συμπόσιον ('Symposium'), transmitted only as a string of brief entries in which individual words are explained through etymology. It opens with a derivation of βολβός and a longer note on ἦδος, which debates the aspiration of trochaic neuter nouns such as εὔχος and ἦχος and quotes a rule by which their initial vowel is made smooth. The remaining entries run through terms for foods, seasonings and vessels of the table, κάραβος, καρκίνος, ὄξος, τάριχος, φιάλη and ψωμοί among them, each given a derivation from some other word, with occasional Homeric quotations and remarks ascribed to Philoxenus standing alongside the notes cited from Herodian's own Symposium.
grc.herodotus.histories: The Histories of Herodotus of Halicarnassus, a Greek prose work in nine books, opens with a proem announcing its aim of preserving the great deeds of Greeks and barbarians and setting out the cause of the war between them. It begins with Persian and Phoenician accounts of a chain of abductions, Io, Europa, Medea, Helen, as the origin of East–West enmity, before turning to Croesus of Lydia and the rise of Persia under Cyrus, Cambyses and Darius. Across its course the narrative of Persian expansion is interwoven with long ethnographic and geographical digressions on Egypt, Scythia and other lands, with histories of Greek states such as Athens and Sparta, and with the Ionian revolt, leading to the invasions of Darius and Xerxes, the battles of Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis and Plataea, and the Greek counteroffensive. The work closes with the Athenian capture of Sestos in the Hellespont and the punishment of the Persian governor Artayctes.
grc.hesiod.theogony: The Theogony is a Greek epic poem of uncertain date, attributed to Hesiod, that sets out a genealogy of the gods from the origin of the cosmos to the established order under Zeus. It opens with an invocation of the Heliconian Muses, who encounter the poet as he tends sheep on the mountain, give him a laurel sceptre, and breathe into him an inspired voice to sing of things past and to come. The poem then traces the first beginnings from Chaos, Gaia, and Eros through the generations of Night, Pontus, and Ocean, the overthrow of Uranus by Cronus and the birth of Aphrodite, and long catalogues of Nereids, Oceanids, rivers, and monsters. Its central narrative follows Cronus's swallowing of his children and Zeus's rise, the war with the Titans, the punishment of Prometheus and the making of Pandora, the defeat of Typhoeus, and Zeus's distribution of honours and his marriages, closing with a catalogue of goddesses who bore children to mortal men and a summons to sing the race of women.
grc.hippocrates.aphorismi: The Aphorisms is a collection of terse medical maxims in ancient Greek, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates and of uncertain date, arranged in seven sections. It opens with the celebrated dictum that life is short, the art long, the occasion instant, experiment perilous and judgement difficult. The work then moves through rules for diet and sleep, the use of purgative drugs such as hellebore, the bearing of the seasons, winds and the ages of life on health, and the effects of heat and cold on wounds and inflammations. Its later sections gather prognostic signs drawn from sweats, urine, dreams and the crisis days of fevers, together with observations on surgery, epilepsy, phthisis and the diseases of women and pregnancy.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_et_locis: On Airs, Waters, and Places (De Aere Aquis et Locis) is an ancient Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic collection, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens by declaring that whoever wishes to investigate medicine correctly must first consider the seasons of the year, the hot and cold winds, the properties of the waters, and a city's position toward sun and winds, together with the mode of life of its inhabitants. The treatise then traces how each exposure, toward hot or cold winds, toward the rising or setting sun, shapes the bodies, illnesses, and dispositions of a city's men, women, and children, classifies waters from rain, snow, springs, and marshes and their medical effects, and shows how the coming year's diseases may be foretold from seasonal signs and the risings and settings of stars, with warnings about dangerous moments of seasonal change. Its closing section compares Asia and Europe, arguing that climate and political institutions account for differences in physique and courage between their peoples, and gives ethnographic accounts of the Macrocephali, the Phasians, the Sauromatae, and the nomad Scythians, whose bodily peculiarities are explained by their environment and way of life.
grc.hippocrates.de_aere_aquis_locis: An ancient Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, On Airs, Waters, Places begins by instructing the physician who would practise medicine aright to examine the seasons, the winds, the waters, a city's situation and the way of life of its inhabitants, so that he may foresee the diseases of any unfamiliar place. It then describes city by city the effects of exposure to hot, cold, eastern and western winds on the bodies and illnesses of their populations, and classifies waters, from stagnant and marshy through rain-fed and melted snow to high spring water, as harmful or wholesome for drinking. Further chapters show how the character of the seasons allows a physician to predict whether the year ahead will prove healthy or sickly, marking the solstices, equinoxes and the risings and settings of stars as dangerous times of transition. The closing part compares the peoples of Asia and Europe, treating the Long-heads, the marsh-dwelling Phasians, the Sauromatae and the Scythian nomads, and argues throughout that climate, terrain, waters and political institutions shape the physiques, customs and courage of peoples.
grc.hippocrates.de_capitis_vulneribus: A Greek surgical treatise handed down among the works of Hippocrates, De Capitis Vulneribus ('On Wounds of the Head') deals with injuries to the cranium and their treatment. It opens with an account of variations in the shape of the skull and the course of its sutures, which resemble the letters T, H, or X according to the head's configuration. The treatise then classifies the ways in which cranial bone may be wounded, fracture, contusion, depression, and indentation, explains how hidden injuries can be detected through questioning the patient, inspection, scraping, and probing, and gives detailed directions for incision, dressing of wounds, and trepanation, with warnings about the proper handling of the saw and drill and the dangers posed to the membrane surrounding the brain. It ends with remarks on the thinner bones of children, the signs by which a fatal outcome may be foretold, such as fever, suppuration, and convulsions that cross from one side of the body to the other, and further technical guidance on completing the operation safely.
grc.hippocrates.de_diaeta_in_morbis_acutis: A Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, on the dietary management of acute diseases. It opens by criticising the writers of the so-called Cnidian opinions for recording patients' symptoms without the physician's own prognostic observations and for relying on a very small number of remedies. The work then argues against prolonged fasting at the outset of illnesses such as pleurisy, pneumonia, phrenitis, lethargy and burning fevers, and sets out when and how to introduce barley gruel and its strained juice, the dangers of sudden changes in a patient's habitual diet, and the discriminating use of drinks such as sweet, dark and white wines, hydromel, oxymel and water. It ends with an account of bathing, covering its benefits in pleuritic conditions, the preparations it requires, and the circumstances in which it helps or harms the sick.
grc.hippocrates.de_flatibus: De Flatibus (Breaths) is a short Greek prose treatise on the causes of disease, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens by discussing medicine as a laborious art and posing the question of what the single cause of diseases might be. The work then argues that air, drawn into the body with food and drink as breath (pneuma, physai), is the cause of all illness, and explains fevers, rigors and tremors, hernias and abscesses, fluxes and hemorrhages, ruptures, dropsy, apoplexy, and finally the so-called sacred disease as effects of breaths moving through the veins and flesh. It closes by claiming to have demonstrated that breath is the dominant cause of all diseases.
grc.hippocrates.de_fracturis: A treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, On Fractures sets out the surgical management of broken and displaced bones. It opens by censuring physicians who fail to extend fractures into the straightest possible position, illustrated by cases of a broken forearm wrongly bandaged. The argument then proceeds through the mechanics of extension, reduction, and bandaging with linen rollers, cerate, and splints for fractures of the forearm, upper arm, thigh, and shin, together with injuries of the heel, ankle, and foot and the slipping of the joints at knee and elbow. Later chapters treat compound fractures with protruding bone, the use of the lever to replace it, dieting and the timing of re-bandaging, the signs by which exfoliation of bone is foreseen, and criticisms of rival practitioners' methods.
grc.hippocrates.de_prisca_medicina: A Greek medical treatise, De Prisca Medicina ('On Ancient Medicine'), attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, which argues that medicine is an art grounded in long accumulated experience rather than in abstract postulates. It opens by attacking those who reduce the causes of disease and death to a single hypothesis such as the hot, the cold, the moist or the dry. The argument then traces the origin of the art in the discovery of a diet suited to human nature, moving from raw and wild foodstuffs to prepared bread, porridge and blended drinks, and goes on to defend the regimen of the sick through discussions of fasting and repletion, the effects of heat and cold, the acridity of humours, and the shapes of bodily organs such as the bladder, head, womb, spleen and lung. It closes with reflections on the powers of the individual humours and their relations to one another.
grc.hippocrates.jusjurandum: The Jusjurandum, or Hippocratic Oath, is a short Greek composition, transmitted under the name of Hippocrates in the Hippocratic Corpus and of uncertain date and authorship, in which a physician swears a formal pledge of professional conduct. It opens with an invocation of Apollo the healer, Asclepius, Hygieia, Panacea, and all gods and goddesses as witnesses to the pledge. The body of the oath sets out obligations to the teacher and the teacher's household, a commitment to treat the sick for their benefit and to abstain from harm and injustice, and prohibitions on giving deadly drugs or abortive pessaries and on cutting patients for stone, together with pledges of sexual propriety, confidentiality about what is seen or heard in patients' houses, and purity of life and art. It closes by promising lasting repute to those who keep the oath and the opposite to those who forswear it.
grc.homer.hymns: The Homeric Hymns, a collection of thirty-three hexameter hymns transmitted under Homer's name and of uncertain date, address the major gods of the Greek pantheon. The opening hymn, fragmentary in transmission, honours Dionysus, weighing conflicting accounts of his birth before Zeus confirms the Nysan version. Four long narrative hymns recount Persephone's abduction by Hades, Apollo's birth and founding of his cult at Delphi, Hermes' invention of the lyre and theft of Apollo's cattle, and Aphrodite's seduction of Anchises, while the remaining shorter hymns invoke deities such as Ares, Helios, Selene and the Dioscuri. The collection closes with the Dioscuri, called upon as saviours of sailors caught in winter storms at sea.
grc.homer.iliad: The Iliad is a Greek epic poem in twenty-four books of dactylic hexameter, attributed to Homer and of uncertain date. It opens with a quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles over a captive woman, which sets the poem's declared subject, the wrath of Achilles and the suffering it brings upon the Achaeans. The narrative follows Achilles' withdrawal from the fighting before Troy, the mounting reverses of the Greek forces, the death of Patroclus at Hector's hands, Achilles' return to battle and killing of Hector, and Priam's ransom of his son's body. The poem closes with the nine days of mourning and the Trojans' funeral rites for Hector, ending with his burial and the funeral feast in Priam's house.
grc.homer.odyssey: The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic poem in twenty-four books, attributed to Homer and of uncertain date. It opens with an invocation to the Muse for the tale of the man of many devices who wandered long after the sack of Troy, kept from his home by the anger of Poseidon, and begins with a council of the gods and Telemachus' voyage to Pylos and Sparta in search of news of his father. Odysseus himself, released from Calypso's island and entertained among the Phaeacians, recounts his wanderings: the Cicones, the Cyclops, Aeolus and the Laestrygonians, Circe, his descent to the underworld, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the cattle of the Sun. Returned unrecognised to Ithaca, he is sheltered by Eumaeus, reunites with Telemachus, endures the insolence of the suitors in his own hall, and the poem closes with the contest of the bow, their slaughter, the testing and reunion with Penelope, the meeting with Laertes, and a truce with the kinsmen of the dead brought about by Athena.
grc.isaeus.speeches: A collection of twelve forensic speeches in Attic Greek attributed to Isaeus, an Athenian logographer and teacher of Demosthenes, probably composed in the fourth century BC. The speeches, all but one concerned with contested inheritances, were written for delivery by clients in Athenian courts arguing over wills, adoption, and claims of kinship. Each speech builds a case through legal argument, appeals to the laws of Athens, examination of witnesses, and attacks on the opposing litigants' claims to kinship or legitimate birth.
grc.isocrates.speeches: The Speeches of Isocrates gather twenty-one separate Greek prose discourses of the Athenian rhetorician Isocrates. The opening speech is an address to the young Demonicus, son of Hipponicus, sending him paternal counsel on piety toward the gods, honour for his parents, disciplined care of body and soul, and the company he should keep. The collection ranges from such protreptic and advisory pieces to public and forensic orations, all cast in the long, carefully balanced periods characteristic of Isocrates' prose.
grc.libanius.declamations_13-30: A collection of declamations in Greek by Libanius, comprising rhetorical speeches composed on themes drawn from Greek history and from imagined situations. The opening speech has the Corinthians address the Greeks in accusation of Athens over the siege of Potidaea. Much of the collection then takes its material from the era of Demosthenes and Philip, with speeches in which a Demosthenes figure laments the disaster at Chaeronea, contemplates death, and answers Philip's demands upon Athens. Others move to invented courtroom pleas, including that of a poor man who asks the council for hemlock to escape the misery of a newly enriched neighbour settled beside him.
grc.libanius.declamations_31-51: A set of twenty-one Greek declamations, numbered 31 to 51 within the corpus of the rhetorician Libanius. Such declamations are fictitious display speeches composed for rhetorical training, delivered in the persons of imagined speakers before courts or councils. The first speech in the collection, addressed to a city council, is spoken by a man whose property has been repeatedly confiscated; he recounts his father's teaching on frugality and argues that death is preferable to living on after the loss of his estate.
grc.libanius.orations_26-50: A group of orations by the Greek author Libanius. It opens with an address to a governor of Antioch who resents the city's attachment to his predecessor Proclus, arguing that recent disorders in the baths and theaters are the work of a few troublemakers rather than of the citizens as a whole. Later speeches combine civic complaints with personal quarrels, most prominently a sustained invective against Silvanus, son of Gaudentius, a former pupil represented as repaying his teacher's kindness with insults, mockery of his lameness, and open hostility. The collection closes with a petition to an emperor protesting the abuses of officials who, under cover of doing favors, compel provincials to furnish donkeys, labor, and goods for public building works.
grc.lucian.alexander: Lucian's Alexander, a Greek prose satire in the form of a reply to his friend Celsus, opens with the author undertaking to set down the life and schemes of Alexander of Abonoteichus, comparing the task with the cleansing of the Augean stables. The narrative then follows Alexander from his youth as a dependent of a Tyanean magus and his partnership with the choreographer Cocconas, through the founding of an oracle at Abonoteichus, where a tame snake is presented as the newly born Asclepius under the name Glycon. It proceeds to expose the devices behind the cult, including the rigged incubation of a goose egg, the mechanical snake's head, the tampering with sealed questions, the oracles in verse, the hostility toward Epicureans and Christians that culminates in the burning of Epicurus's book, and the credulity of prominent dupes such as the senator Rutilianus. The account closes with Alexander's death at seventy of a festering foot, contrary to his own prophecy of a hundred and fifty years, and a final tribute to Epicurus.
grc.lucian.contemplantes: Charon, or the Inspectors (Contemplantes) is a short satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. It opens with Charon, granted a single day's leave from ferrying the dead, persuading a reluctant Hermes to guide him over the upper world. Stacking Pelion on Ossa and Oeta on Parnassus for a vantage point, the pair survey human life from on high: cities swarming like beehives, hopes and fears hovering overhead, the Fates spinning each person's fragile thread, and the impending falls of kings such as Croesus, Cyrus, and Polycrates, while Solon's conversation with Croesus on the uncertainty of happiness unfolds below. The tour takes in tombs, funeral offerings, and the vanished splendour of Nineveh, Babylon, Mycenae, and Troy, and the dialogue closes as Charon descends again, musing that human strivings, golden bricks, battles over burial mounds, leave the ferryman himself unremarked.
grc.lucian.dearum_iudicium: The Dearum Iudicium ('The Judgement of the Goddesses') is a short comic prose dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. Zeus instructs Hermes to carry a golden apple to Paris, the young shepherd on Mount Ida, and have him decide which of Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite is the most beautiful. The dialogue then follows the goddesses' journey across Phrygia, their jealous banter and mutual disparagement en route, Paris's nervous deliberation and his request to inspect the undressed competitors, and the bribes each offers: lordship of all Asia from Hera, victory in war from Athena, and the hand of Helen from Aphrodite. Paris, already smitten by the description of Helen, awards the apple to Aphrodite, who promises to serve as matchmaker with the help of Eros, Himeros, Pothos, and the Charites, thereby setting the abduction that leads to Troy in motion.
grc.lucian.dialogi_meretricii: A collection of short Greek prose dialogues by Lucian of Samosata, staged among the courtesans, mothers, lovers, and confidantes of Athens. The opening exchange has Thais and Glycerion discussing a soldier lover whom the courtesan Gorgona has lured away. The subsequent scenes follow the fortunes and stratagems of the trade: jealous and violent suitors, haggling over gifts and fees, mothers coaching daughters into prostitution, hired witches and love-philtres, and forged letters and wall inscriptions deployed in lovers' quarrels. Among the more extended episodes are the account of the wealthy Megilla, who lives as a man with her female companion, and a soldier whose lurid tales of single combat terrify his mistress and her maid into flight.
grc.lucian.icaromenippus: Lucian of Samosata's Icaromenippus is a satirical dialogue in which Menippus the Cynic recounts to a friend the distances and stages of his winged flight from earth to the moon and on up to heaven. Frustrated by the contradictory teachings of the philosophers on the cosmos and the gods, he fashioned wings from an eagle and a vulture, paused on the moon, met the shade of Empedocles there, and gained an eagle's sharp sight with which to survey human affairs from above. From that vantage he mocked the pettiness of kings, philosophers and ordinary people alike, before being admitted to Zeus's banquet, where he overheard the day's prayers and attended an assembly in which Zeus denounced the squabbling philosophical sects at the Moon's prompting and promised to destroy them. The dialogue ends with Menippus returned to earth by Hermes, resolved to carry what he has seen and heard to the philosophers in the Stoa.
grc.lucian.patriae_encomium: A short Greek prose encomium by Lucian of Samosata arguing that the fatherland deserves the highest honor in human life. It opens by conceding the proverb that nothing is sweeter than one's native land and asking whether anything more august and divine can be named, then answers that the fatherland is the cause and teacher of all that people hold sacred. The argument goes on to treat the native land as a common mother dearer than any parent, cherished by the gods for the places of their birth, repaid through education, wealth, and public service, and longed for in exile and old age, when men wish to end their days and be buried in the soil that reared them. It closes with the observations that lawgivers impose banishment as the harshest penalty for the greatest wrongs, that generals rally their troops with the cry that the war is for the fatherland, and that this name makes the coward brave.
grc.lucian.podagra: Lucian's Podagra ('Gout') is a short Greek dramatic satire that travesties the diction and metres of tragedy, attributed to Lucian of Samosata. A speaker invokes Gout as a hateful child of Cocytus nursed by an Erinys, cataloguing the disease's fire and bitterness in the joints and veins, and contrasts the springtime processions of Phrygian, Lydian, and Cretan worshippers with the mock-rites of gout sufferers, whose 'hymns' are laments over their staff-supported steps. The monody closes as the speaker, summoned out of doors toward the sunlight, asks whether approaching garlanded staff-bearers are celebrating Apollo Paian or dancing in honour of Bacchus.
grc.lucian.rhetorum_praeceptor: The Rhetorum Praeceptor ('The Teacher of Orators') is a short Greek satirical monologue by Lucian of Samosata, in which a self-styled master of eloquence instructs an eager youth. It opens with the young man asking how he may become a rhetor and be admired as a sophist, whereupon the teacher promises him a road far easier than the steep, laborious one traced by Demosthenes, Plato, and the ancients. The bulk of the work sets out mock 'laws' for instant success, boldness, ignorance, and shamelessness as travelling gear, a stock of showy Attic words, contempt for classical reading, digressions to Marathon, Salamis, and Xerxes on any theme, and a theatrical voice, walk, and dress, backed by a dissolute private life. The satire closes with the teacher's own confession of a disreputable career, from his low birth through a fraudulent marriage and forgery to a flourishing practice as a losing advocate, and his parting boast that whoever follows his easy path will soon marry Rhetoric herself and reign in the courts.
grc.lucian.toxaris_vel_amicitia: A Greek prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, conducted between Mnesippus, a Greek, and Toxaris, a Scythian, and concerned with friendship, as its alternative title indicates. The opening exchange turns on the Scythian cult of Orestes and Pylades: Mnesippus questions the worship of foreigners who had plundered the country and slain its king, while Toxaris defends his people's honours to men they judge good and beneficent. Toxaris goes on to describe the bronze stele in the Oresteion recording the friends' deeds and the painted scenes in the temple enclosure, showing the shipwreck, the sacrifice to Artemis averted, and the fight during their escape. The remainder of the work is devoted to stories of devoted friendship told on the Greek and the Scythian side in turn.
grc.lucian.verae_historiae: Lucian of Samosata's Verae Historiae ('True Histories') is a Greek prose narrative whose preface declares that it describes things the narrator neither saw nor suffered nor learned from others, things that do not exist and could never have existed, and that readers should believe none of it. The work is offered openly as fiction, written in ridicule of earlier poets and prose writers, Ctesias, Iambulus and Homer's Odysseus among them, who recorded marvellous voyages and fabulous peoples. The narrative then follows the narrator and his fifty companions beyond the Pillars of Heracles into the western ocean, where, after seventy-nine days adrift in a storm, they land on an island bearing an inscription of Heracles and Dionysus, a flowing river of wine, and fish that taste and colour of it.
grc.lycurgus.against_leocrates: A public prosecution speech (eisangelia) in which the Athenian orator Lycurgus charges Leocrates with treason for abandoning Athens after the battle of Chaeronea. The work opens with an ancient hypothesis summarising the case, and the speech proper begins with the prosecutor invoking Athena and the other gods of the city and pledging a just and pious accusation. The argument establishes that Leocrates fled with his money, household slaves and ancestral sacred objects, went first to Rhodes and then lived for more than five years in Megara before returning to Athens under a defence that he had sailed out on trade. Lycurgus corroborates the charge with witnesses and documents, including a decree of Hypereides, the ephebic oath and the oath sworn at Plataea, reinforces it with exempla from Codrus and the Persian Wars to Euripides' Erechtheus, Homer, Tyrtaeus and Simonides, reviews earlier Athenian and Spartan treatment of traitors and cowards, and closes by urging the jurors to condemn Leocrates to death.
grc.novum_testamentum.actus_apostolorum: The Actus Apostolorum, the fifth book of the New Testament, is a narrative in Koine Greek prose of the Imperial era. It opens with a dedication to Theophilus and an account of Jesus' ascension, then turns to the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost and the founding of the church in Jerusalem. The narrative follows the apostles through Peter's preaching and healing, the martyrdom of Stephen, the conversion of Saul, the admission of Gentiles, and the Jerusalem council, before tracing Paul's missionary journeys across Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia, and Greece. It closes with Paul's arrest and trials before Roman governors and King Agrippa, a storm-driven voyage to Malta, and his preaching under guard in Rome.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_colossenses: A New Testament epistle in Greek, of uncertain date, presented as written by the apostle Paul with Timothy to the Christian community at Colossae while Paul was imprisoned. The letter opens with a salutation and thanksgiving for the Colossians' faith and love, leading into a hymnic declaration of Christ as the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, through whom all things were made and reconciled. Paul then describes his labor and suffering for the churches before warning the Colossians against being taken captive by empty philosophy and against judging one another by rules of food, drink, festival, new moon, and sabbath, arguing instead that believers have died and been raised with Christ. The closing movement gives ethical exhortation, to seek the things above, to strip off the old self and clothe themselves in compassion, humility, and love, a household code for wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves, and masters, counsel on prayer and conduct toward outsiders, greetings from associates including Tychicus, Onesimus, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas, an instruction to exchange the letter with the church at Laodicea, and a final greeting written in Paul's own hand.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_i: A Greek epistle of the New Testament, written in prose during the Imperial era and attributed in its opening verses to Paul, called as an apostle of Christ Jesus, together with Sosthenes, addressing the church of God at Corinth. The letter begins with thanksgiving and a plea that its readers end their factional loyalties to Paul, Apollos, and Cephas. Its course then takes up disorder within the community in turn: wisdom and the cross, immorality and lawsuits, marriage and celibacy, food sacrificed to idols, the abuse of the Lord's Supper, and spiritual gifts, including the hymn to love. It closes with a sustained argument for the resurrection of the dead, instructions for a collection for the saints in Jerusalem, travel plans, and personal greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_corinthios_ii: An epistle of the New Testament composed in Greek during the Roman imperial period, 2 Corinthians is addressed in its opening salutation from Paul and Timothy to the church of God at Corinth and throughout Achaia, followed by a blessing on the God who comforts his servants in every affliction. The letter then explains a change of travel plans, counsels leniency towards a repentant offender, and mounts an extended defence of Paul's apostolate as a ministry of the new covenant, characterised by suffering, integrity and the word of reconciliation. Its later chapters press the Corinthians to complete their collection for the poor at Jerusalem, answer rival preachers through an ironic boast of hardships, imprisonments and heavenly visions, and warn of censure at the writer's impending third visit. Exhortations to restore and perfect the community, mutual greetings and a threefold benediction bring the work to a close.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_ephesios: The Epistle to the Ephesians, a New Testament letter in Greek prose of the Roman imperial period and attributed to the apostle Paul, opens with a salutation to the saints at Ephesus, a blessing over God's grace and election, and a thanksgiving for the recipients' faith and love. Its doctrinal first half sets out redemption through Christ's blood, the revelation of the mystery of God's will to unite all things in Christ, and the reconciliation of Jew and Gentile into one new humanity, with the church portrayed as Christ's body and as a temple built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. The latter half moves into ethical exhortation: the putting off of the old self, truthfulness, mutual kindness, and purity, followed by a household code governing wives and husbands, children and parents, and slaves and masters, and by the image of the whole armor of God against the spiritual powers. The letter closes with word that Tychicus will report on the writer's affairs and with a benediction of peace and grace.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_hebraeos: The Epistle to the Hebrews is a Greek prose epistle of the New Testament, composed in the Imperial era by an author of uncertain name. It opens by declaring that God, who spoke long ago to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken through a Son appointed heir of all things and far superior to the angels. The argument then sets Christ above Moses and the Levitical priesthood as high priest after the order of Melchizedek, contrasts the old covenant's repeated sacrifices with the single offering of Christ once for all, describes his entry into the true heavenly sanctuary, and interweaves warnings against unbelief and apostasy with appeals to enter God's rest. A long catalogue of faithful figures from Abel to the prophets leads into final exhortations to endurance, discipline, holiness, and obedience to leaders, followed by personal notices, greetings from Italy, and a closing benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philemonem: A short Greek prose letter of the New Testament, composed during the Imperial era and attributed to the apostle Paul, written jointly with Timothy and addressed to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church that meets in Philemon's house. It opens with a greeting and a thanksgiving for Philemon's faith and love before turning to its principal request: Paul intercedes for Onesimus, once Philemon's slave and now his spiritual child begotten during Paul's imprisonment, urging that he be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. Paul offers to charge himself with any wrong or debt Onesimus has incurred, expresses confidence that Philemon will comply, asks that lodging be prepared in hope of release through the recipients' prayers, and closes with greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, followed by a benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_romanos: The Epistle to the Romans is a Greek Christian letter ascribed to the apostle Paul and addressed to believers in Rome, composed at an uncertain date during the imperial period. It opens with a salutation in which Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus and called apostle, greets the community and announces that the righteousness of God is revealed through faith. The body argues that Jew and Greek alike stand under sin and are justified by faith apart from works of the law, tracing the theme through the example of Abraham, the reconciliation won by Christ against the backdrop of Adam's transgression, liberation from sin and the law through baptism and the Spirit, God's continued purpose for Israel alongside the Gentiles, and the Spirit's assurance that nothing separates believers from the love of God. A closing hortatory section urges the offering of the body as a living sacrifice, mutual love, subjection to governing authorities, and forbearance between the strong and the weak in matters of food and observance, before Paul sets out his plans to visit Rome en route to Spain and sends greetings to named members of the community.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_i: The First Epistle to Timothy, a New Testament epistle in Greek prose of the Imperial era, attributed to the apostle Paul and addressed to Timothy, his trusted associate at Ephesus. It opens with Paul's charge that Timothy remain at Ephesus to restrain certain teachers of divergent doctrine and endless genealogies. The remainder sets out instructions for the ordering of congregational life: the right use of the law and Paul's account of the mercy shown to himself, directions for public prayer and the conduct of men and women, qualifications for overseers and deacons, the enrolment and support of widows, the treatment of elders and of slaves, warnings against ascetic pretension and the love of money, and a closing charge to Timothy to guard the deposit of faith until the appearing of Christ.
grc.novum_testamentum.apocalypsis: The Apocalypse (Revelation) is the final book of the New Testament, an Imperial-era early Christian apocalypse in Greek prose presented as the revelation of Jesus Christ delivered through an angel to a servant named John. It opens with an epistolary greeting and a vision commanding John to write messages of praise and rebuke to seven churches in Asia. The remainder recounts his visions on Patmos and in heaven: the sealed scroll opened by the Lamb, the seven seals, trumpets, and bowls of wrath, the dragon and two beasts, the fall of Babylon, the thousand-year reign and final judgment, and the descent of the new Jerusalem, closing with promises of Christ's imminent return.
grc.novum_testamentum.iacobi: The Epistle of James is a Greek New Testament letter of the Imperial era, sent in the name of James, who calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and addressed to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. The work proceeds as a chain of moral and paraenetic discourses rather than a sustained argument, teaching endurance under trial, prayer for wisdom, hearing and doing the word, and impartiality toward rich and poor. Later sections set out the harmony of faith and works through the examples of Abraham and Rahab, the danger of the untamed tongue, true and false wisdom, quarrels and friendship with the world, the coming judgment of the wealthy, patience until the Lord's return, the prohibition of oaths, and the anointing and prayer of the elders for the sick, closing with a call to bring back anyone who wanders from the truth.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannes: The Gospel of John, the fourth of the four canonical Gospels of the New Testament, a Greek prose narrative of the Roman Imperial period by an author of uncertain identity. It opens with the prologue hailing the Word that was with God in the beginning and became flesh. The account then follows Jesus from the witness of John the Baptist and an early series of signs, water made wine at Cana, healings, the feeding of the five thousand, and the raising of Lazarus, through long discourses on the bread of life, the light of the world, and the good shepherd, into the farewell discourses and the high-priestly prayer. The work closes with the passion narrative, from arrest and trial before Pilate to crucifixion and burial, and the resurrection appearances to Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and the disciples beside the Sea of Tiberias, ending with a remark on the beloved disciple whose testimony the book records.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_ii: The Second Letter of John is a brief New Testament epistle in Greek prose, composed at an uncertain date in the Imperial period and attributed to an author who identifies himself in the opening only as 'the Elder.' It opens with a greeting to 'the elect lady and her children,' whom the writer loves in truth along with all who know the truth. The body recalls joy at the recipients' conduct and urges them to love one another and to keep the commandments heard from the beginning, before warning against deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, whom the addressee is told neither to welcome into the house nor to greet. The letter closes with the writer's hope of speaking face to face rather than by paper and ink, and with greetings from the children of the addressee's elect sister.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_iii: The Third Letter of John is a brief Greek epistle of the New Testament, written in prose during the Imperial era by an unnamed writer who styles himself 'the elder'. It opens with a greeting to Gaius, whom the writer loves in the truth, together with a prayer for his health and prosperity. The body of the letter praises Gaius for his faithful hospitality to travelling missionaries, contrasts him with Diotrephes, a domineering figure in the church who refuses the elder's representatives and expels members from the congregation, and commends Demetrius as a man attested by all and by the truth itself. The closing lines express a hope of visiting face to face, declining to write more with ink and pen, and pass on mutual greetings among friends.
grc.novum_testamentum.iudae: The Epistle of Jude is a brief New Testament letter in Greek prose, composed in the Imperial era and counted among the catholic epistles. It opens by identifying its author as Judas, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, who addresses the called and beloved and announces his intention to urge his readers to contend for the faith once delivered to the saints. The letter then denounces ungodly intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ, reinforcing the warning with a sequence of exemplary judgments, unbelievers delivered from Egypt, fallen angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Michael's dispute with the devil over the body of Moses, and the prophecy of Enoch, while portraying the offenders as followers of Cain, Balaam, and Korah in imagery of waterless clouds, wild waves, and wandering stars.
