It ends with exhortations to build up faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep in the love of God, and show mercy toward the wavering, closing with a doxology to the only God and Savior through Jesus Christ.
grc.novum_testamentum.marcus: The Gospel of Mark, the second of the four canonical gospels, is a prose narrative in Greek of the Roman imperial period, attributed by tradition to Mark the evangelist. It opens with the preaching and baptism of John the Baptist, the baptism of Jesus, and the temptation in the wilderness. The main body follows Jesus through Galilee and the surrounding regions as he calls the twelve, heals the sick, expels unclean spirits, and teaches the crowds in parables, before the journey to Jerusalem brings the temple confrontations, the eschatological discourse on the Mount of Olives, and the last supper, which lead into the betrayal, trial, crucifixion, and burial. The account closes with the women fleeing the empty tomb, to which the shorter and longer endings preserved in the manuscript tradition are appended.
grc.novum_testamentum.matthaeus: The Gospel of Matthew, a Greek prose narrative in the New Testament, opens with a genealogy of Jesus traced from Abraham through David and an infancy narrative that includes the visit of the magi, the flight into Egypt, and the settlement in Nazareth. It then follows Jesus from his baptism by John and temptation in the wilderness through a Galilean ministry of preaching, healing, and exorcism, punctuated by extended discourses such as the Sermon on the Mount, the parables of the kingdom, and the mission instructions to the twelve disciples. The narrative later turns toward Jerusalem, where the entry into the city, the temple confrontations, and an apocalyptic discourse on the destruction of the temple and the end of the age lead into the Last Supper, betrayal, trial before Pilate, crucifixion, and burial. The work closes with the women at the empty tomb, appearances of the risen Jesus, and his commission to the disciples to baptize all nations.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_i: First Peter is a prose epistle of the Greek New Testament, attributed to the apostle Peter and of uncertain date within the imperial period, addressed to the elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia; it opens with a salutation and a blessing on the living hope secured through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The body of the letter urges its addressees to holiness, sincere mutual love, and good conduct among the nations, presenting them as living stones built upon Christ and as a royal priesthood. It then sets out exhortations to submission to emperor, governors, masters, wives, and husbands, and treats unjust suffering as a share in Christ's own passion, with baptism figured in the deliverance through the flood. The closing sections instruct elders to shepherd the flock, counsel humility and vigilance against the devil, and send greetings through Silvanus from the community in Babylon together with Mark.
grc.oppian.halieutica: The Halieutica, a Greek didactic poem on fish and fishing in 3,506 lines divided into five books, is attributed to Oppian, who addresses it to a Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; his identity and date are uncertain in the record. The poem opens with a proem contrasting the toilsome, perilous craft of the fisherman with the easier hunts of land and air, invoking Zeus, Poseidon, and Hermes as patrons. It surveys the breeding grounds and habits of the sea's many creatures, their loves, fights, and cunning devices, including the mating of the moray and viper, the sponge-hunters, and the dolphin's friendship with a youth of Lesbos. Books on fishing follow, describing hooks, nets, traps, spears, poisons, and the hunting of tunny, swordfish, and great sea-monsters, closing with a prayer for the emperor and an invocation to Eros.
grc.oppian_of_apamea.cynegetica: The Cynegetica ('On Hunting') is a Greek didactic epic in four books attributed to Oppian of Apamea, addressed in its opening lines to the young Antoninus, son of Domna and Severus, who is bidden by Calliope and Artemis to sponsor a song of the chase. The first book treats the hunter's equipment and dress, the seasons and hours suited to the hunt, and the breeds, mating and training of horses and dogs, with an excursus on legendary hunters such as Perseus, Castor and Polydeuces, Meleager, Atalanta, Hippolytus and Orion. The second and third books survey the generations of wild beasts, the horned game, elephants, the rhinoceros and smaller creatures, then the great carnivores, lion, pard, lynx, tiger, bear and wild boar, with close attention to their courtship, parturition and parental behaviour. The final book turns to methods of capture, covering pit traps, nets, fire and mounted drives for lions, the luring of panthers with springs of drugged wine, which occasions an extended account of Dionysus, the Bacchants and Pentheus, and the taking of bears and gazelles with nets and snares.
grc.pausanias.description_of_greece: A periegesis of mainland Greece in ten books by the Greek writer Pausanias, describing the country region by region through its cities, sanctuaries, monuments, and works of art. The first book begins at Cape Sounion and the harbors of Athens before moving into the city itself. Subsequent books pass through the Peloponnese, Corinth, Laconia, Messenia, Elis with Olympia, and Arcadia, and then return to central Greece with Boeotia and Phocis, closing among the towns of the Ozolian Locrians. Descriptions of temples, statues, votive offerings, and tombs are interwoven throughout with local myths, cult practices, historical anecdotes, and notices of artists and Olympic victors.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_mutatione_nominum: A Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus expounding the seventeenth chapter of Genesis. It opens with the divine appearance to the ninety-nine-year-old Abraham (Gen. 17:1), arguing that such visions disclose not the unknowable Existent himself but his kingly and beneficent powers, and that his true name cannot be uttered by mortals. The body of the work interprets symbolically the successive scriptural renamings, Abram as Abraham, Sarai as Sarah, Jacob as Israel, Joseph as Psonthomphanech, Hoshea as Joshua, and others, turning etymologies of each name into moral and psychological readings of virtue, grace, and the self-taught character of wisdom. Later sections treat the promised birth of Isaac as joy generated in the soul, Abraham's laughter and momentary wavering in faith, the significance of perfect numbers, and the purification of thought, word, and deed through the sin offerings of Leviticus.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_posteritate_caini: De Posteritate Caini is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, of uncertain date, expounding the Genesis narrative of Cain's departure from God and of his descendants. It opens with Genesis 4:16, Cain going out from the face of God to dwell in the land of Naid opposite Eden, and argues that since God has no face or parts and fills all things, the Mosaic narrative must be read figuratively. The exposition follows Cain's line, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methuselah, and Lamech with his wives Adah and Zillah and their offspring, taking each name as a personification of impiety, vanity, or bodily passion, and reads Cain's founding of a city as the construction of a doctrine that makes the human mind the measure of all things. Later sections set the Cainites against Seth, the 'other seed' raised up in place of Abel, through extended allegories of watering and irrigation such as Hagar and Rebecca at the well, and the treatise closes with the drunkenness of Lot's daughters, Onan, Phinehas, and praise of peace as the fount of happiness and long life.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sobrietate: A Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus, expounding the scriptural account of Noah's drunkenness in Genesis 9 and framing sobriety as the watchfulness of the rational soul. Opening from the verse in which Noah, waking from wine, learns what his younger son has done, the work first praises the sober mind and then reads scriptural talk of 'younger' and 'older' as descriptions of moral condition rather than age, with examples drawn from Ishmael and Isaac, Rachel and Leah, Joseph, and the naming of Abraham as elder. Its latter half interprets the curse of Canaan, son of Ham, as vice in motion rather than at rest, and expounds the blessings of Shem and Japheth, in which the wise man calls on God to enlarge the mind and to dwell in the purified house of the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_specialibus_legibus_lib: De Specialibus Legibus ('On the Special Laws') is a four-book treatise in Greek by Philo Judaeus, the first-century CE Alexandrian Jewish philosopher, expounding the individual precepts of the Mosaic law as the 'species' that fall under the ten commandments, which he had treated in an earlier work as the 'genera'. The work opens with a defence of circumcision against those who deride the practice, followed by the laws on the worship of the one God and the prohibition of images and of reverence paid to the sun, moon and stars. The remaining books pass in order through the rest of the Decalogue: the Sabbath and the festival calendar, duties to parents and neighbours, marriage and sexual conduct, homicide, theft, judicial procedure, and the duties of magistrates and soldiers. Each precept is supplied with a rational or symbolic explanation, and the treatise closes with the laws of warfare and an extended praise of justice and equality as the ordering principle of heaven and earth.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_virtutibus: De Virtutibus is a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, expounding the virtues as embodied in the Mosaic law and falling into sections on courage, humanity, repentance, and nobility. It opens by passing from a preceding discussion of justice to courage, defining true manliness not as the furious rage the many admire but as knowledge that scorns poverty, dishonour, mutilation, and disease with a firm and high-hearted soul. The bulk of the work follows the law's humane injunctions concerning female captives, runaway and debt slaves, enemies and their beasts of burden, and newborn animals, before treating repentance and, at length, nobility, arguing from the patriarch Abraham, from Tamar, and from Jacob's handmaids that genuine good birth derives from virtue and worship of the one God rather than from ancestry.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_vita_mosis_lib_iii: De Vita Mosis Lib III carries the third book of Philo Judaeus' Greek treatise on the life of Moses, edited in Cohn's Berlin edition of 1902 and running to 627 lines. Philo, a Jewish author writing in Greek, ranks Moses above Greek sages as lawgiver and interpreter of sacred laws and recasts the biblical narrative in the idiom of Greek biography, following him from his Chaldaean lineage and Egyptian birth through exposure on the Nile, adoption by the king's daughter, a royal education in mathematics and philosophy, and the enslavement of his people. The opening prologue defends Moses against the mockery of Greek men of letters and announces an account drawn from the sacred books and from elders of the nation. For readers of intertexts, the work stands among the fullest ancient Greek treatments of Moses, bridging scriptural narrative and the conventions of Greek paideia, biography, and encomium.
grc.philo_judaeus.legatio_ad_gaium: A Greek historical narrative by Philo of Alexandria, who writes as a member of the embassy sent by the Jews of Alexandria to the emperor Gaius Caligula. The work opens with a meditation on the instability of fortune against the steadfastness of nature and divine providence, naming the people Israel as 'he who sees God.' It then traces Gaius's accession after Tiberius, the empire's initial rejoicing, his grave illness, and his growing demand for divine honours, before turning to the order to erect a colossal statue of the emperor in the Jerusalem Temple and the grief and danger this brought upon the nation. The account culminates in the envoys' humiliating audiences before Gaius in Rome, his mockery of their ancestral customs, their narrow dismissal, and closes with a promise to narrate the emperor's subsequent reversal of fortune.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.heroicus: Heroicus is a Greek dialogue by Philostratus the Athenian in which a Phoenician merchant, delayed by contrary winds on the Hellespont coast near Troy, meets a vinedicker who asserts that the hero Protesilaos, first of the Achaeans to fall at Troy and afterwards restored to life, dwells on his land, helps him cultivate it, and shares his counsel. The rest of the work is largely the vinedicker's report of Protesilaos' conversations, in which the hero describes the true deeds, characters, and physical appearance of the Greek and Trojan warriors, corrects what he takes to be Homer's and the poets' inventions, and recounts marvels, oracles, and cult practices connected with the heroes. Its topics range from Palamedes and Ajax to the careers of Odysseus, Hector, and Achilles, the love of Achilles and Helen on the White Island in the Black Sea, and the Amazons' raid on the island's shrine. The dialogue closes as the vinedicker declines to speak of the underworld's rivers and tribunals and sends the merchant back to his ship.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vitae_sophista: The Vitae Sophistarum ('Lives of the Sophists') is a Greek prose work by Philostratus the Athenian, presented in its opening letter as a record, in two books, of celebrated sophists, dedicated to Antonius Gordianus. The selection preserved here comprises the dedicatory letter and the opening of the first book. In it Philostratus surveys the history of sophistic rhetoric, distinguishing an older sophistic founded by Gorgias of Leontini from a second sophistic associated with Aeschines, and illustrates its character with anecdotes about Prodicus, Chaerephon, Demosthenes, and other figures.
grc.pindar.odes: Pindar's Carmina gathers the epinician odes of the Greek lyric poet Pindar in four books, the Olympian, Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian odes, named for the festivals at which the victors they celebrate won. The collection opens with the ode for Hieron of Syracuse, which moves from a catalogue of splendours to the myth of Pelops and Poseidon. Across the four books each poem praises an athletic victor and his city, cataloguing wins at the great games and weaving in heroic myth, local legend and gnomic reflection on wealth, fortune and excellence. The sequence ends with the ode telling of Perseus, Medusa and Athena's invention of the flute.
grc.plato.cleitophon: A short dialogue attributed to Plato, the Cleitophon consists of a single sustained speech in which Cleitophon, son of Aristonymus, responds to a report that he has been disparaging Socrates' company and praising that of Thrasymachus. He opens by assuring Socrates that he admires his exhortations above all others, comparing them to a god's speech from the tragic stage rousing men to care for their souls rather than for wealth or the body. The speech then turns to complaint: having been awakened by such protreptic, Cleitophon repeatedly questioned Socrates' companions and finally Socrates himself as to what justice is and how its study should begin, but the answers offered, benefit, advantage, friendship in the cities, harmony as knowledge, each collapsed under examination, so that Socrates appears able only to exhort, not to teach. It ends with a pointed challenge: Cleitophon asks Socrates to state what treatment the soul requires, declaring that unless he does so Cleitophon will go to Thrasymachus and others, and will count him either a blessing or an obstacle to reaching virtue accordingly.
grc.plato.cratylus: Plato's Cratylus is a dialogue, in Greek, in which Socrates discusses with Hermogenes and Cratylus whether names possess a natural correctness or are fixed only by convention. The conversation opens with Cratylus' claim that names belong to things by nature and Hermogenes' contrary view that names are whatever a community agrees to call them, and Socrates agrees to investigate the question with both. Socrates then offers a long series of etymologies, first of names of gods and heroes and cosmic entities, then of words for virtue and vice, arguing that the original name-makers imitated the essences of things in sounds and letters, while also allowing for names that have been distorted by usage, altered pronunciation, or borrowed from foreign tongues. The discussion closes with Socrates qualifying the theory: names are likenesses of things but can be fitted well or badly, convention plays some part, and things must ultimately be studied through themselves rather than through names, which may themselves mislead those who follow them.
grc.plato.crito: A short Socratic dialogue of Plato set in Socrates' prison cell in Athens, where Crito arrives before dawn with news that the ship from Delos is expected, the signal that the day of Socrates' execution is at hand. Crito urges escape, appealing to public opinion, the danger to his friends' fortunes, and the upbringing of Socrates' children, but Socrates maintains that one must never return injustice for injustice, whatever the many believe. In reply he produces the personified Laws of Athens, who claim that he has tacitly agreed to obey them by remaining in the city, rearing children there, and not once leaving, so that flight would wrong the laws, the city, and himself. The dialogue closes with Socrates resolved to remain and accept death, saying that in this the god leads.
grc.plato.euthydemus: Plato's Euthydemus, a dialogue in Greek, opens with Socrates recounting to Crito a meeting in the Lyceum with the brothers Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, sophists who claim to teach virtue and to refute any questioner regardless of the truth of what is said. Socrates narrates their eristic displays against the young Clinias and Ctesippus, in which verbal tricks are used to argue that only fools learn, that contradiction and false statement are impossible, and that Socrates himself must be fatherless and related to dogs, before turning to his own protreptic account of philosophy as the knowledge of right use, the search for a single royal or political knowledge of good use, and the exposure of false lovers of wisdom. The work ends with Socrates advising the brothers to converse only with paying pupils and with his exhortation to Crito that he test philosophy itself rather than judge it by its bad practitioners, and finally encourage his sons toward it.
grc.plato.gorgias: A dialogue of Plato set in Athens, in which Socrates examines the nature and value of rhetoric with the rhetorician Gorgias. It opens as Socrates and Chaerephon arrive late at Callicles' house, just after Gorgias has given an exhibition there. Socrates first draws from Gorgias the claim that rhetoric produces persuasion before crowds on matters of just and unjust, then answers Polus's defense of the tyrant's power to do what he pleases with the arguments that doing injustice is worse than suffering it and that punishment benefits the wrongdoer. When Callicles rejects this as conventional morality and champions the natural right of the stronger to unlimited indulgence, Socrates replies with an account of self-control and the ordered soul and closes with a myth of the dead judged naked before Rhadamanthus, Minos, and Aeacus, urging that justice and virtue be practiced in life and in death alike.
grc.plato.hippias_minor: A Socratic dialogue by Plato, the Hippias Minor opens as Eudicus prompts Socrates to question the sophist Hippias of Elis about Homer's judgment of Achilles and Odysseus, whose portraits frame the ensuing argument. The discussion first asks whether the truthful and the false speaker are one and the same, drawing on arithmetic, geometry and astronomy to argue that only the capable man can both lie and tell the truth. Socrates then turns to whether one who errs or wrongs voluntarily is better than one who does so involuntarily, testing the claim through examples drawn from running, wrestling, the crafts and the faculties of body and soul. The dialogue ends unresolved, with Socrates professing himself unsettled by the argument's apparent conclusion that the deliberate wrongdoer, if such a person exists, would be the good man.
grc.plato.laches: A dialogue of Plato in which Socrates, Nicias, and Laches are consulted by Lysimachus and Melesias on whether their sons should be trained in the art of fighting in armour. The two generals give opposing assessments of that military instruction, and Socrates redirects the discussion by asking what courage, the virtue such training is meant to instil, actually is. Laches proposes that courage is endurance of the soul, and Nicias that it is knowledge of what is and is not to be feared, but both definitions are tested and found wanting. The dialogue ends in perplexity, with the participants resolving to seek a teacher for themselves as well as their sons and to meet again the next day.
grc.plato.leges: Plato's Laws is a long dialogue in twelve books, conducted between an unnamed Athenian Stranger, Cleinias of Crete, and Megillus of Sparta. It opens as the three men walk from Cnossos towards the shrine of Zeus, asking whether the laws of Crete and Sparta were given by a god or by men. The discussion then moves through the full design of a projected colony at Magnesia: education, choral song and dance, gymnastics, military training, marriage and household life, religious worship and the trial of impiety, together with criminal and civil statutes, courts and penalties, and rules for burial. It ends by proposing a Nocturnal Council of elder guardians, modelled on the union of intelligence and sensation in the soul, to watch over the whole constitution.
grc.plato.lysis: The Lysis is a Socratic dialogue of Plato on the nature of friendship. It opens with Socrates walking outside the city walls between the Academy and the Lyceum, where Hippothales and a group of youths draw him into a newly built wrestling school. After telling Hippothales that a lover should humble rather than flatter his beloved, Socrates questions the boys Lysis and Menexenus about who can be a friend to whom, testing in turn the claims that like is friend to like, that opposite attracts opposite, and that what is neither good nor bad becomes a friend of the good through the presence of evil. Each proposal collapses in its turn, and the conversation ends unresolved when the boys' attendants call them home at dusk.
grc.plato.menexenus: Plato's Menexenus is a Socratic dialogue of uncertain date, opening with a chance meeting between Socrates and the young Menexenus after a session of the council that must choose a speaker for the public burial of the war dead. After playful talk about funeral rhetoric and Socrates' supposed teachers of it, the greater part of the work is Socrates' recitation of a funeral oration, delivered in the voice he attributes to Aspasia. The speech praises the autochthonous birth of the Athenians and their ancestral constitution, recounts the city's wars from Marathon, Salamis and Plataea through campaigns against fellow Greeks to the recent conflicts with Sparta and Persia, and closes with exhortations to the sons of the fallen and consolation to their parents. A brief closing exchange returns the oration to its ironic frame, with Socrates promising further political speeches learned from Aspasia.
grc.plato.meno: A Platonic dialogue in which Socrates and the Thessalian visitor Menon inquire whether virtue can be taught. It opens with Menon's question whether virtue arises by teaching, practice, or nature, and then moves through the demand for a definition of virtue, the eristic puzzle that inquiry is impossible, the demonstration of recollection by means of a geometrical problem put to one of Menon's slaves, and the argument that knowledge is true belief tethered by an account of the cause. Taking up the question again by the method of hypothesis, Socrates concludes that virtue, if beneficial, must be a kind of wisdom, yet since no teachers of virtue exist it must arise neither by nature nor by teaching but by divine dispensation, and the conversation ends with an injunction to Menon to win over the Athenian Anytus.
grc.plato.parmenides: The Parmenides, a philosophical dialogue by Plato of uncertain date, opens with a frame conversation in which Cephalus of Clazomenae and his companions induce Antiphon to recite a reported meeting between a young Socrates, Zeno, and the aged Parmenides. In the first part Socrates questions Zeno's defence of the Eleatic thesis, puts forward an account of Forms, and meets searching objections from Parmenides concerning the participation of sensible things in Forms, before being set an exercise in dialectic. The remainder of the work consists almost entirely of Parmenides' prolonged examination of the hypotheses 'if the One is' and 'if the One is not', deriving contrary and often paradoxical consequences for the One itself and for the others with respect to unity, plurality, wholeness and parts, likeness, contact, motion, rest, and coming-to-be. It concludes that, whether the One is or is not, the One itself and the others, in relation both to themselves and to one another, in every way are and are not, and both appear and do not appear.
grc.plato.phaedo: Plato's Phaedo is a dialogue on the death of Socrates, framed as the narrative that Phaedo of Elis delivers to Echecrates about the conversation in Socrates' prison cell on the day he drank the hemlock. After a preamble in which Socrates explains why the philosopher should face death willingly, the discussion assembles successive arguments for the survival of the soul, drawn from the cycle of opposites, from recollection, and from the soul's kinship with the invisible and intelligible, before objections from Simmias, who likens the soul to a harmony, and Cebes, who doubts its endurance through many bodies, reopen the question. Socrates answers by recounting his youthful disappointments with natural science and his turn toward explanations through Forms, and a final argument presents the soul as the principle of life and therefore immortal. The closing movement carries Socrates' myth of the true earth, the underworld rivers, and the soul's postmortem journeys, followed by the death scene itself, ending with his last words about a debt to Asclepius.
grc.plato.phaedrus: Plato's Phaedrus is a Greek dialogue in which Socrates converses with the young Phaedrus. It opens with the pair meeting outside the walls of Athens, where Phaedrus has been listening to a speech by Lysias urging that a youth should favour a non-lover over a lover, and as they walk beside the Ilissus Socrates offers rival speeches on love, culminating in a palinode and the myth of the winged soul and its charioteer. The work then turns from love to rhetoric, examining how speeches are properly composed and judged, criticising written discourse by contrast with the living dialogue of dialectic, and recounting the story of the Egyptian god Theuth's invention of writing. It closes with Socrates' prayer to Pan and instructions to send messages to Lysias and Isocrates.
grc.plato.protagoras: Plato's Protagoras is a Socratic dialogue in Greek prose in which Socrates recounts to an unnamed companion how Hippocrates roused him before dawn, eager to pay the visiting sophist Protagoras of Abdera for instruction. The opening exchange follows the two to the house of Callias, where Protagoras is lodging, as Socrates questions what such paid teaching would make of a pupil. The dialogue as a whole takes up whether virtue can be taught, leading into debate between Socrates and Protagoras over the nature and unity of virtue.
grc.plato.respublica: Plato's Respublica is a Socratic dialogue in ten books. It opens with Socrates' descent to the Piraeus with Glaucon for a festival, his detention at the house of Cephalus, and a conversation that turns from old age to the question of justice. The dialogue goes on to found an ideal city in speech, treating the education and way of life of its guardians, the analogy between city and soul, the rule of philosophers, and the allegories of the sun, the divided line, and the cave, before examining the degeneration of constitutions, the figure of the tyrant, a criticism of poetry, and the immortality of the soul. It closes with the myth of Er, in which souls choose their next lives before drinking from the river of Lethe.
grc.plato.sophista: Plato's Sophist is a dialogue in which an unnamed Stranger from Elea, a companion of Parmenides and Zeno, is questioned by Socrates on the day after the conversation of the Theaetetus about whether the Eleatic tradition distinguished the sophist, the statesman, and the philosopher as separate kinds. Taking Theaetetus as his respondent, the Stranger seeks a definition of the sophist through dichotomous division, taking the angler as a paradigm and classifying the acquisitive and imitative arts. Midway the hunt is suspended for a prolonged examination of being and non-being, surveying earlier theories of what is, the 'gigantomachy' between materialists and idealists, and the claim that false speech becomes possible once being, sameness, difference, rest, and motion are distinguished as the greatest kinds. The dialogue closes by narrowing the divisions to a final definition of the sophist as an ironic imitator, ignorant of what he imitates, who produces appearances in short private arguments through contradictory speech.
grc.plato.statesman: A dialogue by Plato, opening with a short frame in which Theodorus and Socrates arrange for a visiting Stranger, questioned by young Socrates, to define the statesman by division. The work follows the Stranger's method of diaeresis through successive attempted definitions of the statesman's art, including a long myth of cosmic reversal and the age of Kronos, a parable in which the king is first mistaken for a shepherd and the definition is then corrected, and an extended analogy comparing statesmanship to the art of weaving. The dialogue separates the royal science from rival claimants such as generals, judges and orators, classifies forms of constitution and examines whether law or expert knowledge should rule, discusses measurement and the mean in speech and action, and closes by defining the true statesman as the one who binds courageous and moderate temperaments together into a single fabric for the city.
grc.plato.theages: A brief Socratic dialogue in the Platonic corpus, attributed to Plato and of uncertain date. It opens as Demodocus of Anagyrus asks Socrates for a private word, and the two withdraw to the stoa of Zeus Eleutherios to discuss Demodocus's son Theages, who desires to become wise. Socrates questions the young man about what kind of wisdom he seeks, setting the expertises that govern particular tasks, such as steersmanship, charioteering, medicine and generalship, against the political knowledge by which good men rule willing fellow-citizens as Themistocles and Pericles did, and after jesting that the boy's ambition points toward tyranny he disclaims any such knowledge himself. The closing portion describes the divine sign, the daimonion, that has attended Socrates since childhood and only ever dissuades, illustrated through the stories of Charmides, Timarchus, the expedition of Sannion and Aristides son of Lysimachus, and the dialogue ends with an agreement to test the companionship, with prayers and sacrifices to placate the sign if it should oppose the association.
grc.plato.timaeus: Plato's Timaeus opens with Socrates summarizing the ideal city he had described the previous day and with Critias' report of ancient Athens' victory over Atlantis, a tale traced back to Solon and Egyptian priests. The bulk of the work is Timaeus' long cosmological discourse, in which a divine craftsman shapes the visible universe as a living, intelligent likeness of an eternal model. The discourse goes on to explain the world-soul and its planetary circuits, the generation of time, the four elements built from triangles and regular solids, the characterless receptacle that receives all becoming, and the construction of the human body and its mortal soul. It closes with discussions of sensation, breathing, disease, and the transmigration of degenerate souls into lower creatures, ending with the completed cosmos hailed as one visible living god.
grc.plutarch.aemilius_paulus: Plutarch's Life of Aemilius Paulus opens with a preface shared with its companion Life of Timoleon, in which the author explains his habit of writing parallel lives as mirrors for the ordering of his own character. The narrative then follows Lucius Aemilius Paulus from his patrician Roman lineage and early magistracies, through his commands in Iberia and against the Ligurians, to his election, already in his sixties, to lead the war against Perseus of Macedon. Central chapters recount the campaign culminating in the battle of Pydna, including the lunar eclipse before the engagement, the breaking of the Macedonian phalanx, and Perseus's flight, betrayal, and surrender. The closing sections cover Aemilius's tour of Greece and the devastation of Epirus, his three-day triumph and the deaths of his two young sons, his address to the people on the instability of Fortune, Perseus's end in captivity, and Aemilius's censorship, final illness, and funerary honours.
grc.plutarch.amatorius: Plutarch's Amatorius, a Greek dialogue on love of uncertain date, opens with Autobulus agreeing to repeat for Flavianus the conversations about Eros that he witnessed at the god's festival at Thespiae beneath Mount Helicon. The reported discussion begins from the abduction of the young Bacchon by the wealthy widow Ismenodora, which leads Protogenes, Peisias and the other guests into argument over whether pederastic or conjugal love better deserves the name of Eros. The father of Protogenes then undertakes a sustained defence of Eros as a god and a teacher of virtue, drawing on Platonic doctrine, an Egyptian teaching about three Erotes, and an extended analogy between Eros and the sun, and illustrating his case with stories of lovers' courage and constancy, from Cleomachus of Thessaly and Epaminondas to the Galatian Camma and the hiding of the fugitive Sabinus underground with his wife. The dialogue closes with news that Peisias, once the match's chief opponent, now willingly leads the bridal procession, and the company departs to salute the god and attend the wedding.
grc.plutarch.an_seni_respublica_gerenda_sit: The dialogue is conducted between Plutarch and his friend Euphanes, whose habit of quoting Pindar provides the opening for the question whether old age is a proper season for public life. Against the pretext that retirement befits the old, Plutarch argues from examples of Greek and Roman statesmen, Pericles, Agesilaus, Phocion, Cato, Pompey, Cicero and Masinissa among them, that age brings prudence, authority and experience, while withdrawal into luxury or idleness discredits both the man and the city. He goes on to weigh which offices and burdens an elderly statesman should decline and which he should keep, how he should speak in the assembly without provoking envy, and how he should guide and give way to the young. The discussion closes with the claim that political engagement is not a task with an end but a way of life for a rational and social being, exercised to the last through judgement, speech and care for the common good.
grc.plutarch.animine_an_corporis_affectiones: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia under a title usually rendered 'Whether the affections of the soul are worse than those of the body.' It opens with Homer's verdict that no creature is more wretched than man and proposes to divide human misery between body and soul, to see whether men are unhappy through fortune or through themselves. The argument, conducted largely through medical analogy, holds that psychic affections are the more grievous: bodily diseases announce themselves in pulse and pallor, whereas the soul's maladies, folly, anger, love, envy, cowardice, deceive their bearers, who take them for virtues and flee the philosopher as they would never flee a physician. Drawing on the Aesopic fox's boast of inward variety, on Democritus, and on the madness of Agave, the essay closes with the passions figured as wintry storms that wreck a man's life and the crowded courtroom as a body inflamed.
grc.plutarch.antony: Plutarch's Greek biography of Mark Antony opens with the statesman's ancestry, a grandfather put to death in Marius's purge, and the young Antony's extravagance under Curio, before turning to his campaigns in the East and his service as Caesar's ally and general. The narrative follows him through Caesar's assassination, his ascendancy at the funeral oration, the triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and its proscriptions, and his marriage to Octavia, then dwells at length on the liaison with Cleopatra that estranged him from Rome. A disastrous Parthian expedition, the naval defeat at Actium, and the final collapse at Alexandria lead to Antony's suicide, and the account closes with Cleopatra's death, the fate of their children, and the later fortunes of the family down to Nero.
grc.plutarch.bruta_animalia_ratione_uti: A Greek prose dialogue transmitted among the Moralia of Plutarch, taking its premise from Circe's transformation of Odysseus's companions into beasts. Odysseus asks the sorceress to restore his men to human form, but she produces instead Gryllus, one of the swine, who refuses and undertakes to defend the animal way of life. The ensuing debate measures the reason and virtue of beasts against those of humanity, Gryllus contending that animals possess courage, justice, and the other virtues untaught and according to nature, while human reasoning serves appetite and ambition. From the name of its principal animal speaker the work is also known as the Gryllus.
grc.plutarch.caesar: Plutarch's Life of Caesar, written in Greek, opens with Caesar's marriage to Cornelia, daughter of Cinna, and the enmity it provoked in Sulla. The narrative follows his perilous youth, his capture by pirates and the raid by which he punished them, his rhetorical studies at Rhodes, and his rise through the Roman magistracies amid the Catilinarian debate, the Bona Dea scandal, and the alliance with Pompey and Crassus that brought him the consulship and the Gallic command. Its central portion covers the wars in Gaul, Germany, and Britain, above all the revolt of Vercingetorix and the siege of Alesia, before turning to the rupture with Pompey, the crossing of the Rubicon, and the civil war through Pharsalus, Alexandria, Zela, Thapsus, and Munda. It ends with Caesar's dictatorship for life, his reform of the calendar and his triumphs, the conspiracy of Brutus and Cassius, his murder in the senate-house on the Ides of March at the base of Pompey's statue, and the retribution that pursued the assassins, closing with the omens before Brutus at Philippi.
grc.plutarch.caius_gracchus: A Greek biographical work by Plutarch, belonging to his Lives of Roman statesmen, which opens with Caius Gracchus withdrawing from public life after his brother Tiberius's death, reluctant to take up the political cause that had cost Tiberius his life. The narrative follows his quaestorship in Sardinia, his tribunates and legislative programme of grain distributions, judicial reform, colonies and roads, his rivalry with Livius Drusus and the senate's counter-moves, and his colonial foundation at the site of Carthage. It concludes with the armed confrontation under the consul Opimius, the death of Caius and his ally Fulvius Flaccus, the reprisals that followed, and the later fortunes of his mother Cornelia.
grc.plutarch.camillus: A Greek prose biography of the Roman statesman and general Camillus, one of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, of uncertain exact date. Opening with the paradox of a five-time dictator and four-time triumphator who never held the consulship, the work follows Camillus through his early distinction at the battle against the Aequi and Volscians, the ten-year siege and capture of Veii, the controversy over the owed tithe of spoils, and the charges that drove him into exile. It then recounts the Gallic invasion, the Roman defeat at the Allia, the capture and burning of Rome, the geese that saved the Capitoline, the ransom crisis with Brennus, and Camillus's return from exile at Ardea to defeat the Gauls and restore and rebuild the city. The remaining chapters cover his further dictatorships and campaigns against the Latins, Volscians, Aequi, and Etruscans, his handling of the demagogue Manlius Capitolinus, his arbitration of the conflict between plebs and senate over plebeian consuls, and his death in the plague that followed his final compromise.
grc.plutarch.cicero: A Greek biographical account of the Roman orator and statesman Cicero by Plutarch, opening with traditions about his parentage, omens at his birth, and the 'chickpea' origin of his family name. The narrative follows his education in Greek philosophy and rhetoric, his quaestorship in Sicily and prosecution of Verres, and his consulship, in which he exposed the Catilinarian conspiracy, executed the ringleaders, and was saluted as father of his country. It goes on to recount his exile engineered by Clodius, his triumphant return, his governorship of Cilicia, his wavering between Pompey and Caesar in the civil war, and his later withdrawal into philosophical and rhetorical writing. The account ends with his speeches against Antony, his entanglement with the young Octavian, his proscription and murder, and Antony's public display of his severed head and hands.
grc.plutarch.cleomenes: Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes, a Greek biography belonging to his Lives, opens after the death of Leonidas II with the forced marriage of Agiatis, Agis' widow, to the young Cleomenes, whose character and education under the Stoic Sphaerus are then sketched. The main narrative follows Cleomenes' seizure of power through the killing of the ephors, his cancellation of debts and redistribution of land, and his restoration of the old Spartan discipline, before tracing his campaigns against the Achaean League and Aratus, his capture of Argos and Corinth, and his losing struggle against the Macedonian king Antigonus, which ends with his brother Eucleidas' death at Sellasia and his own flight to Egypt. A closing stretch narrates his detention at the court of Ptolemy in Alexandria, his failed uprising with the suicides of his companions, the execution of his mother Cratesicleia and her children, and the serpent that coils about his exposed body.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pericles_and_fabi: The formal comparison (synkrisis) concluding Plutarch's paired Lives of Pericles and Fabius Maximus opens by observing that both men left many fine examples of political and military virtue. It first weighs their generalship, contrasting Pericles at the head of an Athens at the height of its good fortune with Fabius supporting a Rome battered by defeats, deaths, and the war against Hannibal, taking up such particular deeds as Fabius' rescue of Minucius and Pericles' nine trophies. The discussion then moves to their civic conduct, setting Fabius' gentleness toward Minucius against Pericles' ostracism of Cimon and Thucydides, and to their disinterestedness with money, before closing on Pericles' buildings, whose magnificence the comparison places above all earlier Roman display.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_sertorius_and_eum: The comparison of Sertorius and Eumenes is the short concluding assessment that Plutarch attaches to his paired Lives of the two men. It opens by declaring that everything memorable about Eumenes and Sertorius has now been gathered, and weighs what they shared: both were exiles and foreigners who continually commanded large and warlike armies of many peoples, though Sertorius held his command by the willing deference of his allies while Eumenes won supremacy through his deeds amid contests over leadership. It then contrasts their characters, Eumenes being warlike and contentious though he might have lived securely and with honour, and Sertorius mild and peace-loving though no peace was permitted him, so that each was driven into the opposite role. It closes with their deaths, Sertorius slain unsuspecting through his trust in his friends and Eumenes caught while trying to flee and reduced to pleading with his captor for his body and life.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_solon_and_publico: A brief comparison in Greek prose by Plutarch, forming the formal synkrisis that closes his paired lives of Solon and Publicola. It opens by asking what is proper to this particular comparison, that each statesman was the other's imitator and witness, and cites Solon's answer to Croesus on happiness as spoken more fittingly of Publicola than of Tellus. The body weighs the two careers point by point: Publicola's distinguished lineage and a death mourned by all Rome, his wealth justly gained and generously spent, his borrowing from Solon's laws in framing the constitution, the doubling of the senate, and his rooted hatred of tyranny, displayed in the expulsion of the kings and the unmasking of the Tarquins' conspiracy; Solon, for his part, is credited with the cancellation of debts that secured the citizens' freedom and with a constitution more brilliant in its beginning, though Publicola preserved his and proved the more fortunate at the last. The piece closes with the observation that a statesman's deeds must be judged against the circumstances before him, Publicola having won his greatest contests in person and turned the formidable Porsenna from enemy into friend.
grc.plutarch.conjugalia_praecepta: A Greek ethical essay by Plutarch, the Conjugalia Praecepta opens as a wedding gift to a newly married couple, explaining that philosophy offers a discourse on marriage no less worthy than song and praying that Aphrodite be attended by the Muses, Hermes, Peitho and the Graces. The body of the work consists of a long succession of short precepts, maxims and anecdotes, drawing on figures such as Solon, Socrates, Cato, Philip and Olympias, on the conduct and harmony of husband and wife. Recurring themes include the avoidance of quarrels, the wife's modesty and household management, common property and friends, the control of jealousy and gossip, restraint of luxury, and the proper observance of Aphrodite within marriage. The closing chapters, addressed to the bride Eurydice and the groom Pollianus, urge philosophy and education as the finest adornment of a wife, citing learned and celebrated women from Theano and Sappho to Claudia and Cornelia.
grc.plutarch.de_animae_procreatione_in_timae: Plutarch's De animae procreatione in Timaeo ('On the Generation of the Soul in the Timaeus') is a Greek philosophical treatise handed down among his Moralia. It opens by setting out the Timaeus passage on the blending of the indivisible and the divisible essence and by surveying how earlier Platonists such as Xenocrates and Crantor had interpreted it. The body of the work argues that Plato posits a third principle alongside god and matter, a pre-cosmic and disordered soul which the demiurge reduces to order, and defends this reading against rival interpretations and against the apparent contradiction between the soul's ungenerated status in the Phaedrus and its generation in the Timaeus, with excursuses on the origin of evil in Stoic and Epicurean thought. Its closing chapters follow the mathematical construction of the world soul through the number series, the arithmetic and harmonic means, musical intervals and the Pythagorean tetraktys, ending with reflections on the harmony by which the planets and the whole cosmos are ordered.
grc.plutarch.de_cohibenda_ira: Plutarch's De Cohibenda Ira (On Restraining Anger) is a short Greek dialogue in which Fundanus and Sulla discuss the control of temper. Fundanus recounts how he tamed his own quick anger, and the speakers compare anger to a disease requiring continuous treatment rather than a single remedy, arguing that reason must be cultivated within the soul in advance, since a person in rage admits no outside counsel. The exchange draws on sayings of Musonius, medical and nautical imagery, and anecdotes and verses illustrating how slight provocations kindle wrath. The dialogue is preserved among Plutarch's moral essays (Moralia).
grc.plutarch.de_herodoti_malignitate: Plutarch's short Greek essay On the Malice of Herodotus, part of the Moralia and addressed to an Alexander, is a sustained polemic against Herodotus's Histories. It opens by warning that Herodotus's easy and charming style conceals a malignant character directed chiefly against the Boeotians and Corinthians, and announces a collection of telltale signs of biased storytelling. The essay then catalogs such signs of malice, harsh word choice, gratuitous disgraceful episodes, omission of noble deeds, preference for worse accounts, imputation of base motives, and attribution of success to luck or bribery, and proceeds through the Histories book by book, from Io and the Trojan War to the battles of the Persian Wars, arguing that Herodotus defames leading Greek states and diminishes their achievements at Marathon, Thermopylae, Artemisium, Salamis, and Plataea. It closes by conceding the sweetness of Herodotus's narrative while likening his hidden slander to a beetle among roses.
grc.plutarch.de_liberis_educandis: The De Liberis Educandis is a Greek moral essay attributed to Plutarch, offering precepts for the rearing of freeborn children. It opens by proposing an inquiry into the upbringing of the free-born, beginning from the choice of a wife and the circumstances of conception, before passing through the nursing of infants, the selection of nurses, paedagogues, and teachers, the training of body and memory, and the disciplined use of praise and reproach rather than blows. Later sections treat restraint of the tongue and of anger, truthfulness, the disputed question of the company of lovers, the perils of adolescence and of flatterers, and the arranging of marriages, all illustrated with anecdotes drawn from figures such as Lycurgus, Socrates, and Themistocles. The essay closes with a catalogue of unstable goods, nobility, wealth, beauty, strength, health, beside which education alone is held to be an immortal and divine possession.
grc.plutarch.de_stoicorum_repugnantis: A Greek philosophical treatise by Plutarch arguing that Stoic doctrine is at odds with itself, above all in the writings of Chrysippus. It opens by demanding that a philosopher's life display the same harmony with his teaching that Aeschines required of the orator and the law, before turning to a long catalogue of Stoic inconsistencies. Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus are shown praising the active life while spending their days in secluded study, and Chrysippus is made to contradict himself over the order of philosophical instruction, the unity of virtue, arguing on both sides, law and justice, pleasure, the wise man's earnings, and friendship. The longest sections attack his physics and theology, charging that his accounts of fate, providence, and the gods, of the cosmos's growth and its position in the void, and of the soul and bodily qualities conflict with one another and with his own earlier statements.
grc.plutarch.epitome_libri_de_animae_procrea: A short Greek epitome of Plutarch's treatise on the generation of the soul in Plato's Timaeus, preserved among the Moralia. It opens by announcing that the treatise reports all that Plato and the Platonists have laboured over concerning the making of the soul, introducing geometrical, musical, and arithmetical theorems. The summary follows the argument through matter shaped by soul, soul bestowed on the universe and on each living creature, and evil as a growth of matter; it criticises Posidonius and his circle for placing soul near matter and identifying it with an idea or a harmony constituted by number, and insists that Plato makes the soul not a number but ordered by number. It closes with an account of the world-soul blended from indivisible and divisible substance, in which the same and the different are mixed through intermediate natures and the world's body is harmonised from the four elements.
grc.plutarch.fabius_maximus: This Life by Plutarch, written in Greek as part of his Parallel Lives, treats the Roman statesman and general Fabius Maximus, the dictator famed for his cautious strategy of attrition against Hannibal during the Second Punic War. It opens by recalling the preceding Life of Pericles as a transition and then traces Fabius's lineage from Heracles through the early Roman gens Fabia, before describing his deliberate, slow-tempered character. The narrative follows his first consulship and triumph over the Ligurians, his appointment as dictator after the Roman disaster at Lake Trasimene, his avoidance of battle with Hannibal despite the mockery of his master of horse Minucius, the trick by which Hannibal escaped the pass at Casilinum with burning oxen, Minucius's equal command, defeat, and reconciliation, the catastrophic battle of Cannae under Terentius Varro and Paullus, Fabius's recapture of Tarentum through betrayal, his quarrel with Scipio Africanus over invading Africa, and his death before the war's end, closed with an account of the honour shown him at his burial.
grc.plutarch.instituta_laconica: A brief Greek miscellany of Spartan usages preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch and written under the Roman Empire, the Instituta Laconica gathers short notices of Lycurgan institutions and everyday Laconian practice. It opens with the rule of silence at the common messes, where the eldest diner points to the doors and declares that no word spoken within may pass beyond them. The collection then runs through diet and the celebrated black broth, bodily hardship, the upbringing and discipline of boys and their deference to elders, trained theft and deliberate frugality, music and the three choruses of the age-classes, burial rites, the periodic expulsion of foreigners, and military custom, including scarlet cloaks, sacrifices after victory and the cult of Armed Aphrodite. It closes with anecdotes of magisterial punishments, the annual flogging of youths at the altar of Orthia, the leisure secured by helot labour, and an account of Sparta's departure from Lycurgus' laws down to its subjection under Rome.
grc.plutarch.lacaenarum_apophthegmata: The Lacaenarum Apophthegmata, or Sayings of Spartan Women, is a short Greek collection of anecdotes preserved in Plutarch's Moralia. It opens with Argileonis, mother of Brasidas, questioning visitors from Amphipolis about whether her son fell worthily of Sparta, and next gives Gorgo's warnings to her father Cleomenes against Aristagoras. The body of the work consists of terse replies by named and anonymous Laconian mothers, wives, and daughters: women send sons off to war with their shield, disown or even slay cowards, rejoice over those fallen in the ranks, and answer questions on marriage and household life with pointed brevity, a few entries carrying short epigrams. The collection closes with sayings of Spartan women in captivity or offered for sale, who respond to inquiries about their skills with declarations of free birth and faithful stewardship.
grc.plutarch.lucullus: Plutarch's Greek Life of Lucullus opens with the ancestry of Lucius Licinius Lucullus and his youthful prosecution of Servilius the augur, his father's accuser. The narrative then follows his early service under Sulla, his naval mission to Egypt, Cyrenaica and Cyprus, and his command in the war against Mithridates and Tigranes, including the siege of Sinope, the crossing of the Euphrates, and the march into Armenia. Later chapters treat his orderly administration of Asia, his sumptuous retirement with its daily banquets, the library he kept open to Greek scholars, and his adherence to the Old Academy of Antiochus, together with his gradual eclipse by Pompey in politics. The work closes with the failing mind of his last years, a report of death by poisoning set beside other accounts, and the burial arranged for him by his devoted brother.
grc.plutarch.maxime_cum_princibus_philsopho_: A short Greek treatise by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia under the Latin title meaning 'That a philosopher should converse especially with men in power.' It opens by rejecting the charge that a philosopher's cultivation of friendship with the powerful springs from love of glory, arguing that it is rather the shunning of rulers that betrays ambition and servility. Over the course of the essay the speaker maintains that philosophy sown in the soul of a ruler benefits many at once, illustrated by anecdotes of Anaxagoras and Pericles, Plato and Dion, Pythagoras among the leading men of Italy, Cato and Athenodorus, and Scipio and Panaetius, together with analogies drawn from doctors, priests, farmers, shipwrights, and makers of lyres and rudders. The argument closes with Plato's Sicilian voyages, where his teaching met in Dionysius a stained palimpsest still drinking in the dye of tyranny, while affirming that noble words take on the force of laws when they gain a firm hold on the minds of men in command.
grc.plutarch.nicias: Plutarch's Life of Nicias is a Greek biography of the Athenian general and statesman Nicias, son of Niceratus. An opening preface explains the author's decision to pair Nicias with the Roman Crassus and to keep his treatment of events already narrated in detail by Thucydides deliberately brief. The life surveys Nicias's wealth from the Laurium silver mines, his lavish festival dedications at Athens and Delos, and his pious, superstitious temperament, before following his commands in the Peloponnesian War, his negotiation of the peace that bears his name, and his rivalry with Alcibiades over Athenian policy. It closes with his reluctant leadership of the Sicilian expedition, the siege of Syracuse, the lunar eclipse that checked the retreat, the destruction of the army at the Asinarus river, his capture and execution, and the fate of the Athenian prisoners in the quarries.
grc.plutarch.non_posse_suaviter_vivi_secundu: Non posse suaviter vivi secundum Epicurum is a Greek dialogue by Plutarch, preserved among his moral essays, in which the speakers undertake to show that a pleasant life is impossible on Epicurean principles. It opens with the narrator recalling Colotes' Epicurean book against the other philosophers and his own earlier reply, after which Zeuxippus, Theon, and Aristodemus resolve, during a walk in the gymnasium, to plead the opposite cause. The discussion contrasts the brief and pain-laden pleasures of the body with the abiding joys of noble action, philosophy, and the memory of great deeds, then takes up Epicurus' teaching on the gods, providence, and divination, and his denial of the soul's survival after death. The speakers close by charging Epicurean doctrine with cutting off hope of immortality and the gods' kindness, and with rejecting music, poetry, history, and civic virtue in favour of the belly.
grc.plutarch.otho: Plutarch's Life of Otho is a Greek biography of the Roman emperor whose rule followed the murder of Galba and was undone by the civil war against Vitellius. It opens with Otho sacrificing on the Capitoline and pardoning Marius Celsus, an adherent of the slain Galba. The narrative follows his conciliatory settlements in the senate and with survivors of Nero's and Galba's reigns, the mutinous violence of his soldiers, and the war in northern Italy against the generals of Vitellius, culminating in the confused and bloody defeat near Bedriacum. It closes with Otho's speeches refusing to prolong a struggle of Romans against Romans, his disciplined suicide at Brixellum, the mourning of his troops, the modest tomb and epitaph Plutarch reports having seen, and a verdict that he lived no better than Nero yet died more nobly.
grc.plutarch.philopoemen: Plutarch's Life of Philopoemen, one of the Greek biographies in his series of Lives, treats the Megalopolitan general and statesman who rose to lead the Achaean League in the Hellenistic age. The work opens with Cleander of Mantinea, whose friendship with Philopoemen's father leads him to raise the orphaned boy, and with the philosophers Ecdemus and Megalophanes, who direct his education toward politics and action. It goes on to portray his austere habits, his rejection of athletic training, his farming near Megalopolis, and the career that made him the foremost commander of the Achaeans, including his victories over the Spartan tyrants Machanidas and Nabis, a disputed generalship for the Gortynians in Crete, a naval expedition against Nabis, and uneasy relations with Titus Flamininus and Rome. The narrative closes with his capture by the Messenian rebel Dinocrates, his death by poison in prison, the vengeance of the Achaeans under Lycortas, his funeral in which Polybius carries the urn, and a final notice of the honors his statues enjoyed even after Mummius sought to destroy them.
grc.plutarch.platonicae_quaestiones: Platonicae Quaestiones is a sequence of ten philosophical questions on difficult points in Plato's dialogues, preserved among Plutarch's Moralia. The first asks why the god commanded Socrates to act as midwife to others while forbidding him to beget, and is answered through an account of the elenchus as a purgative remedy and of philosophy as recollection rather than teaching. The remaining questions take up the naming of the supreme god as father and maker, the unequal divisions of the line in the Republic, the birth of body from soul, the rectilinear figures of the elements and the priority of straight to curved, the wing of the soul in the Phaedrus, antiperistasis as a single cause of effects from thunder to magnetism, the sowing of souls as instruments of time in the Timaeus, and the composition of logos from nouns and verbs alone. Each problem is posed as an aporia and resolved at length in Plutarch's own expository voice, with mathematical, physical and grammatical argument applied to the Platonic wording.
grc.plutarch.publicola: A Greek prose biography by Plutarch of Publius Valerius Publicola, the Roman statesman of the early Republic, composed as one of the author's paired lives and matched with his Solon. The work opens by sketching Publicola's lineage and his original name Publius Valerius and by announcing the comparison with Solon. The narrative then follows his part in the expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus, the institution of the consulate under Brutus and Collatinus in place of the kingship, the suppression of a royalist conspiracy, and the defense of the new commonwealth against Tarquin and Lars Porsenna, including the exploits of Horatius Cocles at the wooden bridge and Cloelia among the hostages. Its later course covers Publicola's measures for the new liberty and his repeated consulships, the consecration of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter with a digression on that building's later history, the Sabine wars, the reception of Appius Claudius and his followers at Rome, a victory over the Sabines near Fidenae, and Publicola's death and public funeral.
grc.plutarch.quaestiones_convivales: Plutarch's Quaestiones Convivales (Table Talk) is a collection of sympotic dialogues in which a circle of learned diners debates problems raised over wine, framed as instalments sent to the Roman Sossius Senecio. The opening preface explains the project of gathering remembered conversations from dinners held in Rome and in Greece and takes up the first problem, whether philosophy is fitting at a drinking party. The remaining books pose a new question at each sitting: problems in physics and medicine such as why fasting produces thirst and why snow preserves, natural questions about figs, salt and strained wine, literary and grammatical puzzles drawn largely from Homer, discussion of rites and customs such as the Chaeronean expulsion of Boulimos, and a closing sequence on the Muses, music and the art of dance. The debates recur among a familiar company of interlocutors, above all Plutarch's brother Lamprias and the philosopher Ammonius.
grc.plutarch.quomodo_adulator_ab_amico_inter: A Greek ethical essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia under the Latin title Quomodo adulator ab amico internoscatur ('How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend'), it opens by telling Antiochus Philopappus, on Plato's authority, that self-love makes every man his own first and greatest flatterer and thus opens the way to the external flatterer. The main body shows how flattery counterfeits friendship through shared pleasures, imitation of the friend's tastes and character, eager services, and a sham frankness (parrhesia), and collects signs by which the counterfeit may be exposed, such as inconstancy, servility towards the rich and powerful, and the praising of vices as virtues. Later chapters turn to the genuine frankness that belongs to friendship, prescribing when reproof should be sharp and when gentle, warning against public, drunken, or self-interemed criticism, and urging that admonition be mixed with kindness, timely praise, and due regard for the friend's feelings. The essay closes by recommending the cutting away of self-love and the pursuit of self-knowledge as the surest safeguard against falling prey to flattery.
grc.plutarch.regum_et_imperatorum_apophthegm: Attributed to Plutarch and of uncertain date, the Regum et Imperatorum Apophthegmata ('Sayings of Kings and Commanders') is a Greek collection of brief anecdotes recording the memorable replies, witticisms, and judgements of rulers and generals. It opens with a short preface addressed to the emperor Trajan, arguing that a man's spoken words display his character more directly than his deeds. The sayings proceed in loose chronological order from the Persian kings through the tyrants of Sicily and the Macedonian dynasts to Athenian statesmen, Spartan kings and commanders, Theban generals such as Epaminondas and Pelopidas, and finally Roman leaders from the early Republic down to Caesar and Augustus. The material is grouped under the names of individual rulers, each entry a compact episode in which an answer to a question, an insult, or a crisis serves as a portrait of its speaker.
grc.plutarch.solon: The Life of Solon, one of Plutarch's biographies of Greek and Roman figures, opens with antiquarian discussions of its subject's ancestry, citing Didymus for the claim that Solon's father was Euphorion against the common tradition of Execestides, and noting his Codrid descent and kinship with Peisistratus. The narrative then covers his early trading voyages and poetry, the tripod episode and other stories placing him among the Seven Sages, and his leadership in recovering Salamis from the Megarians, before turning to the Cylonian pollution, Epimenides' purification of Athens, and the conflict between debtors and creditors that brought him the archonship and a mandate to reform the state. Its central sections present his refusal of tyranny, the seisachtheia cancelling outstanding debts, a mixed constitution ranking citizens in four property classes, and a wide body of laws on marriage, funerals, water rights, planting, and public conduct, together with his travels in Egypt and Cyprus and his celebrated meeting with Croesus, whose downfall vindicates his warning to count no man happy until the end. The closing chapters describe his return to an Athens slipping under Peisistratus, his unsuccessful resistance, his death during the tyranny, and the story, judged implausible by ancient writers themselves, that his ashes were scattered on Salamis.
grc.plutarch.theseus: Plutarch's Life of Theseus, written in Greek as one of his Parallel Lives and paired with the Life of Romulus, opens with an address to Sosius Senecio explaining how the mythical element of remote antiquity is to be sifted and set aside. The narrative follows Theseus from his concealed birth at Troezen and his raising of his father's sword and sandals from beneath the rock to his overland journey to Athens, where he clears the road of malefactors such as Periphetes, Sinis, Sciron, and Procrustes, and to his recognition by Aegeus despite Medea's schemes. Later portions recount the Cretan tribute and his voyage to slay the Minotaur with Ariadne's aid, the forgotten sail that brings Aegeus to his death, his unification of Attica and reordering of its civic and religious institutions, the founding of the Isthmian games, the war with the Amazons, and his friendship with Peirithous in the battle with the Centaurs and the fatal descent to the underworld. The Life closes with the abduction of Helen, Theseus' imprisonment and return, his exile to Skyros and death at the hands of Lycomedes, and the honors he receives at Athens, culminating in Cimon's recovery of his remains.
grc.plutarch.tiberius_gracchus: Plutarch's Life of Tiberius Gracchus, a Greek prose biography from the Plutarchan Lives as printed in Perrin's Loeb edition, presents the elder Gracchan brother within the 'Roman pairing' with Gaius announced at its opening. It sets out the family's standing through the elder Tiberius Gracchus and Cornelia, daughter of Scipio Africanus, contrasts the brothers' looks, speech, and habits, and then follows Tiberius through service under Scipio at Carthage, the quaestorship under Mancinus and the negotiated surrender to the Numantines, and his tribunate with its agrarian law, whose defence against the propertied class ends the preserved portion. The 97 lines break off in the conflict with the tribune Marcus Octavius, so the Life's later course is unrepresented. Readers hunting parallels will find Polybius, Fannius, and Gaius Gracchus's memoir invoked as authorities, allusive touches such as the Dioscuri comparison of the brothers' oratory, and the celebrated passage likening landless Italians to beasts that have dens and lairs but no share in the land they fight for.
grc.plutarch.vitae_decem_oratorum: The Vitae decem oratorum, a work of uncertain date transmitted with the Moralia and attributed to Plutarch, comprises brief biographies of the ten canonical orators of Athens. It opens with Antiphon of Rhamnus, whose family and teaching, part in the oligarchy of the Four Hundred, and execution are recounted, with the decree passed against him quoted at length. The sequence then runs through Andocides, Lysias, Isocrates, Isaeus, Aeschines, Lycurgus, Demosthenes, Hyperides, and Dinarchus, before closing with notices of Demochares and of Lycophron son of Lycurgus. Each life records ancestry, deme, teachers, political career, trials, and manner of death, tallies genuine and spurious speeches, comments on style, and appends anecdotes and, at intervals, the texts of public decrees.
grc.plutarch_pseudo.placita_philosophorum: A Greek compendium of philosophical doctrines attributed to Plutarch. The work opens by dividing philosophy into physical, ethical and logical parts after the Stoics and Peripatetics, then defines nature before turning to the principles and elements proposed by individual thinkers. It proceeds topic by topic through the natural world, recording under named philosophers, Thales, Anaximander, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Plato, Aristotle, the Stoics, Epicurus and others, their doctrines on god and daemons, matter, the void, the cosmos and its shape and generation, the heavens and stars, eclipses, the Milky Way and comets, thunder and the rainbow, winds and seasons, the earth and sea, the soul and its faculties, perception, respiration, sleep, semen and embryology, plants, health and disease. Each section juxtaposes conflicting opinions, presenting the disputed teachings of successive schools in brief, systematic form.
grc.polyaenus.strategemata: Polyaenus' Strategemata is a Greek collection of military ruses compiled by a Macedonian author who, in the dedicatory preface, declares himself too old for active service and offers his knowledge of generalship instead to the emperors Antoninus and Verus. The work is announced as eight books and some nine hundred stratagems, arranged for the most part commander by commander in rough chronological order, beginning with Dionysus and passing through figures of myth to generals and kings such as Demetrius, Eumenes, Seleucus, Perdiccas, and Cassander. The individual entries are usually brief, recording devices such as feigned retreats, forged letters, concealed forces, and fires kindled to exaggerate an army's size, whereby a commander might prevail at little risk. The final book departs from the sequence to gather the exploits of women, from queens such as Artemisia, Amage, and Cynane to citizen wives who turned the course of sieges.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_mundo: A Greek cosmological treatise attributed to Aristotle but of uncertain authorship and date, composed in the form of a letter to Alexander. It opens by praising philosophy as a divine expedition of the soul to behold the whole of things. The work then surveys the structure of the universe, the spherical heavens, the aether, the fixed stars and seven planetary circles, and the five concentric elements with the earth at rest at the centre, before turning to the seas and continents, meteorological phenomena such as winds, thunder, rainbows and comets, and terrestrial and maritime disturbances including earthquakes. It closes with an account of the divine power that preserves the cosmic harmony of opposites, likening God to a Persian great king, a lawgiver and a chorus-leader, and gathering his many names as Zeus, necessity and fate.
grc.pseudoarrianus.anonymi_arriani_ut_fertur: A Greek prose periplus of the Euxine (Black Sea) of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted anonymously and attributed to Arrian, whence the designation Pseudo-Arrian. It opens at the sanctuary of Zeus Ourios on the Thracian side of the Bosporus, the landfall for ships entering the Pontus, and traces the right, Asian shore through Bithynia, Paphlagonia, Pontus and Colchis to the Cimmerian Bosporus, then rounds Lake Maeotis and returns along the left, European coast by the Tauric Chersonese and the mouths of the Ister to end at Byzantium. Coastal points are enumerated in sequence with distances in stadia and miles, together with notes on harbours, anchorages, navigable rivers and the safety or danger of particular shores. Woven into the itinerary are notices of Greek colony foundations, of peoples such as the Scythians, Sarmatians, Taurians and Mossynoeci, and of mythical associations, including the island of Achilles, the Amazons of the Thermodon and Iphigenia in the Tauric land, with occasional citation of Herodotus, Xenophon and earlier geographers.
grc.pseudogalen.de_theriaca_ad_pamphilianum: A Greek pharmacological treatise transmitted under the name of Galen and of uncertain date, cast as an address to Pamphilianus, who had asked its author to set out the nature and use of the theriac antidote. The work argues that theriac deserves use not only against venomous bites and poisonings but also prophylactically for health, longevity, and keenness of the senses, citing the practice of Roman magnates who take it at the new moon and an account of a plague in Italy stemmed by the drug. Its central section enumerates the conditions for which the antidote is appropriate, including bites, fevers, coughs, dropsy, jaundice, epilepsy, and disorders of the chest, kidneys, and liver, with dosage, vehicles, and seasons of administration specified for each. It closes with recipes for the preparation of Hedyochrus, for squill troches and theriac pastilles, and for the composite antidote attributed to Andromachus, together with Crito's directions for gathering vipers and squills.
grc.pseudolucian.χαρίδημος_ἢ_περὶ_κάλλους: The Charidemus or On Beauty is a short Greek dialogue transmitted under Pseudo-Lucian's name and of uncertain date. It opens with Hermippus meeting Charidemus, who undertakes to report a symposium given by Androcles in the Peiraeus, where the beauty of the youth Cleonymus had moved the guests to deliver speeches in praise of beauty. The body of the work consists of the three speeches then delivered, by Phylon, Aristippus, and Charidemus himself, arguing that beauty is the most divine and honoured of goods and illustrating the claim with mythological examples such as Zeus's pursuit of Ganymede, the judgement of Paris and the war fought over Helen, Theseus's seizure of Helen, and the suitors who died for Hippodameia. Charidemus's closing speech dwells on beauty's supremacy over every other excellence, and the dialogue ends with Hermippus thanking him for the account.
grc.pseudomenander.sententiae_corresponds_to: The Greek Sententiae transmitted under the name of the comic poet Menander (Pseudo-Menander) is a collection of moral maxims of uncertain date, preserved in the Greek text corresponding to the Arabic tradition of the so-called Menander Sentences. It opens with the precept that one who is human ought to think human thoughts, and continues through several hundred brief sayings, most of them single verse lines, arranged for the most part alphabetically by initial letter. The maxims urge moderation, self-control, and justice, and give particular attention to friendship, wealth and poverty, marriage and women, household management, piety toward the gods, and the workings of fortune, time, and speech.

A short Greek collection of one-line gnomic sayings handed down under the name of the comic poet Menander, preserved here as the Greek wording corresponding to one of the Arabic versions of the so-called Sentences of Menander; the compiler and date of the collection are unknown. It opens with a counsel to speak and learn good things eagerly and to put piety towards God first. The remaining monostichs, composed in iambic trimeters, urge mastery of tongue and temper, honour towards parents, elders and friends, endurance of poverty and distrust of ill-gotten gain, wariness towards women and pleasure, the value of silence and self-knowledge, and the lessons of time and fortune. The collection closes with sayings on the greatness of a gift given at the right moment and on old age as a prayed-for evil.
grc.pseudoplutarch.de_fluviis: The De Fluviis ('On Rivers') handed down under the name of Plutarch is a short Greek prose treatise of uncertain date, a work of geographical paradoxography devoted to rivers and the mountains beside them. It opens with the Hydaspes in India, where a tale of incest, impalement, and a royal suicide explains the river's renaming, and proceeds river by river through the known world, taking in among others the Ismenus and Achelous in Greece, the Hebros in Thrace, the Nile in Egypt, and the Tigris and Indus further east. Each entry gives the water's earlier name, a mythological aetiology in which divine lust, transgression, or misadventure ends in drowning and a change of name, together with the corresponding story of the adjacent mountain, and then catalogues the stones and plants found in or near the water that are credited with marvellous protective, erotic, or medicinal powers. Throughout, the narratives are supported by citations of named authorities, historians and local writers invoked by book number for each account.
