grc.pseudoscymnus.scymni_chii_ut_fertur_peri: A Greek verse periegesis of the inhabited world transmitted under the name of Scymnus of Chios but known as the work of Pseudo-Scymnus, of uncertain date and addressed to a king Nicomedes. It opens with a prologue defending the choice of comic iambic metre for a brief and memorable account, invoking the model of Apollodorus's chronicle dedicated to Attalus and listing the geographers on whom the compilation rests, including Ephorus, Eratosthenes, Demetrius of Callatis and Timaeus. The body then conducts a coastal circuit beginning at the Pillars of Heracles, passing through Iberia and Tartessus, Celtica and Massalia, Italy and Sicily, the Adriatic, Illyria and Epirus, mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, Crete and the islands, Thessaly, Macedonia and Thrace, the Propontis, and the Black Sea with its Scythian hinterland, the Maeotis and the Tanaïs, ending amid the coastal towns of northern Asia Minor such as Sinope and Heracleia. Throughout, it records city foundations and their founders, rivers, islands, harbours and emporia, and the customs of Greek and barbarian peoples.
grc.quintus_smyrnaeus.fall_of_troy: The Fall of Troy, a Greek epic in fourteen books attributed to Quintus Smyrnaeus, a poet of uncertain date, carries the Trojan story from the point where the Iliad ends down to the city's destruction. It opens just after Hector's death and cremation, as the Trojans cower behind their walls and the Amazon queen Penthesileia arrives to aid them. The poem then traces in succession Penthesileia's death at Achilles' hands, the coming and slaying of Memnon, Achilles' own death and funeral, the contest for his arms, Ajax's suicide, the arrival of Neoptolemus and of Eurypylus, the stratagem of the wooden horse, the sack of the city, and the Greeks' departures. It closes with the gods obliterating the Greeks' fortifications at the shore and dispersing the fleet with storms as each hero sails to his appointed fate.
grc.sappho.fragments: The Greek lyric fragments transmitted under the name of Sappho, written in an Aeolic dialect, preserve pieces of songs on love and desire, the worship of Aphrodite and the other gods, weddings, girlhood companions and rivals such as Atthis and Anaktoria, old age, and mythological figures including Helen, Tithonus and Adonis. The collection opens with an appeal to Hera that Charaxus may come home safely in his ship, and among the longer pieces nearby stands the nearly complete hymn summoning Aphrodite from her father's house. Elsewhere the preservation is far poorer: many items are reduced to single broken lines or isolated words, and the remainder comprises wedding songs and congratulations to bride and groom, laments for Adonis, gnomic utterances, and short prose paraphrases in later Greek that summarise poems otherwise lost.
grc.septuaginta.aggaeus: The Aggaeus, or Haggai, is a short prose book of prophetic oracles in the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, among the books of the Minor Prophets. It opens with a word of the Lord in the second year of Darius delivered through the prophet Haggai to Zorobabel son of Salathiel of the tribe of Judah and to Jesus son of Josedech the high priest, rebuking a people who dwell in panelled houses while the house of the Lord lies waste. The remaining oracles, each set to a date in the same reign, urge the people to set their hearts on their ways and rebuild the temple, promise that the glory of the latter house will surpass the former and that peace will be given in that place, put questions of purity and impurity to the priests to show that the people's works are defiled, recount blighted harvests and failing stores, and close with a promise of cosmic shaking in which the thrones of the nations are overthrown and Zorobabel is chosen and set as a signet.
grc.septuaginta.amos: Amos is the Greek Septuagint version of the prophetic book attributed to Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa whose activity the book itself sets in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel; the translation forms part of the Greek rendering of the Hebrew Bible produced by anonymous translators in the Hellenistic period. The book opens by introducing the words Amos saw concerning Jerusalem two years before the earthquake. It proceeds through judgement oracles against Damascus, the Philistine cities, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, and Moab before turning on Judah and Israel, denouncing the sale of the poor, the corruption of worship, and the complacent luxury of Samaria's elite. Visions of coming ruin, a confrontation with the priest Amaziah, and threats of exile beyond Damascus give way to a closing promise that the fallen tent of David will be rebuilt and the people planted once more in their land.
grc.septuaginta.canticum: The Canticum is the Song of Songs as transmitted in the Greek Septuagint, a Hellenistic translation of the Hebrew love poem ascribed to Solomon. It opens with the superscription 'A song of songs, which is to Solomon' and the woman's plea that her lover kiss her with the kisses of his mouth. The poem then proceeds as a cycle of lyric dialogues between a woman and her beloved, punctuated by refrains adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem, episodes in which the woman searches the city streets for her absent lover, the procession of Solomon's palanquin with its armed escort, and extended songs of mutual praise drawn from garden, orchard, and vineyard imagery. It closes with love's strength as great as that of death, an exchange over the vineyard of Solomon, and the beloved's flight to the mountains of spices.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_theodotionis: The Book of Daniel in the Greek version attributed to Theodotion, transmitted with the Septuagint and written in prose. It opens with Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem and the deportation of Daniel and his three companions to the Babylonian court. The narrative follows Daniel's rise as an interpreter of dreams and visions through the episodes of the great statue, the fiery furnace, Nebuchadnezzar's madness, the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and the lions' den, with the furnace story expanded by the prayer of Azariah and the hymn of the three young men. The latter part turns apocalyptic, recounting the visions of the four beasts, the ram and the goat, the seventy weeks, and the wars of the kings of the north and south, and closes with Michael's arising and the command to seal the book until the time of the end.
grc.septuaginta.daniel_translatio_graeca: The Old Greek version of the biblical book of Daniel, preserved in the Septuagint and of Hellenistic date, opens with Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem and the deportation of Daniel and his three companions to the Babylonian court. The work follows their fortunes under successive foreign kings: Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great image and his dream of the felled tree, the three young men withstand the fiery furnace with an inserted prayer of Azariah and a long hymn blessing all creation, Daniel reads the writing on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and he emerges unharmed from the lions' den under Darius. The latter part of the book turns apocalyptic, recounting Daniel's visions of the four beasts from the sea, the ram and the he-goat, the seventy weeks of years, and a final angelic revelation of the wars of kings of north and south, ending with the resurrection of the dead and the command to seal the book until the time of the end.
grc.septuaginta.ecclesiasticus: A Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book preserved in Greek within the Septuagint, the Ecclesiasticus presents itself in its prologue and colophon as the work of Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem, whose sayings were transmitted and gathered by his descendants. It opens with a prose preface describing the book's origin and the kinds of matter it contains. The main body consists of prose maxims and instructions on the fear of the Lord, family duties, friendship, speech, wealth and poverty, women, the discipline of children and slaves, dreams, medicine, and the practical trades, interspersed with longer poems, among them a self-praise of Wisdom recounting her origin and dwelling in Israel. A later section eulogizes the famous men of Israel from Enoch through the patriarchs, kings, and prophets to the high priest Simon, and the work closes with a prayer of thanksgiving and an autobiographical account of the author's lifelong pursuit of wisdom.
grc.septuaginta.epistula_jeremiae: The Epistle of Jeremiah is a short prose work of the Hellenistic period, transmitted in the Septuagint, attributed by its title to the prophet Jeremiah though of uncertain authorship and date. It opens with an address to the Jewish exiles, announcing that for their sins they will be carried captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar and remain there for seven generations before God leads them out in peace. The body of the work is a sustained satirical attack on idols, which are shown to be artefacts of silver, gold, and wood fashioned by craftsmen, adorned and guarded by their priests yet unable to speak, see, move, help their worshippers, or save themselves, while their cults are marked by impurity and corruption. The refrain that these are not gods and should not be feared recurs throughout, and the closing verses contrast the idols with the sun, moon, stars, lightning, wind, and clouds, which carry out the commands of the true God, ending with the declaration that a righteous man without idols stands far from reproach.
grc.septuaginta.esdras_a: A Greek biblical narrative of Hellenistic date and anonymous authorship, preserved in the Septuagint. It opens with Josiah's celebration of the Passover in Jerusalem, narrated through its sacrificial and liturgical arrangements. The story then follows the last kings of Judah from Josiah's death in battle against the Pharaoh of Egypt through the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the exile, before turning to Cyrus's decree that the exiles return and rebuild the temple. Interwoven with the return are the lists of repatriates, the correspondence obstructing the work, the tale of the three bodyguards whose contest over wine, kingship, women, and truth wins Zerubbabel royal favor, the completion and dedication of the temple, and Ezra's later mission under Artaxerxes, which ends with his prayer over mixed marriages, the dismissal of foreign wives, and the public reading of the law.
grc.septuaginta.ezechiel: Ezechiel is the Hellenistic Greek translation of the biblical book of the prophet Ezekiel, transmitted as part of the Septuagint corpus. The work opens with the prophet's vision of the divine chariot-throne by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldaeans and his commissioning to speak to a rebellious house of Israel. From there the narrative moves through oracles of judgement and symbolic acts against Jerusalem and its idolatry, visions of corruption within the temple and the departure of the divine glory, sayings on the watchman's duty and individual responsibility, and a long sequence of oracles against foreign nations including Ammon, Moab, Edom, Tyre, Sidon and Egypt. The closing portion turns to consolation and restoration, the valley of dry bones, the reunion of Judah and Joseph under a single Davidic ruler, the campaign of Gog of Magog, and an extended vision of a new temple with detailed measurements, cultic regulations for priests and prince, a life-giving river, and the division of the land among the twelve tribes.
grc.septuaginta.isaias: The book of Isaiah as rendered into Greek in the Septuagint, a translation made in the Hellenistic period, sets out the prophecies of Isaiah son of Amoz against Judah and Jerusalem in the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. It opens with the prophet's vision and a summons to heaven and earth to hear the Lord's complaint against a rebellious people whose sacrifices he refuses. The work then proceeds through denunciations of Judah's injustice and idolatry, oracles against foreign powers including Babylon, Assyria, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, and Tyre, and narrative episodes in which Isaiah counsels Ahaz and Hezekiah during the Assyrian threat, including the siege of Jerusalem and the king's illness and recovery. Its closing stretch brings oracles of consolation and restoration, songs of a suffering servant, promises of Zion's renewal, and visions of a new heaven and a new earth with worship gathered at Jerusalem.
grc.septuaginta.jeremias: The Greek version of Jeremiah preserved in the Septuagint, of Hellenistic date, opens with the word of God that came to Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth in Benjamin, in the days of the kings of Judah. Its prophecies denounce the idolatry and injustice of Judah and Jerusalem, announce sword, famine and exile from the north, and record the prophet's clashes with priests and rival prophets, together with symbolic acts such as the buried linen girdle, the potter at his wheel and the shattered earthenware flask. The work then turns to sustained oracles against the surrounding nations, Egypt, Philistia, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab, Elam and above all Babylon, framed by the cup of wrath that all peoples must drink. It closes with the narrative of Nabouchodonosor's siege and the fall of Jerusalem, the assassination of Gedaliah, the flight of the remnant to Egypt, words of comfort to Baruch, and promises of return, restoration and a new covenant.
grc.septuaginta.joel: The Greek Septuagint version of the prophetic book of Joel, a Hellenistic-era translation of a Hebrew biblical text, opens with the word of the Lord coming to Joel son of Bathuel and a summons to the elders to hear of a calamity unlike any in living memory. The prophecy describes a devastating locust plague, figured both as agricultural ruin and as an invading army, and calls the priests and people to fasting, mourning, and repentance before the swiftly approaching day of the Lord. In response to their entreaty, the Lord promises restored harvests, the outpouring of the Spirit on all flesh, and the gathering of the nations for judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat. The book closes with Egypt and Edom laid waste, Judah and Jerusalem settled forever, and the Lord dwelling in Zion.
grc.septuaginta.jonas: The Book of Jonah as it stands in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Jewish scriptures translated in the Hellenistic period by translators whose names are unrecorded, tells its story in narrative prose. It opens with the word of the Lord commanding Jonah son of Amathi to preach against Nineveh, from which the prophet instead flees by ship toward Tarshish. A divinely raised storm leads the sailors to throw him into the sea, where a great fish swallows him; from its belly he prays for three days and nights before being cast up on dry land. Under a second commission he preaches in Nineveh, and the city, from king to livestock, repents in sackcloth and fasting so that God relents, provoking Jonah's anger and the closing lesson, taught through a springing and withering gourd, on the Lord's pity for the great city and its many inhabitants.
grc.septuaginta.josue: The Greek book of Joshua, here under its Septuagint title Josue and with its hero called Jesus (Iesous) son of Nave, is a Hellenistic prose rendering of the Hebrew biblical book of Joshua, the work of translators whose names are not recorded. It opens with the Lord addressing Joshua after the death of Moses, charging him to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land sworn to their fathers. The narrative proceeds through the spies and Rahab at Jericho, the miraculous crossing of the river, the fall of Jericho, Achan's offense and the capture of Ai, the treaty with the Gibeonites, and the campaigns against the kings of the south and north, including the battle of Gibeon at which sun and moon stand still. The latter part consists largely of registers, namely the catalog of conquered kings, the boundaries and city lists of the tribal allotments, the cities of refuge and the Levitical cities, and the book closes with Joshua's exhortations and covenant renewal at Shechem, followed by notices of his death and burial and those of Eleazar and Phinees.
grc.septuaginta.judith: Judith is an anonymous narrative book of the Hellenistic period, preserved in Greek as part of the Septuagint. It opens in the twelfth year of Nebuchadnezzar, who reigns over the Assyrians at Nineveh, overthrows Arphaxad king of the Medes, and commissions his general Holofernes to punish the western nations that refused to join his war. The story follows Holofernes' devastating campaign westward to the siege of Bethulia, where the weakening defenders are delivered when the widow Judith prays for strength, enters the Assyrian camp with her maid, and beheads the general as he lies drunk after seeking her favour. The book closes with the rout of the Assyrian army, Judith's hymn of praise, her pilgrimage to Jerusalem, and her long and honoured life, ending in death at Bethulia at the age of one hundred and five.
grc.septuaginta.kritai: The Kritai (Judges) is the Greek Septuagint version of the biblical book of Judges, a prose narrative of the Hellenistic period. It opens after the death of Joshua, as the Israelites inquire of the Lord who shall lead them against the Canaanites. The book recounts the partial conquest and settlement of the land, then follows a recurring cycle of apostasy, foreign oppression, and deliverance through a succession of leaders, including Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak (with the Song of Deborah), Gideon, Abimelech, Jephthah, and Samson, before closing with appendices on Micah's shrine and the Danite migration and on the Levite's concubine and the tribal war against Benjamin. Throughout, Israel's unfaithfulness is set against the repeated raising of saviours, under the refrain that in those days there was no king in Israel.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_b: 2 Maccabees is a Hellenistic-era Greek Jewish historical work, transmitted in the Septuagint, which presents itself as an abridgment by an unnamed epitomator of a five-book history of the Maccabean crisis by Jason of Cyrene. It opens with two letters sent from Jerusalem to the Jews of Egypt concerning the observance of the days of the purification of the temple. The narrative proper recounts the attempted seizure of the temple treasury by Heliodorus, the hellenizing measures and persecutions under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the martyrdoms of the aged Eleazar and of seven brothers and their mother, and the rise of Judas Maccabaeus. It follows his campaigns against Nicanor, Timothy, Gorgias, and other commanders, the death of Antiochus, the rededication of the temple, the wars under Lysias and Demetrius, and closes with the defeat and death of Nicanor.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_d: A Greek prose treatise of the Hellenistic era, preserved among the books of the Septuagint and of uncertain authorship, 4 Maccabees is a philosophical-historical discourse on the thesis that devout reason is sovereign over the passions. It opens by announcing that pious reasoning masters pleasure, pain, fear, and desire, and defines reason, wisdom, and the cardinal virtues before turning to its proof. The greater part of the work narrates in highly rhetorical style the martyrdom of the aged priest Eleazar, of seven brothers, and of their mother under the Seleucid king Antiochus Epiphanes, each death offered as evidence that obedience to the ancestral Law conquers bodily suffering. It closes with praise of the martyrs as champions of piety, the divine punishment of the tyrant, and an exhortation to the nation to hold fast to the law.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_i: First Maccabees is a Hellenistic Jewish historical narrative transmitted in Greek within the Septuagint, anonymous and of uncertain date. It opens with the conquests of Alexander the Great and the accession of Antiochus Epiphanes, whose edicts against the Jewish law and plundering of the Jerusalem temple provoke the revolt of the priest Mattathias and his five sons. The narrative follows Judas Maccabeus through his victories, the rededication of the altar, and his death in battle, then turns to the leadership of his brothers Jonathan and Simon, covering their campaigns, their negotiations with rival Syrian kings, and the embassies to Rome and Sparta. The work closes with Simon's holding of the high priesthood and command, the removal of the Seleucid yoke from the land, and his murder at a banquet by his son-in-law Ptolemy, leaving his son John as heir.
grc.septuaginta.nahum: The Book of Nahum in its Greek form, one of the twelve minor prophets as rendered in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew scriptures produced in the Hellenistic period by translators whose identities are unknown. The book opens with its superscription, 'an oracle of Nineveh, the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite', followed by a theophanic hymn on the Lord as jealous, avenging, slow to anger, and terrible in wrath. The prophecy then announces the doom of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital: God restores the splendour of Jacob and Judah, the enemy is swept away, and the city falls amid plunder, panic, and the flight of her soldiers. The closing oracles denounce the 'city of blood' as a sorceress and harlot, picture her merchants scattered like locusts and her rulers asleep, and end with the verdict that her wound is incurable and that all who hear of her ruin will clap their hands.
grc.septuaginta.odae: The Odae form a collection of prose canticles transmitted in Greek biblical manuscripts and appended to the Psalms in Septuagint tradition. The collection opens with the song of Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea, and proceeds through canticles and prayers drawn from other biblical books, including the song of Moses in Deuteronomy, the prayers of Hannah, Hezekiah, Jonah, and Habakkuk, the prayer and song of the Three Youths, and the Prayer of Manasseh, together with the New Testament canticles of Mary, Zechariah, and Simeon. It closes with a morning hymn of praise. The date of the compilation as a distinct collection is uncertain.
grc.septuaginta.proverbia: The Paroimiai, the Greek Proverbs of the Septuagint, is a Hellenistic prose rendering of the biblical collection attributed to Solomon son of David. It opens with a superscription and a programmatic preamble promising knowledge of wisdom, discipline, and the interpretation of the proverbs, riddles, and sayings of the wise. The body consists chiefly of paternal instructions to a son on prudence, justice, restraint, and the dangers of the adulterous woman, interspersed with speeches of personified Wisdom, including an account of her presence at the creation of the world, together with long runs of aphorisms on speech, wealth, poverty, friendship, and kingship. Toward the end stand numerical and observational sayings, the words of King Lemuel taught by his mother, and a poem praising the virtuous woman.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi: The Psalms in their Greek Septuagint version, a translation made in the Hellenistic period, form the collection of Hebrew psalms as it passed into Greek biblical use, with superscriptions ascribing many of the poems to David and recalling occasions such as his flight from Absalom. The collection opens with the beatitude on the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night. The psalms that follow range over laments and petitions for deliverance from enemies, thanksgivings, royal psalms on the Lord's anointed, wisdom admonitions, and long recitals of Israel's history from the plagues of Egypt and the exodus through repeated apostasy and forgiveness. The sequence closes in a series of hallelujah hymns summoning trumpet, strings, and cymbals to praise the Lord, followed by a short appended psalm narrating David's youth, his anointing, and his beheading of the Philistine.
grc.septuaginta.ruth: Ruth is the Greek version of the biblical book of that name, rendered anonymously into Greek in the Hellenistic period as part of the Septuagint. The narrative opens with a famine that drives Elimelech and his family from Bethlehem to Moab, where the deaths of the men leave his wife Naomi alone with her Moabite daughters-in-law. Naomi's return to Bethlehem at the barley harvest shapes the rest of the book, as Ruth gleans in the field of the kinsman Boaz, approaches him at the threshing floor, and is married to him after he settles the right of redemption before the elders at the gate; the birth of their son Obed is greeted by the women of Bethlehem as a restoration of Naomi. A closing genealogy traces Obed's line through Jesse to David the king.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_theodotionis: Susanna, preserved here in the Greek version attributed to Theodotion, is a narrative in Hellenistic biblical prose set among the Jewish exiles in Babylon. It opens with Susanna, the beautiful and God-fearing wife of the wealthy Joakim, whose garden becomes the scene of the story's crisis: two elders appointed as judges, consumed with desire for her, accost her as she bathes alone and, when she refuses them, denounce her before the people as an adulteress. The assembly condemns her to death, but as she is led away God stirs the spirit of the young Daniel, who separates the two witnesses and exposes their false testimony through questions about the tree under which they claim to have caught the supposed lovers. The elders are put to death according to the law of Moses, Susanna's innocence is vindicated, and Daniel's standing among the people grows from that day onward.
grc.septuaginta.threni_seu_lamentationes: The Greek Lamentations, transmitted in the Septuagint under the title Threni, is a biblical book of Hellenistic date and uncertain authorship. It opens with the cry of how the city once crowded with people now sits solitary like a widow among the nations. The work consists of five laments over the destruction of Jerusalem and the exile of Judah, the first four arranged as acrostics on the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, moving from the city's mourning and the Lord's outpoured wrath through confession of sin and reflections on suffering to a closing communal prayer that God, enthroned for ever, would turn his people back and renew their days as of old.
grc.septuaginta.tobias: The Book of Tobit (Greek Tobias), preserved in the Septuagint, is a Hellenistic Jewish prose narrative of uncertain date and authorship. It opens with the first-person account of Tobit, a man of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, who recounts his almsgiving, his burial of murdered kinsmen, his blindness, and his prayer for death. The story then follows his son Tobias, sent to recover a deposit in Media under the disguised angel Raphael: catching a fish in the Tigris, he marries his kinswoman Sarah at Ecbatana after burning the fish's organs to drive off the demon Asmodeus, who had slain her seven previous husbands, and returns with the money and his bride to heal his father's sight with fish gall. Raphael then reveals his identity, Tobit chants a hymn of praise with prophecies of Nineveh's fall and Jerusalem's restoration, and the book closes with Tobit's final instructions and the deaths of Tobit, Anna, and Tobias in Ecbatana.
grc.septuaginta.zacharias: The Zacharias of the Septuagint is the Greek version of the biblical book of Zechariah, a collection of prophecies attributed to Zechariah son of Barachias of the line of Addo, whose oracles are set in the reign of Darius and whose Greek translation was made in the Hellenistic period. The book opens with the word of the Lord coming to the prophet in the second year of Darius, summoning a people chastened like their fathers to turn back to the Lord. A series of night visions follows, horsemen among the shady mountains, four horns and smiths, a man with a measuring line, the high priest Jesus accused and reclothed, a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, a flying scroll, a woman borne in a measure to Babylon, and four chariots, interspersed with oracles on the rebuilding and repopulation of Jerusalem, the crowning of the high priest, fasts turned to joy, and the gathering of many nations to seek the Lord. Later chapters turn to shepherds who destroy the flock, the thirty pieces of silver and the breaking of the two staffs, a sword roused against the shepherd, the assault of the nations on Jerusalem, the Lord's standing on the Mount of Olives, living waters flowing from the city, and all peoples ascending yearly to keep the feast of tabernacles.
grc.sophocles.ajax: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, dramatizing the fate of Ajax after the arms of Achilles are awarded to Odysseus. In the prologue Athena shows Odysseus that she has turned Ajax's murderous rage upon the army's flocks and herds, which he has slaughtered in the belief that they were the Atreidae and their followers, and she holds him deluded inside his tent. The play goes on to depict Ajax's recognition of his disgrace and his suicide, the laments of Tecmessa and the chorus, the quarrel between Teucer, Agamemnon and Menelaus over his burial, and its settlement through Odysseus's intervention.
grc.sophocles.antigone: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, set in Thebes after the deaths of Eteocles and Polynices, who killed one another in the war for the city. It opens with Antigone telling her sister Ismene of Creon's edict forbidding any burial of Polynices and declaring her resolve to bury him in defiance. Antigone is caught and condemned despite her appeal to divine ordinance, and neither the pleas of Haemon for his betrothed nor the warning of the seer Teiresias turns Creon in time: Antigone hangs herself, Haemon and then Eurydice kill themselves, and Creon is left to lament his ruin. The play closes with the chorus's reflection that wisdom comes only through suffering, that reverence is owed to the gods, and that great words bring great blows upon the proud.
grc.sophocles.ichneutae: The Ichneutae is a satyr play by Sophocles that survives only in papyrus fragments, with many lines lost or broken. It opens mid-speech with a proclamation of a reward for anyone who can find Apollo's stolen cattle, as a tracker recounts following traces through Thessaly, Boeotia and other lands toward Cyllene. The surviving action follows the satyrs, sent out under their father Silenus to hunt the missing herd, whose search brings them to a cave on Cyllene whence issues a sound never before heard among mortals; the nymph Cyllene comes forth and explains that the infant Hermes concealed there has killed a tortoise and fashioned the lyre from its shell. The later fragments consist largely of the ensuing exchanges over the theft, in which the satyrs, Silenus and Cyllene dispute the child's deed, though the close of the play is badly damaged.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_at_colonus: A tragedy by Sophocles, the Oedipus at Colonus dramatises the final episode of the Oedipus story, from the blind hero's arrival in Attica to his enigmatic end. The opening scene presents Oedipus, led by his daughter Antigone, reaching a grove at Colonus and asking to be set down while she inquires where they have come. Learning that the spot is inviolable ground of the Eumenides, Oedipus takes it as the resting place promised to him and gains the protection of Theseus and the Athenians, while Creon's attempt to force him back to Thebes, carrying off Antigone and Ismene, and Polynices' appeal that ends in his father's curse supply the conflicts of the central action. The closing scenes follow Oedipus away to a hidden grave from which he vanishes, an end reported by a messenger, and conclude with Antigone and Ismene lamenting their loss as they prepare to return to Thebes.
grc.sophocles.oedipus_tyrannus: Oedipus Tyrannus is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, following the ruin of the king of Thebes within a single day. It opens with the plague-stricken city supplicating Oedipus, who sends Creon to Delphi and receives the oracle that the killer of Laius must be found and driven out before the sickness will cease. The ensuing search brings Oedipus into angry conflict with the seer Tiresias and with Creon, whom he accuses of plotting against him, until Jocasta's recollection of an abandoned child and Oedipus' memory of a killing at a triple crossroads set the recognition in motion. A messenger from Corinth and an aged Theban herdsman complete the evidence that Oedipus is Laius' murderer and Jocasta's son, whereupon Jocasta takes her own life, Oedipus blinds himself, and, after a last leave-taking of his daughters, he passes under Creon's charge into exile while the chorus reflects that no man should be counted happy before the end of his life.
grc.sophocles.philoctetes: A Greek tragedy by Sophocles, dramatising the attempt of Odysseus and the young Neoptolemus to obtain the bow of Heracles from Philoctetes, who has been marooned on Lemnos for ten years with a festering snake-bite. The play opens on the desolate shore of the island, where Odysseus coaches Neoptolemus in the deceit by which the bow is to be won. After gaining Philoctetes' trust and seizing the weapon, Neoptolemus is overcome by conscience and pity, reverses the treachery, and at last Heracles appears to command Philoctetes to sail to Troy, where he is promised healing and victory. The drama turns throughout on the conflict between expedient cunning and honourable integrity.
grc.sophocles.trachiniae: The Trachiniae is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, dramatising the final catastrophe of Heracles through the story of his wife Deianira. The play opens with Deianira at Trachis lamenting her long separation from Heracles and recounting her wooing by Heracles and the river-god Achelous; a messenger soon brings news of his victories and of the captive Iole. Deianira, hoping to win back her husband's love, sends him the robe she has unknowingly soaked in the poisoned blood of the centaur Nessus, and when she learns what she has done she kills herself; the dying Heracles, brought home in agony, extracts from his son Hyllus the promise to burn him alive on Mount Oeta and to marry Iole.
grc.soranus.de_signis_fracturarum: De Signis Fracturarum ('On the Signs of Fractures') is a short Greek medical treatise transmitted under the name of Soranus. It opens by defining the cranial fracture and distinguishing its principal varieties, such as fissure, incision, depression and splintering. The treatise then works through the skeleton site by site, from nose, jaw and clavicle to spine, sternum, ribs, pelvis and the bones of the limbs, describing the visual and tactile signs by which each kind of fracture is diagnosed. It ends with general criteria for judging the danger of fractures complicated by open wounds, protrusion of bone, or involvement of vital parts.
grc.soranus.gynaeciorum_libri_iv: A Greek medical treatise on women's medicine in four books by the physician Soranus, of uncertain date. The opening explains how the discipline is best divided and then defines the qualities required of the ideal midwife, from literacy, memory and steady nerves to long, slender fingers and short-trimmed nails. The work proceeds to the anatomy and nomenclature of the womb and the management of pregnancy and childbirth, sets out the care of the newborn and young child, swaddling, bathing, nursing, the timing of teething and weaning, and the treatment of infant ailments, and then turns to the pathological conditions of women, discussing at length the causes and correction of uterine prolapse. It closes with a sequence of chapters cataloguing affections of the female parts, among them abscesses, ulcers, cancers, fistulas, warts and haemorrhoids of the womb.
grc.themistocles.epistulae: Attributed to Themistocles and of uncertain date, the Epistulae is a series of Greek letters composed in the voice of the exiled Athenian statesman. The opening letter, addressed to Aeschylus, recounts his ostracism from Athens and the sympathetic encounters with Argive friends on his journey toward Delphi. The remaining letters, to correspondents including Pausanias, Aristides, Polygnotus, Habronichus, Autolycus, and Alcetas, rehearse his exile at Argos, his flight by way of Corcyra and the court of Admetus in Molossia, his perilous voyage to Asia, and the honours and cities granted him at the Persian court, while also rebuking Pausanias for treasonable dealings with Persia and narrating his downfall and death. A final short note orders the dispatch of silver kraters and golden thuribles by a trustworthy carrier.
grc.theocritus.epigrams: The Epigrams are a collection of short Greek poems transmitted under the name of Theocritus, composed in literary dialects with marked use of Doric. The pieces include dedications to gods such as Pan, Priapus, and Aphrodite, epitaphs for figures ranging from herdsmen to physicians and sophists, and verses on statues, votive offerings, and choregic victories. Varied in subject and scale, they stand as a brief epigrammatic complement to the bucolic poetry of the Theocritean corpus.
grc.theocritus.idylls: The Idylls are a collection of thirty short poems in Greek by the poet Theocritus, composed for the most part in the Doric dialect. The opening poem brings together a goatherd and the herdsman Thyrsis, who for a wager undertakes to sing of the sufferings of Daphnis. From there the collection ranges over pastoral singing matches, laments, and love talk among herdsmen and reapers; urban mimes, notably the Syracusan women at the festival of Adonis; encomia of patrons such as Hiero and Ptolemy; an epithalamium for Helen; mythological episodes concerning Hylas, Heracles, and the Cyclops; and closing poems in which a speaker complains of his bondage to Eros, who drags him by a yoke whether he wills it or not.
grc.theophrastus.characters: The Characters of Theophrastus is a Greek collection of brief ethical portraits, each devoted to a single disreputable type of person. A prologue addressed to Polycles, spoken by a writer who claims ninety-nine years of observation of human nature, announces the plan of setting down the ways (tropoi) of men by kinds, before the work turns to the sketches themselves. Each sketch opens with a compact definition of a character, the ironist, the flatterer, the chatterer, the superstitious man, the penurious man and the rest, and then catalogues the tell-tale words, gestures and petty dealings by which that type betrays itself in ordinary life. The behaviours described are drawn from every quarter of everyday experience, from dinner parties, the agora and the bathhouse to dealings with friends, slaves and tradesmen, so that the whole forms a systematic taxonomy of everyday vice.
grc.tryphiodorus.the_taking_of_ilios: The Taking of Ilios (Iliou Halosis) is a short Greek epic in hexameters by Tryphiodorus, of uncertain date. It opens with a prayer to Calliope to sing of the end of the ten years' war, then recounts the building of the Wooden Horse by Epeius at Athena's prompting, the Greeks' feigned departure for Tenedos, Sinon's deception of Priam, and the Trojans' fatal resolve to haul the horse into their city despite Cassandra's prophecies. The latter part describes the night of the sack: the warriors emerging from the horse, the slaughter of Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios and of Astyanax on the walls, the violation of Cassandra by Ajax, the sparing of Antenor's house and the rescue of Aeneas, and the Greeks' departure with Helen and the captives after burning Ilios.
grc.zenobius_sophista.ἐπιτομὴ_ἐκ_τῶν_ταρραίο: The collection transmitted under the name of the sophist Zenobius is a Greek epitome of proverbs compiled, as its title records, from the proverb-collections of Tarrhaeus and Didymus. It opens with the entry 'Abydenon epiphorema' and proceeds alphabetically through a long series of sayings, each glossed with its meaning and, in many cases, with the mythological or historical story from which it arose. Entries cite poets, historians, comic writers and oracles as witnesses to usage, and the accompanying narratives range from the labours of Heracles and the myths of Perseus, Oedipus and the Danaids to Athenian institutions, Sicilian and Corinthian affairs, and local customs across the Greek world.
grc.aelian.epistulae_rusticae: The Epistulae Rusticae, or 'Rustic Letters', is a short collection of twenty fictitious letters in Greek attributed to Aelian, composed in a polished literary style shot through with rustic vocabulary and dialect forms and exchanged among imagined country-dwellers. The opening letter, from Euthykomides to Blepaios, recounts a flirtation with a girl among the vines and closes with a jesting oath by the great mysteries of Pan. The remaining letters are self-contained vignettes of rural life: farmers trade banter and seasonal gifts of fruit and wine, a beekeeper mourns his absconded swarms, neighbours quarrel over water and stolen grapes, the misanthrope Knēmōn trades insults with his well-meaning correspondent Kallippidēs, and senders write of hunting, of a bride swapped for a courtesan, of a neighbour who has abandoned his farm for the sea-trade, and of the honest virtues of the farming life.
grc.aelian.ἀποσπασμάτια: A collection of short Greek excerpts, transmitted under the name of Aelian and consisting chiefly of fragments of his works On Providence and On Divine Manifestations, together with pieces of uncertain position drawn from the Suda and from later commentators such as Eustathius. It opens with brief notices of the frugal lives of Chrysippus of Soli and Cleanthes. The body of the work gathers moralising anecdotes in which divine providence is shown at work: the impious, whether Epicurean philosophers, tyrants, temple-robbers, oath-breakers or mockers of the gods, meet with punishment, while the pious are protected through dreams, oracles, providential rescues and the healings of Asclepius. Scattered among these stories are episodes from Greek and Roman history, accounts of sacrilege and its retribution, and short glosses on rare words.
grc.aelius_aristides.ars_rhetorica: A Greek treatise on rhetoric transmitted under the name of Aelius Aristides and of uncertain date. It opens by enumerating the virtues, or ideai, of political discourse, solemnity, gravity, circumlocution, credibility, force, emphasis, cleverness, care, sweetness, clarity, brevity, and correction, and then shows how each arises from thought, figure, and diction, illustrating the lessons chiefly from Demosthenes, with Isocrates and Thucydides also drawn on. Along the way it treats the kinds of discourse and their mixtures, the subjects of deliberative oratory, praise and blame, and the periodic arrangement of clauses and sentences. The latter part turns to the plain style, setting its thoughts, figures, rhythms, and diction against those of political oratory largely through extended analysis of Xenophon, and closes with discussions of the beginnings of a discourse, the conveyance of character, and the special case of Homer.
grc.aelius_herodianus.on_enclitics: A brief Greek grammatical treatise by the grammarian Aelius Herodianus on enclitic words and their accentuation. It opens with definitions distinguishing the enclined word, the enclitic particle, and the synenclitic sequence of successive enclitics. The discussion then works through the parts of speech that admit enclisis, among nouns only the indefinite tis, among verbs phemi and eimi, together with pronouns, interrogative adverbs, and conjunctions, setting out rules for how enclitics surrender or shift their accents and raise the grave accent of the preceding word, with examples drawn chiefly from Homer alongside citations of Hesiod and Callimachus. The closing line notes that the remaining material of the treatise has dropped out.
grc.aelius_theon.progymnasmata: A Greek rhetorical treatise, the Progymnasmata of Aelius Theon, a handbook of preliminary exercises for students of rhetoric that has been transmitted together with the Ars rhetorica printed in Spengel's Rhetores Graeci. The work opens by urging that orators should first train in philosophy and the general curriculum before pleading causes, mocking those who skip such preparation, and announcing that it will set out the exercises to be practised before one undertakes full hypotheses, together with definitions and methods of use for each. The body of the treatise treats the exercises in turn, beginning with chreia and continuing through myth, narrative, and the methods of refutation and confirmation, with detailed instructions on clarity, brevity and plausibility in narration, the treatment of evidence and topics, and the varied ways of paraphrasing and recasting material. Extensive illustrative passages are drawn from Homer, Hesiod, Herodotus, Thucydides, Plato, Demosthenes, Lysias and Isocrates, while guidance is also given to teachers on choosing models, correcting pupils' work, avoiding rhythmic or ornate composition, and adapting instruction to the natural strengths of individual students.
grc.aeschines.against_timarchus: An Athenian forensic speech in which the orator Aeschines prosecutes Timarchus under the law subjecting public speakers to scrutiny, seeking to bar him from addressing the assembly on the ground of a dissolute life. Aeschines opens by denying that he has ever injured any citizen and by casting himself as avenger of the city, the laws, and himself against Timarchus' lawless demagogy. He then recites the archaic laws governing the upbringing of boys, conduct in schools and gymnasia, prostitution, and hubris, before narrating at length Timarchus' alleged career as the kept companion of Misgolas, Pittalakos, and Hegesander, his squandering of his patrimony, and his misconduct in public offices and embassies. The later portion attacks Demosthenes as the author of Timarchus' defense, contrasts honourable eros with hired prostitution through examples from Homer and tragedy, and closes with an exhortation to the jurors to punish wrongdoers for the sake of civic order.
grc.aeschylus.libation_bearers: A Greek tragedy by Aeschylus, the second play of his Oresteia, the Libation Bearers dramatizes Orestes' revenge for the murder of his father Agamemnon. It opens at Agamemnon's tomb, where Orestes and his sister Electra meet at the grave and join a chorus of captive women in lament, prayer, and invocation of the dead king. Acting on an oracle of Apollo, Orestes and his companion Pylades gain entry to the palace in disguise, kill Clytemnestra's lover Aegisthus and then Clytemnestra herself, and display the net in which Agamemnon died. As Orestes asserts that his deed was just, the avenging Furies become visible to him alone, and the play ends with him driven mad and fleeing toward Apollo's seat at Delphi while the chorus wonders where the house's cycle of bloodshed will end.
grc.aeschylus.prometheus_bound: Prometheus Bound is a Greek tragedy attributed to Aeschylus and of uncertain date. It opens with Power and Force compelling a reluctant Hephaestus to rivet the fire-thief Prometheus to a desolate crag in Scythia as punishment for his gifts to mortals. The play consists almost entirely of the chained Titan's encounters with successive visitors, the chorus of Oceanids, Oceanus, the heifer-maiden Io, and finally Hermes demanding the secret prophecy that threatens Zeus's rule, while Prometheus foretells Io's wanderings, the hero who will one day free him, and his own eventual reconciliation with Zeus. Refusing throughout to submit, he is engulfed with his chorus by thunder, earthquake and storm in the closing cataclysm.
grc.aesop.fabulae: A collection of Greek prose fables transmitted under the name of Aesop, of uncertain date, in which many stories survive in two or more parallel recensions and most are closed by a brief moral comment (epimythium). It opens with the tale in which the goods, driven out by the evils, ask Zeus how they may come among men, and then runs through a long series of short narratives of animals, gods, and ordinary human figures: eagles, foxes, fishermen, frogs, farmers, snakes, asses, and slaves. Among them stand such familiar tales as the fox and the sour grapes, the frogs begging Zeus for a king, the north wind and the sun, and the farmer who tells his sons to dig for a treasure in the vineyard, alongside hundreds of briefer anecdotes whose morals touch on greed, ingratitude, flattery, and the persistence of nature. Many fables recur in variant versions across the collection, differing in wording, detail, and the moral appended to them.
grc.aesop.αισώπειων_μύθων_συναγωγή: A collection of Greek prose fables transmitted under the name of Aesop, of uncertain date. It opens with the fable of the Good and the Evil Things, in which goods descend from heaven to humanity one by one while evils assail them in a body. The work then runs through several hundred short narratives, drawn mostly from the doings of animals, foxes, wolves, lions, eagles, asses, mice and the like, but also from fishermen, farmers, astrologers, debtors and other human types, each fable typically closing with a one-line moral maxim. Alongside these stand fables of Zeus, Hermes and Prometheus, anecdotes attached to named figures such as Aesop himself, Demades, Socrates and Stesichorus, and an extended account of the Choice of Heracles.
grc.agatharchides.ex_agatharchidis_de_maris_: Excerpts from On the Erythraean Sea, a five-book geography and ethnography of the Red Sea and its coasts by Agatharchides of Cnidus, a Greek prose writer of the Hellenistic age, preserved in abridged form as a series of summaries. The opening excerpts consider Ptolemy's institution of elephant hunting and the rival explanations of why the Red Sea bears its name, together with a polemic against earlier mythographers. The sequence then ranges over Egypt and the sufferings of its gold-mine convicts, the coasts of the Troglodytes and the fish-eating Ichthyophagi, and the Arabian Gulf and its tribes, recording customs, flora, fauna, and trade before closing with accounts of exotic animals and the cause of the Nile's summer flood.
grc.alcidamas.ὀδυσσεύς: A Greek prosecution speech attributed to Alcidamas and of uncertain date, in which Odysseus accuses Palamedes of treason before the assembled Greeks at Troy. The speaker alleges that Palamedes conspired with Alexander (Paris), citing an arrow bearing an inscribed message and a shield emblem as evidence, and repeatedly dwells on Palamedes' character as a sophist and philosopher. The latter part digresses into the stories of Nauplius, the violation of Auge by Heracles, the birth and upbringing of Telephus, and Alexander's voyage to Greece that ended in the abduction of Helen. The piece belongs to the tradition of rhetorical exercises composed on themes from the Trojan War.
grc.anacharsis.epistulae: The Epistulae attributed to Anacharsis are a short pseudepigraphic collection of Greek letters ascribed to the Scythian sage of Greek tradition, of uncertain date. The collection opens with a letter to the Athenians in which the writer answers their mockery of his imperfect Greek by arguing that a man's worth lies in judgement and deeds rather than in purity of speech. The remaining letters, composed in the persona of a plain-spoken barbarian and addressed to figures including Solon, Cyrus and a king of the Lydians, defend Scythian frugality and hospitality while denouncing drunkenness, envy, ingratitude and the pursuit of wealth, with one extended rebuke illustrated by the parable of a ship on the Danube that founders under stolen cargo. The closing letter to the Lydian king declares that the writer has come to Greece to learn its customs and has no need of gold.
grc.andocides.against_alcibiades: A political speech, transmitted in the corpus of Andocides under the title Against Alcibiades, cast as an Athenian ostracism contest in which the speaker, Alcibiades and Nicias compete for the exile. It opens with reflections on the danger of meddling in public affairs and the duty of a good citizen to risk himself for the many, together with a protest that the speaker, four times tried and acquitted, should not be ruined by slander. The bulk of the work is a sustained attack on Alcibiades' life and character: his mistreatment of his wife and his dealings in Callias' household, the coercion of the painter Agatharchus and the assault on the choregos Taureas, a son begotten on a captive Melian woman, the doubling of the allies' tribute after Aristides' assessment, and the extravagance of his Olympic victories. Against this the speaker sets his own embassies and self-funded liturgies, arguing that ostracism serves the city only if the worse man is exiled, and that Alcibiades, a tyrant in deed while posing as a democrat, is the man who must go.
grc.andocides.on_the_peace: A deliberative speech in Attic Greek attributed to the Athenian orator Andocides and addressed to the assembly, opening with the charge that Athens' politicians favour peace in name while opposing the terms on which it could actually be concluded. The speaker, presenting himself as one of an embassy sent with full powers to Sparta, surveys the earlier peace settlements with Lacedaemon, including the peace of fifty years, the Thirty Years' Peace in which his grandfather served as envoy, and the peace made by Nicias, arguing that the democracy was never overthrown under any of them and that a peace on equal terms differs from the truces dictated by a victor. He then weighs the case for continuing the war over Corinth and Boeotia, dismisses the value of the Argive alliance, recalls past misjudgements such as the dealings with the Great King, the desertion to Amorges and the Sicilian expedition, and contrasts the favourable terms now on offer with those imposed after defeat. The speech closes by inviting the assembly, within the forty days allowed for debate, to amend the written terms as it wishes and to choose for itself between peace and war.
grc.anonymous.geographiae_expositio_compendi: A short anonymous Greek compendium of geography, of uncertain date, offering a schematic account of the inhabited world. It opens with the earth's circumference in stadia and the length and breadth of the oikoumene, measured from the Ganges to the Sacred Promontory beyond Lusitania. Having divided the earth into Europe, Libya and Asia by isthmuses and straits, the work surveys the peoples and regions of each continent, then ranks its largest islands, mountains and rivers and describes the oceans and inland seas with their principal gulfs and their dimensions in stadia and miles. It closes with a treatment of the twelve winds and of the lengths, breadths and coastlines of the main seas, straits and islands of the world.
grc.antiphon.speeches: A collection of six speeches in Attic Greek attributed to Antiphon, an orator of uncertain date. The corpus consists of forensic orations for prosecution and defence in homicide cases, together with the tetralogies, paired sets of model speeches arguing alternately for and against a single murder charge. The collection opens with a young prosecutor's case against his stepmother, whom he accuses of poisoning his father, while his half-brothers and their mother appear for the defence.
grc.antisthenes.αἴας: A short Greek rhetorical speech of uncertain date attributed to Antisthenes, in which Ajax, son of Telamon, contests before the assembled Greeks the award of the arms of Achilles, claiming them against Odysseus. The speech opens with a protest that judges who were absent from the deeds are adjudicating matters only eyewitnesses could judge rightly. Ajax then contrasts his own open conduct, bearing Achilles' body out of the battle, with the secrecy, cowardice, and greed of his rival, whom he accuses of a nocturnal theft of a goddess's image and of willingness to endure any indignity for gain, and he urges the judges to decide by deeds rather than words, since war is settled by action, while those who sit as appraisers of opinions rather than true judges themselves stand in need of a verdict.
grc.antisthenes.ὀδυσσεύς: A short Greek oration entitled Odysseus, attributed to Antisthenes and of uncertain date, in which Odysseus delivers a defence speech before the assembled Greeks, contesting with Ajax for the arms of the dead Achilles. He opens by addressing not Ajax alone but the whole army, claiming that his services to the camp exceed those of every other warrior. The body of the speech contrasts his own craft with Ajax's brute strength: he credits himself with recovering the image of the goddess stolen by Alexandros, with entering the enemy walls alone and by night, and with guarding the army like a pilot or general, while dismissing Ajax's impregnable armour and boastful courage as the recklessness of a wild boar. It closes with the prediction that a wise poet will one day portray Odysseus as much-enduring, many-counselled and the sole taker of Troy, and liken Ajax to sluggish donkeys and ploughing oxen.
grc.apollodorus.epitome: The Epitome is an abridged continuation of the Greek mythographic handbook known as the Bibliotheca or Library, attributed to Apollodorus and of uncertain date. It opens mid-narrative with Theseus' roadside killings of the sow Phaia, Sciron, Cercyon and Damastes, and follows his career through the Minotaur and Ariadne, Daedalus and Icarus, the Amazons, Phaedra and Hippolytus, and his descent with Pirithous to the underworld, before turning to the houses of Pelops and Atreus. The narrative then runs through the Trojan cycle from the judgment of Paris and the muster at Aulis, past Achilles' exploits and the deaths of Achilles and Ajax, to the capture of Troy by means of the wooden horse. It closes with the returns of the Greek leaders, covering Agamemnon's murder and Orestes' vengeance, Menelaus' wanderings, and Odysseus' journey from the Cyclops and Circe to the slaughter of the suitors and his death at the hand of Telegonus, regularly recording variant traditions with the formula 'as some say'.
grc.apollonius_dyscolus.περὶ_ἀντωνυμίας: A Greek grammatical treatise by Apollonius Dyscolus, of uncertain date, on the pronoun (Περὶ Ἀντωνυμίας). It opens with a preface defending concise exposition and a review of the names given to the pronoun by Aristarchus, the Stoics and others. The main discussion defines the pronoun as a word standing in place of a noun and representing definite persons, then takes up its division into deictic and anaphoric classes, the three grammatical persons and their combinations, the possessive and reflexive derivatives, questions of number, case, gender and accentuation, and the contrast between orthotone and enclitic forms. Individual forms are examined dialect by dialect, chiefly Attic, Ionic, Doric, Aeolic and Boeotian, with Homeric and lyric quotations as evidence, and the argument repeatedly refutes rival views, including Stoic classifications and the readings of Aristarchus and Zenodotus.
grc.appian.civil_wars: Appian's Civil Wars is a Greek prose history in five books dealing with the internal conflicts of the Romans. Its opening survey traces the course of civil strife from early disputes between plebs and senate over laws, debts and land, through the killing of Tiberius Gracchus, the dictatorship of Sulla and the rivalry of Caesar and Pompey, to the triumvirate of Antony, Lepidus and Octavian and the war around Actium. The account closes with Antony's defeat, the taking of Egypt and the elevation of Octavian as Augustus, ruler of Rome and the nations under her.
grc.archimedes.ad_eratosthenem_methodus: A Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes, cast as a letter to Eratosthenes, which opens by recalling theorem statements sent earlier without proofs and by explaining why the author now publishes the mechanical method behind them. The work then sets out that method, in which plane figures and solids are conceived as cut into parallel slices and balanced against one another on a lever, so that results can first be surmised mechanically and afterwards confirmed by strict geometric demonstration. After a series of lemmas on centers of gravity, it applies the procedure to a sequence of theorems: that a segment of a right-angled conoid is four-thirds of the triangle on the same base and height, that a sphere is four times the cone on its greatest circle while the circumscribed cylinder is half again the sphere, and comparable results for spheroids, segments of spheres and conoids, and their centers of gravity. It closes with the mechanical investigation of the solid cut from a cylinder by a plane through the center of its base and one side of the circumscribed square, which is shown to be one-sixth of the enclosing prism.
grc.archimedes.fragmenta: A short collection of Greek fragments transmitted under the name of Archimedes. It opens by setting the five regular solids known to Plato against the thirteen semiregular polyhedra credited to Archimedes, and then lists each of those thirteen in turn, giving its faces, triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons, octagons or decagons, its solid angles and its edges, together with the regular solid from which each is generated by truncation. A further fragment discusses a fourteen-faced solid that Plato is said to have known, and the closing piece, framed around Ptolemy, explains why stars appear larger near the horizon by appealing to refraction in the moist air about the earth, with reference to Archimedes' work on mirrors.
grc.aretaeus.signorum_acutorum_morbum: A Greek medical treatise on the signs of acute diseases, by the Cappadocian physician Aretaeus, of uncertain date. It opens with the premonitory symptoms of epilepsy, tracing the affection from flashes before the eyes and ringing in the ears through the convulsion itself to its fatal or favourable outcome. Later chapters set out the characteristic symptoms of tetanus, of suffocating affections of the throat such as synanche and cynanche, of pleurisy and peripneumonia, of the spitting or bringing up of blood, and of syncope, cholera, and the intestinal obstruction called ileus. The closing portions deal with inflammatory fevers of the liver, disorders of the kidneys and bladder with retention of urine, suffocation arising from the womb, and the condition known as satyriasis.
grc.aristophanes.acharnians: A comic play by Aristophanes, first produced in 425 BC, in which the Attic farmer Dicaeopolis, weary of the Peloponnesian War, arranges a private peace with Sparta and opens his own marketplace to enemy traders. The opening scene finds him attending an assembly that refuses to discuss peace, and after ambassadors recount their extravagant missions to Persia, he seals a thirty-year truce for himself alone, drawing the wrath of the Acharnian charcoal-burners, who pursue him. To defend himself he borrows tragic rags from Euripides and, dressed as a beggar, argues that the war sprang from petty private grievances such as the Megarian dispute, before deflecting them by holding a basket of charcoal hostage. The second half follows the private peace in action: Megarians selling their daughters disguised as piglets, a Boeotian trading eels for a captured informer, festive celebrations of the wine god, the marriage-bed aphrodisiac granted to the bride, and the general Lamachus marching off to a winter campaign while Dicaeopolis departs to a drinking party, returning victorious from his feast just as Lamachus limps home wounded.
grc.aristophanes.birds: A comedy by the Greek poet Aristophanes, in which two Athenians abandon their native city to live among the birds. The play opens with Pisthetairos and Euelpides wandering a trackless wild, led by a crow and a jackdaw in search of Tereus, once a man and now a hoopoe. On his advice they persuade the birds to fortify the air as their own city, Nephelokokkygia, whose commanding position intercepts sacrificial smoke and forces the Olympians to terms. The middle of the play brings a procession of human visitors, a poet, an oracle-monger, the geometer Meton and a seller of decrees among them, while the birds assert in a formal address to the audience that they are older than the gods; divine envoys, from Iris to an embassy of Poseidon, Heracles and the Triballian god, are rebuffed until Pisthetairos is granted the goddess Basileia in marriage, and the play closes with his wedding and elevation as supreme ruler.
grc.aristophanes.thesmophoriazusae: A comedy by Aristophanes in which Euripides, threatened by the women gathered at the festival of the Thesmophoria with death for his slanders against them in tragedy, first seeks aid from the tragedian Agathon, who declines to enter the women's assembly in disguise. The task falls instead to Euripides' kinsman, who is shaved, dressed as a woman and smuggled into the meeting, where he answers the women's indictments of the poet until his sex is discovered and he is seized; taking hostage a baby that is in fact a wine-skin, he holds off arrest while Euripides arrives in a series of disguises parodying his own Helen and Andromeda, with Echo repeating his laments, until he promises to speak well of women and the captives are freed. The closing scenes leave the Scythian archer who guarded the prisoners duped into chasing the disguised kinsman and a dancing girl through the streets, before the chorus bids farewell to the Thesmophorian goddesses.
grc.aristotle.categoriae: A Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle, the Categoriae opens by distinguishing homonyms, synonyms, and paronyms and by dividing what is said into simple and composite expressions, before listing the ten categories under which terms spoken without combination fall. The body of the work takes up the categories in turn, dwelling at greatest length on substance, where primary individual substances are distinguished from the species and genera called secondary substances, and then treating quantity, quality, and relation together with what is proper to each, such as the receptivity of substance to contraries and the reciprocity of relatives. The closing chapters examine the four modes of opposition, the senses in which one thing is prior to or simultaneous with another, the six species of motion and their contraries, and the various senses of having.
grc.aristotle.constitution: A Greek treatise on the history and workings of the Athenian constitution, transmitted under Aristotle's name though its authorship has long been debated. It opens with Athens' earliest kings and the mythical origins of its institutions before proceeding through the reforms of Draco, Solon, and Cleisthenes, the tyranny of Peisistratus and his sons, and the successive oligarchic and democratic regimes down to the author's own day. The latter part sets out in detail the machinery of the contemporary democracy: the council, the magistracies, the courts, and the procedures by which citizens, jurors, and officials were enrolled and held accountable. The work concludes with an account of how judges are selected by lot and how verdicts are reached in the Athenian lawcourts.
grc.aristotle.de_anima: Aristotle's De Anima, a treatise on the soul, opens by ranking the inquiry into the soul among the highest of subjects and by surveying the doctrines of earlier philosophers before offering its own account of the soul as the first actuality of a natural body endowed with life. The treatise then proceeds through the soul's faculties in order of generality: the nutritive faculty shared by plants and animals, sensation examined sense by sense, imagination, desire, and thought. Along the way it treats the interdependence of soul and body, distinguishes a mortal passive intellect from an active intellect that is separable, unmixed and immortal, and closes with a discussion of the cause of animal movement and of the senses of taste and touch.
grc.aristotle.de_insomniis: A short Greek treatise on dreams attributed to Aristotle. It opens by asking to which faculty of the soul the dream appears, whether the thinking or the perceptive, and argues that dreaming belongs neither to bare sensation nor to opinion but to the faculty of imagination, which is one in subject with the perceptive faculty yet distinct in activity. The body of the work sets out the mechanism: sense impressions leave behind movements that persist in the sense organs after the stimulus has ceased, illustrated by after-images from bright objects, flowing water, strong noises and smells, and by the clouded mirror held by a menstruating woman, and these residual movements, normally drowned out by waking perception, surface in sleep when the senses lie idle, so that dreams are strong and clear for the healthy but distorted in the feverish, the drunk and the melancholic, while none occur after meals, in young children, or in the rare people who never dream at all. It closes by defining the dream as the phantasm arising from the movement of sense impressions during sleep, distinct from the faint perceptions and stray thoughts that can accompany slumber.
grc.aristotle.de_iuventute_et_senectute_de_v: A Greek prose treatise by Aristotle, known by the Latin title De Iuventute et Senectute, De Vita et Morte (On Youth and Old Age, On Life and Death), belonging to his writings on natural philosophy about the functions shared by living things. It opens by announcing an account of youth, old age, life and death, undertaken together with an inquiry into the causes of respiration. The argument locates the nutritive and sensitive soul in the middle of the body, in blooded animals the heart, in bloodless ones its analogue, and treats death as the loss of innate heat, old age being its gradual exhaustion from want of nourishment and violent death its quenching by an opposing cold. Its discussion of how plants and animals must continually cool this heat by means of food, water or air ends at the point of passing on to a fuller explanation of breathing.
grc.aristotle.de_longitudine_et_brevitate_vi: A short Greek treatise by Aristotle on the causes of long and short life in living things. It opens by setting out problems for inquiry, asking whether one cause governs longevity in both animals and plants and whether long life belongs to the healthy constitution. The argument then considers what is easily destroyed in natural compounds and holds that life depends on a warm and moist principle that must be neither small nor readily dried up, whence it explains why large land animals such as man and the elephant are the longest-lived of animals, why warm regions, males, and fatty or whole-blooded creatures outlast others, and why trees, whose parts are perpetually renewed, surpass all living things in the length of their existence. It closes by announcing that youth, old age, life, and death remain to be treated for the study of animals to be complete.
grc.aristotle.de_partibus_animalium: The De Partibus Animalium is a treatise in four books by Aristotle on the causes of the parts of animals. It opens with reflections on the education that enables a hearer to judge well and on the method proper to natural inquiry, arguing that form and purpose rank above matter and rejecting dichotomous division of animal kinds. The remaining books proceed from the homogeneous constituents of animals, blood, marrow, fat, flesh, and bone, to the principal organs, including heart, lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, and bladder, and then to the external parts of blooded animals such as teeth, horns, tongue, eyes, limbs, and the organs of speech and respiration. The discussion then passes to insects, crustaceans, shellfish, and molluscs, and to the anatomy of fish, birds, and egg-laying quadrupeds, throughout asking what each part is for and why animals are constituted as they are.
grc.aristotle.de_sensu_et_sensibilibus: De Sensu et Sensibilibus (On Sense and Sensibles) is a short Greek treatise attributed to Aristotle, one of the minor natural works that take up questions of living things as affections common to soul and body. It presents itself as the continuation of an enquiry into the soul, turning from the De Anima to powers such as sense, memory, pleasure and pain that belong to animals in respect of both soul and body. The argument first examines the sense organs, allotting each to an element and refuting accounts of vision as an emanation of fire, then defines colour as the limit of the transparent in a determinate body and derives the varieties of colour and flavour from mixtures of white and black and of sweet and bitter according to numerical ratios. Smell is treated as intermediate between touch and sight, its kinds distinguished and the pleasant odours of flowers assigned peculiarly to man in connection with respiration and the cooling of the brain, before the closing discussion of whether perception proceeds through a medium, whether several objects can be perceived at the same instant, and the unity of the common faculty that judges them.
grc.aristotle.de_somno_et_vigilia: A short Greek treatise by Aristotle, De Somno et Vigilia investigates what sleep and waking are, whether they belong to the soul, the body, or both, why they occur, and which living things share them. It opens by posing these questions together with further puzzles about dreams, their causes, whether dreamers always dream but forget, and whether dreams can foretell the future, questions it refers for treatment elsewhere. The work then argues that sleep and waking are affections of the common faculty of sense, possessed by all animals that have touch though by no plants, and offers a physiological explanation: vapours arising from food are carried upward by innate heat, cooled in the region of the brain, and by their recoil seize and inhibit the primary sense organ. It concludes by defining sleep as the seizure of the primary sense organ preventing its activity, occurring of necessity and for the sake of preservation, since rest preserves the animal.
grc.aristotle.eudemian_ethics: A Greek ethical treatise by Aristotle, the Eudemian Ethics inquires into happiness and the character of the good life. Its opening takes its cue from the Delian inscription distinguishing the good, the beautiful, and the pleasant, and asks how living well is acquired, by nature, learning, habituation, a divine gift, or chance, insisting that a life must be ordered toward a definite end. The body of the work treats the virtues of character as means between excess and deficiency, among them liberality, magnanimity, and justice, and then examines friendship at length in its kinds and conditions, together with concord, goodwill, and friendship toward oneself. It concludes with an account of good fortune, natural or divine in origin, and of kalokagathia as perfect virtue, whose standard is the contemplation of God.
grc.aristotle.fragmenta_deperditae_partis_pr: Attributed to Aristotle, the work preserves the surviving fragments of the lost first part of the Constitution of the Athenians (Athenaion Politeia), transmitted chiefly as quotations in later lexicographers, scholiasts, and Plutarch. It opens with an account of Athens' earliest kingship and of the citizens' renaming as Ionians after Ion, accompanied by lexicographical notes on Apollo Patroos. The remaining fragments concern Theseus, crediting him with the synoikismos, the first move toward democracy, and the division of the people into eupatridae, geomoroi, and demiourgoi, and then set out the pre-Cleisthenic organisation of the citizen body into four tribes, twelve trittyes or phratries, and thirty gene of thirty men apiece, whose members were called gennetai. A notice of Theseus' death at Scyros and the recovery of his bones after the Persian Wars precedes a closing editorial remark that further fragments sometimes assigned to the treatise do not belong to it.
grc.aristotle.poetics: A Greek treatise by Aristotle on poetry in general and its principal kinds. It opens by announcing a complete treatment of the poetic arts and distinguishing the forms of imitation, epic, tragedy, comedy, dithyramb, and music, by their medium, their objects, and their manner. From there it traces the origins of poetry in the human instinct for imitation and rhythm, defines tragedy and enumerates its six parts, and gives extensive discussion to plot, covering unity of action, reversal, recognition, the kind of hero who best serves the tragic effect, and the pity and fear proper to the genre. Later sections take up character and diction, including metaphor, set out methods for answering objections to particular poems, weigh epic against tragedy, and conclude that tragedy, despite its shorter compass, achieves the aims of poetic imitation more fully than epic.
grc.aristotle.topica: The Topics is a Greek philosophical treatise by Aristotle on dialectic, setting out a method for reasoning from accepted opinions about any problem proposed. Its opening defines syllogism, distinguishes the demonstrative, dialectical and eristic varieties, and states the purposes of the inquiry for exercise, debate and the philosophical sciences. The greater part of the work collects topoi, or strategies of argument, concerning the four predicables of definition, property, genus and accident, showing how propositions about each may be established and refuted and what counts as a correctly laid-down definition or property. The final book prescribes the roles of questioner and answerer in a dialectical exchange, classifies the faults of faulty reasoning, and closes with advice on training, the choice of interlocutors and the ready command of propositions and definitions.
grc.aristotle.μηχανικά: The Μηχανικά is a short Greek treatise on mechanics transmitted under Aristotle's name, of uncertain date. It opens by defining mechanics as the art that assists human purposes in what lies contrary to nature, and traces all such effects to the properties of the circle, from which the balance and the lever derive. The remainder consists of a long series of problems treated in question-and-answer form, explaining by the principle of the lever the working of balances, pulleys, the wedge, oars and rudders, nutcrackers, forceps, ship's windlasses, and human movements such as rising from a seat. Later problems concern projectiles, why thrown objects stop moving, and why bodies carried in whirling water drift toward the centre.
grc.aristoxenus.elementa_harmonica: The Elementa Harmonica of Aristoxenus is a Greek theoretical treatise on the science of melody. It opens by ranking harmonics first among the branches of the science concerned with music and defining its goal as the theory of systems and tones, before criticising the achievements of earlier writers such as Eratocles. The argument then proceeds through the ordered movement of the voice and the definitions of note, interval, and system, the three genera of melody, enharmonic, chromatic, and diatonic, with the divisions of the tetrachord, and the principles governing consonance, succession, and the melodic composition of systems. The work closes with demonstrations of the melodic paths open from each kind of interval and of the three species into which the fourth can be cast.
grc.arrian.anabasis: Arrian's Anabasis, a Greek prose history of Alexander the Great in seven books, opens with a preface in which the author states that he records as wholly true whatever Ptolemy son of Lagus and Aristobulus agree upon about Alexander, choosing the more credible and more noteworthy account where they differ.
