The narrative then follows Alexander from his accession to the Macedonian throne after Philip's death as a young man of about twenty, through campaigns against the Thracians, Triballi and Illyrians, the crossing into Asia, and the major battles with the Persians and their satraps. Later books carry the story through the reduction of the coastal cities and Egypt, the conquest of the Persian heartland, and the hard-fought campaigns in Bactria and Sogdiana against Spitamenes and the Scythians, including the siege of the Sogdian rock, before turning to India and the return westward. The work closes with Alexander's death in Babylon, the divergent accounts of his final days and of rumours of poisoning, and a long final assessment of his character and achievements.
grc.artemidorus.onirocriticon: Artemidorus of Daldis wrote the Onirocriticon, a Greek treatise on the interpretation of dreams as divinatory signs of future events. The work opens with a preface defending dream divination against its critics, followed by definitions distinguishing the meaningless enypnion from the true dream (oneiros), which is classified as either theorematic, fulfilling exactly what is seen, or allegorical, signifying one thing through another. The main body proceeds through the manifold dream images, animals, insects, bodily acts, gods, vehicles, journeys, and contests among them, stating for each the outcome it portends to dreamers of differing condition, from slaves and the poor to rulers and athletes. A concluding series of actual dreams with their observed fulfillments, many involving sacred contests and the god Sarapis, rounds off the treatise.
grc.aspasius.in_ethica_nicomachea_paraphrasi: Aspasius's Greek exposition of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics opens by weighing ethical and political philosophy against theoretical wisdom, judging the former necessary for living well while the latter is superior in honor. It then follows Aristotle's argument section by section, introducing art, method, action, and deliberative choice as paths toward the good, with happiness as the human end, before treating the moral virtues, at greatest length liberality, magnificence, and magnanimity understood as greatness of soul measured by honor. The closing portions are devoted to friendship: its division into kinds grounded in the good, the pleasant, and the useful; the question of equality and superiority between friends such as parents and children or ruler and ruled; the correspondence of friendship and justice with the various constitutions from kingship to tyranny; and the claims of kinship and of mutual benefit, including disputes over the repayment of favors.
grc.athenaeus.deipnosophists: A Greek prose dialogue, of uncertain date, in which Athenaeus addresses Timocrates with an account of a sumptuous banquet given by the wealthy Roman Larensis, attended by grammarians, philosophers, physicians, jurists, and musicians. The dinner talk moves from fish, vegetables, and other fare to music, jests, drinking cups, the wealth of kings, and ships, threading long quotations from poets, historians, and philosophers, comic poets especially, through the conversation. As the meal proceeds the diners treat of parody and comedy, proverbs and rare words, and the vocabulary of lamps and torches, until the evening closes with a libation and a paean to Hygieia, Health.
grc.babrius.fabulae_aesopeae: A collection of Aesopic fables in Greek verse by Babrius, a poet of uncertain date, who recasts traditional tales of animals and men in short limping iambics. The prologue, addressed to a boy named Branchus, recalls the mythic ages of mankind, when even beasts had articulate speech and mortals kept company with gods, before announcing that the fables of 'our wise old Aesop' will be set down as broken limbs of bitter iambic verse. The individual fables, a hunter and a lion, a fisherman and his catch, a goatherd and a wounded she-goat, a horse forced to carry a fallen donkey's load, among others, are brief narratives, each furnished with a short moral lesson on prudence, fortune, or human folly.
grc.barnabas.barnabae_epistulae: A Greek Christian epistle of uncertain date, attributed in tradition to Barnabas. It opens with a greeting in which the writer rejoices at the spiritual gifts of his addressees and undertakes to share with them a portion of the knowledge he has received. The main body argues that the literal observances of the Mosaic law, sacrifice, fasting, food prohibitions, circumcision, and the sabbath, were never what God desired, reading them instead as figures pointing to Christ, baptism, the cross, and the moral life, and warns that evil days precede the approaching end. The letter concludes with a teaching on two ways, contrasting the way of light, set out as commandments, with the way of darkness, a catalogue of sins, and closes by asking to be remembered by those who profit from its exhortation.
grc.basil_of_caesarea.de_legendis: A Greek exhortation to young men attributed to Basil of Caesarea, bishop of Caesarea, setting out how pagan learning may profit readers raised in the Christian life. It opens with the speaker, commending his counsel by the goodwill he bears the youths and by long experience of human affairs, promising to point out the safest road for those just entering upon life. The work distinguishes the present human life from the life to come, arguing that external studies are valuable only as preparation, like leaves adorning the fruit of truth, and cites Moses and Daniel as men who first disciplined their minds in Egyptian and Chaldean learning before turning to divine things. It then reviews what should be accepted and what passed over in the poets, adducing examples of self-command and endurance from Socrates, Pericles, Euclides, Alexander and Cleinias, and closes with warnings against sloth, wealth, pleasure and love of reputation, urging that virtue be gathered from every source as provision for the journey.
grc.callimachus.aetia: The Aetia ('Causes') of the Hellenistic Greek poet Callimachus was a four-book aetiological elegy explaining the origins of cults, rites, festivals, names, and local customs, and it survives only in papyrus fragments and quotations by later writers. The extant material opens with a cluster of ancient epigrams and testimonies about the poet and his work, followed by the dream prologue in which the poet is carried to Helicon and questions the Muses. Across books one and two the fragments range over aetiologies of heroes, foundations, and rituals, among them the Locrian maidens sent to Troy, Coroebus, and Phalaris' bull, while book three preserves the longest continuous narrative, the courtship of Acontius and Cydippe on Ceos, woven together with an account of the island's settlement. Book four carries the poem on to further local aetiologies, such as the Deipnias festival and the hero Androgeos.
grc.carmina_delphis_inventa.carmina_delphis_: Carmina Delphis Inventa collects the Greek cult songs for Apollo that were recovered from the Athenians' treasury at Delphi, printed with their surviving musical notation aligned beneath the words and accompanied by a Latin editorial apparatus on the notation and harmonies. The work opens with an inscribed decree of the Delphians honouring the Athenian melody-composer Cleochares, son of Bion, whose prosodion, paean, and hymn the boys of the city were instructed to sing at the Theoxenia; the poems themselves are of uncertain date. The hymn that follows invokes Apollo as the famed son of Zeus who slew with his arrows the serpent that guarded the tripod, and recalls the god's repulse of the Galatian war-host that had ventured against him. The remaining pieces call on the deep-wooded Helicon and the daughters of Zeus, summon singers to the twin-peaked heights of Parnassus, and close with prayers that Apollo, lord of the Cretan traders' shrines at Delphi, keep the Bacchic bands unharmed upon the mountain and make the musical contests flourish with unwithering praise.
grc.chariton.de_chaerea: Chariton's Chaereas and Callirhoe is a Greek prose romance of uncertain date; the narrator introduces himself as Chariton of Aphrodisias, clerk to the rhetor Athenagoras, and announces an account of a love affair that befell at Syracuse. The story opens with the marriage of Callirhoe, daughter of the Syracusan general Hermocrates, to the young Chaereas, whose jealous rivals provoke a quarrel in which he strikes his bride so that she collapses and is buried as dead. Buried alive, Callirhoe is freed by tomb robbers and sold into slavery at Miletus, where the wealthy Dionysius marries her, while Chaereas, searching the seas for her, is shipwrecked, enslaved, and finally brought with her to trial before the Persian king Artaxerxes at Babylon. The Egyptian revolt that interrupts the trial leads to Chaereas's naval command and victories, a reunion with Callirhoe on Aradus, and the couple's return to Syracuse laden with Persian spoils.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.eclogae_prophetica: The Eclogae Propheticae is a short Greek miscellany of scriptural interpretation by Clement of Alexandria, of uncertain date, gathering notes and extracts on prophetic and other biblical passages. It opens with the hymn of the three young men in the fiery furnace, which Clement reads as evidence for the purity of the heavens and the waters and for the ordered ranks of the angelic powers. The collection then ranges across allegorical interpretations of Genesis, Daniel, Hosea and the Psalms, with discussions of baptism through water, spirit and fire, of fasting, prayer and the fear of God, and of the soul's purification from matter and advance toward divine knowledge. It closes with notes on angels and the restoration of souls in ranks, on the fate of exposed infants as reported from the Apocalypse of Peter, and on the significance of the stars, of day and night, and of particular psalm verses and divine names.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.paedagogus: The Paedagogus of Clement of Alexandria is a Christian instructional treatise in which the divine Word is presented as the tutor who trains human souls in virtue and sobriety of life. The opening chapters define the educator's office, describing his philanthropy, his equal guidance of men and women, his instruction through law and prophets, and the healing of the passions that must precede higher teaching. The body of the work turns to practical daily conduct, regulating eating and drinking, behaviour at table, music and laughter at banquets, the use of garlands, ointments, jewellery, and cosmetics, hairstyle, deportment in public and at spectacles, and the manner of men, women, and children in church. It closes by gathering commandments from the Decalogue, the prophets, and the apostles into a summary of the life required of the tutor's pupils, followed by a prayer and a hymn of thanksgiving to Christ, who now hands them over to the teacher.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.quis_dives_salvetu: Quis Dives Salvetur ('Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?') is a Greek homily by Clement of Alexandria on the question whether the wealthy can attain salvation. It opens with a censure of those who flatter the rich with encomia, before turning to the Gospel episode in which a rich man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life and is told that it is easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. The main body expounds that passage, arguing that the command to sell all one has must be understood chiefly of the passions of the soul rather than of outward property, that wealth is an indifferent instrument to be used rightly, and that almsgiving, love of God and neighbour, illustrated from the parable of the Good Samaritan, and true repentance leave the rich a path to eternal life. The work closes with the story of the apostle John pursuing and reclaiming a young man turned bandit chief, offered as a great example of repentance, followed by a doxology.
grc.colluthus.rape_of_helen: The Rape of Helen is a Greek poem in epic hexameters by Colluthus, an author of uncertain date, recounting the events that led to Helen's journey from Sparta to Troy. It opens with a prayer to the nymphs born of the river Xanthus to tell of the shepherd Paris and of the first beginning of the strife. The narrative then moves from the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, where Eris, barred from the feast, casts a golden apple among the goddesses, to Hermes' bringing of Paris from Mount Ida and the judgment in which Hera offers rule over Asia, Athena prowess in war, and Aphrodite the hand of Helen. The remainder follows Paris by ship to Sparta, where Helen, persuaded by Aphrodite's command, departs with him by night, and closes with Hermione searching in vain for her vanished mother and with Cassandra tearing her hair as Troy opens its gates to Paris.
grc.cratetis_epistulae.epistulae: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to the Cynic philosopher Crates, of uncertain date. The opening letter urges its recipient to hasten to greet Diogenes while he still lives. The remaining letters, mostly brief and gnomic, exhort their addressees to a Cynic life of toil, cold water, plain food and the rough cloak, argue that philosophy teaches justice better than law, defend the name of 'dog' as a badge of endurance rather than a reproach, and include advice to women disciples on philosophy, adornment, childbirth and the rearing of children, a warning against drunkenness illustrated from Homer, and a longer narrative epistle recounting Diogenes' capture by pirates and his conduct when exposed for sale in the slave market.
grc.demosthenes.against_androtion: Against Androtion is a forensic speech of the Demosthenic corpus, delivered in an Athenian court in support of Euctemon's prosecution of the politician Androtion over a decree conferring a crown on the Council. It opens with the speaker, who has himself suffered wrongs at Androtion's hands, promising to help Euctemon win redress and to defend the city. The argument contends that the Council could not lawfully be crowned while it had failed to build the triremes required by law, and then surveys Androtion's public career: his conduct in collecting the eisphora, where he is accused of dragging defaulters and even metics from their homes with the aid of the Eleven, his insults and cruelty toward citizens, and his melting down of allied dedicatory crowns to make gold phialai inscribed with his own name. The closing appeals urge the jurors to uphold the laws and convict rather than be deceived by Androtion's eloquence.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_1: A forensic oration by Demosthenes, the first of his speeches against Aphobus, a guardian whom he sued on coming of age for the mismanagement of the estate left by his father. It opens with an address to the jurors observing that Aphobus had refused arbitration and evaded those who knew the family's affairs, and then recounts how the father died leaving a son of seven, a daughter of five, a mother with a dowry of eighty mnas, and property of nearly fourteen talents entrusted to three guardians. For most of its course the speech itemizes that property, two workshops of knife-makers and couch-makers, household goods, sums on deposit with bankers and out at maritime interest, and, with testimony read aloud, reckons up the money allegedly taken or wasted by Aphobus, Demophon, and Therippides, covering the unpaid dowry, the concealed will, and the unsupported claim of buried treasure. It closes with a warning that defeat would expose the speaker to a penalty of a hundred mnas, an appeal to the laws and the jurors' oath, and a plea for pity on a household wronged by those bound to protect it.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristocrates: A forensic speech of Demosthenes, composed for delivery in an Athenian court as a prosecution by graphē paranomōn against Aristocrates, the proposer of a decree making anyone who killed the mercenary commander Charidemus liable to seizure without trial. The speaker opens by disclaiming private enmity and declaring that his real concern is that Athens securely hold the Chersonese. The argument then shows the decree to be contrary to the Athenian homicide laws, from Draco's code to the procedures of the Areopagus and the other homicide courts, and reviews at length Charidemus's career in the service of Cotys, Cersobleptes, and other Thracian dynasts, his alleged betrayals of Athenian interests, and the machinations by which the decree was brought forward. The closing sections contrast the honors lavished on Charidemus with the treatment of earlier benefactors such as Miltiades and Themistocles and urge the jurors to annul the decree.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_1: A forensic prosecution speech attributed to Demosthenes, brought against Aristogiton, a public debtor who nonetheless presents himself in court as an informer and accuser of others. The opening remarks that Lycurgus, the joint prosecutor, has already stated the legal case, and that the verdict will turn less on arguments than on the jurors' attitude toward wickedness. The speech then catalogs Aristogiton's misdeeds, including his betrayal of his father in prison, the sale of his sister, his treatment of Zobia, who sheltered him after his escape, his assault on a fellow prisoner and theft of a document, and attacks his professed goodwill toward the people, likening him to a scorpion or viper in the city's midst. It closes by urging the jurors, in view of citizens and foreigners watching their verdict, to impose either death or a fine he cannot pay.
grc.demosthenes.against_aristogiton_2: An Athenian forensic oration attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus, of uncertain date; it is the second speech in the prosecution of Aristogiton, supporting the earlier case in which Lycurgus had already exposed the defendant's character, and it opens by asserting that Aristogiton owes money to the public treasury, stands disfranchised, and is therefore barred by the laws from addressing the people. The speaker argues that men convicted of lawbreaking must be excluded from public life, since the offences of office-holders injure the whole city as a helmsman's error ruins an entire ship's company, and he appeals to Solon's swifter punishments for demagogues and to the penalties once paid by Aristides, Miltiades and Pericles. He then recounts how Aristogiton twisted Hyperides' decree, passed after the disasters at Chaeronea had restored disfranchised citizens to their rights, into a personal privilege, reviews his barren record as a politician, and closes by urging the jurors to defend the laws, whose ordering governs even the cosmos, and to condemn the wrongdoer.
grc.demosthenes.against_boeotus_1: An Athenian forensic speech from a private suit (dike), transmitted among the orations of Demosthenes and generally counted among the private speeches of the corpus. It opens with the speaker, Mantitheus, disclaiming any meddlesome fondness for litigation and explaining that he has sued his half-brother Boeotus to prevent him from claiming the same name. The argument contends that their father Mantias, when obliged to enrol the younger son in his phratry, registered the boys as Boeotus and Mantitheus respectively, and that a father has sole legal authority to give or revoke his children's names. The bulk of the speech enumerates the practical confusion two identically named citizens would cause in liturgies, court summonses, military levies and public offices, rebuts the anticipated charge that the name was imposed under provocation or mockery, closes with hostile characterisation of Boeotus and appeals to the laws, the jurors' oaths and his self-contradictions.
grc.demosthenes.against_callippus: Forensic speech in Greek from the corpus attributed to Demosthenes, written for the defense in an Athenian private suit over a money deposit left with a bank. The opening observes that no opponent is harder to refute than a man of reputation who lies boldly and can produce witnesses. The narrative then explains that Lycōn of Heraclea left sixteen minae and forty drachmae with the banking house of Pasiōn, to be repaid to Cephisiadēs, a metic of Scirus, whom Archebiades was to present, and argues that Callippus, proxenos of the Heracleots, inspected the bank's record at the time, stayed silent for more than five months, and later fabricated both a claim to the money and a suit for damages. The speaker contests Callippus's account of an oath before the arbitrator Lysitheides, discredits the relatives testifying for him, and supports his case with documents, laws, and witness testimony before closing with a plea for acquittal.
grc.demosthenes.against_dionysodorus: Against Dionysodorus is an Athenian forensic speech of Demosthenes, arising from a commercial suit over a maritime loan. It opens with the speaker presenting himself as a partner in a bottomry loan of three thousand drachmae advanced to Dionysodorus and his associate Parmeniscus for a voyage from Athens to Egypt and back. The narrative then shows how the defendants, bound by a written contract to return the ship to the Piraeus, instead sailed to Rhodes, sold the grain cargo there in concert with the agents of Cleomenes, who had cornered the Egyptian grain trade, and thereafter withheld both principal and interest. The remainder of the speech reads out the contract and a formal challenge, rebuts the defendants' claims of shipwreck and of concessions from other lenders, and closes by urging the jurors to enforce the stipulated penalty of double repayment, since the verdict will determine confidence in maritime agreements and the security of the city's commerce.
grc.demosthenes.against_eubulides: A forensic speech transmitted among the private orations of Demosthenes, in which a defendant answers Eubulides' prosecution on a charge of falsely claiming Athenian citizenship. The speech opens with the speaker's protest against Eubulides' slanders and his appeal for a hearing equal to that granted his accuser. It then recounts the night-time scrutiny (diapsephismas) held in his deme of Halimous, alleging that Eubulides and his associates contrived the vote against him, and proceeds to establish the speaker's citizen birth through a genealogy of his mother's family, testimony from kinsmen, phratries and demesmen, his enrolment in the deme, and his preliminary selection for the priesthood of Herakles. Censure of Eubulides' record of expelling citizens for money gives way to a closing plea that the speaker be allowed to keep his civic status and bury his mother in the ancestral tombs.
grc.demosthenes.against_lacritus: Athenian forensic speech for a commercial suit (dikē emporikē), transmitted in the corpus of Demosthenes, in which the speaking litigant identifies himself as Androcles of Sphettus, a merchant who lent money for a voyage to the Black Sea. The speech opens with a general attack on the Phaselites as inveterate defaulters in maritime lending. It then recounts the loan of thirty minas to Artemon and Apollodorus of Phaselis under a written contract stipulating a cargo of Mendean wine, and the action brought after Artemon's death against his brother and heir Lacritus, a pupil of Isocrates, who denies liability for the debt. The body of the speech sets the contract's terms against the brothers' conduct, a cargo far short of the stipulated three thousand jars, a second unauthorized loan on the same security, failure to bring return freight to Athens, a claimed shipwreck near Panticapaeum that witness testimony contradicts, and the pledging of the collateral to a Chian creditor, and closes with an appeal to the jurors to uphold the binding force of maritime agreements.
grc.demosthenes.against_leochares: A forensic oration of uncertain date, attributed to Demosthenes and transmitted among the private speeches of the corpus, delivered in an Athenian inheritance suit over the estate of the childless Archiades. It opens with an accusation that Leochares has lodged a false diamartyria, or challenge, asserting that Archiades left legitimate sons and thereby barring the family's claim to the estate. The speech then traces the descent of the Otryneis from Euthymachus through his sons Meidylides, Archippus, and Archiades, argues that kinship through males makes the speaker and his father Aristodemus the nearest heirs, attacks the irregular deme and phratry enrolments by which Leocrates had himself and his son Leochares entered as Archiades' adopted children, and cites the succession laws, including Solon's provision that an adopted son may not dispose of the estate. Witness testimony and deme registers are marshalled throughout to show the challenge to be untrue, and the jurors are asked to reject it and assign the inheritance to the closest kin.
grc.demosthenes.against_macartatus: Against Macartatus is an Athenian courtroom speech in Greek, attributed to Demosthenes, delivered in an inheritance dispute (a diadikasia) over the estate of Hagnias. It opens by recalling earlier contests with the same opponents over the estate and announces a narrative of the whole affair from its beginning. The speaker then traces the descent of both parties from Bouselos of Oinoe, recounts how the widow Philomache won the estate at law while her rivals produced forged wills, and describes the adoption of her son into the house of Euboulides and his enrolment among the phrateres, supporting the case with testimonies and with laws of Solon on inheritance, the epiklerate, and the duties of kin to the dead. Running through the speech are accusations that Theopompus and his son Macartatus practised collusion and perjury and uprooted more than a thousand olive trees from the land, and it closes with an appeal to the jurors to protect the boy and keep the household of Hagnias from desolation.
grc.demosthenes.against_nausimachus_and_xeno: A forensic speech in Attic Greek attributed to Demosthenes and of uncertain date, delivered in an Athenian court by one of two orphan brothers whom Nausimachus and Xenopeithes were prosecuting over the administration of their inheritance. It opens with the speaker's account of the paragraphe by which he and his brother seek to have the case ruled inadmissible, since their father had already been sued by the same men and released from those actions. The greater part of the speech argues from the settlement and the father's death soon after, from laws forbidding renewed litigation over released claims, and from the five-year limit within which orphans must sue former guardians, contrasting the opponents' present written charge with the opposite claims of their earlier complaint and attacking their squandered estates and poor record in liturgies. It closes with the reading of testimony, laws and the original charge, and a plea that the brothers be left in possession of their property.
grc.demosthenes.against_olympiodorus: A private forensic speech of the Athenian orator Demosthenes, composed for a plaintiff bringing suit in a jury court against his brother-in-law Olympiodorus over an inheritance. It opens with the speaker's defence of the necessity, painful to him, of litigating against a kinsman. The core of the speech is a narrative: the childless kinsman Comon died, the speaker called in Olympiodorus to help with the funeral, the two men divided the estate under written contracts and mutual oaths deposited with Androcleides, joint litigation against rival claimants ended in Olympiodorus' victory, and he then refused to share the proceeds, including money obtained through a tortured slave, as the oaths required, with laws, contracts and testimony cited throughout. The closing sections rebut the defendant's excuses, press challenges to have the deposited contracts opened before the jurors, attack his treatment of the speaker's wife, her sister and their daughter, denounce his life with a hetaera, and end with an appeal for a just verdict.
grc.demosthenes.against_onetor_31: A forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus, belonging to the series of private actions arising from Demosthenes' lawsuits against his former guardians and their associates in fourth-century BC Athens. It opens by recalling the argument left over from the earlier speech, that Onetor never paid the dowry owed with his sister's marriage to Aphobus, and announces an exposure of the defendant's falsehoods. The argument then tracks Onetor's shifting statements: the valuations he first placed on the house and country estate, his change of the dowry's stated amount from eighty minae to a talent, his removal of the boundary markers once litigation began, and the oath he would have sworn had the dowry actually been given. The speaker contends that these acts themselves prove the dowry was never paid and that Onetor's conduct as guarantor for Aphobus shows collusion, closing with questions of justice toward an orphaned heir left defrauded and unpaid.
grc.demosthenes.against_phaenippus: A forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, addressed to an Athenian jury in a suit arising from an antidosis, the procedure by which a citizen assigned a public liturgy could summon a wealthier man either to undertake it or to exchange properties with him. It opens with praise of Solon's law governing such exchanges and an account of the speaker's formal challenge to Phaenippus, including his inspection of the estate at Cytherus and his marking of its buildings and produce. The body of the speech documents Phaenippus' defiance of the exchange: the late filing of his sworn valuation, the unsealing of marked storehouses and carting off of grain, wine and timber, and the debts and dowry claim produced to inflate his liabilities, supported throughout by inserted laws, witness depositions and the valuation itself. The closing plea asks the jurors to compel the exchange and so relieve the speaker, impoverished by misfortunes in the silver mines and assessed three talents by the city, of the burden.
grc.demosthenes.against_stephanus_1: A forensic speech in the Demosthenic corpus for a private suit of false witness, spoken by Apollodorus son of Pasion against Stephanus of Acharnae. The opening has Apollodorus tell the Athenian jurors that, wronged through Stephanus's testimony and by Phormion's outrages, he has come before them to obtain redress. The speech then centres on the deposition in which Stephanus attested a challenge and a purported will of the banker Pasion: Apollodorus has the witness statements, the challenge, the will, and the lease of the bank read out in turn, arguing that the documents are fabricated, that the testimony contradicts itself and the pleadings, and that the witnesses have become accusers of their own case. Turning from legal argument to invective, he dwells on Stephanus's servile origins in the household, his greed and neglect of liturgies, and Phormion's alleged treatment of Apollodorus's mother, before closing with an appeal that the jurors punish the false witness as a warning to others.
grc.demosthenes.against_theocrines: Against Theocrines is a forensic speech attributed to Demosthenes, delivered in an Athenian court in support of an endeixis (denunciation) brought by a young man against Theocrines. It opens with the speaker explaining that his father, fined ten talents after Theocrines laid an information (phasis) against a ship of Micon and then abandoned the case for money, has left the prosecution to his son. The body of the speech assembles the charges: Theocrines' repeated acceptance of payment to withdraw prosecutions, his unpaid fines owed to the state, his betrayal of the speaker's father in a case concerning an illegal decree, and the misconduct of his brother while holding public office, with laws, decrees, a stele and witness testimony read into the argument. It closes by urging the jurors to enforce the laws against a professional sycophant and to come to the aid of a young man pleading his father's cause.
grc.demosthenes.erotic_essay: A short Greek epideictic oration of the Demosthenic corpus, the Erotic Essay (Erotikos) is attributed to Demosthenes and composed in the voice of a lover addressing the young Epicrates, whom he reckons the most attractive and promising of the city's youth. It opens with a frame in which the speaker announces that he will read out a composition he has written, in a style meant for display rather than the courtroom, designed both to praise the youth and to counsel him on education and the conduct of life. The main body celebrates Epicrates' beauty, his moderation towards his admirers, and his manliness shown in his choice of training with arms and in a chariot-race victory, and cites mythological exemplars and figures such as Pericles, Alcibiades, Timotheus, and Solon as men formed or improved by association with philosophers. The oration closes with an exhortation to take up philosophy, to choose his friends with care, and so to prepare for a leading part in the city's affairs.
grc.demosthenes.for_the_megalopitans: A deliberative oration by Demosthenes, delivered before the Athenian assembly on the question of aiding the Megalopolitans of Arcadia against the Lacedaemonians. It opens with the speaker rebuking both the Arcadian and the Lacedaemonian envoys for trading accusations before the city instead of advising on the common interest. The argument then holds that Athens' true policy is to keep both Thebes and Sparta weak, taking up in turn the claim that alliance with the Megalopolitans would make enemies of Sparta and hinder the recovery of Oropus, the charges brought against the Megalopolitans and Thebans for their earlier dealings, and the proposals for restoring Thespiae, Orchomenus, and Plataea and pulling down the old stelai. Appeals to the oaths sworn for the Messenians and to the city's habit of saving the wronged lead to the closing admonition not to abandon the Megalopolitans, nor any weaker state to a greater.
grc.demosthenes.funeral_speech: A Greek funeral oration (epitaphios) attributed to Demosthenes, composed for delivery at the public burial of Athenians fallen in war. The speaker opens by professing the difficulty of finding adequate praise for men who chose a noble death over life. The speech then surveys the autochthonous nobility of the Athenian people and the mythical exploits of their ancestors, the repulse of the Amazons, Eumolpus, and the Heraclids, and the burial of the Seven against Thebes, before passing to the Persian Wars and the valour of the recently fallen, whose defeat it recasts as a victory of spirit that had preserved the freedom of all Greece. Its closing sections credit the democracy with fostering such courage, recall a hero of each of the ten Attic tribes as a model for the dead by tribe, and end with consolation to parents and orphans before dismissing the mourners to perform the customary rites.
grc.demosthenes.letters: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to Demosthenes and addressed to the council and people of Athens. The first letter, prefaced by a prayer to the gods, presents the writer as an exile offering political counsel, urging concord among the citizens, forbearance toward former opponents, and united action among the Greeks now that Alexander is dead. Combining formal salutation with sustained advice on public affairs, the correspondence also touches on the question of the writer's own return home.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_1: An address to the Athenian assembly by the orator Demosthenes, the first of the Olynthiac orations urging the city to defend Olynthus against Philip of Macedon. It opens with the claim that the Athenians would do well to choose good counsel over money and should therefore listen readily to anyone who comes forward with advice. The speaker presents the Olynthians' war with Philip as an unlooked-for opportunity that must be seized at once, rehearsing earlier missed chances at Euboea, Amphipolis, Pydna, Potidaea and Methone on which Athenian inaction allowed Philip to grow great, and he warns that if Olynthus falls nothing will stop Philip from marching on Attica, even as Thessalian, Paeonian and Illyrian resistance troubles Philip's position. He proposes a twofold response, soldiers sent to save the Olynthic cities and other forces to ravage Philip's own territory, and closes by urging that the campaign be financed from the funds reserved for military purposes, with rich and poor alike serving and contributing as the need requires.
grc.demosthenes.olynthiac_3: A deliberative speech addressed to the Athenian assembly and the third of Demosthenes' Olynthiac orations, it urges vigorous military aid to Olynthus against Philip of Macedon. Opening with the complaint that talk of punishing Philip has distracted the Athenians from the real task of saving their allies, the speech reviews past delays and missed opportunities since Philip's siege in Thrace, blames flattering politicians for the city's passivity, and proposes appointing lawmakers to suspend the laws concerning the theoric fund so that money and citizens return to military service. The closing section contrasts the discipline, frugality and conquests of the ancestors, Aristides, Miltiades, Nicias, Pericles, with the private luxury of present-day statesmen, and ends with a call for the Athenians to serve in person and restore the civic order their forebears left them.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_halonnesus: An Athenian deliberative speech by Demosthenes, of the age of Philip II of Macedon, composed in answer to a letter in which Philip professed to be giving Athens the island of Halonnesus. The speaker begins by insisting that Philip's complaints cannot bar Athenians from giving counsel at the bema, and undertakes to examine both the letter and the arguments of Philip's ambassadors. He then rebuts the letter point by point, denying that Halonnesus is Philip's to give, exposing his proposals on pirates and commercial treaties as devices to consolidate his seizures at Potidaea and Amphipolis, and citing his actions at Pherae, Ambracia and in Cassopia as proof that his professed care for Greek freedom is empty. Recalling the decree of Philocrates and the earlier embassy under Python, the speech attacks Philip's encroachments on the Chersonese in favour of Apollonides of Cardia, and closes with the speaker reserving a further reply to the ambassadors' arguments.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_liberty_of_the_rhodia: An Athenian deliberative oration by Demosthenes, urging the assembly to restore the exiled democracy of Rhodes, which had been overthrown by oligarchs acting with the support of Mausolus of Caria. It opens by defending the right of every counsellor to speak freely on matters of great consequence. The speaker then reviews the recent war provoked by Chios, Byzantium, and Rhodes, recalls the precedent of Timotheus' aid to Ariobarzanes and the liberation of Samos, and argues that the King's success in Egypt would leave Artemisia free to secure Rhodes for herself. The closing sections broaden into a defence of democracy at large, presenting oligarchic revolution as the common enemy of all who value freedom and calling on Athens, as protector of Greek liberty, to act worthily of her ancestors.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_navy: A deliberative speech addressed to the Athenian assembly, handed down in the corpus of Demosthenes and of uncertain date, urging naval preparation against the Persian king. It opens by faulting speakers who court favour with praise of Athens' ancestors and promises counsel of more practical worth. The speaker argues against beginning the war with the king, since the Greeks are divided and Athens would bear the brunt, and instead proposes that the city make its power visibly ready: two thousand men enrolled in symmories, three hundred triremes with their crews and costs assigned by lot among these groups, ship-sheds redistributed by tribe and trittys, and contributions of money deferred until the danger is manifest, since the wealthy will part with it only when danger is real. The speech ends with a summary of the whole policy: to prepare against present enemies, to resist king or Greek alike who attempts wrong, and to see that Athens' deeds rather than the words spoken at the bema prove worthy of her ancestors.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_peace: An Athenian deliberative oration by Demosthenes, addressed to the assembly at a moment of tension following the conclusion of a peace with Philip of Macedon. The speech opens with the speaker confessing the difficulty of advising on present affairs and censuring the Athenians for deliberating only after events have gone against them. He then defends his past counsel, recalling his opposition to the Euboean expedition in aid of Plutarchus and his denunciation of Neoptolemus, before reviewing the promises made when the oaths of peace were sworn and the circumstances of the Phocian surrender. The greater part of the speech argues that Athens should preserve the existing peace, judge each question on its merits rather than be drawn into a common war under Amphictyonic auspices over Delphi and Phocis, and weigh the security of quiet against the perils of quarrelling over Oropus, Amphipolis and the islands.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_trierarchic_crown: On the Trierarchic Crown is a short oration in Greek attributed to the Athenian orator Demosthenes and belonging to the corpus of classical Attic oratory. Addressed to the council, it presents the speaker's plea for a crown in recognition of his service as a trierarch, contrasting his own expenditure in fitting out and fully manning a trireme with the conduct of rivals who hired substitutes for the liturgy and failed to equip their ships. Drawing on earlier Athenian practice, including the punishment of trierarchs after a naval defeat, he argues that those who discharge public duties deserve honour, while those who neglect them merit censure rather than reward.
grc.demosthenes.philip: A short Greek letter preserved in the corpus of Demosthenes, composed in the voice of Philip II of Macedon and addressed to the Athenian council and people, with both authorship and date uncertain. It opens with Philip announcing his intention to set out plainly the wrongs he claims to have suffered at Athenian hands despite his repeated embassies and his observance of the oaths. The letter is largely a catalogue of grievances: the ten-month imprisonment of the herald Nicias, Athens' toleration of pirates and of the Thasians and Byzantines, the raids and enslavements of the general Diopeithes in Thrace, the embassy sent to the Persian king to incite him against Macedon, decrees concerning Teres and Cersobleptes, the grants of citizenship to Evagoras of Cyprus and Dionysius of Syracuse, and the disputed status of Halonnesus, which Philip says he took from the pirate Sostratus. He ends by defending his title to Amphipolis as ancient, based on conquest, and acknowledged in Athens' own letters and treaties, and by urging that the quarrel be settled by argument and arbitration rather than by arms.
grc.didymus_alexandrinus.mensurae_marmorum_a: A short Greek treatise on the measurement of marble and timber, attributed to Didymus Alexandrinus and of uncertain date. It opens by distinguishing linear, planar, and solid modes of measurement and by setting out the differences among cubits. The body consists of worked problems computing the solid contents of marble slabs and of round, half-round, square, and triangular timbers, along with the diagonals of square pieces, followed by conversion rules among the cubit, the Ptolemaic foot, the Roman foot, palms, and digits, including the ratios of the Ptolemaic and Roman feet to the royal cubit. It closes with procedures for converting lengths and areas measured in cubits, palms, and digits into plane measurements.
grc.dinarchus.against_aristogiton: A forensic prosecution speech attributed to Dinarchus, directed against Aristogeiton on a charge of taking bribes, in a trial conducted on the report (apophasis) of the council of the Areopagus in the aftermath of the Harpalus affair. It opens with the speaker declaring that the present case is the most astonishing yet to arise from such reports, since the most notorious wrongdoer in the city now stands judgment. The argument surveys Aristogeiton's record of earlier crimes, imprisonment, debts to the state, and denunciation by Lycurgus, rebuts appeals to spare him for his ancestors' sake and his moderation, and invokes the ancestral expulsion of Arthmius of Zeleia and the convictions of Demades and Demosthenes as precedents for treating bribe-taking as a betrayal of the city. It closes by urging the judges to condemn him to death as both punishment and a cleansing of corruption from Athenian public life.
grc.dinarchus.against_demosthenes: An Athenian forensic speech by Dinarchus, prosecuting Demosthenes before a jury of Athenians in the affair of the money brought into the city by Harpalus. It opens with the speaker announcing, after Stratocles' preliminary charges, that the demagogue has been caught taking gifts from those against whom he once professed to act, and that the case now rests with the jurors. Over the course of the speech Dinarchus defends the investigation and verdict of the Areopagus council, recounts Demosthenes' alleged misdeeds, the betrayal of Thebes, his flight after the battle of Chaeronea, his failures on embassies, and the favors and citizenships he is said to have sold, and contrasts him with earlier benefactors of the city such as Timotheus and Conon, urging the conviction and death penalty that Demosthenes himself had set down in his own decree. It closes with the speaker handing the prosecution over to the remaining accusers.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.ad_ammaeum: A short Greek treatise in the form of a letter from Dionysius of Halicarnassus to Ammaeus, written to refute the claim that Demosthenes modelled his speeches on Aristotle's rhetorical treatises. It opens with Dionysius reporting a Peripatetic who promised to show that Demosthenes, having learned the art from Aristotle, transferred its precepts into his own orations. Dionysius then reconstructs the chronology of Demosthenes' public career from the biographers, running from the Against Androtion through the deliberative speeches against Philip, and sets it beside the life of Aristotle as handed down. Calling the philosopher himself as witness, he argues from passages in the rhetorical technai, whose examples are drawn from the Olynthiacs, On the Crown, and other speeches, that Demosthenes' forensic and deliberative orations were composed before Aristotle's treatises.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.antiquitates_: The Antiquitates Romanae of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a Greek prose history of Rome running from the city's legendary origins to the war with Pyrrhus. It opens with a methodological preface in which the author defends his choice of subject, arguing that Rome's dominion surpassed in extent and duration the earlier empires of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, Macedonians, Athenians and Spartans. The narrative then covers the regal period and the early Republic, with sustained attention to the struggles between patricians and plebeians and to the speeches of statesmen, ambassadors and tribunes that shaped them, including the conflict surrounding Gaius Marcius. The work closes with episodes of the early third century, among them Pyrrhus' campaigns and defeat, the censorship of Fabricius, an embassy to Ptolemy Philadelphus, and the subjugation of the Brettii and other Italian peoples.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_antiquis_o: A Greek critical essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to one Ammaeus under the title De Antiquis Oratoribus ('On the Ancient Orators'). It opens by declaring that the author's own age deserves thanks for restoring the ancient, philosophical rhetoric that, since the death of Alexander, had been supplanted in the Greek cities by a theatrical Asianic manner, a change Dionysius ascribes above all to the educating influence of Rome and its well-judging leading men. The essay then surveys that transformation across the cities and announces its programme: an examination of the six orators Dionysius judges the finest, namely Lysias, Isocrates, and Isaeus from the older generation and Demosthenes, Hyperides, and Aeschines from those who flourished after them, treating each man's life, character, and style in two successive parts, of which the discussion of the earlier three comes first.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_demosthene: A Greek rhetorical treatise in the form of a letter to Ammaeus by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, written in the first century BC, examining the style of Demosthenes. It opens with a detailed taxonomy of literary diction, distinguishing the austere style of Thucydides, the plain style of Lysias, and the mixed middle style practiced by Isocrates and Plato, each illustrated with lengthy quotations and criticism. The central argument holds that Demosthenes, imitating no single model, wove the finest features of all these styles into one flexible manner of speaking, and the work compares passages from Isocrates, Plato, Herodotus, and Demosthenes himself to demonstrate his superiority in the grander genres. The treatise concludes with an analysis of Demosthenic word arrangement, identifying its hallmarks in melody, rhythm, variation of periodic form, and delivery, and answering the hostile criticisms of Aeschines point by point.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_dinarcho: A short Greek treatise in which the rhetorician Dionysius of Halicarnassus assesses the orator Dinarchus, opening with his explanation that, having passed Dinarchus over in his writings on the ancient orators because he neither founded a distinctive style nor perfected that of others, he now judges him worthy of a separate account. The work then recounts Dinarchus's life: his Corinthian origins, his coming to Athens and association with Theophrastus and Demetrius of Phalerum, his fifteen years of speech-writing that followed the fall of Demosthenes and the other leading orators after Alexander's death, his flight to Chalcis under Cassander's oligarchy, and his lawsuit in old age against Proxenus over entrusted money. Dionysius characterizes his style as imitative rather than original, resembling at different points that of Lysias, Hyperides, and Demosthenes, and establishes his dates by a list of Athenian archons from Nicophemus to Philip. It ends with catalogues of speeches attributed to Dinarchus, genuine public speeches, spurious ones, and private ones, each cited by its opening words, together with the grounds for accepting or rejecting each attribution.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_lysia: A Greek critical essay by Dionysius of Halicarnassus on the style of the Attic orator Lysias. It opens with a life of Lysias, his Syracusan parentage, birth at Athens, sojourn in Thurii, and return to Athens as a prolific writer of courtroom, deliberative, and display speeches, before turning to his qualities as a stylist. The main body takes up these virtues in turn: purity of Attic diction, the use of plain and ordinary words, clarity, brevity, vividness, characterisation, propriety, persuasiveness, and the pervasive charm treated as the surest test of genuine Lysian authorship, together with his powers of invention and arrangement and his standing in the judicial, deliberative, and epideictic kinds of oratory. Extended excerpts illustrate the argument, including the speech against Diogeiton, the Olympic oration urging the Greeks against Dionysius of Syracuse, and a deliberation on preserving the ancestral constitution, while speeches on Lysias's name such as those for Nicias and Iphicrates are questioned, and the essay closes by announcing Isocrates as the next orator in chronological order.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydide: The De Thucydide of Dionysius of Halicarnassus is a Greek critical essay addressed to Quintus Aelius Tubero, opening with the author's explanation that, having touched on Thucydides only briefly in an earlier survey of writers and poets, he now sets out, at his correspondent's request, a fuller study. The work first surveys the historians before Thucydides, from the old local chronographers to Herodotus, to show how his choice of the Peloponnesian War alone as his subject and his devotion to truth set him apart, and praises the justice and restraint of his factual narrative. Dionysius then faults the composition of the history, its division by summers and winters, its arrangement of the causes of the war, and its uneven treatment of battles, embassies, and public funerals, before turning to Thucydides' style, with its archaic and figurative vocabulary, harsh arrangement, and dense, often obscure diction, illustrated from the narrative of the Corcyrean stasis and from speeches such as the defense of the Plataeans, the Melian dialogue, and the addresses of Pericles and Hermocrates. The essay closes by rejecting those who defend Thucydides' obscurity as fitting for history, commending the parts that stay within ordinary usage, and crediting Demosthenes alone among later orators with a successful imitation of his manner.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.epistula_ad_p: A letter in Greek from Dionysius of Halicarnassus to Pompey, who is addressed in the text as Geminus; it opens with a reply to the recipient's complaint that, in weighing Demosthenes against Isocrates and Plato, Dionysius had brought accusations against Plato. The letter then defends comparison as the surest method of critical testing, noting that many before him, Aristotle among them, had censured Plato, and examines Plato's style at length, praising his plain and precise manner while finding the ornate, figurative and dithyrambic vein defective, with examples drawn from the Phaedrus. It closes with critical estimates of the historians Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Philistus and Theopompus in their choice of subject, arrangement and diction, and a reference to the author's memoranda on imitation addressed to Demetrius.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.libri_secundi: Fragments in Greek of the second book of the treatise On the Ancient Orators by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, preserved as a short series of scholia and critical notices. The remains open with a scholion quoting Dionysius on a metaphor in Demosthenes, judged more tragic in its original form than the political phrasing of the same thought in the speech On the Embassy. The remaining fragments likewise concern Demosthenes and Aeschines: they criticise the prooemium of the Embassy speech as epilogic in tone and unduly ornate, praise a colon borrowed from Euripides as expressed with sound judgement rather than levity, and censure Aeschines' use of παρακαταθέσθαι of bodies and of a phrase about contending for victory over virtue.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnassus.de_compositio: A short Greek rhetorical treatise on the arrangement of words, transmitted in epitomized form under the name of Dionysius of Halicarnassus. It opens as a birthday gift from the writer to a young friend named Rufus Melitius, offered as equipment for every profitable use of language. The work defines synthesis as the fitting placement of words into clauses and periods, ranks it above the mere choice of words as the source of charm, persuasion and power in style, and examines the sounds of letters and syllables, the rhythms and metres that run through even unmetrical prose, and the imitation of nature's sounds. Its later chapters distinguish three styles of harmony, the austere, the polished and the well-blended, illustrating each with extended quotations from Homer, Pindar, Thucydides, Sappho and Isocrates, and discuss the propriety of arrangement suited to subject and feeling, together with the ways prose can carry hidden measures and verse can loosen its metre toward the freedom of prose.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.de_imitatione_: The surviving fragments of Dionysius of Halicarnassus' treatise On Imitation set out how a writer should study and emulate earlier Greek authors. It opens with definitions of rhetoric, of imitation and of emulation, and a plea for close reading of the ancients, illustrated by the story of the plain wife made beautiful by gazing at portraits and by Zeuxis painting his Helen from the finest features of the maidens of Croton. The body of the work reviews the qualities to be drawn from individual models, characterising Hesiod, Pindar, Simonides, Stesichorus and Alcaeus among the poets, Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides among the tragedians, Herodotus, Thucydides, Philistus, Xenophon and Theopompus among the historians, Plato and Aristotle among the philosophers, and Lysias, Isocrates, Lycurgus, Demosthenes, Aeschines and Hyperides among the orators. Short closing pieces contrast Gorgias' poetic manner with Lysias' plainness and argue that the apparent artlessness of Lysias' style is itself highly wrought.
grc.epictetus.gnomologium_epicteteum_e_stoba: A collection of Greek moral maxims attributed to Epictetus, drawn from the anthology of Stobaeus. It opens with the saying that a life entangled with fortune resembles a winter torrent, turbulent and short-lived, in contrast to the soul that keeps company with virtue like an ever-flowing spring. The remaining sayings, mostly brief aphorisms built on similes, treat the opposition of virtue to fortune, wealth, and luxury; moderation in food, drink, and conviviality; true freedom of the soul against bodily slavery; household order and friendship as against flatterers; the duty of just judgment; and the conduct of the citizen and statesman, ending with the image of the man who benefits his city as unprompted as the rising sun.
grc.epicurus.ratae_sententiae: The Ratae Sententiae (Greek Kyriai Doxai, 'Principal Doctrines') is a short Greek collection of forty numbered maxims setting out the central ethical teachings of Epicurus. The sayings were transmitted by Diogenes Laertius in his life of Epicurus. The maxims treat the blessed and untroubled nature of the gods, death as nothing to us, the measure of pleasure and pain, the need for the study of nature to dispel fear, the classification of desires as natural, necessary, or vain, and the role of friendship and justice in the secure life. Some of the sayings are accompanied by brief explanatory glosses in parentheses.
grc.euripides.heracles: Euripides' tragedy Heracles opens in Thebes, where the hero's wife Megara, their children, and his aged father Amphitryon shelter at an altar of Zeus while the usurper Lycus, who has killed the ruling house of Creon, prepares to put them to death. Heracles, away in the underworld fetching Cerberus, returns in time to slay Lycus and rescue his household. Madness sent by Hera then drives him to murder his own wife and children, and on waking, bound to a pillar, he confronts the deed in a long scene of grief and despair. Theseus arrives, argues him out of suicide, and leads him to Athens for purification, leaving the destroyed family to lament their fate in Thebes.
grc.euripides.iphigenia_aulis: A Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizing the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigenia at Aulis. It opens with Agamemnon's account to an old retainer of the oath binding Helen's suitors, the muster of the Greek armament at Aulis, and Calchas' oracle demanding the death of his daughter in exchange for sailing. Menelaus intercepts Agamemnon's letter countermanding the summons, Clytemnestra arrives with Iphigenia and the infant Orestes under the pretense of marriage to Achilles, and the hero, discovering the misuse of his name, first rages at the deception and then resolves to defend the girl against an army that clamors for the sacrifice. Iphigenia ultimately chooses to die freely for the sake of Greece, and a messenger reports that Artemis substituted a deer and carried the maiden away, releasing the fleet for Troy as Agamemnon sends Clytemnestra home with an ominous farewell.
grc.eusebius_caesarea.historia_ecclesiastica: A Greek church history in ten books attributed to Eusebius of Caesarea, setting out the story of the Christian church from the incarnation and apostolic age down to Constantine's victory over Licinius. Book 1 opens with a chapter-by-chapter outline of its contents and then argues from prophecy for the pre-existence, incarnation and ancient roots of the Christian name before turning to Herod, the census of Quirinius, John the Baptist and Jesus. The later books trace the succession of bishops in Jerusalem, Rome, Alexandria and other sees, the careers of figures such as Clement, Origen and Dionysius, the arguments with heresies including Marcion and Montanus, the series of persecutions under Roman emperors, and end with the conversion of Constantine, the Edict of Milan and the rebuilding of churches.
grc.flavius_josephus.contra_apionem: Contra Apionem is an apologetic treatise in two books written in Greek by Flavius Josephus. Addressed to Epaphroditus, it opens with the author explaining that his Antiquities has already set forth the antiquity of the Jewish people, and that he now writes briefly against those who slander the Jews or distrust his account because Greek historians record nothing of them. The first book defends the antiquity and careful transmission of Jewish records, outlines the twenty-two books of the Hebrew scriptures, and cites Egyptian, Phoenician, Chaldean, and Greek writers as witnesses to the Jews' early history, before refuting the hostile Egyptian narratives of Manetho, Chaeremon, and Lysimachus. The second book answers the accusations of Apion and Apollonius Molon and closes with a summary of the Mosaic constitution, its theocratic government, priesthood, and laws, arguing that the law has remained unaltered and has spread among many peoples.
grc.flavius_josephus.de_bello_judaico_libri_: The Bellum Judaicum is a historical narrative in seven books by Flavius Josephus, who introduces himself in the preface as Josephus son of Matthias, a priest from Jerusalem who first fought against the Romans and later accompanied them. It recounts the great war between the Jews and the Romans, from the turmoil that followed Nero through the outbreak of the revolt and the Roman campaigns to the siege of Jerusalem and its destruction under Titus. Josephus presents the work as a Greek rendering of an account he had earlier composed in his ancestral language for the peoples beyond the Euphrates, and defends its accuracy against writers whom he accuses of flattering the Romans or slandering the Jews. The narrative stresses the part played by internal tyrants and factions in the city's fall, and joins the historian's account of events to the author's lament for the misfortunes of his homeland.
grc.galen.ad_glauconem_de_methodo_medendi: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, addressed to a friend named Glaucon and framed as advice for the treatment of diseases by a general method. The work opens by defending the need for a physician to know not only the common human constitution but each individual patient's, and outlines a dialectical method of dividing diseases into genera and species, praising Hippocrates, Mnesitheus, and Plato for their use of such division. It then proceeds systematically through fevers, first the simple ephemeral fevers arising from fatigue, insomnia, grief, anger, and other causes, with their signs in pulse, urine, and complexion, then the periodic fevers (tertian, quartan, quotidian, and continuous), covering their diagnosis and dietary and pharmaceutical treatment, and turns next to fevers accompanied by symptoms such as vomiting, syncope, and hemorrhage, discussing when evacuation of blood or humors is safe. The treatise closes with a series of accounts of local diseases and swellings, including inflammations, erysipelas, herpes, scirrhus, oedema, abscesses, fistulae, gangrene, and cancerous tumours, giving for each the method of treatment by purging, venesection, plasters, and surgery, and ends with a promise of a fuller work on the powers of drugs.
grc.galen.an_in_arteriis_sanguis_contineatur: A short Greek treatise by Galen arguing that the arteries naturally contain blood, written against Erasistratus and his followers, who held that the arteries carry only pneuma and admit blood only at the moment of wounding. It opens with a syllogistic proof that, since blood escapes at once from a wounded artery and no pneuma is seen to escape beforehand, blood must already have been present in the vessels. The argument then answers the Erasistratean objection that pneuma, being subtle and light, could pass out unobserved whether borne by itself or driven from the heart, and supports Galen's case with appeals to the visible behaviour of exposed arteries, anatomical observations on the mesenteric vessels, and a demonstration with cannula and ligature showing that the pulse ceases beyond the ligature because arterial dilatation stems from a power of the heart rather than from transmitted pneuma. Along the way Galen defends the use of logical method in medicine, criticizes the reasoning of both Skeptics and Dogmatists, and closes with the anatomical demonstration of the ligated artery.
grc.galen.de_anatomicis_administrationibus: A Greek anatomical manual by the physician Galen, written, as its opening states, while the emperor Antoninus was on the throne. The work begins with Galen's account of rewriting his anatomical books after the originals were lost in Rome and at the request of the consul Flavius Boethus. Thereafter it proceeds as a sustained practical instruction in dissection, leading the dissector from the skeleton, studied on human bones where possible and otherwise on apes, through the muscles, vessels and nerves to the viscera of chest and abdomen, the peritoneum and its reflections, and the organs of nutrition and excretion. Later parts describe procedures on living animals, including the exposure of the beating heart, the section of nerves and spinal cord that abolishes respiration and voice, and the dissection of the brain's coverings, ventricles and contained vessels.
grc.galen.de_antidotis: Galen's De Antidotis is a Greek pharmacological treatise on antidotes, the drugs physicians administer internally to counteract poisons and venomous bites. It opens with a definition of the antidote and an account of the two most famous compound preparations, the Mithridatium of Mithridates of Pontus and the theriac of Andromachus, Nero's archiater. The greater part of the work gives detailed instructions for compounding the theriac, covering the selection and testing of ingredients such as vipers' flesh, squill and theriac tablets, opium, honey, wine and numerous aromatics, with warnings about adulteration, notes on the regions that yield the best simples, and recipes in prose and verse drawn from Andromachus, Damocrates and Criton. Closing sections assemble further antidotes ascribed to named physicians and rulers, including the Mithridatium itself and remedies for the bites of vipers, scorpions, spiders and mad dogs.
grc.galen.de_causis_morborum: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Causis Morborum opens by recalling an earlier work that classified diseases by species and genus into simple and compound kinds, and announces that the causes of each disease will now be examined, beginning with the simple, homoeomerous parts of the body and then proceeding to the organic ones. The discussion first takes up the causes of diseases of immoderate heat, cold, dryness and moisture, listing sources such as excessive exercise, putrefaction, exposure to sun or cold, and unsuitable food and drink, and explains how fevers, apoplexies and comas arise from them. It then treats compound diseases and the affections of organic parts, covering faulty conformation from conditions in the womb or the careless rearing of infants, corruption of cavities and pores, and abnormalities of position, number and size. The work ends with the common genus of dissolution of continuity, including fractures, wounds and contusions, and anticipates a following account of the differences of symptoms.
grc.galen.de_constitutione_artis_medicae_ad_: Galen addresses Patrophilus, whose eagerness to learn the healing art with demonstration and method he undertakes to serve by setting down memoranda, the present work being the second of two, devoted to showing how the single method that founds every productive art also constitutes medicine. It first classifies the arts as theoretical, practical, productive and acquisitive, and establishes medicine as a productive art of the corrective kind, which repairs the body as a builder mends a damaged house rather than creating something new. The argument then requires knowledge of the body's parts, simple and organic, in their substance, size, shape, number and arrangement, together with their activities and uses, and passes from anatomy through the four elements and the mixtures that yield health and disease to the therapeutic method, whose general aim, as Hippocrates is cited as saying, is that contraries cure contraries. Worked diagnoses such as pleurisy, an account of prognosis as a weighing of disease against nature, and brief sketches of the preventive and recuperative branches of hygiene complete the demonstration that medicine, like the other productive arts, is built from the concept of its end.
grc.galen.de_consuetudinibus: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, of uncertain date, defending habit (ethos) as one of the legitimate therapeutic indications in the art of medicine. It opens by answering detractors of this doctrine, appealing to Hippocrates on acute diet and to Erasistratus on paralysis and recounting the death of Aristotle of Mytilene, who refused a cold drink that might have saved him. The bulk of the work seeks the cause of habit's power: repeated use of foods and drinks is said to produce a qualitative alteration and a natural affinity in the body, and the same reasoning is extended to external agents such as heat, cold, bathing and sun, and to gymnastic training of body and mind, with a long quotation from Plato's Timaeus. It closes by discussing habitual evacuations, nosebleeds, haemorrhoids, venesection and purges, which it explains not from habit as such but from the causes of the original evacuations.
grc.galen.de_crisibus: Galen's Greek treatise On Crises deals with the diagnosis and prognostication of critical days and turning points in disease. It opens by declining to fix a single definition of crisis and undertaking instead to teach how crises, whether already present or still to come, may be discerned. The argument then moves through the four periods of illness (beginning, increase, acme, and decline), the signs of concoction or its failure shown in urine, sputum, and bowel evacuations, the discrimination of fever types such as tertian, quartan, and quotidian from the first days of sickness, and the prediction of when, how, and how favorably a crisis will fall, with sustained quotation and exegesis of Hippocratic passages from the Aphorisms, Prognostic, and Epidemics and attacks on later physicians such as Thessalus who neglect these doctrines.
grc.galen.de_curandi_ratione_per_venae_secti: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on treatment by venesection, directed in part against physicians of the Erasistratean school who rejected the practice. It opens by setting out the questions a physician must settle before bleeding anyone: which bodily conditions require evacuation, which of them call for venesection in particular, and which patients can bear the loss of blood. The work then takes up the choice of vein and incision point, the quantity of blood to be drawn and its timing by season, age and bodily strength, and the distinction between evacuant and revulsive uses of bleeding, illustrated with case histories from Galen's practice at Rome; a closing section extends the discussion to arteriotomy and reports operations performed at Pergamum and elsewhere, some undertaken on the strength of dreams. Throughout, Hippocratic authority is invoked and the doctrines of Erasistratus and his followers, including Chrysippus of Cnidus, are attacked.
grc.galen.de_diebus_decretoriis: De diebus decretoriis (On Critical Days) is a Greek medical treatise by Galen concerning the days on which crises in disease occur and how far they can be trusted. The opening argues that a sudden resolution of illness counts as a genuine crisis only when accompanied by visible evacuations such as sweats, abundant urine, haemorrhages, or discharges, and that convalescents must accordingly be kept under strict regimen. Crises are then classified as complete or incomplete, trustworthy or unreliable, dangerous, clear, obscure, or plainly foreshadowed, with the seventh day presented as the most reliable crisis day and those on the sixth, twelfth, and sixteenth as rare, incomplete, or generally unfavourable. In support of this scheme the treatise appeals to Hippocrates and to the accumulated experience of earlier physicians including Archigenes, Heracleides of Tarentum, Philotimus, and Diocles.
grc.galen.de_difficultate_respirationis: A Greek treatise by Galen on difficult breathing, arguing that dyspnoea is a form of disturbance affecting respiration just as disturbances affect sensation and movement. It examines the natural components of breathing, inspiration, expiration, and the pauses between them, and classifies forms of dyspnoea as simple or compound, arising in the speed, size, or spacing of the breath. Galen further criticises newer physicians who departed from the names for breathing defects customary among Hippocrates and the older medical writers.
grc.galen.de_elementis_ex_hippocrate: A Greek treatise on the elements of bodies according to Hippocrates, attributed to Galen (2nd century AD), which sets out the doctrine that the fundamental constituents of all things are the hot, the cold, the dry and the wet, and that Hippocrates was the first to establish this correctly. It opens by distinguishing elements as they appear to the senses from elements as they are in nature, arguing from the experience of pain that man cannot be composed of a single principle. The argument then ranges over rival theories, refuting in turn the atomists, monists who identify the element with water, air, fire or earth, and physicians such as Athenaeus of Attalia and Asclepiades who place the elements too near to sense, before turning to a second book on the four humours, blood, phlegm and the two biles, as the elements proper to animals with blood, with discussion of embryonic formation, the varieties of blood, the selective attraction exercised by drugs, and nutrition and evacuation as grounded in a faculty that draws to each body its like.
grc.galen.de_foetuum_formatione: A brief Greek treatise by Galen, On the Formation of the Foetus, on embryonic development. It opens by criticising philosophers who wrote about the shaping of the embryo without anatomical evidence, contrasting them with Hippocrates, whose observational account of a six-day embryo Galen then quotes at length. The body of the work describes the membranes and vessels surrounding the foetus, the chorion, amnion and allantois, and the veins and arteries of the umbilicus, and argues that the vessels are formed first from the seed, drawing the mother's blood like the roots of a plant, followed by the liver and heart and, last of all, the brain and sense organs. Against Stoic and Peripatetic doctrines that make the heart the first-formed part and ruler of the living creature, Galen distinguishes the principles of generation from those of governance, and the treatise closes with the question of the forming cause, an artisan of supreme skill and power evident in every part of the body, whose identity he confesses himself unable to determine.
grc.galen.de_hirudinibus_revulsione_cucurbit: A brief Greek therapeutic treatise by Galen, covering leeching, revulsion, the cupping-glass, and incision and scarification. It opens with practical directions for catching, keeping, and applying leeches to draw blood, together with the care of the bitten part and the stopping of any resulting bleeding. The remainder sets out three further procedures: revulsion, whereby violent flows of humours are diverted from one region of the body to another by counter-attracting remedies; the use of the cupping-glass, with its applications and limitations in inflammatory and plethoric conditions; and incision and scarification, recommended as a lighter alternative to frequent venesection, with indications for which parts of the body to cut and which complaints each operation relieves.
grc.galen.de_inaequali_intemperie: De Inaequali Intemperie is a short Greek treatise in which Galen examines anomalous or uneven dyscrasia, an imbalance of bodily qualities that afflicts one part of the body differently from another. The opening chapters distinguish such irregular imbalances, whether affecting the whole body or a single member, from uniform ones, illustrating them with conditions such as erysipelas, phagedaena, herpes, and elephantiasis, and then survey the body's structures from the largest visible parts down to the homogeneous tissues. The remainder follows the course of a hot flux invading a muscle, explaining how inflammation and pain arise as the parts are heated and compressed, and how recovery proceeds either by dispersion of the flux or by its concoction into pus, together with an account of which cavities offer the safer sites for suppuration. Hippocratic sayings on pain arising during alteration of nature are invoked along the way.
grc.galen.de_instrumento_odoratus: The De Instrumento Odoratus is a Greek treatise by Galen on the anatomy and physiology of the organ of smell. It opens by distinguishing the perception of odours from the faculty that effects it and by asking whether the nose itself can be that organ. From there the work traces the nasal passages, the ethmoid bone and the membranes continuous with the mouth, pharynx and brain, arguing from anatomical observation and experiments with odorous substances and sneezing remedies that the seat of olfaction lies deeper, in the anterior cavities of the brain. In the course of the argument Galen rejects the hypothesis, which he reports from Aristotle, that breathing uncovers special odour-bearing pores, holding instead that odours are perceived only during inhalation.
grc.galen.de_locis_affectis: Galen's De Locis Affectis ('On the Affected Locations') is a Greek medical treatise of uncertain date within his oeuvre that opens by explaining why physicians distinguish the precise bodily parts, topoi, affected by disease, since treatment varies according to those differences. The work then develops a systematic method for diagnosing hidden rather than visibly apparent diseased locations, drawing on anatomical knowledge of each organ's substance, position, and function, and proceeds organ by organ through the head and brain, nerves, spinal marrow, lungs and chest, heart, liver, spleen, stomach, intestines, kidneys, bladder, uterus, and external genitalia, illustrating each discussion with case histories from Galen's own practice and with critiques of predecessors such as Archigenes, Erasistratus, and Asclepiades.
grc.galen.de_marcore: De Marcore ('On Marasmus') is a brief Greek medical treatise by Galen.
