It defines marasmus as the destruction of a living body through dryness, distinguishing a simple form arising from starvation from compound forms accompanied by excessive heat or cold, as in certain fevers and in old age. An opening digression recalls a philosopher who promised to rear infants immune to aging, an anecdote Galen uses to illustrate how plausible but unproved arguments persuade. The discussion then investigates the cause of aging, rejecting the doctrine that innate heat consumes the body as a flame consumes its fuel, and engages with a Hippocratic saying on the killing power of the heat that shaped the body.
grc.galen.de_morborum_differentiis: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, transmitted under the Latin title De Morborum Differentiis (On the Differences of Diseases), setting out a systematic classification of diseases. It opens by defining disease as an affection contrary to nature that impairs bodily function, distinct from both symptom and cause, and argues that health is a due symmetry of the body's elements while disease is their asymmetry. The argument then enumerates the primary simple diseases of the homoiomerous parts, first as excess and defect of porosity on the hypothesis of passive elements, then as the four dyscrasias of hot, cold, wet and dry on the hypothesis of active qualities, before passing to the diseases of the organic parts, which arise from defects of shape, number, size, composition or continuity, with examples ranging from inflammations, ulcers, tumours and abnormal growths to fractures, dislocations and amputations. It ends by showing how compound diseases of whole organs are built up out of these simple affections, and by separating what is disease proper from what is merely its cause or symptom.
grc.galen.de_motu_musculorum: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on the movement of muscles, which identifies the muscles as the organs of voluntary motion and surveys their great number, varied shapes, and points of attachment to bone. It distinguishes tendons, ligaments, and nerves, describing the tendon as a mixed nature between ligament and nerve, and traces the powers of motion and sensation from the brain and spinal cord through the nerves into the body of the muscle, which is also nourished by artery and vein. It sets the psychic, voluntary movements of the muscles apart from the natural movements of arteries and veins, and closes with a physiological account of how the tendon, formed from both nerve and ligament, binds the muscle to the bone and draws it in movement.
grc.galen.de_nervorum_dissectione: A short Greek anatomical treatise by Galen on the dissection of the nerves. It opens with points conceded by all physicians, that no part of the animal possesses voluntary motion or sensation apart from a nerve, and that nerves take their origin from the brain and spinal cord. The body of the work proceeds pair by pair through the cranial nerves, numbered after Marinus, and then through the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral pairs of the spinal marrow, tracing each from its bony exit to its distribution among the muscles, sense organs, and viscera, while repeatedly pointing out where earlier anatomists went astray. It closes by presenting the whole as a compressed summary for beginners, with exact detail referred to Galen's fuller anatomical procedures.
grc.galen.de_parvae_pilae_exercitio: Galen's short Greek treatise On Exercise with the Small Ball argues that exercising with a small ball surpasses all other forms of gymnastics for health. The opening, addressed to Epigenes, concedes that earlier philosophers and physicians have said enough about gymnastics in general but observes that ball exercise in particular has never been adequately explained. The treatise then praises the exercise for its accessibility, since it requires only a small ball rather than the wealth and leisure demanded by hunting, and for training every part of the body evenly while also sharpening the mind through the attention needed to catch and throw; it further discusses how the exercise can be intensified or softened to suit the old, the young and the convalescent, likening its quick seizure and guarded retention of the ball to a general's skills. It concludes by weighing these advantages against the dangers of other pursuits, which injure runners, riders, jumpers, wrestlers and discus-throwers, whereas ball exercise, properly practised in moderation, brings benefit without hazard to body and soul alike.
grc.galen.de_placitis_hippocratis_et_platoni: A Greek medical-philosophical treatise by the physician Galen, De Placitis Hippocratis et Platonis sets out the agreement of Hippocratic medicine with Platonic teaching on the soul. The work opens in the midst of an extended anatomical argument, appealing to dissection and vivisection to show that the left ventricle of the heart holds blood rather than pneuma and that the psychic pneuma resides in the ventricles of the brain. Galen presses the case against Chrysippus, Erasistratus, Aristotle, and Praxagoras, whom he charges with placing the ruling part of the soul or the origin of the nerves in the heart contrary to what observation of the body reveals.
grc.galen.de_plenitudine: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on fullness (plethos), the excess of fluids in the body and its vessels. It opens by surveying and ridiculing the definitions of quantity given by contemporary physicians, some of whom measure it against the capacity of the containing vessels and some against the dynamic power (dynamis) of the body. The discussion then distinguishes these two senses, criticises Erasistratus' account of how plethora arises and is diagnosed, attacks the Stoic and Herophilean doctrines of the cohesive cause, and dissects the cluster of symptoms - bodily weight, tension, swelling and redness of the veins, sluggishness, a sedentary life and suppressed evacuations - by which the empiric doctors justified phlebotomy. Its closing sections set out how the several kinds of humoral excess are recognised through colour, pulse, sleep, appetite and previous regimen, together with contributory factors such as season, region and the density of the patient's body.
grc.galen.de_praenotione_ad_epigenem: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on prognosis, addressed to Epigenes. It opens with a denunciation of physicians who pursue favour through flattery, display, and attendance on the wealthy, and who persecute those claiming foreknowledge of the course of disease. The main part is a narrative account of the quartan fever of Eudemus, a Peripatetic philosopher whom Galen attended in Rome, recording his pulse-based predictions of the fever's critical days and his disagreements with rival physicians over treatment, notably their administration of theriac. The account also refers to anatomical demonstrations on voice and respiration given before distinguished Romans, including men of consular rank.
grc.galen.de_praesagitione_ex_pulsibus: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Praesagitione ex Pulsibus ('On Prognosis from the Pulse') teaches how to draw prognostic signs from the pulse, taking prognosis to cover present and past conditions as well as things to come. Its discussion centers on the pulse conventionally called 'great,' examining how changes in size, speed, and density arise from causes such as bodily constitution, thinness, exercise, bathing, food and wine, anger, warming drugs, and the onset of fever. It also treats the examination of patients who conceal their condition, including an anecdote in which Galen detects that a wealthy man has secretly taken medicine despite his denials. Throughout, the argument presupposes Galen's earlier treatises on the diagnosis, differences, and causes of pulses.
grc.galen.de_propriorum_animi_cuiuslibet_aff: A short Greek ethical treatise by Galen, cast as a reply to an interlocutor who asked for a summary of the book Galen had written for Antonius the Epicurean on watchfulness over one's own passions. It distinguishes errors, which arise from false opinion, from the passions, which arise from an irrational power in the soul that disobeys reason, and argues that self-love blinds everyone to his own failings. Following the fable of Aesop's two sacks and sayings of Plato, it prescribes entrusting self-knowledge to an impartial observer, neither loved nor hated, who will report one's faults, and counsels patience under criticism. Practical directions follow for testing such a companion's honesty and for treating able critics, in Zeno's phrase, as paedagogues.
grc.galen.de_ptisana: A short Greek treatise by Galen on the preparation and medical use of ptisan, the barley gruel and its juice. It opens with the observation that physicians administer the drink to patients without defining what it can and cannot provide, whereupon Galen undertakes to set out its proper boiling, its powers, and the manner, quantity, and timing of its administration. The discussion proceeds through the choice of pure water and of sound barley neither too new nor too old, the correct method of cooking, and the properties of the well-boiled ptisan, its smoothness, moistness, and power to cleanse and nourish, which make it suited above all to acute fevers. The treatise closes with the necessary qualifications, indicating when, in what amount, and to whom the drink should or should not be given, and how dosage should be graduated from the juice alone to the whole ptisan.
grc.galen.de_pulsibus_ad_tirones: A short Greek introductory treatise by Galen on the pulse, addressed to a certain Teuthras and opening with the promise to set out what beginners need to know about pulses, the fuller art being treated elsewhere. After explaining which arteries are palpable and why the wrist is the most convenient site, it sets out the elementary differences of the pulse in size, speed, force, the texture of the arterial coat and the intervals between beats, together with regularity, periodic order and compound deviations such as the worm-like, ant-like and hectic pulses. A second part lists the factors that alter the pulse in health, including sex, temperament, age, season, climate, pregnancy, sleep, exercise, bathing, food, wine and water. The last and longest section treats pathological changes, giving the characteristic pulse of emotions, pain, inflammation and a long list of diseases, from pleurisy and empyema to phrenitis, lethargy, tetanus, paralysis, dropsy and jaundice, and closing with the effects of hellebore.
grc.galen.de_purgantium_medicamentorum_facul: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on the action of purgative drugs, De Purgantium Medicamentorum Facultate ('On the Faculties of Purging Medicines'). Galen argues that cathartics possess an attractive power proper to each humour, drawing out that humour alone from the veins, and directs the argument against Erasistratus, who allowed no such faculty, and against the followers of Asclepiades, who held that purgatives transform all the humours indiscriminately rather than evacuating one. The treatise invokes Hippocratic authority for the doctrine of attraction and repeatedly challenges its opponents to public demonstrations of treatment on patients suffering from jaundice and dropsy, to be decided by deeds rather than long speeches.
grc.galen.de_sanitate_tuenda: A Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Sanitate Tuenda ('On the Preservation of Health') sets out the hygienic half of the art concerned with the human body, arguing that the preservation of health must be examined before the treatment of disease. It defines health as a due proportion of the elementary qualities in the body's parts and surveys the harms to which the body is subject, both those innate from conception, such as the progressive drying that constitutes old age, and those arising from outside. The discussion then turns to the replenishment of lost substance through food, drink, respiration and the pulse, the digestion of nutriment into matter resembling the body, and the formation and evacuation of residues as the chief means of keeping the body free of corruption.
grc.galen.de_sectis_ad_eos_qui_introducuntur: Galen's short Greek treatise De Sectis introduces newcomers to the principal schools of ancient medicine and the disputes among them. It opens by defining medicine as knowledge of the healthy and the diseased and by naming its two earliest sects, the Empiric and the Logical or Dogmatic. The work then sets out how the Empiricists derive remedies from accumulated experience, how the Dogmatists proceed by reasoning or 'indication' from hidden causes, ages, seasons, regions, and bodily conditions, and how the two schools accuse one another of inadequacy over anatomy, dialectic, and demonstration. A final section presents the Methodist school with its 'commonalities' of constriction and flux, its dismissal of causal inquiry, its boast of teaching the whole art in six months, and closes with a dogmatic speaker's rebuttal addressed to beginners.
grc.galen.de_sophismatis_seu_captionibus_pen: A short Greek treatise by Galen on fallacies arising from wording, preserved under the Latin title De Sophismatis seu Captionibus penes dictionem. It sets out Aristotle's six modes of verbal sophism, homonymy, amphiboly, accent, combination, division, and figure of speech, judging Aristotle's own supporting argument entirely obscure and the explanations of earlier interpreters unsuccessful. Galen then argues that diction has a single virtue, clear signification, and a single vice, ambiguity, so that every fallacy dependent on language ultimately arises from a word's double meaning.
grc.galen.de_substantia_facultatum_naturaliu: A Greek fragment of On the Substance of Natural Faculties by Galen, the second-century CE Greek physician. The fragment takes up the apparent discrepancy in claims that animals are hot and plants cold, defending Plato against the charge of inconsistency between his ordinary statements and the doctrine of the Timaeus that the world's soul extends through the whole cosmos. It then distinguishes the natural faculties of attraction, retention, alteration, and expulsion from psychic powers, maintains that bodies arise from a thorough mixture of the four elements, and argues that questions about the substance and immortality of the soul need not be settled by the physician, since such knowledge is unnecessary for curing disease, preserving health, or the practical part of moral philosophy.
grc.galen.de_symptomatum_differentiis: Galen's De symptomatum differentiis (On the Differences of Symptoms) is a Greek medical treatise that takes up symptoms after a separate treatment of diseases and their causes, so that the account of all abnormal bodily conditions may be complete. It opens by defining the symptom and distinguishing it from disease, cause, and related terms such as pathos and pathema, defending these usages against less exact medical vocabulary. The body of the work divides symptoms into three genera: abnormal dispositions of the body itself, impairments of the body's activities, and phenomena attending excretions, retentions, and audible signs, with the impairments traced through the psychic faculties of sensation, movement, and the ruling faculty of imagination, reasoning, and memory, and through the natural faculties of attraction, retention, alteration, and evacuation. Examples range from blindness, pain, tremor, epilepsy, and madness to indigestion, atrophy, jaundice, dropsy, and disordered discharges, throughout which symptoms are shown to arise from diseases as their causes, often following one another in sequence like a row of tiles set in motion.
grc.galen.de_temperamentis: A Greek medical treatise by Galen on temperaments (kraseis), the mixtures of the elementary qualities, hot, cold, dry and wet, in bodies. It opens by showing that bodies are composed of these four qualities and that mixtures differ in proportion, then surveys earlier doctrines that recognize only four or five mixtures, arguing that the best-tempered (eukratos) constitution must be counted first and that there are in all nine kinds. Galen discusses how mixtures are diagnosed by touch and reason, the balance found in man and especially in the skin of the hand, and the variations of temperament with age, season and race; later books treat the qualities of foods and drugs, distinguishing what nourishes from what alters the body, and explaining why some substances act hot or cold only in potentiality. The work closes by summarizing how things potentially hot, cold, dry or wet are to be tested and judged.
grc.galen.de_theriaca_ad_pisonem: A Greek prose treatise on the theriac, the compound antidote against venomous bites and poisons, in which Galen addresses a friend named Piso. The opening praises Andromachus, a Cretan physician esteemed by the emperors of his time and credited with a treatise on the antidote, and recounts Galen's observation of Piso tending his own son's injury. Later sections celebrate the drug's reputation and power, explain how a batch of theriac may be tested for adulteration using cockerels and purgatives, and condemn vendors who trade on its name. The closing portion credits the emperor Marcus with habitual use of the remedy, praises the liberality with which the reigning emperors dispense medicines, and recounts cures such as those of Antipater and of Arrhia.
grc.galen.de_totius_morbi_temporibus: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen on the 'times' (kairoi) of the whole disease, distinguishing four phases analogous to the ages of living creatures: genesis or onset, ascent, acme, and decline. The discussion rehearses disputes among physicians over how these phases are to be defined and whether some diseases lack one or another of them, then applies the scheme to inflammation, fever, ulcers, ophthalmia, and discharges from the head, holding that the stage reached is recognized through signs of defective or completed digestion in the evacuations, urine, and sputum. Hippocratic sayings on the timing of remedies such as venesection, clysters, and purging are cited in the course of the argument about treatment at each phase.
grc.galen.de_tremore_palpitatione_convulsion: A short medical treatise by Galen on four abnormal bodily motions, tremor, palpitation, convulsion, and rigor, which opens by objecting to Praxagoras for classing all of them indiscriminately as affections of the arteries. The body of the work defines each condition and marks it off from its neighbours: tremor is traced to weakness of the power that moves and carries the body, palpitation to the gathering of thick vaporous pneuma in hollow parts such as muscles or skin, rigor to a sudden and painful whole-body chilling of the innate heat, and convulsion to over-tension of the nerves and muscles from excess moisture, dryness, or inflammation. Galen weighs the views of earlier physicians and philosophers, including Herophilus, Hippocrates, Plato, and Asclepiades, on the seat and cause of each affection, cites Hippocratic case material and reports observations of his own, and closes with an account of the different treatments the conditions require.
grc.galen.de_tumoribus_praeter_naturam: A short Greek medical treatise by Galen, De Tumoribus Praeter Naturam ('On Tumours Contrary to Nature'), sets out the varieties of abnormal swelling of the body. It opens by analysing the term onkos, distinguishing mere increase beyond the natural state, such as fatness, from swellings contrary to nature, which are marked by damage to function. The argument follows inflammation in detail, arguing that the swollen part is filled with blood rather than pneuma, and then passes to abscesses, fistulas, and cystic growths such as atheromata, steatomata, and melicerides. Later sections cover anthrax, gangrene, cancer, erysipelas, herpes, oedema, scirrhus, aneurysm, and the ulcerations bred by black bile, together with diseases of the skin, tumours and hernias of the groin, varices, and growths of the throat and eye, closing with the claim that no kind of abnormal swelling has been left undiscussed.
grc.galen.de_uteri_dissectione: Galen's De Uteri Dissectione is a Greek anatomical treatise on the womb, opening with a programme of topics to be treated: the uterus's position, size and shape, the structures by which it is suspended and nourished, the vessels that weave it, and what grows within it during pregnancy. The discussion proceeds through the organ's placement between the bladder and the rectum, its dimensions in women of different ages and conditions, and its shape, recording earlier descriptions of its horn-like processes by Herophilus, Diocles, Eudemus, Praxagoras and Philotimus. Later sections treat its attachments, ligaments and nourishing vessels, its two coats, the cervix with its changes over the reproductive cycle, the female testicles and seminal vessels, and finally the chorion, the amnion and allantois, the umbilical vessels and the cotyledons, ending with the promise of a separate account of the embryo's anatomy.
grc.galen.de_utilitate_respirationis: De Utilitate Respirationis (On the Use of Breathing) is a Greek medical-philosophical treatise by Galen on why living creatures breathe. It opens by asking what benefit breathing confers and cataloguing the answers of earlier doctors and philosophers, among them Asclepiades, Praxagoras, Philistion, Diocles, Hippocrates, and Erasistratus. The body of the work tests these doctrines against observable phenomena, breath-holding and suffocation, the movements of the heart and arteries, the extinction of flames cut off from air, and the breathing of people in baths, during exercise, and at different ages and seasons, refuting Erasistratus' account at length. Galen concludes that the chief use of respiration is the preservation and moderation of the body's innate heat, with the nourishment of the psychic pneuma through inspiration as a secondary benefit.
grc.galen.de_venarum_arteriarumque_dissectio: De Venarum Arteriarumque Dissectione is a Greek anatomical treatise by Galen which opens as a note to his friend Antisthenes, promising a synopsis of the veins and arteries as demonstrated on the body of a dissected monkey, the vascular system being likened to a tree with roots, trunk, and branches. The account first follows the portal vein from the gates of the liver to the stomach, intestines, spleen, and omentum, then the hollow vein (vena cava) upward through the diaphragm to the heart, neck, arms, and head and downward to the kidneys, genitals, and legs, and then the arteries arising from the left cavity of the heart, including the great artery (aorta) and the vessels to the lungs, brain, and spinal column. Throughout, Galen distinguishes superficial from deep vessels, records variations among individual specimens, notes which veins run without accompanying arteries, and repeatedly defers fuller detail to the anatomical dissections. The survey closes with the vessels of the unborn animal, the umbilical arteries and vein.
grc.galen.de_victu_attenuante: A short Greek dietary treatise by Galen on the so-called thinning regimen, the diet that attenuates thick and viscous humours in the body. It opens by arguing that most chronic illnesses, nephritis, arthritis, breathlessness, enlarged spleen, indurated liver, and epilepsy, can be relieved or even cured by such a diet alone, without drugs. The work then surveys foods in turn: pungent vegetables and wild greens, seeds and pulses, cereals and breads, fish, birds and quadrupeds, roots, tree fruits, and foods preserved in vinegar or brine, grading each by its capacity to thin or thicken the humours, and closing with an account of honey, named wines such as the Ariousian, Lesbian, Falernian, and Theraean, and milk. Throughout it insists that the physician must control both the occasion and the measure of use, and it commends oxymel, honey tempered with vinegar, as the drink most suited to the regimen.
grc.galen.institutio_logica: A Greek introduction to logic by the physician and philosopher Galen, of uncertain date, transmitted under the title Institutio Logica. The work opens with an account of how things are known through perception, understanding and demonstration, and defines propositions, axioms and syllogisms. It proceeds through categorical and hypothetical propositions, the figures and moods of the syllogism, proof, and relational arguments of the kind used in mathematics, drawing repeatedly on Stoic, Peripatetic and Aristotelian doctrine, with examples from Plato, Euclid and medicine. The treatise closes with criticism of Chrysippean and Peripatetic classifications of syllogisms and of forms it judges redundant.
grc.galen.quod_optimus_medicus_sit_quoque_ph: A short Greek treatise by Galen arguing that the best physician must also be a philosopher. It opens by comparing most physicians to athletes who long for Olympic victories yet undertake none of the training needed to win them, praising Hippocrates in words while neglecting the studies he prescribed. The discussion then examines why those who extol Hippocrates neither read nor understand his writings, ascribing their failures in logical method, knowledge of the body, classification of diseases and prognosis to the love of money and pleasure, and it sets out what a true physician requires: contempt for wealth, self-discipline, tireless effort and first-hand observation of cities, climates and waters. It concludes that the logical, physical and ethical parts of philosophy are all indispensable to medicine, so that whoever would practise the art worthily in Hippocrates' manner must philosophise rather than quarrel over names.
grc.gorgias_of_leontini.ἑλένης_ἐγκώμιον: The Encomium of Helen is a short prose defence of Helen of Troy by Gorgias of Leontini, undertaking to free her from the censure of the poets by showing that she does not deserve blame for the voyage to Troy. After an opening meditation on praise and blame as the fitting honours of city, body, soul, and speech, the speaker recounts Helen's parentage and beauty and then examines the four possible causes of her journey to Troy, the designs of gods and fortune, abduction by force, persuasion by speech, and love kindled through sight, acquitting her in each case. The treatment of persuasion presents logos as a great dynast and as a drug upon the soul, illustrated from poetry, incantation, the discourses of students of the heavens, debate, and painting, before the closing declaration that the speech is both Helen's encomium and its author's plaything.
grc.hermogenes.progymnasmata_dub: An ancient Greek rhetorical handbook on the progymnasmata, the preliminary exercises of the rhetorical school, attributed to Hermogenes and of uncertain date. It opens with the myth, arguing that fable is set first before the young because it shapes their souls toward what is better, and illustrating its handling with the fables of the nightingale, the fox, and Aesop. The treatise then works through the standard sequence of exercises, narrative, chreia, gnome, refutation and confirmation, common place, encomium, comparison, ethopoeia and prosopopoeia, ekphrasis, thesis, and introduction of a law, defining each form, classifying its kinds, and showing how it is to be elaborated. Definitions are throughout paired with worked specimens, such as monkeys debating the founding of a city, Isocrates' saying on the root and fruit of education, Medea's betrayal of the golden fleece, and an invective against a temple-robber.
grc.hermogenes.περὶ_τῶν_στάσεων: A Greek rhetorical treatise on the stases, or issues, of civic disputes, attributed to Hermogenes and of uncertain date. It opens by ranking the division and determination of civic questions into their so-called heads as the greatest part of rhetoric, closely allied to invention. The work then defines the civic question, distinguishes the persons and things open to examination, and sorts questions that can sustain a dispute from those that cannot, before setting out a method that moves through the logical stases of conjecture, definition, counterplea, transference, and antithesis, through the legal stases arising from written instruments, antinomy, ambiguity, and syllogism, and finally through the practical stases of the lawful, the just, the expedient, the possible, and the honorable. Hypothetical cases, a man found burying a murdered body, rival claimants to a priesthood, ambassadors accused of taking bribes, and examples drawn from Demosthenes illustrate each head, and the treatise closes with criticism of how division is handled in other writers' rhetorical arts.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.belopoeica: Attributed to Hero of Alexandria, the Belopoeica is a Greek technical treatise in prose on the design and construction of artillery engines. It opens with a philosophical preface presenting engine-making as a means of securing tranquillity in both peace and war, and objects that earlier writers recorded dimensions without explaining how the machines were actually built. The body of the work defines the art, distinguishes straight-spring arrow-shooters (euthytona) from palintone stone-throwers, and traces the engines' development from the hand bow through the belly-bow (gastraphetes) to torsion machines, describing component by component the frames, washers, sinew springs, bases, winches and catapult strings, together with assembly, tensioning and maintenance procedures and guidance on materials such as sinew and hair cord. It closes with rules of proportion for scaling engines from the diameter of the spring-hole, including a geometrical method for finding two mean proportionals between given lines.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_automatis: A Greek treatise in two books by the mechanician Hero of Alexandria on the construction of automata. It opens by distinguishing the two kinds of devices treated in the work: the self-moving shrines and altars called hypagenda, whose figures act out a myth, and the stationary display boards (stata), whose doors open of themselves to reveal successive painted scenes. The first book gives practical directions for level ground, light materials, cords, axles and sand-driven regulators, and details a moving shrine of Dionysus in which an altar kindles and dancing Bacchae perform; the second explains the stationary boards, worked out at length through a tableau of the myth of Nauplius, with ships under repair, a sailing expedition, dolphins, a beacon fire, the wreck of the fleet, the appearance of Athena and a thunderbolt striking Ajax. Hero also evaluates the earlier treatment of the same myth by Philon of Byzantium, and the treatise closes with a note on timing the motions by a steady flow of water.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.de_mensuris: The De Mensuris is a short Greek treatise on measurement attributed to Hero of Alexandria and of uncertain date. It opens by dividing measures into three kinds, the linear, the planar and the solid. The bulk of the work consists of worked numerical examples, computing the volume or capacity of pits, wells, squared and rounded stones, beams, columns, walls, ships, cisterns, theatres, hippodromes, circles, spheres, pyramids, cones and plots of land, all reckoned in feet, fingers and cubits. The closing sections form a glossary of weights, coins and dry and liquid measures, defining units such as the talent, mina, shekel, drachma, modius, xestes, artabe and kor and explaining their Hebrew, Greek and Roman names.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.mechanicorum_fragment: A short collection of Greek fragments from the Mechanics of Hero of Alexandria, a writer on mechanics, handed down as excerpts and paraphrases that repeatedly refer to Hero's own demonstrations and note that the compiler had encountered corrupted and incomplete copies of the books. The collection opens with the problem of moving a given weight by a given force by means of meshing toothed drums, illustrated by the gear train of the Baroulkos with stated ratios of drums, axles, and a hand-turned screw, together with the report of Archimedes' saying about moving the earth. It then gives a mechanical construction for finding two mean proportionals between two given straight lines, followed by an epitome of the five mechanical powers, wheel and axle, lever, polyspaston, wedge, and screw, with the construction and use of each. A further fragment demonstrates the centre of gravity of a triangle, and the collection ends with descriptions of lifting machines with one to four uprights and of sled-like 'turtles' for hauling heavy loads over the ground.
grc.hero_of_alexandria.metrica: The Metrica is a Greek treatise on geometric mensuration by the Alexandrian mathematician and engineer Hero of Alexandria; its date of composition is uncertain. It opens with a preface tracing geometry to the measuring and dividing of land, recalling the achievements of Eudoxus and Archimedes, and announcing a collection of the useful results recorded by earlier writers together with the author's own contributions. The work proceeds from plane figures, triangles, quadrilaterals, regular polygons up to the dodecagon, the circle and its segments, the ellipse and the parabola, including the general rule for a triangle's area from its three sides alone, demonstrated through the inscribed circle, to solid bodies, giving rules and demonstrations for prisms, cylinders, cones, pyramids and their frusta, the sphere and its segments, the five Platonic solids, and irregular objects measured by displacement of water. A concluding section treats the division of lands and figures, both plane and solid, in prescribed ratios.
grc.heronis_alexandrini.liber_geeponicus_sp: The Liber Geeponicus, a Greek collection attributed to Hero of Alexandria but of uncertain date, opens in question-and-answer form with definitions of plane and solid figures, covering the circle and its parts, then triangles, quadrilaterals, gnomons and trapezia, together with such terms as base, diagonal, perpendicular and parallel. The bulk of the work is a practical manual of mensuration: worked problems compute areas, perimeters, heights and volumes for squares, oblongs, triangles of every kind, circles, apses, stoas, pyramids, regular polygons, wells, cisterns, jars, ships, vaults and tiled roofs, with rules for converting among body-based measures such as the finger, palm, span, foot, cubit, pace and fathom. Further sections measure land in iugera and differentiate soils of differing quality, treat measures of lime, stone, timber, rafts, walls, discs, towers, hippodromes, spheres and ovens, give a general rule for passing between the side and diameter of any regular polygon, and provide reckonings for stored wheat and barley in modii and sextarii. Headings naming Hero, a section bearing Euclid's name, and grain reckonings authenticated in the prefecture of a Modestus mark the collection as a composite of surveying practice rather than a unified treatise.
grc.hesiod.works_and_days: Works and Days is a didactic poem of uncertain date by the Greek poet Hesiod, framed as admonition to his brother Perses after their dispute over the family inheritance. It opens with an invocation to the Pierian Muses and to Zeus, by whose will the low are raised and the proud abased, and who sends mankind both the bad and the good Strife. The poem recounts the myths of Prometheus and Pandora and the five races of men from gold to iron, and warns rulers against injustice in the fable of the hawk and the nightingale. Its greater part is practical instruction on ploughing, sowing, harvesting, seafaring, marriage and household economy, closing with a calendar of days favourable and unfavourable for the month's undertakings.
grc.hippocrates.coa_praesagia: The Coa Praesagia, a prognostic treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, sets out numbered maxims on the signs by which acute diseases declare a fatal, dangerous, or hopeful outcome. It opens with shivering fits that follow chills and the symptoms accompanying them, then proceeds in short books through fevers and their critical days, head, eye, ear, facial, and dental signs, the tongue, sputum, voice, and respiration, and the throat, chest, and abdomen. Later sections cover haemorrhages, spasms, quinsy, pleurisy and empyema, consumption, liver disease, dropsy, dysentery, bladder complaints, apoplexy, wounds of head and body, disorders grouped by age, and ailments of women, closing with vomitings, sweats, urine, and bowel discharges.
grc.hippocrates.de_alimento: De Alimento (On Nutriment) is a short Greek medical treatise of uncertain date attributed to Hippocrates. It opens by defining nutriment as one and yet many, single in kind but manifold in its wet and dry forms and in its power to grow and strengthen like and unlike parts according to the nature of each. The work proceeds as a string of compressed, often antithetical dicta surveying how nourishment reaches every tissue, humour and organ, the unity of beginning and end in all things, evacuations according to and contrary to nature, remedies and wounds and their discharges, the porosity of the body and its respiration, the rooting of veins in the liver and arteries in the heart, the nourishment of embryo and infant through blood and milk, numbered periods of formation and movement, the nutrition of bone, pus and marrow, and the merits of moist against dry food and of power against bulk. It closes with remarks on the assimilation of liquid and solid nutriment and on the dicta that power augments, nourishes and sprouts all things and that moisture is the vehicle of nutriment.
grc.hippocrates.de_arte: De Arte (On the Art) is a short Greek treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates, composed as a defence of medicine against those who deny that it is a genuine art. It opens by rebuking men who make a practice of reviling the arts and announces that the present argument will answer those who attack medicine in this way. The argument then establishes that every art has a subject-matter that can be seen and known, defines medicine as the removal of the sick person's sufferings and the blunting of disease's violence, and answers the objections that recoveries come by luck, that physicians fail and prescribe wrongly, and that they rightly refuse cases mastered by disease. It closes by showing that ailments hidden from sight may still be overcome through reasoning and through signs such as voice, breath, and discharges, so that medicine holds ample resources for its task of aid.
grc.hippocrates.de_genitura: A short treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, ascribed to Hippocrates, setting out a physiological account of human generation in eleven chapters. It opens with the doctrine that seed is separated off as the strongest part of all the body's moisture, tracing its passage through veins and the spinal marrow and explaining nocturnal emissions and the infertility of eunuchs. The argument then turns to women, describing female seed and pleasure in intercourse, the retention of seed in the womb, determination of the child's sex by the stronger and more abundant seed of either parent, and the basis of the child's resemblance to its parents. It closes with explanations of weak or maimed offspring, attributing small stature and deformity to the narrowness of the womb or to injury suffered by the mother.
grc.hippocrates.de_humoribus: A brief Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and preserved in the Hippocratic Corpus, of uncertain date, composed in an aphoristic, enumerative manner rather than continuous argument. It opens with the colours of the humours and with rules for drawing them off in whatever direction they tend. The remaining sections catalogue the signs by which evacuations and crises are recognised, in urine, sputum, stools, sweat and dreams, discuss the timing of purgation with respect to critical days and paroxysms, and note the deposits of humours in the joints and elsewhere. Later parts treat the effects of winds, waters and seasonal changes on the character of diseases, the constitutions suited to each season and age, and the work closes with remarks on sufferers from haemorrhoids and on the thick white urine of Antigenes as a sign of recovery.
grc.hippocrates.de_liquidorum_usu: A short Greek treatise on the therapeutic use of liquids, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus. It opens by distinguishing drinking water from sea water and by setting out the effects of hot and cold affusions on the body, together with the care needed to judge the proper degree of heat. Further sections treat sea water and vinegar for wounds, itching and skin conditions, the astringent and softening properties of sweet and dark wines, and the many affections, erysipelas, gouty and articular swellings, tetanus, head injuries, and disorders of the eyes, ears and womb, in which cooling or warming helps or harms. The treatise closes by summarising the modes of application: pouring of liquids, anointing with oils, and the application of leaves, linen or plasters, each judged by whether cold or heat proves beneficial or injurious.
grc.hippocrates.de_natura_hominis: A Greek medical treatise of uncertain date attributed to Hippocrates, De Natura Hominis opens by attacking those who reduce human nature to a single element and physicians who identify man with blood, bile or phlegm alone. The argument that follows maintains that the body contains four humours, blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, whose balanced mixture constitutes health, while their excess, deficiency or separation breeds disease, and it traces their seasonal predominance through the year. Later chapters set out treatment by opposites, attribute epidemic disease to the air men breathe rather than to individual diets, describe the courses of the principal veins and where phlebotomy should be performed, and interpret signs in sputum, urine and stools, before distinguishing four types of fever according to the bile from which each arises.
grc.hippocrates.de_salubri_diaeta: De Salubri Diaeta (On a Salubrious Diet) is a short Greek prose treatise of the Hippocratic corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens by prescribing a seasonal regimen for laypeople, with copious eating and undiluted wine in winter, softer and wetter fare in spring and summer, and gradual transitions between the regimes. Subsequent chapters adapt diet, exercise, bathing, and clothing to bodily type, age, and locality, give regimens for the fat who wish to grow thin and the thin who wish to grow fat, set out the seasonal use of emetics and clysters, and offer guidance for infants, women, and athletes in training, together with the ailments that follow exertion. The work closes with the maxim that a sensible man, reckoning health the most precious of human possessions, should know from his own judgment how to benefit himself in sickness.
grc.hippocrates.praeceptiones: A short treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, the Praeceptiones sets out counsel on the theory and conduct of medicine. It opens by distinguishing time from the critical moment (kairos) and arguing that healing must rest on experience joined with reason rather than on plausible argument alone. The remainder offers precepts on medical practice: learning from observation and even from laymen, calling in and cooperating with other physicians, moderation over fees with occasional free treatment of those in need, and avoidance of pretension, affected obscurity, and late-learned, merely verbal display. It closes with brief aphoristic remarks on signs, symptoms, and judgments in disease.
grc.hippocrates.prognosticon: The Prognosticon is a Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens by declaring that the best physician practises prognosis, foretelling present, past, and future symptoms so that patients will trust him, while conceding that not all the sick can be saved. The body of the work sets out the signs by which recovery and death in acute diseases may be judged: the appearance of the face, the patient's posture and position in bed, the hands, breathing, sweats, the hypochondrium, dropsies, sleep, bowel movements, urine, vomits, and sputum, together with chapters on the days of suppuration and on the critical days of fevers, and on pains of the head, ears, and throat. It closes by urging the physician to master all the signs and weigh them against one another, noting that they hold true in every land and season.
grc.hippocrates.vectiarius: A Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and transmitted in the Hippocratic Corpus, of uncertain date. It opens with an anatomical survey of the bones and their articulations, running from the fingers through the leg, spine, ribs, shoulder and arm. The bulk of the work treats dislocations throughout the body, of the ribs, jaw, shoulder, hip, knee and foot, setting out diagnostic signs, methods of reduction, bandaging, apparatus such as levers and stretching-benches, and rules of diet and prognosis, with repeated warnings of gangrene and death where reduction fails or is misapplied. It closes with general observations on which joints slip most readily, on the errors of practitioners, and on the deformities left by congenital or untreated dislocations.
grc.isidore_of_charax.mansiones_parthicae: A short Greek geographical itinerary attributed to Isidore of Charax, an otherwise obscure author of uncertain date, the Mansiones Parthicae (Stathmoi Parthikoi) records the stages of the overland route from the Euphrates to the eastern provinces of the Parthian empire. It opens with the crossing at Zeugma and the road down the river through Apameia, then proceeds station by station through Mesopotamia and Babylonia to Seleucia on the Tigris, onward across Media and the Caspian Gates to Hyrcania, Parthia, Aria, and Sakastane, naming villages, fortified posts, Greek foundations, rivers, temples, treasuries, and royal residences, with distances given in schoeni. The itinerary ends at Alexandropolis in Arachosia, the stated limit of Parthian rule, and the surviving corpus closes with a few fragments of Isidore, including an account of pearl-fishing in the Persian Gulf and notices of Persian kings quoted from Athenaeus and Lucian.
grc.isocrates.letters: A collection of nine short letters in classical Attic prose attributed to Isocrates. Most are cast as epistles of counsel addressed to rulers and dynasts: the opening letter urges a powerful addressee, at war with Carthage while Spartan supremacy recedes, to weigh the safety of the Greeks and the perils of rash boldness against the pursuit of martial glory. The letters reflect on the limits of advising in writing rather than in person, on the difference between flatterers and honest counsellors, and on the conditions under which a death in battle brings honour rather than disgrace.
grc.libanius.declamations: The Declamations of Libanius, the fourth-century AD rhetorician of Antioch, are a collection of imaginary courtroom speeches composed in the tradition of Greek rhetorical display on fictitious legal situations set largely in classical Athens. The collection opens with a speech in which a companion of Socrates pleads before the Athenian jurors against the philosopher's condemnation, urging them to judge by their oath rather than by hostility. The remaining declamations put words into the mouths of a varied cast of hypothetical litigants, among them a husband who asks the council for release from a life made intolerable by his wife's incessant chatter and a man who laments the theft of treasure he had buried in the ground for safekeeping. Each speech elaborates the arguments, commonplaces, and emotional appeals appropriate to its imagined case.
grc.libanius.orations: Greek orations of the fourth century CE by Libanius of Antioch, a sophist and teacher of rhetoric. The opening oration is autobiographical, narrating his upbringing in a prominent Antiochene family, his education, and his career, and composed to correct the opposing verdicts of those who counted his fortune the happiest and those who counted it the most wretched. Subsequent speeches carry the self-defence further, answering complaints from rivals, students, and the city over his teaching and conduct, and include a rebuttal of slanders against the emperor Julian. The collection closes with an oration in defence of the pantomime dancers, addressed to Aristides, which presents the art as a public schooling in the deeds of myth and history after the manner of the poets and tragedians.
grc.libanius.orations_1-11: Orations 1-11 gathers the opening speeches of Libanius, a Greek rhetorician of Antioch, printed here from Richard Foerster's Teubner edition. The first oration is his autobiography, in which he corrects those who call him either the most fortunate or the most wretched of men by narrating his family history at Antioch, his orphaned childhood, and his ardour for the study of rhetoric. Because Libanius frames his life through allusion to earlier Greek literature, citing Aristophanes' Acharnians outright and recalling his memorization of the ancient orators, the autobiography offers rich pickings for readers tracing intertextual parallels.
grc.lucian.abdicatus: A short forensic speech in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, belonging to his rhetorical declamations and delivered in the person of a young physician answering his father's lawsuit to disinherit him a second time. The speaker opens by protesting that, having been cast off once and then readmitted after curing his father's madness, he now faces renewed expulsion for refusing to treat his stepmother, a case he judges incurable. He argues that a father who has voluntarily taken back a son has exhausted his legal power of renunciation, that decisions once rendered in court must stand, and that medicine is a free art in which no one may be commanded against his judgment. In the course of the plea he reviews his own conduct toward both parents, refutes the charge of disobedience with a discussion of the differing constitutions of bodies, of women's susceptibility to illness, and of the many forms and causes of madness, and closes by urging that a son who has saved and restored his father merits gratitude rather than expulsion.
grc.lucian.adversus_indoctum_et_libros_multo: A short Greek satirical invective by Lucian, addressed to a wealthy but ignorant man who buys up fine old books in the hope that mere possession will pass for culture. It opens with the speaker charging the addressee that his conduct defeats his own purpose, since he can neither distinguish valuable ancient books from worm-eaten rubbish nor use what he owns. A string of analogies and anecdotes then drives the point home: a man with wooden feet buying costly clogs, Thersites in Achilles' armour, Euangelos of Tarentum flogged from the theatre at Delphi despite his gem-studded cithara, the Lesbian tale of Orpheus' lyre and its ill-fated purchaser Neanthus, Dionysius composing verses on Aeschylus' writing-tablet, Demetrius the Cynic tearing a copy of the Bacchae, and Pyrrhus' flatterer-induced delusion of resembling Alexander. The speech closes with the advice to sell the library to the educated and a final comparison of the owner to the dog in the manger, which neither eats the barley itself nor allows the horse to do so.
grc.lucian.anacharsis: A short dialogue by Lucian between the Scythian sage Anacharsis and Solon concerning the training of Athenian youths. It opens with Anacharsis asking what good lies in young men strangling and rolling one another in the mud, pommelling each other in the dust, and performing what to him looks like madness. Solon defends the exercises as preparation for a greater civic contest, describing Athenian education in letters, music, the poets, the laws, and the theatre, the discipline of the body in the palaestra, the prizes at Olympia, the Isthmus, Nemea, and Delphi, the practice of the Areopagus, and Spartan customs under Lycurgus, while Anacharsis objects from the Scythian point of view. The dialogue closes with the two withdrawing to the shade and arranging to continue the next day with an account of the Scythians' own training.
grc.lucian.bacchus: A brief Greek prose piece by Lucian, the Bacchus is framed as a Bacchic tale that turns into a defence of unexpected styles of discourse. It opens with the speaker announcing a myth of Dionysus' campaign against the Indians, who at first ridicule his army of maenads, satyrs, Pan and the drunken old Silenus, only to be routed when the forces meet in battle. The narrator then explains that most people behave toward unfamiliar kinds of speech, including his own, as the Indians did toward Dionysus, expecting from him only satyric and comic matter, and proceeds to a second Indian story of a grove with three springs, of the satyrs, of Pan and of Silenus, whose waters affect boys, men and old men each in their own way, giving the aged a sudden torrent of eloquence. The piece closes with a jest that any foolishness in the telling is due to drunkenness, while any wisdom must be set down to Silenus' favour.
grc.lucian.calumniae_non_temere_credundum: Calumniae Non Temere Credundum ('On Not Readily Believing Slander') is a short Greek essay by Lucian of Samosata against credulity toward calumny. It opens with ignorance pouring a mist over human affairs, blinding people so that they stumble at what lies at their feet yet dread what is far off, and supplying tragedy with its disasters. The discussion takes the painter Apelles as its model, slandered before Ptolemy and barely spared, he depicted Calumny in an allegory, and follows suit, defining slander as accusation made in the accused's absence and credited without rebuttal, then anatomizing the slanderer, the slandered, and the credulous listener, with anecdotes of Ptolemy's court, of Alexander after Hephaestion's death, and of wronged figures from Bellerophon and Hippolytus to Aristides and Socrates. The essay closes by prescribing that every charge be examined on its own merits, with reason posted as doorkeeper of the ears as in Homer's tale of the Sirens, and looks to a time when, lives being illuminated by truth, slander would find no ground to stand on and flee to the pit.
grc.lucian.cataplus: Lucian's Cataplus is a short comic dialogue set on the shore where the dead embark for the underworld. It opens with Charon complaining to Clotho that the ferry stands fully ready while Hermes lingers above among the living. When Hermes finally arrives with the newly dead, among them the tyrant Megapenthes, who begs for more life and pleads in vain to learn what will become of his possessions and household after him, and the cobbler Mikyllos, who goes gladly, the crossing gives the tyrant occasion to lament his abandoned riches while the poor cobbler laughs at the equality of death. Before Rhadamanthys the philosopher Kyniskos indicts the tyrant, whose lamp and couch testify against him, and he is condemned to be bound beside Tantalus and denied the water of Lethe, so that he must remember forever what he was.
grc.lucian.de_domo: A short Greek prose piece attributed to Lucian, transmitted under the title De Domo ('On a House'), is a rhetorical exercise defending the delivery of formal speeches in praise of a splendid building. The speaker holds that a cultivated viewer who meets a beautiful hall with silence is a philistine, and that settings of great beauty naturally call forth eloquence, adducing Alexander's longing to bathe in the Cydnus and Socrates' conversation by the Ilissus as instances. The argument proceeds to praise the proportions, light, and judicious use of gold in the house, contrasting them with the ostentatious but artless luxury of the Persian kings, and closes with the figure of the modest woman who wears gold only in measured ornament.
grc.lucian.de_luctu: Lucian's De Luctu (On Mourning) opens by proposing to observe what the common people say and do at funerals, lamenting death as unbearable while ignorant of whether it is an evil or a good. The work then rehearses in mocking detail the popular underworld drawn from Homer and the other poets, Pluto and Persephone, the rivers and the Acherusian lake, Cerberus, the judges Minos and Rhadamanthys, the delights of Elysium and the torments of the wicked, before turning to the funeral customs such beliefs sustain: the obol for the ferryman, the washing, anointing, and garlanding of the corpse, and the hired wailing of the women. A long imagined speech in which the dead son rebukes his grieving father, cataloguing the hunger, disease, and old age he has escaped, exposes the folly of the lament. The piece closes with a survey of national burial customs, the Greek burning, the Persian burying, the Scythian eating, the Egyptian mummifying the dead, and the funeral feast at which the mourners are at last coaxed into eating.
grc.lucian.de_mercede: De Mercede ('On Pay') is a short Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, addressed to the young Timocles; it opens with the speaker promising to set out, from the accounts of men who have endured the life, what those who attach themselves to rich households for a salary must suffer and do. The main body likens paid friendship to slavery and catalogues the dependent's humiliations, servile flattery at lavish dinners, the worst of the food and wine, enforced attendance on the patron's walks and journeys, and the pettiness of the fee itself. A comic inset recounts the Stoic TheSmopolis being made to mind his patroness's lapdog on a journey, and later passages touch on women who keep rhetoricians and philosophers as ornaments and on the envy and slander that meet the dismissed dependent. The work closes with a spoken allegory of Wealth's house, in which the suitor enters led by Hope, passes through Deceit, Servitude, Toil and Old Age, and leaves naked and despairing, under the maxim that the god is blameless and the responsibility lies with the chooser.
grc.lucian.de_sacrificiis: A brief satirical essay in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, the second-century CE rhetorician and satirist. It mocks the anthropomorphic piety of traditional cult, arguing that a religion in which gods need offerings, sulk when slighted, and sell their favours for hecatombs makes them less than noble. To make the point it rehearses mythic exempla drawn largely from Homer and the poets: Artemis's vengeance on Oeneus, Chryses' bargaining with Apollo, Apollo's servitude to Admetus and Laomedon, Zeus's overthrow of Cronus and his many amours, the births of Athena and Dionysus, the lameness of Hephaestus, and Prometheus chained on the Caucasus.
grc.lucian.de_saltatione: De Saltatione ('On Dancing') is a Greek dialogue by the satirist Lucian of Samosata in which Lycinus defends pantomime dance against attack. It opens with Crito rebuking Lycinus for his devotion to the theatre, dismissing the art as frivolous and effeminate. Lycinus replies with a sustained encomium: he traces dancing back to the primal movement of the cosmos, catalogues the enormous range of mythological subjects a dancer must command, Heracles, the Theban and Argive cycles, the Trojan war and nostoi, and stories from Thrace, Asia, Italy, and Egypt, and sets out the memory, quick intelligence, and bodily discipline required of the ideal performer. Anecdotes about celebrated and ridiculous dancers, observations on audiences and on the dance's moral and educational power, and a survey of its faults carry the argument to its close, where Crito is won over and asks to share Lycinus' seat at the theatre.
grc.lucian.de_syria_dea: A brief Greek prose treatise attributed to Lucian and written in Ionic Greek, describing the great sanctuary of the Syrian goddess in a city of Syria near the Euphrates, sacred there as the Assyrian Hera. It opens with the narrator, presenting himself as an Assyrian, promising an account of the temple, its gods and its rites drawn from his own observation and from the priests, with an early digression on the ancient shrines of Phoenicia, including the Adonis rites at Byblus. The body of the work recounts the sanctuary's foundation legends, Deucalion's flood, Semiramis, Derketo, and the story of Stratonice and Combabos, to whom the present temple is ascribed, then describes its precinct and colossal phalli, the gold-clad images of Hera and Zeus, the self-moving oracle of Apollo, the clergy, the self-castrated Galli, and the sacred lake with its venerated fish. It closes with the great festivals, processions to the sea, the spring rite of burning trees, practices of tattooing, self-laceration and castration, and the dedication of consecrated locks of hair.
grc.lucian.deorum_consilium: A short satirical dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, opening with Zeus convening an assembly of the gods to hear complaints about the crowd of mortals and foreigners lately admitted to divinity. Momus, urged to speak with frankness, derides the newcomers in turn, Dionysus and his rustic retinue, Asclepius and Heracles (whom Zeus silences), Egyptian animal cults, bogus oracles, and the philosophers' empty personifications such as Virtue and Fortune, while reproaching Zeus himself for setting the precedent through his own amours. The dialogue closes with the reading of a decree appointing seven judges to review each god's credentials, expel the unqualified to their ancestral tombs or Tartarus, and restrict each deity to its proper function.
grc.lucian.dialogi_marini: The Dialogi Marini is a collection of brief dramatic dialogues in Greek, set among the sea gods and sea-nymphs of myth, variously dated to the second century AD and attributed to Lucian of Samosata. The dialogue that opens the collection, between Galateia and Doris, mockingly appraises the Cyclops Polyphemos as a lover, and an exchange between Polyphemos and Poseidon recounts his blinding by Odysseus; later pieces carry the theme of divine passion through encounters of Poseidon, Proteus and Menelaos, a retelling of the judgement of Paris, the wooing of Amymone, Io, Helle, and the rescue of Ariadne and Andromeda. The dialogues conclude with a pair of winds describing Zeus's abduction of Europa, carried over the sea in the form of a bull to Crete.
grc.lucian.dialogi_mortuorum: The Dialogues of the Dead is a collection of short comic dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, set almost entirely among the shades in the underworld. It opens with Diogenes instructing Polydeuces to summon Menippus down to Hades, where satraps, tyrants, and rich men are now recognizable only by their weeping. The remaining scenes range widely through myth and history: Hermes and Charon process the new arrivals, Pluto and Minos hold court, Alexander, Hannibal, and Scipio dispute military precedence, Diogenes contrasts his enduring fame with Mausolus' vast monument, Helen survives only as a nameless skull, Protesilaus wins a single day's return to his bride, and Menippus tours the famous dead, from the Seven Sages and Empedocles to Socrates and Tiresias. Throughout, the dialogues press the leveling equality of death, mocking the wealthy, legacy-hunters, tyrants, philosophers, and prophets, with the Cynics Diogenes, Crates, and Antisthenes laughing at the reversals.
grc.lucian.dipsades: A short comic piece in Greek prose by Lucian, the Dipsades opens with a description of the scorched southern sands of Libya, waterless, fruitless, and uninhabited save by the tent-dwelling Garamantes, who venture out to hunt wild asses, ostriches, and elephants when rain briefly tames the heat. The piece then catalogues the land's monstrous serpents before settling on the dipsas, a snake whose bite kindles an insatiable and incurable thirst, an affliction illustrated by an epitaph in which a dead traveller is likened to Tantalus and the Danaids. It closes playfully as the speaker, confessing no firsthand knowledge of Libya, compares his own growing thirst for the audience's attention to the doomed thirst of the serpent's victim.
grc.lucian.electrum: A short satirical dialogue by Lucian, opening with the speaker's recollection of the myth that the poplars on the river Eridanus weep drops of amber as tears for Phaethon, whose transformed sisters they were, and that he once hoped to gather some himself. Sailing up the river in later life he finds neither poplars nor amber, and when he retells the tale of Phaethon the local boatmen, who have never heard the name, ridicule him for trusting the poets. His second expectation, that Apollo's musical swans haunt the banks there, meets the same dismissal, the boatmen knowing only a few unmusical birds in the marshes. The piece closes with the moral that believing poets, who inflate everything toward the grandiose, leads to such disappointments, and with the speaker's warning that his own plain and unpoetic discourse holds out no such treasures to his listener.
grc.lucian.eunuchus: A short comic dialogue in which Lycinus, arriving from the marketplace in high spirits, tells Pamphilus of a lawsuit he has just witnessed between rival philosophers. The occasion is the filling of a well-paid chair of philosophy maintained at the king's expense, vacant since the death of a Peripatetic, where the elderly disputant Diocles opposes the candidacy of Bagoas, a eunuch said to know his doctrines but derided as neither man nor woman and therefore unfit for philosophy, sacred rites and the company of the young. Bagoas replies that judgment should fall on the soul rather than the body, appealing to Aristotle's admiration for the eunuch tyrant Hermias of Atarneus and jesting that were philosophers judged by their beards, the goat would be preferred before all. After proposals to examine the candidate bodily, general laughter and an inconclusive verdict sending the case off to Italy, the dialogue closes with Diocles preparing an added charge of adultery and with Bagoas confident of victory.
grc.lucian.gallus: A short comic Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, opening with the poor cobbler Micyllus cursing the cock whose crowing has cut short a dream of boundless wealth. The bird answers in human speech and reveals itself as the soul of Pythagoras, which has passed through many lives, from Euphorbus at Troy through Aspasia, Crates, kings, horses and frogs to its present form. Using a feather of Hermes that opens any door unseen, it leads Micyllus by night into the houses of the rich, the tanner Simon, the moneylender Gniphon and the wealthy Eucrates, to display the anxieties, fears and hidden miseries that accompany their fortunes, while narrating its own past lives and the lavish banquet of Eucrates' dream. At daybreak Micyllus is persuaded that his humble poverty, untroubled by such cares, is happier than the wealth he coveted.
grc.lucian.harmonides: A brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, it opens with the aulete Harmonides asking his teacher Timotheus how he might win renown for his art, having already mastered the technical demands of the instrument. Timotheus answers that fame sought directly from the crowds is a slow business, and that the surest path is to win the approval of a few acknowledged experts, whose verdicts the multitude will simply follow; the narrative adds that Harmonides himself died uncrowned at his very first competition at the Dionysia, bursting a breath-vessel in his eagerness. A closing speaker extends the lesson beyond musicians to all who display themselves publicly for applause, and, applying it to his own pursuit of reputation in speech, resolves to submit his work to the judgment of one supremely learned and cultivated man whose approval outweighs the votes of all.
grc.lucian.hercules: A short prose piece by Lucian of Samosata, the Hercules takes its departure from a painting of the Celtic Heracles, whom the Gauls call Ogmius, portrayed as a shrunken old man in the god's lion-skin and carrying his club and bow. A Celtic bystander explains the image to the puzzled narrator: the god draws a crowd of men by golden and amber chains fastened from their ears to his pierced tongue, and the Celts take him for Heracles rather than Hermes because he is eloquence itself, whose winged arrows are words that wound the soul. The closing pages turn the figure back on the aging author, who defends his return to public rhetorical display after long retirement and, invoking Hippoclides' remark that such things are no concern of his, asks the gods for a fair wind as he relaunches his refurbished little boat upon the sea.
grc.lucian.hermotimus: A dialogue of Lucian in which Lycinus, meeting Hermotimus hurrying along the road to his Stoic teacher after twenty years of study, draws him into conversation about the path to philosophy. Lycinus questions the promised rewards of the sect and presses the problem of how anyone could tell which of the many rival schools follows the one true road to the happy city of the wise, arguing through a series of analogies, the wine jar, the seed merchant's sample, the drawing of lots at Olympia, that testing every doctrine would outrun a human lifetime. Anecdotes about Hermotimus's own teacher, his harshness over fees and his violent temper, undercut the school's pretensions, and the criterion that might judge between teachers and doctrines proves to lead only to an endless regress. Hermotimus ends by renouncing philosophy altogether and resolving to live the common life among the many.
grc.lucian.hippias: A short Greek encomium by Lucian, the Hippias praises an engineer of that name, a man of the speaker's own day. It opens by arguing that true wisdom shows itself in deeds rather than words alone, citing physicians, musicians, generals, and master builders such as Archimedes, Sostratus of Cnidus, Thales, and Epeius as earlier examples of men who left monuments of their craft. The greater part of the piece is a detailed praise of Hippias's bathhouse: his levelling of an awkwardly sloping site and laying of firm foundations, then the entrance, dressing rooms, and cold and hot plunge halls with their marbles, statuary, and abundant light, the orientation of each chamber to sun and winds, and the adjoining palaestra and cloakrooms. The speaker ends by enumerating the bath's virtues, usefulness, brightness, proportion, and security, and by repaying both work and craftsman with his speech.
grc.lucian.iudicium_vocalium: A short Greek mock-forensic oration by Lucian, cast as a courtroom trial in which the letter Sigma prosecutes the letter Tau before the seven vowels sitting as judges. The piece opens with Sigma's written charge, laid under the archon Aristarchus of Phalerum, alleging violence and robbery in Tau's usurpation of his place in spelling. Sigma's speech catalogs his grievances with comic examples of words disfigured by the substitution, reports the parallel complaints of Delta, Theta and Zeta, and broadens to Tau's supposed tyranny over human speech, including a fanciful derivation of crucifixion from the letter's shape. The oration ends with Sigma demanding that Tau be punished by suffering death in its own form.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_confuatus: A satirical Greek dialogue by Lucian in which Zeus is cross-examined by the Cynic Cyniscus, who begins by asking whether the Fates celebrated by Homer and Hesiod really fix everything that happens, leaving no room even for divine intervention. From that premise Cyniscus presses a chain of questions: whether Zeus himself hangs subject to the thread of the Moirai, what good sacrifice and prayer can do if nothing can be altered, why providence lets the wicked prosper while men like Phocion, Aristides and Socrates suffer, why thunderbolts strike the innocent more often than temple-robbers, and whether prophecy has any value when oracles are deliberately ambiguous. He argues that if all things are fated, Minos in the underworld ought to sentence Heimarmene instead of Sisyphus, and that the gods are at best mere instruments of the Fates, like the adze and auger of a carpenter. Zeus, alternately evasive, indignant and threatening, is at last reduced to silence and departs, denouncing his questioner as a bold sophist.
grc.lucian.iuppiter_tragoedus: A comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata that parodies tragedy, epic and political oratory together opens with Zeus pacing pale and distracted while Hera, Athena and Apollo press him for the cause of his distress. He explains that the Stoic Timocles and the Epicurean Damis have been disputing in Athens whether the gods exist and exercise providence, and an assembly of the gods is convoked: Hermes issues a proclamation stitched together from Homer, the divine statues take their seats strictly by material worth, with the Egyptian idols outshining the bronzes of Myron and Phidias, Momus speaks with his habitual bluntness, and Apollo delivers an oracle so opaque that Momus takes it as plain abuse. Word then arrives that Timocles and Damis are about to renew their debate, and the gods eavesdrop from a cloud. Timocles defends providence from the order of the heavens and the image of a well-governed ship, while Damis replies with the gods' loves and feuds in Homer, ambiguous oracles such as the one that ruined Croesus, the discordant worship of the nations, and the mismanagement of the world-ship, and carries the assembly until Timocles, out-argued and out of temper, drives his opponent away with insults.
grc.lucian.marcrobii: A short Greek essay by Lucian of Samosata, addressed to one Quintillus and framed as a birthday gift prompted by a dream that instructed the author to send him examples of long-lived men. After a prefatory word on races and peoples famed for extreme longevity, such as the Seres, the Chaldaeans and the Brahmans, whose long life is ascribed to climate, water or regimen, the work turns to individuals, arranged by occupation. Kings and generals come first, from Numa, Arganthonius and Hiero to Mithridates, the Artaxerxeses and Tigranes, followed by philosophers, historians, orators, poets, a grammarian and the lawgiver Lycurgus, each entry giving the age attained, often with the reporting authority and an anecdote such as Isocrates composing the Panegyricus at ninety-six or Sophocles defending his sanity by reading the Oedipus at Colonus. The essay ends with the author promising an account of long-lived Romans and Italians in a separate work.
grc.lucian.muscae_encomium: The Muscae Encomium is a short mock encomium in praise of the fly by Lucian of Samosata. It opens by setting the insect's size against that of gnat and bee and by describing its delicate, iridescent, membranous wings and its melodious flight. The speech then surveys the fly's anatomy and bloodsucking proboscis, its birth from a worm, its lifelong table companionship with humankind, its cunning evasions of the spider, and the boldness for which Homer repeatedly likens his heroes to it, before turning to the fly's revival from ashes as proof of the soul's immortality, its freeloading ease, its nomadic sleeping habits, the myths and poetesses named Myia, and the long-lived soldier-flies. It ends by cutting the discussion short with the proverb about making an elephant out of a fly.
grc.lucian.navigium: A comic dialogue of Lucian of Samosata, opening as Timolaos explains to Lykinos why he and his companions hurried to the Piraeus to view a colossal Egyptian grain ship newly arrived there. The conversation dwells on the vessel's gigantic dimensions, its Isiac figurehead and gilded ornaments, the multitude of its crew, and the captain's account of a storm-tossed voyage from Egypt in which a star of the Dioscuri saved the ship near the Chelidonian islands. When the strayed companion Adiamantos is overtaken on the road back to Athens, he confesses that he had been lost in a daydream of sudden wealth, and the friends successively frame extravagant mock wishes: a fleet of grain ships, a self-won kingdom extending to the Euphrates, and rings granting health, invisibility, strength, flight, eternal youth, and universal charm. Lykinos deflates each fantasy in turn by exposing the anxieties, dangers, and brevity that attend riches and power, and the party reaches the Dipylon gate laughing at the emptiness of such dreams.
grc.lucian.necyomantia: A satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which the Cynic Menippus, clad in grotesque costume of cap, lion-skin and lyre, arrives among his friends straight from the world below and tells of his journey to Hades. He recounts how the contradictions between the poets and the laws, together with the fruitless wrangling of the philosophers, left him unable to decide how to live, until he sought out a Babylonian Magus, Mithrobarzanes, who purified him with lengthy rites and led him down through the marshes of the Euphrates into the underworld. There he watches Minos try the dead, sees kings, satraps and moneylenders stripped of wealth and rank and punished beside their inferiors, and attends an assembly at which the dead vote that the rich should return to life as beasts of burden, while Tiresias whispers that the best life is the plain, unpretentious one of the ordinary man. His question answered, he escapes back to the surface through the sacred cave of Trophonius and finds himself suddenly at Lebadeia.
grc.lucian.philopseudes: The Philopseudes, a Greek satirical dialogue by Lucian, opens with Tychiades asking Philocles why some men love and tell falsehoods although nothing obliges them to. In reply he recounts a visit to the house of the ailing Eucrates, where Ion the Platonist, Deinomachus the Stoic, Cleodemus the Peripatetic, the physician Antigonus, and the Pythagorean holy man Arignotus trade marvels: a Babylonian exorcist heals a snakebite, a Hyperborean magician conjures the dead, Hecate, and Selene, a bronze statue of Pellichus walks and bathes by night, Eucrates describes an encounter with Hecate and a descent into Hades, Arignotus lays the ghost of a haunted house at Corinth, and the Egyptian priest Pancrates turns a doorbolt into a water-carrying servant. Tychiades punctuates each tale with skeptical mockery, and the talk drifts toward oracles and a prophetic ring of Apollo before he leaves the company in disgust. The frame closes with Philocles observing that Tychiades, bitten by Eucrates' falsehoods like a victim of rabid dogs, has passed the infection on to him, and that truth remains the surest antidote.
grc.lucian.pro_imaginibus: The Pro Imaginibus is a short Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as an apology for the extravagant praise of a woman's beauty in an earlier encomium, which had likened her to Hera and Aphrodite. It opens with the woman herself rebuking Lycinus for hyperbolic flattery, objecting that to compare a mortal with goddesses is an affront to divine honour. The greater part of the work takes the form of a mock trial in which Polystratus prosecutes and Lycinus defends himself, arguing that elevated comparison is the essence of true encomium rather than of flattery, and citing Homer's likening of his heroes and heroines to gods, Phidias' willingness to correct the Zeus of Olympia at the public's insistence, and Alexander's refusal to have Mount Athos carved into his image. The dialogue closes with Lycinus delivering his defence as if in the woman's presence, turning her very piety into grounds for still higher praise.
grc.lucian.prometheus: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, staged on the Caucasus.
