It opens with Hephaestus and Hermes surveying the cliffs for a suitable spot on which to nail the condemned Prometheus. Chained to the rock and awaiting the eagle, the Titan demands a hearing, and the piece unfolds as a mock forensic exchange in which Hermes prosecutes him for cheating Zeus over the sacrificial portions, for fashioning humankind, and for stealing fire, while Prometheus defends each exploit at length, portraying the god's wrath as petty ingratitude. The exchange closes with Prometheus hinting that the secret of Thetis may yet purchase his release and foretelling the coming of a Theban archer to save him.
grc.lucian.prometheus_es_in_verbis: A short Greek comic dialogue by Lucian, entitled Prometheus Es in Verbis, in which a speaker answers a critic who likens him to Prometheus for fashioning what seem to be living creations out of lowly clay. He weighs and largely rejects two flattering readings of the name, that his works are masterfully wrought and that they are original creations like Prometheus's moulding of mankind, illustrating the peril of mere novelty with the story of Ptolemy son of Lagus, whose exhibition in Egypt of a gold-harnessed Bactrian camel and a piebald man ended in ridicule. The greater part of the piece turns on his experiment of yoking Dialogue, a stately companion of philosophical walks, to Comedy, the Dionysiac mocker of philosophers who trips to anapaestic measures, a hybrid as monstrous as the hippocentaur unless the mixture is harmonious. He closes by resolving to stand by what he has once chosen, since to change one's mind is the work of Epimetheus, not of Prometheus.
grc.lucian.saturnalia: A short satirical dialogue in Greek by the second-century AD writer Lucian of Samosata, on the festival of the Saturnalia. It opens with the priest Cronosolon asking Cronos for riches, only to be told that wealth lies in Zeus's gift, while Cronos's seven-day kingship grants only licence: drinking, gaming, and the temporary equality of slaves and masters. The conversation passes into mythological banter about Cronos's devouring of his children, his abdication to Zeus, and the vanished golden age, before Cronos commissions the priest to draft a comic code of laws obliging the rich to share their wealth at the festival. The work closes with an exchange of letters, in which Cronos and Cronosolon, and then Cronos and the rich themselves, debate the claims of the poor, the hidden burdens of wealth, and the terms on which the well-to-do might justly keep their feast.
grc.lucian.soleocista: The Solecist (Σολοικιστής) is a short comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata. It opens with one speaker asking whether a man who professes to be expert at detecting solecisms can avoid committing them himself. The rest of the piece stages a running contest in which the interlocutor repeatedly catches this self-professed expert in solecisms that go unnoticed even as he censures the errors of others, and it inserts a long series of anecdotes about Socrates of Mopsus, whom the speaker had met in Egypt, gently mocking the barbarisms and false Atticisms of those around him. The dialogue closes with discussion of fine distinctions between easily confused words and forms, such as ὑπαλλάττειν and ἐναλλάττειν or κάθισον and καθέζεσθαι, and breaks off with the remaining lessons deferred to another occasion.
grc.lucian.symposium: A satirical Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata. It opens with Philo asking Lycinus to confirm the story that a dinner at Aristaenetus' house the previous day ended in brawling and bloodshed. The bulk of the work is Lycinus' narrative of the wedding banquet given for Aristaenetus' daughter and the moneylending philosopher Eucritus, where guests drawn from the rival philosophical schools, together with a grammarian and a rhetor, move from table talk and the reading of a slanderous letter to quarrels over seating and portions of food, then to a drunken melee of blows, broken skulls, an overturned lamp and injuries dealt in the darkness. The account closes with the wounded bridegroom led home in bandages, the company dispersing, and the narrator's conclusion that it is unsafe to feast with such wise men, seasoned with a tragic quotation on the gods' unexpected dispensations.
grc.lucian.zeuxis: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata on the tendency of audiences to admire novelty at the expense of genuine artistry. It opens with the narrator leaving after reading a discourse, showered with congratulations from hearers who praise only its originality. The bulk of the work consists of two illustrative stories: that of the painter Zeuxis and his picture of a female centaur suckling twin young, seen by the narrator in a copy at Athens, whose spectators admire the unheard-of subject rather than the craftsmanship; and that of Antiochus surnamed Soter, whose victory over the Gauls was won when the unexpected sight of sixteen elephants threw the enemy into confusion. In closing, the speaker treats his own situation as a third instance of the same phenomenon, complaining that the strangeness of his subject is applauded while the real merits of his writing pass unnoticed.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.excerpta: Short excerpts transmitted under the name of Nicomachus of Gerasa and dealing with Greek music theory, of uncertain date and compilatory character. The opening excerpt recounts the legend of the lyre's invention by Hermes and its transmission through Orpheus, Linus, Amphion, and Terpander; the remainder sets out arithmetical demonstrations of the ratios governing the tone, the fourth, and the fifth, explains why the outer strings bear the names hypate and nete and are assigned to the Moon and Saturn, and tabulates the note names of the greater perfect system across its five tetrachords. A closing passage maps the five tetrachords onto the celestial spheres and the tetraktys, appealing to Plato's Laws, where harmonics is placed last among the sciences.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἐγχειρίδιον_ἁρμονικ: The Ἐγχειρίδιον Ἁρμονικῆς (Manual of Harmonics) is a short Pythagorean treatise on music theory in twelve chapters by Nicomachus of Gerasa. It opens with a list of chapter headings and an apology for its brevity, the author explaining that he has drawn up the summary at a lady's request while travelling and promises her a fuller treatment later. The chapters cover the distinction between continuous and intervallic voice, the naming of notes from the seven planets, Pythagoras's discovery of the numerical ratios of the concords through the blacksmith experiment, the diatonic division of the octave, the harmonic doctrine of Plato's Timaeus, and the testimony of Philolaus. They close with the tuning of the octave by ratios, an account of the fifteen-note double-octave system, and definitions of the three genera of melody, diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic.
grc.nonnus_of_panopolis.dionysiaca: The Dionysiaca of Nonnus of Panopolis is a Greek epic in dactylic hexameters, of uncertain date, devoted to the life of the god Dionysus. It opens with an invocation of the Muse to sing of Semele killed by the thunderbolt and of the half-formed infant Dionysus whom Zeus carried in his own thigh until birth. The poem follows the god from his upbringing through his long campaign against the Indians, filled with battles, transformations, divine interventions, and love affairs, including his union with Ariadne. It closes with Dionysus's apotheosis and the establishment of his worship in rites and dances celebrated at Athens together with Iacchus.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_galatas: The Epistle to the Galatians is a letter of the Greek New Testament, composed in Koine prose during the Imperial period and addressed to the churches of Galatia under the name of the apostle Paul. It opens with a salutation in which Paul claims his commission directly from Jesus Christ and rebukes the Galatians for so quickly turning to a different gospel. The body defends his apostolic independence from the Jerusalem leaders through autobiographical narrative, including the confrontation with Cephas at Antioch, and argues at length that justification comes through faith in Christ rather than works of the law, drawing on the example of Abraham, the contrast between promise and law, and the allegory of Hagar and Sarah. It concludes with ethical exhortations to stand in freedom, walk in the Spirit, and bear one another's burdens, ending with a note in Paul's own hand and a final blessing.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_philippenses: The Epistle to the Philippians is a Greek letter of the New Testament composed in the names of Paul and Timothy to the Christian community at Philippi, opening with a salutation of grace and peace and a thanksgiving for the Philippians' partnership in the gospel from the first day onward. From the writer's account of his imprisonment and his tension between the desire to depart and be with Christ and the necessity of remaining for the community's sake, the letter proceeds to an exhortation to unity and humility grounded in a hymnic passage on Christ's self-emptying, death on a cross, and exaltation. Travel plans involving Timothy and the ailing Epaphroditus, warnings against opponents, and an autobiographical passage in which the writer counts his pedigree and attainments as loss for the knowledge of Christ occupy the middle chapters. The closing sections urge steadfastness, continual rejoicing, prayer free from anxiety, and reconciliation between Euodia and Syntyche, thank the Philippians for the material support they sent, and end with greetings from those with Paul, including the saints of Caesar's household, and a benediction of grace.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_ii: The second letter to the Thessalonians is a prose epistle of the New Testament, written in the names of Paul, Silvanus and Timothy and addressed to the church of the Thessalonians. It opens with thanksgiving for the recipients' growing faith and love amid persecutions, together with a vision of judgment repaid at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven. The body corrects a report that the day of the Lord has already come, setting out instead a prior rebellion and the revelation of the man of lawlessness, whom the Lord will destroy at his appearing, and it urges the believers to stand firm and hold fast to the traditions they were taught. The closing chapters request prayer for the spread of the gospel, command the members to work quietly and eat their own bread rather than live in idleness, prescribe withdrawal from the disobedient coupled with admonition as for a brother, and end with a prayer for peace, a greeting in Paul's own hand, and a benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_titum: The Epistle to Titus is a short Greek prose letter of the New Testament, presented as a message from Paul to his coworker Titus during the Roman imperial period. It opens with Paul's self-identification as a servant of God and apostle of Jesus Christ and a greeting to Titus as his genuine child in the shared faith. The body instructs Titus to appoint blameless elders in each Cretan town, to silence false teachers who upset whole households for shameful gain, and to counsel older men and women, younger women, younger men, and slaves on orderly conduct, grounding the exhortations in the grace of God that has appeared and in salvation by mercy rather than works. It closes with warnings against quarrels and genealogies, an order to shun the divisive person after repeated admonition, travel plans involving Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos, and final greetings.
grc.novum_testamentum.lucas: The Gospel of Luke, a Greek prose narrative preserved in the New Testament, recounts the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus in an Imperial-era biblical idiom. It opens with a preface addressed to Theophilus explaining the aim of an orderly account, followed by the annunciations and births of John the Baptist and Jesus under Herod and Augustus. The narrative then traces Jesus's baptism and temptation, his Galilean ministry of preaching, healing, and parables, including the good Samaritan and the prodigal son, the sending out of the disciples, and the long journey toward Jerusalem. The final chapters cover his entry into the city and teaching in the temple, the Last Supper, betrayal, trial before Pilate and Herod, crucifixion and burial, the women's discovery of the empty tomb, appearances on the road to Emmaus and to the assembled disciples, and the ascension from Bethany.
grc.novum_testamentum.petri_ii: The Second Epistle of Peter is a Greek New Testament letter attributed to the apostle Simon Peter and of uncertain date. It opens with 'Symeon Peter' greeting those who have received a faith like his own and exhorting them to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love. The letter then affirms the apostolic witness to Christ's transfiguration and the reliability of prophecy before turning to a sustained denunciation of false teachers, illustrated with scriptural examples of divine judgment such as the fallen angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Balaam. Its closing chapter answers scoffers who mock the promise of Christ's return, proclaims that the day of the Lord will come like a thief and the heavens be dissolved by fire, and ends with exhortations to holiness in expectation of new heavens and a new earth.
grc.orphica.fragmenta: A short collection of Greek fragments attributed to Orpheus and the Orphic poets, of uncertain date and authorship, preserved as quotations and testimonies in authors ranging from Plato and Aristotle to Athenagoras, Clement and Damascius. It opens with the report in Plato's Philebus of Orpheus' injunction to cease from the strain of song in the sixth generation. The material is chiefly theological: cosmogonic and theogonic verses on Ocean and Tethys, Night, the serpent Chronos, the cosmic egg and Phanes, together with statements about the soul's divine origin and the body as its prison, and notices of rites, initiations and purifications ascribed to Orphic books. To the quoted verses are added Orphic gold funerary tablets from Petelia, Eleutherna and Thurioi addressed to the dead at the spring of Memory, a papyrus paraphrase of an Orphic Demeter hymn, and allegorical explanations of Orphic doctrine.
grc.paradoxographus_florentinus.mirabilia_de: An anonymous Greek collection of marvels concerning waters, conventionally known as the Paradoxographus Florentinus from its Florentine manuscript and of uncertain date. It opens with a spring at Potniae near Thebes whose water drives horses that drink it mad, and continues as a terse catalogue of springs, lakes and rivers credited with strange or harmful properties, from waters that intoxicate, petrify or make drinkers hate wine, to lakes with floating islands, sunken cities visible beneath the surface, and combustible naphtha, located across Greece, Asia, Africa and Italy. Many entries close with the name of a source authority such as Isigonos, Ctesias, Aristotle or Theopompus, and several quote epigrams said to be inscribed at the springs themselves.
grc.phalaridis_epistulae.epistulae: A collection of Greek prose letters attributed to Phalaris, the tyrant of Acragas in Sicily, of uncertain date, composed in the tyrant's own voice and addressed to poets, philosophers, physicians, kinsmen, and Sicilian cities. The opening letter thanks the physician Polyclitus for curing an incurable disease and rebukes the citizens who accuse his benefactor of treachery. Across the collection Phalaris reports victories over Leontini and other towns, sends gifts, loans, and invitations to Acragas, consoles the family of Stesichorus on the poet's death, instructs his wife Erytheia and son Paulola, and answers charges of cruelty, above all the brazen bull devised by Perilaus, whom he professes to have executed in his own machine. The letters mix diplomacy and threats, reflections on tyranny, fortune, and death, and self-defence, presenting a ruler at once boastful and conciliatory.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_abrahamo: De Abrahamo, by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, is a Greek philosophical exposition and rewriting of the Genesis narrative of Abraham, belonging to a larger series of treatises on the Mosaic laws. It opens by introducing the five books of the law and the three pre-Abrahamic figures Enos, Enoch and Noah, who stand for hope, repentance and righteousness. The main course of the work follows Abraham from his migration out of Chaldaea and his recognition of the invisible God through his hospitality to the three visitors at Mamre, the destruction of Sodom, his rescue of Lot, the intended sacrifice of Isaac, and the death of Sarah, reading each episode on both a literal and an allegorical level as an account of the soul's progress toward God. It closes with praise of Abraham's faith, his standing as the first 'elder' of the race, and his fulfilment of the divine law without written instruction.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_aeternitate_mundi: A Greek philosophical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the eternity and incorruptibility of the cosmos. The work opens with an invocation of God as the source of the knowledge needed for an inquiry into the world's indestructibility. It then surveys earlier opinions on whether the world is generated and perishable or eternal, covering Democritus and Epicurus, the Stoic doctrine of conflagration and palingenesis, Aristotle, the reading of Plato's Timaeus, Hesiod, and the Mosaic account of Genesis. The remainder assembles proofs that no cause within or without can destroy the world, weighs the arguments of Critolaus, answers the Stoic case for ekpyrosis and rebirth, reports that Boethus of Sidon and Panaetius abandoned the conflagration doctrine, and closes by replying to objections drawn from mountain formation, the shrinking of the sea, the mutability of the elements and living kinds, and the alleged youth of the arts, with catastrophes of fire and flood invoked on both sides.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_agricultura: A Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus that reads Genesis 9:20–21, where Noah 'began to be a husbandman of the earth,' as an allegory of the cultivation of the soul. It opens by distinguishing, on the exactness of Mosaic naming, the husbandman Noah from the mere tiller of the ground, the figure of the wicked man who labours only for the body and its pleasures. The argument then proceeds through paired terms: shepherd against cattle-driver, with Jacob and Moses as shepherds of the soul's flock and God as shepherd of the cosmic whole through his firstborn Logos, and skilled horseman against unskilled rider, with the passions as horses, the serpent of Dan biting the horse's heel, and virtue as the only truly sacred contest. It closes on Noah's having only 'begun' the art, drawing lessons on beginnings without ends, on voluntary and involuntary transgression, and on the stages by which virtue is planted, advanced, and brought to completion.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_cherubim: De Cherubim ('On the Cherubim') is a Greek allegorical commentary on Genesis by Philo Judaeus. It opens by citing Genesis 3:24, in which cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way to the tree of life after Adam's expulsion from Paradise. Philo first distinguishes being cast out, which admits no return, from being sent forth, and reads Hagar's departures as the removal of encyclical education once Sarah, virtue, has borne fruit; the cherubim and the fiery sword are then expounded in turn as the two spheres of the heavens with the sun, and as symbols of God's two eldest powers, goodness and sovereignty, joined by the Logos, the fiery word between them. The closing part takes Cain, whose name means 'possession', as the mind born of its union with sense-perception and puffed up into claiming created things as its own, and concludes that God alone truly owns all things while humans are settlers and sojourners, God being the cause of what comes to be and the divine Logos only the instrument through which it was made.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_confusione_linguarum: De Confusione Linguarum is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus expounding the confusion of tongues in the Tower of Babel narrative of Genesis 11:1–9. It opens as the continuation of a preceding discussion, quoting the biblical passage in full and answering critics who deride the ancestral laws. The body of the work surveys and rejects rival accounts of the episode, including the myth of the Aloeidae who piled mountains to reach heaven and the fable that animals once spoke a single language, and then reads the story allegorically of the soul: the builders' one speech becomes the harmonious consensus of the wicked in wrongdoing, the tower a citadel of vice and impiety, and God's 'descent' a figurative expression for a God who fills all things, works through ministering powers, and is the cause of goods alone. The treatise closes with an analysis of confusion as the dissolution of the alliance of vices, distinguished from mere mixture, and with the scattering of the impious builders as God's dispersal of impiety from the world.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_congressu_eruditionis_g: A Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus on Genesis 16:1–6, the account of Abraham, Sarah and Hagar, which opens by citing the scriptural passage and identifying Sarah with virtue, barren in appearance yet endlessly fertile in good words and deeds. The greater part of the work develops the further equation of Hagar with the encyclical or preliminary studies, grammar, geometry, music, rhetoric and dialectic, through which the mind must pass before it can receive the true offspring of virtue. Later sections turn to numerical symbolism, dwelling on the pre-eminence of the number ten, the tithe, and related legislation concerning firstfruits, festivals and sacrifices, illustrated from the stories of Abraham, Melchisedek and the wilderness wanderings. The treatise closes by interpreting Hagar's affliction at Sarah's hands as the salutary hardship that divine discipline imposes on the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_decalogo: A Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish writer Philo Judaeus, De Decalogue expounds the Ten Commandments as the summary heads of the Mosaic law. It opens by asking why the laws were given in a deep wilderness rather than in cities, and dwells at length on the perfection of the number ten and on the theophany at Sinai, where the divine voice sounded from fire to a purified people. The main body discusses each commandment in turn, first the five duties concerning God, his name, the sabbath and parents, then the five prohibitions against adultery, murder, theft, false witness and desire, treating them as the heads of whole classes of particular laws. A closing section explains why the commandments were issued as bare injunctions without specified penalties, since God is the cause of goods alone.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_fuga_et_inventione: De Fuga et Inventione ('On Flight and Finding') is a Greek allegorical commentary by the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria on Genesis 16:6–12, the episode of Hagar's flight from Sarah and her encounter with the angel at the well. After citing the biblical lemmata, the treatise sets out three causes of flight, hatred, fear, and shame, and traces them through the scriptural careers of Jacob, who flees both Laban and Esau, and Hagar, before turning to the Mosaic law on involuntary homicide and the six cities of refuge, whose number, location, and connection with the Levites and the death of the high priest are expounded at length. The second half takes up the complementary themes of seeking and finding, illustrated chiefly by Joseph, by Isaac as the self-taught sage who finds wisdom without seeking, and by the several senses of 'well' or 'spring' in Scripture, and closes with a symbolic reading of the names and places in Hagar's story.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_gigantibus: A Greek prose treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, De Gigantibus offers an allegorical exposition of Genesis 6:1-4, the passage on the multiplication of mankind, the 'sons of God' who took the daughters of men, and the giants. It opens by asking why the human race proliferated after the birth of Noah and his sons, and then interprets the 'angels of God' as bodiless souls, some of which descend into bodies while others remain in the service of the creator. Philo argues that the divine spirit cannot dwell in flesh, that wisdom requires detachment from the body and its pleasures, and that the giants are not mythological beings but figures for men 'of the earth', 'of heaven', and 'of God', exemplified respectively by lovers of pleasure, students of the arts, and priestly prophets such as Abraham. The treatise ends by reading Nimrod, the first giant, as the soul's desertion from God, and Babylon, whose name is explained as 'migration', as the change of mind with which every defection begins.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_josepho: De Josepho is a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish-Hellenistic writer Philo Judaeus presenting the biblical Joseph as the exemplar of the political life. It opens with a programmatic announcement that, after lives of Moses exemplifying learning, natural wisdom, and ascetic practice, the author will now portray the statesman through Joseph, whose youthful dreams, his brothers' jealousy, and his sale to merchants bound for Egypt begin the narrative. The retelling runs through servitude in the house of the chief cook, the attempted seduction by his master's wife, imprisonment, the interpretation of the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer, baker, and then Pharaoh himself, Joseph's elevation to governor of Egypt, his stewardship of the seven years of plenty and famine, the brothers' journeys for grain, the planting of the silver cup in Benjamin's sack, the self-revelation and reconciliation, Jacob's migration to Egypt, and Joseph's death at a hundred and ten. Throughout, the story is interspersed with allegorical and moral commentary in which the crowd appears as a eunuch chief cook, the politician as a dream-interpreter of waking life, and human fortune as unstable as a dream.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_migratione_abrahami: De Migratione Abrahami ('On the Migration of Abraham') is a Greek allegorical treatise by Philo Judaeus on the divine command to Abraham to leave his land, his kindred, and his father's house (Genesis 12:1–3), which it quotes at the outset. Philo interprets the summons as the soul's threefold migration away from the body, from sense-perception, and from mere spoken utterance, so that the mind may advance toward the intelligible and toward God. Working verse by verse through the call of Abraham, the treatise takes up the gifts promised to the wise, a great nation, blessing, and a magnified name, the relation between inner thought and the speech that expresses it, the worth of literal observance alongside symbolic meanings, and the danger of the 'mixed multitude' of confused opinions that accompanies the exodus from the life of the senses. Later passages attack the Chaldean doctrine that the visible cosmos is divine and trace Abraham's progress out of Haran, figured as the cave of sense-experience, and on to Sychem.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_opificio_mundi: De Opificio Mundi is a Greek philosophical treatise by the Jewish author Philo Judaeus on the creation of the world as narrated in the opening chapters of Genesis. It opens by contrasting Moses with other lawgivers, who either set down bare laws or veiled the truth in myth, whereas Moses began his legislation with the noblest of all subjects, an account of the world's generation in which law and cosmos accord. The argument follows the six days of creation: the intelligible world contemplated in the divine logos before the visible one, the making of heaven, the elements, plants, animals, and man as the image of God, with extended discussions of the properties of the numbers six, four, and seven and the sanctity of the seventh day. It closes with the first man, paradise, the serpent as a symbol of pleasure, and five doctrines drawn from the cosmogony, namely that God exists, that he is one, that the world is generated, that it is single, and that God exercises providence over it.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_plantatione: The De Plantatione, written in Greek by the Jewish exegete Philo Judaeus, forms part of a sequence of allegorical commentaries on Genesis and opens by turning from agriculture in general to viticulture in the person of Noah, the first to plant a vineyard. God is portrayed as the supreme planter, the cosmos as a plant rooted in the divine Logos, and the rational soul as a garden whose senses, intellectual faculties and virtues are divinely cultivated trees. Later allegory reads Eden and its trees as symbols of the soul's virtues, Abraham's grove beside the well of the oath as an emblem of God as beginning and end, and the law concerning the fruit of the fourth and fifth years as an occasion for symbolic readings of the numbers four and five. The treatise concludes with a two-sided philosophical debate, supported by etymology, on whether the wise man will fall into drunkenness, taking its departure from Noah's wine-drinking.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_praemiis_et_poenis_et_d: On Rewards and Punishments and on Curses, a Greek treatise by Philo Judaeus, opens by dividing the oracles delivered through the prophet Moses into three kinds, cosmogony, history, and legislation, and announces as its subject the prizes set before the good and the penalties laid upon the wicked. Its first part interprets patriarchal figures as victors in sacred contests, assigning hope, repentance, and justice to Noah's line and faith, joy, and the vision of God to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, while Moses alone receives four prizes, kingship, lawgiving, prophecy, and the high priesthood, and the twelve tribes draw their privileges from the blameless house of the founders. The treatise then sets out the goods promised to the obedient, victory over enemies human and animal, material plenty, fertility, and bodily soundness, together with the rest that sabbaths and sabbatical years afford, against the curses that overtake transgressors, from failed harvests, drought, and locusts to enslavement, sickness, panic in battle, and the desolation of a land deprived of its fallow rest. It ends with the assurance that repentance can avert the curse, and that scattered exiles who return to the ancestral way of life will be forgiven and brought back to their homeland in sudden and unexpected freedom.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_sacrificiis_abelis_et_c: De Sacrificiis Abelis et Caini is a Greek allegorical commentary by Philo Judaeus on the offerings of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4. It opens with the verse 'And she added to bear his brother Abel' and a meditation on how the soul gains the God-loving Abel and sheds the self-loving Cain. From there the work allegorizes the two brothers as warring dispositions within one soul, illustrated from Rebekah's pregnancy and from an extended personified scene in which Pleasure, attended by her retinue of vices, and Virtue, accompanied by the virtues, each solicit the mind with rival promises. Later sections examine Cain's faults in offering sacrifice only 'after days' and not from the 'firstfruits,' reading the Mosaic laws on the firstborn, unleavened loaves, the fat portions, the Levites as ransom, and the cities of refuge as rules for consecrating to God what is first and best in the soul.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_somniis_lib_iii: De Somniis Book III is a Greek prose treatise by Philo Judaeus offering a philosophical and allegorical interpretation of divinely sent dreams recorded in Genesis. It opens by distinguishing two classes of God-sent dreams and takes as its subject the second kind, in which the human mind, set in motion by the mind of the whole, appears to be god-possessed and to foresee the future. Its principal example is Jacob's dream of the ladder reaching from earth to heaven (Genesis 28:12–15), expounded through symbolic readings of details such as the well called 'of the oath' as an image of knowledge, together with discussions of the four elements of the cosmos and the boundless nature of learning.
grc.philo_judaeus.quis_rerum_divinarum_heres: A Greek philosophical commentary by Philo Judaeus, the Alexandrian Jewish writer, presenting an allegorical exposition of Genesis 15, in which Abraham's question about his inheritance becomes an inquiry into who is worthy to become heir of divine things. Opening with Abraham's petition to God, the treatise moves through discussions of the wise man's boldness before God, the meaning of names such as Masek, Damascus and Eliezer, the division of the soul, God's cutting of the sacrificial animals into equal and opposing halves, the seven-branched lampstand as a symbol of the heavens, the four kinds of ecstasy and the prophetic state, and the covenant promise of the land stretching from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, read throughout as an account of the soul's migration from the senses toward the intelligible realm.
grc.philo_judaeus.quod_deterius_potiori_insi: Quod deterius potiori insidiari soleat ('That the worse person assails the better under a pretext') is a Greek allegorical commentary on Genesis 4:8 by Philo Judaeus, opening with Cain's luring of Abel into the plain. Philo takes the plain as a symbol of rivalry and dispute, and reads the episode together with related passages, such as Joseph sent to his brothers and Isaac meditating in the field, as a contest between self-love, figured in Cain, and the love of virtue, figured in Abel. The argument runs that the wicked man who attacks the better destroys himself, since in killing Abel Cain kills the finest part of his own soul, while the virtues themselves remain imperishable. Later sections expound the voice of Abel's blood, the meaning of blood and of the soul's substance, the curse on Cain and the tilling of the ground, and the sevenfold vengeance as an allegory of the seven parts of the irrational soul, closing with the mark set upon Cain as the sign of a folly that escapes death but knows every other calamity.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.de_gymnastica: A Greek treatise on athletics by Philostratus the Athenian, of uncertain date. It opens by ranking gymnastics among the branches of wisdom rather than mere banausic craft, and undertakes to set down memoranda for those who train athletes. The body of the work gives the origins and aetiologies of the Greek contests, foot races, the hoplite race, pentathlon, boxing, wrestling, and pankration, interspersed with stories of athletes from Peleus and Milo to Glaukos and Arrhichion, then turns to the trainer's art: judging an athlete's inborn nature from his parents and physique, classifying bodily types and temperaments, and managing training cycles, diet, oiling, dust, sun, and apparatus. It closes with a picture of the robust training of the ancient athletes and a denunciation of the luxury, corrupt diet, and bought victories by which, in the author's account, the discipline of his own day had declined.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.epistulae_et_d: Short Greek love letters and two prose declamations by Philostratus the Athenian, a Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period. The collection opens with letters that send roses to a beloved and dwell on the flower as an image of spring, desire, and beauty quickly withering. The many letters that follow, addressed for the most part to unnamed boys and women but also to named friends, to Epictetus, and to the empress Julia Augusta, range from praise of the poor lover, of love for a foreigner, of blushes, and of long hair lamenting its cropping to more public letters on the study of erotic poetry and on the proper character of epistolary style. The work ends with two dialexeis, in the first of which the author, a Lemnian, professes his devotion to his native Lemnos and to Imbros, and in the second of which he argues that law and nature are kindred rather than opposed.
grc.philostratus_the_athenian.vita_apollonii: The Vita Apollonii is a Greek prose biography in eight books by Philostratus the Athenian of the sage Apollonius of Tyana, compiled, as the narrator explains, from the travel notes of Damis of Nineveh, the subject's will, and other written accounts. The opening defends the undertaking by surveying earlier figures in the Pythagorean and divine-man tradition and by denying that Apollonius was a magician. The narrative then follows Apollonius from his birth at Tyana, marked by an omen of the Egyptian god Proteus, through his ascetic Pythagorean discipline, his journeys to Babylon and India, and his travels, teaching, and interventions across Greece, Egypt, and Ionia, including his encounter with Vespasian at Alexandria and his trial and defense before Domitian in Rome. The closing books recount his miraculous escape from imprisonment, his public vindication at Olympia, his counsel to Nerva, and rival traditions about his death and possible immortality at Ephesus, Lindus, and Crete.
grc.philostratus_the_lemnian.imagines: The Imagines (Eikones) attributed to Philostratus the Lemnian is a Greek prose collection of ekphraseis, that is, rhetorical descriptions of individual paintings. A prologue sets the scene at a gallery in a seaside suburb of Naples, where the speaker, a guest of Aristodemus of Caria, expounds the pictures to his host's young son and a circle of studious youths. The descriptions take mythological and Homeric subjects, beginning with the contest of fire and water at the Scamander from Iliad 21 and continuing with figures such as the personified Comus, and discuss in detail how each painting renders its story, its figures, and its effects of colour and light.
grc.phlegon.de_mirabilibus: A short Greek prose work, the De Mirabilibus ('On Marvels') attributed to Phlegon, preserved as a single narrative episode. It recounts the story of Philinnion, a young woman who returned from the dead to visit Machates, a guest lodging in her family's house, told as a report addressed to a king. The account follows the alarm of her parents Charito and Demostratus, Machates' production of the ring and breastband she had left with him, the opening of her tomb, and the chthonic purifications ordered after her final disappearance. It closes with the narrator's offer to send further witnesses and particulars to the king.
grc.plato.alcibiades_2: A short Socratic dialogue in which Socrates, meeting Alcibiades on his way to the temple to pray, warns him that people often ask the gods for evils in the belief that they are goods, as in the case of Oedipus. The discussion goes on to classify forms of folly, to argue that every skill, from generalship and rhetoric to the manual crafts, is useless or harmful apart from knowledge of what is best and when to employ it, and to depict a city governed by such expertise without that knowledge as full of disorder. Socrates praises the Spartan custom of praying only for good things, recounts how the Athenians once consulted the oracle of Ammon about their failures against Sparta, and cites Homer and Euripides on the gods' refusal of offerings from the wicked. The dialogue closes with Alcibiades agreeing to postpone his sacrifice until the mist is removed from his soul and he learns how he ought to conduct himself toward gods and men.
grc.plato.apologia: Plato's Apologia is an Ancient Greek prose work presenting the defence spoken by Socrates before an Athenian jury on charges of impiety towards the city's gods and of corrupting the young. It opens with Socrates confronting the slanders of both early and recent accusers and asking the jurors to bear with his plain, unpolished manner of speech as a seventy-year-old appearing in court for the first time. The speech then cross-examines Meletus on the indictment, recounts the Delphic oracle's answer that no one was wiser and the lifelong mission of examining politicians, poets, and craftsmen that followed from it, and defends his divine sign, his poverty, and his conduct under both the democracy and the oligarchy of the Thirty. After the verdict it renders his counter-proposal of maintenance in the Prytaneum, his refusal of exile or silence, a warning to his condemners, reflections on death addressed to those who voted for acquittal, and a closing request that his sons be held to the same scrutiny of virtue.
grc.plato.charmides: A dialogue in ancient Greek by Plato, cast as a conversation between Socrates, Critias, and the young Charmides. The scene is set in the palaestra of Taureas at Athens immediately after Socrates' return from the fighting at Potidaea, where Critias presents his nephew Charmides, famed for both beauty and philosophical promise, under the pretext of a headache remedy. The ensuing discussion pursues the question of what sophrosyne, temperance or sound-mindedness, is, examining a succession of candidate definitions, including modesty, quietness, doing one's own things, self-knowledge, and knowledge of knowledge itself.
grc.plato.euthyphro: Euthyphro is a short Platonic dialogue in which Socrates questions Euthyphro, a man who claims exact knowledge of divine matters, about the nature of piety. The scene is set at the stoa of the Athenian king-archon, where Socrates reports the indictment for impiety brought against him by Meletus and learns that Euthyphro has come to prosecute his own father for murder. Socrates then asks for a definition of the pious, and each of Euthyphro's successive answers, piety as prosecuting wrongdoers, as what the gods love, as the part of justice concerned with the service of the gods, and as a knowledge of sacrifice and prayer, is tested and found wanting. The argument repeatedly circles back on itself without reaching a settled definition, and the dialogue ends aporetically as Euthyphro hurries away.
grc.plato.hipparchus: Hipparchus, a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and printed in Burnet's Oxford text, opens with Socrates and an unnamed friend attempting to define the lover of gain (philokerdes) and to settle whether gain itself is good. A string of elenctic exchanges, built on analogies with the farmer, horseman, helmsman, and other experts who know the worth of their equipment, dismantles the friend's successive accounts, until the two concede that everyone loves gain and that the reproached philokerdes is the one who profits from things from which the good do not dare to profit. A later digression praises Hipparchus, son of Pisistratus, as a benefactor who brought the poems of Homer to Athens, giving the dialogue its title. Its aporetic handling of value, profit, and the appetite for more affords close parallels with the definitional dialogues of the Platonic corpus and with later Greek discussions of pleonexia and acquisition.
grc.plato.hippias_maior: The Hippias Major is a Socratic dialogue of Plato in which Socrates questions Hippias of Elis, a travelling sophist celebrated for his eloquence, memory and earnings. It opens with Hippias's boasts about his lucrative embassies and public displays, until Socrates, prompted by a challenger who had confounded him, asks what the beautiful itself is. Proposed answers, a beautiful maiden, gold, the fitting or appropriate, the useful and beneficial, and pleasure received through sight and hearing, are each examined and refuted, and Socrates's own attempts fare no better. The discussion ends without a definition, in aporia, on the proverb chalepa ta kala, 'beautiful things are difficult.'
grc.plato.ion: Plato's Ion is a short Socratic dialogue in which Socrates questions Ion of Ephesus, a prize-winning rhapsode who recites and interprets Homer. It opens with Socrates' greeting and inquiry into Ion's visit to the festival of Asclepius at Epidaurus and his success in the rhapsodic contest held there. Socrates then presses whether Ion's command of Homer alone amounts to a craft, arguing by analogies with painting, sculpture, and music that rhapsody, as Ion practises it, is not a technē but a divine inspiration, conveyed like the power of a lodestone from the Muse through the poet and the rhapsode to the audience. After testing whether the rhapsode knows the several arts Homer describes, chariotry, medicine, fishing, divination, and whether rhapsody and generalship are the same, Socrates leaves Ion to choose between being deemed unjust or divine.
grc.plato.lovers: The Lovers (Erastai), a short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato though of disputed authenticity and uncertain date, opens with Socrates entering the school of the grammarian Dionysius, where two well-born youths and their admirers are quarrelling about Anaxagoras and Oenopides. Asked whether philosophy is a fine thing, the disputants define it as polymathia, the pursuit of learning in many arts and crafts. Socrates cross-examines the definition through the analogy of the pentathlete, who ranks second in every contest, arguing that a dabbler in the arts would be useless while genuine craftsmen are to hand, and drives the argument towards the unity of justice, temperance, statesmanship, kingship and household management as a single art of judging rightly. The dialogue closes abruptly, with one interlocutor silenced by shame and the other still objecting that matters stand otherwise.
grc.plato.philebus: Plato's Philebus is a Socratic dialogue on whether pleasure or intelligence constitutes the good for human life. It opens with Socrates restating the dispute between Philebus, who holds that enjoyment is the good for all living creatures, and the advocates of thought, knowledge, and true reasoning. The discussion then moves through questions of method and the four classes of being to a detailed classification of pleasures, including mixed and false varieties, an account of the kinds of knowledge, and the construction of a blended life in which both pleasure and intelligence participate. The argument concludes that the good is to be sought in measure, proportion, and truth, with mind placed closest to it and pleasure ranked far below, and the closing exchange leaves a few remaining points of the summary to be supplied on a later occasion.
grc.plato.symposium: Plato's Symposium, a dialogue in ancient Greek, opens with Apollodorus agreeing to describe for his companions a dinner party held years earlier at the tragedian Agathon's house after a dramatic victory, as he had it from Aristodemus, who was present. The guests agree to moderate their drinking and instead each deliver a speech in praise of Eros: Phaedrus, Pausanias, the physician Eryximachus, and Aristophanes, whose myth of primordial split beings seeking their lost halves precedes Agathon's celebration of Love's youth and beauty, and finally Socrates, who first questions Agathon and then reports the teaching of the priestess Diotima of Mantinea on Love as a daimon between mortal and divine and on the soul's ascent toward Beauty itself. The evening is interrupted by the drunken Alcibiades, who substitutes an encomium of Socrates himself, likening him outwardly to satyrs and Silenus figures and recounting his own failed attempts to seduce him. As the party breaks up toward dawn, Socrates is left arguing that the same man could write both comedy and tragedy before proceeding, as on other days, to the Lyceum.
grc.plato.theaetetus: Plato's Theaetetus is a dialogue devoted to the question of what knowledge (epistēmē) is. It opens with a short frame in which Eucleides of Megara tells Terpsion that Theaetetus, wounded in the fighting at Corinth and stricken with dysentery, is being carried home to die, and that he once wrote down an account of Socrates' conversation with the youth. A slave then reads that record, in which Socrates questions the young Theaetetus before the geometer Theodorus: Theaetetus proposes in turn that knowledge is perception, true judgement, and true judgement accompanied by an account, and Socrates tests each definition through discussions of Protagoras' measure doctrine and Heraclitean flux, the philosophical life contrasted with that of the courts, Socratic midwifery, memory as a wax tablet, and knowledge as an aviary of captured birds. The enquiry ends aporetically, with no definition accepted, and Socrates departs to answer the indictment of Meletus, arranging to meet Theodorus again the next morning.
grc.plutarch.ad_principem_ineruditum: A brief moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to an uneducated ruler and known by its Latin title Ad Principem Ineruditum. It opens with the story of the Cyrenaeans who begged Plato to write laws for them and were refused, on the ground that legislating is hard for men so fortunate. From there the essay argues that a ruler must take philosophy as an attendant counsellor and guardian, first ordering his own soul before governing others, since the true king obeys the law, the living reason enthroned within him, and imitates the god who orders all things rather than brandishing sceptre and thunderbolt. Plutarch supports the argument with a broad range of exempla, Theopompus moderating the Spartan kingship, Alexander and Dionysius, Epaminondas keeping watch while Thebes feasted, Cato's death at Utica, the fearful tyrants Clearchus and Aristodemus, and closes with reflections on how power exposes untrained souls and how in rulers punishment, driven by anger, outruns accusation and proof.
grc.plutarch.adversus_colotem: A polemical treatise by Plutarch, addressed to one Saturninus, rebutting the Epicurean Colotes' book, which had argued that on the doctrines of the other philosophers it is not even possible to live. It opens with the arrival of Colotes' treatise, addressed to King Ptolemy, and a reading among friends at which the Platonist Aristodemus of Aegium and others urge a reply, before Plutarch takes up the accusations one by one. The greater part of the work defends Democritus, Empedocles, Parmenides, Plato, Socrates, and Stilpon against Colotes' charges, then turns to his treatment of the Cyrenaics and of Arcesilaus and the suspension of judgement, holding that the Epicurean position undermines itself. The closing section contrasts Epicurean withdrawal from public affairs with the laws, cities, and political service owed by philosophers, cataloguing the civic deeds of those Colotes had attacked.
grc.plutarch.agesilaus: Plutarch's Life of Agesilaus, the Spartan king, opens with an account of the ruler's lineage, his upbringing in the agoge despite a lameness he bore cheerfully, and his contested accession to the throne over Leotychides. The narrative follows his campaigns in Asia Minor against Persian forces, his estrangement from Lysander, and his command at the Battle of Coronea, before tracing the rise of Thebes under Epaminondas, the Spartan defeat at Leuctra, and the Theban invasion of Laconia. The work concludes with Agesilaus's mercenary expedition to Egypt in the service first of Tachos and then Nectanabis, and his death at the age of eighty-four while returning home.
grc.plutarch.agis: Plutarch's Life of Agis gives a biographical account of the Spartan king Agis, son of Eudamidas, who sought to restore the Lycurgan constitution in a Sparta corrupted by the influx of wealth. It opens with an essayistic reflection on love of glory and its dangers, illustrated from the careers of the Gracchi, before introducing Agis and Cleomenes as a Lacedaemonian pair of demagogue kings comparable to those Roman reformers. The narrative then follows Agis's proposals for the cancellation of debts and the redistribution of land, the resistance of King Leonidas and the wealthy, the treachery and greed of Agesilaus, the burning of the debt records, Agis's campaign in support of the Achaeans against the Aetolians, his arrest and summary trial before the ephors, and his execution by strangling together with his mother and grandmother. The life ends with observations on Agis as the first Spartan king put to death by the ephors and on the gentleness that, in the author's judgment, contributed to his undoing.
grc.plutarch.alcibiades: Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades, one of his Greek Lives, is a biographical account of the Athenian statesman and general, opening with his lineage from Eurysaces and the Alcmaeonids, his upbringing under the guardianship of Pericles, and his boyhood attachment to Socrates. The narrative then follows his entry into politics, his rivalry with Nicias and Phaeax and the ostracism of Hyperbolus, the Argive alliance that unsettled Spartan power in the Peloponnese, and his advocacy of the great Sicilian expedition. Accusations connected with the mutilation of the Herms and the profanation of the Mysteries bring condemnation and exile, after which the Life traces his defection to Sparta, his dealings with Tissaphernes, a triumphant recall and naval victories at Abydus, Cyzicus, and Byzantium, and his renewed disgrace after the reverse off Notium. It closes with the fall of Athens, his wanderings in Thrace, Bithynia, and Phrygia, and his death in a burning house, which the final chapters attribute variously to Lysander and Pharnabazus or to private revenge.
grc.plutarch.alexander: The Life opens with Plutarch's declaration that he writes lives rather than histories, gathering from small words and deeds the signs of character. It follows Alexander from his birth amid portents and his schooling under Aristotle and the taming of Bucephalus, through his accession at twenty, the destruction of Thebes, and the expedition proclaimed against Persia. The main course of the narrative covers the crossing into Asia, the victories at the Granicus, Issus, and Gaugamela, the siege of Tyre, the founding of Alexandria, the journey to the oracle of Ammon, the capture of the Persian court, and the death of Darius, together with Alexander's adoption of Persian dress and customs and the crises over Philotas, Cleitus, and Callisthenes. The latter part carries the army into India, through the battle with Porus and the devastating return march through Gedrosia, to the deaths of Hephaestion and of Alexander himself in Babylon, ending with the rumors of poisoning and the fates of Roxane, Stateira, and Arrhidaeus.
grc.plutarch.amatoriae_narrationes: Amatoriae Narrationes is a short Greek collection of five local love stories transmitted with the Moralia and attributed to Plutarch, of uncertain date. It opens with the tale of Aristocleia of Aliartos, a Boeotian maiden whose choice between two suitors ends in her violent death as she goes to sacrifice before her wedding. The remaining narratives follow the same pattern of desire, abduction, and retribution through local legend: Actaeon of Corinth, killed by his admirer Archias in a botched abduction, whose death brings plague, oracle, and Archias's flight that leads to the founding of Syracuse; the outrage against Skeadas's daughters at Leuktra, avenged by omens before the Spartan defeat there; the killing of Phokos by Callirhoe's rejected suitors and their punishment after the siege of Hippotas; and the Spartan Alkippos's daughters, slain with their mother Damokrita after his unjust exile. Each tale is set in a named Boeotian or Peloponnesian town and closes with vengeance, a divine sign, or a foundation bound to the disaster.
grc.plutarch.an_recte_dictum_sit_latenter_es: A short Greek philosophical essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, which takes up and refutes the Epicurean maxim lathe biōsas, 'live unnoticed.' The opening remarks on the paradox that Epicurus, in urging withdrawal from public life, did not himself conceal the precept, since to proclaim it was already to seek fame. The argument then likens hidden vice to sickness concealed from the physician, insists that virtue needs recognition in order to act, citing Epaminondas, Themistocles, Camillus, and Dion as benefactors who could not have helped humanity in obscurity, and treats knowledge as the light that gives honour and effective exercise to the virtues. It closes with a vision of the afterlife in which the wickedly obscure are punished not with bodily torments but in a realm of darkness, oblivion, and utter loss of reputation.
grc.plutarch.an_virtus_doceri_possit: A short moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia under the title 'Whether Virtue Can Be Taught'. It opens by asking why, since singing, letters, farming, riding, and countless other skills are all learned, prudence and right living alone are held to be untaught, so that good men exist in name only, like centaurs or giants. The argument then ranges over examples from crafts, households, and public life, including anecdotes about Diogenes, Aristippus, and Iphicrates and a reference to Plato on harmony, contending that forbidding instruction would abolish virtue altogether and that denying its teachability, while granting it to minor accomplishments, resembles the Scythians' blinding of their slaves. It closes by presenting prudence as the guiding order of all the other arts, of no avail unless those who practise them are themselves trained and orderly, as at a dinner served by educated attendants.
grc.plutarch.an_vitiositas_ad_infelicitatem_: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia under the question of whether vice by itself is sufficient to make a person unhappy. It opens with the case, illustrated from Euripides, of a man whose circumstances are shown to be 'brief and insecure', a Tantalus-like wealth that its possessor has no leisure to enjoy. The argument goes on to establish that vice needs neither instruments nor assistants to render people wretched, being more violent than fire or iron, and stages Fortune and Vice as rival contractors bidding for the making of an unlucky man, with Fortune's menaces of poverty, slavery, poison and the pyre all met by the composure of figures such as Metrocles, Diogenes, Socrates and the Roman general Decius. The essay closes by denying that Fortune can complete misery without vice as its co-worker, since vice alone softens and hollows out its victims, making wretched even those who are rich, prosperous and secure.
grc.plutarch.aratus: Plutarch's Life of Aratus, written in Greek as part of his Lives, opens with an address to Polycrates framed around an old proverb about fathers who can be praised only through their sons, explaining the work as an ancestral model for Polycrates' children. The narrative follows Aratus of Sicyon from his childhood escape from the tyrant Abantidas and the moonlit scaling of Sicyon's walls to overthrow Nicocles, through his city's adhesion to the Achaean League and his covert capture of the Acrocorinthus from its Macedonian garrison. Later sections recount his campaigns against the tyrants of Argos and Megalopolis, his feud with Lydiades, the war with Cleomenes of Sparta and the appeal to Antigonus Doson that placed Corinth back in Macedonian hands, and his growing estrangement from Philip V, whose slow poison is said to have killed him. A closing notice describes the honors paid to Aratus at Sicyon, including the annual Arateion, the madness of his son under Philip's drugs, and Philip's own downfall at Roman hands.
grc.plutarch.brutus: Plutarch's Life of Brutus is a Greek prose biography of Marcus Junius Brutus, the assassin of Julius Caesar. It opens with Brutus's claimed descent from Junius Brutus, who expelled the Tarquins, and with the conflicting ancient reports about his ancestry through his mother Servilia. The narrative follows his upbringing under his uncle Cato, his attachment to the Old Academy of Plato, his terse Laconic manner in Greek letters, his mission to Cyprus on Cato's behalf, and his choice to join Pompey in the civil war against Caesar.
grc.plutarch.caius_marcius_coriolanus: The work is a Greek biography of the Roman patrician Gaius Marcius Coriolanus, composed by Plutarch among his Lives. It opens with the distinction of the Marcian house and the orphaned Marcius's upbringing by his widowed mother Volumnia. The narrative follows his rise through youthful military distinction and the capture of Corioli, whence he takes the surname Coriolanus, through his conflict with the plebs over grain, his failed bid for the consulship, his prosecution and exile, his generalship for the Volscians alongside Tullus Aufidius, his campaigns through Latium to the walls of Rome, and the supplication of the Roman matrons led by his mother that turns him back from the city. Digressions treat the plebeian secession and Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly, Roman religious scruples over rites interrupted, customs of personal naming, and the broken standing of Coriolanus among the Volscians, which ends in his violent death at Antium.
grc.plutarch.caius_marius: A Greek biographical account of the Roman general Gaius Marius, written in Greek by Plutarch as part of his Parallel Lives. The work opens with a discussion of Roman naming customs and Marius's humble origins at Cirrhaeaton near Arpinum, then traces his career from early service under Scipio Aemilianus through his tribuneship, his rise to command in the war against Jugurtha, and his successive consulships against the Cimbri and Teutones, including the battles at Aquae Sextiae and Vercellae. The narrative follows his later years through political rivalry with Sulla, exile and wanderings through Italy and Africa, his violent return to Rome alongside Cinna, a seventh consulship, and his death seventeen days into it, ending with the downfall of his son Marius.
grc.plutarch.cato_minor: A Greek biographical account by Plutarch of Cato the Younger, the Roman senator remembered for his stubborn defence of the republic. The opening traces Cato's lineage from his great-grandfather Cato the Censor and gathers anecdotes of the severe, unyielding temperament he showed as an orphaned child under Sulla's domination. The narrative then follows his whole public career, covering his austere private life, his service in Rome's offices, the mission in which he conveyed the royal treasure from Cyprus, his quarrels with Cicero, Clodius, Pompey, and Crassus over elections and laws, and his leadership of the republican side in the civil war against Caesar. It closes with his suicide at Utica as Caesar approached, Caesar's reported remark on his death, and brief notices of the son and daughter who carried on his cause at Philippi.
grc.plutarch.cimon: Greek Life of Cimon by Plutarch, paired in his Parallel Lives with the Life of Lucullus. It opens with a long anecdote about Damon of Chaeronea, an ancestor of Plutarch whose murder of a Roman officer nearly ruined the city until Lucullus's testimony saved it, and the preface justifies pairing the two generals as alike in valour, magnificence and unfinished campaigns. The work then follows Cimon's career from his obscure youth and devotion to his sister Elpinice through his leadership of the Delian League, the victory at the Eurymedon, the capture of Eion and Skyros and the return of Theseus's bones, his lavish public generosity, his philolaconian politics, ostracism and recall, and his death during the expedition to Cyprus, closing with an account of his burial and the veneration of his memory.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aegisalius_pompey: A short Greek synkrisis attributed to Plutarch, the formal comparison that closes his paired biographies of the Spartan king Agesilaus and the Roman general Pompey. It opens by announcing that, since the two lives have been set out, the writer will run quickly through the points of difference, beginning with their contrasting rises to power. The essay then weighs the men point against point: their dealings with Sulla and Lysander, their transgressions in civil life, their political virtue and moments of good fortune or error, and finally their generalship, where Pompey's abandonment of Rome and defeat at Pharsalus are set against Agesilaus's defence of a weakened Sparta and his later conduct in Egypt, with faults on either side acknowledged and each man's failures traced to his character.
grc.plutarch.comparison_agis_cleomenes_gracc: A short Greek composition by Plutarch, the work is the formal comparison that closes his paired Lives of Agis and Cleomenes and of the Gracchi, weighing the Spartan kings against the Roman brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. It opens by announcing that, the narrative being brought to an end, there remains the comparison to be drawn from the parallel lives, and turns first to the natural gifts and upbringing of the two pairs. The body then weighs the four men point by point: their continence with money, the scale and character of their political innovations, their achievements in war, their deaths, their conduct of their respective revolutions, and the specific charges brought against Tiberius, Gaius, and Cleomenes. It closes with an overall judgment that awards the first place in virtue to Tiberius, finds Agis the least at fault of the Spartans, and ranks Gaius and Cleomenes together in deed and daring.
grc.plutarch.comparison_alcibiades_coriolanu: A short comparative essay in Greek by Plutarch, the formal closing comparison to the paired Lives of the Athenian Alcibiades and the Roman Coriolanus. It opens by judging their military exploits as a whole evenly matched, neither commander holding a decisive advantage in daring or generalship. The essay then contrasts their political careers and characters, Alcibiades' brilliant but demagogic charm against Coriolanus' proud and unyielding oligarchic temper, and goes on to weigh their conduct over money, the resentment each aroused at home, the disasters each brought upon his city through anger, and their differing ends in exile, before concluding that Coriolanus, for all his harshness, surpassed Alcibiades in temperance and self-command and deserves to be ranked with the purest of the Greeks rather than with so reckless a man.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_demosthenes_with_: A short Greek synkrisis by Plutarch, forming the formal comparison that concludes his paired Lives of Demosthenes and Cicero. It weighs the two orators' rhetorical powers and styles, then turns to their characters as these appear in their speeches, treating their humour, gravity, and self-display. Further sections contrast the authority each held and how he used it, their conduct toward money and royal gifts, and the differing circumstances of their flights and downfalls.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_dion_and_brutus: Plutarch's Comparison of Dion and Brutus is the formal concluding comparison, written in Greek, that weighs the Syracusan statesman against the Roman tyrannicide in the manner of his paired Lives. Opening from the premise that both men achieved great things with very slight advantages, it notes that Dion lacked a partner of Cassius's calibre and that he, unlike Brutus, advanced his own fortune for the war. The comparison then sets their dissimilar tyrants side by side, judging Dionysius's open tyranny an easier and more legitimate mark than Caesar's popular rule, before assessing their conduct as generals, the purity of their motives against tyranny, and their choice of friends and partisans, where Dion's trust in corrupt associates and Brutus's single-minded purpose are each examined. It closes with the anecdote of the bronze statue of Brutus at Mediolanum, which Caesar, after threatening the city, smilingly praised the Gauls for their fidelity and ordered to remain in place.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lucullus_and_cimo: A short formal comparison in Greek that closes Plutarch's paired biographies of Lucullus and Cimon. It opens by judging Lucullus fortunate in his end, since he died before the civil wars he foresaw, while his country was still free, a lot shared with Cimon. The remainder weighs the two men point against point: their contrasting use of wealth and taste for luxury, their successes by land and sea, Cimon's single-day victory combining land battle and naval action for Greece and Lucullus's campaigns beyond the Taurus and across the Tigris to the capture of Tigranocerta, Cabira, Sinope and Nisibis, their standing with soldiers and allies, and their common experience of political prosecution and ostracism. It concludes that both were favoured by the gods, the one shown what to achieve and the other what to guard against.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lycurgus_and_numa: A short Greek comparison by Plutarch, the formal synkrisis attached to his lives of the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus and the Roman king Numa Pompilius. It opens by undertaking, now that both lives have been treated, to collect the points of difference between the two men. The body first sets out their shared qualities, moderation, piety, civic and educational concern, and divine sanction for their legislation, and then weighs their contrasts: Numa's receiving of kingship against Lycurgus's voluntary surrender of it, the harsher task of taming Sparta against Numa's gentler ordering of Rome, the treatment of helots and slaves, land redistribution, marriage customs and the exposure of Spartan maidens, and the training of the young. It closes by observing that Lycurgus's laws endured over five hundred years while Numa's peace collapsed soon after his death, yet that Numa's achievement in winning a still-unsettled city through wisdom and justice, without arms or force, is great and divine.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_philopoemen_and_t: A brief Greek synkrisis in which Plutarch weighs the Achaean general Philopoemen against the Roman Titus Quinctius Flamininus, rounding off the pair of lives devoted to them. It opens by conceding Titus's superiority in the magnitude of his services to Greece, since he defeated Philip and liberated the Greek cities at a time when Philopoemen, unable to aid his hard-pressed countrymen, had withdrawn to Crete. The argument then sets their failings side by side, ascribing Philopoemen's missteps to ambition and a hot temper and Titus's to contentiousness, before crediting Philopoemen with far wider and more personal military experience, gained in countless battles and in his own redesign of arms and tactics, and no less effective as a private citizen than as a commander. It ends by finding the balance hard to determine and proposing to award the Greek the crown of martial skill and the Roman that of justice and goodness.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_theseus_and_romul: Plutarch's Comparison of Theseus and Romulus is the short formal synkrisis that closes the paired biographies of the two founders in his Lives. It opens by weighing the heroes' first motives, contrasting Theseus's self-chosen ambition from a secure kingship at Troezen with Romulus's flight from servitude. The comparison then proceeds point by point through their exploits against tyrants and robbers, their daring in war, the love of Ariadne, their divergent political temperaments, their lapses toward brother and son, the founding and unification of cities, and the abduction of women, where the seizure of the Sabines is judged to have served civic concord. It closes on matters divine, contrasting Romulus's providentially favored preservation with the oracle to Aegeus that cast Theseus's begetting as against the will of the gods.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_apollonium: A consolatory essay in Greek, preserved among Plutarch's Moralia, addressed to Apollonius on the early death of his son, a young man of disciplined, pious, and phil-anthropic character. After conceding that some grief is natural, the speaker argues that mourning must be kept within rational and moderate bounds, drawing on Homer, Pindar, Euripides, Simonides, Crantor, and Socrates for arguments that death is no evil, whether likened to sleep, to a long journey, or to complete dissolution. The essay also incorporates Plato's myth of the judgement of souls from the Gorgias, stories of divine favour shown to the prematurely dead, and exempla of fathers who bore the loss of children with composure, from Anaxagoras, Pericles, and Xenophon to Demosthenes, Dion, and Antigonus, while treating untimely death as possibly a blessing that spares future suffering. It closes by urging Apollonius to honour his son through grateful memory and a return to his customary manner of life rather than fruitless lamentation.
grc.plutarch.consolatio_ad_uxorem: A letter of consolation in Greek by Plutarch, addressed to his wife Timoxena on the death of their infant daughter and transmitted with the Moralia. It opens with news of the child's death, directions for a simple burial, and an appeal to the mother to moderate her sorrow. The remainder argues that excessive grief is irrational and harmful: Plutarch praises his wife's composure before visitors, recalls the daughter's affectionate and winsome nature, warns against ostentatious lamentation and against letting mourning efface memory of the good the child brought, and urges that the mind dwell on the bright and honorable parts of a life rather than its losses. A closing section appeals to Dionysiac teaching on the soul's immortality and to ancestral custom concerning the burial of very young children.
grc.plutarch.crassus: Plutarch's Life of Marcus Licinius Crassus, the Roman triumvir, opens with his family and frugal upbringing in a modest household and turns at once to the avarice that Romans regarded as his one dominant vice. The narrative traces the building of his vast fortune out of Sulla's proscriptions and the cheap purchase of burning and ruined houses, his flight from the Marians to Spain and eight months' concealment in a seaside cave, his service under Sulla, and his sustained rivalry for public standing with Pompey. Its central section gives a continuous account of the gladiatorial war led by Spartacus, from the outbreak at Capua and the defeats of Roman commanders to Crassus' appointment, the decimation of cowardly troops, the wall across the Bruttian isthmus, and the final battle in which Spartacus died while Pompey claimed the credit for ending the war. The life closes with the joint consulship and its reconciliation engineered by Caesar, the triumvirate and the conference at Luca, Crassus' Syrian command and Parthian invasion against omens and warnings, the disaster of the desert march and the death of his son Publius, his own death amid Surena's treachery at Carrhae, the insulting mock triumph and grotesque scenes at the Parthian court, and the retribution that later overtook Surena and Hyrodes.
grc.plutarch.de_alexandri_magni_fortuna_aut_: A Greek declamatory essay from Plutarch's Moralia, On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander stages a contest between Fortune and Virtue for credit with Alexander's conquests. It opens with Fortune personified, claiming Alexander as her own peculiar work and provoking an answer on behalf of philosophy. The argument that follows attributes his empire instead to his virtue: his philosophical schooling under Aristotle, his founding of cities and mingling of Macedonians and Persians in one common civic life, his magnanimity toward the family of Darius, his maxims and patronage of artists, and a long catalog of wounds and hardships suffered in his campaigns. The closing contention is that Fortune opposed rather than aided him at every stage, so that his greatness belongs to virtue and not to chance.
grc.plutarch.de_amore_prolis: De Amore Prolis (On Affection for Offspring) is a Greek prose treatise by Plutarch, transmitted among the Moralia. The work argues that parental love is natural and freely given, contrasting the laws, honours, and incentives by which human beings are induced to marry and rear children with the untutored devotion of animals to their mates and young. Its case rests on copious natural observation, describing the kingfisher's woven nest, the viviparous sharks, the bear's licking of her formless cubs, the partridge's diversion of hunters, and the care shown by hens, dogs, and horses, and it closes by setting the beasts up as witnesses against a human nature that alone appears to love for a price.
grc.plutarch.de_capienda_ex_inimicis_utilita: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, addressed to Cornelius Pulcher, on the theme of turning hostility to one's advantage. It opens by observing that no public life is free of envy and strife and that friendships and enmities interweave, so that profiting from enemies deserves serious examination. The discussion then ranges widely: enemies watch a man's affairs more closely than friends do, so their scrutiny encourages vigilance and self-improvement; abuse and insult can serve as correction where flattery has silenced candid friendship; enduring reviling without anger exercises self-command; and showing fairness and generosity toward an enemy, even praising a rival's merits, purges envy and contentiousness that would otherwise be spent on friends. Instances drawn from Greek and Roman history, from Chilon and Socrates to Themistocles, Cicero, and Cato, illustrate the argument throughout.
grc.plutarch.de_communibus_notitiis_adversus: A Greek philosophical dialogue of Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, in which Lamprias opens by telling Diadoumenus how his Stoic friends have disturbed him by philosophizing contrary to the common conceptions shared by all humankind. The greater part of the work is a systematic prosecution of Stoic doctrine on those grounds, taking up in turn the Stoic account of goods and indifferents, the paradoxes concerning the sage, the claim that vice is useful to the whole, the theology of the conflagration in which only Zeus survives, and the physical teachings on mixture, the infinite division of bodies, time, growth, the soul, and the elements. Chrysippus is quoted extensively throughout, and his formulations are repeatedly charged with overturning the universal preconceptions that the Stoics themselves claim to follow.
grc.plutarch.de_cupiditate_divitiarum: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia and devoted to the love of wealth. It opens with the anecdote of the trainer Hippomachus, who says of a long-armed boxer that he ought to take down the hanging crown, an image applied to those who marvel at fine estates, great houses, and heaps of silver as though happiness were for sale. The argument, illustrated with anecdotes of Aristippus, Demades, and Phocion, is that wealth cures no evil but love of wealth itself, since greed is an insatiable sickness of the soul that calls for purgation rather than acquisition: no one is poor who has enough, while the acquisitive man, supplied with necessities, is filled instead with desires for gold, ivory, and emeralds, and passes his life in debts, lawsuits, and anxiety. Plutarch distinguishes the petty, ant-like miser from the beastly, rapacious kind who takes from others what he cannot use, condemns parents who bequeath avarice to their children along with the inheritance, and closes by contrasting wealth, which is blind without spectators and stages its banquets for an audience, with virtue and wisdom, which keep their own light even when no one is watching.
grc.plutarch.de_curiositate: A short Greek moral treatise by Plutarch, transmitted with the Moralia and known by its Latin title De Curiositate, on polypragmosyne, the invasive curiosity that hunts out other people's affairs and misfortunes. It opens with the image of a dark and unhealthy house that cannot be fled but can be brightened by shifting the light and rearranging the doors, a figure applied to the treatment of the disease of curiosity.
