It opens as a letter announcing that proofs are given both of theorems earlier circulated and of others more recently discovered, and then supplies definitions of these solids, their axes, vertices, centres, and segments. The body of the work first states lemmas drawn from proportion theory and conic geometry, then proceeds through a series of propositions, proved largely by inscribed and circumscribed figures built out of cylinders, establishing the volumes of segments of conoids and spheroids: a segment of a right conoid cut off by a plane perpendicular to the axis is half of the cone on the same base and axis, segments cut in any planes are in duplicate ratio of their axes, half of an oblong spheroid cut through its centre is double a cone, and the greater and lesser segments of an oblique cut have ratios expressible in terms of the axes; it also determines which plane sections of each solid are circles, parabolas, or ellipses and proves that a tangent plane touches such a solid at a single point. A closing set of propositions and problems includes the task of cutting from a given conoid or spheroid a segment equal to a given cone, cylinder, or sphere.
grc.archimedes.de_sphaera_et_cylindro: Archimedes' Greek treatise on the sphere and cylinder opens with a dedicatory letter announcing results earlier sent to Conon, chiefly that the surface of a sphere is four times its greatest circle and that a cylinder circumscribing the sphere is half again as large in volume. After a preface of definitions, axioms, and lemmas on circumscribed and inscribed figures, the first book proves in succession the areas of pyramids, cones, cylinders, spherical segments and sectors, and finally that a sphere equals four times the cone over its great circle while the enclosing cylinder is hemiolic to it. The second book consists largely of problems: finding a plane figure equal to a spherical surface, finding a sphere equal to a given cone or cylinder, cutting a sphere so that its segments bear a given ratio, and constructing segments equal to one given segment and similar to another.
grc.archimedes.liber_assumptorum: The Liber Assumptorum, or Book of Lemmas, is a short collection of geometrical propositions in Greek attributed to Archimedes and of uncertain date. It opens with a proof that, when two internally tangent circles have parallel diameters, the lines drawn from the point of contact to the ends of the diameters lie in a single straight line. The remaining propositions cover the geometry of the circle and the semicircle: tangents drawn from external points, chords intersecting at right angles, and the areas and diameter ratios of figures bounded by semicircular arcs, including the arbelos and the lune, with one proposition posed as a problem requiring the ratio between a semicircle's diameter and that of the circle inscribed in its arbelos. The work closes with two porisms, one establishing that a side of the regular pentagon inscribed in a circle is cut in extreme and mean ratio.
grc.archytas_of_tarentum.fragmenta: Fragments of Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher whose surviving words are preserved as quotations in later authors such as Porphyry, Nicomachus, Iamblichus, Stobaeus, and Theon of Smyrna, transmitted in literary Doric Greek. The collection opens with the longest fragment, from a treatise on mathematics or harmonics, in which astronomy, geometry, arithmetic, and music are called sister sciences, and the pitch of sound is explained through the speed of motion, rapid movement producing sharp notes and slow movement heavy ones. Shorter fragments define the three musical means, arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic, distinguish learning from another person from discovering by oneself, and credit the discovery of calculation (logismos) with ending civil strife by establishing equality. The collection closes with an inventory of titles ascribed to him, ranging from works on principles, being, the soul, wisdom, and law to a treatise on cookery and letters exchanged with Plato and Dionysius, together with testimonies to writings on machines and agriculture.
grc.aristophanes.plutus: The Plutus, a comedy of Aristophanes, opens with the slave Carion grumbling as he escorts his master home from Apollo's oracle, for the god has bidden the man to follow Wealth himself, blind and helpless, when the god might as well have cured him. The plot turns on the restoration of Wealth's sight, after which he bestows riches on the just and abandons sycophants and wrongdoers, despite Poverty's warning that a world rid of her would be destitute. Subsequent scenes bring the healed god to the temple of Asclepius, and an elderly woman is undone when her young lover, no longer dependent on her money, deserts her. The play closes with Plutus reinstated in his former seat within the temple, led in procession with torches and sacred vessels.
grc.aristotle.de_memoria_et_reminiscentia: A short Greek treatise by Aristotle on memory and recollection, transmitted as one of the essays of the Parva Naturalia. The work opens by turning from the senses and their objects to memory and remembering, asking what memory is, from what cause it arises, and in which part of the soul the affection occurs. It argues that memory is neither sensation nor belief but a lasting state or affection of the primary perceptive faculty, arising from imagination and bound up with the perception of time, and it explains such phenomena as the poor memory of the very young and the very old through the analogy of an imprint made in the soul. The remainder treats recollection as a deliberate act of searching, a kind of syllogism in which movements in the soul proceed from a starting point to what is sought by similarity, contrast, or contiguity, an act found among known animals only in human beings, and ends with a summary of the conclusions on both memory and recollection.
grc.aristotle.economics: The Economics is a short Greek treatise on household management attributed to Aristotle. It opens by distinguishing economics from politics and by tracing the household's natural constitution, the conjugal relation, children, property, and slaves. The work then surveys the duties of the household head toward wife, offspring, servants, and possessions, including provisions on training, discipline, and the management of resources, before distinguishing four kinds of economy (royal, satrapic, political, and private). It closes with a collection of anecdotes showing how rulers and cities from Cypselus of Corinth to Alexander's commanders raised money in wartime and other emergencies.
grc.aristotle.metaphysics: The Metaphysics of Aristotle is a Greek prose treatise in fourteen books on first philosophy, the inquiry into being qua being and into the principles and causes of things. It opens with the claim that all human beings by nature desire to know, tracing the ascent from sensation and memory through experience to art and science. The work then sets out the aporiai concerning first principles, examines the four causes, and analyses substance as matter, form, and the composite, together with potentiality and actuality. Its later books argue for an unmoved first mover and examine the doctrines of Plato's followers and the Pythagoreans on separate Forms and numbers.
grc.aristotle.res_publica_atheniensium: A Greek treatise on the Athenian state, transmitted among the works of Aristotle and of uncertain date. It opens amid the aftermath of the Cylonian conspiracy and the harsh oligarchic order of the hektemoroi that preceded Draco and Solon. The historical first half traces the development of the Athenian constitution through Draco's code, Solon's reforms and debt-cancellation, the Pisistratid tyranny, Cleisthenes' reorganization, and the oligarchic upheavals of the late fifth century down to the author's own day, while the second half sets out the working constitution in detail: the council of five hundred and its supervision of magistrates and finances, the nine archons and their religious and judicial duties, the military and festival offices, and the courts, including the allotment of jurors, the use of ballots and water clocks, and the conduct of trials.
grc.aristotle.rhetoric: Aristotle's Rhetoric, a Greek prose treatise on the art of persuasion, opens by defining rhetoric as the counterpart of dialectic and by criticising earlier handbooks for dwelling on matters outside the cause instead of on proof. The work then sets out the three species of oratory, deliberative, forensic and epideictic, and the sources of persuasion in character, emotion and argument, with a central book analysing the passions, from anger and fear to shame and pity, together with the ages and characters of audiences, as material for enthymematic reasoning. Its final book treats style and arrangement, covering correctness of language, metaphor and simile, periodic composition, and the parts of a speech from proem to epilogue, with guidance on questioning, answering and the use of the laughable.
grc.aristotle.virtues_and_vices: A short Greek ethical treatise attributed to Aristotle and of uncertain date, transmitted in the Aristotelian corpus under the title Virtues and Vices (Peri areton kai kakion). It opens by ranking the noble among things praiseworthy and the base among things blameworthy, and, adopting the Platonic division of the soul into three parts, assigns virtues to each: phronesis to the rational part, gentleness and courage to the spirited, temperance and self-control to the appetitive, and justice, liberality, and magnanimity to the soul as a whole. The rest of the work defines each virtue and its corresponding vice in turn, folly, irascibility, cowardice, licentiousness, incontinence, injustice, illiberality, and small-mindedness, cataloguing the traits and behaviours that accompany each. It concludes with general characterisations of virtue as a well-ordered disposition of the whole soul, likened to a model of a good constitution, and of vice as its contrary.
grc.aristotle.περί_χρωμάτων: A short Greek treatise on colours, transmitted under the name of Aristotle and of uncertain date, which investigates how colours arise in the natural world. It opens by defining the simple colours as those that follow the four elements, with air and water naturally white, fire and the sun yellow, and earth white though appearing variegated through staining. The remainder derives the many colours from the mixture of these simples and from the varying strength of reflected light, discussing blackness and shadow, the hues of sea and sky, the ripening and changing colours of fruits and flowers, and finally the colouring of hair, wool, and feathers in animals, including greying and whitening with age. It closes by observing that the whole inquiry into colours can best be grasped from the mingling of the rays of sunlight and firelight.
grc.aristotle.ἐκ_τοῦ_περὶ_ἀκουστῶν: A short Greek treatise on sound and the voice, of uncertain date, transmitted as an excerpt from a work On Things Heard and attributed to Aristotle. It begins with the claim that every voice and every noise arises when bodies, or air striking against bodies, set the air in motion, not because the air is given a shape, as some suppose, but because it is driven, compressed and struck by the impact. The argument then sets out a general mechanics of sounding: a blow of air propagated onwards carries the voice to the ear, and the qualities of sound, high and low pitch, hardness and softness, thinness and thickness, hoarseness, harshness, nasality, broken or stammering utterance, are traced to the size, shape and condition of the lung, windpipe and mouth and to the quantity and force of the breath. Examples are drawn throughout from human and animal voices, from instruments such as strings, auloi, horns and trumpets, and from natural phenomena like rivers and thunder, closing with an account of how rapid, imperceptibly successive impacts on the ear produce the appearance of continuous sound and of concord.
grc.arius_didymus.liber_de_philosophorum_sec: The work is a Greek doxographic epitome, attributed to Arius Didymus and preserved by Stobaeus, which surveys the ethical doctrines of the ancient philosophical schools. It opens with an account of happiness as activity in noble and preferred actions, then passes through notices of Xenophanes and Philo of Larissa to definitions of ethos and passion as framed by the followers of Plato, by Zeno, and by Aristotle. The longest portion sets out Stoic ethics at length: the four primary passions and their many species, the paradoxes concerning the wise man, and discussions of friendship, law, and the city. It closes with the doctrines of Aristotle and the later Peripatetics, treating virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency, the classification of goods, and finally household management and constitutional matters.
grc.callistratus.statuarum_descriptiones: A collection of fourteen rhetorical descriptions of works of art, attributed to Callistratus and of uncertain date. The first piece depicts a statue of a pipe-playing Satyr in a grotto near Egyptian Thebes; the sequence then proceeds through further statues, Scopas' Bacchante, Praxiteles' Eros, a drunken Indian, Narcissus at the spring, Lysippus' personification of Opportunity, Orpheus on Helicon, Dionysus, the vocal colossus of Memnon, Asclepius, an ephebe, a Centaur, and Medea, and closes with a painting of Athamas and Ino amid a storm-tossed sea filled with dolphins and sea deities. Each description sets the artwork in a landscape or sanctuary and dwells on how stone, bronze, or pigment can be made to seem alive, breathing, moving, and displaying the passions of the soul.
grc.chionis_epistulae.epistulae: A series of seventeen Greek letters attributed to Chion of Heraclea and of uncertain date, composed as correspondence between the young Heracleote Chion and his father and Plato. The opening letter, sent from Byzantium, answers parental anxiety over his prolonged absence by asking his father to see his education not as a consolation but as a pledge of future excellence. The sequence then follows his voyage from the Black Sea toward Athens, detained at Byzantium, where he witnesses Xenophon restraining the Greek soldiery from sacking the city, and by a storm that drives him to Perinthus, before turning to his philosophical life at Athens with Plato and Speusippus and to his return to a Heraclea oppressed by the tyrant Clearchus, against whom he begins to conspire. The collection closes with a farewell to Plato written on the eve of the attempt on Clearchus, in which Chion embraces the prospect of a noble death for his city's freedom.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.musica: A short Greek collection of definitions and notes on music transmitted under the name of Claudius Ptolemaeus and of uncertain date. It opens with a numerical scheme of the cosmic system, assigning ratio-numbers to the standing notes of the spheres from the moon and Hermes to Aphrodite, the Sun, Ares, Zeus, Kronos, and the fixed stars. The remainder gathers memoranda on music theory at large: definitions of music, melody, and harmonics; the kinds of rhythm and of metrical feet (dactylic, iambic, and paeonic) with their time values; the measurement of tones, semitones, and dieses in twelfths of a tone after Eratosthenes; the qualities of the four elements; the three things subject to rhythm (word, melody, bodily movement); a table of the lyre's notes for the left and right hands in kithara-playing; and a closing remark on the manly Dorian and mournful Phrygian rhythms.
grc.clement_of_alexandria.excerpta_ex_theodo: A Greek compilation transmitted under the name of Clement of Alexandria, preserving in excerpt and note form the Gnostic teaching of Theodotus, a follower of Valentinus. The collection opens with a Valentinian exposition of the Saviour's words 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit', read through the myth of Sophia and the spiritual seed. It then moves through the whole Valentinian system: the emanation of the aeons and Sophia's fall, the unknowable Father and the Monogenes, the Saviour and the psychic Christ, the three natures of human beings descended from Adam, the Demiurge and the creation of the world, the meaning of baptism and its liberating power, and the deliverance of the faithful from fate and the astral powers. Short notes on other Gnostic teachers, including followers of Basilides, and running exegesis of individual scriptural passages, from the transfiguration and John's prologue to the wedding garment and the money of Caesar, are interspersed throughout.
grc.cleonides.εἰσαγωγὴ_ἁρμονική: Of uncertain date and attributed to Cleonides, the Eisagōgē harmonikē is a short Greek treatise on musical theory that opens by defining harmonics as the theoretical and practical science of the harmonized, divided into seven parts: notes, intervals, genera, systems, tonos, modulation, and melopoeia. The body of the work defines these elements in turn, treating the eighteen notes of the system as fixed or movable, the three genera (diatonic, chromatic, enharmonic) with their tetrachordal divisions and six colourings expressed in numerical fractions of the tone, and the arrangement of tetrachords in the lesser and greater perfect systems. It then sets out the species of the octave with their traditional names, Mixolydian, Lydian, Phrygian, Dorian, Hypolydian, Hypophrygian, Hypodorian, and the thirteen tonoi counted according to Aristoxenus, illustrating the term with quotations from Terpander and Ion. The treatise closes with the four kinds of modulation, including change of tonos and of melopoeia with its ethical characters suited to tragedy, laments, or hymns, and with melopoeia itself as the practical employment of conduction, interweaving, repeated striking, and sustained tone.
grc.demades.on_the_twelve_years: Attributed to the Athenian orator Demades, On the Twelve Years is a short forensic defense in which a statesman of the age of Philip and Alexander answers charges arising from his political career before an Athenian court. The speech opens by comparing the juror to a physician who cannot treat the sick without knowing the cause of the disease, and by asking for a hearing untainted by the slanders of rival orators. The speaker defends the peace he wrote with Philip and the honors he conferred on him as acts of necessity that won back two thousand captives without ransom and a thousand citizens without a herald, vilifies Demosthenes as a bitter sycophant, and insists that decisions taken in war cannot be judged by the standard of present peace. Aphoristic sayings on fortune, rhetoric, the taming of Alexander, sycophants, and the jurisdiction of the Athenian courts are scattered through the argument, and the speech closes on further such sententiae.
grc.demosthenes.against_apatourius: A short Athenian forensic speech from the Demosthenic corpus, delivered by a defendant in a maritime commercial suit in support of a paragraphe, the plea that the case brought against him is inadmissible. It opens by citing the laws that give merchants and shipowners prompt commercial dikai and allow those disputing alleged contracts to have the issue settled by the paragraphe procedure. The speaker recounts his dealings with Apatourius and the fugitive Parmenon of Byzantium: a loan of thirty minae raised from the banker Heraclides on his guarantee, the ship and children taken in pledge, the mutual release of all contracts once the debt was paid, the vanishing of the original written agreements, and a disputed arbitration by Aristocles held in Parmenon's absence after an earthquake destroyed his family. He denies ever having stood guarantor for Parmenon, argues from the passage of time and the annual term allowed for guarantors, and concludes that his paragraphe was entered rightly and that Apatourius has sued falsely and contrary to the laws.
grc.demosthenes.against_aphobus_2: A forensic speech of Demosthenes, the second of two delivered against Aphobus, concerning the estate that the speaker's dying father entrusted to Aphobus and two fellow guardians. It opens with the speaker announcing that he will refute Aphobus' many falsehoods, beginning with the claim that the grandfather owed money to the state and that the father therefore refused to lease the house for fear of penalty. The argument shows that the family's wealth was openly held and liberally assessed for liturgies, that the guardians concealed the will by which alone the truth could be learned, and that they misappropriated the workshop, the slaves and other assets while lodging contradictory accounts against one another. It recalls how the father on his deathbed placed his children and property in the three men's hands, exposes the antidosis contrived to bar the speaker's lawsuits, pleads on behalf of the impoverished mother and sister, and closes by urging the jurors to grant the speaker his day in court.
grc.demosthenes.against_callicles: Against Callicles is a short Athenian forensic speech transmitted among the works of Demosthenes and of uncertain date, in which a landowner answers a private suit for damages brought by his neighbour Callicles over rainwater draining between their farms. The opening laments that nothing is harder to bear than a wicked and grasping neighbour and recounts Callicles' record of vexatious litigation, including suits routed through a cousin, a brother, and the slave Callarus. The argument then maintains that the disputed walling was built by the speaker's father more than fifteen years earlier while Callicles' father lived beside him and never objected, that the land is planted with vines and figs and holds ancestral tombs and so cannot be a gully, and that the alleged spoilage of grain and oil was trivial, with testimony and a formal challenge read out in support. The speech closes with an appeal to the jurors not to abandon a man being driven from the city by sycophants.
grc.demosthenes.against_evergus_and_mnesibul: A forensic speech of Demosthenes composed for an Athenian jury in a suit for false testimony. The opening praises the laws that allow a party injured by perjured witnesses to bring a separate action against them, and asks the jurors to hear the affair from its beginning. The speaker, a former trierarch, then recounts how he was compelled by decree and law to recover naval equipment owed to the state by Theophemus, how his seizure of pledges led to blows between the two men, and how Theophemus retaliated by plundering the speaker's house and property; against this background he prosecutes Theophemus's brother Evergus and brother-in-law Mnesibulus, whose testimony that Theophemus had once offered to surrender a female slave for the torture-test proved decisive in the earlier assault trial. The speech argues that this testimony is demonstrably false because the slave was repeatedly demanded and never produced, supporting the narrative throughout with the reading of decrees, laws and depositions.
grc.demosthenes.against_nicostratus: An Athenian forensic oration of the private class, transmitted in the corpus of speeches attributed to Demosthenes, arising from an apographē, the registration of property for confiscation by the state. The speech opens with the speaker's insistence that he registered slaves claimed as the property of Arethusius not as a professional informer but as a man wronged and outraged, citing the size of the registered estate and his having filed it in his own name. The central narrative recalls a long friendship and neighbourly dealings with the opponent Nicostratus, the speaker's ransom of him after his capture by a trireme and sale at Aegina, the loans and mortgage extended to him, and the injuries that followed, including a judgment in default, the forcible removal of household goods, the felling of trees, an ambush near the stone quarries, and the speaker's successful action for false summons, in which he induced the jury to impose a fine of a talent rather than the death penalty. The closing portion marshals witnesses to establish that the slaves belong to Arethusius, recounts the mutual challenges to have them tortured in public before the council or the Eleven, and argues that men who owe the treasury a pledged sum have no right to contest the state's claim upon their property.
grc.demosthenes.against_spudias: A Greek forensic oration of uncertain date, transmitted among the private speeches of the Demosthenic corpus, in which a plaintiff brings suit against his brother-in-law Spudias before an Athenian jury. The speech opens with the speaker explaining that he and Spudias have married two sisters, the daughters of Polyeuctus, and that he is compelled to litigate over the property that man left behind. It then recounts Polyeuctus's marriage settlements and dowry arrangements, the thousand drachmae of dowry still outstanding and secured by boundary stones on a house, and a series of further grievances, the price of a slave with interest, money lent to Polyeuctus's widow, pledged jewellery and a tent never returned, and a mina the speaker's wife spent on the Nemesia, all of which Spudias allegedly refuses to honour or disputing. Anticipating the defence that Polyeuctus acted of his own free will, the speaker answers it with laws, wills, deposited documents, and witness testimony, weighs the rival valuations of the dowry goods, and closes by urging the jurors not to let Spudias prevail through false accusations.
grc.demosthenes.against_zenothemis: A short Athenian forensic speech transmitted in the Demosthenic corpus, arising from a maritime loan on a grain cargo shipped from Syracuse. It opens with the speaker citing the laws under which he has lodged a paragraphe, arguing that the suit Zenothemis has brought against him is inadmissible because no written contract existed between the parties. The narrative that follows shows Zenothemis and the shipowner Hegestratos conspiring to scuttle the vessel and defraud its lenders; Hegestratos drowned when the plot failed, and Zenothemis then sought to divert the ship at Cephallenia and later laid claim to the grain at Athens. The latter part of the speech introduces evidence and testimony, attacks Zenothemis' record in other litigations, and closes with the speaker's report that Demosthenes, his kinsman, declined to intervene in the dispute.
grc.demosthenes.philippic_2: A speech of Demosthenes addressed to the Athenian assembly, the Second Philippic warns the Athenians that Philip of Macedon is exploiting the peace to expand his power and is preparing against their city. The speech opens by observing that orators denounce Philip's aggression on every occasion yet nothing is ever done to check it. It then surveys Philip's conduct since the peace, his favour to the Thebans, his dealings with the Messenians, Argives and Lacedaemonians, and his interventions in Thessaly, arguing that all his actions converge on a design against Athens, and reports the speaker's earlier warning to the Peloponnesians against trusting the friendship of a tyrant. The closing section recalls the peace embassies, the surrender of Phocis and Thermopylae, and the unfulfilled promises made to the city, ending with the demand that the ambassadors responsible be summoned to answer for them.
grc.demosthenes.reply_to_philip: The Reply to Philip is a short Athenian assembly speech by Demosthenes, framed as an answer to a letter sent by Philip of Macedon, and it opens by charging that Philip never made peace with the Athenians in earnest but only postponed the war, his letter now openly admitting the breach. The speaker argues that Philip should be neither feared nor resisted half-heartedly: divine favour lies with Athens against an oath-breaker, distrust of him spreads among the Thessalians, Thebans and the cities he has attacked, and the Persian king could be persuaded to finance an Athenian-led coalition. The Macedonian kingdom is depicted as inherently fragile, dependent on the king's own campaigning yet resented by subjects who sacrifice their lives and families to his love of glory, and dreaded at court as much by flatterers and mercenary captains as by enemies. Turning to Athens, the speaker attributes the losses of the former war to negligence and to politicians bought with Philip's gifts, and closes by urging the Athenians to spare neither public nor private resources, to take the field with better generals than before, and to rally the other Greeks to the alliance by deeds rather than words.
grc.dinarchus.against_philocles: A Greek courtroom oration by Dinarchus, prosecuting Philocles for bribery and treachery in connection with the money Harpalus brought into Attica. The speaker recalls that Philocles, though repeatedly condemned by the council of the Areopagus and sworn to keep Harpalus out of the Peiraeus, took bribes while holding the generalship over Mounichia and the ship-sheds, and now stands trial only for the assessment of his penalty. Treating the charges as admitted rather than disputed, the speech weighs fine, death, and confiscation, and presses for the harshest sentence, warning that a commander who sells his trust would as readily betray the fleet, the harbors, and the city itself.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_compositio: A Greek rhetorical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, addressed to Rufus Metilius, on the arrangement (synthesis) of words in both verse and prose. It opens with a dedication comparing the work to Helen's gift of the peplos, setting out its programme: the nature of word-arrangement, its aims, its chief varieties, and the source of the poetic and melodious quality in prose. The treatise defines arrangement and its priority over word-choice, demonstrates its power by rearranging passages of Homer and Herodotus into different metres and styles, surveys the three tasks of the art (fitting, shaping and modifying words), and analyses the contributions of melody, rhythm, variation and propriety, with extended discussions of letters, syllables and rhythmical feet. It then classifies the three general types of arrangement, the austere (exemplified by Pindar and Thucydides), the smooth and flowery (Sappho, Isocrates), and the well-blended mean (Homer, Stesichorus, Herodotus, Demosthenes), closes with an argument that good prose contains concealed metres and rhythms, and shows how verse can be made to resemble prose.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_isaeo: The essay opens by assembling what can be known of Isaeus the logographer: his disputed origins as Athenian or Chalcidian, his training under Isocrates, his role as teacher of Demosthenes, and the silence of earlier writers about his life and dates. It then treats his exclusive practice of forensic oratory and his style, which largely imitates Lysias yet differs from it in greater artifice of composition, arrangement and emotional effects, so that Isaeus appears as the source from which Demosthenes' power grew. Extended comparisons of passages from speeches of the two orators, including the speech for Eumathes the metic, the Callimachus concerning the estate of Ferenicus, the speeches on guardianships, and the oration for Euphiletus against the deme of the Erchieis, illustrate the contrast between Lysias' natural simplicity and Isaeus' technical elaboration. The work ends with brief assessments of other rhetoricians such as Isocrates, Gorgias, Alcidamas, Anaximenes, Antiphon and Thrasymachus, explains why Dionysius of Halicarnassus took Lysias and Isaeus as his exemplars, and announces a further discussion of Demosthenes, Hyperides and Aeschines.
grc.dionysius_of_halicarnasus.ars_rhetorica: A Greek treatise on rhetoric attributed to Dionysius of Halicarnasus, the work opens with praise of festivals as a gift of the gods and, in an address to one Echecrates, teaches how a festival speech should commend the presiding god, the city, the contest, the crown, and the king. It then passes in turn through the chief occasions of epideictic oratory: wedding speeches and the speech in the bridal chamber, addresses on the day of a child's birth, words of welcome to governors arriving in a city, public and private funeral orations, and exhortations delivered to athletes at the games. The latter part is devoted to figured speeches, in which a speaker says one thing while meaning another, with extended analyses of passages from Demosthenes, Thucydides, Plato, Xenophon, Euripides, and Homer. A closing section catalogues the faults that disfigure rhetorical exercises in character, judgment, technique, and diction, and proposes those four criteria as the standard for judging any speech.
grc.epictetus.fragments: A collection of short Greek fragments, dialogues, and maxims transmitted under the name of Epictetus, several of them headed as drawn from Arrian's compilations of the philosopher's sayings. The opening piece questions in dialogue form whether a philosopher must concern himself with the physical composition of existing things, taking up the Delphic precept to know oneself. The excerpts that follow treat what lies within our power and what does not, acceptance of nature and providence, friendship, pleasure, wealth, and moderation, with sections headed as coming from Arrian's protreptic lectures, from the memorabilia of Epictetus, and from Rufus's excerpts on friendship. The collection closes with a string of aphorisms, some marked as taken from the Enchiridion, on friendship, household order, wealth and luxury, sound judgment, and the conduct of citizens and rulers.
grc.euripides.medea: Medea, a Greek tragedy of the fifth century BCE by Euripides, opens with the Nurse's lament that Jason has forsaken Medea, the Colchian princess who once saved him, to marry the daughter of Creon, king of Corinth, and that Medea and her children have been condemned to exile. Creon, fearing her reputation for cunning, grants her only a single day's delay, and her quarrel with Jason, who defends the new marriage as advantageous to the family, ends in stalemate. Assured of asylum by Aegeus, king of Athens, Medea sends her children to the bride with a poisoned robe and golden crown that destroy both princess and father, and she then kills her own sons so that Jason is left wholly bereft. The play closes with Medea appearing above the house in the chariot of the Sun, refusing Jason the bodies of the children for burial and foretelling his dishonourable death, before departing for Athens.
grc.euripides.suppliants: Suppliants is a classical Greek tragedy by Euripides. It opens at Eleusis, where the childless mothers of the Seven who fell before Thebes supplicate Demeter, and Aethra, mother of Theseus, pleads their cause with her son. Theseus wins the Athenian assembly's approval to recover the dead, rebuffs the herald sent by Creon in a debate on monarchy and democracy, defeats the Thebans in battle, and brings the bodies back for cremation; the play then presents the mothers' laments, Evadne's self-immolation on her husband Capaneus's pyre, and Athena's closing epiphany, which imposes an oath of peace on Adrastus and foretells the vengeance of the dead men's sons.
grc.galen.de_comate_secundum_hippocratem: Galen opens by asking what the name 'coma' signifies in Hippocrates, drowsy sinking into sleep, sleep itself, or a lethargic torpor, and reviews the divergent answers of earlier interpreters. Drawing chiefly on the third book of the Epidemics and on the Prognostic, he argues that Hippocrates repeatedly pairs coma with sleeplessness, so that the word cannot simply mean sleep or drowsiness. He distinguishes two kinds of sinking (kataphora), the heavy sleepiness proper to lethargic patients and a heavy but rousable, sleepless torpor that occurs in cases of phrenitis, maintaining that both fall under the name of coma. A final discussion defends the interrogative force of Hippocrates' phrase 'are they phrenitic?', reading his hesitation as a sign of an early stage of illness that may end either in lethargy or in phrenitis.
grc.galen.de_compositione_medicamentorum_sec: A Greek pharmacological treatise by Galen, De Compositione Medicamentorum Secundum Locos sets out compound drug recipes arranged according to the parts of the body they treat. It opens by arguing that therapy is indicated not by the disease alone but also by the patient's constitution and the nature of the affected part, and announces a survey of suitable remedies beginning with the head. The work proceeds through preparations for scalp and hair complaints such as alopecia and baldness, dentifrices and mouth remedies, and plasters and ointments for sciatica, gout, and arthritis, many of the formulas ascribed to earlier physicians such as Andromachus, Asclepiades, Heras, Timocrates, and Damocrates, accompanied by Galen's comments on the powers, proportions, and correct preparation of the ingredients.
grc.galen.de_experientia_medica: The De Experientia Medica (On Medical Experience) is a Greek polemic by the physician Galen against the Empirical school of medicine, cast in the form of a dialogue. The Greek opens and closes in mid-argument, with a speaker mocking an Empiricist opponent who still awaits the seventh and eighth observations before conceding anything to experience. The debate then demands that the Empiricists state how many observations suffice for a reliable generalisation, faults them for supplying no measure of the 'often', and weighs their appeals to Democritus' distrust of the senses and to Plato's definition of an art as unreasoning practice. It concludes that, even if countless similar observations were granted, the Empiricists could establish no medical doctrine, since no measure of frequency exists across the differing conditions of patients.
grc.galen.de_simplicium_medicamentorum_tempe: A Greek pharmacological treatise by Galen, De Simplicium Medicamentorum Temperamentis ac Facultatibus sets out how single, uncompounded drugs act on the body through the primary qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. The opening argument defines the terms pharmakon and dynamis, distinguishes simple from compound medicines, and rejects the position of the Sceptic philosophers and the Empiric doctors that such powers are unknowable, holding instead that they arise from the four elemental qualities. Galen lays down a method of testing each drug by its observed effect on the body to which it is administered, insisting that judgement rest on the substance itself rather than on colour, texture, or incidental properties. Examples drawn from substances such as pepper, hellebore, henbane, and mandrake illustrate the classification of simple drugs by their degrees of heating, cooling, drying, and moistening.
grc.galen.de_venae_sectione_adversus_erasist: Galen's Greek prose treatise De Venae Sectione Adversus Erasistratum ('On Venesection Against Erasistratus') is a polemical defence of phlebotomy aimed at the school which, following Erasistratus, declined to employ it. The opening asks why an author so meticulous over trifles such as recipes for boiled vegetables and poultices should have passed over venesection in near-total silence. The body of the work reports the objections of Erasistratus' followers and of Chrysippus of Cnidus, rehearses the Erasistratean physiology in which fever and inflammation arise from blood driven into the arteries, and answers it with Hippocratic passages prescribing the cutting of veins, nature's ordinary evacuations in menstruation, haemorrhoids and lactation, the concordant practice of physicians of every sect, and the argument that drawing blood is easier to control in measure than drugs, clysters or fasting. The closing argument turns Erasistratus' own admissions against him, contending that since he concedes the need to evacuate plethora while denying that fasting evacuates, venesection remains the speedy and safe remedy his silence had omitted.
grc.galen.natural_faculties: A Greek treatise in three books by Galen on the natural faculties through which living bodies are governed. The opening separates the works of the soul, such as perception and voluntary movement, from the works of nature, growth and nutrition, which animals share with plants, and announces an inquiry into the powers by which these works are accomplished. The argument maintains that every part of the body possesses innate attractive, retentive, alterative, and expulsive faculties, demonstrated through digestion, the formation of blood, the secretion of urine and bile, growth, generation, and the working of organs such as the stomach, womb, kidneys, and spleen, while Erasistratus, Asclepiades, and their followers are attacked for denying such powers. Throughout, Hippocrates and Aristotle serve as authorities for a physiology of alteration by the hot, the cold, the dry, and the wet.
grc.galen.protrepticus: A Greek prose protreptic by Galen urging young men to devote themselves to education in the arts. It opens by asking whether the so-called irrational animals share in reason, concluding that man alone is properly called rational because of his command of the arts and sciences. The argument then contrasts the unstable goddess Fortune with Hermes as master of reason and inventor of every craft, depicting the ruin that overtakes the pursuers of wealth, noble birth, and beauty, before passing to a sustained attack on athletic training as useless for war, health, and livelihood, illustrated from Euripides and Hippocrates and by the story of Milon of Croton and the fable of animals crowned at Olympia. In closing it commends the liberal arts, and above all medicine, as the worthiest object of a young man's labour.
grc.galen.synopsis_librorum_suorum_de_pulsib: Galen's Greek synopsis of his own books on the pulse opens with a defence of epitome-writing: because learners shrink from detailed treatises yet are harmed by faulty summaries made by others, he explains, he was driven to compress his own sixteen-book work on the pulse, four books each on its differences, diagnosis, causes, and prognosis, into a single overview. The treatise then defines the pulse as the artery's perceptible expansion and surveys the kinds of difference pulses exhibit in size, speed, strength, hardness, rhythm, and regularity, teaching how each is distinguished by the fingers and how the hand should be laid on the vessel. Later chapters take up the causes that produce and alter the pulse, the variation proper to sex, age, season, climate, and locality, and the prognostic value of pulse diagnosis in fevers and crises, naming aberrant forms such as the wave-like, gazelle-like, worm-like, ant-like, and mouse-like pulses. Along the way it criticises Herophilus' rhythmic reckoning of pulse-times and Erasistratus' account of the pulse as a movement of pneuma, before breaking off before its exposition is complete.
grc.hanno.periplus_hannonis: The Periplus of Hanno is a short Greek narrative, of uncertain date, cast as the report of Hanno, a Carthaginian sent beyond the Pillars of Heracles to found cities of the Libyphoenicians on the Atlantic coast of Africa. It opens with the Carthaginians' decision to equip sixty penteconters carrying men and women to the number of some thirty thousand, together with grain and other provisions. The account then follows the fleet down the coast through settlements such as Thymiaterion and the island Kernē, meetings with the friendly Lixitae and their Ethiopian neighbours, lakes and great rivers teeming with crocodiles and hippopotamuses, and a succession of wonders, nocturnal fires, a burning and impassable country, a mountain called the Chariot of the Gods, an island resounding with flutes, cymbals and drums, until, in the Horn of the South, three hairy women whom the interpreters call Gorillas are seized and their skins carried back to Carthage, where dwindling stores end the voyage. The narrative closes with this return rather than any formal conclusion.
grc.hippocrates.de_articulis: A Greek surgical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, De Articulis treats the diagnosis, reduction, and aftercare of dislocated and subluxated joints. It opens with the shoulder, distinguishing the directions in which the humeral head may slip and comparing methods of forcing it back, from the heel and the ladder to a shaped wooden lever that its author ranks best of all. The discussion then proceeds joint by joint through the elbow, wrist, fingers, jaw, nose, ear, spine, ribs, hip, knee, ankle, and foot, giving the signs of each displacement, techniques of leverage, extension, and bandaging, and the complications to be expected. Extensive passages cover the fatal danger of reducing open dislocations, gangrene and amputation, the wasting and shortening that follow unreduced dislocations, and congenital deformities such as club foot, with digressions on anatomy, on the constitution of patients and the physiology of cattle, on the legendary Amazons, and on a quotation from Homer.
grc.hippocrates.de_morbis_popularibus: A Greek medical treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, conventionally titled in Latin De Morbis Popularibus and known in English as the Epidemics. It opens with a record of the seasons and weather at Thasos around the autumn equinox, followed by an account of the year's constitution and the disorders that prevailed in it. The work proceeds through general descriptions of the epidemic ailments, continued and intermittent fevers, consumption, erysipelas, phrenitis and bowel complaints, along with discussions of the types of fever and of the critical days on which crises, relapses and recoveries fall. Its largest portion consists of individual case histories of named patients, at Thasos, Abdera, Larisa, Cyzicus and other towns, each traced day by day through symptoms, excretions, crises and outcomes in survival or death.
grc.hippocrates.de_officina_medici: De Officina Medici is a short Greek treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date. It opens with a reflection on knowledge gathered through the senses and then enumerates, in terse, list-like prose, the elements of the surgical setting: the patient, the operator, the assistants, the instruments, the light, the place, the manner and the time. The bulk of the work prescribes the physician's posture, bearing, and training of both hands, and sets out detailed rules for bandages, padding, splints, the reduction of fractures and dislocations, the use of warm water, massage, and the timing of dressing changes.
grc.hippocrates.epidemiarum: Epidemiarum (Epidemics) is a Greek medical treatise of the Hippocratic Corpus, attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, which records the seasonal 'constitutions', the weather and prevailing diseases, of particular places together with clinical case histories. It begins at Thasos with an account of one year's autumn, winter, spring, and summer conditions and the illnesses that followed, above all a widespread and fatal outbreak of phthisis among the young. The work proceeds in the same manner through further years and localities, describing fevers, bowel complaints, and other epidemic ailments, and interleaves these surveys with a long series of brief case notes naming individual patients, wrestlers, women in childbirth, children, and wounded men, whose symptoms, crisis days, outcomes, and occasional dietary or pharmacological treatments are set down in sequence.
grc.hippocrates.prorrheticon_i: The Prorrheticon is a prognostic treatise attributed to Hippocrates and of uncertain date, made up of short, often aphoristic statements of the signs from which the course and outcome of disease may be foretold. It opens with signs present at the onset of illness, taking drowsiness combined with pains of the head, loins, flanks, and neck, together with wakefulness, as pointing to phrenitis. The main body catalogues such indications for acute fevers, delirium, tremors, sweats, the state of the tongue, urine, and bowel discharges, loss of voice and nosebleed, repeatedly marking them as fatal, doubtful, or favourable, with occasional reference to named patients, several of them from Cos. Toward the end the terse entries give way to fuller discussions that instruct the physician in questioning patients, covering disorders of menstruation and the womb, chronic headache, night blindness, sciatica, and other long-standing complaints.
grc.libanius.declamations_1-12: A collection of twelve declamations by Libanius, Greek speeches cast as pleas before courts or assemblies and delivered in the personae of figures from myth and classical history. The opening speech is a defence of Socrates at his trial, in which a companion of the philosopher answers the charges of Anytus, Meletus and Lycon before the Athenian jurors. The remaining declamations carry the same form through other subjects and speakers drawn from the Trojan cycle and Athenian public life, among them an Achilles who justifies his anger and refuses the gifts and marriage alliance offered by Agamemnon, and, at the close, a Timon who laments that love for Alcibiades has overthrown his celebrated misanthropy. The speeches throughout treat both legendary and historical characters within the fixed shape of an imagined address to judges or listeners.
grc.lucian.de_astrologia: A short Greek dialogue by Lucian, composed in an archaizing Ionic style, opens with the speaker's complaint that the learned cultivate every other art while neglecting astrology, which he champions as the oldest of sciences and the work of god-favored early kings. The work then traces the art's descent from the Ethiopians, who first observed the moon's phases and the wandering planets, to the Egyptians, who fixed the twelve zodiacal signs and the measures of months and years, and onward to the oracle of Ammon among the Libyans and the Babylonians, before reaching the Greeks through Orpheus. A long central sequence rereads Greek myths, Tiresias' double nature, the golden ram in the strife of Atreus and Thyestes, Bellerophon, Phrixus, Daedalus, Icarus and Pasiphae, Phaethon, Endymion, the divine parentages of Minos, Aeneas and Autolycus, Cronus' slow course, episodes in Homer and Hesiod, the oracles of Delphi and Didyma, Odysseus' consultation of Tiresias, and Lycurgus' Spartan laws, as distorted memories of celestial knowledge. The dialogue closes by rebutting objections that astrology is impossible or useless, arguing that the stars' movements bring foreknowledge that makes coming goods and evils easier to bear.
grc.lucian.de_parasito_sive_artem_esse_paras: A short comic dialogue by Lucian of Samosata in which Tychiades asks the parasite Simon what art he practises, and Simon, conceding knowledge of no conventional craft, claims mastery of one only: the 'parasitic art' of dining at other men's tables. The body of the work consists of Simon's mock-serious defence of parasitism as a genuine technē, with a formal definition, an argument that it surpasses rhetoric and philosophy, examples of philosophers such as Aeschines, Aristippus and Plato said to have lived as parasites at tyrants' courts, and Homeric heroes, notably Nestor and Patroclus, claimed as practitioners of the same art. Simon then compares the parasite favourably with orators and philosophers in both war and peace, extols his freedom from fear, ambition and love of money, and presents him as a blessing and guardian to the rich man he attends, whereupon Tychiades declares himself Simon's first pupil in the art.
grc.lucian.dialogi_deorum: The Dialogues of the Gods (Dialogi Deorum) is a set of miniature comic dialogues in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, staged among the Olympians and conducted in everyday colloquial speech. The collection opens with Prometheus chained on the Caucasus bargaining with Zeus for his release. From there the dialogues range over Zeus' love affairs with Ganymede, Io, Semele, Danaë and Alcmene, Hera's jealous quarrels, Ixion's cloud-bride, the births of Athena, Dionysus and Heracles, the net in which Hephaestus traps Ares and Aphrodite, Apollo's mourning for Hyacinthus, Pan's claim to divine parentage, and Hermes' laments over his endless errands. Throughout, the gods appear as a quarrelsome, amorous household, their mythic exploits recounted as gossip, bickering and domestic comedy.
grc.lucian.herodotus: A short Greek prose piece by Lucian of Samosata bearing the title Herodotus. It opens with the wish that one might imitate even a single excellence of Herodotus, such as the beauty of his language, his Ionic harmony, or the wit of his judgment. The narrative recounts how Herodotus, sailing from Caria, read his nine books, later called the Muses, before the assembled Greeks at Olympia and so won a pan-Hellenic reputation, notes the sophists and writers who afterward followed the same route to fame, and describes at length the painter Aetion's picture of the marriage of Alexander and Roxane exhibited at the same festival. It closes with Lucian likening his own presentation of his works to the assembled Macedonians to Herodotus' recitation, in hope of a similar renown.
grc.lucian.hesiod: A brief Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, conducted between Hesiod and an unnamed critic. The critic opens by charging Hesiod with breaking the promise made in his verse that the Muses granted him knowledge of things past and to come, since he recounted the births of the gods and gave farming counsel yet never foretold anything useful to life. Hesiod replies that the Works and Days offers practical instruction on agriculture, seasons and labour rather than divination, that the Muses bestow their gifts as they please, and that poets fill out their lines for metre and euphony without incurring a duty of literal completeness. He then ridicules the idea that weather-wisdom in ploughing and sowing amounts to true mantic art, and the exchange closes with the retort that Hesiod's claimed inspiration was not even reliable, having left its promised foreknowledge unfulfilled.
grc.lucian.imagines: A Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, cast as a conversation between Lycinus and Polystratus. It opens with Polystratus recounting how, on catching sight of a beautiful woman, he stood all but petrified like one who has looked upon the Gorgon. The dialogue then proceeds to a sustained verbal portraiture: her bodily beauty is assembled feature by feature from celebrated sculptures, including the Cnidian Aphrodite of Praxiteles and works of Phidias, Alcamenes, Calamis and Sosandra, and given colour by the most famous painters, after which she is identified as Panthea, the companion of a king. The second half paints images of her soul in turn, praising her education, wisdom, goodness, temperance and modest bearing in high fortune, and it closes with the proposal to combine body and soul into a single written portrait more lasting than any work of brush or chisel.
grc.lucian.phalaris: Phalaris is a pair of rhetorical speeches in Greek by Lucian of Samosata, staged at Delphi over the question of whether to accept the bronze bull dedicated by Phalaris, tyrant of Acragas. It opens as the tyrant's envoys address the Delphians, relaying his request that the god receive the offering and his plea that his reputation for cruelty is undeserved. The envoys' speech then unfolds a sustained apology, narrating Phalaris's seizure of power amid faction at Acragas, his professed moderation, his justification for punishing plotters, and the story of Perilaus, the craftsman who devised the bull as an engine of torture and was shut inside it as its first victim. A Delphian speaker closes the work by arguing that the dedication must be received, since the sanctuary has never examined the character of donors and doing so now would profane established custom.
grc.lucian.pro_lapsu_inter_salutandum: A short prose piece by Lucian of Samosata in which the speaker recounts a slip of the tongue: greeting a patron at daybreak, he has wished him 'hugiainein' ('be in good health') where custom demanded 'chairein', and stood rebuked before the onlookers. The bulk of the work is the written apology the speaker resolves to compose, a survey of greetings and the openings of letters in antiquity: the use of 'chairein' in Homer, tragedy and comedy, Plato's replacement of it with 'eu prattein', the Pythagorean and Epicurean preference for 'hugiainein', and anecdotes of Alexander and Hephaestion, Antiochus, Ptolemy, Pyrrhus and Augustus. The argument turns the lapse into a propitious omen, attributed to the favour of Hygieia or Asclepius, and the piece closes with the apology addressed to the speaker's friend Asclepius.
grc.lucian.pseudologista: The Pseudologista is a short Greek invective by Lucian of Samosata, in which a speaker denounces a malicious critic who has taunted him as a barbarian and jeered at his declamations. Threatening repayment in the biting iambs associated with Archilochus, the speaker appeals to the prologue-figure of a Menandrian comedy as an ally in frank speech and rehearses the man's notorious conduct. The closing portion recounts an anecdote from Olympia, where a sophist passed off as his own improvisation a written speech about Pythagoras that had been patched together from borrowed material, while the audience recognised each stolen passage.
grc.lucian.quomodo_historia_conscribenda_sit: The Quomodo Historia Conscribenda Sit ('How History Should Be Written') is a satirical treatise on the craft of historiography by Lucian of Samosata, cast as advice to a friend named Philo. It opens with the comic story of the Abderites, who fell into collective madness and declaimed Euripides after a performance of the Andromeda, a condition Lucian likens to the epidemic of would-be historians that followed a recent war between Romans and Parthians. The greater part of the essay mocks the faults of these contemporaries, among them bombastic prologues, servile imitation of Thucydides and Herodotus, flattery, implausible exaggeration, and gross errors of geography. It then turns to positive precepts: the historian should be politically perceptive, fearless and impartial, devoted above all to truth, writing for posterity rather than present applause, and setting out events in plain, clear diction, carefully ordered and proportioned like a sculptor shaping given material.
grc.lucian.scytha: The Scythian is a short prose piece by Lucian of Samosata in which a Syrian speaker tells of Scythians at Athens, opening with the story of Toxaris, a man of common Scythian stock who came to Greece before Anacharsis in his desire for Greek learning, died at Athens, and received heroic honours as a healer. In the Ceramicus Toxaris greets the newly landed Anacharsis, who in his bewilderment is on the point of sailing home, and hears from him a request to be guided through the finest of Athens and of Greece. Toxaris instead leads him to Solon, presenting the aged lawgiver as Greece entire and the touchstone of Attic wisdom, and Anacharsis goes on to be initiated and, as the account runs, made a citizen of Athens. The speaker closes by comparing his own arrival in the city, years later, with Anacharsis' perplexity, and reports the Athenians' counsel that he attach himself to an eminent father and son, whose further praise he promises to give.
grc.lucian.tyrannicida: A short Greek declamation by Lucian, cast as the defense speech of a man claiming the public reward for tyrannicide after killing two tyrants in a single day. The speech opens with the speaker presenting his exploit to the judges: he cut down the tyrant's son with his own sword and then brought the aged father, through grief, to slay himself with the same blade. The bulk of the work answers an objector who holds that the law's reward belongs only to the man whose own hand did the killing: the speaker recounts his storming of the acropolis and defeat of the bodyguard, dwells on the son's harsher tyranny and the father's doting subjection to him, and dramatizes the old man's lament over his dying child and his trembling suicide. He argues that whoever supplies the cause of death counts as the killer under the law, and closes by asking the judges to weigh the design and entire outcome of the deed rather than the exact manner of the tyrant's death.
grc.lucian.vitarum_auctio: Vitarum Auctio is a short comic dialogue in Greek by Lucian of Samosata: Zeus orders Hermes to prepare a marketplace and herald an auction at which the lives of the philosophers are to be sold. A would-be purchaser examines each lot in turn, beginning with a long-haired Pythagorean who teaches the harmony of the universe and transmigration, and going on to a dog-like Cynic, a drunken Cyrenaic hedonist, a laughing philosopher from Abdera and a weeping one from Ephesus, an Athenian expounding the theory of forms and community of women, an Epicurean gourmet, a Stoic expert in syllogisms and paradoxes, a double-natured Peripatetic, and a Pyrrhonian skeptic who professes ignorance of everything. The exchanges trade in mockery of each school's doctrines and jargon, and the lots are variously bought, refused, or left unsold. At the close Zeus and Hermes dismiss the crowd with a promise to auction the lives of ordinary and tradesman-like men on the following day.
grc.maximus_of_tyre.dialexeis: The Dialexeis of Maximus of Tyre, also transmitted under the title Philosophumena, is a collection of philosophical lectures composed in Greek. It consists of orations on ethical and philosophical subjects, the first of which contrasts the actors of Dionysus with the philosopher, who plays many roles in a civic drama directed by god. That opening oration argues that the philosopher's logos must adapt to every occasion of human life, illustrating the point with Homeric quotations and analogies drawn from musical harmonies, rivers, and athletic contests.
grc.niciae_epistula.epistula: A single Greek letter attributed to Nicias, the Athenian general in Sicily, addressed to the Athenians during the campaign against Syracuse. It opens with a reminder that earlier deeds are known to the recipients from previous letters, and then reports the arrival of the Spartan Gylippus with reinforcements, a battle lost before the walls, and the abandonment of the siege works. The greater part recounts the decay of the fleet and its crews through rotten hulls, casualties, desertion and the hostility of the countryside, together with the weakness of the remaining allies, before closing with an urgent demand for fresh land and naval forces, money and a successor commander on account of the writer's kidney illness, and a warning that decisions must be taken at once with the coming of spring.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_timotheum_ii: The Second Letter to Timothy, one of the Pastoral Epistles of the Greek New Testament, is framed as a letter from the apostle Paul, presented as imprisoned and near death, to his beloved associate Timothy; its date is uncertain. It opens with a greeting and thanksgiving in which Paul recalls Timothy's sincere faith, inherited from his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to rekindle his gift and not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul's chains. The body of the letter moves through images of the soldier, athlete and farmer, warnings against vain disputes and teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus, a catalogue of the vices that will prevail in the last days, an appeal to remain in the inspired scriptures, and a solemn charge to preach the word in season and out of season. It closes with Paul's sense that the hour of his departure has come, requests that Timothy bring Mark, his cloak and the parchments, reports on companions who have left or stayed, and greetings that lead into a final benediction of grace.
grc.philip_ii_king_of_macedonia.epistulae: A brief Greek collection of royal letters attributed to Philip II of Macedon. The opening letter, addressed to the council and people of Athens, announces Philip's campaigns in Phocis and warns the Athenians to abide by their sworn agreements. The remaining pieces deal chiefly with relations with Athens: a long letter catalogs grievances ranging from the imprisonment of the herald Nicias and the conduct of the general Diopeithes to the dispute over Halonnesus and rival claims to Amphipolis, while shorter notes to the Thebans and to the Peloponnesian allies take up peace overtures and a summons to arms against the Locrians who had violated the sanctuary at Delphi. The collection closes with a correspondence with Aristotle, in which Philip announces the birth of a son and asks that Aristotle rear and educate him, followed by a reply on virtue and the conduct of rule.
grc.philo_judaeus.de_ebrietate: De Ebrietate ('On Drunkenness') is a Greek allegorical treatise by the Jewish philosopher Philo Judaeus, which opens by recalling what other philosophers had said about drunkenness in a preceding book and turning to what Moses the Lawgiver holds on the subject. The work surveys the Law's differing commands concerning wine, from the Nazirites and the priests to the drunken and disobedient son condemned to be stoned, and interprets drunkenness as a figure for the folly that springs from lack of education, ignorance, and insatiable appetite. Biblical episodes throughout, Noah's nakedness, Jacob and Esau, Jethro, Laban, Rachel and Leah, the Levites' slaughter at the golden calf, Phinehas, Lot with his daughters, Pharaoh's chief butler and baker, and Hannah the mother of Samuel, are expounded as symbols of vice and of knowledge, set against the sobriety of those who follow right reason and virtue.
grc.philo_judaeus.in_flaccum: A Greek historical and moralising treatise by Philo Judaeus on the fall of Aulus Avillius Flaccus, Roman prefect of Alexandria and Egypt under Tiberius and Gaius. It opens by ranking Flaccus as heir to Sejanus's designs against the Jewish nation, then catalogues his capable and orderly early administration. With Tiberius's death and Gaius's accession the prefect degenerates, and the narrative follows his connivance at mob violence against the Alexandrian Jews, the desecration of their synagogues, the public floggings and the forcing of Jewish women to eat pork, together with his obstruction of the embassy bearing a decree of homage to the emperor until King Agrippa secures its passage. The work closes with Flaccus's arrest at a banquet, his banishment to Andros, and a violent death presented as retribution for the innocent blood he shed, framed throughout as proof that the Jewish nation did not lack divine aid.
grc.plato.alcibiades_1: A Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato, in which Socrates converses with the young Alcibiades shortly before the latter's first appearance in Athenian public life. The conversation opens with Socrates explaining his long attachment and declaring that a daimonic opposition to their association has now ceased. Socrates then subjects Alcibiades' political ambitions to questioning, showing that he cannot say what justice is, that the just and the advantageous coincide, and that the many are incompetent teachers of such matters; the discussion passes to self-knowledge and the care of the soul, which is identified as the true self, and to the contest Alcibiades must prepare for against the kings of Sparta and Persia rather than his fellow citizens. It closes with Socrates presenting himself as the only genuine lover of Alcibiades' soul and warning that only virtue, cultivated through mutual self-examination, will secure the happiness of both and of the city.
grc.plato.critias: Plato's Critias is a short, unfinished dialogue, presented as the continuation of the Timaeus, in which Critias undertakes to describe a war fought some nine thousand years before between primordial Athens and the island of Atlantis. Opening with Critias' plea for indulgence after Timaeus' speech, the work first recounts the ancient constitution of Athens, its warrior class living in common around the temple of Athena and Hephaestus, and the pristine fertility of Attica. It then turns to Atlantis, describing Poseidon's union with Cleito, the island's division into ten kingdoms among his sons, the concentric rings of land and water about the royal city, its temples, palaces, canals, harbours, military organisation and royal laws, and the corruption that overtakes its kings as the divine element in them wanes. The narrative breaks off abruptly just as Zeus gathers the gods to deliver judgement on the Atlantians.
grc.plato.epinomis: A short Greek dialogue attributed to Plato, the Epinomis serves as an appendix to the Laws and reopens the conversation of the Athenian Stranger, Cleinias, and Megillus over the question left unfinished there: what learning makes a human being truly wise. Surveying the practical arts, farming, building, generalship, medicine, divination, music, and the rest, the speaker argues that none of them yields wisdom, which rests instead on number and mathematics, crowned by astronomy. A theology follows in which the celestial bodies are visible, ensouled gods, soul is older than body, and the cosmos is filled with the five kinds of living beings born of fire, air, water, earth, and aether. The work closes by prescribing this mathematical and astronomical study, pursued through a life of piety, as the proper discipline of the nocturnal council and the source of virtue and happiness for the city.
grc.plato.minos: A short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato and of uncertain date, in which Socrates discusses the nature of law with an unnamed companion. It opens with the question of what law is and the suggestion that law is simply whatever is held or decreed by a city, which the two speakers proceed to examine and revise. The argument develops the claims that law aims at the discovery of truth, that the writings of doctors, gardeners, cooks, and kings are the laws of their respective arts, and that the variation and change of laws among peoples show that most people have not found what truly is, before turning to an encomium of Minos, defended from Homer and Hesiod as a pupil of Zeus and a beneficent lawgiver whose unchanging Cretan laws were slandered by Athenian poets because of the tribute. The dialogue closes with Socrates asking what the good lawgiver distributes to the soul to make it better, a question the companion is unable to answer.
grc.plutarch.apophthegmata_laconica: A Greek collection of brief sayings of Spartan kings and citizens, preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch. It opens with the answers of Agasicles, including his reason for refusing to study under the sophist Philophanes, and passes to Agesilaus, whose terse replies are interleaved with episodes from his campaigns against Tissaphernes and the Persian king and his dealings with Greek cities. Later sections gather the remarks of Cleomenes, Labotas, Leotychidas, and other royal and private Spartans on command, warfare, piety, wealth, and laconic brevity of speech. The work closes with anecdotes of anonymous Laconians, including their answers to Philip of Macedon and Antipater and vignettes of Spartan conduct at Olympia and elsewhere.
grc.plutarch.aquane_an_ignis_sit_utilior: Aquane an Ignis Sit Utilior ('Whether Water or Fire Is the More Useful') is a short Greek treatise by Plutarch, preserved among his Moralia. It opens from Pindar's verdict that water is best, weighed against the view of those natural philosophers who make fire the first principle of all things. The body of the work consists of antithetical arguments: the case for water rests on its constant necessity for all creatures, its priority over the fire later ascribed to Prometheus, its role in the growth of plants and crops, its harmlessness and equal availability to rich and poor, and the sea's power to join humankind in exchange, while the opposing case credits fire with sustaining the heat on which life depends, with the invention of the crafts under Hephaestus, with the extension of the usable day, and with the kinship of sight, the keenest sense, to flame.
grc.plutarch.aristides: The Aristides is one of Plutarch's Greek biographies (Lives) of the Athenian statesman surnamed 'the Just'. It opens by weighing conflicting reports about Aristides' poverty, answering the objections of Demetrius of Phalerum before turning to the career itself. The narrative follows his long rivalry with Themistocles, his part at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea, where the battle is recounted in unusual detail down to the dispute over the award of valour, together with his ostracism and recall. Later chapters cover his assessment of the allies' tribute after Athens assumed command, anecdotes of his incorruptibility, his death, and the public honours paid to his family.
grc.plutarch.comparationis_aristophanes_et_m: A brief Greek comparison of the comic poets Aristophanes and Menander, preserved among the Moralia attributed to Plutarch, which opens by pronouncing Menander by far the superior poet in general terms. The essay then censures Aristophanes' diction as coarse and ill-suited, adducing its antitheses, like word-endings, paronomasia, and jumbled stylistic registers, illustrated with quotations from his plays. Menander's language is in turn praised for its blended consistency, fitting every character, age, and circumstance as no craftsman's product fits all wearers, while remarks on the poets' audiences and reputations contrast Aristophanes' bitter, biting salt with the universal charm that made Menander at home in theatres, schools, and symposia.
grc.plutarch.comparison_aristides_cato: The Greek synkrisis, the formal comparison Plutarch appended to his paired Lives of Aristides and Cato the Elder, opens by observing that each life set whole against the other makes their difference hard to discern amid many great resemblances, since both men rose to office and renown without inherited advantage. It then weighs the pair point by point: their different entries into public life amid the still modest wealth of Athens and the grandee politics of Rome; their military records, with Aristides serving at Marathon, Salamis and Plataea while Cato distinguished himself in Spain and in the war against Antiochus; and their political fortunes, Aristides' ostracism by Themistocles set against Cato's escape from repeated public prosecutions. Further sections compare their household economy and attitude to money, defending Aristides' voluntary poverty as a mark of self-sufficiency while questioning Cato's thrift, and take up self-praise, frankness and political ambition. The comparison ends with their marriages, charging that Cato's wedding in old age to the daughter of a serving man brought scandal upon his reputation for temperance.
grc.plutarch.comparison_demetrius_antony: A short formal comparison (synkrisis) in Greek, closing the paired Lives of Demetrius and Antony by Plutarch. The piece opens by observing that great reversals of fortune befell both men and proposes to weigh first their power and prominence, noting that Demetrius inherited an empire largely made by his father Antigonus while Antony raised himself from obscure origins to claim Caesar's place. It then sets their careers point against point: Demetrius' liberation of Greek cities against Antony's war on Cassius and Brutus, their generosity, their luxury and love affairs, with Cleopatra's hold on Antony likened to Omphale's stripping of Heracles, their marriages, acts of impiety, treatment of parents and kin, breaches of sworn agreements, and the differing ways each lost his cause. The comparison ends by finding neither man's death praiseworthy, though Demetrius' endurance of captivity is judged the more disgraceful.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_lysander_sulla: A brief comparison by the Greek author Plutarch that formally closes the paired Lives of Lysander and Sulla, opening by turning from the two biographies just completed to the synkrisis. The body of the work sets the men's common rise from obscurity against their different roads to power, Lysander gaining command in a well-ordered Sparta while Sulla emerged amid the corruption and faction of Rome, and then compares their conduct toward friends, their attitudes to money and pleasure, and their private morals. Military achievement is weighed next, Lysander's two naval victories and his inglorious death before Haliartus against Sulla's many pitched battles, his twice holding Rome, and his storming of the Piraeus, with each man's treatment of Athens supplying a final point of moral contrast. The closing verdict judges that Sulla accomplished more while Lysander erred less, awarding the primacy in self-control and temperance to the latter and in generalship and courage to the former.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_nicias_and_crassu: A short Greek prose synkrisis, the formal comparison that Plutarch appends to his paired Lives of the Athenian Nicias and the Roman Crassus. It opens by weighing the two men's wealth, finding Nicias' mining revenues less disreputable than Crassus' gains from Sulla's proscriptions and his fire-brigade speculation. The comparison then proceeds point by point through their public expenditure, their political conduct, and their commands, contrasting the Sicilian expedition with the Parthian campaign, before touching on their attitudes to divination and closing with an assessment of their deaths, in which Crassus' end is judged the more blameless.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_pelopidas_and_mar: A short Greek comparative essay by Plutarch, the formal comparison (syncrisis) closing his paired lives of Pelopidas and Marcellus. It opens with the judgment that the two men matched one another in courage, industriousness, fiery temper, and magnanimity, differing chiefly in that Marcellus inflicted slaughter on the cities he subdued, whereas Pelopidas and Epaminondas never killed a captive or enslaved a city. The discussion then weighs their campaigns, Marcellus's victory over the Celts and capture of Syracuse against Pelopidas's exploits at Tegyra and Leuctra and the liberation of Thebes, alongside their conduct against Hannibal and Sparta and the credit due to each for his deeds. Plutarch ends by lamenting the irrational deaths of both men in battle and by observing that Pelopidas received burial from the allies for whom he fell, while Marcellus was buried by the enemies by whom he fell.
grc.plutarch.comparison_of_timoleon_and_aemi: Plutarch's Comparison of Timoleon and Aemilius Paullus is the short formal synkrisis that concludes the pair of Lives of the Greek liberator of Sicily and the Roman conqueror of Macedon. It opens by observing that the two careers leave little room for contrast, since both men won famous victories over distinguished foes, Aemilius over the Macedonians and the line of Antigonus, Timoleon over the Carthaginians and the tyrants of Sicily. The argument then weighs their unequal circumstances, judging Timoleon's successes over broken tyrants and a great Carthaginian force, achieved with mercenary and disorderly troops, the more creditable, and it praises the purity and justice of both commanders, remarking that no Greek general who touched Sicily, Dion alone excepted, escaped corruption. Further points treat their disinterestedness, since Aemilius enriched himself by not a drachma from the kingdom he overthrew and Timoleon accepted but did not need rewards, and their bearing, with Aemilius proving unbowed by either good fortune or the great calamity of his children's deaths, while Timoleon's remorse over his brother reveals a gentler and more yielding disposition.
