grc.plutarch.de_amicorum_multitudine: A short Greek moral essay by Plutarch from the Moralia, arguing that the pursuit of many friends is a maimed and blind kind of philia and that true friendship cannot be multiplied. It opens with the anecdote of Menon the Thessalian, whose sweeping catalogue of virtues for every age and station draws from Socrates the remark that a man who names many virtues knows none, just as one who falls into many friendships may possess none. The argument plays on the images of Briareus's hundred hands and Argus's watchful eyes, compares affection divided among many to a river split into thin and weak streams, observes that no one can attend to many friends' competing claims at once, and notes that many friends bring many enemies in their train, recalling famous pairs such as Theseus and Pirithous, Achilles and Patroclus, Orestes and Pylades, Damon and Phintias, and Epaminondas and Pelopidas. It concludes that friendship, arising from likeness of character, demands a steadfast disposition rather than the Proteus-like versatility of the man who conforms himself to everyone, whence the rarity of a firm friend.
grc.plutarch.de_faciae_quae_in_orbe_lunae_ap: A dialogue in Greek by Plutarch, De facie quae in orbe lunae apparet ('On the Face Which Appears in the Moon'), opens mid-conversation when Sulla asks the assembled speakers, among them the narrator Lamprias, Lucius, Pharnaces, Apollonides, Theon, and the mathematician Menelaus, to set out the opinions already canvassed about the face visible on the moon. The discussion attacks rival explanations of the markings by reflection from the outer ocean, mixed vapour, or Stoic fire, and argues for a moon compounded of earth and ether, lit by the sun and marked by deep, shadow-holding hollows. Later portions treat the geometry of eclipses and the earth's shadow, questions of weight and cosmic position, and whether the moon could sustain inhabitants, vegetation, and dew of its own. The dialogue closes with Sulla's retelling of a stranger's tale of the northern islands where Cronus sleeps guarded by daimones, and of an afterlife in which earth supplies the body, the moon the soul, and the sun the mind.
grc.plutarch.de_fortuna: De Fortuna (On Fortune), a short Greek essay preserved among the Moralia of Plutarch, argues that human affairs are governed not by chance but by reason and good counsel. It opens by voicing the claim that fortune, not sound deliberation, directs mortal things, and immediately rebuts it with paired exempla: Aristides enduring poverty and Scipio refusing the spoils of Carthage set against Philocrates, Lasthenes, and Euthycrates corrupted by Philip's gold, and Alexander's restraint set against Priam's ruin. The argument goes on to contend that the crafts accomplish their works by rule, measure, and skill rather than luck, that prudence is accordingly the greatest of the arts, and that man, physically naked and defenceless among the beasts, prevails over them through reason, memory, and technique. Drawing on sayings of Sophocles, Plato, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Aeschylus, Hesiod, and Demosthenes along the way, the essay closes with the thought that wealth, fame, and success apart from prudence become sources of harm and disgrace to their possessors.
grc.plutarch.de_sera_numinis_vindicta: Plutarch's dialogue On the Delays of Divine Vengeance, preserved among his Moralia, examines why the gods defer punishment of the wicked. The conversation opens just after an Epicurean speaker has departed following an attack on providence, leaving Plutarch with his companions Patrocleas, Timon, and Olympichus to take up the question. In answer to a series of objections, that late punishment fails to reform or deter, that the gods penalize descendants for ancestors' crimes, and that divine anger falls capriciously on later generations, the speakers argue that postponement allows for repentance and correction, that vice itself torments the evildoer, and that cities and families persist as continuous moral agents across time. The dialogue culminates in the tale of Thespesius of Soli, who, revived after an apparently fatal fall, is conducted through the afterworld and reports on the survival of the soul, its judgment and punishments, a region of Dionysian delight beside Lethe, and the reincarnation of souls, including that of Nero, into new bodies.
grc.plutarch.de_superstitione: De Superstitione is a short Greek moral essay by Plutarch, preserved among the Moralia, treating the passion of deisidaimonia. It opens by dividing ignorance concerning the gods into two currents, atheism arising in harsh temperaments and superstition in softer ones. The argument then sets the two conditions side by side: atheism is defined as a false judgment that produces apathy toward the divine, while superstition is a passion born of false belief, filling its victims with dread of the gods, robbing them of sleep through frightful dreams, driving them to degrading purifications, laments, and self-mortification, and conceiving the divine as cruel and vengeful. Historical exempla, Midas, Aristodemus, Nicias at the lunar eclipse, the Jews keeping the sabbath under siege, Carthaginian child sacrifice, illustrate superstition's ruinous effects in crisis and festivity alike, and the essay closes with the warning that those fleeing superstition too rashly may leap over the piety that lies between and fall into atheism.
grc.plutarch.demetrius: A Greek prose biography by Plutarch of Demetrius Poliorcetes, son of Antigonus and king of Macedon. It opens with a prologue defending the portrayal of men whose great natures carry great vices as well as virtues, and announces that the book will treat Demetrius alongside Antony. The narrative follows Demetrius from his first campaigns under his father, victory over Ptolemy at Salamis in Cyprus, his reception at Athens as saviour and god, and the vast siege of Rhodes that won him the title 'Besieger of Cities', through the disaster at Ipsus where Antigonus fell, his seizure of the Macedonian throne, and renewed wars against Pyrrhus, Lysimachus and the Greek cities, to his final defeat and capture by Seleucus. It closes with his three years of captivity in the Chersonese, his death there, and the royal funeral procession by which his son Antigonus conveyed his remains to Demetrias.
grc.plutarch.galba: Plutarch's Life of Galba, written in Greek, gives a biographical account of the elderly Roman aristocrat who was proclaimed emperor after the fall of Nero and murdered within months. It opens with a general reflection on military discipline, drawn from the disorder of Roman armies and the rapid succession of rulers following Nero's death. The narrative then follows Galba's noble lineage and wealth, his governorship of Spain, the revolt of Vindex that led to his acclamation, the intrigues of Nymphidius Sabinus at Rome, his march to the city, and the growing resentment of soldiers denied their promised donative. It closes with the adoption of Piso, the German legions' proclamation of Vitellius, Otho's conspiracy, Galba's assassination in the Forum, and a concluding assessment of his character and misjudgements.
grc.plutarch.mulierum_virtutes: Plutarch's essay on the virtue of women opens as a letter to Clea that rejects Thucydides' saying about the silence of a good woman and argues that the same virtue belongs to men and women, adducing the Roman custom of public funeral praises. The remainder of the work assembles a series of historical and legendary episodes in which women save, found, or liberate their communities: Trojan women burning the ships in Italy, the women of Phocis, Chios, and Argos with the poet Telesilla against Cleomenes, Persian and Celtic women, Cloelia's escape with the hostages, and the tyrannicides Camma, Aretaphila, and Xenocrite. The collection closes with domestic examples, including Stratonice, Chiomara, Timoclea's defiance of Alexander, Eryxo, and the wife of Pytheas, some episodes reported in variant versions and with occasional citation of earlier authorities.
grc.plutarch.parallela_minora: A short Greek collection of paired anecdotes transmitted in Plutarch's Moralia. It opens with a preface defending ancient history against those who dismiss it as myth: the compiler explains that for each older Greek story he has set a more recent Roman parallel, citing the writers who recorded both. The pairs that follow run through battle narratives such as Marathon beside Metellus's victory and Leonidas beside Fabius Maximus, self-sacrifices like the leaps of Curtius and Anchurus into chasms, tales of cruel hosts and tyrants such as Busiris, Faunus and Phalaris with their Roman counterparts, stories of plague, sacrifice and averted maiden-death, foundlings nursed by she-wolves, strange births and metamorphoses, and city foundation legends like those of Praeneste, each item closing with a named source. The same handful of stories thus reappear on both the Greek and the Roman side throughout, from Cynaethus and Salia to Romulus and Remus.
grc.plutarch.pericles: A Greek biographical essay by Plutarch pairing the life of the Athenian statesman Pericles with that of Fabius Maximus, prefaced by a methodological discussion of how virtuous deeds arouse emulation in the reader. Opening with a genealogy of Pericles, his distinguished ancestry, his unusual physical appearance mocked by comic poets, and his education under musicians, sophists, and above all Anaxagoras, the life then traces his cautious entry into democratic politics, his rivalry with Cimon and Thucydides son of Melesias, and his consolidation of popular power through pay for jury service and public building works. Substantial sections treat the monumental construction programme overseen by Phidias, including the Parthenon and Propylaea, the ensuing accusations against Pericles' associates, his relationship with Aspasia, the Samian revolt and its suppression, and his role in the coming of the Peloponnesian War, the Megarian decree, and his refusal to lift it. The final portion follows the war's outbreak, the plague that destroyed his family and reputation, his brief restoration, his death, and the closing assessment that under his rule Athens was great in deed while no Athenian had cause to wear mourning clothes because of him.
grc.plutarch.praecepta_gerendae_reipublicae: Plutarch's 'Precepts of Statecraft' (Praecepta Gerendae Reipublicae), a treatise in Greek preserved among the Moralia, addresses Menemachus, a young man of good family entering public life, and sets out advice on political conduct. The work opens by contrasting philosophers who merely exhort with the practical statesman, and proceeds through topics such as the motives for entering politics, reading the character of one's citizens, the proper use of speech and rhetoric, the choice of entry into public life, the selection and treatment of friends, the handling of rivals and enmities, conduct under Rome's imperial power, relations with co-officials, and the dangers of ambition and flattery. It closes with counsel on stirring civic concord, avoiding faction and quelling private quarrels before they inflame whole cities, all illustrated with anecdotes and sayings drawn from Greek and Roman history.
grc.plutarch.themistocles: A Greek prose biography by Plutarch, one of the Parallel Lives, devoted to the Athenian statesman and general Themistocles. It opens with his undistinguished parentage: an Athenian father, Neocles, and a mother variously reported as Thracian or Carian, so that his birth was open to question. The narrative follows his rise in politics and rivalry with Aristides, his persuasion of the Athenians to spend the Laurium silver on warships, his leadership against Xerxes at Artemisium and above all at Salamis, and the rebuilding of the walls and the fortification of the Piraeus, before turning to his ostracism, the accusations of collaboration with Persia that arose from Pausanias' treason, his flight through Greece, and his final reception at the Persian court and death at Magnesia. Anecdotes, sayings, and discussion of conflicting traditions handed down by earlier historians run throughout, and the life closes with notices of his children, his tomb, and the honors retained by his descendants.
grc.plutarch.titus_flamininus: A life of the Roman consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus, one of Plutarch's paired biographies and the counterpart to his Philopoemen, opening with a description of Titus's bronze statue in Rome and his quick, ambitious character. The narrative traces his early service in the war against Hannibal and his capture of Tarentum, his unusually early consulship, and his command against Philip V of Macedon, culminating in the defeat of the Macedonian phalanx and his proclamation of the Greeks' freedom at the Isthmian games in Corinth. Later chapters treat his restrained settlement of the war with the Spartan tyrant Nabis, his diplomacy among the Greek cities when Antiochus invaded Greece, his role in Hannibal's death in Bithynia, and the humiliation of his brother Lucius at Cato's hands, and the work ends with a formal comparison of Titus and Philopoemen.
grc.polyaenus.excerpta_polyaeni: The Excerpta Polyaeni is an excerpted collection of military stratagems transmitted under the name of Polyaenus, a Macedonian author of uncertain date. It opens with an encomium of the ideal general, enumerating the endurance, courage, prudence, frugality and piety expected of a commander. The remainder of the work consists of a long series of brief anecdotes, each introduced by the formula Ὅτι ('How...'), in which generals of Greek, Macedonian, Persian, Carthaginian and Roman history, Philip, Alexander, Iphicrates, Agesilaus, Epaminondas, Hannibal, Scipio and Caesar among them, defeat or escape their enemies by feigned retreats, ambushes, spies, forged letters, disguises, deceptions in battle and siege, and tricks at sea. The entries are grouped broadly by subject, moving from ruses in the field and matters of discipline and encampment through sieges, escapes, and naval engagements to wiles of treachery, treason and pursuit.
grc.pseudoaristotle.de_spiritu: A short Greek physiological treatise transmitted under Aristotle's name with the title De Spiritu (On Breath) and of uncertain authorship and date. It opens with the question of how the innate pneuma persists and grows, whether it is nourished through respiration or through the digestion of food carried in with the blood. The body of the work raises puzzles about respiration and its cooling function, the pulse as a movement distinct from breathing and nutrition, the conveyance of nourishment through veins and arteries to flesh, bone and sinew, and the purposes served by bones in movement and support. It concludes by rejecting the notion that a single kind of fire acts alike in all bodies and by asking whether the innate heat of each part operates as instrument, as material, or as both.
grc.pseudogalen.ad_gaurum_quomodo_animetur_f: Ad Gaurum (Πρὸς Γαῦρον περὶ τοῦ πῶς ἐμψυχοῦνται τὰ ἔμβρυα, 'On How Embryos Are Ensouled') is a Neoplatonic treatise of uncertain date and authorship, falsely attributed to Galen and cast as a disputation addressed to a certain Gaurus. It opens by surveying the longstanding perplexity over whether the embryo is an animal or lives only in the manner of a plant, whether potentially or actually alive, and over when the soul may be said to enter the body. The argument then marshals Plato's Timaeus and Phaedrus to distinguish the vegetative from the self-moving soul, rebuts Hippocratic, Stoic (notably Chrysippus's spermatic logoi) and popular explanations, including tales of the father or womb snatching a soul from the air and Chaldaean doctrines of the eastern 'gate of souls', and answers objections drawn from foetal movement and maternal cravings. Its own thesis, supported by analogies of the ship and its steersman, musical harmony, the magnet and naphtha, is that neither parent transmits the rational soul, that embryos live a merely plant-like life in the womb, and that the completed body receives its proper soul from outside at birth, while the closing section, on whether like proceeds from like, survives in damaged condition.
grc.septuaginta.bel_et_draco_theodotionis: The Greek text of Bel and the Dragon, a short prose addition to the Book of Daniel transmitted with the Septuagint tradition in the version associated with Theodotion, opens with the death of Astyages and the accession of Cyrus, as the honoured Daniel disputes with the king over worship of the idol Bel. Daniel proves the idol to be clay and bronze by strewing ashes in its temple and exposing the priests, with their wives and children, who secretly consume its offerings; the king has them slain and gives Bel over to Daniel, who dismantles its temple. Turning to the great dragon venerated by the Babylonians, Daniel kills it with cakes of pitch, fat and hair, and in consequence is cast into the lions' den for six days, where the prophet Habakkuk, carried from Judaea by an angel of the Lord, brings him food.
grc.septuaginta.machabaeorum_g: A Hellenistic Greek prose narrative of uncertain authorship and date, preserved in the Septuagint as the third of the books called Maccabees, recounting the peril and deliverance of the Jews of Egypt under Ptolemy IV Philopator. It opens with Ptolemy, learning that Antiochus has seized territory from him, marching with his sister Arsinoë to Raphia and defeating him in battle, after which he visits Jerusalem and insists on entering the inner sanctuary, from which attempt he is struck down by God. The story then turns to his persecution of the Jews of Alexandria and Egypt: a decree of registration and branding with the ivy mark of Dionysus, imprisonment in the hippodrome, and the twice-delayed stampede of five hundred elephants maddened with wine and frankincense. The aged priest Eleazar intercedes in a prayer recalling past deliverances of Israel, two angels appear and turn the elephants upon the king's own troops, and the work closes with the king's reversal, letters releasing the captives, the punishment of apostate Jews, and the establishment of annual days commemorating the salvation.
grc.septuaginta.malachias: Malachias is the Greek Septuagint version of a short biblical prophecy attributed to the prophet Malachi, of uncertain date in its Hebrew original, rendered into Greek in the Hellenistic period. It opens as a burden, or oracle, of the word of the Lord to Israel, delivered by the hand of an angel. The work proceeds through a series of disputations in which God rebukes the priests for offering blemished sacrifices and profaning the covenant of Levi, and the people for faithlessness, wrongful divorce and withheld tithes, while promising a coming day of the Lord that refines like fire, a sun of righteousness for those who fear his name, and the sending of Elijah the Thesbite before the great and manifest day, closing with an admonition to remember the law of Moses.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_i_sive_chronic: A Greek biblical book preserved in the Septuagint, the First Paralipomenon or Chronicles, rendered from Hebrew into Greek by an anonymous translator in the Hellenistic period. It opens with an unbroken chain of genealogies running from Adam through Noah, Abraham, the twelve tribes, the priestly and Levitical houses, and the settlers of Jerusalem, together with notices of the Edomite kings and the return from Babylon. The narrative portion recounts the death of Saul, David's anointing at Hebron, his capture of Zion and victories over the Philistines and neighboring nations, the transfer of the ark to Jerusalem, the census and ensuing plague, and his extensive military, cultic, and administrative preparations for the temple that Solomon is to build. It closes with David's assembly of all Israel, his charge to Solomon and provision for the temple service, Solomon's enthronement, and David's death after forty years of reign.
grc.septuaginta.psalmi_salomonis: The Psalms of Solomon are a collection of Greek prose psalms of Hellenistic date, transmitted with the Septuagint corpus and bearing Solomon's name in the title, though the works are anonymous. The opening psalm cries out to the Lord in affliction as sinners press upon the speaker, recalling the profanation of Jerusalem's holy places and the mockery of its captors. Across the collection the poems lament the arrogant foreign ruler who trampled the sanctuary and the sins of Jerusalem's own people, denounce hypocrites and the insolent rich, and give voice to the prayers of the pious poor. Later pieces express confidence in God's just judgment, the hope of a purified Zion gathered from exile, and the promise of a Davidic king and resurrection for those who fear the Lord.
grc.soranus.de_fasciis: A short Greek surgical treatise on bandages by Soranus, preserved in some sixty numbered sections. It opens in the midst of instructions for winding a bandage across the brow and over the crown of the head, and the work proceeds part by part through the body, each section prescribing how a named bandage, among them the mitra, basiliskos, charax, sphendone, and thorax, is to be applied. The sequence runs from the skull and face, with dressings for the eyes, nose, jaw, and cheeks, to the chest, shoulder, and collarbone, then to supports for the breast, the groin, the genitals, the arm and hand, and finally the lower leg, ankle, and heel. Each entry states the manner of application together with the injury or condition the bandage suits, keyed to numbered illustration plates.
grc.tryphon_i_grammaticus.περὶ_τρόπων: A short Greek treatise on tropes (peri tropōn) attributed to the grammarian Tryphon and of uncertain date. It opens by defining phrasis as diction conveying heightened signification, dividing it into kuriologia, the proper use of words, and tropos, a turn away from proper usage, and enumerating fourteen principal tropes. The work then proceeds trope by trope through metaphor, catachresis, allegory, riddle, metalepsis, metonymy, synecdoche, coinage, periphrasis, anastrophe, hyperbaton, pleonasm, ellipsis and parapleroma, each defined and illustrated chiefly from Homer with some examples from tragedy, comedy and lyric. A final section catalogues twenty-seven further figures of diction, from hyperbole, emphasis and irony to sarcasm, wit and proverb, with a brief notice distinguishing komma from kolon and assigning the three stylistic characters, austere, middle and slender, to Thucydides, Demosthenes, Lysias and other orators.
grc.xenophon.anabasis: A Greek prose narrative by Xenophon, the Anabasis opens with the rivalry between Cyrus the Younger and his elder brother Artaxerxes and recounts Cyrus' secret assembly of a Greek mercenary force under cover of campaigns against the Pisidians and Tissaphernes. The work takes its name from the army's march up-country from Sardis into the interior of the Persian empire, and goes on to follow the fortunes of the Greek soldiers after Cyrus' death in battle. Xenophon himself appears in the narrative among those who lead the retreat.
grc.archimedes.dimensio_circuli: The Dimensio Circuli ('Measurement of a Circle') is a brief Greek mathematical treatise by Archimedes consisting of three propositions on the geometry of the circle. It opens by proving that every circle is equal to a right triangle whose one leg about the right angle equals the radius and whose base equals the circumference. The second proposition establishes that the area of a circle has to the square on its diameter the ratio of 11 to 14. The third and longest proposition demonstrates, by successively bisecting the angles of inscribed and circumscribed polygons, that the circumference of any circle exceeds three times its diameter by less than a seventh and by more than ten seventy-firsts.
grc.aristotle.de_divinatione_per_somnum: A short treatise by Aristotle, transmitted among the Parva Naturalia, on the divination that is said to occur through dreams. It opens by observing that such divination is neither easy to despise nor easy to credit, since dreams appear significant to many people although no evident cause for them can be found. The argument distinguishes dreams as causes, signs, or coincidences of what comes to pass, notes that reputable physicians attend closely to dreams as indications of bodily conditions, and concludes that most dreams, especially those concerning distant events, are mere coincidences, which is why many fail to come true. Dreams are held to be daimonic rather than god-sent, arising from faint natural movements that the sleeping mind perceives more readily by night, so that prophetic aptitude belongs to ordinary, excitable, and melancholic characters rather than to the wisest, while the best judge of dreams is one who can discern resemblances in their distorted images; the closing sentence recalls that sleep, dreaming, and divination from dreams have now all been discussed.
grc.artaxerxis_epistulae.epistulae: Two royal letters in Greek attributed to the Persian king Artaxerxes and preserved among the Greek epistolographers. The first purports to be the decree ordering the extermination of the Jews throughout the empire at Haman's instigation, the second the revocation of that decree, the crucifixion of Haman at Susa, and the granting of peace and honour to Mordecai and Esther on the thirteenth of Adar. Together they retell the story of the Book of Esther in the king's own voice, in the elevated prose of an imperial rescript. The composition is of uncertain date.
grc.critias.fragmenta: The Fragmenta collect the surviving remains of Critias of Athens, son of Callaeschrus, a poet, sophist, and politician numbered among the Thirty, transmitted as quotations in authors such as Athenaeus, Plutarch, Galen, Sextus Empiricus, and Pollux. The collection opens with an elegiac passage praising the songs of Anacreon, and the elegiac corpus further comprises sympotic verse on the kottabos and drinking customs, a poem in honour of Alcibiades, and short gnomic sayings. Alongside the poetry stand substantial prose fragments from works on the constitutions of Sparta and Thessaly, on the nature of love or of virtue, on aphorisms, and on conversations, together with tragic speeches from plays such as Peirithous and Sisyphus, several of which are transmitted under Euripides' name and assigned by the sources to Critias or to Euripides. Lexical and grammatical gleanings on individual words complete the remains.
grc.demosthenes.against_pantaenetus: A courtroom speech by Demosthenes, delivered in an Athenian private action. It opens with the speaker's defence of the preliminary plea (paragraphe) by which he argues that the suit brought against him by Pantaenetus is inadmissible. The greater part of the oration recounts the underlying affair: the joint loan of a hundred and five minae made by the speaker and his partner to Pantaenetus for the purchase of a mining workshop and thirty slaves at Maroneia, the tenancy of the workshop under Mnesicles, the quarrel between Pantaenetus and the partner that ended in the partner's victory at law, and the settlement in which Pantaenetus released the speaker from every charge before bringing a fresh action. The speaker then answers each count of the new indictment, producing laws, witness testimony and formal challenges to show that both the release and the mining statutes bar the suit, and closes with a character defence of lending money and a plea that a settlement once made should stand.
grc.demosthenes.on_the_accession_of_alexande: A short deliberative speech in Attic Greek, attributed to Demosthenes and dating from the period of Alexander's accession, addressed to the Athenian assembly. It opens by conceding that those who urge the Athenians to abide by their oaths and treaties are right in principle. The speaker then argues at length that Alexander himself has violated the terms of the Common Peace, citing his installation of the sons of Philiades as tyrants at Messene and of Chaeron at Pellene, his dissolution of democracies in the Peloponnese, the forcible escort of shipping to Tenedos, and the provocative entry of a Macedonian trireme into the Piraeus. Since justice, expediency, and the treaty clauses alike condemn these acts, he concludes by urging the Athenians to vote, as the treaties prescribe, for war against the transgressors.
grc.dionysius_halicarnassensis.de_thucydidis: De Thucydidis Idiomatibus is a short Greek rhetorical treatise by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, of uncertain date, cast as a letter to one Ammaeus. It opens with a preface explaining that, having treated Thucydides in earlier works addressed to Aelius Tubero, the author now sets out the distinctive traits of his style by gathering examples rather than by demonstrative proof. The body of the work characterizes Thucydides' language as a mixture of prose and poetry, archaic, poetic, and foreign words alongside common usage, and then surveys, with passages quoted from the History, his grammatical figures: exchanges of nouns for verbs and of active for passive voice, shifts between singular and plural, between genders, and between cases, personification of abstractions, long parenthetical insertions that obscure the argument, and strained antitheses in the manner of Gorgias. It ends by presenting the observations assembled from the continuous narrative as the requested demonstrations of the four instruments of Thucydidean style: poetic vocabulary, variety of figures, harshness of harmony, and speed of expression.
grc.epicharmus.fragmenta: The Fragmenta of Epicharmus gathers the surviving remains of the Greek poet's verse, composed in Doric dialect. The pieces are short and largely gnomic or dialectical, treating subjects such as the usefulness of maxims, the ceaseless change of all things, the difference between perceiving through the senses and understanding, and the presence of intelligence in living creatures. The fragments stand embedded in excerpts from the later ancient writers who quote them, and the collection closes with a passage in which Epicharmus foretells that his sayings will one day be recast in new dress.
grc.euripides.ion: Euripides' Ion is a Greek tragedy whose opening speech by Hermes recounts how Apollo fathered a son on Creusa, daughter of Erechtheus of Athens, and how the exposed infant was carried to Delphi and reared as a servant in Apollo's temple. The action centres on the grown Ion's meeting with Creusa and her husband Xuthus, who have come to the oracle seeking heirs: Xuthus is instructed to claim the youth as his own son, while Creusa, believing herself wronged, attempts to poison him. The plot fails, and the tokens of exposure, the woven cloth, the olive wreath, and the cradle basket, establish Creusa as Ion's mother, after which Athena appears to explain Apollo's design and to foretell that Ion's descendants will become the Ionians while Xuthus' line will found the Dorians and Achaeans. The play closes with the family preparing to leave Delphi for Athens, where Ion is to take up his ancestral rule.
grc.eutropius.breviarium_historiae_romanae: A Greek version of the Breviarium Historiae Romanae, the compressed history of Rome from the foundation of the city composed by Eutropius. The work recounts how Roman power grew from the humblest beginnings to a dominion without equal in memory, opening with the birth of Romulus to Rhea Silvia and Mars and his founding of the settlement on the Palatine hill. The narrative proceeds reign by reign through the seven kings, Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Marcius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus, down to the rape of Lucretia, the expulsion of the Tarquins and the end of the monarchy.
grc.galen.de_bono_habitu: A short Greek treatise by Galen on euexia, good condition of the body. It opens by distinguishing hexis, a stable and hard-to-dissolve state, from the qualified conditions called euexia and cachexia, defining simple good condition as the perfection of health found in the best-constituted bodies and contrasting it with the merely relative condition of athletes such as Milo or Achilles. Drawing on Hippocrates' dictum that peak athletic fitness is precarious and on Plato's critique of athletic bulk in the third book of the Republic, the treatise sets out what the two kinds share, namely good mixture of the bodily parts, sound functioning and good humours, and where they diverge, in the proportion or disproportion of blood and flesh. It ends with a physiological account of how excessive repletion overfills the veins, smothers the innate heat and can rupture the vessels of lung, liver and chest, corroborated by a Hippocratic saying on sudden repletions of the veins.
grc.galen.de_humero_iis_modis_prolapso_quos_: A brief Greek medical treatise by Galen on dislocations of the shoulder occurring in ways that Hippocrates had not described. Galen contrasts the single mode of dislocation recorded by Hippocrates with the additional modes known to later physicians and recounts five cases he himself witnessed, one in Smyrna during his student years and four in Rome, arguing that their frequency reflects the size of those cities and the unskilful practices of doctors and wrestling trainers. The work then describes reduction techniques, including countertraction, a broad strap around the chest, slings, and the Hippocratic bench, and closes with a discussion of how muscle tension or laxity and bodily condition, whether lean or fleshy, make dislocation and reduction easier or harder, with remarks on the interpretation of Hippocratic wording.
grc.galen.de_usu_partium_corporis_humani_ixi: A Greek prose treatise on teleological anatomy by the second-century physician Galen, On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body argues that each bodily part exists for the sake of the soul's activities. The portion here contains the work's opening argument, which defines a part as something with its own outline yet joined to other parts, presents the body as the soul's instrument, and surveys how the endowments of different animals, horns, tusks, speed, strength, match their several natures. Humans, alone naked and unarmed yet rational, receive hands in place of natural weapons, and Galen follows Aristotle in holding that man possesses hands because he is wisest, the hand serving as an organ before all organs as reason is an art before all arts. Hippocrates, Plato, and Aristotle are invoked by name throughout the argument.
grc.gregory_of_nazianzus.theological_oration: The Theological Orations of Gregory of Nazianzus form a sequence of five Greek orations on the doctrine of the Trinity. The first opens with a rebuke of clever disputants who turn argument into a game, laying down that only the purified may philosophise about God, and only at the proper season and within limits. The subsequent discourses treat the incomprehensibility of the divine essence and the weakness of human knowledge of God, defend the Son's eternal generation and consubstantiality with the Father against objections drawn from scripture while expounding the names ascribed to him, and argue at length for the divinity of the Holy Spirit and his procession from the Father. The sequence closes with an account of the unity of the one divinity in three hypostases and a doxology to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
grc.herodian.ab_excessu_divi_marci: Herodian's Ab Excessu Divi Marci is a Greek historical work covering Roman imperial history from the death of Marcus Aurelius to the accession of Gordian III. The opening proem criticises earlier historians for favouring elegance over truth before introducing Marcus's deathbed anxieties for his young son Commodus. The narrative then proceeds through a rapid sequence of reigns, Commodus, Pertinax, Didius Julianus, Septimius Severus, Caracalla, Macrinus, Elagabalus, Alexander Severus, and Maximinus Thrax, recounting assassinations, civil wars, foreign campaigns against Parthians, Persians, and Germans, and the growing political power of the army in imperial succession.
grc.hyperides.speeches: Forensic speeches and fragments by the Athenian orator Hyperides, active in the fourth century BC. The remains consist of excerpts of speeches addressed to Athenian jurors, including a defence against a public indictment (eisangelia) and material from private causes touching marriage, adoption, and inheritance, while the public charges alleged range from the betrayal of the dockyards to the seizure of a stronghold. Much of the wording survives only in passages quoted by later grammarians, notably Pollux, so the speeches are preserved discontinuously.
grc.lucian.bis_accusatus_sive_tribunalia: A Greek dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, bearing the Latin title Bis Accusatus sive Tribunalia ('Double Indictment, or Tribunals'). In the opening scene Zeus complains to Hermes of the endless toil of divine rule and of the suits long lodged by the arts and sciences against mortals who have abandoned them, which have lain untouched through the gods' supposed idleness. Hermes is sent to proclaim a day of court, and Justice (Dikē) is appointed to sit in judgment on the Areopagus over the accumulated cases.
grc.lucian.demonax: Lucian of Samosata's Demonax is a short biographical encomium of the Cypriot philosopher Demonax, whom the author knew at Athens and presents as a model of philosophical life. The work opens with Lucian's claim that his own age was not wholly without men worthy of remembrance, naming the athlete Sostratus and, above all, Demonax. The body of the piece sketches Demonax's origins, his self-directed turn to philosophy and eclectic refusal of any single school, his mildness, frankness, and ready wit, and his successful defence before the Athenian assembly against charges of impiety, before passing to a long series of apophthegms and repartees addressed to sophists, philosophers, and officials such as Favorinus, Peregrinus, Herodes Atticus, and Epictetus. It closes with the philosopher's death at nearly a hundred, his public burial and lasting honours from the Athenians, and Lucian's note that he has recorded only a few episodes from many, enough to show what sort of man he was.
grc.lucian.fugitivi: A short comic prose dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, traditionally titled the Runaways (Fugitivi), cast as a conversation in which Zeus and Philosophy herself are the chief speakers. It opens with the two recalling an aged enthusiast who burned himself alive on a pyre at Olympia. Philosophy then recounts her mission from Zeus to civilize humankind, among the Brahmans of India, the priests of Egypt, the Chaldaeans, Scythians, and Thracians, and finally the Greeks, and laments that her work is undone by impostors who dress and brawl in the philosophers' manner while living in greed, flattery, and debauchery, so that the ordinary people revile philosophy for their sake. Zeus, Philosophy, Hermes, and Heracles accordingly descend to a city on the Hebrus in Thrace to hunt the fugitives, and a herald's proclamation, with Orpheus's help, brings about the identification of three runaway slaves who had taken up the Cynic guise, Cantharus, Licythion, and Miropnoun, whose capture, punishment, and return to their masters close the piece.
grc.lucian.lexiphanes: Lexiphanes is a short satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata, whose title character affects an ostentatiously archaic and outlandish style of speech. It opens with Lexiphanes presenting to his friend Lycinus a freshly minted composition, an 'anti-symposium' written against Plato's Symposium, and asking for a judgment on it. At Lycinus' urging he recites a long specimen, a narrative of exercise, bathing, drinking, and a sumptuous dinner party told in a grotesque jumble of rare, technical, and invented words that bewilders its hearers. Lycinus then pronounces the speech a disease, brings in the physician Sopolis, whose emetic literally purges the offending vocabulary, and closes with precepts directing the offender to form his style on the best poets, orators, Thucydides, and Plato.
grc.lucian.nigrinus: The Nigrinus of Lucian is a short satirical dialogue framed by an opening letter, in which Lucian addresses the philosopher Nigrinus and undertakes to report to a friend a conversation he once heard. The dialogue proper presents the narrator's account of a visit to Nigrinus, a Platonist living in Athens, whose speech praises philosophy and the frugal, frank, poverty-embracing life of the Athenians while deriding the luxury of Rome. Its episodes cover sycophants and flatterers of the rich, gluttony and elaborate baths, extravagant funerals and wills, the mania for chariot-racing, and philosophers who peddle virtue, all under the recurring image of philosophy as a healer's well-aimed arrow. The work closes with the narrator declaring himself wounded by the words and asking his friend to seek with him a common cure, after the manner of Telephus.
grc.lycophron.alexandra: A Greek dramatic monologue in iambic trimeters attributed to Lycophron and of uncertain date, spoken throughout by a servant of Priam who reports to the king the prophecies uttered by his captive daughter Cassandra. The poem opens with the servant describing how Cassandra, once struck dumb, has broken into prophecy, veiling her meaning in deliberately obscure and riddling language. Her vision sweeps from the judgment of Paris through the Trojan War and the deaths of heroes on both sides to the wanderings of the returning Greeks, above all Odysseus, and the fortunes of Aeneas and his descendants, ending with the future greatness of Rome. At the close the frame resumes, as Cassandra withdraws again into her prison and the servant finishes his report with a prayer for his master's house.
grc.marcus_aurelius.m._antonius_imperator_ad: A Greek work of philosophical reflection in prose, presented under the title 'M. Antonius Imperator ad Se Ipsum' (Marcus Aurelius, 'To Himself') and conventionally known as the Meditations. It opens with a book of thanks in which the author credits his family, teachers and the gods with the virtues he has learned from them, before moving into sustained Stoic exhortation on the governance of the mind, the acceptance of fate, the transience of all things, death, and the duties of a rational, social being; the notes record where the entries were written, such as among the Quadi on the river Granua and at Carnuntum. The whole is a private commonplace book of short maxims, arguments and self-addresses rather than a continuous treatise, distributed across the twelve books in which the tradition transmits it.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.problemata_arithmet: A short collection of six numbered arithmetical problems (α–ϛ) preserved with the Introduction to Arithmetic of Nicomachus of Gerasa, to whom they are attributed. The first problem gives a rule, with proof, for summing any run of consecutive numbers beginning from unity, distinguishing an odd from an even count of terms. The remaining items supply a quicker reckoning for such sums with worked examples, a rule for series in equal difference, a ten-number puzzle said to have been set out by King Leo together with a criticism of earlier solutions and a fresh division of it, a trick for discovering a number secretly held in the mind by successive removals of three, five and seven, and the testament of a dying man apportioning a hoard of gold coins among three sons and three daughters.
grc.novum_testamentum.ad_thessalonicenses_i: A Greek prose epistle of the New Testament, composed in the Imperial era, the First Letter to the Thessalonians opens with a salutation from Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the church of the Thessalonians and a thanksgiving for the converts' faith, love, and endurance. The body recalls the missionaries' toil and persecution in bringing the gospel to Macedonia, rejoices in Timothy's report of the Thessalonians' steadfastness, and exhorts the readers to holiness, sexual restraint, brotherly love, quiet work with their hands, and esteem for those who lead them. A later section teaches that the dead in Christ will rise first at the Lord's descent from heaven, warns that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, and urges watchfulness and mutual encouragement. Short closing commands on rejoicing, prayer, testing prophecy, and greeting are followed by an injunction that the letter be read to all the brothers and a final benediction.
grc.novum_testamentum.ioannis_i: The First Epistle of John is a Greek prose epistle of the New Testament, of the Imperial era and traditionally attributed to John, though the work itself names neither its author nor its addressees. It opens with a prologue in which the writer, speaking as an eyewitness, announces the word of life that was from the beginning and has been manifested in Jesus Christ. The body alternates ethical exhortation with polemic: God is light and believers must walk in the light, confess sin, keep the commandments, and love one another, while the writer warns against antichrists who deny the Son, against love of the world, and against spirits that do not confess Christ, setting out the marks by which children of God are distinguished from children of the devil. A sustained meditation declares that God is love and that love reaches perfection in those who abide in him, before closing with assurance of eternal life, discussion of sin that leads to death, and a final admonition to guard oneself from idols.
grc.plato.epistles: A Greek collection of thirteen letters transmitted under Plato's name, addressed for the most part to Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse, and to the circle of Dion, with shorter notes to other friends and correspondents. The opening letters rebuke Dionysius for ingratitude, refuse his gifts, and reflect on a philosopher's reputation and conduct in dealings with power. The longest and central letter gives an autobiographical account of Plato's voyages to Sicily, his hopes and disappointments at the Syracusan court, and a digression on why the deepest philosophical teaching cannot be set down in writing. The later letters arrange practical affairs, money, gifts, marriage settlements, and journeys, and the collection closes with greetings and instructions to Iatrocles.
grc.plutarch.epitome_argumenti_stoicos: A short Greek epitome of an argument against the Stoics, attributed to Plutarch and of uncertain date. It opens by setting Pindar's Caeneus, rendered impervious to wounds, against the Stoic sage, who is struck, tortured and maimed yet remains fearless, painless and unconquerable. The argument then works through a series of Stoic paradoxes: the overnight conversion of the utterly vicious man into a sage, compared with Euripides' Iolaus suddenly made young and with Athena's removal of Odysseus' ugliness; the claim that virtue brings instant wealth, kingship, wisdom and the granting of any wish, like the horn of Amalthea; and a contrast with Heracles, who never ceases to need necessities, culminating in the Stoic, who begs for food and a cloak at other men's doors while shouting that he alone is king and rich.
grc.pseudogalen.de_optima_secta_ad_thrasybul: A Greek medical treatise of uncertain date and authorship, transmitted among the works of Galen and addressed to a certain Thrasybulus, the De optima secta asks how the doctrines of medicine are to be judged. It opens by stipulating that every medical thesis must be true, useful, and consistent with its assumed principles, and defines criteria for testing each of these three qualities. The body of the work sets out what the Logical, Empiric, and Methodist schools of medicine hold in common and what distinguishes each, then refutes in turn the Empiric reliance on observation, recorded history, and transition to the similar, and the Methodist doctrines of the commons, the uselessness of symptoms and affections, and the seasons of disease as guides to diet and remedies. The Rationalist position, which grasps hidden causes through reason, is vindicated throughout as the soundest, in keeping with the work's title.
grc.pseudolucian.ἔρωτες: The Erotes is a short Greek prose dialogue attributed to Lucian and of uncertain date; it opens with Theomnestus regaling Lycinus with erotic tales at dawn as the pair celebrate a festival of Heracles. At Lycinus's prompting they agree to weigh love of women against love of boys, and Lycinus recounts a voyage to Italy that brought him, with his companions Charicles of Corinth and Callicratides of Athens, to the temple of Aphrodite at Cnidus, where they admired Praxiteles' statue and heard a temple attendant tell of a youth who defiled it. Charicles then delivers a set speech defending heterosexual love and attacking women's vanity and luxury, while Callicratides answers with a defence of pederasty that invokes Socrates, Achilles and Patroclus, and Orestes and Pylades; Lycinus awards the victory to Callicratides, allowing marriage to all but reserving philosophic love for the wise. Theomnestus responds with a racy speech on the ascending stages of physical love before Lycinus cuts the discussion short so that the party may attend the god's sacrifice.
grc.septuaginta.paralipomenon_b: Paralipomenon B is the second book of Chronicles in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Hebrew Bible, a prose biblical narrative of Hellenistic date whose translator is unnamed. It opens with Solomon's accession, his prayer for wisdom at Gibeon, and the building and dedication of the temple at Jerusalem, together with accounts of his wealth and glory. The work then follows the kings of Judah reign by reign, from Rehoboam to Zedekiah, recording alternating religious reform and apostasy, wars with neighbouring peoples and with Assyria and Babylon, temple restorations, and prophetic rebukes, until the burning of the temple, the deportation to Babylon, and Cyrus's proclamation permitting the exiles to return.
grc.septuaginta.susanna_translatio_graeca: The Greek Susanna, preserved in the Septuagint among the additions to the Book of Daniel, is a short prose narrative of uncertain date from the Hellenistic period. It opens in Babylon with the household of the wealthy Joakim, whose wife Susanna, the beautiful and God-fearing daughter of Helcias, walks daily in his garden. Two elders appointed as judges covet her, try to force themselves upon her, and, when she refuses, falsely accuse her of adultery, winning the assembly's assent to her condemnation. The youthful Daniel, given a spirit of discernment by an angel, separates the elders and cross-examines each about the tree beneath which they claim to have seen the supposed lovers, exposes their contradictory answers, and the law's penalty is carried out on them as false witnesses, after which Susanna is vindicated and a closing admonition praises the piety of the young.
grc.sextus_empiricus.pyrrhoniae_hypotyposes: The Pyrrhoniae Hypotyposes, a Greek prose treatise by the sceptical philosopher Sextus Empiricus of uncertain date, offers a systematic account of Pyrrhonian scepticism. The first book opens with a list of its chapters and then treats the division of philosophy into dogmatic, Academic and sceptical tendencies, the concept, principles, criterion and end of scepticism, the ten, five and two modes that lead to suspension of judgement (epochē) and tranquillity (ataraxia), and the characteristic sceptical phrases such as 'no more' and 'I suspend judgement'. Its remaining chapters distinguish scepticism from the Heraclitean, Democritean, Cyrenaic and Protagorean philosophies, from the Academy, and from empirical medicine.
grc.theophrastus.enquiry_into_plants: Concerning Weather Signs (De signis) is a short Greek prose treatise by Theophrastus, transmitted together with his Enquiry into Plants. The opening announces a collection of signs of rain, winds, winter storms and fair weather, gathered partly from the author's own observation and partly from trustworthy informants, and explains the risings and settings of stars and the divisions of year, month and day by which such signs are to be read. The greater part of the work catalogues prognostics drawn from the sun, moon and stars, from clouds, haloes, thunder and lightning, from mountains and the sea, and from the behaviour of birds, beasts, insects and household objects, distinguishing rain from wind and from southerly or northerly weather. Later sections gather the signs of winter and of fair weather, and the treatise closes with predictions concerning the character of whole years and seasons.
grc.bion_of_phlossa.fragmenta: Fragments of the Greek bucolic poet Bion of Phlossa, preserved in Doric dialect and comprising short poems, epigrams, and isolated lines on love, song, and pastoral life. The remains open with a dialogue weighing which of the four seasons is sweetest, answered in favour of spring; there follow an episode in which a young bird-catcher first sees Eros, a scene in which Aphrodite brings Eros to be taught music, reflections on the brevity of mortal toil and the blessedness of mutual love, a prayer to Hesperus, a reproach to Aphrodite for the harshness of her son, an account of Apollo's vain efforts to heal a stricken lover, and the Cyclops' wooing of Galatea. Aphoristic verses on the kinship of Eros and the Muses, with a handful of single-line remains, conclude the collection.
grc.claudius_ptolemaeus.apotelesmatica_tetra: The Tetrabiblos of Claudius Ptolemy is a Greek treatise in four books on astrology, the art of prognostication from the celestial bodies. The work opens with an address to Syrus defending the possibility and usefulness of such prediction, while insisting on its merely probable character and distinguishing it from the certain knowledge of astronomy itself. Book 1 sets out the physical doctrine of planetary natures, the signs of the zodiac, aspects, houses, exaltations, and bounds, and book 2 treats 'mundane' or national astrology, covering climates and peoples, eclipses, planetary stations, comets, and the weather. Books 3 and 4 turn to genethlialogy, the judgment of nativities, proceeding from parents, siblings, and length of life through bodily form, disease, the soul and its affections, wealth, rank, occupation, marriage, children, friendship, and foreign travel to the quality of death, and closing with methods for dividing time and assigning events to particular years.
grc.demosthenes.against_conon: An Athenian forensic speech written by Demosthenes for the private suit for assault (dike aikeias) brought by the young Ariston against Conon. It opens with Ariston explaining that, beaten so severely that his family long expected him to die, he has recovered to prosecute his attacker. The speech then recounts the hostile quarrel during garrison service at Panakton and the night-time attack near the Leokorion in the agora, where Conon, his son Ctesias, and their companions knocked Ariston down, stripped him, and beat him, before presenting eyewitness and medical testimony about his injuries. Its later sections argue that Conon is liable under the laws on outrage (hybris) and on stripping a victim's clothes, expose the perjured evidence of his drinking companions, and close with a formal challenge to a solemn oath and an appeal to the judges for punishment.
grc.demosthenes.against_leptines: An Athenian public prosecution speech by Demosthenes, written for the opponents of Leptines' law repealing the exemptions from liturgies held by benefactors of the city, among them the son of Chabrias. The opening addresses the jurors on the question whether it profits the city to annul the law, and the argument then sets out the wrongs the measure would do, stripping honours already granted and making future gratitude unsafe. In support the speaker surveys the grants of citizenship and exemption conferred on such men as Leucon of Bosporus, Epicrates of Cyrene, the Corinthian exiles, the Thasians, the Byzantines, Conon and Chabrias, reading out the decrees in their favour and recounting the deeds of Chabrias at length. Further sections defend the honouring of benefactors against appeals to Spartan and Theban practice, invoke Solonian legislation on how laws are to be framed, exhibit the substitute statute proposed in place of Leptines' measure, and note that its terms would expose to severe penalties any who asked a reward for services.
grc.euripides.electra: A Greek tragedy by Euripides dramatizing the revenge of Orestes and Electra upon Agamemnon's murderers, Aegisthus and Clytemnestra. The play opens with a prologue by the peasant to whom Aegisthus has married Electra, explaining how Agamemnon was slain on his return from Troy, how Orestes was smuggled into exile, and how the forced marriage was meant to forestall any avenger. Orestes and Pylades arrive in disguise, meet Electra at a spring, and are recognized through an old servant; the siblings kill Aegisthus at a country sacrifice and lure Clytemnestra to the house with false news of Electra's childbirth, where they kill her as well. The drama closes with the appearance of the Dioscuri, who pronounce the matricide a mistake, send Orestes to stand trial in Athens, and give Electra in marriage to Pylades.
grc.lucian.apologia: The Apologia is a short Greek dialogue in which Lucian of Samosata answers the charge of inconsistency levelled against him after his invective upon men who attach themselves to rich households for pay. It opens with Lucian voicing, as though for his friend Sabinus, the objection that the author of so fierce a condemnation of salaried dependence has now himself accepted such a position. Sabinus then presses the case at length, likening him to a tragedian off stage and to a monkey betrayed by a fig, while Lucian replies by distinguishing his salaried judicial and secretarial office in the Roman administration of Egypt from servile attendance on a private patron, and by arguing that everyone acts for reward, kings not least. The dialogue ends on a lighter note, with Lucian conceding that he is no sage and waving his critics away with the words 'Hippocleides does not care.'
grc.lucian.de_morte_peregrini: A short satirical epistle addressed to Cronius, in which Lucian of Samosata recounts the life of the Cynic Peregrinus, who styled himself Proteus, down to his self-immolation after the Olympic festival. The opening mocks the old man's love of glory and reports his recent death by fire, then traces his career: adultery and flight in Armenia, the murder of his aged father, a sojourn among the Christians of Palestine that ended in imprisonment and expulsion, and a series of wanderings through Egypt, Italy, and Greece marked by theatrical asceticism and quarrels. The account follows the narrator to Elis and Olympia, where Peregrinus announces his intention to burn himself, his follower Theagenes extols him amid rival harangues and invented oracles, and after the games the narrator witnesses the night-time cremation at nearby Harpina. The letter closes with the mocking aftermath, including a tale that a vulture rose from the pyre, plans for statues and cult, and an anecdote about the dead man's fear of pain shortly before the end.
grc.lucian.piscator: A satirical dialogue by the Greek author Lucian of Samosata, composed as a defence of the author's public mockery of the philosophers. It opens with the philosophers of the past, Plato, Chrysippus, Aristotle, Pythagoras, Diogenes and the rest, returned from the dead, pelting a reviled offender with stones; the offender is Lucian's own spokesman Parrhesiades, who had put philosophy up for auction and ridicule, and he buys a formal trial instead. Philosophy herself, attended by personified Truth, Justice, Education and their companions, comes to the Acropolis to judge the case: Diogenes prosecutes, Parrhesiades pleads that his abuse was aimed only at charlatans who wear the philosopher's cloak for money and vanity, and Philosophy acquits him and enrols him as a friend of the sect. A second hearing then summons the philosophers with promises of pay and honours, crowns the few genuine ones, puts the impostors to flight, and ends with Parrhesiades fishing from the wall with a hook baited with gold, landing a string of fraudulent Cynics, Platonists, Aristotelians and Stoics to be branded.
grc.lucian.somnium: The Somnium ('The Dream') is a short Greek prose work of Lucian of Samosata in which the speaker recounts, before a live audience, a formative dream from his boyhood. It opens with his father deliberating with friends over what trade the boy should learn and apprenticing him to an uncle skilled in sculpting, whose harsh correction of the boy's first botched stroke sends him home in tears. That night two women contend for him in a vivid dream, the rough-handed Sculpture and the radiant Paideia, or Education; he judges for Paideia, who rewards him with a winged ascent over cities and nations, and he wakes to a changed appearance that astonishes his father. The speaker rebukes scoffers among his hearers and explains that he has told the story so that the young, and especially any tempted by poverty to abandon learning, may take his own rise from obscure origins as an example and pursue education.
grc.lucian.timon: A comic Greek dialogue by Lucian that dramatises the story of Timon of Athens, the legendary misanthrope. It opens with a mock-solemn invocation in which Zeus, roused by complaints that his thunderbolt has gone cold and idle, sends Hermes and Plutus back to Timon, who after being stripped of his fortune by ungrateful flatterers now digs the land in solitary bitterness. Along the way Hermes and Plutus discourse on the inconstancy of wealth, the follies of hoarders and spendthrifts, and the virtues of Poverty, whose company has restored Timon's integrity; when he uncovers a buried treasure he drafts a self-imposed code of total withdrawal from mankind. The former hangers-on, a parasite, a sycophant, a self-serving rhetorician and a poseur philosopher, soon return to court his renewed riches, and the piece closes as he drives them off with blows from his mattock and reaffirms his hatred of men.
grc.plutarch.artaxerxes: A Greek biographical life by Plutarch of the Persian king Artaxerxes II, surnamed Mnemon. The opening distinguishes this second Artaxerxes, son of Darius and Parysatis, from a gentler earlier namesake and sets his rivalry with his brother Cyrus. The narrative then follows Cyrus's bid for the throne and his death at Cunaxa, with Plutarch weighing the conflicting accounts of Ctesias, Dinon, and Xenophon, before turning to the fate of the captured Greek generals, Parysatis's vengeance against them, and her poisoning of Queen Stateira. Its later course covers the war with Sparta ended by the King's Peace of Antalcidas, the unsuccessful Egyptian and Cadusian campaigns, Artaxerxes's marriage to his daughter Atossa, the conspiracies of Teribazus that led to the execution of crown prince Darius, and the king's own death at ninety-four after a reign of sixty-two years.
grc.aristotle.de_respiratione: A short Aristotelian treatise on why animals breathe, De Respiratione (Peri anapnoēs) opens by reviewing earlier natural philosophers who held that all living creatures respire, and arguing that fish and many bloodless animals plainly do not. The bulk of the work sets out Aristotle's own explanation: the innate heat whose seat is the heart must be tempered by cooling, which lunged animals achieve by breathing air and gilled animals by taking in water through the gills. It goes on to explain why air-breathers suffocate in water and fish die on land, describes the working of the lungs, gills, windpipe and heart, and treats the course of life from generation and youth through old age to natural death. A final section considers the pulse and heartbeat alongside respiration and touches on the border between natural philosophy and medicine in questions of health and disease.
grc.demosthenes.against_timotheus: Against Timotheus is a Greek forensic speech handed down among the orations of Demosthenes, argued in an Athenian private suit in which the speaker pursues a claim for debts owed to his deceased father, a banker of the Piraeus, by the general Timotheus. It opens with an appeal to the judges not to find it strange that the son prosecutes a man whom his father once helped freely in his hours of need. The narrative then sets out the successive transactions one by one: a first loan at the Piraeus for Timotheus' departure as general, a second of a thousand drachmas raised at Calaureia to keep the Boeotian trierarchs supplied and repaid to the shipmaster Philip, freight money for timber brought from Macedonia, and the valuation of two silver phialai deposited at the bank. Supporting the account with witnesses, bank memoranda, and inferences from Timotheus' embarrassments, the speaker rebuts the claims that the money was lent to Antimachus or to a Boeotian navarch, explains his refusal of the oath Timotheus offered, and closes by asking the judges to help him recover the sums his father left.
grc.demosthenes.against_neaera: An Athenian forensic speech of the fourth century BCE, preserved among the orations of Demosthenes, in which the prosecutor brings a charge of xenia against Neaera, a Corinthian courtesan accused of living as the wife of the citizen Stephanus and of passing off her daughter as an Athenian. The opening presents the suit as the speaker's answer to a series of injuries and plots endured at Stephanus's hands. The body of the speech recounts Neaera's early career as a slave prostitute at Corinth, Stephanus's blackmail of her lovers, the marriage of her daughter Phano to Theogenes the king archon and her performance of the city's secret rites before the scandalised Areopagus, and the prosecutor's challenge to test the household slaves under torture, which Stephanus refused. The closing appeal urges the jurors to convict in defence of the laws, the gods, and the standing of citizen women.
grc.libanius.orations_51-64: A group of speeches by Libanius, the fourth-century AD rhetorician of Antioch, numbered 51 to 64 in the standard collection of his works. The first opens as a direct address to the emperor on justice and the twin supports of arms and laws, and goes on to denounce the throngs who besiege governors at their houses, baths, and tables, and the letters and intermediaries that corrupt their verdicts. Elsewhere in the range a panegyric weighs an emperor's sons, sent east and west after their father's death, against Cyrus, Darius, and Alexander to their advantage, while a long defence of pantomime dancing, addressed to an Aristides, sets the dancer beside the poets and orators as a teacher of audiences in justice and endurance.
grc.lysias.speeches: The collected speeches of the Athenian orator Lysias, active in the late fifth and early fourth centuries BCE, comprise thirty-four forensic and deliberative orations transmitted under his name, several of uncertain authenticity. The corpus opens with On the Murder of Eratosthenes, a husband's defense before an Athenian court of his killing of an adulterer caught in his house. The remaining speeches range over private litigation concerning homicide, inheritance, property, assault, and family affairs, alongside public orations on political matters, including defenses of men accused under the restored democracy, pleas against confiscations, and addresses urging civic concord and resistance to renewed oligarchy.
grc.nicomachus_of_gerasa.ἀριθμητικὴ_εἰσαγωγή: The Arithmetikē Eisagōgē ('Introduction to Arithmetic') is a Greek treatise on Pythagorean number theory attributed to Nicomachus of Gerasa, of uncertain date. It opens by defining philosophy as the love of wisdom and arguing, with appeals to Pythagoras, Plato and Archytas, that the mathematical sciences, arithmetic, music, geometry and spherics, lift the mind from the sensible to the intelligible. The body of the work classifies numbers in themselves (even and odd, prime, composite and perfect, figurate and polygonal numbers) and their ratios, multiples, superparticulars and related forms, illustrated with letter-number diagrams, before treating quantity in relation and cataloguing the arithmetic, geometric, harmonic and further means. A set of short appended problems and methods, covering the summation of series, a riddle ascribed to a king Leo, a trick for divining a number held in someone's mind, and the division of gold cups among a dying man's children, follows the treatise proper.

it.dante.inferno: The first cantica of Dante's Commedia, thirty-four cantos in which the poet, lost in a dark wood in 1300, is led by Virgil down through the nine circles of Hell. Each circle punishes a class of sin by a penalty that mirrors it, and the damned tell their stories as the travellers descend to the frozen centre of the earth.
it.dante.purgatorio: The second cantica, thirty-three cantos on the mountain of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed of the seven capital vices on ascending terraces. Virgil guides Dante to the summit and the earthly paradise, where he departs and Beatrice takes his place.
it.dante.paradiso: The third cantica, thirty-three cantos ascending through the spheres of the heavens with Beatrice as guide, ending in the vision of God. Its subject matter is theology, light, and the limits of speech, and it repeatedly stages the poet's inability to report what he saw.

fro.chanson_de_roland: The oldest surviving French epic, about four thousand assonanced lines from the Oxford manuscript of the twelfth century. Roland, commanding Charlemagne's rearguard, is betrayed at Roncevaux and refuses to sound his horn for help until his men are lost, and the poem ends with Charlemagne's vengeance and the trial of the traitor Ganelon.

gmh.nibelungenlied: The Middle High German heroic epic of about 1200, in some 2,400 stanzas. Its first half tells of Siegfried's courtship of Kriemhild, his dragon-won invulnerability, and his murder by Hagen; its second half of Kriemhild's marriage to Etzel and the annihilation of the Burgundians at his court.

en.blake.songs_of_innocence: Songs of Innocence is a collection of short lyric poems by William Blake. It opens with an 'Introduction' in which a piper, bidden by a laughing child seen on a cloud, plucks a hollow reed and writes down his happy songs so that 'every child may joy to hear'. The lyrics that follow, largely in simple quatrains and other brief measures, are voiced by or about children and their guardians: shepherds and lambs, a black child of the southern wilds taught by his mother, a young chimney sweep comforted by an angelic dream, charity children filing into St Paul's, infants, nurses, and mothers at evening play. Across the collection, pastoral delight, maternal tenderness, and a divinity identified with the lamb and the child frame scenes of cradle-song, springtime, and angelic watchfulness, closing with the assurance that God shares every human sorrow and weeps beside the sufferer.
en.bunyan.pilgrims_progress: Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is a prose allegory cast as a dream narrative and interspersed with short verses, opening as the narrator, sleeping in a den, beholds a man clothed in rags who carries a great burden and cries out for deliverance from coming judgment. The dream follows this man, Christian, as he flees the doomed City of Destruction, is directed by Evangelist to the wicket-gate, and journeys along the narrow way through the Slough of Despond, the Interpreter's house, the cross where his burden falls away, Hill Difficulty and Palace Beautiful, a combat with Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation, and the Valley of the Shadow of Death. Joined by his townsman Faithful, he is arrested and tried at Vanity Fair, where Faithful is condemned by Lord Hate-good and burned, after which Hopeful becomes Christian's new companion. Together the two pass By-ends and the silver mine of Demas, are imprisoned by Giant Despair in Doubting Castle until the key called Promise frees them, rest on the Delectable Mountains and in the land of Beulah, cross the river of death, and are received into the Celestial City, while Ignorance, arriving without a certificate, is turned away at the gate.
en.carroll.alice_in_wonderland: Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland is a prose fantasy recounting a young girl's adventures in a nonsensical underground world. It opens with Alice following a hurried White Rabbit down a rabbit-hole into a hall of locked doors, where potions and cakes alternately shrink and enlarge her. The narrative then carries her through a sequence of encounters: a sorrowful Mouse and a Dodo's caucus-race, a hookah-smoking Caterpillar, the peppery Duchess and her grinning Cheshire Cat, an endless tea-party with the Hatter and March Hare, croquet with the tyrannical Queen of Hearts, the Mock Turtle's lament, and a chaotic trial of the Knave of Hearts for stolen tarts. Alice finally grows to full size, denounces the court as a pack of cards, and wakes on the riverbank to find the whole adventure has been a dream.
en.coleridge.rime_of_the_ancient_mariner: Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a narrative poem in archaic ballad style that opens with an ancient Mariner detaining a Wedding-Guest on his way to the feast and beginning the tale of a ship driven by a storm southward into icy seas, where the Mariner shoots the albatross that had befriended the crew. Under a becalmed sky a spectre-ship crewed by Death and Life-in-Death wins the sailors' lives, and the Mariner alone survives, cursed among his dead shipmates until, blessing the water-snakes unawares, he is able to pray and the albatross falls from his neck. Angelic spirits, mysterious voices, and the risen corpses work the ship homeward, where the vessel sinks in a whirlpool and the Mariner, shriven by a Hermit, is condemned to wander from land to land, seized at uncertain hours by the agony that forces him to tell his tale. The poem ends with the Wedding-Guest departing a sadder and a wiser man, having heard the Mariner's closing moral that prayer avails best for those who love all things, both great and small.
en.cowper.task: Cowper's The Task is a long reflective poem in blank verse, divided into six books, which opens in mock-heroic vein with a history of the sofa, a light tribute undertaken at a lady's command. From that playful beginning the poet turns to the country walks that frame the whole work, meditating on nature, rural retirement, and the changing seasons along the Ouse. Its digressive course ranges widely, surveying city luxury and fashionable folly, corrupt public life and careless clergy, the slave trade and cruelty to animals, providence, kingship, and political liberty, together with extended passages on domestic happiness, gardening, winter scenes, and the evening newspaper. The poem closes with a portrait of the contented retired man, an argument that true freedom comes through God alone, and a vision of a restored creation.
en.edgar_allan_poe.the_raven: The Raven is a narrative poem by Edgar Allan Poe, composed in stanzas of insistent internal rhyme built around the single-word refrain 'Nevermore.' It opens on a bleak December midnight as a grieving scholar, brooding over books and the memory of the lost Lenore, hears a tapping at his chamber door and finds, instead of a visitor, a stately raven that perches on a bust of Pallas. The speaker moves from amused speculation about the bird's one utterance to anguished questioning, asking whether there is any balm for his sorrow and whether he will clasp Lenore again in a paradise beyond death, and to every question the raven answers 'Nevermore.' The closing stanzas leave the bird still sitting above the chamber door, its shadow cast on the floor, from which the speaker's soul 'shall be lifted, nevermore.'
en.keats.eve_of_st_agnes: The Eve of St Agnes, a narrative poem by John Keats composed in Spenserian stanzas, opens on a bitter wintry night as an aged beadsman says his prayers in a castle chapel while a baronial feast is prepared above. It follows Madeline, who observes the rituals that, by an old superstition, are to bring a sleeping virgin a vision of her future husband on St Agnes' Eve, and Porphyro, her lover from a hostile family, who is led by the aged Angela into her chamber, where he spreads a lavish feast and wakes her from her dream. The lovers escape through the sleeping household into the storm, and the poem closes with the baron's nightmarish visions and the deaths of Angela and the beadsman.
en.keats.fancy: Fancy is a short lyric in rhymed couplets by John Keats. It opens with the maxim 'Ever let the Fancy roam, / Pleasure never is at home', judging that delight melts at a touch like bubbles under rain. The poem then addresses a hearer seated at the winter fireside and dispatches the personified Fancy to gather the pleasures of the scattered seasons into one vision, mingling May blossoms and birdsong, summer swarms, harvest carols and autumn fruit with the muffled snow outside. It closes by bidding Fancy find the hearer a mistress likened to Ceres' daughter before she learned to frown and to Hebe with her slipping golden clasp, before returning to its opening maxim that pleasure is never at home.
en.keats.hyperion: Keats's Hyperion is an unfinished epic in blank verse dramatising the overthrow of the Titans by the younger gods, opening with the fallen Saturn sitting silent in a shadowy vale while Thea mourns the loss of his dominion. The poem follows them to a cavern where the defeated Titans gather in grief: Oceanus argues that a race more strong in beauty must rightly succeed them, Clymene recalls hearing Apollo's new music, and Enceladus calls for a second war, at which the sun-god Hyperion appears in disconsolate splendour. The third book shifts to Apollo on Delos, who pours out to Mnemosyne his anguish and his hunger for knowledge until, deified in an agony of dying into life, he shrieks and the narrative breaks off abruptly.
en.keats.isabella: Isabella is a narrative poem by John Keats, composed in eight-line stanzas, retelling a tale told by Boccaccio. It opens with the secret, mutually consuming love of fair Isabel and young Lorenzo within her brothers' Florentine merchant household. The brothers, intending to marry her to a nobleman, lure Lorenzo into the Apennine forest and murder him, reporting that he has sailed abroad; his ghost later reveals the crime, and Isabel digs up the body, buries the head in a garden pot, and rears a basil plant above it, feeding it with her tears. When the brothers steal the pot and recognise their victim's face they flee into banishment, leaving Isabel to pine away and die; the story is interspersed with addresses to Boccaccio, Melancholy, Music and Echo, and with stanzas condemning the mining, trade and labour by which the brothers grew rich.
en.keats.lamia: Lamia is a narrative poem in rhymed couplets by Keats, telling how a serpent is transformed into a beautiful woman who wins the love of the young Corinthian Lycius. It opens in a fabled Cretan forest, where Hermes, searching for a hidden nymph, grants the serpent Lamia a human body in exchange for revealing the nymph's whereabouts. Lamia then makes her way to Corinth, enthrals Lycius, and conjures a palace and marriage feast, until the philosopher Apollonius, whom Lycius had kept from the guest list, arrives uninvited and fixes her with a penetrating gaze; her serpent nature is exposed, she vanishes with a scream, and Lycius is found dead upon the couch.
