An appended note quotes Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, in which the tale of Menippus Lycius and the lamia at Corinth is told.
en.keats.lines_on_the_mermaid_tavern: A short lyric in octosyllabic couplets by the early nineteenth-century poet John Keats. The poem opens with an apostrophe to the souls of dead poets, asking whether any Elysium they knew, happy field or mossy cavern, could be choicer than the Mermaid Tavern with its Canary wine and its venison pies dressed as if for Robin Hood and Maid Marian. It then tells a fanciful tale of the tavern's sign-board flying away, until an astrologer records on sheepskin that the poets drink in glory beneath a new old sign, the Mermaid now set among the constellations of the Zodiac. The opening stanza returns at the close as a refrain, framing the whole in the same teasing question.
en.keats.ode_on_a_grecian_urn: Ode on a Grecian Urn is a five-stanza lyric ode by Keats, spoken in apostrophe to an ancient Greek urn. It opens by hailing the vessel as 'unravish'd bride of quietness' and 'sylvan historian', asking what leaf-fring'd legend of deities or mortals haunts its shape. The middle stanzas dwell on the scenes it bears: soft pipes playing melodies unheard, a bold lover forever short of an unattainable kiss, boughs and an unwearied melodist held in perpetual spring, and a mysterious priest leading a garlanded heifer to a green altar from a little town left eternally silent. The close addresses the 'Attic shape' as 'Cold Pastoral', musing on its endurance when old age has wasted successive generations and voicing its final maxim, 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.'
en.keats.ode_on_melancholy: An ode in three ten-line stanzas by the English Romantic poet John Keats. The opening stanza forbids the sufferer of melancholy all recourse to death and mourning, from Lethe and wolf's-bane to nightshade, yew-berries, the death-moth and the owl. The poem then advises that when the melancholy fit falls sudden from heaven like a weeping cloud, the sufferer should glut his sorrow on a morning rose, the rainbow of the salt sand-wave, the globed peonies, and his mistress's peerless eyes. The final strophe sets Melancholy in the very temple of Delight, dwelling with Beauty that must die and Joy that is ever bidding adieu, her sovran shrine seen only by him whose strenuous tongue can burst Joy's grape and taste the sadness of her might.
en.keats.ode_to_a_nightingale: John Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' is a lyric ode in eight stanzas. It opens with the speaker's heart aching and his senses drowsed, as though he had drunk hemlock, at the sound of a nightingale singing of summer among the trees. The poem follows an imagined flight, sought first through wine and then on the viewless wings of poesy, away from a world of weariness, fever, and death into a dark, fragrant forest where the speaker, listening among unseen flowers, contemplates an easeful death at the height of the bird's song. He then hails the nightingale as an immortal bird whose voice has sounded since ancient days, cheered Ruth amid the alien corn, and charmed magic casements on perilous seas, before the word 'forlorn' tolls him back to his sole self and the fading anthem leaves him asking whether he wakes or sleeps.
en.keats.robin_hood: John Keats's short lyric 'Robin Hood' opens with the declaration that the days of the greenwood are gone, their hours old and gray and their minutes buried under the leaves of many years. The poem then catalogues what has vanished with the outlaw band: the bugle and twanging bow, the mid-forest laugh, the morris dance, the song of Gamelyn, and the tough-belted outlaw idling in the green shawe. It goes on to imagine Robin and Marian restored to a changed world, where he would craze to see his oaks felled by dockyard strokes and she would weep that her wild bees sing no more and honey cannot be got without hard money. A closing litany of toasts bids honour to the bow-string, the bugle-horn, Lincoln green, Little John, Maid Marian, and all the Sherwood clan, before inviting the speakers to try 'a burden' in their memory.
en.milton.comus: Comus is a masque by Milton, a dramatic entertainment in blank verse interspersed with lyric song and dance. It opens with the prologue of an Attendant Spirit who explains that the Lady, benighted and parted from her brothers in a tangled wood, must be protected from Comus, son of Bacchus and Circe, whose enchanted liquor transforms travellers into beasts. The action then follows the brothers' search and debate over chastity, the Lady's captivity in the enchanter's palace, where she meets his pleas for pleasure with a defence of temperance, the breaking of his glass although he escapes with his wand, and the invocation of the river-nymph Sabrina, who dissolves the spell that holds her fixed. In the closing scene the company arrives at Ludlow Castle, where the three children are restored to their parents amid country dances and songs, and the Spirit's epilogue ends the piece with the declaration that virtue alone is free.
en.milton.il_penseroso: John Milton's Il Penseroso is a lyric in rhymed octosyllabic couplets that celebrates the contemplative life under the patronage of Melancholy. It opens with the speaker banishing 'vain deluding joys' and hailing 'divinest Melancholy' as a sage goddess of ancient descent, attended by Peace, Quiet, Leisure and Contemplation. The poem then courses through the nocturnal pleasures of the solitary mind, the nightingale's song, the wandering moon, the far-off curfew bell, midnight study of Platonic and Hermetic lore, and the delights of tragedy and of the half-told tale of Cambuscan, before turning to dawn in twilight groves, mysterious dreams, and the organ and anthems of the cloister. It closes with the hope of a studious old age in a peaceful hermitage, devoted to star and herb, that may attain 'something like prophetic strain' and live with Melancholy for ever.
en.milton.l_allegro: Milton's 'L'Allegro' is a lyric poem in octosyllabic couplets that opens by banishing loathed Melancholy to her Stygian haunts and summoning the goddess Mirth, Euphrosyne, with her train of Jest, Jollity and Laughter. The poem then courses through a day of cheerful delights, from lark, cock-crow and hunting horn at dawn, past ploughman, milkmaid and mower in the fields, to cottage dinners, village dances and fireside tales of Fairy Mab and the drudging goblin. It turns next to towered cities, courtly revelry, the stage of Jonson and Shakespeare, and music so sweet it might rouse Orpheus, closing with the speaker's resolve to live with Mirth.
en.milton.lycidas: Lycidas is a pastoral elegy by John Milton, composed in irregularly rhymed pentameter stanzas, mourning the death by drowning of the young shepherd-poet Lycidas. The song begins as the speaker plucks the berries of laurel and myrtle before their mellowing season and calls on the Muses to sing for one 'dead ere his prime'. The body of the poem moves through memories of shared shepherding, the absence of the nymphs at the shipwreck, a dialogue with Phoebus on fame, the sea-gods' report of the 'fatall and perfidious Bark', the lament of Camus, and a stern rebuke of negligent clergy delivered by the 'Pilot of the Galilean lake', before a catalogue of flowers is gathered to strew the 'Laureat Herse'. It closes in consolation, as Lycidas, sunk like the day-star, rises through the might of 'him that walk'd the waves' to the company of the saints and becomes 'Genius of the shore', while the frame returns to the 'uncouth Swain', who has sung from grey dawn to sunset and departs 'To morrow to fresh Woods, and Pastures new'.
en.milton.paradise_lost: Milton's Paradise Lost is a blank-verse epic in twelve books on the fall of humanity. It opens with an invocation to the heavenly Muse announcing man's first disobedience and the loss of Eden. The narrative follows Satan and the rebel angels from their fall into Hell through the infernal council at Pandemonium, Satan's voyage across Chaos to the newly created world, and the assembly in Heaven at which the Son offers himself for mankind's redemption. Raphael warns Adam and recounts the war in Heaven and the creation before Satan, in the serpent, seduces Eve, and the poem concludes with judgement on the first parents, Michael's prophetic visions of human history, and their expulsion from Paradise.
en.milton.paradise_regained: Paradise Regained is a short epic poem in four books of blank verse by John Milton, dramatizing the temptation of Christ in the wilderness. Opening with a proem in which the poet turns from the fall of man to sing paradise recovered 'to all mankind' by one man's obedience, the poem follows the newly baptized Son of God into the desert, where Satan, after a council of the fallen angels, resolves to try him. Over forty days the Tempter assays hunger with a conjured banquet, then offers riches, glory, arms, the empires of Parthia and Rome, and the philosophy and eloquence of Athens, and at last assails the Saviour with a night of storms and a dare to cast himself from the Temple pinnacle. Unshaken through every trial, the Son of God refutes each solicitation, Satan falls baffled from the pinnacle, angels bear the victor to a celestial feast, and Christ returns quietly to his mother's house.
en.milton.sonnets: A small collection of sonnets by John Milton, written in English and Italian, with a single canzone among them. The opening poem invokes the nightingale as a herald of successful love and places the speaker in the joint service of the Muse and of Love. The Italian poems follow the amorous conventions of the tradition, praising a lady whose name honours the valley of the Rhine, addressing his friend Diodati on an unexpected fall in love, and defending the choice to write of love in a foreign tongue, while the English sonnets offer meditations on youth, time and the will of Heaven, and an appeal to an armed officer to spare the poet's defenceless house.
en.shakespeare.a_midsummer_night’s_dream: A Midsummer Night's Dream is a comedy in five acts by William Shakespeare. It opens in Athens as Duke Theseus anticipates his marriage to Hippolyta, while Egeus insists that his daughter Hermia wed Demetrius on pain of death or lifelong seclusion. Hermia and Lysander flee into a wood outside the city, where the fairy king Oberon and queen Titania quarrel over a changeling boy and the misapplied juice of a magic flower entangles the affections of four young Athenians; the same night the weaver Bottom, transformed with an ass's head, becomes the object of the charmed Titania's devotion. The work closes with the lovers restored and wed, the amateur tradesmen's performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' before Theseus, the fairies' blessing of the bridal house, and Puck's epilogue inviting the audience to take the whole as a dream.
en.shakespeare.hamlet: An English tragedy in blank verse and prose by William Shakespeare, it opens at midnight on the battlements of Elsinore, where sentries and Horatio meet the apparition of the recently dead king of Denmark. The ghost tells Prince Hamlet that Claudius, his uncle and the new king, murdered him and has married the widow Gertrude, and Hamlet, feigning madness while hesitating over revenge, stages a play mimicking the murder to test the king's conscience. The drama then moves through the killing of the courtier Polonius, Hamlet's dispatch to England with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern and his escape at sea, the gravedigging scene over the drowned Ophelia, Laertes' rebellion and alliance with Claudius, and the fencing match with an envenomed foil and poisoned cup that leaves the king, the queen, Laertes, and Hamlet dead as Fortinbras of Norway arrives to take the throne.
en.shakespeare.richard_iii: Richard III, a history play by William Shakespeare, opens with the Duke of Gloucester's soliloquy declaring that, deformed and unfit for the peacetime court, he is 'determined to prove a villain'. The ensuing action traces Richard's rise to power: he has his brother Clarence murdered in the Tower, woos Lady Anne over the corpse of Henry VI, schemes against the family of Edward IV's queen as the king sickens and dies, and gains the crown through a staged show of reluctance before having his nephews, the young princes, killed in the Tower. Buckingham's rebellion, the ghosts who visit Richard and Richmond on the eve of Bosworth Field, and Richard's famous cry for a horse carry the drama to its close, in which Richmond slays the tyrant and proclaims the union of the houses of York and Lancaster.
en.shakespeare.sonnets: A sonnet sequence of 154 poems in iambic pentameter by William Shakespeare, mostly in the English form of three quatrains and a closing couplet; the opening group urges a fair young man to marry and beget heirs so that his beauty may survive time and decay. The sequence then follows the poet's devoted attachment to this young friend, treating his worth, absence and reconciliation, betrayal by the friend with the poet's own mistress, the rivalry of other poets, and the recurring claim that verse will confer immortality against time and death. From sonnet 127 onward the addressee becomes a dark-complexioned woman, and the poems explore desire, lust, deceit and disillusionment with unusual directness. The collection closes with two allegorical sonnets on Cupid's brand, quenched in a fountain whose healing bath proves powerless against love.
en.spenser.faerie_queene: Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene is a long allegorical romance-epic composed in the late sixteenth century, cast in the nine-line Spenserian stanza and dedicated to Queen Elizabeth under the figure of Gloriana, the Faerie Queene. It opens with the Redcrosse Knight riding out over a plain with the veiled lady Una, sent from Gloriana's court to prove his prowess against a dragon. The six completed books follow a series of virtuous champions, Redcrosse for Holiness, Guyon for Temperance, Britomart for Chastity, and knights of Friendship, Justice, and Courtesy, through episodic adventures of monsters, magicians, false ladies, and enchanted houses, with Prince Arthur repeatedly intervening in their aid. Designed for twelve books but left incomplete after the sixth, the poem also carries the two Mutability cantos of the projected seventh book, together with the Letter to Raleigh expounding the whole design, dedicatory sonnets, and commendatory verses.
en.swift.gullivers_travels: Jonathan Swift's prose satire presents itself as the truthful memoir of the ship's surgeon Lemuel Gulliver, opening with a mock publisher's note and a letter in which Gulliver protests at editorial alterations to his papers. The narrative then follows four voyages: a shipwreck leaves Gulliver prisoner among the tiny Lilliputians, whose court factions and war with Blefuscu over egg-breaking caricature English politics; later voyages take him to Brobdingnag, a land of giants whose king condemns European institutions; to the flying island of Laputa, the projectors of Balnibarbi, and the islands of Glubbdubdrib, Luggnagg and Japan; and finally to Houyhnhnmland, where rational horses govern the brutish Yahoos. The work closes with Gulliver back in England, estranged from his family and humankind, and with a concluding chapter defending his veracity and his declared design of reforming readers.
en.wordsworth.prelude: The Prelude is Wordsworth's long autobiographical poem in blank verse, cast in fourteen books and addressed throughout to Coleridge as 'O Friend!'. It opens with the poet, newly escaped from the city, greeting a gentle breeze and resolving to trace the making of a poet's mind. The narrative follows his childhood among the lakes and fells of the Lake District, his school days and undergraduate years at Cambridge, a walking tour through the Alps, residence in London, and sojourn in revolutionary France, recording his early devotion to Nature alongside his deepening engagement with human life and politics. The later books treat his disillusionment with the French Revolution, the intellectual and moral crisis that followed, and the gradual restoration of imaginative faith through remembered 'spots of time', culminating in the ascent of Snowdon and valedictions to his sister and to Coleridge.
en.world_english_bible.new_testament: The New Testament of the Christian Bible in the King James Version, the English translation that takes its name from King James I. It opens with the Gospel according to Matthew, beginning with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David and the son of Abraham, and the account of his birth. Across its course the work sets out the four gospels, which narrate Jesus' teaching, miracles, crucifixion and resurrection; the Acts of the Apostles, which follows the growth of the early church from Pentecost through the missionary labours of Peter and Paul; and a series of epistles, from Paul's letters to the congregations through the general letters of Hebrews, James, Peter, John and Jude, that instruct and admonish the first Christian communities. It ends with the Book of Revelation, an apocalyptic vision of judgment and the new heaven and earth.
en.world_english_bible.pentateuch: The Pentateuch comprises the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy, in the English rendering of the King James Bible, a composite of narrative and law traditionally ascribed to Moses. Genesis opens with God's creation of the heaven and the earth in six days. The narrative continues through the fall, the flood, and the tower of Babel to the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, whose family settles in Egypt; Exodus recounts the Israelites' bondage there and their deliverance under Moses, followed by the covenant and the giving of the Law at Sinai. Leviticus codifies sacrifice, priesthood, and purity; Numbers records the census and the years of wandering in the wilderness; and Deuteronomy restates the law in Moses' farewell discourses, closing with his death in Moab and the charge given to Joshua.
en.world_english_bible.revelation: The Book of Revelation, given here in the King James translation, is the apocalyptic work that closes the Christian New Testament, of uncertain date and set down in the voice of a prophet who names himself John and places his visions on the island of Patmos. It opens with a vision of the glorified Christ commanding John to send letters of praise and rebuke to seven churches in Asia. The body of the work unrolls a chain of visionary scenes: the heavenly throne and the Lamb opening a book sealed with seven seals, the sounding of seven trumpets and the pouring out of seven vials of wrath, the dragon Satan and two beasts bearing the number six hundred sixty-six, and the destruction of the harlot Babylon amid plagues and lamentation. It closes with the binding of Satan, a final battle and last judgment, and the descent of the new Jerusalem into a new heaven and new earth, followed by exhortations to keep the words of the prophecy.
en.blake.songs_of_experience: William Blake's Songs of Experience is a collection of short lyric poems in quatrains and other brief stanzas, opening with an 'Introduction' in which the Bard calls upon the Earth to rise from the night of despair. The poems that follow treat childhood, repressed desire, institutional religion, and social misery, as in 'The Chimney-Sweeper', 'The Garden of Love', and 'London', with its 'mind-forged manacles'. Short emblem pieces on flowers, insects, and beasts, including 'The Sick Rose', 'The Fly', 'Ah! Sun-flower', and 'The Tyger', with its interrogation of the tiger's creator, stand beside ballad-like narratives such as 'The Little Girl Lost' and 'The Little Girl Found', and a sequence of paired dramatic voices like the clod of clay and the pebble debating the nature of love. The collection closes with 'The Voice of the Ancient Bard', an address summoning youth away from the tangled maze of folly toward the opening morn.
en.keats.ode_bards_of_passion: An ode by John Keats, addressed to the bards of passion and of mirth, who are told that they have left their souls on earth while living again in heaven. The poem imagines the heavenly souls communing with the spheres, the fountains, and heaven's trees, seated at ease on Elysian lawns where the nightingale sings not a senseless tranced thing but divine melodious truth and golden histories of heaven and its mysteries. The earth-born souls left behind speak to mortals each day of their sorrows and delights, passions and spites, glory and shame, teaching wisdom though the bards themselves are fled far away. The lyric closes by repeating the address of its opening lines, hailing the bards as double-lived in regions new.
en.keats.ode_to_psyche: Ode to Psyche is a lyric poem in irregular stanzas by Keats. It opens with an apology to the goddess for singing her secrets in 'tuneless numbers', and recounts the speaker's vision of Cupid and Psyche lying embraced in a flowered forest glade beside a hidden brook. The poem then laments that Psyche, the latest born of Olympus' faded hierarchy, possesses none of the temples, altars, choirs, or oracles of the older gods, being too late for antique vows. The speaker thereupon vows himself her priest, promising to build a fane in an untrodden region of his mind, where branched thoughts replace pines and Fancy dresses a rosy sanctuary with a bright torch and casement open at night to let the warm Love in.
en.keats.to_autumn: To Autumn is a short lyric ode by John Keats addressed to the personified season, arranged in three eleven-line stanzas. It opens with an apostrophe to autumn as the close bosom-friend of the maturing sun, conspiring to load the vines, cottage-trees, gourds and hazel shells with ripeness until the bees' summer cells seem to overflow. The second stanza pictures the drowsy season amid the harvest, resting on a granary floor, asleep in a half-reaped furrow, keeping steady a gleaner's laden head, or watching the last oozings of the cyder-press. The closing stanza turns aside the question of spring's vanished songs to insist that autumn has its own music, cataloguing the gnats mourning among the river sallows, the bleating lambs, hedge-crickets, the red-breast's soft treble and the gathering swallows twittering in the rosy light of the stubble-plains at day's end.
en.milton.arcades: Arcades is a short pastoral entertainment by John Milton, presented to the Countess Dowager of Derby at Harefield by noble members of her family, who approach her seat of state in pastoral dress singing in praise of her almost divine presence. The Genius of the Wood then addresses the singers, hailing them as descendants of Arcadia, describing his guardianship of the grove against blighting winds, cankered worms and thunder, and telling of the celestial harmony by which the Sirens upon the ninefold spheres lull the daughters of Necessity and hold nature to her law. He leads them onward with songs toward the lady's glittering state, and the piece closes with lyrics bidding the Arcadian nymphs and shepherds forsake their old hills and streams for a better soil, where they may serve a rural queen surpassing all Arcadia.
en.world_english_bible.prophets: The Prophets division of the King James Bible comprises twenty-one books of the Old Testament in English, following the traditional order from Joshua to Malachi. It opens after the death of Moses, with God commanding Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan and take possession of the promised land. The narrative then traces the conquest and settlement of Canaan, the rule of the judges, the united monarchy under Samuel, Saul, David, and Solomon, the division into the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the fall of each to Assyria and Babylon, and the return from exile. The latter portion presents the prophets themselves, from Isaiah's oracles of judgment and consolation for Judah and the nations, through Hosea's lament over Israel's unfaithfulness, Jonah's mission to Nineveh, and Micah's call for justice, to the visions of Zechariah and Malachi's closing promise that Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers and children before the day of the LORD.
en.shelley.adonais: Adonais is a pastoral elegy in Spenserian stanzas in which Shelley mourns the death of a young poet under the classical name Adonais. It opens with a summons to weep for the dead youth and with the rallying of Urania, his mighty mother, to his grave. The course of the poem takes in the lament of nature and the procession of personified mourners, including a self-portrait of the poet as a frail and hunted form, an attack on the reviewer held responsible for the young poet's death, and a turn toward consolation in which the dead poet is welcomed by Chatterton, Sidney and Lucan and absorbed into the one sustaining spirit of the universe. The final stanzas set the scene at Rome, among the flowering graves beside the pyramid, where the speaker feels his own spirit drawn to follow Adonais to 'the abode where the Eternal are'.
en.world_english_bible.writings: The Writings (Ketuvim), the third division of the Hebrew Bible as given in the King James translation, comprise thirteen books of narrative, poetry, and wisdom. The collection opens with the tale of Ruth the Moabite, who leaves her homeland to follow Naomi, gleans in the fields of Boaz, and enters the lineage of David. It proceeds through the genealogies and royal histories of 1 and 2 Chronicles, the post-exilic restoration in Ezra and Nehemiah, and Esther's deliverance in Persia, then turns to the wisdom and lyric books: the affliction and restoration of Job, the Psalter, the proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes' meditation on vanity, the Song of Songs, and Lamentations over fallen Jerusalem. It closes with Daniel's court narratives in Babylon and his visions of empires and the end of days.
en.browning.sonnets_from_the_portuguese: Sonnets from the Portuguese is a sequence of love sonnets by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, written in Petrarchan form and addressed by a woman speaker to her beloved. The opening sonnet contrasts the sweet years of Theocritus's song with the melancholy years of the speaker's own life, until a figure that seems to be Death is revealed as Love. The sequence then traces a movement from grief, self-doubt, and the pull of the grave toward the acceptance of an earthly union, weighing worldly opposition and the threat of separation against vows of constancy that neither sea, tempest, nor heaven's distance can dissolve. It closes with poems that measure love against old griefs, childhood faith, and lost saints, and with a final gift of flowers whose roots, the speaker says, are left in her own.
